EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Behind the northward retreat of a warm front, a cluster of showers moved along and just ahead of a cold front from Virginia into northwest North Carolina during the evening hours. These showers deepened and led to growing clusters of storms, along with one sustained supercell that brought a swath of large hail (0.75 to 1.25) and sporadic power outages and downed trees to the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One hundred power outages from trees on powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media partner relayed a photo of approximately tennis ball size hail in Emory.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported 1 inch hail north northwest of Commerce.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought created an environment ripe for wildfire through much of May. Sporadic thunderstorm activity produced lightning which ignited a few wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Highway 41 wildfire lingered into early May burning a total of 9,149 acres in Miami-Dade County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.

Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th and 19th. On the 19th, a cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms produced widespread lightning (over 2500 strikes), heavy rainfall of 1 to over 2 inches and several reports of flash flooding in western NV from Stagecoach to southeast Reno/Hidden Valley, east Sparks to Lockwood and Spanish Springs. Hail up to 1��� diameter and wind gusts of 60-75+ mph also occurred with these storms as they pushed across northwest and west central NV.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station JSPN2 Juniper Springs measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 86 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of minor weather disturbances moved through the region from April 9th through the 11th. These combined with increased moisture to bring showers and storms to the region. With enough wind shear available in the atmosphere, some of these storms brought severe wind gusts to the region. Dry and windy conditions were in place on April 9th and that helped drive the spread of a wildfire known as The Smooth Eddy Incident which was over 500 acres. Additionally, the Purple Monster Wildfire would be sparked due to dry lightning in Oldham County on the evening of April 9th. That fire would go on to burn 1,911 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm moved across Dalhart during the afternoon of April 10, 2026. It produced penny to quarter size hail on the north side of town, including along highway 54.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.

High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.

A closed low off the Southern California coast pulled in some deep atmospheric river moisture ahead of a shortwave trough dropping southward across northwest Colorado. This led to moderate snow accumulations in the northern and central Colorado mountains with much less elsewhere. Warm temperatures also resulted in high snow levels with most accumulations above 9000 feet and rain or rain/snow mix in the valleys limiting accumulations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 4 to 8 inches of snow fell across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting northern to central Maryland during the late afternoon hours with swaths of 60 to 70 mph wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down between Lake Drive and North Bel Air Drive Southwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning, afternoon and evening hours of April 26 through April 29 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail and a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball-sized hail was reported in Sallis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms moved across the area on the evening of the 30th into the early morning hours of the 31st, producing a couple rounds of heavy rain and several reports of accumulating hail, with hailstones as large as ping pong balls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to the size of nickels in the Comins/Fairview area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Ohio Valley with showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging wind gusts.

A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms around 11 AM in northwest Mississippi with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of northwest Mississippi, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed hitting powerlines causing a power outage at Pleasant Hill and Laughter Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved east toward the area that helped to produce severe thundertorms over a good portion of the CWA. Flooding also occurred in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Lambert MT-200 DOT site (MTLBT) recorded a 73 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An incoming shortwave trough brought showers and some thunderstorms to west Texas and southeast New Mexico overnight April 30th and especially during the morning of May 1st. During the morning of the 1st, rainfall became locally heavy at times, which resulting in flash flooding in urban and low-lying areas. Showers largely cleared the area during the afternoon of the 1st as the shortwave moved east of MAF's CWA, taking the best lift and moisture with it.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report from the public of flooded streets near the intersection of Hermosa Drive and 1st Street. The total time of occurrence is estimated by radar. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms organized into a squall line and moved eastward into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 15th. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the second segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado crossed into Washington County, AR, near the 4765 Road. It crossed the Baron Fork River, and damaged outbuildings, uprooted trees, and snapped numerous large tree limbs along Salem Springs Road. Trees were uprooted or snapped along Highway 59 and Sugar Hill Road, before the tornado dissipated southwest of Lincoln. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down along Perch Road near its intersection with US Highway 52.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across eastern Arkansas. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill value of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass overspread the southern Appalachians in the wake of a strong cold front throughout the 26th and 27th. Widespread air temperatures in the single digits combined with gusty northwest winds to produce wind chill values of 5 to 10 below in the valleys. Temperatures near or below zero combined with generally stronger winds to yield wind chills of 15 to 25 below above 4000 feet.

An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Stark County Emergency Management relayed numerous damage photos from across the city of Dickinson. Damage includes trees down, fences down, minor roof damage, and other various property damage. A very large tree was uprooted by Dickinson City Hall that cracked the sidewalk and ripped the gutter out of the street. Overall damage is consistent with wind speeds of 80 to 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Newland Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Tuesday, April 14th, a southwest flow pattern transported a warm, humid air mass into central New York, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. The combination of sufficient instability, strong wind shear, and an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary ingredients for thunderstorm development. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on Wild Turnpike Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 2, thunderstorm development was initiated by a weak backdoor cold front moving in from the northeast. The resulting activity was primarily concentrated within and surrounding the DFW Metroplex, leading to instances of marginally severe hail and strong to severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported some utility poles and tree limbs down on Seagoville Rd near Interstate 635 in Balch Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. The strongest winds were generally west of the James River Valley where gusts to 60 to 70 mph were common. While areas of light snowfall generally on the order from a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, there were only very spotty and brief instances of visibility below one mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 40 to 44 mph at times with a peak gust of 62 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 2 miles south-southwest of Beresford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The side of a large steel outbuilding was ripped off at a property on Fort Loramie-Swanders Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front began tracking east from lee of the Appalachians to the Triad region of North Carolina during the late morning and afternoon hours of Monday March Sixteenth. Out ahead of this front, a prefrontal trough developed across the Coastal Plain. With ample moisture, instability, as well as low level and deep layer wind shear noted across North Carolina, scattered shower and thunderstorm activity developed along and out ahead of the prefrontal trough. Given the favorable conditions a few of the thunderstorms became strong in nature producing a mix of waterspouts and strong wind gusts across  the Pamlico, Croatan, Roanoke, and Albemarle sounds and coastal waters north of Ocracoke Inlet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was recorded as thunderstorms were moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall during February combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in continuing Extreme Drought (D3) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a slow-moving cold front. Some of these storms produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced quarter size hail north of Barksdale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall and snowmelt resulted in flooding across the south-central U.P.  Many roads were flooded and several closed.  The flooding also caused damage at the Escanaba Airport (KESC) due to standing water on the runways and power failure. Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th for Menominee and Marquette counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County emergency management reported Delta County Airport closed on the 13th due to water over the runways. Power was cut to the VOR facility and water was at least 3 feet deep. At least 4 roads in the city of Escanaba were closed on the 13th. In Rapid River, water over the road closed the US-41 and US-2 intersection. A culvert washout closed County Road 503 in Bay De Noc Township from the 16th to the 17th. Water over the road on County Road 497/GG in Nahma caused the road to be closed from the 17th to the 27th. Drone footage along the Ford River provided by the emergency manager highlighted multiple structures threated, surrounded, or inundated by high water. County emergency manager estimates private property damages around 300 Thousand $USD and the public damages at approximately 250 Thousand $USD.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued to burn into June. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May helped the final containment of local ongoing wildfires in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pace CT wildfire near Interlachen began on January 31, 2026 and continued to burn through most of June. Per the Florida Forest Service,  the fire remained at 343.35 acres with 90% containment. On June 8th, the fire had a containment of 95%. The fire remained at 343.35 acres and became 100% contained on June 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A small area of D2 Severe Drought conditions were in place to start the month of April in northeastern Minnesota. Above normal rainfall during the first part of the month led to a reduction in area of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 7th before the complete removal of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 21st. Rainfall for the month ranged from around 0.5 to 2 inches above normal in the affected area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: April began with D2 Severe Drought conditions across the far southeastern corner of southern St. Louis County and the western two-thirds of Carlton County. Above normal rainfall over the first half of the month led to the complete removal of D2 Severe Drought with the update on the 21st. Rainfall for the month was around 1.5 to 2 inches above normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported in the Tiburon neighborhood in North Bossier City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of East Texas along with an isolated report of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from quarter to golf ball size reported in Bullard. Quarter size hail was also reported east of U.S. Highway 69 along FM Road 344.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a strong arctic high pressure system and very dry air resulted in very cold temperatures ranging from zero to 10 degrees above zero on the morning of January 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures ranged form zero to 5 above zero across Jones County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An inside slider pattern developed over May 15 to May 18 as a low pressure system over the Great Basin and high pressure in the eastern Pacific combined to create a strong pressure gradient, resulting in strong gusts and turbulent wind-driven seas. A Beach Hazards Statement was placed in effect for the entire weekend, while two separate Wind Advisories were put in place, one for coastal regions through Saturday and another for the interior mountains of the Bay Area Sunday night through Monday morning. The strong winds caused an estimated 13,000 customers across the Bay Area to lose power.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ormsey Cutoff Trail station operated by PG&E reported a gust of 53 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Edinburg International Airport recorded freezing temperatures (32F degrees or lower) for 9 hours from 11:35pm CST on January 26th to 8:35am CST on Tuesday January 27th. A Hard Freeze (temperatures at or below 27F degrees) occurred for over 3.5 hours from 4:15-7:55am CST January 27th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon. This resulted in locally heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of high water on Coastal Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast Georgia with significant snow accumulations and very cold wind chill temperatures. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type. Rain quickly transitioned to snow during the afternoon hours, which continued into the evening before ending. Most of the snow accumulation impacted areas along and north of Interstate 16, with the highest amounts reported across Screven, Bulloch, and Effingham counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. The wind chill temperature first fell below 10 degrees at the Metter Airport (KMHP) at 18:55 EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of March 15th. Several tornadoes occurred within this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds snapped off a few limbs southwest of Saint James.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system developed from storms in south Texas and moved across the northwestern Gulf into coastal Louisiana.  This complex produced severe marine wind gusts, including a measured 81 mph gust near Cocodrie.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KOYE measured a marine thunderstorm wind gust of 70 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas.  Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were multiple reports of several trees down along State Road 64 near Kyana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Ohio Valley into the northern Mid-Atlantic region. A mid-level system tracked in from the west and led to numerous showers and storms across the Coastal Plain and Piedmont of Central North Carolina. Numerous wind damage reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on Kennebec Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 8.0 inches of a combination of snow and sleet. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Central Montana and surrounding mountains received a good amount of snow, with some lower-elevation locations seeing up to 13 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fisher Creek reported 1.6 of SWE. White Mill reported 1.3 of SWE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 6 to 8 inches of snow across Vermilion County...including 7.2 inches in Danville.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms developed in a northwest to southeast orientation across northwest Kansas during the early morning hours on the 1st and moved east to northeast. Quarter size hail was reported northwest of Goodland in Sherman county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail size ranged from nickel to quarter size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: We had a few wildfires that occurred in early April.  A couple in Hutchinson County (North and South Twin), and another Fire in Potter County (Meadow View).  The fires ranged from 365-1262 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Twin fire ignited 2 miles northwest of Sanford, TX and would go on to burn 365 acres.  The cause of the fire was unknown.  Both North and South Twin fires were noted as contained by the evening of the 5th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery revealed a tornado track which started around 3 miles southeast of Terril one-half mile south of 250th Street along 330th Avenue.  The tornado tracked to the northeast before crossing over into Emmet County around one-half mile north of 250th Street along 340th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 30 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Warren County in early to mid March after an ice jam broke loose on the Hudson River from the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. According to these sources, water and large chunks of ice flowed rapidly downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In Thurman, portions of River Road became inundated, specifically near The Glen Bridge, by both rapidly flowing water and large pieces of ice. This lead to the closure of the road for several days. In Warrensburg, portions of the Warren County Fish Hatchery also became inundated with some water and ice from a nearby branch of the Hudson River. Additionally, Cronin's Golf Course, which lies right along the Hudson River, became inundated with significant amounts of water. Areal drone images from a local news outlet showed what appears to be the entire golf course covered in water and ice. Due to the substantial nature of this ice jam, flooding impacted these areas for several days after the initial onset.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Warren County Emergency Managers, with the help of local broadcast media partners, reported that at 10 A.M. on Thursday, March 12th, an ice jam that had accumulated near the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg, NY broke free and rapidly flowed downstream. Large chunks of ice were swiftly carried downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In the town of Warrensburg, Cronin's Golf Course, which lies right along the Hudson River, became inundated with water and some pieces of ice. Areal drone images from a local news outlet showed what appears to be the entire golf course covered in water and ice with significant ice cover on the river next to it.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon and early evening hours of June 24th. As activity moved to the east and southeast, storms became severe with strong winds and large hail. Hail up to the size of baseballs was reported near Wauneta and wind gusts up to 77 MPH were reported near Grant. Thunderstorm wind damage, with winds estimated at 80 MPH overturned multiple pivots and damaged buildings south of Madrid.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report. VFD reports multiple pivots overturned in the area. Significant building  damage from apparent straight line winds. Time estimated from radar. Emergency management and print media reports damage to homes, vehicles and severe damage to crops.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement report of hail measured at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low moved across northern Mexico bringing a strong cold front through South-Central Texas. This resulted in very cold air in the boundary layer with a layer of above freezing air aloft which produced sleet and freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mix of sleet and freezing rain began during the evening of the 24th. Storm total accumulations included 0.03 of ice at Del Rio International Airport and 0.3 of sleet in Del Rio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down along County Road 110.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multicell thunderstorms over eastern Indiana moved into northwest Ohio resulting in sporadic reports of damaging wind gusts and sub-severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed in Gas City on South 5th Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portion of east-central and northeast Nebraska during March. Monthly precipitation totals were generally 0.5 to 1.5 inches below average.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A D3 (Extreme) drought was introduced across the southwestern portion of the county on March 3. Through the remainder of the month, D3 drought conditions expanded to encompass the northwestern majority of the county, with D2 conditions across the remainder of the county. The mesonet station near St. Helena, Nebraska recorded 0.55 inches of precipitation for the month, which was 1.12 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms that reached as far south as North Carolina. One storm in particular sent a swath of trees and power lines down in Mount Airy of Surry County. This storm formed and intensified after crossing the Blue Ridge and shortly dissipated in Stokes County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of trees were reported in the White Plains community at near I-74. The reports are as follows:||Two trees were reported down along McKinney Road.|A tree was reported down near the intersection of McKinney Road and Old Highway 601.|Two trees were reported down along Perry Taylor Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southeast South Dakota during the evening of February 17 and into the morning of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 50 mph with gusts as high as 66 mph were reported across the area. The strongest winds were along and west of the James River Valley. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of widespread wind gusts from 45 to 55 mph and light snow resulted in brief reductions in visibility to one-half mile or less, resulting in difficult travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms moved over portions of SE Texas, bringing large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the pubic reported quarter size hail along I-45 near exit 136 off Spur 67.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down on the Natchez Trace Parkway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down on CR 73 blocking both lanes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system emerged out of the Southern Plains and Texas and rode northeast through the Tennessee Valley and the Appalachians, before emerging just off the New Jersey coast. This produced a heavy snowfall across all of Northeastern New Jersey, with sleet, some of it heavy across a large portion of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Newark Airport reported 11.7 inches of snow and sleet. A trained spotter reported 11.2 inches of snow and sleet in Cranford. Broadcast media reported 9.6 inches in Linden. Cocorahs reported 11.8 inches at 0.6 NNW Cranford. Average snowfall totals across the zone were estimated to be just above 10 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions across Lawrence County from April 2026 improved to moderate drought in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported 2 inch diameter hail between Southmayd and Sherman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite episodic rounds of precipitation throughout the month, above-normal temperatures and prolonged stretches of mostly dry weather continued to maintain severe (or worse) drought conditions across portions of northern, central and western Oklahoma.

At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed a little less than one mile north of Webb just east of 290th Avenue in an open field.  The tornado was documented by numerous individuals as it tracked east-northeast for a little over a minute. The tornado crossed 300th Avenue near a farmstead where trees were damaged along the north side of the property and the resultant winds caused minor damage to the residence.  The tornado continued toward the east-northeast for a little over a minute over open fields and lifted just before 310th Avenue south of 470th Street. The tornado was rated EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 75 mph. The average path width was 30 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported quarter sized hail 6 miles east-northeast of Wonewoc.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of upper disturbances and fast moving cold fronts cause multiple rounds of stormy weather across portions of Louisiana. Several severe storms occurred. Behind the fast paced systems, tides fell below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beauregard Electric reported a tree downed onto power lines which was causing outages in Moss Bluff.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening line of thunderstorms moving northeast over East Central CO produced an outflow boundary that rushed east ahead of the storm activity into Kansas.  This boundary broke a healthy tree limb in Goodland.  As the weakening thunderstorms moved northeast into Kansas they produced wind gusts up to 76 MPH, the highest gust occurring at St. Francis.  Northwest of St. Francis these storms produced dust storm conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station northeast of Sharon Springs measured a high wind gust with no thunderstorm activity nearby.  This was from outflow winds from the thunderstorms west of Cheyenne Wells, CO.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 45 mph wind gust was recorded at the New York State Mesonet site near Oppenheim.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Mesonet station, GW3917, in Versailles measured a 60mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak brought 4 tornadoes to portions of western Wisconsin during the mid to late afternoon hours on April 17th. One of these tornadoes was a strong EF-3 tornado near the unincorporated community of Cream, Wisconsin. This intense tornado was responsible for substantially damaging a home with much of its exterior walls collapsed. Additional tornadoes occurred as these storms traveled into Trempealeau and Jackson counties, with tree and minor structural damage along their paths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado continued from northeast Trempealeau County where it crossed Interstate 94, moving northeast into far northwest Jackson County where it caused roof damage to two residences and damaged a significant number of trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 19th afternoon, an unstable airmass ahead of an approaching surface trough triggered a cluster of severe thunderstorms across central Indiana.  Convection initially intensified over the western and northern portions of the Indianapolis metropolitan area shortly after 1500 EST, capitalizing on strong low-to-mid level wind shear. These storms quickly organized into severe segments that tracked eastward and southward, producing a concentrated swath of damaging straight-line winds across Hendricks, Hamilton, Delaware, and Bartholomew counties before exiting the IND CWA by 1700 EST.||Damaging winds were the primary hazard with this event, resulting in structural damage, power outages, and travel disruptions. Hamilton County was particularly hard hit, where estimated wind gusts up to 55 knots (63 mph) downed multiple utility lines, left a power pole leaning in Noblesville, and knocked a large tree through the roof of a residence.  Transportation infrastructure was also impacted:  in Delaware County, estimated gusts of 55 knots blew over a semi truck on Interstate 69 near mile marker 249.  Earlier in the afternoon, severe gusts in Hendricks County downed several trees, including one that blocked a roadway southwest of Danville.  As the severe weather pushed into south-central Indiana, the KBAK AWOS at Columbus Municipal Airport in Bartholomew County recorded a peak measured wind gust of 52 knots (60 mph).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew over a semi on I69 at Mile Marker 249 Southbound Lanes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken band of supercell thunderstorms developed across Southeast Oklahoma late in the afternoon on April 28th, with this convection being largely focused along an outflow boundary and warm front lifting northward. The downstream air mass on the western edge of an earlier cold pool in far Southwest Arkansas adjacent to Southeast Oklahoma was still recovering with MLCAPE values rebounding to 2500-3500 J/kg. This recovering air mass coupled with an environment featuring 50-55 knots of effective bulk shear and effective storm-relative helicity (SRH) of around 200 m2/s2 supported the continuation of these supercells. As a result, one report of large hail and a couple of isolated damaging wind gusts were recorded across parts of McCurtain County during the late afternoon on April 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on Madge Tyler Road just north of U.S. Highway 70 near Millerton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: March 31, 2026, was a red-letter day for the southern tip of Texas in terms of drought.  Months of dry, top-five to ten warmest, low humidity, and breezy weather took its toll - and by the 31st, all areas were at Severe (D2) or higher, with 95% of the region at Extreme (D3) or higher, and a whopping 54.79% at Exceptional (D4) conditions.  Soon after, on Easter Weekend, the worst drought in 13 years would begin to crack with the start of spring rains, which continued through at least the end of May. ||Still, there were likely notable crop production/harvest losses in the Valley, and cattle herd production losses across the ranchlands, who had the longest duration of D3 and D4 conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The March 31, 2026 Drought Monitor removed the last of Severe (D2) Drought in central Kenedy County and replaced it with Extreme (level 3 of 4, D3) conditions. Unknown as of this writing were impacts on cattle ranches, including the King, Kenedy, and Yturria ranch, in the county. Herd impact estimates may be provided later this summer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several reports of trees down throughout Henrico County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated storms developed along a prefrontal trough by mid day on May 20. Later in the afternoon, a broader multicellular cluster of storms associated with the slow moving cold front moved into the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires blown down onto River Road between PA-611 and Narrows Hill Road. River Road was closed as a result for a period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 50 to 70 mph wind gusts across northern NY that resulted in several reports of tree limbs or trees in utility lines and several thousand power outages across northern NY. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across northern NY just prior to midnight on the 16-17th with a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts and some additional damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in excess of 40-45 mph from the south of March 16th and then 50-55 mph from the west during the early morning hours of March 17th after the passage of a sharp cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A convective complex moved through the region during the day on June 21st. Though it remained sub-severe for most of its life, the complex did intensify in south-central Illinois where it produced tornadoes, wind damage, and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between 3 and 5 inches of rain fell in a short period of time. This led to water over several roadways including at least 2 vehicles that got stuck in flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reports that a large limb fell onto a camper and injured the person inside.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved across Southeastern Arizona on January bringing light to moderate rainfall beginning at 5 AM on the 7th and continued off and on through 10 PM on the 8th. This heavy rainfall caused an anchor became loose leading to a power outage to 1400 people. A nearby CWOP station reported a rainfall total of 1.49 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused an anchor became loose leading to a power outage to 1400 people. A nearby CWOP station reported a rainfall total of 1.49 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed quarter to half dollar size hail fell on LCR 433 around 7 miles south of Mexia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed across Highway 480 near Campti.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

A sharp cold frontal passage on March 16th in southeast brought the last surge of winter weather in the form of snow. Precipitation transitioned from rain to snow on the afternoon of the 16th and prevailed into the next day. One to four inches of snow fell across southeast Ohio as a result, with locally higher amounts noted in Athens County in response to a heavy snow band that laid across the county and into north-central West Virginia. Much quieter weather returned to the area later on March 17th under the guise of building high pressure.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mobile home rolled over on Glister Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought a sharp transition from record-breaking warmth to severe weather across eastern Kentucky on March 11th. Ahead of an approaching cold front, unseasonably warm air surged into the region on a potent low-level jet, with temperatures reaching record levels at London and Jackson. Widespread non-convective wind gusts between 30 and 50 mph occurred during the afternoon.||As the cold front moved in during the evening, a pre-frontal squall line (QLCS) developed in a high shear environment and tracked across the Commonwealth. The most intense measured wind gust was 70 mph at the London-Corbin Airport ASOS. Elsewhere, the storms resulted in structural damage, scattered downed trees, and a few power outages before a sharp cold front crossed the area, ushering in a much drier and colder airmass.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A picture on social media showed a tree that had been blown down onto an old mobile home in the vicinity of Martin, resulting in substantial roof damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in Missouri during the morning of May 31st. As they passed through central Missouri, one cell was able to produce minor flooding in Boone and Moniteau counties. The thunderstorms then congealed before producing a swath of wind damage in southeast Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds estimated to be about 60 mph in magnitude downed large, healthy branches in and near Fredericktown. Some fell on a residence and damaged its gutters and roof, though the true extent of the damage is unknown. Other large trees and power lines were downed through the county. Notably, winds caused extensive damage across a farmstead near Junction City. A farm outbuilding was collapsed, and a wooden beam was drilled into the top of a garage. Debris was all over the yard, including atop a GMC Denali and Buick crossover. The debris did damage both vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold temperatures and wind chills affected the region on January 30th and 31st. A few individuals died or were hospitalized due to hypothermia or house fires during this cold weather episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the county fell as low as 0 degrees during the early morning of January 31st. One female died due to cold exposure, and another individual was hospitalized due to hypothermia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed south of Wakita and a mobile home was unroofed and at least two buildings were destroyed along Harper Road. A number of power poles were damaged along State Highway 11 as the tornado moved northeast. Although the last damage was noted by the survey team along State Highway 11, a storm chaser observed the tornado at least a couple of miles farther northeast and the tornado is estimated to have dissipated about 5 miles southeast of Wakita.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another in a week of extremely strong winds occurred with the strongest wind day with a peak of 89 mph at East Butte and several gusts over 70 mph throughout the state.  Interstate 15 was pre-emptively closed from Shelley to north of Idaho Falls in anticipation of the extreme event.  It was a widespread event with some damage and power outages occurring as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extremely strong winds occurred throughout the day with a peak wind of 73 mph at the Palisades Dam mesonet site.  Antelope Flats recorded 63 mph and extensive wind gusts of 60 mph plus occurred.   Glass shattered on a rear window of a vehicle parked at the Swan Valley gas station thought to be from wind or flying debris from the wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across the majority of Southwest Arkansas throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since late December 2025. A combination of above normal temperatures and below normal monthly rainfall ranging from 2-4 inches, which remained 50-75% of normal, maintained these drought conditions across this area throughout the month. As a result, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal stock pond levels and thus, water to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow on area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

The month of June saw overall above normal temperatures and a mixed bag of precipitation with some areas seeing above normal precipitation and others below normal precipitation. This is very reflective of the early summer thunderstorm activity that saw daily rounds of thunderstorms pass over some areas repeatedly, while missing other areas entirely. As a result, most of New Mexico saw no change in drought conditions while around a quarter to a third of the state saw either a 1 class degradation or improvement in drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought was introduced to a central swath of the zone with severe drought persistent elsewhere.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell in the Joinerville community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A departing cold front brought winds in excess of 55 mph late on the 27th into the early hours of the 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The C-MAN Station ROAM4 Rock of Ages Lighthouse reported wind gusts in excess of 55 mph for at least between 5:49 PM and 9:54 PM on the 27th, with a peak gust of 61 mph 7:44 PM out of the northwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 35 to 55 mph with gusts as high as 75 mph across southeast South Dakota. When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches north of Highway 18, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and very brief blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds were sustained from 40 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 61 mph at Mitchell and 58 mph at a South Dakota Mesonet site near Mount Vernon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 71 mph wind gust measured at the Base of Howe Peak mesonet station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushed across eastern New York during the afternoon hours on June 6, 2026 within the warm sector of a low pressure system. The strongest and most organized thunderstorms moved across Ulster and Dutchess Counties where numerous reports of downed trees and wires occurred. More isolated thunderstorms also produced some downed trees across far northern Washington County and near North Creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed on Trotting Lane in Napanoch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass setup over southern Wisconsin in late June.  Low temperatures struggled to get into the 70s while high temperatures in the 90s combined with high dew points led to heat indices reaching the 105F-110F range.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina throughout the afternoon. Several of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.

Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 6 tornadoes were confirmed across southwest Mississippi and multiple  reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The damage path of an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph and max width of 200 yards was identified via high resolution satellite imagery in northwest Amite County, north of Gloster, MS. This tornado caused damage and displacement to several trees including a swath west of Hwy 33 concurrent with an EF-1. Additional tree damage was identified along Hwy 33 near Homochitto Rd. This was corroborated by EM report of tree damage north of Gloster which also was collocated with a strong area of rotation on KHDC radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens. There were numerous social media posts of frozen and burst water pipes across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of June saw overall above normal temperatures and a mixed bag of precipitation with some areas seeing above normal precipitation and others below normal precipitation. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening mesoscale convective system (MCS) advanced east southeast into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours on June 24th, just north of an outflow reinforced frontal boundary which extended from Northeast Texas into North Central Louisiana and eastward into Mississippi. Behind the MCS, showers and thunderstorms increased in coverage from North Louisiana into Southwest Arkansas. Wind profiles in the 925-850 millibar layer showed some modest strengthening into the 25-30 knot range from the south southwest, helping to remove lingering lower level convective inhibition centered near 850 mb. Low level flow overrunning the surface boundary set up a convergence axis in the 925-850 millibar layer, aligned from Southeast Oklahoma into Northwest Louisiana. This zone of convergence focused increasing coverage of elevated thunderstorms throughout the morning, beneath increasingly diffluent flow aloft in the 300-400 millibar layer. The convergence axis was aligned with a gradient in MLCAPE of 500 to 1500 J/kg noted to the southwest of the axis. Precipitable water (PWAT) values ranged from 1.7 to near 2 inches across the region. As a result, hourly rainfall rates of 1 to 2+ inches occurred within areas of training storms with localized rainfall totals of 2 to 6+ inches common across Southwest Arkansas. Thus, numerous reports of flash flooding were recorded throughout the morning into the mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported to be entering 8-10 homes on North Main Street in Nashville.
