EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a slowly advancing cold front across south-central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and nighttime hours of April 17. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and up to 70 mph wind gusts. Wind damage was also noted across a couple locations across southeast Kansas from these storms.

A powerful and expansive storm system brought widespread heavy wintry precipitation across nearly two thirds of the width of North America, stretching from the southern Rockies and southern Plains, across portions of the Midwest, Deep South, and Southeast, into the Mid-Atlantic and New England. For the Mid-Atlantic region, this was an overrunning precipitation event, with a very cold and dry, arctic airmass in place ahead of the storm. The main low pressure center passed offshore just to the south of the forecast area.||Precipitation began as all snow across the local region during the very early morning hours of January 25th. A transition to sleet occurred from south to north after dawn, reaching as far north as the I-78 to I-80 corridors by the evening before precipitation ended. Some freezing rain occurred across the coastal plain of New Jersey and Delmarva during the afternoon and evening hours. The marine front remained south and east of the I-95 to I-195 corridors. North of the front (along and north of the I-95 to I-195 corridors, including much of the Philadelphia metropolitan area, central and northern Delmarva) into the I-78 corridor, temperatures remained in the 10s (and even single digits near the I-78 corridor) when snow changed to sleet. Total sleet accumulations between 1-3 were reported in this region, on top of approximately 5-10 of snow. North of the I-78 corridor, precipitation remained mostly all snow, where near a foot or more of accumulations were reported, though at least some mixing of sleet was reported as far north as I-80.||The snow and sleet proved very challenging to remove following the storm due to the weight and density of the ice-capped snowpack and below freezing temperatures. At least 3 fatalities related to snow removal occurred in the Lehigh Valley. Snow removal took a few days in some places. Untreated or unplowed pavement remained covered in snow and/or ice for one to two weeks following the storm.||A 17 day period of largely well below freezing temperatures began the day before this storm on January 24th and continued through February 9th. This was one of the coldest 17 day periods in several decades for much of the region at the time. Mean temperatures in the period ranged from the mid 10s to low 20s. The extreme cold preserved the ice-capped, glacier-like snowpack for approximately 3 to 4 weeks following the storm. The snowpack remained across the entire region until about the third week of February, before melting away completely in most areas due to light rainfall and low temperatures remaining above freezing for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow and sleet accumulation totals mainly ranged from 10-17. The highest report received was 19.2 in Portland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One downed tree was observed along Brier Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An strong upper-level low with an associated surface cold front allowed to ample lift in an environment with sufficient shear and instability for a line of showers and isolated thunderstorms to form during the afternoon and evening hours of March 13, 2026. Strong-to-damaging wind gusts were observed across northwestern Pennsylvania with these features with the most widespread wind damage in portions of Clearfield County during the late afternoon to early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of showers producing wind gusts estimated at 70 mph knocked a tree down onto a house approximately 3 miles southeast of Curwensville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of strong thunderstorms shifted into northwest Alabama during the late afternoon and early evening hours.  The storms produced strong and gusty winds knocking down a few trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down along Wagon Mountain Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down three separate trees to fall down within a short distance. One tree fell along on Cornfield Lane, another tree fell on a power line on Church Street, and a third tree fell along Redfields Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

A strong upper level disturbance and associated cold front translated into the Southern Plains on the 8th. An unseasonably warm and moist air mass had spread into eastern Oklahoma ahead of this system, which resulted in weak instability across the area. A line of thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma from the west during the morning hours of the 8th. Strong wind fields and wind shear associated with the approaching upper level system, combined with the weak instability, supported an environment in which the stronger thunderstorms within the squall line were able to develop low level circulations. One such circulation resulted in a brief, weak tornado and wind gusts to 88 mph in Osage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oklahoma Mesonet station near Wynona measured thunderstorm wind gusts up to 88 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multicell thunderstorms over eastern Indiana moved into northwest Ohio resulting in sporadic reports of damaging wind gusts and sub-severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles down west and northwest of Ottoville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

A second day of high winds occurred for Northwest Kansas.  The high winds began after 9 AM MT and continued as late as 5:30 PM MT.  The peak gust was 76 MPH reported at the Goodland airport.  The combination of high winds and loose soil led to dust storm conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dust storm conditions were reported at 1 ESE of Ruleton (MM 10 on I-70) and 2 E of Caruso.

This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 900-1200 J/kg, resulted in severe thunderstorms that blew a few trees down in Greenbrier and Mercer Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm moved through La Porte County on the afternoon of March 6 and produced 1.75 inch diameter hail. The storm went on to produce multiple tornadoes in southern Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received a report from the public of 1.75 inch diamater hail near Westville, IN.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front opened up the month of April across northeast Kentucky, supplying a brief burst of strong to severe thunderstorms. The first storm of note passed through Lawrence County shortly after midday, leading to local power outages from downed trees and power lines. A few hours later, one more storm pressed through the county and prompted a single downed tree. The bulk of the convective activity then became focused in West Virginia, bringing the severe threat to northeast Kentucky to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage in the Georges Creek area resulted in 54 customers to be without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms ahead a cold front produced isolated severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fallen trees or limbs resulted in a power outage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record dry winter in Southeast Missouri led to dry conditions heading into April from Bollinger to Mississippi Counties. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. Severe (D2) drought developed mid-month along that corridor, diminished some with heavy rain the following week, then expanded for the end of April with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed in Leon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees and wires down across Pine Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather system moved into Wyoming and mixed strong winds aloft down to the surface, bringing high wind to much of central Wyoming. The highest wind occurred in the mountains, with a maximum wind gust of 95 mph at Red Canyon over South Pass in the Wind River Range. In the lower elevations, some notable wind gusts included 74 mph at the Lander Airport, 75 mph at Twenty Mile Hill to the north of Casper, 75 mph in Clark, and 69 mph near Buffalo.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 63 mph wind gust was recorded at the Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport near Rock Springs. A 64 mph wind gust was recorded along Interstate 80 near Tipton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pictures of hail measured at 3 inches in diameter were received from the public. This hail fell in a mostly rural location though a few homes in the area received hail damage to roofs, outbuildings and equipment.  A few vehicles suffered damage as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface shortwave troughing allowed for ample lift in an environment with increasing instability as skies began to clear out during the early afternoon hours. Sufficient deep-layer shear across the region allowed for some thunderstorm development with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms across much of southern Pennsylvania during the late afternoon and evening hours. Thunderstorms across south-central Pennsylvania during the late afternoon hours gradually pulsed up to severe limits, causing an area of tree and building damage in Franklin County before a similar instance occurred in Adams County with a small barn collapse. Residual convection from western Pennsylvania began moving into portions of central Pennsylvania during the evening hours, causing isolated tree damage in Somerset County along with some damage in Bedford County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a tree onto Rosenbaum Road north of the intersection with Lincoln Highway east of Stoystown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours. Strong storms developed and produced damaging wind gusts and localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Upper Bellbrook Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 15-18. The highest reliable measurement received was 19.3 from Robbinsville Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front, combined with scattered thunderstorms embedded in southwest flow, interacted with an anomalously warm and dry air mass across southwest Montana. High temperatures were in the 80s, creating large dewpoint depressions. High winds aloft, reaching 65 knots between 16,000 and 18,000 feet MSL, were brought to the surface by both convective downdrafts and evaporative cooling, as well as the passing cold front. This synoptic setup led to severe and high wind gusts across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An initial thunderstorm produced a 54 MPH wind gust just west of Homestake Pass at 1254MST. This gust resulted in a power outage that lasted until 1930MST. Later, at 1629MST, a 67 MPH wind gust was measured at the Bert Mooney Airport (KBTM). This severe gust was associated with a weak thunderstorm that mixed down stronger winds from aloft, aided by evaporative cooling. The strong winds caused a tree branch to fall onto a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley region, pulling a cold front through the area. Showers and thunderstorms developed out in front of and along the front. Some storms produced instances of damaging wind gusts and heavy rainfall, leading to isolated flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed across a roadway. Additionally, the trees knocked down several power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on Saddle Hollow Road near Mint Spring Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong and gusty north to northeast winds impacted many areas of Southwestern California. Wind gusts up to 83 MPH were reported across the mountains and foothills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong and gusty north to northeast winds impacted the area. Some peak gusts include: Crystal Lake (gust 59 MPH) and Clear Creek RAWS (gust 58 MPH).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to Zero to 15 below zero across much of VT with wind chill temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero across much of VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures around 5 to 15 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 15 to 25 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While some rainfall did occur, below the monthly average rainfall occurred for most of the county, which produced continued dry conditions. This allowed drought to range from Extreme (D3) to Abnormally Dry (D)) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought all severe hazards to portions of Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail larger than baseballs (up to 3 inches in diameter) was reported near Interstate 35 near Bridgeport by a deputy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system moved over the Great Lakes region Saturday evening, resulting in warm air advection in the mid-levels. Deep warm nose led to sleet, and then a sleet/freezing rain mix early Sunday morning in the north and Central Highlands region. Very cold low-level layer helped precipitation to refreeze. Roughly an inch or so of snow fell in the north, alongside an inch to an inch and a half of sleet by Sunday morning. Impacts were mainly just a messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly an inch of snow and sleet fell in Northern Piscataquis by early morning Sunday.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over southeast Louisiana, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D3 to include St Tammany, southern Tangipahoa, and St James Parishes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D3 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of Upper Terrebonne Parish according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued to burn into June. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May helped the final containment of local ongoing wildfires in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Sargent wildfire developed in northwest Baker county, northern Osceola National Forest on April 2, 2026 around 350 PM EDT and grew to 2,523 acres by the end of April. Per the Florida Forest Service, the Sargent fire was 100% contained on June 3rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.
Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.
Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted through much of the month before improving to Severe (D2) late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 0.70 to 1.00 inches across the month of February. This maintained D3 conditions across all of Howard county through the month. These drought conditions continued into at least March 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between large air masses funneled strong and severe winds through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple observations in central and southern Valley County recorded wind gusts in excess of 59 mph, the strongest of which was 75 mph, measured at the Glasgow Airport ASOS site (KGGW).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions persisted through the month of April.

Above normal rainfall in portions of north central, central, southwestern and western Nebraska led to improvements in drought conditions across western and north central Nebraska in June. There were a few local areas where drought conditions remained unchanged in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions improved to severe (D2) drought conditions across most of Hayes County by the end of June. Across far southwestern portions of the county, severe (D2) drought conditions improved to moderate (D1) drought. Across far southeastern portions of the county,  exceptional (D4) drought improved to severe (D2) drought conditions. Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread into northwestern Arkansas during the evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma and northwestern Arkansas, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to golf ball size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to half dollar size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Craig county in May after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Johns Creek, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rain across parts of central Illinois from the evening of June 10th into the pre-dawn hours of June 11th.  Rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches were common, with some locations exceeding 3.50.  Excessive rainfall rates associated with strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of June 10th resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding across Knox, Peoria, Tazewell, McLean, and Sangamon counties.  In addition, sharp rises on area creeks and streams led to overland flooding in a few spots...most notably on the north side of Lexington in McLean County.  The flood waters gradually receded after sunrise on June 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing across parts of Carl Sandburg Drive in Galesburg with one car stalled in the flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees downed along Boyd Road and Pleasant Hill Cemetery Road near Plain Dealing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees and power lines were downed in the 8000 block of Orangeburg Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. By the end of the event, snowfall totals of 6 to 15 inches were observed across western Pendleton and western Grant Counties with lesser amounts of 3 to 6 inches across western Mineral. Further east across the eastern panhandle, totals were elevation dependent with the ridges observing 2 to 4 inches and the valleys observing a coating to 2 inches.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Walters (WAL2) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the late afternoon and early evening of May 18, 2026, severe thunderstorms and heavy rain triggered flash flooding across central Johnson County. Because the area was already saturated from several consecutive days of rain, the ground could not absorb the sudden deluge. Driven by intense downpours of 1 to 2 inches per hour, total accumulations rapidly reached 3.00 to 4.50 inches. Emergency management reported localized flooding through Tecumseh, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A potent Arctic Front across southern Ontario and western New York began to shift southeasterly during the late evening hours of December 31, 2025 and continued into the early morning hours of January 1, 2026. This potent cold front allowed for a line of snow squalls to form across all of central Pennsylvania, with widespread whiteout conditions are the line of squalls moved through the area. Whiteout conditions were observed at the NWS State College office, along with by multiple spotters in Centre, Mifflin, Blair, and York counties. No accidents or injuries were reported during these snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall brought visibility less than one quarter of a mile with heavy snow observed on Interstate 83 south of New Cumberland. Heavy snowfall allowed for quick accumulation on the roadway in a span of 10 to 15 minutes. Winds were observed to gust near 30 mph as these snow squalls moved through the county during the early morning hours of January 1, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Franklin County averaged 2.62 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.79 inches below normal. Since June, deficits grew to over 9 inches making it the driest stretch on record. The USDM on March 31st had 52% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 48% in Moderate Drought (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree branch was snapped by thunderstorm wind gusts across a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large pine tree was downed in Hemphill.

Precipitation initially began as freezing rain at many locations but quickly switched to sleet as the lower levels of the atmosphere cooled. Despite temperatures well below freezing into the single digits by the morning of the 24th, sleet continued to be the dominant precipitation type. A strong warm layer aloft allowed for much of this precipitation to remain as sleet. By the afternoon of the 24th, the warm layer aloft cooled enough to allow mostly snow to fall as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Snowfall continued through the night of the 24th ending late in the afternoon on the 25th. The heaviest amount of snow fell over the western South Plains into the extreme southern Texas Panhandle where totals of six to eight inches were observed. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the second time in a week, a winter storm impacted the mountains and foothills of North Carolina as an area of low pressure intensified across the Deep South. In this case, all precipitation fell as snow. Snow began falling during the late evening of the 30th and continued off and on for around 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the morning of the 31st. By the time the snow tapered off, 5 to 8 inch totals along with locally higher amounts were reported across the area.

An upper level disturbance moving across the central Rockies combined with higher moisture across the southeast plains of NM resulted in the development of multiple severe thunderstorms across southern Roosevelt County during the mid afternoon to mid evening hours. These thunderstorms resulted in three rounds of hail up to ping pong diameter between Pep and the Roosevelt and Lea County border. Back building of severe thunderstorms across this area resulted in some minor flooding in culverts and low lying areas. Thunderstorms tapered off just before sunset on May 21st due to the loss of daytime heating. Two more rounds of thunderstorms developed across the northeast and east central plains of NM during the afternoon on May 22nd and 23rd. These storms resulted in a severe wind gust at a public weather station near Melrose on May 22nd and at Tucumcari Municipal Airport on May 23rd. Storms exited into west Texas during the evening hours. The Trigg wildfire was also discovered in far eastern San Miguel County, burning through May 25th before coming under control.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter 7 miles south-southeast of Pep observed quarter size hail from the second severe thunderstorm of the afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The McIntosh County Warning Point reported a tree down at 5th Street West.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass surged into southern Mississippi behind a strong cold front on January 25���26, 2026, resulting in dangerously cold temperatures and wind chills across the region.  Strong cold air advection, driven by a 1040+ mb surface high building southward into Texas and Louisiana, combined with persistent north winds of 10 to 15 mph to produce hazardous conditions.  By the morning of January 27th, air temperatures had fallen into the teens and 20s across southern Mississippi. When combined with strong northerly winds, wind chills dropped into the single digits across southwest Mississippi and values generally ranging from 10 to 15 degrees along the Mississippi Gulf Coast. These conditions persisted for several hours during the early morning, prompting an Extreme Cold Warning for the entire area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local observations showed wind chills dropped into the single digits for several hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 5 degrees or less across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 8F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the county fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe storms developed along a slow moving cold front as it creeped across the area through the afternoon and into the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 2-inch hail along with estimated winds up to 90 mph. Multiple structures were damaged across south-central Kansas due to these storms.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inch hail reported south of Paola.
