EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very isolated rain events brought some moisture to the eastern Panhandles during the month. However, this did not put a dent in the 120 departure from normal with values staying 2 to 4 below normal. Mites were appearing on stressed winter wheat crop and wildfires became an increasing concern across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate Drought (D1) conditions persisted in the NW TX Panhandle until the third week of March. At that point, the drought intensified, with Dallam, Hartley, Sherman, and Moore Counties all escalating to Severe Drought (D2). This transition was marked by an additional 1 to 2 being added to the existing 120-day precipitation deficit. Furthermore, the severity of the drought's impact on winter crops was worsened by record monthly maximum temperatures recorded during the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hirschville NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper low moved through the region bringing widespread light snow to the U.P. Moderate to heavy lake effect snow developed over the northern and western U.P. as an arctic air mass moved into the Great Lakes, disrupting travel and resulting in school closures. In addition to snowfall, winds and arctic air brought very cold windchills in the -20s across the U.P.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill of -20F reported at the Copper Harbor ASOS KP59 at 0151 EST, 1/20.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours. ||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS KMER Merced-Castle Air Force Base reported quarter-mile visibility in dense |fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

Surface low pressure supported by vigorous mid-level shortwave moved across northern NY and northern New England during the afternoon and evening hours of June 18th.||Moderate instability combined with directional wind shear at multiple levels and a cold front helped develop a line of thunderstorms in NY that increased in intensity and coverage as it moved across VT with wind damage as well as weak, isolated tornadoes in VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous powerlines and trees blown down by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th, and across far southeastern Oklahoma on the 18th.

An intense thunderstorm cluster, exhibiting occasional supercell character, moved from the western suburbs of Oklahoma City, OK southward towards Lawton, OK. In addition to reports of large to very large hail, a concentrated corridor of thunderstorm wind damage occurred on the east and southeast sides of Lawton, OK. This included several observations of significant severe winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage occurred near Fort Sill. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold high pressure settled in the Northern and Central Plains the morning of the 19th. With low pressure near the Straits of Mackinac, winds persisted through the night allowing wind chills to drop into the -40F to -45F range across portions of northeastern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -43F were reported in the central part of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Pacific weather system crossed western and central Wyoming and brought heavy snow west of the Continental Divide and high wind to the east of the Divide. Notable accumulations fell throughout the western mountains. The highest amount was in the Salt River and Wyoming Ranges where 34 inches of new snow fell at the Spring Creek Divide SNOTEL site. Other notable amounts included 30 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL in Yellowstone National Park, 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL in the Absarokas and 24 inches over Togwotee Pass. High winds occurred along and East of the Divide as well as across Sweetwater County. Some of the more notable wind gusts included 82 mph along South Pass and 81 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 69 mph wind gust was reported on the north side of Casper. At the Lander airport, a 58 mph wind gust was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station measured a wind gust to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From June 2-4, 2026, a series of disturbances tracking across the region within broad zonal flow set off several rounds of thunderstorms to the region. A slow-moving front on June 2 set off the first round of thunderstorms, producing widespread heavy rain and localized flash flooding. The most significant impacts occurred in Oglala and surrounding communities, where 6 to 7 inches of rain fell in a short period, causing streets and ditches to fill extremely quickly. Some storms also produced large hail and strong winds. Some storms also produced large hail and strong winds.||June 3 brought another round of storms as a disturbance moved across the Northern Plains. Clearing over Wyoming and the Black Hills allowed storms to redevelop along a boundary across southern South Dakota. Several became supercells, including the storm that produced the rain-wrapped Ideal tornado in Tripp County. The tornado mainly affected agricultural land but damaged multiple outbuildings and caused additional RFD���related damage to a nearby modular home.||On June 4, the severe threat was more limited. Lower dewpoints over Wyoming and a strong cap over the Black Hills and western South Dakota kept storm coverage down, though a few storms still became severe with larger hail and strong wind gusts. A landspout also occurred in northeast Wyoming with one of the isolated storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms repeatedly developed over the same areas on June 2, 2026 leading to flash flooding, that turned into pluvial flooding. Runoff from an estimated 5 to 7 inches of rain caused considerable damage in Oglala. Seven buildings were destroyed, 24 buildings had major damage, and 10 other structures reported minor damager. Highway 18 and BIA 41 were also inundated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

A disturbance moved through Northeast Pennsylvania. and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region. With one storm, lightning struck a church and led to a fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree onto roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on power line along Dan Parrish Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed large tree onto 9th Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A ridge of high pressure moved into the region on the morning of the 1st. Temperatures plummeted into the single digits. Although winds were mainly light, a few locations still manage to see wind chills fall between -5 to -10.

A deep occluded low approaching the UP from the west on the 18th brought a warm front just south of the UP and eventually the occluded front moved over the UP as the low weakened by the 19th. This brought a mess of heavy wet snow and freezing rain as well as high winds. Impacts included a majority of school districts closed, municipal facilities closed, power outages, and near-impassible roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While Southern Houghton County is in a data-sparse area, surrounding zones reported snowfall between 5 and 10 inches, with municipal resources strained including a Houghton County snowplow being totaled after a crash from slick roads. Key impacts: hazardous travel, closed municipalities.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across the South Carolina Piedmont during the afternoon. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility company reported trees blown down on power lines causing outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass combined with moderate or gusty winds to bring extreme cold conditions to portions of northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Montana Climate Office mesonet site Fort Kipp NW (FTKM8) measured a wind chill of -41 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portion of a barn roof was removed on Farris Loop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to Zero to 15 below zero across much of VT with wind chill temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero across much of VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures around 5 to 15 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 15 to 25 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary arctic frontal zone crashed southeast across the region with yet another increase in winds, spotty light snowfall, and areas of blowing snow.

When snow was falling, even lightly, area Department of Transportation cameras and automated instruments indicated visibility as low as one-quarter mile or less at Windom and near Mountain Lake. Travel was not advised along State Highway 60 for portions of the afternoon and evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably cold airmass, originating from central Canada, brought record and near-record cold temperatures to the region. A deep and cold upper low pinched off and became centered over southern Saskatchewan and Montana during the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures dropped into the low to mid 20s for lower elevation sites such as just west of Lolo, around Sula, and along Rock Creek on the mornings of the 25th and 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail reported in the Chireno community.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Riverside Fire began near Espanola, NM near the Santa Claran Hotel within the Santa Clara Pueblo. The fire grew to 44 acres destroying 5 structures, including one single-wide trailer, one home, one recreational vehicle, and two sheds. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Damage is an estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough approached Georgia on the morning of Sunday, January 18th, drawing Gulf moisture northward into central Georgia. Meanwhile, a cold front brought an influx of colder air into the area. This interaction led to a few hours of snowfall across much of central Georgia on the morning of January 18th. Snowfall accumulations were generally in the 1-2 range across this stretch of the state, though a few spots received near 3 of snow. After a brief period of slowed travel and snowy scenes, afternoon sun brought warmer temperatures which quickly melted the snow, bringing a quick end to this relatively uncommon central Georgia snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain transitioned to snow in the early morning hours of the 18th. Snow accumulations of T to 1.5 inches were reported across the county. All snow tapered off by late morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water 4 feet deep near exit at Labonte Park / I-37.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe t-storms developed during the late afternoon into the evening of April 23rd.  Large hail, damaging winds and a few tornadoes were documented.  The strongest tornado damaged structures at lake kahola near the Morris and Chase County line.  The other tornadoes were rated EF0 or EFU due to lack of documented damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Relayed report by Emergency Manager.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front draped over the Ohio Valley tracked into the central and southern Appalachians by the late evening and overnight period. Ahead of the front, scattered showers and storms tracked from the North Carolina mountains into the Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the evening hours. Numerous wind damage reports were observed over the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down at Millennium Drive and North Church Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limb downed by thunderstorm wind gusts onto a house which caused a gas leak.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts measured by South Dakota Mesonet station MNMS2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of western Massachusetts from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across western Massachusetts from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, declared a state of emergency prior to this event which authorized additional local resources as well as orders for travel restrictions. NWS Albany additionally received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across western Massachusetts. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 15.5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated damaging winds occurred with a line of storms on April 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered trees down between Plainwell and Pine Lake. Scattered power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported quarter sized hail in New York Texas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet accumulation up to 1/2 inch, followed by 1/4 to 1/2 inch of ice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms following the Appalachian mountains reorganized later in the afternoon and brought damaging wind gusts to parts of south-central Virginia. Surface heating and mixing resulted in MLCAPE values of 750-1000 J/kg and low level lapse rates of 7-8��C/km. Mid-level lapse rates were not as impressive which may have limited the coverage of severe storms but DCAPE values of 700-900 J/kg contributed to some downed trees in Charlotte and Halifax Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on Clover Road near the Charlotte County border.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-wave severe event unfolded from the afternoon of January 9 through the morning of January 10. While the first wave featured no severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall over Birmingham led to numerous flooding issues. Early the next morning, additional heavy rainfall led to more flooding issues in parts of Jefferson, Shelby, and St. Clair counties. A bowing line segment moved across Marengo, Dallas, Autauga, Elmore, Montgomery, and Lee counties, with scattered instances of wind damage. In addition, a cell in advance of the main QLCS produced an EF-0 tornado in northern Cleburne County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines were downed in the Salem community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure tracked across the central Great Lakes, into southern Ontario and then into southwest Quebec on December 29th. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking Mannington Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees down throughout Berlin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low to mid level east-southeasterly flow and moderate instability favored sea breeze convection that produced a waterspout over the Caloosahatchee River near Whiskey Creek and a strong marine wind gust over Tampa Bay waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS site KPIE St Pete-Clearwater International Airport reported a 43 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of  west central and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening period, with very large hail and severe winds reported. One supercell produced 3 inch hail in Moorhead, MN. One EF-0 tornado developed with a supercell in Clay County 6 miles northwest of Hawley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 12 inch tree branch split off the main trunk relayed via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low deepened as it moved through North Dakota, leading to high non-thunderstorm wind gusts. By the early afternoon, the strong winds were producing blowing dust and significantly reduced visibility across western North Dakota, with a Blowing Dust Warning and Blowing Dust Advisory issued for much of western and central North Dakota. Visibility was under one quarter of a mile at times. The strongest wind gust reported was 76 mph near Crosby in Divide County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ray NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 71 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement or maintenance of the drought. Dimmit, Medina, and Travis Counties all improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Hays County remained in D3. Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 20.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were still below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 5.7 feet but was 11.1 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in April and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.7 feet and was 69.8 feet below normal. Medina Lake rose 0.3 feet but was still 87.1 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina and Blanco Rivers; below normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal to much above normal (90%-95%).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching warm front produced showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Delaware Valley up through northern New Jersey. A few of these storms produced heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: North Beechwood Street flooded with water almost halfway up the side of multiple cars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of damaging wind gusts. A few destructive wind gusts were noted in north-central Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees blew down between Rapidan and Locust Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size in North Liberty.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree and adjacent power lines were observed along WV Route 5 between Gluck Run Road and Duck Run Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple organized QLCSs push across central Mississippi and produced damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began near the eastern end of Mapp Turner Road and tracked across Lily Rose Road, downing large tree limbs. It crossed MS Highway 13 near the intersection with Greens Creek Road, uprooting trees and damaging siding at a home along Clay Lee Johnson Drive. The tornado then made a leftward turn as it occluded, downing additional large tree limbs as it lifted near the intersection of Greens Creek Road and Jot-Em Down Road. Estimated peak wind speeds were 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low deepened as it moved through North Dakota, leading to high non-thunderstorm wind gusts. By the early afternoon, the strong winds were producing blowing dust and significantly reduced visibility across western North Dakota, with a Blowing Dust Warning and Blowing Dust Advisory issued for much of western and central North Dakota. Visibility was under one quarter of a mile at times. The strongest wind gust reported was 76 mph near Crosby in Divide County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dickinson Airport ASOS reported wind gusts up to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Manager reported wind gusts up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. Several wildfires developed due to the dry grasses, low relative humidity and high wind gusts. One wildfire in Beaver County burned into Kansas and consumed over 200,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Stevens Fire ignited around 11:45 a.m. on February 17, 2026, approximately seven miles northwest of Hooker, Oklahoma, in Texas County. The fire burned 12,894 acres and was caused by human activities. Smoke from this fire reduced visibility along US Highway 54, which resulted in a seven vehicle accident and additional fire start(which became the Side Road Fire). Mandatory evacuations occurred for the town of Tyrone on the 17th and were lifted by the morning of February 21st. US Highway 54 was closed between Tyrone and Hooker due to smoke and fire activity.  Five structures were burned: 4 barns and one house per OEMA. About 263 homes were threatened by this fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front associated with an upper-level system moved into the local area from the northwest on March 7th. As the upper trough weakened, the front began to stall across the region. Ample moisture was already in place across south Louisiana and south Mississippi, as evidenced by the afternoon KLIX sounding, which showed record precipitable water values. In addition, sufficient instability aloft supported persistent and robust thunderstorm development along and ahead of the boundary. The combination of these factors resulted in flash flooding across portions of southwest Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sheriffs Office reports several county roads flooded in Wilkinson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After an active period of multiple systems moving through the area bringing periods of high winds to the southern panhandle, a stronger system arrived bringing high winds to majority of the Panhandle on the 13th into the 14th. This low center tracked northward through the eastern gulf, while deepening, along with a storm force front. The low center moved onshore along the NE Gulf Coast in vicinity of Yakutat overnight Tuesday the 13th. As the low jumped inland, winds spiked up through the inner channels, lasting longest for the Skagway area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Annette Island saw high winds during the afternoon of the 13th including a tree down in downtown Metlakatla between 2-215pm. The Annette Island Packing company measured wind gusts in excess of 58mph during this period, included a peak gust of 74mph at 127pm and sustained winds of 40mph from 3 to 4pm. The CWOP station at the weather service office measured a peak gust of 59mph at 143pm and the AWOS station in town measured a peak gust of 55mph at 118pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system over the Mid Mississippi Valley lifted into the Great Lakes on the 20th, driving a warm front north towards New England. By the evening of the 20th an occlusion developed along the front in the vicinity of Chesapeake Bay and secondary low pressure began to deepen. Snow moved into the region and got heavier during the evening and overnight as the secondary low pressure became dominant and moved to a position east of Cape Cod. The upper trough trailing the system prolonged light snowfall into the early morning hours of the 21st before coming to an end. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents, dangerous travel.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began during the mid afternoon on the 20th and quickly became moderate to heavy at times. Snow tapered off in the late evening and light snow continued into the early morning hours of the 21st before ending. Snowfall totals ranged from 4 to 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm moving over Ortonville on the evening of June 4 produced large hail and strong winds. The Automated Weather Observing System at Ortonville municipal airport recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph, while a resident adjacent to the airport property observed hail to the size of golf-balls. The storm produced additional quarter-sized hail as it continued eastward.

Discrete thunderstorms in southeast Oklahoma congealed into a mesoscale convective complex as they moved southeast into northern Louisiana early morning of May 9th. The system consisted of clusters and linear segments moving rapidly eastward, while localized cell mergers and brief training occurred within the broader complex. The storms produced widespread damaging winds from the northshore of Lake Pontchartrain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS station KNEW New Orleans Lakefront Airport measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 55 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a six-month respite (since early-September 2025) with no worse than Moderate Drought (D1) assigned to any portion of this 24-county South Central Nebraska area by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM), unfortunately March 2026 brought a steadily worsening drought situation back into the spotlight as much of the area not only spiraled into Severe Drought (D2), but also Extreme Drought (D3). This marked the first D3 within the area in 10 months (since May 2025) and marked the highest areal coverage of D3 in at least 2.5 years (since Sept. 2023). These rapid degradations not only stemmed from an incredibly dry March, but also from the inevitable consequence of cumulative dryness that had been building for six months...as October 2025-March 2026 ranked among the Top-4 driest October-March periods on record across most of the area (see below for more detailed precipitation info).  Breaking down the significant changes in county-level USDM drought categories during March, the month opened with the vast majority of the 24-county domain assigned either D1 (mainly counties along/north of Interstate 80) or Abnormally Dry/D0 (most places south of I-80). Only a small sliver of the area (around 2 percent of it) was void of all drought categories whatsoever...mainly southeast Thayer County. As March unfolded, degradation came swiftly, with portions of several counties designated D2 on the very first USDM issuance of the month, and a steadily expanding introduction of D3 arriving just a few weeks later. As a result, the end-of-March categorical breakdown stood as follows (in order of drought severity): 1) roughly 52% of South Central Nebraska featured D3 (most prevalent within counties along/north of I-80)...2) approximately 32% of real estate contained D1...3) around 15% of the area was in D1 (almost entirely within southern-most counties along the Kansas border)...4) the remaining sliver of the area (far southern Thayer/Nuckolls counties) was allotted D0. ||Turning to the dire precipitation details, and starting with the longer-term dryness (including a pronounced lack of snow) that defined Oct. 2025-March 2026, this six-month stretch registered among the Top-4 driest on record across South Central Nebraska. More specifically, based on a mix of observations from over 100 NWS and NeRAIN/CoCoRaHS observers along with some radar estimation, the majority of the 30-county area (roughly 80% of it) measured merely between 1.65-4.45...only 25-67% of normal. The highest concentration of amounts 2-or-less focused within primarily far northern and western counties, particularly: Dawson, Gosper, Furnas, Valley, Greeley, Buffalo. Citing six-month totals from just a few longtime NWS Cooperative Observer sites, the Canaday Power Plant (near Lexington) incredibly registered just 0.87 (17% of normal...driest on record), Arcadia 2W reported only 1.29 (21% of normal...driest on record) and Elwood 8S tallied just 1.36 (25% of normal...driest on record). At the Tri Cities airports, October-March ranked between the 2nd-4th driest on record, with totals ranging from 1.69 (Kearney) to 2.68 (Hastings). The only part of the area where precipitation amounts were even remotely close to normal (but still below it)...with at least 5...focused within portions of Thayer and Nuckolls counties. Drilling down to March itself, while October-February were dry enough, March truly brought things to a whole other level. In fact, the majority of South Central Nebraska measured somewhere between a paltry trace and 0.27 (essentially zero to 20% of normal). In fact, around 96% of the 24-county area observed LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH NORMAL March precipitation. Among the very driest of the dry, the following NWS stations were just a few of several that received a paltry trace for the month: Cambridge, Elwood 8S, Beaver City and Orleans 2W. In the Tri Cities, the airports registered just 0.12-0.14. Even the wettest parts of the domain were still significantly below normal, including totals of 0.63 at Hebron, 0.36 in St. Paul, and 0.35 at Belgrade. Needless to say, the significant dryness that spanned the end of 2025 into the start of 2026 set the stage for not only a rough start to the 2026 agricultural growing season in South Central Nebraska (meager soil moisture profiles) but also sparked an above-average early-spring wildfire threat. In addition to several smaller fires across the 24-county area, portions of southwestern Dawson County were ravaged by the massive Cottonwood Fire that ignited on March 12th in far southeastern Lincoln County.

A remnant Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) interacted with a sheared and unstable environment to produce numerous supercells in southeast Illinois on June 21st.  13 tornadoes were documented, the strongest being two EF-2 tornadoes near Newton.  Storms training over the same areas led to widespread heavy rainfall and several occurrences of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limbs were blown down onto a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong cold air advection in wake of a passing cold front led to gusty wind conditions capable of producing damage across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree down and blocking one lane near the intersection of Augusta Highway and Powder Horn Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed within the vicinity of a strong mid-upper level shortwave trough and a surface low. One supercell tracked from southeast Minnesota through northeast Iowa and into southwest Wisconsin while maintaining is strength during the late afternoon. The storm evolved into a line as it trtacked through south central Wisconsin during the early evening and produced a swath of damaging winds and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado appears to have started southwest of Ridgeway, hitting the Town of Ridgeway salt shed near Highway 18/151.  It then tracked to the southeast and destroyed a metal shed along County Road H.  Otherwise, sporadic tree damage was noted along the end of the path with rear flank downdraft winds occurring to the south-southeast of the path.  Some tree damage was noted east of the end of the path but appeared to fan out and not be a path near County Rd K and Mounds View Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.

A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. Training along the boundary mostly resulted in a flash flooding threat, though moisture pooling ahead of the front supported MLCAPE values reaching 1000 J/kg, and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported some storm organization for a damaging wind and embedded tornado threat with locally backed surface wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down across roadway on Hamer Road near Navajo Valley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of a southeastward-moving upper system (and associated surface front) fostered scattered severe thunderstorms during the evening of the 9th, focused across portions of western Oklahoma. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard amid steep lapse rates and strong wind shear, sufficient for supercells. Focused areas of wind damage occurred near Sayre and northeast of Lawton as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down near the intersection of Oklahoma Highway 65 and Townley Road. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

A disturbance moved through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on River Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multicell thunderstorms over eastern Indiana moved into northwest Ohio resulting in sporadic reports of damaging wind gusts and sub-severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Manager reports a tree downed on State Route 613.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front blasted southeast across the region, with high winds ranging from 55 mph to 76 mph in wake of the front during the nighttime hours through the day on the 15th. The highest wind gust was measured near Winona. The high winds caused blowing dust and dust storm conditions in various places across Northwest Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusts up to 70 mph were measured two miles east-southeast of Quinter, with additional gusts of 58 to 62 mph reported across the county. The high winds contributed to a two person injury accident east-bound on Interstate 70 just south of Grinnell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of May, D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Issaquena County to Forrest County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Franklin County decreased from D1 (Moderate Drought) to D0 (Abnormally Dry) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The first round of storms arrived during the early morning hours of the 27th, associated with a warm front lifting northeastward across the region. Being elevated storms, large hail was the primary impact. Additional isolated to scattered storms developed during the midday hours, also tracking northeastward with large hail. ||In Southern Illinois, early morning MLCAPE values were around 750-1000J/kg, DCAPE was 700-900J/kg, effective bulk shear was a very robust 50-60kts, and mid-level lapse rates were around 6.5C/km.||Southern Illinois received primarily hail with early to mid morning thunderstorms, with the largest reports to golf ball size in Vergennes and Dowell. The one wind damage report involved portions of trees falling at a home in Anna, damaging a porch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated up to ping pong size fell near Goreville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Berkeley County Emergency Management reported a tree down along Red Bank Road near Henry E Brown Boulevard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ongoing severe drought (D2) persisted across portions of southeast West Virginia, including: Boone, southern Braxton, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Lincoln, Logan, McDowell, Mingo, Nicholas, Raleigh, southern Roane, southern Wayne, and Wyoming counties.  Moderate drought (D1) also remained present just north and west of the D2 area. ||Significant improvements occurred during the second half of the month as multiple rounds of rain and storms produced four to eleven inches of rain that resulted in weekly category improvements. By the second week of the month, D2 was confined to Mingo, McDowell, and portions of Kanawha, Clay, Nicholas, Fayette, Raleigh, Wyoming, and Logan counties. Minimal improvements to D1 also occurred. In the third and fourth weeks of the month, both D2 and D1 eroded from all but McDowell, and parts of Wyoming and Raleigh counties.

High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down onto a house and a car on Harding Avenue in Lincolnwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate. The report was relayed by emergency management.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 26th an approaching cold front associated with an upper level shortwave trough brought strong shear and modest mid level instability to New Hampshire.  Daytime heating was near seasonable norms, but still enough to create amble low level instability as highs reached the lower 80s.  A few long track storms created a swath of hail and wind damage from Sullivan to Rockingham Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed a tree down on Southington Rd. in Kensington. One lane closed during time of report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm and moist airmass was in place across southeast Louisiana on April 2nd, with scattered to numerous thunderstorms developing during the afternoon and evening hours. Storms became oriented north to south and repeatedly redeveloped while slowly shifting east across Tangipahoa Parish. This allowed heavy rainfall to fall over some of the same areas for an extended period. A stronger storm also produced localized wind damage near Tickfaw.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed an oak tree onto a powerline along North Oller Road near Tickfaw.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mountrail County Emergency Manager reported 3 campers turned over by strong thunderstorm wind gusts in White Earth Bay. Numerous properties in the same area with  south facing hail damage to siding and windows. Damage is consistent with wind speeds of approximately 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Approximately 86% of Arkansas was locked in Severe Drought (D2) or worse. Crucially, Northeast Arkansas remained the epicenter of Exceptional Drought (D4) and Extreme Drought (D3) conditions. Because the topsoil lacked the basic moisture required for seed germination, row-crop farmers across the Northeast Arkansas Delta had to run irrigation pivots continuously through the first three weeks of May just to get cotton, corn, and soybeans to sprout. Relief finally arrived during the last week of May, with widespread storms dropping several inches of rain across the region. Despite the rain, it took a bit of extra time to make up for the extreme rainfall deficits and drought continued into June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought persisted through the whole month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The most intense and deadly tornado of the cyclic tornadic|supercell touched down in northwest Branch county, northwest of|Union Lake between Blossom Rd and Mendon Rd. This tornado was|well photographed from multiple angles, and it quickly turned|into a multi-vortex wedge. After destroying a pole barn and|damaging a residence, the tornado deposited a 500 gallon propane|tank in a field. Drone footage also showed ground scouring in the|same field. The tornado continued northeast and caused the most|widespread and intense damage along Prairie Rose Ln. Every|residence along this stretch was either heavily damaged or|completely destroyed. Tragically, three individuals lost their|lives here when their manufactured homes were lofted and tossed.|One of these trailers was well anchored and tossed approximately|100 yards, badly twisting the frame. Numerous vehicles were also|tossed in this area. The maximum peak intensity of 160 mph was|estimated to be at the corner of Tuttle Rd and Prairie Rose Ln.|This 2 story block home was completely destroyed. Construction|quality and older building codes of all homes in this area|contributed to their failure and precluded the survey team from|being able to rate higher than an EF-3. The tornado continued off|to the northeast into Union City producing EF-1 to EF2 damage|along the way before dissipating at the Branch/Calhoun county|line. Special thanks to the various subject matter experts on the|Quick Response Team that helped NWS Northern Indiana determine|this tornado's intensity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions at the start of the month ended on the March 10th issuance as a result of heavy rain in the early portions of the month. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 6 to 7 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following an Arctic cold front passage on the afternoon of January 22, a bitterly cold air mass settled into southern Wisconsin and much of the Upper Midwest. The conditions prompted Extreme Cold Warnings across all of southern Wisconsin, with most school districts canceling classes on January 23. The school cancellations extended all the way up to the university level, with both the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Marquette University among major colleges electing to close on January 23. Extreme cold conditions continued over portions of central and east-central Wisconsin into the morning of January 24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: January 2026 was generally a mild and wet month for most of northern and central New Mexico. There were two active periods during the month, with the first being from January 7th to 9th and the other from January 23rd to 25th. This resulted in well above average precipitation across southern and central areas and near to slightly above average precipitation across east central and northern areas. Temperatures for the month were well above average across western and central areas and well below normal across the southeast plains. The well below normal temperatures across the southeast plains were due to a potent arctic like airmass impacting eastern NM during the 2nd aforementioned active period with the cold temperatures continuing through the end of the month due to extended periods of low clouds and freezing fog over the lingering snowpack. The wetter than average conditions for the month resulted in the removal of extreme drought across the San Francisco River Valley and removal of severe drought across almost all of southern Chaves County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought remained persistent over the far northwestern portion of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions as covering approximately 50% of Colorado Zone 003 - Roan and Tavaputs Plateaus, with the remainder of the zone under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. Conditions remained unchanged for most of the month. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, the coverage of Exceptional (D4) Drought was reduced to just 2% of the zone, with the remaining 98% of the zone under Extreme (D3) Drought. While there have been no direct effects from the drought noted as yet, there is increasing unease among those who live and work in this zone. There are concerns over water availability through the summer for ranching and farming, as well as drinking water quality and sourcing. There is also increasing concern over what the current drought means for the summer wildfire season.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto Shaffer Mountain Road near Central City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck southern Vermont on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast.||The forecast for this system was a very complicated one. Model guidance in the days leading up to the event was highly variable in their depictions of the track and strength of the system. Ultimately, the track of the storm remained farther south and east than what was anticipated, leading to a fairly steep south to north gradient in snowfall totals. This also led to much lower snowfall totals across southern Vermont than what were initially anticipated. The highest snowfall totals were recorded across the highest elevations of the southern Green Mountains where about 7-9 inches were recorded. Across lower elevations, only 0.5 to isolated amounts of 6 inches were reported. And while blizzard conditions were not a threat across this region, gusty winds did reduce visibility at times, making travel particularly difficult when combined with snow covered roadways. ||Key Impacts: road closures, traffic accidents, school closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 4.8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
