EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed in the city of Murray.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported 2 inch diameter hail about 7 miles north of Oak Center.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Jefferson County received 5 to 8 inches of snow and sleet, in addition to around 0.10 inches of ice accumulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak short wave trough tracked across the higher terrain along the New Mexico/Colorado border during the evening of the 26th. Large scale ascent from this short wave along with low level convergence in a surface pressure trough in eastern New Mexico initiated thunderstorms during the evening hours across eastern New Mexico. This initial thunderstorm activity generated a strong outflow boundary which then moved into the South Plains of West Texas. A very dry lower atmosphere allowed these storms to produce widespread severe wind gusts as they tracked eastward across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle through the early morning hours of the 27th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Automated Weather Observing System at Hale County Municipal Airport measured a severe wind gust of 59 mph at 2230 CST. From 2232 CST through 2240 CST, a Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Plainview measured severe wind gusts with a peak gust of 70 mph at 2232 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms rolled across the Denver Metro area mid afternoon on June 8th producing up to golf ball sized hail. Isolate severe wind gusts were recorded as well. As the storms progressed east of the Denver their intensity increase. A supercell thunderstorm continued to track eastward, stay south of I-70. Farther north, thunderstorms organized into a broken line, producing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph across far northeast Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved through the region in early February, spawning deepening surface low pressure offshore. A very steep pressure gradient resulted in strong winds across northeast North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherstem sensor at Jarvisburg Elementary School experienced strong winds as low pressure deepened offshore. Sustained winds were above 40 mph from 2:30-3:30 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread storms developed across central Virginia in the afternoon of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. Upscale growth into a few storm clusters produced swaths of damaging winds across central Virginia, eventually progressing eastward toward eastern Virginia in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 call center reported a power line down on Riddick Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front moved across Minnesota during the early morning of April 17th which ultimately produced two rounds of thunderstorms.  The first line of storms was associated with a warm front which produced quarter size hail across south-central Minnesota mid-morning. The secondary and stronger line of storms tied to the cold front itself moved through in the early afternoon across eastern MN. This line produced a swath of large hail measuring from quarter size up to ping pong ball size hail in Cannon Falls (Goodhue County) which ended up being the largest measured hailstone from this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo measurement provided via Facebook.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.

A strong cold front dove through the area from north to south ushering in strong cold advection in its wake. A narrow, strong line of convective snow developed along the boundary sinking across the entire county warning area. There were numerous reports of visibility of a quarter mile or less, wind gusts greater than 30 mph, and rapid accumulation on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: PennDOT sensor I-70 Eastbound at Mile Marker 48 measured less than a quarter mile visibility in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved through South-Central Texas. Some of these storms produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced nickel size hail in Doss.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved into Eastern Pennsylvania, producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm and moist airmass was in place across southeast Louisiana on April 2nd, with scattered to numerous thunderstorms developing during the afternoon and evening hours. Storms became oriented north to south and repeatedly redeveloped while slowly shifting east across Tangipahoa Parish. This allowed heavy rainfall to fall over some of the same areas for an extended period. A stronger storm also produced localized wind damage near Tickfaw.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video showed water surrounding a home and beginning to enter the garage in Tickfaw.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 5 degrees or less across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 6F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oswalt Road Fire burned 346 acres across northwestern Love County, north of Rubottom. The end/control time is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The winter of 2025-2026 has been, overall, a dry and warm one. And as such, drought has clung on across eastern Utah and western Colorado, especially across the Central Divide Mountains. Areas in the eastern Uinta mountains have also seen drought linger.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of January, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering 25% of Utah Zone 023 - Eastern Uinta Mountains. Severe (D2) Drought covered 70% of the zone, and Moderate (D1) Drought covered the remaining 5%. With the 1/7 Drought Monitor update, the area of Extreme (D3) Drought was removed, with 30% of the zone now under Severe (D2) Drought conditions, and the remaining 70% under Moderate (D1) Drought. No reports of impacts or damages have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ongoing severe drought (D2) persisted across portions of southeast West Virginia, including: Boone, southern Braxton, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Lincoln, Logan, McDowell, Mingo, Nicholas, Raleigh, southern Roane, southern Wayne, and Wyoming counties.  Moderate drought (D1) also remained present just north and west of the D2 area. ||Significant improvements occurred during the second half of the month as multiple rounds of rain and storms produced four to eleven inches of rain that resulted in weekly category improvements. By the second week of the month, D2 was confined to Mingo, McDowell, and portions of Kanawha, Clay, Nicholas, Fayette, Raleigh, Wyoming, and Logan counties. Minimal improvements to D1 also occurred. In the third and fourth weeks of the month, both D2 and D1 eroded from all but McDowell, and parts of Wyoming and Raleigh counties.

Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Exceptional Drought (D4) to Extreme (D3) on June 23rd and then to Severe (D2) on June 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fisherwoman was swept to sea by a sneaker wave on the morning of June 16 near Pacifica south of the local pier, which was closed due to damage. The fisherwoman estimated that the wave dragged her around 30 feet into sea, and after several minutes, she resurfaced , and fellow anglers helped to rescue her. First responders arrived within minutes and transported her to the hospital, where she was treated for hypothermia before being released. At 8 AM local time on the day of the incident, the San Francisco buoy (46026) reported waves of 3.5 feet high, with a south-southwest swell of 3.5 feet at 14.8 seconds and westerly wind waves of 0.5 feet at 3.5 seconds. A Beach Hazards Statement was in place for long period swell resulting in an increased risk of sneaker waves.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A fisherwoman was swept to sea by a sneaker wave on the morning of June 16 near Pacifica south of the local pier, which was closed due to damage. The fisherwoman estimated that the wave dragged her around 30 feet into sea, and after several minutes, she resurfaced , and fellow anglers helped to rescue her. First responders arrived within minutes and transported her to the hospital, where she was treated for hypothermia before being released. At 8 AM local time on the day of the incident, the San Francisco buoy (46026) reported waves of 3.5 feet high, with a south-southwest swell of 3.5 feet at 14.8 seconds and westerly wind waves of 0.5 feet at 3.5 seconds. A Beach Hazards Statement was in place for long period swell resulting in an increased risk of sneaker waves.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limb downed near intersection of Ferndale Street and Rhawn Street. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several calls for trees blown down around Glen Echo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported along Harris Rd and Hogan Rd following 4 to 5 inches of rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad low pressure system over the Northern Plains combined with an upper level trough pushing through the region to produce heavy snow over northwest and north central North Dakota. The greatest snow amounts reported were around nine inches, which occurred in Divide, Bottineau, and Pierce Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rolla received seven inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One side of Laurel Creek Road was impassable due to a downed tree near Lenore. In Belo, a tree blew down onto power lines along Dog Fork Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over the region, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D2 to include all of the Coastal Mississippi counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of Harrison County according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Town of Blythewood shared photos of damaged amphitheater cover, with metal sheeting blown off. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of southern Illinois. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Roads were particularly bad near Glendale in Pope County, IL. Ice on rural roadways in Saline County, IL caused one vehicle to overturn with a person trapped. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell over much of northwest Illinois during the early morning of March 16th, where a swath of 6 to 9 inches of snow fell.  Storm total snowfall amounts included 8.7 inches four miles north northwest of Rockford; 8.2 inches five miles west northwest of Rochelle; 7.7 inches near Timberlane; 7.5 inches four miles north northeast of Harvard; 7.2 inches in Capron and 6.0 inches in Marengo.  Rockford Airport reported 5.7 inches of snow. Snowfall amounts across the rest of northern Illinois including much of the Chicago metro area were generally in the 1 to 3 inch range.||Strong winds caused significant blowing and drifting snow across much of northern Illinois through the evening of March 16th as scattered snow showers moved across northern Illinois. While blizzard criteria were not met, near blizzard conditions were reported at times in open and rural areas.

As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarters in size were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northwest Pennsylvania. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northwest Pennsylvania, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters, particularly near the OH/PA border across Northwest Pennsylvania where a few tornadoes also occurred. At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado began over a farm field where a few small limbs were downed.  The tornado continued to the northeast, snapping a few trees and downing several large limbs. Further to the northeast, the view was not accessible with the tornado ending southwest of Big Muskego Lake, south of the Big Muskego Lake Wildlife area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts moving through western and central North Dakota combined with a series of short-wave troughs resulted in an extended period of strong winds. The strongest reported wind gust was 74 mph at the Bowman Airport in Bowman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gladstone NDDOT site reported wind gusts to 69 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front moved across the area during the evening hours of January 15th. Strong winds continued overnight and into the following day. Numerous power outages, damages, and road closures were reported with the abnormally strong northwest winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 62 MPH was observed at a sensor 6 ESE Bridgeport at 10:15 AM MST on 1/16. Power outages were reported in the city of Bridgeport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The beginning of February featured very cold temperatures and wind chills that began during late January across southwest Virginia. Temperatures as low as minus 8 degrees were recorded by a local cooperative observer in Clintwood during the first few days of the month, with similar temperatures observed in Buchanan County. The cold across this portion of the Appalachians was short-lived for the month, as temperatures quickly rebounded above freezing on February 3rd and once again by the middle of the month, where afternoon highs ranged in the 50s and 60s.

Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.

A frontal boundary interacting with southerly flow produced a period of heavy rainfall across Puerto Rico from February 2 through February 4, 2026. Abundant moisture and an advective pattern supported widespread showers and periods of moderate to heavy rainfall across the region.||Significant rainfall amounts fell across portions of PR. These conditions resulted in urban and small-stream flooding, localized flash flooding, and minor landslides, particularly across the interior, southern, and western parts of Puerto Rico. Elevated streamflows were observed, with some rivers reaching action stage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A portion of Santiago Palmer Sur Street in Guayama was closed after heavy rainfall caused the collapse of a brick wall in the area. Based on radar estimates, between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in the area during the day. For safety reasons, the damaged structure was removed, and work was carried out in the zone. Authorities urged the public to avoid the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds caused trees to fall in the Dundee area. There was also a vehicle fire according to the county dispatch feed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported 1 inch hail in Tin Top.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees fell down on Fredericks Hall Road near the border with Hanover County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail north of Maple Bluff.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May started with severe drought (D2) present across much of eastern WV, including: Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and most of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Moderate drought (D1) also persisted across most of western and north-central WV, with the exception of Pleasants, Wood, northwest Jackson, northern Mason, western Ritchie, western Tyler, and western Wirt counties where conditions were merely abnormally dry (D0). Only minimal changes to D0 and D1 occurred in the second week of the month. D2, however, spread out across all of Boone and Kanawha counties; most of Lincoln, Logan, and Putnam counties; and portions of eastern Cabell, southern Jackson, southern Roane, and eastern Wayne counties. Conditions worsened even more the following week, as D2 engulfed most of southern, central, and eastern West Virginia, and a sliver of extreme drought (D3) crept into eastern McDowell, southeast Raleigh, and eastern Wyoming counties. Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth. Fortunately, enough precipitation fell at the end of the month to eradicate D3 and confine D2 to mainly Boone, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Nicholas, Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Raleigh, Webster, Wyoming, southern Braxton, eastern Lincoln, southern Roane, and southern Wayne. D1 improved to D0 in southern Tyler, Doddridge, northern Harrison, northern Taylor, part of northern Barbour, Ritchie, Wirt, northwest Gilmer, northern Calhoun, northern Roane, northern Jackson, northwest Mason, northwest Cabell, and part of northern Wayne. Meanwhile, drought was completely eliminated from counties, or at least portions of counties, bordering the Ohio River.||Generally less than an inch of rain fell during the first week of May. Around an inch or less accumulated during the second week. During the third week of the month, much of the area received around an inch and a half or less of rain, though a strip of up to two inches fell along the Ohio River. More substantial precipitation occurred at the end of the month, when one to three inches of rain fell to the south of I-64 and one and a half to over four inches fell to the north of I-64. Highest amounts were observed across portions of Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Taylor, Randolph, and Upshur counties. Multiple rounds of rain during this time finally allowed for significant improvement to drought conditions, particularly across the northern and western part of the state.||The six climate sites in West Virginia were evenly split between above and below normal total precipitation for the month, with Beckley, Charleston, and Elkins on the below normal side and Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg on the above normal side. On the 22nd, Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg each received enough rain to break their existing daily precipitation records. Beckley was also able to tie a standing daily precipitation record on the 24th of the month.

A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SCDPS report of tree on road near between I-95 and Dingle Pond Rd. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to nickel-size in Iberia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough stationed over western Pennsylvania during the early morning hours with ample moisture and lift allowed for snowfall to begin across much of western Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of January 24th and the early morning hours of January 25, 2026. Moderate-to-heavy snowfall rates were observed at onset with low-level frontogenesis allowing for a moderate snowfall band across portions of western Pennsylvania prior to sunrise. Ample moisture in place with an approaching area of low pressure from the Lower Ohio River Valley also allowed for snowfall to begin across portions of southeastern Pennsylvania ahead of sunrise on January 25th. The progressive movement of the aforementioned trough and low pressure system allowed for a shorter duration of snowfall than could have occurred, with snowfall gradually tapering off across much of the area by the evening hours of January 26th. Westerly flow in the wake of the system did allow for continued upslope snow showers across the western highlands, which continued to allow for additional accumulations. Much of central Pennsylvania observed heavy snowfall, with Harrisburg International Airport and Williamsport Regional Airport breaking daily snowfall records, which have been tracked since 1888 and 1895, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow began in the evening of January 24 and continued into the evening of January 25, with most of Huntingdon County seeing 8-10 inches of snow. The highest snowfall total in the county occurred near Wood, where 11 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree blew down along Waveland Farm Road near Governor Ritchie Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow but heavy band of snow developed near the Wisconsin-Illinois border during the evening hours. Enhanced hourly snowfall rates within the snow band led to snow accumulations of 2 to 4 inches, with locally higher totals. Overlapping with the evening commute, the snowfall led to slippery road conditions. Winds became gusty after the snow ended, leading to blowing snow and reduced visibilities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between 1 to 3 inches of snow observed countywide, with locally higher totals. Greatest accumulation of 3.1 inches observed in Burlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across the South Carolina  Piedmont and foothills continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.

A winter storm brought sleet/snow to much of west central Texas. Some freezing rain resulted in a light glaze of ice across the Northwest Hill Country. The snow/sleet amounts ranged from 1 to 4 inches across the northern 2/3 of the area. The winter storm caused disruptions to travel and one fatality due to an accident on Interstate 10 east of Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 1 to 2 inches of snow/sleet across Runnels County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail sizes increased from quarter to half dollar at this location during the event time. The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Harris County experienced a significant degradation into D3 (Extreme Drought) during January. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on September 23, 2025, the county sustained 19 consecutive weeks of D2 or greater intensity. This streak includes the intensification to D3, which was officially recorded on January 20. The drought persisted into February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum windchill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across Maryland. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 12 to 16 across Garrett County, with a general 8 to 12 across the remainder of the area aside from southern Maryland where 4-8 was observed. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed across southern Maryland. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state.

During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado with path length of 10.53 miles and maximum width 75 yards traveled across mostly rural areas of northern Warren County. The peak winds were 85 mph with the tornado causing mainly sporadic tree damage with corn fields showing clear convergence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

Despite the seasonal transition, New Hampshire remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 41% of New Hampshire were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. New Hampshire exhibited highly variable precipitation patterns in March 2026. While the state continued to observe below-normal accumulations and persistent hydrologic strain, central sections along the Merrimack valley and White Mountains experienced modest precipitation surpluses. The onset of seasonal thaw provided minor, superficial relief to shallow soil layers, but slow-responding deep groundwater tables remained severely depleted, with many monitoring locations lingering near or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Carroll County averaged 3.39 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.58 inches below normal, extending the deficits since June up to 11 inches. The USDM on March 31st had 98% of the county in Severe Drought (D2). It was the driest June through March stretch on record.

The combination of greater instability, strong wind shear, and abundant moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon and evening. Daytime clearing likely increased instability, while both cooler incoming air and strong winds aloft supported organized storms capable of producing large hail, and damaging winds.

A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mixed precipitation occurred throughout the 25th. A member of the public reported 2.0 inches of snow and sleet by 0730EST. An estimated 0.25 inches of flat icing was noted in social media from the Broadhead area at 1011EST. Multiple photos showed pine trees drooping heavily under the ice load.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snowfall around 20-30 inches across the county, with a few inches of sleet, and a couple tenths of freezing rain reported, especially across the eastern/southeastern half of the county...upwards of three-tenths of an inch or more of ice accretion reported near the town of Presque Isle. Some county offices and the courthouse were closed through the 17th due to the storm and resultant clean up.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured at 1.50 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.

While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Worsening drought conditions continued into early May across Central Alabama. Following a severe weather event on May 6-7 in which 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across southern counties of Central Alabama, conditions began to slowly improve. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 19th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the Ohio River, with storms moving from southwest to northeast across northern Kentucky and southern Indiana. While effective bulk shear was relatively unsupportive of organized convection around 20 knots, a few stronger cores were able to develop thanks to 2000-2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. These stronger cells were able to produce a few instances of wind damage vai downed trees as well as near-severe level hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged hot and dry period was set up for the Panhandles in mid May.  And with the lack of significant rainfall to help transition the grasses from cured to green, the fuels were well above the 90th percentile in dryness.  While it's not uncommon for a high based storm or two to occur west of the dryline and create dry thunderstorms, on May 14th it was certainly more scattered to nearly widespread storms that occurred.  Several lightning ignitions occurred, and given that the storms had severe dry microbursts associated, the fires that ignited would spread quickly.  Thereafter the Panhandles would go through several consecutive days of critical to extremely critical conditions.  And the issues of any new starts, as well as active fires that ignited on May 14th would take another run were of high concern.  Overall 20 wildfires ranging from over 34,000 acres to some as small as a few acres would ignite in the TX/OK Panhandle between the 14th and the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Rita Blanca Unit 32 Incident was ignited the evening of May 15th and would go on to quickly burn 8,907 acres, before being controlled overnight that night.
