EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching low pressure over northwest Ontario draped a stationary front over Lake Superior on the 24th and a tightening pressure gradient forced wind gusts in excess of storm force.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The C-MAN Station STDM4 Stannard Rock Lighthouse reported wind gusts of over 55 mph from 8:50 AM to 11:40 AM on the 24th, including a peak wind gust of 62 mph at 11 AM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe thunderstorms produced flooding and marginally severe hail in the early morning of April 15th across far northern Illinois.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of northern Illinois during the evening of April 15th producing localized wind damage, hail and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree down northeast of Byron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced isolated flash flooding and damaging in Jones County Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Swift water was flowing across Maybelle Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure stationed across southern Ontario gradually shifted eastward throughout the afternoon hours of May 13, 2026. Some showers and thunderstorms forming ahead of a surface cold frontal passage and along the cold front was stationed in an environment of sufficient deep-layer shear along with steepening low- and mid-level lapse rates that brought a marginal wind threat during that afternoon and evening hours. This severe wind threat allowed for scattered instances of tree damage across central Pennsylvania with the most damage across the Lower Susquehanna Valley where slightly better shear and moisture was available during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 45 mph, knocked down wires south of Oregon Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into northeast PA, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50-60 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked a tree down on Main Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the parish fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of substantial rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of June with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across coastal Miami-Dade County in the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms after 10 AM in southwest Tennessee with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of southwest Tennessee, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed into powerlines at Wilcox Ave and Walters St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed multiple trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper low moved through the region bringing widespread light snow to the U.P. Moderate to heavy lake effect snow developed over the northern and western U.P. as an arctic air mass moved into the Great Lakes, disrupting travel and resulting in school closures. In addition to snowfall, winds and arctic air brought very cold windchills in the -20s across the U.P.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy lake effect snow brought periods of visibility as low as 1/4 mile (IWD ASOS) and snow accumulations around 7 in the Ironwood area. The highest reported snowfall was 7.1 at the Ironwood No. 2 COOP (IWOM4). Key Impacts: Transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level storm system took up residence in the northern Gulf of Alaska during the second weekend of April. Abundant moisture was drawn up by the circulation of this system which managed to wrap around the storm center and push into the Interior of Alaska. This resulted in 24 to 36 hours of steady, and at times heavy, snowfall that affected travel along Interior highways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS spotter in Tok reported a storm total snowfall amount of 8.8 inches of snow. In addition reports from the Alaska DOT indicated difficult road conditions from Dot Lake to Delta Junction along the Alaska Highway due to deep snow and icy conditions along the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the southern North Carolina Piedmont during the early morning of the 25th. The precipitation began as mostly sleet before mixing with, and eventually changing to freezing rain later in the morning. The precipitation finally tapered off during the evening. Total sleet accumulations of around an inch occurred, with 0.10 to 0.25 inch of ice accreting on top of the sleet. This made for very hazardous driving conditions. Due to unusually cold weather following the event, a couple of days of refreezing resulted in travel difficulties continuing during the overnight and morning hours.

Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reports 1.5 inch diameter hail in Madison.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down blocking both lanes of Johnson Road near its intersection with Siloam Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convection along a southwest to northeast oriented cold front caused isolated wind damage in central Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking Sims Cemetery Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex of thunderstorms developed across portions of north-central Kansas during the late afternoon hours of June 8th. These thunderstorms rapidly intensified and moved south and southeast across the I-70 corridor. Widespread wind damage occurred across portions of Lincoln, Ellsworth, Saline, McPherson, Marion, and Chase counties. In fact, a wind gust of 113 mph was measured at the Salina Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust from thunderstorm outflow at Great Bend Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple photos showed large broken tree limbs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 6 to 10.3 inches from both the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated in the central portion of the county. Measured wind gusts of 20 to 30 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around three-quarters of a mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two different barns had roof and structural damage along Harrison Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the early evening of 4/9, enough surface convergence from a front was able to take advantage of 2000 J/kg CAPE with sufficient moisture for modest convection. With the strongest of the storms, 1 inch hail was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 1 inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of thunderstorms formed downstream of a mid-level wave in an environment with around 500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 40 knots of effective shear. Despite the meager instability, thunderstorms were able to reach severe levels with areas of tree and power line damage reported in Northwestern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damage to numerous trees, a few uprooted.  Barn damaged with roof decking blown across the intersection of County Rd V and F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lexington County 911 dispatch reported a tree fell on a vehicle near Crown Point Rd and Cabin Creek Ct.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grayson County received a combination of heavy snow and sleet totaling 4 inches. Grayson County also reported ice accumulation ranging from 0.10 to 0.25 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped into the area after a prolonged period of humid conditions. A few bands/clusters of thunderstorms developed resulting in several damaging wind gusts and sporadic large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees blew down along Airlie Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Immediately following the strong winds, snow enveloped much of the state. Many areas saw 6 to 15 inches of snow across the lower elevations, much higher in the mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received 6 to 9 inches across multiple locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland, producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree blown down into wires. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media post indicated quarter sized hail in Preston Shores on the south side of Lake Texoma.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.

Supercell thunderstorms which developed along a dryline produced several instances of large hail and isolated damaging winds as they moved through western and northwestern portions of North Texas the evening of April 15.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio reported quarter sized hail 4 miles southwest of Graham.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weather observer estimated wind gusts of 70mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree branches snapped by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across parts of east central Illinois during the afternoon of April 13th, producing isolated hail and localized wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two utility poles were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An off duty Storm Prediction Center employee observed a tornado north of Highway 29 east of Wynnewood. No damage was reported and the specific location of the tornado is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 4 to 12 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, moderate to heavy at times, developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 8 and 12 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. There was a report of 12.0 inches of total snow accumulation in New Mt Pleasant. Roads were snow covered and slick with numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image of a caliper-measured hailstone was shared on social media. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines fell down at the intersection of Dodlyt Road and Northumberland Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms ahead of a cold front brought several measured gusts of 34 knots or greater along the coast.
D2-D3 conditions persisted throughout all of June across portions of the Florida Big Bend.
A front moving through brought a squall line through western Massachusetts and into central Massachusetts producing pockets of damaging winds which downed several trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Rutland, a tree was downed on wires near Turkey Hill Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fallen trees damaged power equipment, causing a power outage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A left-moving supercell moved into Fillmore County from northeast Iowa and brought hail up to ping pong ball sized to the county during the afternoon hours on April 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported ping pong ball sized hail near Harmony.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.75 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front swung through the area in the evening kicking off mostly sub severe storms, though a few did produce damaging winds in MA and CT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Wethersfield, a tree was down on house and car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed along a strong cold front which triggered snowfall, with accumulating snow mainly confined to eastern portions of Southern Connecticut. Advisory level snow occurred primarily across portions of New London County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cocorahs observers reported 3.0 inches at Killingworth and 3.0 inches at 2.9 NNE Old Saybrook.  Broadcast media reported 2.5 inches a 2 S Killingworth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure moved across the Upper Great Lakes on Jan 16-17 bringing moderate to heavy lake effect snow to the western U.P.  The heaviest snow fell across Gogebic County with 6-10 of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread moderate to heavy lake effect snow fell over much of Gogebic County on Jan 16-17 with snowfall up to 10.5 at 5 NNW Bessemer, MI-GG-11.  Key impacts: transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved across the area and brought heavy snow, especially to the  mountains. The heaviest snow fell in the Tetons, where there were many reports of over a foot of new snow with a maximum amount of 25 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort. Other notable amounts included 20 inches in the Salt and Wyoming Range, 15 inches in the Bighorn Range, 14 inches in the western Wind River Range and 12 inches on Casper Mountain. Lesser amounts fell in the lower elevations. However, in northern Johnson County, a combination of snow and wind gusting to 50 mph brought closures of Interstates 25 and 90 for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell through much of the Tetons. The highest reported snow was 25 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few large tree limbs were broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist southwest flow between low pressure passing well inland and high pressure offshore led to an environment supportive of strong thunderstorms across warm Atlantic waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow sensor at Fort Sumter Range Front Light measured a peak wind gust of 35 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -11 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -33 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale low with embedded thunderstorms tracked northeast across the Blue Mountain foothills, producing strong wind gusts across portions of Umatilla, OR and Walla Walla, WA counties the afternoon of the 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale low with embedded storms moving northeast across the Blue Mountain foothills produced strong wind gusts in the region, with a 61 mph gust measured by the mesonet station OD185 at 1713 PDT, and a 58 mph gust measured by the KPDT ASOS at 1706 PDT on the 1st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down onto Courthouse Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. The most significant damage came from a surging portion of the line with an embedded supercell that resulted in two tornadoes: 1. an EF-0 tornado which crossed from northeastern Hopkins County into McLean County, and 2. an EF-1 tornado which caused damage from southeast of Rumsey to north of Livermore in McLean County. A swath of straight-line winds accompanied the first tornadic circulation. The tornadoes damaged numerous trees, some electrical lines and power poles, and a few homes and outbuildings. Several other straight-line wind damage reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado, with estimated peak winds of 85mph, began along Ashbyburg Rd and tracked eastward. Trees were snapped and uprooted, and numerous large limbs were downed. Two electrical transmission line cross members were broken. The tornado crossed into McLean County near Jewel City. A swath of straight line winds accompanied the tornadic circulation across far eastern Webster County, far northern Hopkins County, and into southwestern McLean County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado crossed from Christian County into Macon County 0.6 miles north of State Route 48, damaging trees and structures in Blue Mound, including the roof of|Meridian Elementary School. It also destroyed 2 grain bins south|of the school. It tracked east-southeast, taking down electrical|transmission lines and numerous large tree branches to the southeast of Route 51 before crossing into far northern Shelby County near Long Grove Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered snow showers moved across northwest Indiana beginning in the early morning of March 16th and continuing through the early morning of March 17th.  Snowfall amounts were generally 1 to 3 inches.  Strong winds caused significant blowing and drifting snow with near white out conditions at times in open and rural areas.

System snow overspread southern Lower Michigan during the evening hours of January 18th which was followed by periods of lake effect snow on January 19th behind an arctic front. Storm total snowfall accumulations ranged from 2 to 6 inches across southwest Lower Michigan with the greatest amounts reported closer to Lake Michigan.  Strong winds coupled with the snow and blowing snow produced significant visibility reductions at times and hazardous travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light system snow during the late afternoon and evening of January 18th was followed by bands of lake effect snow. The combination of west wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and the snowfall resulted in significant visibility reductions at times due to snow and blowing snow. While storm total snow accumulations were only reported in the 1 to 2 inch range, the combination of snow and blowing snow produced hazardous travel conditions. The heaviest snowfall rates of the event occurred during the early morning of January 19th as a dominant band of snow tracked across the county. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported across the region. In addition, wind chills dropped to as cold as 15 below during the early morning hours of January 19th extending into early afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. A swath of 1 to 1.75 inch hailstones were observed from Putnam and Logan Counties over to Kanawha and Clay Counties. The severe risk subsided as the sun began to set for the evening and the cold front began its passage through the forecast area.
Thunderstorms produced damaging winds in northeastern Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few power lines were blown down with many power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This very brief EF0 tornado with estimated peak winds of 75-mph began just west of Granny Creek Road, southwest of Fredericktown. The tornado ripped off part of a barn's metal roof and scattered the debris southeastward before the tornado ended in vicinity of the road. Radar data suggest this tornado was associated with an anticyclonic mesovortex along the equatorward side of the descending rear-inflow jet of a bow echo and the bow echo was embedded in the flanking line of a cyclonic supercell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mesoscale convective system of thunderstorms dropped southward out of Ontario into Central NY, moving into an unusually unstable and sufficiently sheared environment. This supported severe thunderstorms with widespread damaging winds, an isolated EF1 tornado, and hail. Heavy rainfall also occurred as deep moisture surged northward from the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds brought down multiple trees and wires down with vehicles caught in between.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow accumulation of 1 to 4 inches, followed by 1/4 to 1/2 inch of ice across the southern and eastern part of Marshall County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covering FM Road 248 in Bivins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms affected the combined Panhandles each afternoon and evening in the early parts of June. With enough moisture, instability and sources to provide atmospheric lift, these storms were able to become severe each day and bring large hail to the region. A few instances of damaging winds and flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hailstones up to golf ball sized fell 5 miles north of Stinnett off of Highway 207. In addition, mostly pea to penny size hail fell at the intersection of Texas Highways 136 and 207, with some quarter size hail mixed in.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed along a trough axis during the evening hours on June 6, resulting in multiple reports of thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto a vehicle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures cooled across SE Alaska along with outflow winds during the first couple days of January after December's big snow dump. This allowed the next system that moved in from the west on the 4th and 5th to start out as snow. Prefrontal snow showers during the evening of the 4th added to the storm total snow for parts of the northern and central panhandle, then the main system moved in overnight with heavy snow on Monday the 5th (set to be the first day back at school after Winter Break for most locations). The southern panhandle saw a change over to rain during the day on the 5th, then the rain/snow line pushed northward through the night and into the morning of the 6th. Some strong winds accompanied the front, starting out of the north then shifting to the south with the front and causing temperatures to rise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light, dry, fluffy snow fell through the evening of the 4th with social media reports of around 5 inches between Lena Point and the Mendenhall Valley by 8-930pm. Periods of moderate to heavy snow fell through the night and east winds increased after midnight, gusting 20-30mph at the airport. By 730am around 7 inches of snow was reported out the road and other reports from around the area ranged from 4-7 inches. Snowfall rates increased through the morning of the 5th with visibility falling to a half mile at the airport and sustained winds of 20-30mph with gusts of around 40mph. This caused blowing and drifting snow, which hampered accumulation measurements at the airport. At 1130am, reports from Douglas Island were 9 inches and counting, then at noon a measurement from downtown Juneau had reached 11-12 inches. A large tree was reported across Glacier Highway out the road at 1250pm and brief power outages were also noted during the day. Temperatures steadily warmed through the event with continued wind and a transition to rain occurred in the evening between 6-10pm. Final snowfall reports from Douglas reached 12-15 inches in the evening. The NWS office in the Mendenhall Valley measured 7.1 inches out of this event and the Lena Point COOP measured 6.9 inches, both with some compaction due to the change to rain. ||Monday the 5th was set to be the first day back to school after winter break, but the district opted to close schools the evening of the 4th based on anticipated heavy snowfall rates during the middle of the day Monday, tall snow banks, and unsafe walking conditions. Similarly, after the significant snowfall in December and this additional snow, plus the expected transition to rain adding to the weight, closures to borough facilities and other businesses were made for the 5th and 6th while inspections could be made along with roof clearing. An avalanche advisory was issued by CBJ on the 5th due to elevated risk for the downtown and Thane areas. Numerous small avalanches were noted over the subsequent days, but did not reach any structures. Damage to roofs, outbuildings, and a vehicle were reported via social media on the 6th and two additional boats sunk in Juneau harbors. Total value of property damage from just this January storm is unknown. The State approved a joint disaster declaration for the City and Borough of Juneau and the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska on January 6th for the culmination of December and January snows, plus the added snow weight with rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant storm damage caused by powerful thunderstorm wind gusts across nearly a mile in a neighborhood west of Williston. Emergency manager reported debris in a  southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. One roof blown 100 yards away. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage also noted. Damage is consistent with winds around 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado touched down just east of Old Lucile Road south of Blakely, initially causing damage to oak and pine trees. The tornado flipped a storage shed and damaged a well-constructed farm equipment shelter along Lucile Road. The roof of a business housing several large trucks was severely damaged  along Lucile Road as well. The overhead doors in the structure failed, allowing the roof and wall structure to be lifted and flipped over the rest of the building. The highest winds, approximately 95 mph were estimated to have occurred at this location. The tornado continued east-southeast, with a scattered path of damage to trees. The porch of a manufactured home was damaged on Crystal Springs Loop. An adjacent manufactured home was damaged by debris. After another stretch of isolated damage, additional more significant tree damage was observed along Sandy Bottom Road. The tornado appears to have dissipated shortly after crossing Sandy Bottom Road in a heavily wooded area. The overall damage was consistent with an EF-1 tornado with maximum winds of approximately 95 mph. Thanks to Early County Emergency Management for assistance with this assessment.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles were damaged. The report was relayed through mPING. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather pattern in the upper atmosphere favored the development of showers and thunderstorms across the area. At the surface, a stalled frontal boundary stretched from west to east near the I-12 corridor and provided a focus for repeated thunderstorm development. Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of metro Baton Rouge and the Northshore region of metro New Orleans and resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nobles Cemetery Road was flooded due to heavy rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in wind damage and a large number of power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Management reported trees down on Macedonia Rd near Springfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large cyclonic trough occupying the eastern third of the US was the instigating force behind snow showers and northwest orographic snow. This snow resulted in light snow at lower elevations, with several inches of accumulating snow at higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow eventually yielded 2.9 inches of snow in Mountain City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic front brought prolonged frigid temperatures to southeast Wyoming Sunday, January 25 through the morning of Monday, January 26. The coldest temperatures occurred Sunday night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overnight low temperatures ranged from -15 F to -20 F across Niobrara County from 1/25 into 1/26. The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds resulted in a period of extreme wind chills under -25 F. Minimum observed wind chill values reached -34 F at a Union Pacific Railroad sensor (7 WNW Van Tassell) at 10:55 PM MST on 1/25.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 and D3 drought conditions continued or developed across mainly the southeastern half of the CWA during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions occurred across Freestone County for the entire month. Near the end of the month, conditions in parts of the county worsened to D3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blew down along Spriggs Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over May 29 and 30, a shortwave trough brought light rain to numerous parts of the Intermountain West. Surface conditions remained unsaturated in spite of this, but portions of northern Colorado saw moisture linger into the morning of May 31. With this, as temperatures cooled and winds weakened overnight, the environment supported brief dense fog development within the Yampa River Basin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed within the Central Yampa River Basin during the morning of May 31. The KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport reported a brief period spanning less than ten minutes of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic front brought prolonged frigid temperatures to southeast Wyoming Sunday, January 25 through the morning of Monday, January 26. The coldest temperatures occurred Sunday night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overnight low temperatures ranged from -5 F to -10 F across the South Laramie Range from 1/25 into 1/26. The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds resulted in a prolonged period of extreme wind chills under -25 F. Minimum observed wind chill values reached -34 F at the Vedauwoo WYDOT sensor at 9:36 PM MST on 1/25.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 12th, the San Juan streamer persisted over the same areas across the San Juan metro area and nearby counties, leaving between 1 and 2 inches of rain during the mid-afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 Call Center reported flooding in San Juan along Ave Barbosa near the Walgreens area. A vehicle was reportedly affected by floodwaters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Easterly flow afternoon sea breeze convection produces a funnel cloud near Ft. Myers in Lee County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pictures and video shared by the public via social and broadcast media showed a funnel cloud west of the intersection of U.S. Hwy 41/Cleveland Ave and Winkler Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tideland Electric Cooperative reported three damaged power poles due to strong winds. The time was based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rains washed out a bridge on County Road 1100 North at Wolf Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across the North Carolina  Piedmont and foothills continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.

A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large tree limbs were blown down, including one that fell onto a vehicle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward and generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage in Erie County during the early evening of the 31st. The ambient environment of these storms included moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees downed and a portion of a house's roof was damaged in Waterford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Wales AWOS site (PAIW) first reported blizzard conditions at 20:10L on 2/16 and continued through 17:39L on 2/17. Blizzard conditions were met at 23:10L on 2/16. Winds were consistently greater than 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 21:30L on 2/16 with 56 mph sustained winds gusting to 66 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility less than 1/4 miles. Wind observations went down from 21:35L on 2/16 to 02:35L on 2/17, but winds were gusting well over 50 to 60 mph on each end of the outage. Additionally, blizzard conditions stopped briefly between the hours of 04:30L to 0800L on 2/17, but quickly started again shortly afterwards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure and a warm front brought a round of severe thunderstorms to southern WI during the evening. Large hail and damaging straight-line winds occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and powerlines down near Whitewater.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills. By Friday morning, much of the area was seeing temperatures of at least 20 degrees below zero, and as cold as 25 degrees below zero measured at the South Dakota State University mesonet stations in Gettysburg and 23 miles north of Highmore. With these cold temperatures and a northwest breeze, wind chills across much of the area had fallen to 40 degrees below zero and colder, with the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Summit coming in with a wind chill of 53 degrees below zero. Temperatures failed to warm much during the day, with highs in the single digits to teens below zero. Watertown set a record for the lowest daily high temperature, reaching only 11 degrees below zero.

Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong southwesterly flow developed across the southwestern United States on May 13, bringing with it hot and dry near-surface air. By mid-day, a well-mixed atmosphere supported strengthening surface winds across much of western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 5:31 PM MDT, the Colorado Department of Transportation road weather mesonet site at the Mesa County Line recorded a gust of 60 mph. Other sensors around the zone recorded gusts of 45-50 mph. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nassau County EM reported a gas pump awning structure was blown over in Hilliard, FL. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported golf ball size hail in downtown Whitewright.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hardin County received 4 to 6 inches of heavy snow and sleet. Hardin County also saw ice accumulation of 0.10 to 0.25 inches. Numerous traffic accidents occurred, including one involving a commercial vehicle that blocked one lane on Interstate 65.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down near East Baltimore Avenue.

In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tornadic supercell developed near or along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line during the evening of May 20, 2026. The storm tracked southeastward through Kenedy County before weakening just offshore Kenedy County that evening. A large hail and a very high wind gust (possible tornado) was reported as the supercell moved southeast and crossed Laguna Madre toward the nearshore Gulf waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A quarter inch hail was reported by the public in Sarita, TX. The report was from a photo posted onto our NWSChat 2.0/Slack page. Time radar estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.

Another Spring storm brought mountain snow, rain and thunderstorms to the area from April 20th through April 22nd. There were numerous reports of roadway flooding due to heavy rain and thunderstorms. There was also a report of a rock slide on State Route 16 from the heavy rain with rocks all over the road. Moderate mountain snow brought periods of chain controls over the mountain highways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public shared a picture of roadway flooding in a neighborhood in Salida.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 13th.
Severe thunderstorms moved into Eastern Pennsylvania, producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down near Bellemans Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of May with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across Glades County in the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Highline Ridge station within Taos Ski Valley recorded a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions redeveloped during the middle of January and continued into February.
A severe thunderstorm dropped one inch diameter hail during the afternoon of May 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report came from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the zero to 5 above zero range at times.
