Light snow overspreads Vermont just before midnight on January 15th, ending by mid-morning.||Snowfall amounts were generally 2 to 4 inches across central VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals of 1 to 4 inches were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCS moved out of Kentucky into East Tennessee during the early morning hours of June 28th. This laid out a boundary that acted as a focus for additional shower and thunderstorm development through the late morning hours, resulting in training storms across the central Tennessee valley and numerous reports of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several inches of standing water were flooding the front yard in front of a home in  Andersonville. The road is not covered by water, but water is next to the pictured home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weak, short-lived EF0 tornado touched down on the southeast side of Dyersburg shortly after midnight Tuesday, April 28. The most significant damage occurred at a warehouse on E Court St, where ten skylights were blown out, and a large metal panel was pulled from the side of the building. The tornado continued southeastward almost parallel to E Court Street, causing tree damage on both sides of the road. Minor roof damage was noted at a house on Auburn Ave. The tornado lifted just before reaching U.S. Highway 412.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed a band of heavy snow through the North Idaho Panhandle on late January 7. It brought widespread snowfall amounts ranging from 4 to 13 inches. Lookout Pass received 21 inches of new snow for the period January 6 through 8.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported an estimated 13 inches of snow in Hauser. Time is based off of Sandpoint Airport weather station. Athol had a range of 4 to 5 inches of snow. Spirit Lake received 5 to 6 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 2 to 4 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell over much of northwest Illinois during the early morning of March 16th, where a swath of 6 to 9 inches of snow fell.  Storm total snowfall amounts included 8.7 inches four miles north northwest of Rockford; 8.2 inches five miles west northwest of Rochelle; 7.7 inches near Timberlane; 7.5 inches four miles north northeast of Harvard; 7.2 inches in Capron and 6.0 inches in Marengo.  Rockford Airport reported 5.7 inches of snow. Snowfall amounts across the rest of northern Illinois including much of the Chicago metro area were generally in the 1 to 3 inch range.||Strong winds caused significant blowing and drifting snow across much of northern Illinois through the evening of March 16th as scattered snow showers moved across northern Illinois. While blizzard criteria were not met, near blizzard conditions were reported at times in open and rural areas.

A highly unstable environment developed across western Montana, fueled by pooling moisture and steep lapse rates. Shortwave energy rotating around a broader upper-level trough provided the necessary lift for convective initiation which resulted in large hail. As storms moved into the Idaho Panhandle and interacted with the local terrain, they organized into two distinct quasi-linear convective systems, producing widespread severe wind gusts across Lincoln and Flathead Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple photos of oblong hail placed on top of a ruler were shared on Facebook. Another person who lives south of MT-83 reported that they lost their greenhouse and their patio furniture went flying across the patio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a downed power pole along Hodges Chapel Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of multiple roads flooded throughout Topeka.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal warmth statewide and well below normal precipitation over the eastern half of the state resulted in a one level degradation of drought conditions to Moderate Drought conditions over much of the eastern plains of New Mexico. Drought conditions over the western half of the state remained persistent from January.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought remained persistent over the far northwestern portion of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of thunderstorms formed downstream of a mid-level wave in an environment with around 500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 40 knots of effective shear. Despite the meager instability, thunderstorms were able to reach severe levels with areas of tree and power line damage reported in Northwestern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees reported down making the road impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

A cold front was approaching the region during the evening of May 3rd. Concurrently, a low-level jet was ramping up in the area. This resulted in the development of thunderstorms, some of which became severe and produced large hail in Macoupin and Madison counties.

A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down over inaccessible areas west of Bayou Dularge and tracked northeast toward Crozier Drive. Predominantly minor to moderate patches of tree damage were visible on high resolution satellite imagery along its path which were collocated with a tornado debris signature on Climavision radar V014. Trees were more evidently displaced and damaged as the tornado exited the inaccessible marsh and forested areas and moved over Crozier Drive. A NWS survey team observed two homes on Crozier Drive that had significant roof loss and at least one exterior wall collapsed for both homes. The tornado continued northeast across Bayou Dularge Rd and into more inaccessible marsh and forest vegetation where more minor damage was evident on satellite imagery. The end point of this tornado is estimated and it's possible it extended further northeast though no conclusive evidence of damage was identified.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm sector convection ahead of an approaching cold front spawned thunderstorms, some of which were severe. An axis of up to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE nosed up to Pittsburgh metro with strong effective shear as high as 60 knots. Hail and wind damage were reported with up to 1.5 inch hail, a measured 64 mph wind gust at a home weather station, and trees down on wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down along Bracken Ridge Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 61 MPH were reported at the Elwood Ridge sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A heavy snow event impacted Two Rivers, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. A Local Storm Report indicated that eighteen inches of snow accumulation occurred five miles east of Fox. The Ladd Army Airfield ASOS, located at Fort Wainwright, reported visibilities of one-half mile in snow during the peak of the event at 1255AKST on February 23. The first verifying observation occurred at 1010AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

A windy day was observed on March 13th across southeast Ohio as a result of a passing low pressure system and an accompanying low level jet. While breezy winds were noted in the late morning, daytime mixing aided in the stronger winds from aloft to mix down to the surface, with local AWOS and Mesonet stations observing gusts on the upwards of 40 to 54 miles per hour across southeast Ohio. As these winds prevailed into the late afternoon and evening, numerous 911 call center reports noted downed trees and power lines across the area. The wind gradually declined after sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area.

Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of  west central and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening period, with very large hail and severe winds reported. One supercell produced 3 inch hail in Moorhead, MN. One EF-0 tornado developed with a supercell in Clay County 6 miles northwest of Hawley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated max hail size 2 SSW Moorhead, MN. Time estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced wind damage, mostly to trees and vegetation, in portions of central and southwestern Mississippi during the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree as blown down, blocking a road. Multiple large trees were blown down across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted through the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal system brought widespread light to moderate snowfall accumulations to the area. Total snowfall amounts ranged from a light coating to 1 near the coast to 1-4 farther inland. Temperatures near freezing during daytime snowfall fell well below freezing overnight, resulting in slippery road conditions in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 2-4. The highest reported amount was 4.2 in Warwick Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow accumulation up to 1 inch, followed by 1/2 to 3/4 inch of ice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A low water road was flooded town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple mesoscale convective vortices triggered a line of storms that brought damaging wind gusts the New River Valley and the Piedmont. Mesoscale conditions were not the most ideal for severe weather development. Bulk shear struggled to get above 20 knots, mid-level lapse rates were about 5.5 C/km, and DAPE only up went up 500 J/kg. However, sufficient surface heating and moisture resulted in CAPE of at least 1000 J/kg which allowed for some decent thunderstorm development after the MCV trigger. There was one notable storm that brought down a swath of trees in Roanoke County and went straight eastward and brought more trees down in Charlotte County. Broad rotation was noted in the SRV data by the time it reached Charlotte County with a 59.3 mph velocity gate recorded at around 7250 feet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds uprooted numerous trees, snapping several in half, and brought down many large branches west of the community of Bent Mountain. Most of the reported damage was in a corridor near the intersection of Bottom Creek Road and Rocky Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple organized QLCSs push across central Mississippi and produced damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down across Spillway Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving north of the area brought periods of rain Wednesday morning (13th), followed by scattered showers as a cold front approached. Partial clearing during the afternoon allowed for modest destabilization across western portions of the area. Combined with wind shear and unstable temperature lapse rates, thunderstorms organized along the front as they moved east through the evening. A few storms produced isolated damaging wind gusts and small hail. The strong gusts and small hail resulted in some crop damage according to a state emergency declaration, though estimated costs were unknown.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds brought down a tree in one area and power lines in another near Adams Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow developed across western Kansas during the early morning hours of the 9th before ending during the late afternoon/early evening hours on the 9th. The highest snowfall amounts occurred across Greeley and Wichita counties with 3 inches reported in Tribune and 5-7 inches in Wichita county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wichita Emergency Manager estimated 5-7 inches of snow in the southern portion of Wichita county. 5 inches of snow was reported in Leoti at 1353 CST with snow still falling at the time of report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Em reports tree down on jimm star rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid air to the south of a warm frontal boundary spawned heavy rain producing thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Storms repeatedly moving over the same regions produced pockets of 3 to 4 inches of rain which triggered areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported that several roads are flooded in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Saint Mary's 911 Call Center reported about a dozen or so calls for trees and wires down from Leonardtown to Hollywood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 70 mph blew the roof off of a barn and knocked down trees and wires on Prescott Road between Birch Road and Fox Road in South Lebanon Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front moved across Minnesota during the early morning of April 17th which ultimately produced two rounds of thunderstorms.  The first line of storms was associated with a warm front which produced quarter size hail across south-central Minnesota mid-morning. The secondary and stronger line of storms tied to the cold front itself moved through in the early afternoon across eastern MN. This line produced a swath of large hail measuring from quarter size up to ping pong ball size hail in Cannon Falls (Goodhue County) which ended up being the largest measured hailstone from this event.
A cold front moved through the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours. Strong storms developed and produced damaging wind gusts and localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was downed onto Brunson Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across White Oak Road near Danese.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ward County had estimated wind gusts to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two large trees blown down and a pine tree snapped at 80 feet high in a neighborhood.  Additional trees and tree limbs down in the neighborhood and across Columbus. One tree felled on a home causing roof damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Employee reported roadway flooding along the PX Store on Procurement Road in Tafuna Village. Pictures show at least 6 inches of water pooled onto the roadway and parking lot. Flooding was caused by heavy rainfall and within an area of poor storm water drainage. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak continued into the first couple days of February. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, as it extends well back into January. For the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Highlands, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For the Shenandoah Valley, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. For the Virginia Piedmont to I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through New Jersey producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of trees and wires down. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported tennis ball sized hail near Monona.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level system drove strong cold front eastward across the region, including adjacent coastal waters. Ahead of the boundary, a robust low-level jet brough in warm, buoyant, and very moist air northward from the Gulf. Night timing of the line of storms that developed along the front did limit low level instability, however, elevated instability and frontal lift were more than enough to overcome the lack of surface heating. A few storms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of a tree down high winds caused by severe thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist onshore flow above the existing snow pack ahead of an advancing warm front resulted in widespread dense fog late on February 17th and early on February 18th. The fog dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Wilmington Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. The rate of falling and blowing snow reduced visibility to whiteout conditions, making many roadways impassible. Snow lingered for several hours before finally dissipating the afternoon of the following day. Storm total snowfall ranged between a few inches up to 9.5 inches.||The highest measured snowfall totals from this event are:|9.5 inches ENE of Prior Lake (Scott)|8.5 inches in Shorewood (Hennepin)|7.7 inches in Waconia (Carver)|7.0 inches 1 E of Granite Falls (Chippewa)|7.0 inches 3 SSW of Elko New Market (Rice).||The strongest wind gusts measured from this event were: |50 mph at Canby Municipal Airport (Yellow Medicine)|48 mph at Redwood Falls Municipal Airport (Redwood)|48 mph at New Ulm Municipal Airport (Brown)|44 mph at Mankato Regional Airport (Blue Earth).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS Station located at Olivia Regional Airport reported several hours of blizzard conditions with visibility less than one-quarter mile and a max wind gust of 44 mph. Additionally, Emergency Management reported significant visibility issues across the county with ten motorists ending up in the ditch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken band of thunderstorms developed across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 6th, as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Low level wind shear increased with the approach of the disturbance, and this wind shear combined with a moderately unstable air mass that had developed, resulted in some of the storms developing low level rotation, which supported the formation of three tornadoes across Sebastian and Crawford Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed along Watson Road, west of Highway 71 and north of Young Ridge Road. It moved northwest across Vineyard Creek Road, Hendrix Road, and Nickletown Road, before dissipating just south of Highway 10. The tornado uprooted trees, damaged an outbuilding, and snapped numerous large tree limbs. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KSRX WSR-88D radar. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Beaufort County 911 Call Center reported a tree down at 1501 Ivy Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest Arkansas experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one tenth to one half inch across portions of Benton and Carroll Counties to as much as two to three inches across portions of Sebastian and Crawford Counties. The rainfall that fell across northwest Arkansas in February was below average monthly amounts for the region, with much of Benton and Carroll Counties only receiving between 10 and 25 percent of average monthly precipitation. These dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Benton and Carroll Counties and into portions of Washington and Madison Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Benton and Carroll Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.
A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornadic damage was on Wenger Road, where two barns were destroyed. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped and a residence had minor roof damage. Additional damage was noted along Amsterdam Road where a roof was lifted off of a barn and several trees were uprooted. Farther east, more trees were uprooted and a garage was damaged along County Road 25A. The tornado dissipated just west of I-75.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into Lower Michigan on June 10 resulting in tens of thousands of power outages statewide from wind damage and down trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At Muskegon County Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The emergency manager relayed a report of a tree down near tallapoosa highway, north of steadman road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs were downed on a house in Webb City.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts along the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Melbourne International Airport measured a peak wind gust of 40 knots from the northwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms produced localized wind damage, localized flooding and one brief tornado during the afternoon and evening of June 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed several inches of standing water on a residential street in Addison.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brough freezing rain accumulations of up to 0.25 inches and sleet accumulations of up to 5 inches to the county. Sleet covered roads across the county before transitioning to primarily freezing rain after 2:30 PM local time on the 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a large tree onto Highway 96 in Fairview. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down and an unanchored shed was flipped over in Bellmont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of North Louisiana along with a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail reported in the Three States community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 4:21 AM CST, a brief tornado developed northeast of Nehawka, Nebraska, near 12th Street and Beccard Drive, and moved southeast. The tornado caused fairly extensive tree damage at a residence, including several large broken branches. Based on this damage, peak winds were estimated around 90 mph. The tornado continued southeast, producing additional sporadic tree damage with estimated winds of 65 to 74 mph, before dissipating near 6th Avenue and Hoback Road at approximately 4:24 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported low temperatures ranged from 30 to 32 across much of western Polk County. The lowest reported temperature of 30 was at the Beltrami, MN DOT site at 5:30 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire and rescue reports a fallen tree on powerlines. Wind gust estimated from radar data, nearby observations, and damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were blown down in Buffalo Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 85 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.  At one point, there were around 600 customers without power due to downed lines and poles in parts of Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds knocked down several trees, damaged an outbuilding, and removed shingles from a roof southeast of Wilder.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few clusters of thunderstorms moved east to southeast across portions of northeast and east-central Colorado from the mid-afternoon through the early evening hours on the 21st, in vicinity of a dryline and warm front intersection. Wind gusts up to 67 mph occurred in Yuma County, and nickel sized hail occurred in Cheyenne County.

A mid-level shortwave and associated surface cold front and pre-frontal trough moved towards the area. Isolated showers and thunderstorms developed and given moderate instability and shear, a few thunderstorms became severe, producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree snapped in on 73rd Place near Metropolitan Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 30 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 55 to 65 mph across southwest Minnesota.  When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted to 46 mph at Slayton and 44 mph near Dovray. These winds combined with periods of light snowfall which totaled around 1 inch to produce visibility briefly as low as one-quarter to one-half mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Curlew Junction mesonet station recorded an initial wind gust of 60 mph, shortly followed by an additional wind gust of 60 mph, as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front moved across west Texas and southeast New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level trough neared the region from the west. Widespread rain began during the morning of the 23rd in western portions of the area and gradually transitioned eastward through the day. As the front moved across the area, rain transitioned to sleet and snow from north to south (with freezing rain being more common south of the Pecos River and in the Davis Mountains). Off and on bands of sleet and snow continued across the Permian Basin and southeast New Mexico on the 24th, and became mostly snow by the 25th before moving east of the area late in the afternoon. Snowfall/sleet totals reached winter storm criteria across much of the northern basin and in southeast New Mexico. Lower snow and ice totals were reported further south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported an estimated 3.0-3.5 inches of snow on Facebook. The estimation was based on a measuring stick. The total duration of the event is estimated from radar and nearby AWOS reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System moved across the Ohio Valley on the night of June 17th, 2026 and the morning of June 18th, 2026. Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frog Branch Road was flooded. Water almost reached a residence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency managers reported that a landslide occurred along PR-348 km 14.6. The roadway was partially obstructed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms impacted north central and northeast Kansas on June 4th with wind damage including a short lived but strong tornado that developed over the community of Riley and moved northeast for approximately 4-5 miles.  It produced EF2 damage with winds to around 120 mph at one home just northeast of Riley.  No injuries were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding occurring over highway K9 of eight inches in depth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public mPING report of hail measured at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong ridge of high pressure set up across much of the western United States and brought an long period of record breaking warmth. The most impressive stretch was from March 18 through March 21. In total, 71 new daily record high temperatures were set out of a possible 126 high temperatures at RIW CLI sites (longer term climate sites), greater than half of the daily highs. Every location was at least 10 degrees above normal through the period. Every location had their all time warmest period for these two weeks, with three locations; the Riverton Airport, the Sweetwater County airport near Rock Springs, and the Lander airport; more than 8 degrees above the previous warmest period. All locations set their all time high temperature March multiple times in this stretch. Six locations had their earliest 80 degree high temperature, with four stations having their first 80 degree or greater March high temperatures in station history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Record warmth occurred over the latter half of March in Big Horn County. The period from March 17 through March 30 averaged more than 12 degrees above normal. Every day but one had above normal daily average temperatures, with ten days more than 10 degrees above normal. Seven new daily record high temperatures were set. The previous monthly record high temperature of 81 was tied or broken on three consecutive days from March 19 to March 21, including a new monthly record high temperature of 85 on March 21. The previous earliest occurrence of 80 degrees was broken by 12 days. Records at the South Big Horn County airport near Greybull date back to 1998.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fast moving water over FM 1352 near FM 2508 east of Ben Bolt.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported giant size hail of 3.25 inches in diameter just west of Hatchel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For far western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. Along and east of I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

A decaying thunderstorm produced isolated wind damage in the northern portions of the city of Florence. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall led to flash flooding in Marshall, Jackson, and Cullman Counties in Northeastern Alabama, flooding roads and causing them to become impassable.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of CR 200 and CR 234.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large, long-period northwest to northerly swell affected the Atlantic waters and local passages of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands from February 2 through February 3, 2026. Seas built rapidly to 12-16 feet, with higher values observed during the peak of the event. Post-event analysis indicated that offshore seas reached 15 to 20 feet, with breaking waves along exposed coastlines estimated at 17 to 22 feet.||This swell generated dangerous marine conditions, large breaking waves, and life-threatening rip currents along north- to northeast-facing beaches, including areas from Rinc��n to Fajardo, as well as Culebra, Vieques, and the northern U.S. Virgin Islands. The most significant impacts occurred from late February 2 through February 3.||High surf conditions led to beach erosion, wave overwash, and minor to locally moderate coastal flooding in low-lying, vulnerable coastal areas, particularly during high tide.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coastal flooding occurred along PR-102 (Guanajibo Boulevard) near the mouth of the Guanajibo River in Mayag��ez during the morning of February 3, 2026. High surf caused waves to break over the shoreline and inundate the roadway, leaving debris, including small to large tree branches, across the street. Emergency managers responded to the scene and conducted debris removal operations. The flooding was associated with large breaking waves generated by a long-period northerly swell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a passing shortwave trough and strong jet stream aloft produced high winds across portions of central Wyoming. The highest wind gusts occurred in the Bighorn Mountains of Johnson County, where the School House RAWS site had a maximum wind gust of 85 mph. The strong wind was accompanied by heavy snow showers at times, bringing reduced visibility and wintry travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High wind occurred across portions of Natrona County. Some of the more notable gusts included 72 mph at Scenic Drive and 62 mph at the Natrona County airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 3/4 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 20 mph with frequent gusts over 25mph. The 2-day snowfall reports ranged from about 4 to 7 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 7 inches in Richmond. The highest reports and greatest impacts were generally in the southern portion of the county. Road conditions became dangerous Saturday night and much of Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of upper level disturbances pushed through southeast Texas causing multiple days of stormy weather. A pair of severe weather reports were received. Behind the fast paced fronts that caused the unsettled weather, tides fell below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto Allison Cemetery Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-wave severe event unfolded from the afternoon of January 9 through the morning of January 10. While the first wave featured no severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall over Birmingham led to numerous flooding issues. Early the next morning, additional heavy rainfall led to more flooding issues in parts of Jefferson, Shelby, and St. Clair counties. A bowing line segment moved across Marengo, Dallas, Autauga, Elmore, Montgomery, and Lee counties, with scattered instances of wind damage. In addition, a cell in advance of the main QLCS produced an EF-0 tornado in northern Cleburne County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed around the Sylacauga area, including Odens Mill Rd and New County Line Rd at Coaling Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down along Mulberry Road at Moores Mill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon hours of May 17th, storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of NW Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured 58 mph wind gust north of Maryville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving boundary was the focus for afternoon thunderstorms as the day's capping inversion lifted. Pea and dime-size hail reports were common, with a handful of reports for 1 inch hail or larger.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo from Emergency Management indicates quarter-size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed late Sunday afternoon near the Yellow Medicine - Chippewa County line and strengthened as they moved east towards Sibley and McLeod Counties. There were a few isolated reports of severe wind and hail during this time. The storms reached peak intensity as they turned south and moved through southern Sibley, Nicollet, and eastern Brown Counties. ||The largest hail reports of the evening were half dollar size in Sibley County, and the strongest wind was observed in Nicollet County (estimated 60 mph) where large amounts of dirt and dust were lofted just ahead of the storm along the gust front. It is rare to see this phenomenon occur in Minnesota, but several weeks of below normal precipitation meant many fields were dry and primed for dirt to be blown.

Near record dry conditions in February with half an inch to an inch of precipitation for the month, around 2.5-3 below normal, and a near record to record dry winter across Southern Illinois, including a record dry 2.52 at Carbondale, resulted in northwestern portions of Southern Illinois entering D2 (Severe Drought) mid-month. Occurring in between the '25 and '26 growing seasons, impacts from drought in February were very limited. Drought conditions continued into March.

At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to nickel-size in Rootstown. The hailfall lasted for about three minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees and wires near Coryville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree fell onto a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

A strong cold front moved across southeast Missouri, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the afternoon and evening hours and continued into the afternoon of the 24th. After a brief lull at night, another interval of dangerous wind chills occurred during the morning and early afternoon hours on the 25th. The one exception was New Madrid County, MO where wind chills remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought. Conditions worsened through the month with the county being upgraded to Exceptional (D4) drought on March 24, 2026.  Exceptional drought then continued for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clear skies and calm winds following a cold frontal passage allowed for locally dense fog to form over far Southwestern Kentucky late evening on the 21st through the early AM hours of the 22nd. Patches of freezing fog occurred, with icy roads reported in the town of Dublin in far western Graves County. Northerly winds increasing to 4-7mph before dawn brought an end to fog conditions.

A line of strong to severe storms organized over southwest Kentucky during the early morning hours of June 1, 2026. These storms moved south into West Tennessee and along the Tennessee River into northeast Mississippi during the morning hours. The storms fed on strong instability and adequate deep-layer shear to produce isolated wind damage and large hail. This first round of storms left behind an outflow boundary extending from eastern Arkansas across the Memphis metropolitan area into north Mississippi. Storms ignited along this boundary during the late afternoon and evening hours, fueled by strong instability and an upper-level trough overspreading the region. There were several additional reports of large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were knocked down on Star Landing and Goodman Roads in Walls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down at German Chapel Road and Solomons Island Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ten healthy trees with snapped trunks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite a rather volatile airmass for severe weather across Oklahoma and north Texas on the 26th, misaligned synoptic features (i.e., neutral-to-rising mid-level heights) and remnant convective inhibition limited the overall number/coverage of thunderstorms during the evening. The most significant storm was a slow-moving supercell storm near and north of Wichita Falls, Texas. This thunderstorm produced large to very large hail and yielded a pair of left-moving supercells that went on to produce hail into portions of adjacent southern Oklahoma. This included confirmations of baseball-size hail in areas east of Lawton, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Maximum hail size increased from quarter to golf ball during the event time. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary arctic frontal zone crashed southeast across the region with yet another increase in winds, spotty light snowfall, and areas of blowing snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Even though snowfall was just a few tenths of an inch, northwest winds gusted as high as 45 to 55 mph during the afternoon and evening of January 18.  When snow was falling, even lightly, area Department of Transportation cameras and automated instruments indicated visibility as low as one-quarter mile or less at Tracy and Marshall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few power lines were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement or maintenance of the drought. Dimmit, Medina, and Travis Counties all improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Hays County remained in D3. Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 20.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were still below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 5.7 feet but was 11.1 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in April and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.7 feet and was 69.8 feet below normal. Medina Lake rose 0.3 feet but was still 87.1 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina and Blanco Rivers; below normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal to much above normal (90%-95%).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement or maintenance of the drought. Dimmit, Medina, and Travis Counties all improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Hays County remained in D3. Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 20.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were still below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 5.7 feet but was 11.1 feet below normal.
