EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on March 14th, a narrow band of snow developed across portions of southeast MN with snowfall rates rapidly increasing through the early morning hours on March 15th. Near I-90, a band of heavy sleet occurred that transitioned over to snow near daybreak. Overall, snowfall totals of over a foot were noted in Winona, Olmsted, Dodge and Wabasha counties with even amounts over 18 inches in Wabasha County. After a brief lull during the late morning, a secondary round of snow moved in for the afternoon and into the overnight hours on March 15th bringing additional accumulations accompanied with gusty winds which resulted in localized whiteout conditions. One vehicle accident occurred in Winona County after the snow departed on March 16th resulting in 3 non-life threatening injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This winter storm brought snowfall totals between 8 and 14 inches to Dodge County. The highest reported snowfall total was 2 miles northeast of Kasson where 13.5 inches of snow was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 conditions persisted throughout all of June across portions of the Florida Big Bend.
Strong and gusty north to northeast winds impacted many areas of Southwestern California. Wind gusts up to 83 MPH were reported across the mountains and foothills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong and gusty northwest to north winds impacted the area. The Rehabilitation Ranch sensor reported gusts up to 59 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grain bin, hog barn, large limbs damaged. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a large tree limb which blocked the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photos showed tree limbs at least 6 inches in diameter blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a tree in the vicinity of East Beaver Street and North Monroe Street in Bellefonte.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level trough moved along the international border with a strengthening southerly flow of moisture and instability into southeast South Dakota. With the terminus of the transport near the mid-James River Valley, isolated storms developed by very late afternoon with strong updrafts and large hail up to ping-pong ball size. A more linear system developed along the dry line in central South Dakota during the early evening and produced damaging wind gusts up to 70 mph near and south of Interstate 90.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms organized over southwest Kentucky during the early morning hours of June 1, 2026. These storms moved south into West Tennessee and along the Tennessee River into northeast Mississippi during the morning hours. The storms fed on strong instability and adequate deep-layer shear to produce isolated wind damage and large hail. This first round of storms left behind an outflow boundary extending from eastern Arkansas across the Memphis metropolitan area into north Mississippi. Storms ignited along this boundary during the late afternoon and evening hours, fueled by strong instability and an upper-level trough overspreading the region. There were several additional reports of large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four trees were knocked down on Carlton Drive just south of Arkabutla Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KOMA ASOS measured wind gust of 60 mph a the Omaha Eppley Airfield. Personal weather station measured wind gust of 60 mph near Fort Calhoun, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet accumulation up to 1 inch, followed by 1/4 to 1/2 inch of ice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Alberta Clipper and associated upper trough tracking over the Great Lakes resulted in light fluffy snow with snow-to-liquid ratios ranging from 18:1 to 21:1. Snow amounts generally ranged from 1 to 3 inches in the lowlands initially, but was followed by scattered snow bands/squalls with locally heavy rates during the evening along and behind an the cold front during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS station KPIT Pittsburgh International Airport reported 1/4 mile visibility with a 41 mph wind gust in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms pushed southeastward across central Kansas and the Flint Hills during the evening hours of June 19. These storms produced up to quarter size hail and 75 mph winds.

A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Marion County weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Dell Rapids.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mostly near to above average precipitation supported steadily improving drought conditions across far southwest Nebraska, especially for Dundy County very early in the month, and by mid to late June for Hitchcock and Red Willow counties. Near to below average precipitation prevailed across portions of Red Willow County where drought persisted the longest. D2 Severe Drought only persisted through the 1st for Dundy County, with D2 Severe Drought to D4 Exceptional Drought persisting through mid to late June for the northeast half of Hitchcock County, and through the entire month for all of Red Willow County. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about two inches over northern Red Willow county, to a whopping ten inches over northwest Hitchcock county. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and three-quarters of an inch over western Dundy county, to about three and one-half inches over eastern Red Willow county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from just under two inches to about four and one-half inches (one and one-half inches below average to one and one-half inches above average), lowest over northwest portions of the county. Normal monthly precipitation across the county ranges from about three to three and one-half inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported quarter sized hail in Lake City. The report was relayed via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across eastern North Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KBWP AWOS at Wahpeton, ND frequently reported wind chills -40 or lower from the evening of January 22 through the morning hours of January 23. The lowest wind chill value during this period at that site was -46.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved east toward the area that helped to produce severe thundertorms over a good portion of the CWA. Flooding also occurred in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported (via Facebook) quarter size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions redeveloped during the middle of January and continued into February.
Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported half dollar size hail near Ripley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roadways had several inches of flowing  water over them in Scammon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over southeast Louisiana, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D3 to include St Tammany, southern Tangipahoa, and St James Parishes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 to D3 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of Northern St. Tammany Parish according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in several area rivers reaching flood stage. Some rivers reached moderate to major flood stage, with the Lemonwier River at New Lisbon approaching its flood of record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in the Wisconsin River at Muscoda rising into flood stage during the early morning hours on April 18th. The river crested in minor flood stage on April 19th during the early morning before falling below flood stage during the morning on April 21st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Southerly flow on the backside of high pressure warmed the Delta region and portions of eastern Arkansas. Moisture pulling from our north also resulted in increased dewpoints in these areas. Temperatures in the 90s and dewpoints in the 70s resulted in dangerous heat with heat indices in excess of 105F in the aforementioned areas. Luckily, a cold front translated across the Mid-South the next day, providing some relief from the heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Maximum heat index estimated to be 106F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 2, thunderstorm development was initiated by a weak backdoor cold front moving in from the northeast. The resulting activity was primarily concentrated within and surrounding the DFW Metroplex, leading to instances of marginally severe hail and strong to severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported flooding and road closures on FM 1187 from Ben Day Murrin Rd to Hwy 377, and on Hwy 377 from Pyramid Blvd to FM 1187.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across southern Illinois, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the afternoon and evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. Areas along and northwest of interstate 57 experienced another interval of dangerous wind chills during the morning and afternoon hours on the 25th while areas to the southeast remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy thunderstorm rainfall of up to 2.50 inches in under 2 hours, produced flash flooding in central Martin County that crossed US Highway 50 near Stiles Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A blown transformer was reported on Carters Circle in Greenhead.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm began Saturday night and continued through Sunday as it passed over an entrenched arctic airmass. A strengthening surface low over the Tennessee Valley combined with upper level dynamics to produce snowfall of up to a foot in some areas. The Dayton airport DAY set its highest 24 hour snowfall on record with 12.4 inches on the 25th, breaking the previous record of 12.2 inches set on January 26, 1978.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The observer southwest of Franklin measured 14.1 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on Glenn Highway near Savage Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed in numerous locations around Hamilton, with at least one tree on a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kidder County had estimated wind gusts to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry spring continued across Middle Tennessee during April 2026. Precipitation amounts were generally 3 to 5 inches across with most of this rain recorded during the last week of the month. While these rain amounts were higher compared to the past couple months, it was still below normal for the month. Drought conditions worsened through the month of April. By the end of the month, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least severe drought with about 38 percent of this classified as extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Abnormally dry conditions from March 2026 worsened in April with severe drought conditions developing across Clay County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex setup characterized by moisture overrunning an entrenched wedge of cold air at the surface led to freezing rain and sleet beginning across north Georgia late on the night of January 24 and persisting through much of the day on January 25. Widespread ice accretion of one-tenth to one-quarter inch ice occurred with some areas receiving over a half inch of freezing rain accumulation. ||Significant tree damage and power outages occurred in the worst-affected areas of northeast Georgia, while spotty tree damage and isolated power outages occurred in other areas. Additionally, a layer of sleet occurred in much of northeast Georgia, leading to hazardous roadways. ||The hardest hit areas locally were White County as well as portions of Dawson and Lumpkin counties. The vast majority of the White County lost power with many locations remaining without power for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light rain showers began on the evening of the 24th. Rain briefly transitioned to ice on the morning of the 25th, however temperatures warmed through the day and quickly melted any accumulations which managed to stick on elevated surfaces. Eastern portions of the county which were in the wedge were able to remain colder for a little longer and resulted in ice accumulations on elevated surface up to 0.15 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity resulted in an unsettled weather pattern across the Ohio Valley for the start of June. Each day yielded developing showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest and travelling eastward along the front before dissipating after sunset. On June 6th, storms remained strong to severe as it dashed across Ohio, and caused scattered tree and power line damage across Perry County from the damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dozens of homes around Thornville observed power outages from downed trees in the vicinity of County Route 87.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported two separate instances of severe hail as storms moved through Winona on June 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported golf ball sized hail 1 mile east of Winona Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving south along the west coast brought a strong cold front with valley and mountain snow across far northern California on 02/16 into 02/17. Snow showers followed on 02/18 before they increased in coverage and intensity late on 02/18 into the morning of 02/19.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Gridded Snowfall Analysis indicated storm totals of 4 to 12 inches. Precipitation amounts in the zone included 0.46 inches at Ash Creek, 0.51 inches at Mount Shasta, 0.75 inches at Mt. Shasta Ski Bowl, and 1.58 inches at Dunsmuir.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There were a few rounds of thunderstorms through this period. A few storms were severe with large hail and damaging winds and an isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds of 65 mph from a storm southeast of Woodson along county line. Reported by Woodson VFD.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 conditions persisted throughout all of June across portions of the Florida Big Bend.

During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Courtesy of spotter network.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.

Drought conditions continued during the month of February as below-normal rainfall was observed through the first two months of the year. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across southeastern Central Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The majority of Marengo County was removed from Severe (D2) drought on February 3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.

Snow developed across east central and northeast Illinois during the afternoon of January 24th and continued through the afternoon of January 25th.  Snowfall amounts were generally 2 to 4 inches through the Interstate 55 corridor and 4 to 6 inches along and east of the Interstate 57 corridor.  Lake enhanced snow developed on January 25th with higher snowfall amounts across eastern Cook County.  Snowfall amounts there included 10.5 inches in the Chicago Loop; 9.1 inches in Garfield Park; 9.0 inches in Avondale and Bridgeport; 8.8 inches in Glenview and 8.5 inches in Logan Square.  Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 4.4 inches.
A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.

A shortwave dropping down in northwest flow, paired with a weak cold front and most unstable CAPE around 450 J/kg, produced showers and isolated thunderstorms across western Montana during the evening hours of May 20th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Falling trees and branches brought down power lines and damaged a number of power poles, which sparked two small fires along Highway 200 west of Thompson Falls. Several trees were reported on power lines from Trout Creek to Noxon, as well as on Blue Slide Road and Highway 200. The damage resulted in overnight power outages for roughly 400 customers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique snow setup for South Carolina developed as a strong coastal low strengthening offshore, while a upper level disturbance shifted over our area. This provided sufficient synoptic and mesoscale lift for widespread heavy snow across SC along with unusually high snow to liquid ratios between 15-20 to 1. A brief period of sleet-graupel occurred at the onset of the event following by 12 hours of light-moderate snow across the area, with highest amounts in the Pee Dee region of SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous public, COOP, CoCoRAHS, and spotter reports across Lexington county of 2 to 4 inches of snowfall accumulation. Highest amount in the county was measured via CoCoRAHS north of Lake Murray. Official NWS observation at CAE was 2.8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A stream (quebrada) overflowed its banks in the El Tamarindo sector of Barrio Saltos. Water is inundating the low level crossing at Camino El Tamarindo. Cars observed at both sides of the bridge unable to cross.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were in place across most if not all of the Northern Outer Banks, Washington, East Carteret, West Carteret, Southern Craven, Coastal Onslow, Inland Onslow, and Pamlico Counties from the beginning of June until June thirtieth according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Coastal Onslow County from the beginning of June until June twenty-nineth. Severe drought conditions then ended across the county on June thirtieth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto Friendship Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through northwest Connecticut, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Warming temperatures led to a mix of both rain and snow during this event with some short-duration sleet and freezing rain. ||The highest accumulations of snow fell across northern portions of Litchfield County where 0.5 to about 2 inches were reported. For the southern portion of the county, generally a trace to 0.5 were common. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 1.4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down in western portions of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms developed in north central Kansas during the mid afternoon on 4/26 and tracked eastward through northeast Kansas, producing large hail to ping pong ball size and wind gusts estimated to around 70 mph. Clusters of late evening severe storms impacted much of northeast Kansas through the early morning of 04/27. Large hail to Golfball size and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported. Flash flooding also occurred in Shawnee, Jefferson, and Douglas counties as in upwards of 5 inches of rain fell.

A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Hoboken Police Department reported via social media that Burton Boulevard was closed between Brantley  Street and Kelly Street due to flood waters  inundating the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. With abnormally high amounts of atmospheric moisture, these thunderstorms were able to produce very heavy rainfall with rain amounts of five to seven inches reported across portions of Sumner and Robertson counties. This caused flash flooding for these areas, particularly in low-lying areas and those along area creeks. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Stop Thirty Road in Hendersonville. Extent of damages is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of strong winds and accumulating snowfall resulted in a brief period of near-whiteout conditions across portions of northeast Iowa. While snowfall amounts generally ranged from 1 to 3 inches, 35 to 45 mph wind gusts resulted in a period of visibilities of 1/2 mile or lower during the afternoon and evening on January 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of strong winds of 35 to 45 mph and accumulating snow resulted in a period of blowing snow across Floyd County that reduced visibilities to under 1/2 mile at times. Additionally, snowfall accumulations of 1 to 3 inches were observed throughout the county on January 21st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper-level system brought scattered showers and storms across central North Carolina in the afternoon and early evening. A few storms produced damaging winds across Moore, Randolph, and Chatham Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell in the roadway, blocking one lane of travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough brought an increase in southerly winds aloft on the 13th. This combined with a strongly unstable atmosphere brought severe thunderstorms producing scattered severe wind gusts across the region. High synoptic wind gusts also accompanied thunderstorms on the 13th and 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTM06 Arc-N Havre thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A midlevel shortwave trough plus a very moist airmass combined to produce an isolated severe thunderstorm over Knox County in East Tennessee, leading to several reports of thunderstorm driven wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree felled by severe thunderstorm winds partially blocked the eastbound lanes of a local road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several businesses in Picayune have been flooded from heavy rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another extreme wind event impacted the entire state of Montana, producing gusts up to 77 mph across much of the lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reed Point S gusted to 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northern Nebraska Panhandle, bringing hail, tornadoes, and torrential rain fall with flooding occuring in Kimball and Dawes Counties. No verification occurred in southeast Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KSNY ASOS 3 miles south of Sidney reported a measured gust of 71mph around 6:11pm on May 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spell of strong to near gale force easterly trade winds produced high surf of up to 8 to 12 feet along east facing shores of Kauai, Oahu, Molokai, Maui, Kahoolawe, and the Big Island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A harbor pilot fell into rough waters Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026. He slipped on a rope ladder while attempting to board a ship as it prepared to enter Nawiliwili Harbor on Kauai. He was retrieved safely by crew members.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on power lines on Skipperville Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across western Kentucky, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -1 to -9 degrees during the evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. Southwest portions of the Kentucky Purchase region experienced another interval of dangerous wind chills on the 25th while the Kentucky Pennyrile region remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across much of East Texas throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-5 inches, with isolated higher amounts across Northeast Texas, which remained near to 50% of their normal monthly rainfall. Even with the rains, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.
A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A metal awning was torn from a home into power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Post measured severe wind gusts from 1838 CST through 1843 CST. A peak wind gust of 65 mph was measured at 1839 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As southwest winds brought warm temperatures and moisture to the region, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed and worked east through the Lower Ohio Valley, resulting in flash flooding and a single report of wind damage across central Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Emergency Management reported a  submerged vehicle and water rescue on the  900 block of West Broadway in downtown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southern Illinois on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Williamson County, IL on the 26th. Northwest portions of southern Illinois and areas south of route 13 only experienced advisory criteria with values of -9 to -14. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the early morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Alexander, Pulaski, and Massac County, IL where wind chills warmed above -5 the morning of the 26th due to calmer winds.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to half-dollar size fell west of Browns.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 30 ft long healthy tree branch 7 to 8 inches diameter was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts across Peterman road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 16th, storms brought all severe hazards to Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported at Leisure Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak wind gust in Moore County was 70 mph  and this was observed at the mesonet site located one mile west-northwest of Fritch at 1217CST. Most gusts greater than 58 mph were observed in the county from about 1145CST through 1400CST, with a couple more high wind gusts in Dumas occurring closer to 1800CST. In addition, these high winds caused a semi truck to overturn on northbound Highway 87,three miles south of Dumas. Wind gusts up to 67 mph were measured by a nearby mesonet at time of incident. This occurred around 1245CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.

A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down along Buggs Island Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles and trees were downed in Beecher. A fire was started when one branch fell onto a power line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.
Bitterly cold air moved across northwest Indiana on January 23rd and January 24th with wind chills 20 below to 30 below zero.

A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front. Gusty winds occurred with the cold front passage during the evening of March 16.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station 3 miles east of Knotts Island measured a gust to 50 knots (58 miles per hour).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Wythe county in mid April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front moved through Central New York late in the daytime hours. This front provided enough lift to support isolated thunderstorms in a slightly unstable environment. One storm had strong gusts that resulted in several trees and wires down throughout the Hornell area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees and wires throughout Hornell. One tree fell onto a house on Church St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Ebenezer Church Road near its intersection with Muddy Flats Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.

The Inland Northwest region was impacted by two winter storm systems during February 16 through 19. A cold front brought lower snow levels to the valley floors. It was followed by a warm and moist weather system from California. While most locations had 1 to 3 inches, a few locations received 4 to 8 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported 6 inches of snow 6 miles southeast of Porthill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The difference in pressure between a departing high pressure system to the east and a low to the north helped generate strong winds on the morning of May 14th across northeast South Dakota. A peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station near Summit, while the ASOS at the Aberdeen Regional Airport recorded a peak gust of 59 mph.

Well above normal April rainfall upstream along the Ohio River from East Central Missouri and Central Illinois to Iowa/Wisconsin resulted in river levels on the Mississippi River rising into minor flood at Cape Girardeau to end the month, with minor flooding continuing into May. Impacts were limited to bottomland agricultural areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor flooding began at the very end of April along the Mississippi River across from Cape Girardeau, with limited impacts to low-lying areas. Flooding continued into May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread and consistent rainfall following a pattern change in mid-May led to reductions in drought severity across Central Alabama from late May into early June. As two-month rainfall totals heading into June were near or above average, along with recovery in stream flows around the state, Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Central Alabama during the first week of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lingering Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Chambers County in early June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KEWN ASOS measured a severe thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late morning and early afternoon on the 15th or March. Strong winds around 30 to 35 mph sustained began gusting to 58 mph plus across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. The strongest gusts measured was 71 mph measured by the Dalhart ASOS and 70 mph measured by the Guymon ASOS.

A cold front helped force a line of showers and weak thunderstorms that crossed from west to east across East Tennessee. Winds aloft were quite strong, and convective transport in the strongest cells helped bring those winds to the surface in the form of convective downdraft gusts, producing damage and high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strips of green tin roof were peeled off an inn on Chapman Highway by severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure supported by vigorous mid-level shortwave moved across northern NY and northern New England during the afternoon and evening hours of June 18th.||Moderate instability combined with directional wind shear at multiple levels and a cold front helped develop a line of thunderstorms in NY that increased in intensity and coverage as it moved across VT with wind damage as well as weak, isolated tornadoes in VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and powerlines downed by thunderstorm winds outside of the verified EF1 tornado path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong cold air advection in wake of a passing cold front led to gusty wind conditions capable of producing damage across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported power lines down in the 1000 Block of Ashley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several videos and photos via social media showed large trees down, including some on  houses or other structures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rain and mountain snow showers moved across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening of May 4th. Widespread snow then formed over the mountains and northern foothills during the early morning hours of May 5th and continued for most of the day. Across the lower elevations (below 6000 feet), precipitation type was mainly rain through the morning of the 5th and slowly began to turn over to snow during the afternoon. Snow then continued through the night of the 5th and early morning hours of the 6th. The heaviest snow occurred across the foothills and mountains of Boulder and Larimer Counties where 18 to 36 inches of snow fell. Areas west of I-25 to the base of the foothills received 4 to 12 inches, heaviest near the foothills. Main impact was broken tree branches on deciduous trees, some of which fell on powerlines leading to sparse power outages. Power outages topped 50,000 overnight the 5th and early morning the 6th. Denver International Airport (DIA) had over 700 flight delays and 40 cancellations for May 5th and May 6th. Numerous schools were closed on May 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on spotter and snotel reports, 7 to 16 inches fell across the area with the heavier snow falling east of the Continental Divide.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed large tree limbs broken just west of Randall Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large branches were knocked down onto North Enon Church Road at Meadowville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A villager living in the Ofu/Olosega islands region reported a series of small landslides across both islands. These landslides occurred during heavy rainfall on the 18th. Estimated rainfall over the islands is 5 inches throughout the day. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Electrical Transmission Lines (ETL)/wood poles leaning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter low pressure system brought heavy snow to the high terrain in Inyo County and high winds to areas of San Bernardino County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gust of 60mph was recorded at the Daggett-Barstow airport (KDAG).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple segments of heavy showers and a few thunderstorms moved across north Alabama during the evening hours. This resulted in a power pole being snapped and trees being knocked down in Jackson and Marshall Counties.  A couple of trees were also knocked down blocking roads in Lauderdale and Morgan Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13.
