EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills dropped below 15 degrees across Coryell County the morning of the 28th of January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. Cost of debris cleanup in Hyde county alone topped out at 1.4 million dollars. ||Electrical infrastructure was severely disrupted, causing $2.4 million in utility distribution damage across Hyde and Hand counties. Power was knocked out to 1,072 residents in Hyde County (94% of the county). Power generation was heavily impacted; at least 20 wind turbines were damaged or destroyed at the Triple H and North Bend wind farms, with replacement costs estimated at $50 million.||Day County suffered extensive damage, particularly around Andover, where straight-line wind speeds reached 100 mph. Extensive tree stands were leveled, grain bins dented, and buildings damaged at the Andover Threshing Grounds. Day County power damage reached $18,000, leaving 487 residents without electricity. A brief EFU tornado was confirmed near Andover.||Even as the storm system departed, wrap around high winds caused additional tree damage in areas that had just missed out on thunderstorm wind damage, with several trees and limbs down in parts of Aberdeen, and a peak wind gust measured on a personal weather station of 88 mph in the town of Westport (Brown county).||Governor Rhoden requested a Presidential Disaster Declaration to assist with damage cleanup and repairs for Hyde, Hand, Hughes, Buffalo and Stanley counties including Lower Brule and Crow Creek reservations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread thunderstorm wind damage occurred in the town of Highmore, including trees uprooted or snapped, grain bins dented, knocked over farm implements and trailers, and broken power poles. Almost every building in town suffered some form of straight-line thunderstorm wind damage. The South Dakota State University mesonet station 1 mile west northwest of Highmore, located on the municipal airport grounds, recorded a peak wind gust of 131 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of freezing rain moved across portions of central and southern MN. Despite ice accumulations accreting to less than a tenth of an inch, travel conditions were very slippery which results to numerous vehicle accidents and spin outs across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS station located at the Mora Municipal Airport observed approximately an hour of light snow. Although, snow accumulations were light, they did make for slippery travel conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph wind gust was measured at the Rexburg-Madison airport ASOS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the region and spread thunderstorms across far eastern Montana, a few of which became severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Wolf Point NW Montana Climate Office mesonet site (WOFM8) measured a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rare strong and damaging downslope wind event started in the early morning hours of March 12th and continued through March 13th. Intense mountain wave activity was also a contributing factor to widespread wind gusts between 80 to 110 MPH across southeast Wyoming. Numerous reports of tree damage, power outages, and property damage including flipped over sixteen-wheeler tractor trailer trucks were reported to WYDOT and the National Weather Service. Areas of blowing dust also resulted in lower visibility on area roadways, which added to the already difficult travel scenario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: All reporting observation sites across the northern Snowy Range Foothills measured persistent wind gusts over 58 MPH in a long duration wind event. Peak wind gust of 97 MPH was measured at Cooper Cove, northwest of Laramie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 4 to 12 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 3 and 4 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. Roads were snow covered and slick with reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported a 100 ft tall empty grain bin that collapsed in addition to a large tree that was pushed over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching surface low with a trailing cold front, southern winds brought warmer temperatures and moisture into central Kentucky. Highs temperatures and dew points reached into the 60s. This helped to generate enough instability to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. A couple of these storms dropped severe hail in Nelson and Fayette Counties.

The event, which peaked between Saturday, Jan 24, and Sunday, Jan 25, resulted in double-digit snowfall totals in some areas and widespread, dangerous travel conditions. Heaviest snowfall occurred near the Missouri-Arkansas border, with many locations receiving over 6 inches of snow. Moderate to heavy snowfall then occurred during through the day January 24 and into midday January 25th. Between 4-6 inches of snow were reported across the County, causing multiple schools and roads to close.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads were covered in high water north of De Kalb, with vehicles stranded in the flood waters. Report from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down wires onto a house that led to a fire that was then quickly put out.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 145 mph touched down in a field southwest of the intersection of E 2600 North Road and N 190 East Road. The tornado moved north through Long Point where it caused tree damage. Sporadic tree damage continued near Ancona and in Reading Township. The tornado intensified as it crossed Route 23 where it blew a grain bin off its foundation and dragged it for approximately 700 yards. Drone imagery near this location showed a truck that was dragged at least 200 yards through a field. Damage to trees and utility poles also occurred near Route 23. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system tracking through the western Great Lakes Thursday evening (3/12) through Friday morning (3/13) brought a swath of heavy snow to northern Wisconsin. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Management reported trees down along State Route 1061 and J T Conerly RD.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

A cold front brought several days of showers and thunderstorms to the region as it moved through the area, stalled, and then retreated back to the north. Isolated instances of hail, severe winds, and flooding occurred with this activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter measured a 64 mph wind gust with a handheld anemometer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Turkey measured a severe wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. The warm front lifted north Monday night, which brought the hot and humid weather further north and east to include northeast Wisconsin and the lakeshore with similar temperatures and dew points. The combination of hot temperatures and high dew points allowed heat index values to soar to 105 to 110 degrees both days. ||In addition to the hot temperatures, overnight lows only fell into the upper 70s to lower 80s Monday night (6/29) into early Tuesday morning (6/30), providing minimal relief from the hot temperatures. The heat wave broke when an area of showers and thunderstorms tracked through the area Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday evening (6/30).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong westerly winds aloft were able to mix down to the surface during peak afternoon heating coincident with mountain wave activity, leading to impactful high winds along the Rocky Mountain Front. Isolated instances of high winds spread farther east to the adjacent plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTFPS Flesher Pass measured a 60 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County comms reported multiple trees blown down along Highway 70 west of Morganton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following an Arctic cold front passage on the afternoon of January 22, a bitterly cold air mass settled into southern Wisconsin and much of the Upper Midwest. Air temperatures in the single digits to teens below zero would reach southern Wisconsin by the morning of January 23, combining with brisk northwest winds to create widespread wind chills between 35 and 45 below. The conditions prompted Extreme Cold Warnings across all of southern Wisconsin, with most school districts canceling classes on January 23. The school cancellations extended all the way up to the university level, with both the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Marquette University among major colleges electing to close on January 23. Extreme cold conditions continued over portions of central and east-central Wisconsin into the morning of January 24.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread wind chills between 35 and 40 below zero observed countywide on the morning of 01/23, with widespread wind chills between 30 and 35 below zero observed countywide during the late overnight of 01/23 through the early morning of 01/24. Coldest wind chill of 37 below zero observed at the West Bend Airport on the morning of 01/23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of Ten Mile Creek rose out of its banks and flooded Ten Mile Creek Road. North of Minerva, portions of Four Mile Creek spilled out of its banks and flooded Four Mile Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across the area with a line of showers and thunderstorms. The storms produced several tornadoes and gusty winds across southwest Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Straight line winds resulted in damage to roofs at a nursery. A trailer was also blown over. Time estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system developed along a baroclinic zone off the coast of Georgia during the overnight hours between Friday January thirtieth and Saturday January thirty-first. This low then began to rapidly deepen during the evening hours of January thirty-first while tracking northeastwards along the Carolina Coast making its closest point of approach to the coastal waters near North Carolina during the early morning hours of Sunday February first with a minimum pressure around 994 mb before the system departed off to the north and east. With strong high pressure ridging building in from the north and west a tight pressure gradient spread over most of our waters bringing Storm Force wind gusts to much of the coastal and interior waters of eastern North Carolina during the evening of January thirty-first to the morning of February first.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pamlico Sound XPM2 WeatherFlow site measured several hours of frequent storm force wind gusts between the evening of January thirty-first and the morning of February first. Reports came in via WeatherFlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video from broadcast media showed a small, rain-wrapped tornado moving generally eastward just south of Road 733A and Highway 75. Damage consisted of a small cluster of large downed tree branches, with estimated maximum winds of 80 mph.

An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Following 1.5 inches of snow reported at Keavy via amateur radio at 1930 EST on the 24th, freezing rain resulted 0.35 inches of flat ice accretion at KLOZ by 653 EST on the 25th. Additionally, 0.52 inches of measured flat ice was reported in London at 1131EST and an estimated 0.50 inches of flat ice was observed on utility lines in East Bernstadt, as per a social media picture report from 1158 EST on the 25th.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across parts of East Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only further expanded during the month of April.

CZ_NAME: SOUTH SLOPES OF THE CENTRAL BROOKS RANGE
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Middle June saw a disturbance track over the Central Brooks Range resulting in anywhere from 1 to 1.5 inches of rain in about a 24 hour period. While most rivers were ice free, plenty of snowpack remained across the higher slopes. With high temperatures generally in the 60's and overnight lows remaining above freezing, excessive snowmelt combined with heavy rainfall lead to rapid rises along area streams and rivers, including the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River. As a result, flooding was reported from Coldfoot to Wiseman.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to 1.5 inches of warm rain fell on remaining snowpack across the Central Brooks range resulting in a rapid rise of the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River between Coldfoot and Wiseman. Late evening on Monday the 15th, the public reported that water was moving over the road to Wiseman. A social media comment on the NWS Warning post came in just after midnight on the 16th stating that the water was high enough that it would be very difficult if not impossible to get in or out of Wiseman by road. In addition the NWS received reports from the general public stating that the water came up very fast, but did begin to slowly subside through the day on the 16th as the rain tapered off and came to an end.
