EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree limb was blown down onto a house, breaking the sunroof.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Anomalously dry conditions persisted across much of central Pennsylvania through February 2026, with USDM D2 (severe) drought persisting across portions of southern and eastern Pennsylvania. Multiple counties were added to Drought Warning status by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (PA DEP), including Adams, Franklin, Cumberland and Schuylkill counties, while Fulton County remained in Drought Warning status.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 (severe) drought conditions continued through the month of February 2026. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (PA DEP) maintained Drought Warning status for Fulton County through the month. Residents in Fulton County were urged to reduce their water use due to the ongoing drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably warm and humid airmass developed across central Illinois on March 26, 2026, with some locations recording record high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s. Dewpoints also surged into the lower 60s. As a cold front approached during the evening, scattered to widespread strong to severe storms developed along and ahead of the front, primarily in areas north of I-70. These storms produced hail as large as golf balls, as well as a few wind damage reports.

Numerous thunderstorms occurred over far southern WI as a warm front approached from the south. Repeated rounds of storms resulted in flash flooding in the Racine area, while some large hail occurred across far southern WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Five vehicles reported stranded in floodwaters in Racine from the Racine Police Department. 30 service calls taken by the Racine PD related to the flooding, including flooded roadways, underpasses, and uncovered manholes. Many yards and basements flooded. Flooding impacts also affected communities just to the west of Racine.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.
Isolated thunderstorms move southeast across the eastern Colorado plains during the late afternoon and evening of May 9th. Wind gusts up to 70 mph accompanied the stronger thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station LIC located in Limon Colorado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed along an Arctic front crossing the region late on the 15th. The low tracked from southern Piscataquis county to northern Washington county exiting across New Brunswick during the morning of the 16th. Snow developed to the north of the low track during the early morning hours of the 16th...persisting into the afternoon. The greatest snow accumulations occurred across northern portions of Aroostook county where total snow accumulations generally ranged from 4 to 6 inches...locally up to around 8 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations were estimated to range from 2 to 5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Louisiana and Arkansas and produced damaging wind gusts and hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown onto homes at 121 and 126 Gaylane Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into central NY, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked wires down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2) expanded across southeast Kansas especially towards the end of the month impacting all or portions of five counties. The combination of below normal precipitation by an inch to two along with early season temperatures in the low to mid 90s were two factors.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2) entered the far southeast corner of the county at the start of the month then expanded to most of the southern half of the county at very end of the month. The rest of the county was in moderate drought conditions (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on Battles Road in the Rehobeth area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport (BRO) recorded freezing temperatures (32F degrees or lower) for 4.5 hours from 4:15-8:55am CST on Monday January 26th. Harlingen/Valley International Airport (HRL) recorded freezing temperatures (32F degrees or below) for 11 hours from 10:30pm (Jan 25th) to 9:30am CST January 26th.  Minimum temperatures were in the mid to upper 20s.||An unknown amount of minor damage was likely to winter crops, mainly due to the sharp temperature change from prior to the freeze until after it.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the mid-60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2500J/kg in Southeast Missouri with DCAPE of 900J/kg, 0-6km shear of 35-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from Southeast Missouri were primarily hail based. The largest hail occurred in the town of Advance which had numerous reports of golf ball to tennis size hail and a couple reports of baseball size hail, producing damage. Straight line wind damage was observed with a supercell in Bollinger County, downing a tree and damaging a barn roof.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lots of tree limbs and a few larger branches were downed in the Leopold area as a supercell moved into eastern Bollinger County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system developed over the Northern Plains and tracked across the Upper Midwest. This brought a series of heavy snow bands to eastern ND and Northwest MN from the afternoon of April 3 through the evening of April 4. A large swath of heavy snow was reported across southeast North Dakota, with highest values 10 to 17.5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cocorahs station ND-GG-3 Cooperstown ND measured 7.1 inches for a storm total.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 6 to 10 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, moderate to heavy at times, developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 8 and 10 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. There was a report of 9.6 inches 2 miles south-southeast of Brailey. Roads were snow covered and slick with numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLNK ASOS measured wind gust of 68 mph at the Lincoln Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure passed to the south of Wyoming and brought snow to central and southern portions of the state. The heaviest amounts of snow fell in the favored northeast upslope areas. Some notable amounts in the mountains included 23 inches on Casper Mountain and 19 inches above Sinks Canyon Park near Lander. In the lower elevations, 8 inches of new snow fell in Casper and Jeffrey City and 5 to 12 inches fell near Lander. In Eastern Sweetwater County, the Green Mountains and Wind River Range, winds gusting as over 55 mph brought local blizzard conditions, leading to closure of Interstate 80, US 287 and South Pass during the storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of heavy snow and winds gusting as high as 65 mph brought blizzard conditions to eastern Sweetwater County, leading to the closure of Interstate 80 for many hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated thunderstorm developed during the late afternoon hours of April 11th. This thunderstorm resulted in damaging winds across Reno County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A semi was blown over near K14 and Parallel Road. A separate vehicle was also damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak clipper system moved from the Great Lakes across NY and New England during the night of January 6th through the morning of January 7th. Snowfall developed during the evening of January 6th and ended across northern NY just before daybreak on January 7th.||Snowfall totals ranged from 1-2 inches across the St. Lawrence valley to 3 to 5 inches in the Adirondacks of Essex county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches fell across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

Strong south-southwest wind developed within a tight surface pressure gradient between a departing high pressure system and developing low pressure system across the Northern Rockies. Deep daytime mixing allowed for isolated sustained winds around 40 mph and gusts to 63 mph across southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 43 mph at times at a Minnesota Department of Transportation site near Rushmore.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed along East County Road 125 South.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A semi was blown over near the city of Chenoa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded into Bedford county in the middle of May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm storm brought mountain snow-melt, heavy rain and gusty winds as a potent low pressure system pushed across the area March 16-17th.  This caused some minor ice jams, but no ice left its banks during this event.  Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches fell over the 36 hour period leading to rapid stream and river rises across the state.  A few rivers reached minor flood stage, with most other rivers remaining just below flood stage or in action stage.  Long term drought helped mitigate flood conditions as base flow river levels where very low.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Saco River at Conway reached minor flood conditions on the morning of March 17. Numerous campgrounds flooded. The river reached 9.23 ft, exceeding the 7 ft flood stage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds, gusting to 67 MPH, were reported at the Clear Creek RAWS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

Light west winds with seas of 2 to 3 ft prevailed in the morning of June 2nd ahead of an approaching front. Winds quickly increased and shifted to northeasterly in the afternoon as the front passed through. Breezy winds and elevated waves developed in the late afternoon into evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flagler Beach fire department, Flagler Beach Ocean Rescue and Flagler Beach Police department reported four individuals were swept into deeper waters due to rip currents at Flagler Beach. Two of the four were juveniles and were transported to the hospital in stable condition for further evaluation. No major injuries or fatalities were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported 2 inch diameter hail near Humbird.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second strong cold front moved into the region with high pressure slowly drifting across the area. This kept tides below normal for the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tide fell below -1 foot MLLW for multiple hours falling to a low of -1.29 foot at Cameron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Pre-frontal convection ahead of a cold front moving across the region produce a severe wind gust near Brooksville in Pasco County and downed trees and power lines near Chiefland in Levy County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed just north of intersection of U.S. Hwy 19 and NW 21 Ave near the Chiefland Regional Shopping Center.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported baseball sized hail in Saratoga.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second day of high winds occurred across East Central CO.  The high winds started after 9 AM and continued through 4 PM.  The peak gust was 72 MPH recorded at the Burlington airport.  The loose soil and high winds caused a dust storm to occur on the west side of Yuma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind speeds ranged from 58 to 63 MPH across the county, with the highest gust reported from a personal weather station near Idalia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Modest shear and instability associated with an approaching frontal boundary resulted in a line of pre frontal thunderstorms moving across interior southeast GA during the morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous mobile homes suffered major damage to roofs and siding in the Odum area. Many roofs were peeled off completely destroying the roof. A shipping container was also flipped onto its side. Time was estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 71 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Water Moccasin Fire burned 601 acres across northwestern Love County, north of Rubottom.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several reports of trees and power lines down throughout Hanover County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 70 mph wind gust recorded at Medicine Lodge mesonet site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 10th, a discrete supercell moved from Illinois into northwest Indiana. It produced an EF-2 tornado in Starke County with maximum winds of 115 mph, prompting a rare Tornado Emergency for the area near Knox, IN. Following the initial supercell, a line of storms moved through on the morning of March 11th. Training storms produced significant rainfall between 1 and 3, with localized amounts reaching 4-5, resulting in Flash Flood Warnings and Flood Advisories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on radar, an NWS Survey and reports from numerous spotter|and emergency management officials, one final tornado has been|confirmed with a cyclic supercell that originated in eastern|Illinois. The tornado quickly developed about 3 miles northeast|of the end of the Wheatfield, IN tornado, starting southwest of|the intersection of US 421 and CR W 400 S where 2 large pole|barns suffered extensive damage, as well as 3 empty grain bins.|The debris was carried up to a half mile downstream. Videos and|eyewitness reports indicate a large cone shaped funnel continued|northeast causing damage to trees, some center pivot irrigation|systems and a few other barns and homes, eventually crossing|State Road 39 near CR W 150 S. It then continued over mainly over|unplanted fields before causing some additional damage at SR|8 and CR N 250 E. It lifted just southeast of the Starke county|airport. The tornado has a few areas which suggested some multi|vortex funnels caused damage in the larger swath. After careful|analysis, along with storm chaser video footage and high|resolution satellite data, it was determined that a second weaker|tornado touched down south of Jackson for a brief period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing strong winds and dangerous marine conditions as the line moved offshore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XCLP at Clear Lake Park measured a 34 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between a half inch to one and a half inches of snow and sleet fell, along with a quarter inch of ice near the town of Oxford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ice accumulation of at least 0.25 inches, along with 2-3 inches of snow and sleet, impacted Adair County. The ice accumulation resulted in power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees fell down throughout Goochland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported low temperatures ranged from 28 to 30 across much of western Marshall County. The lowest reported temperature of 28 was at the Stephen, MN NDAWN at 4:50 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of a southeastward-moving upper system (and associated surface front) fostered scattered severe thunderstorms during the evening of the 9th, focused across portions of western Oklahoma. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard amid steep lapse rates and strong wind shear, sufficient for supercells. Focused areas of wind damage occurred near Sayre and northeast of Lawton as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hinton (HINT) Mesonet observation. Wind gust associated with a probable heat burst event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mixed precipitation briefly swept through southeast Ohio on March 2nd in the midst of a passing disturbance. These showers arrived into the area just before dawn when temperatures were still below freezing, keeping hydrometeors as wintry precipitation before fully transitioning over to rain in the afternoon. Local members of the public noted freezing rain during the morning, causing a glaze of ice to form along cars. Additionally, a cooperative observer in Perry County measured an inch of snow during this brief stint of winter weather.

A southern stream disturbance brought moisture over a very cold low level airmass on January 24 and 25th, 2026. Precipitation began as snow late on January 24 across the region but transitioned to a mix of mostly sleet and some freezing rain as temperatures warmed aloft on the 25th and 26th of January.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall ranged from 2-4 across the county. A trained spotter reported 4 of snow just across the state line in Shelbyville, DE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm began Saturday night and continued through Sunday as it passed over an entrenched arctic airmass. A strengthening surface low over the Tennessee Valley combined with upper level dynamics to produce snowfall of up to a foot in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A dispatcher measured 15.5 inches of snow 6 miles south-southeast of Laurel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from severe drought to moderate drought as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 100th to 200th percentile across much of SE West Virginia. Rainfall totals over the past 30 days ranged from 5.0 to 8.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to near normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Both Mercer and Monroe counties continued to remain in Severe drought as portions of those counties received rainfall totals closer to 3-4 inches over the 30 day period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Mercer county by late June after repeated rounds of rainfall during the month of June. The previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 30th to 70th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Bluestone River, which was observed to be below the 25th to 75th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought isolated flash flooding to the Heartland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Coleman County Sheriff Office reported street flooding in Coleman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Both on the evening of the 30th and late afternoon of the 31st, the southeast TX Panhandle was impacted by severe storms that formed as a small complex. Each day looked very similar on radar. These storms produced wind gusts up to 64 mph and hail up to the size of quarters on the 30th. On the 31st the storms did produce hail up to quarters but no wind gusts were recorded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail fell southwest of Hedley for about an hour and a half. Hail ranged from dime to quarter size, although damage occurred to skylights which would suggest that some larger hailstones also fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local emergency management relayed a report of an 80x200 storage building with structure damage consistent with winds around 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite a couple of periods of heavier precipitation, most of the month remained on the dry side with average temperatures near normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions temporarily improved to moderate (D1) during the first half of June but returned to severe (D2) late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered, high-based showers and isolated thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late evening of the 15th and early morning of the 16th, as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Isolated damaging wind occurred with a few of the thunderstorms. ||Strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts occurred with some of the showers. The ASOS at the Tulsa International Airport measured wind gusts up to 69 mph, and large tree limbs were snapped across Tulsa County by non-thunderstorm wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at the Tulsa International Airport measured wind gusts up to 69 mph. Large tree limbs were snapped across Tulsa County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 61 mph was measured at the Montrose Harbor Light.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued to burn into June. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May helped the final containment of local ongoing wildfires in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history across three counties, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. Per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC), the fire was 98% contained on June 3rd. The fire became 100% contained on June 10th. The total cost of the fire across three counties was $19,371,895.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southwest Indiana on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Vanderburgh County, IN on the 26th. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th with wind chill values warming above -5.

Low pressure moved from the Northern Rockies the morning of the 12th to the Upper Great Lakes the morning of the 13th and deepened as it moved east. This brought heavy snowfall to the region starting the afternoon/evening of the 12th and continued into the morning of the 13th. Snowfall totals of 4 to 8 inches were seen across the area with higher pockets of 7 to 10 inches plus, including a high report of 14 inches in Hovland. Additionally, strong winds off of Lake Superior led to a period of blizzard conditions along the North Shore into the Twin Ports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow and strong winds off Lake Superior led to a 9 hour period of blizzard conditions in the Duluth area during the event. Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were reported across the area with a high report of 11 inches from Esko.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near to below normal precipitation amounts over southwest New Mexico kept Severe(D2) drought conditions going through the month of March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe(D2) drought continued across the entire zone in March.  The Hillsboro Cooperative Observer reported just a trace of precipitation which was 0.30 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced a low end squall line of thunderstorms, which in turn produced several reports of damaging winds. After the cold front's passage, a much colder airmass moved in and snow showers developed, leading to light snowfall for much of northeastern Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow fell in Hawkins County, with 1 inch measured in Mooresburg and 1 inch measured in Rogersville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Most locations saw a dry start and middle of the month before more numerous convective systems impacted parts of the area toward the end of the month. This was especially true across far north-central Oklahoma and near the Red River, with central Oklahoma seeing near- to below-normal monthly rainfall totals. As a result, severe (or worse) drought persisted during the month, with some general category improvement towards the last days of the month.
Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts along the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The WeatherFlow station at Jensen Beach measured a peak wind gust of 37 knots from the southeast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System moved across the Ohio Valley on the night of June 17th, 2026 and the morning of June 18th, 2026. Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with a gusts to around 60 mph occurred across west central, southwest, and central Nebraska during the early morning hours until the early afternoon hours on March 15th. Peak wind gusts reached 60 mph or higher at the Imperial, Broken Bow and North Platte ASOS stations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts to around 50 mph or higher were common across McPherson County during the morning hours into the mid afternoon hours. A mesonet site 3 miles east southeast of Tryon recorded a peak wind gust of 56 mph at 505 am CST. The nearby North Platte ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 1107 am CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of a very subtle reinforcing front and high pressure settling over the region and gradually progressing eastward through the night, locked in light, variable, but mostly offshore winds for a cool, dry overnight into Sunday morning. This set us up for a chilly night, with light freezes experienced across much of the northern CWA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KNQI reported temperatures of 32 degF or less for a least 2 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Modest shear and instability associated with an approaching frontal boundary resulted in a line of pre frontal thunderstorms moving across interior southeast GA during the morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports of trees and powerlines down and property damage occurred in the Douglas, GA area. A carport was destroyed along Sinkhole Rd. Trees fell onto a couple of mobile homes along Bear Creek Rd destroying their roofs. The siding was blown off of mobile home along Worth Lane. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water resulted in a water rescue at a home near U.S. Route 50 and Stonelick Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received from Mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe weather occurred across west Michigan with 2 tornadoes causing damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires down at Cutler and Cedar Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted far southern and southeastern parts of Montana, producing low elevation snow up to a foot and up to 2-3 feet in the mountains. Some freezing rain was also reported during this weather system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet reported 6 inches of snow in southeast part of county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly sinking cold front provided lift for thunderstorm development during the evening hours across north Mississippi. Partial clearing of skies prior to the frontal arrival resulted in moderate destabilization. Climatologically, February is cooler, which increases confidence in very cold air aloft. The lift from the front, an unstable environment, and cold air aloft raised a primary concern for large hail. Elevated MUCAPE values (up to 1500 J/kg) and steep lapse rates resulted in hail up to golf ball size to occur.

Despite a rather volatile airmass for severe weather across Oklahoma and north Texas on the 26th, misaligned synoptic features (i.e., neutral-to-rising mid-level heights) and remnant convective inhibition limited the overall number/coverage of thunderstorms during the evening. The most significant storm was a slow-moving supercell storm near and north of Wichita Falls, Texas. This thunderstorm produced large to very large hail and yielded a pair of left-moving supercells that went on to produce hail into portions of adjacent southern Oklahoma. This included confirmations of baseball-size hail in areas east of Lawton, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Maximum hail size increased from quarter to golf ball during the event time. An image showing a ruler-measured hailstone was also shared. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were in place across most if not all of the Northern Outer Banks, Washington, East Carteret, West Carteret, Southern Craven, Coastal Onslow, Inland Onslow, and Pamlico Counties from the beginning of June until June thirtieth according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Southern Craven County from the beginning of June until June twenty-nineth. Severe drought conditions then ended across the county on June thirtieth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to its neighbors across the Mississippi River, West Tennessee spent April 2026 battling a persistent, long-term moisture deficit dating back to July 2025. While central and northern parts of the Midwest received heavy spring rains that broke their droughts, West Tennessee experienced a highly regionalized spring recharge gap. Abnormally hot temperatures and meager rainfall caused drought conditions to actively worsen across the region during the first half of the month, though patchy late-month systems provided highly localized stabilizing relief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions worsened to D3 conditions mid month and persisted through the end of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the overnight hours of January 20th into the 21st, a cold front with a strong pressure gradient brought gusty winds into the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. While most places in the Panhandles saw northerly winds gusting up to 45 to 55 mph, there were isolated instances of measured gusts in the 58 to 66 mph range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS located at the Dalhart Municipal Airport recorded the first high wind gust around 1250CST and the last high wind gust occurred at 1255CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant short-term drought relief was observed across Maine in May 2026, highlighted by a mid-May soaking rain that markedly improved drought categories in the mountains and foothills. In the single week ending May 19, the state's Severe Drought (D2) coverage fell from 11% to 2.2%. While this spring precipitation effectively mitigated immediate agricultural and hydrological impacts���replenishing topsoil moisture, restoring streamflows, and bringing surface water storage like lakes and reservoirs back to near-normal seasonal baselines���long-term deficits endure. Deep groundwater aquifers are slower to react, leaving deep water table levels substantially below historical averages due to these ongoing groundwater deficits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had 57% of Waldo County in Severe Drought (D2), but by the end of May severe drought was completely gone (0%), with 71% in Moderate Drought (D1) and 29% Abnormally Dry (D0). May rainfall averaged 4.62 inches, well above normal by 1.02���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 11-month period ending May 2026 still ranked as the 6th driest on record, leaving the area with a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through eastern New York, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Most of this precipitation fell in the form of snow, though some higher terrain areas received minimal accumulations of freezing rain and sleet with some lower-lying areas conversely receiving some plain rain. ||The highest accumulations of snow fell across portions of the Southwest Adirondacks and Upper Hudson Valley where 6 to nearly 10 inches were measured. Elsewhere, a couple of tenths up to 5 inches were common with the highest of these reported across the Catskills, Helderbergs, and Taconics. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: school delays and traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 5.9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed a large tree limb blown down along Ashley Road just south of Minooka Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees down in Cornplanter Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto the road at Green Road and Ward Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of gale-force wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 44 knots (51 MPH) was measured by the Herring Bay WeatherFlow sensor (XHEB).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near average rainfall for many areas kept drought conditions the same in May. The one change was in northern Sierra county where there was slightly below normal precipitation and the area was put in Extreme(D3) drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe(D2) drought remained over the far northern portions of the zone while Moderate(D1) drought existed elsewhere. The White Sands National Park Cooperative Observer reported 0.63 inches of precipitation which was 0.18 inches above normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.75 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Comanche Springs (COMA) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked east of the Ohio Valley before redeveloping off the Northeast coast on Sunday the 25th. Snow spread from south to north Sunday morning, becoming heaviest from mid-morning through the early evening. The snowfall gradually tapered off early Monday morning, though pockets of freezing rain and drizzle lingered across central New York. Light snow showers and flurries continued into Monday afternoon, accompanied by strong, gusty winds that caused localized blowing snow and reduced visibility. By Monday night, lake-effect snow showers developed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulated between 6 and 12 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports of trees and powerlines down across all of Kent County, including near Betterton. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through northeast Pennsylvania on Sunday, April 19th, ushering in a much colder air mass. Temperatures dropped into the mid-20s to lower 30s overnight and remained well below normal through Tuesday, April 21st. This event occurred before the Frost Freeze program was even underway for the season, but due to how far below freezing some areas reached, this unfortunately led to costly crop damage in northeast Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell below freezing for multiple nights in April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reports trees and power lines down near the intersection of bonds lake road and irwin bridge road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines were downed in the county. Estimated freezing rain accumulation was 0.25 inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on a daily basis across the region over Memorial Day weekend as a result of several passing upper level disturbances. Some storms produced severe hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Significant flash flooding occurred in North Richland Hills in Tarrant County on May 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video showed creek flooding near Precinct Road and Trinity Boulevard on the east side of Fort Worth. Walker Branch overflowed its banks, covering the road with what looked like water up to a foot deep in some places.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
A trough moving across the United States/Canadian border brought much needed mountain snow to the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges in southeast Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak snowfall reported in the Sierra Madres came from the Old Battle SNOTEL (OLDW4) with 9.1 inches. Several other SNOTELs reported snow accumulations above 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on powerlines along US Highway 117.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of slow moving storms, trained over the area producing flooding on several creeks and streams with rainfall amounts in excess of 3 to 5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kansas Route 31 between Kansas Routes 7 and 69 at Clever Creek was flooded and impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong clipper low tracked through the Upper Great Lakes, bringing widespread heavy snowfall which transitioned to lake enhanced/effect as the storm progressed. Over a foot of snow fell at several locations. Many school districts, colleges and a few businesses were closed across the U.P.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall created difficult travel conditions in Dickinson County.  Snowfall analysis and observations showed 6-12 of snowfall over much of the county.  Key impacts: travel delays, school closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the late morning of May 18th producing severe wind gusts, wind damage and one brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few tree limbs were broken in Roseland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm spotter reported a large tree branch snapped off near the base of the trunk west  of Palatka. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large section of aluminum siding blown off a building.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters and broken lines of thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of 4/15 in Ohio and progressed east into the local area. Beneath a belt of enhanced mid-level flow, effective shear values reached 40-50 knots with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE in place. This supported swaths of straight-line wind damage with damage to trees, power lines, and structures as well as hail up to golf ball sized.

Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed, with some on power lines, near Trotman Rd, west of Pike Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Gusty northeasterly winds behind a front, along with very low humidity and dry fuels, combined to create conditions favorable for fire starts and spread across Oklahoma on the 22nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Cross Timber Fire burned 857 acres across southern Pottawatomie County, northwest of Asher.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station UP856 recorded a wind gust of 51 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow showers developed through the day on the 31st with the heaviest amounts on the east side of the county. Total snowfall amounts ranged from 1 to 2 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although northwestern Arkansas received between three and ten inches of rain during May, much of the area experienced below average precipitation during the month. The exceptions were in northern Benton and eastern Carroll Counties, where monthly precipitation was 125 to 175 percent above average monthly precipitation amounts. Much of the region only received between 50 and 75 percent of the average monthly rainfall.  This resulted in severe (D2) drought conditions being maintained in portions of Madison and Carroll Counties, and expanding into portions of Crawford and Franklin Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.
Scattered thunderstorms produced localized wind damage, localized flooding and one brief tornado during the afternoon and evening of June 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Street flooding was reported in and near Naperville. Around one foot of standing water was reported covering a portion of Riverlea Circle. One to two feet of standing water was reported on Gartner Road and Charles Street. Six inches of standing water was reported on Washington Street between 75th Street and 87th Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful and expansive storm system brought widespread heavy wintry precipitation across nearly two thirds of the width of North America, stretching from the southern Rockies and southern Plains, across portions of the Midwest, Deep South, and Southeast, into the Mid-Atlantic and New England. For the Mid-Atlantic region, this was an overrunning precipitation event, with a very cold and dry, arctic airmass in place ahead of the storm. The main low pressure center passed offshore just to the south of the forecast area.||Precipitation began as all snow across the local region during the very early morning hours of January 25th. A transition to sleet occurred from south to north after dawn, reaching as far north as the I-78 to I-80 corridors by the evening before precipitation ended. Some freezing rain occurred across the coastal plain of New Jersey and Delmarva during the afternoon and evening hours. The marine front remained south and east of the I-95 to I-195 corridors. North of the front (along and north of the I-95 to I-195 corridors, including much of the Philadelphia metropolitan area, central and northern Delmarva) into the I-78 corridor, temperatures remained in the 10s (and even single digits near the I-78 corridor) when snow changed to sleet. Total sleet accumulations between 1-3 were reported in this region, on top of approximately 5-10 of snow. North of the I-78 corridor, precipitation remained mostly all snow, where near a foot or more of accumulations were reported, though at least some mixing of sleet was reported as far north as I-80.||The snow and sleet proved very challenging to remove following the storm due to the weight and density of the ice-capped snowpack and below freezing temperatures. At least 3 fatalities related to snow removal occurred in the Lehigh Valley. Snow removal took a few days in some places. Untreated or unplowed pavement remained covered in snow and/or ice for one to two weeks following the storm.||A 17 day period of largely well below freezing temperatures began the day before this storm on January 24th and continued through February 9th. This was one of the coldest 17 day periods in several decades for much of the region at the time. Mean temperatures in the period ranged from the mid 10s to low 20s. The extreme cold preserved the ice-capped, glacier-like snowpack for approximately 3 to 4 weeks following the storm. The snowpack remained across the entire region until about the third week of February, before melting away completely in most areas due to light rainfall and low temperatures remaining above freezing for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow and sleet accumulation totals mainly ranged from 8-12. The highest report received was 12.5 in Malvern.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system and arctic blast brought strong winds and pockets of light to moderate snow showers.  ||A peak wind gust of 71 mph was observed 1 mile north northwest of Lees Corner in Buffalo County by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Information Weather System (RWIS), and by a personal weather station 2 miles north of the Pierre Regional Airport. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded by the SDDOT RWIS station 1 mile northeast of Stephan in Hyde county, while 66 mph wind gusts were measured by the SDDOT RWIS stations 5 miles south southwest of Klein Ranch in Corson county and 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake in Dewey county.  A total of 39 weather stations recorded a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. These high winds flipped a semi and damaged a grain elevator near the town of Murdo on the morning of the 16th. ||While snow accumulations were limited, snow showers of moderate intensity combined with these strong winds to produce temporary white-out conditions. No Travel Advised was issued by both the Walworth and Day county Sheriffs. Various SDDOT RWIS webcams showed visibility in blowing snow fluctuating significantly over short distances in the matter of a few minutes. An emergency vehicle rendering assistance for an accident on Interstate 29 near Watertown was struck with minor injuries. A separate accident along Interstate 90 resulted in a 5 vehicle chain reaction crash which resulted in 2 fatalities and a number of injuries.  ||80 residents of Deuel county reported power out during the event.
Diurnal convection interacted with a very moist atmosphere across portions of Louisiana. These slow moving storms produced flooding and a report of damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple roads were flooded in Breaux Bridge and Cecelia and some were impassable with cars stalled. Water also briefly entered Saint Martin Hospital  in Breaux Bridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a 70 MPH wind gust as measured by a home weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The weather pattern began to turn more rainy/stormy during April 2026 across Oklahoma and western-north Texas, especially late in the month along and east of the Interstate 44 corridor. This helped to generally improve drought conditions here. Continued below-normal early spring rain totals across western and portions of northern Oklahoma intensified prolonged drought conditions for this region.

There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Rock River at Lake Koshkonong rose to Moderate flood stage. There was widespread flooding of roads and docks in the Town of Koshkonong and Town of Sumner including Vets Lane, Blackhawk Island Road and Oxbow Bend Road. There was knee-deep water over Blackhawk Island Road. Lamp Road on the west side of the river also became flooded. Lake Koshkonong merged with Mud Lake to the east of Lake Koshkonong.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly amplified synoptic pattern over the CONUS generated an environment with 50-60kt+ wind barbs in the 850-700mb layer and mixing layer winds of 45-50kts. This resulted in numerous 50-70 mph gusts across the entire CWA with a couple reported gusts of 70+ mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station Beef_Belt_LLC recorded a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A barn wall was blown down.
