EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grenora NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree uprooted about one-mile east of Brooklyn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees across Coffee County and caused roof damage to the library in Manchester. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down on power lines on Sherri Lynn Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass settled over the region behind a strong cold front crossing the area. The combination of cold temperatures and breezy conditions caused wind chills in the 20 to 40 degrees below zero range. Daytime highs only reached the||Notable wind chill values across the area include: -43 degrees Fahrenheit at Philadelphia, -37 degrees Fahrenheit at Cape Vincent and -34 degrees Fahrenheit at Redfield and Grove.

Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 25th ahead of a slow-moving cold front situated near the Ohio River, with precipitable water values reaching into the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the Southside area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis. Abundant daytime heating allowed CAPE values to reach in excess of 1,500 J/kg during the evening. A line of slow-moving thunderstorms developed along a nearly-stationary surface trough that extended from Carroll County through central Halifax and Charlotte Counties, with multiple cells observed training along this boundary. The heaviest rain was observed within the Polecat Creek and Miry Creek basins, where nearly 5.5 inches fell within a 3-hour period. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to be producing rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour. Cells began to develop over the basins at around 6:00 pm EDT, with training reaching a maximum at around 8:00 pm EDT. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D3: Extreme Drought highlighted for all of Halifax County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 200-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration along a east-west strip within the west-central portion of the county, with rainfall totals reaching 150 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 350 to 650 cfs per mi^2 during the storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chatham Road was observed flooded and impassible as heavy rain caused Polecat Creek to rise out of its banks several inches deep across the roadway surface.  No damage was observed to the road, which was reopened to traffic after the flooding receded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 16th, storms brought all severe hazards to Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported in New Hampton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system moved over the Great Lakes region Saturday evening, resulting in warm air advection in the mid-levels. Deep warm nose led to sleet, and then a sleet/freezing rain mix early Sunday morning in the north and Central Highlands region. Very cold low-level layer helped precipitation to refreeze. Roughly an inch or so of snow fell in the north, alongside an inch to an inch and a half of sleet by Sunday morning. Impacts were mainly just a messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: System brought up to 1 inch of snow in Northeast Aroostook, alongside 1-1.5 inches of sleet as snow transitioned to sleet. Caribou ASOS also recorded a trace of freezing rain. NWS employee measured 1.2 inches of sleet in Caribou.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread synoptic snow caused a moderate snowfall across Western and North Central New York on Sunday January 25th through the most of the day on Monday January 26th. Snowfall was the result of a couple of passing surface lows over the region, including a stronger coastal low. Lake enhancement and upsloping caused greater and more prolonged snow to fall closer to the lakes. Widespread snowfall amounts of 6 to 10 inches were observed across most of the Buffalo forecast area, with higher amounts of 10 to 16 inches reported closer to the lakes. ||Some of the notable snowfall reports include: 17.5 inches in Oswego, 16.0 inches in Penfield, 15.0 inches in Hilton, 13.4 inches in Eden, 13.2 inches in Sodus Point, 12.9 inches in West Carthage, 11.5 inches in Adams, 11.3 inches in Wyoming, 11.0 inches in Stafford and Lowville, 10.7 inches in Lockport, 10.0 inches in Cheektowaga and 8.0 inches in Medina.
Thunderstorms moving across eastern Iowa produced hail up to the size of pennies as they moved across eastern Iowa during the early morning hours in Johnson and Scott Counties.

A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in western Maryland across Garrett and western Allegany counties where 3 to upwards of 15 inches of snow fell. A secondary max associated with an inverted trough was observed from the Catoctins down to northern Montgomery county where 3 to 8 inches fell. Upwards of 12 inches were observed across the Catoctins. Another max of 3 to 6 inches was observed across Calvert and St. Mary's counties. The final max was Carroll to Cecil counties where 4 to 9 inches fell. Elsewhere across the DC and Baltimore metro, there was a relative minimum of 2 to 4 inches. Very little snow fell across eastern Allegany into far western Washington County.

A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple areas of minor street flooding around Central Ave and Nicholson Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Antecedent arctic air mass, combined with some radiational cooling on the night of the 7th into the 8th, resulted in a very cold night. Light winds of 5mph or less resulted in apparent temperatures of -15F or colder in many locations, some for several hours, but briefly in a few sites.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gaylord Regional Airport in Gaylord, MI reported an apparent temperature of -22F. Low temperature reported by cooperative observer 11mi ENE of Vanderbilt was -17F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures cooled across SE Alaska along with outflow winds during the first couple days of January after December's big snow dump. This allowed the next system that moved in from the west on the 4th and 5th to start out as snow. Prefrontal snow showers during the evening of the 4th added to the storm total snow for parts of the northern and central panhandle, then the main system moved in overnight with heavy snow on Monday the 5th (set to be the first day back at school after Winter Break for most locations). The southern panhandle saw a change over to rain during the day on the 5th, then the rain/snow line pushed northward through the night and into the morning of the 6th. Some strong winds accompanied the front, starting out of the north then shifting to the south with the front and causing temperatures to rise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Start and end times are estimated based on surrounding observations and measurements from Kake, Hoonah, and Juneau since the Angoon Seaplane Base AWOS was down at the time. The Hidden Falls Hatchery COOP on Baranof Island, across Chatham Strait from Angoon (not in the same zone but another reference station), measured 12 inches of new snow at their 5pm report on the 5th. At 425pm on the 5th Angoon School District announced on social media that a delayed start was planned for the following day due to weather. At 908am on the 6th the decision was made to shift to remote learning due to hazardous icy road conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.

A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down near the intersection of hwy 29 and cedar creek rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions persisted across the tri-state area through April and into May with D3-D4 drought continuing.

The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions,  Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural  activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred, despite a significant snow event, which produced little changed in drought conditions through the month leaving Severe (D2) drought and Moderate (D1) drought conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the region Wednesday and Thursday that brought heavy rain, damaging wind, and several brief tornadoes to eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO.  The more widespread wind damage occurred Wednesday afternoon June 10th from a derecho that developed in eastern Iowa and moved east. This downed trees, power lines primarily along and north of I-80. The more significant winds between 70-80 mph winds were seen north of the Hwy 20 corridor. A second round of storms later on produced isolated wind damage, including some damage north of Geneseo, IL that was due to straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down near the intersection of County Road  64 and 200th Ave. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines and poles were reported down causing power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 4 to 12 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 4 and 6 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. Roads were snow covered and slick with reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wildfire near Cross Creek, FL of 134 acres remained ongoing during the month of April, increasing containment to approximately 75% by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms developed in north central Kansas during the mid afternoon on 4/26 and tracked eastward through northeast Kansas, producing large hail to ping pong ball size and wind gusts estimated to around 70 mph. Clusters of late evening severe storms impacted much of northeast Kansas through the early morning of 04/27. Large hail to Golfball size and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported. Flash flooding also occurred in Shawnee, Jefferson, and Douglas counties as in upwards of 5 inches of rain fell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lawn furniture was blown around and into the side of the house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon hours of March 10th, supercells brought massive hail to portions of eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar sized hail reported near I-435 and Leavenworth Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low in the Central Plains moved northeast into the Great Lakes late on Sunday the 15th. Ahead of its attendant cold front that passed later in the evening, a low level jet developed in the late morning and moved east. Daytime heating gave added energy to mix the lower levels of the atmosphere and bring strong winds from this feature to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down on Fair Road in Sidney.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated strong summer thunderstorms formed during the afternoon in central Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced a 62 mph wind gust at the Riverton airport.

CZ_NAME: MOUTH OF CHESAPEAKE BAY FROM NEW POINT COMFORT TO LITTLE CREEK, VA
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front. Gusty winds occurred with the cold front passage during the evening of March 16.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Poquoson River Light (XPQR) mesonet measured a gust to 52 knots (60 miles per hour).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected portions of Hancock and Pearl River Counties from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding reported on Springfield Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Georgia Automated Environmental Network  rain gauge at the Alma / Bacon County  Airport measured 6.63 inches of rainfall since midnight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Large hail and heavy rain impacted lower Michigan on March 10-11. Between 1 to 3 inches of rain fell in a short period of time, resulting in localized flash flooding and closed interstates with trapped cars in several counties.
Some severe thunderstorm outflow winds occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 64 mph wind gust measured at Oneida Narrows mesonet station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.

A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow associated with a coastal system began during the early morning hours of February 22, 2026 become heavier during the evening hours and into the morning hours of February 23rd across Lancaster County. Lingering light snow did occur throughout the day on February 23rd before slowly tapering off during the evening hours. Snowfall totals generally ranged between three to five inches with the multiple reports across eastern portions of the county ranging between five to seven inches of snowfall from this system. A tractor trailer overturned on State Route 272 in Drumore Township due to slick roadways on February 22nd, injuring one person. During the early morning hours of February 23rd, another tractor trailed jackknifed on US Route 222 in Manheim Township closing the roadway for a period of time. Winds associated with this system also knocked down a tree onto wires in Ephrata Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought as covering approximately 35% of Colorado Zone 009 - Grand and Battlement Mesas, with 55% of the zone under Extreme (D3) Drought, and 10% under Severe (D2) Drought. Drought conditions remained unchanged for much of the month. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought was reduced to 15% coverage, with 70% of the zone now under Extreme (D3) Drought, and 15% under Severe (D2) Drought. Impacts thus far from the drought have been limited to economic losses due to the lack of snowpack, mainly focused on tourism and the one ski area in the zone. The Colorado State Climatologist has referred to the 2025-2026 winter as historically bad. Those who live and work in the zone are beginning to be concerned with what the drought means for the summer wildfire season. Additionally, there is concern over water quality and availability as many who live in this zone draw their water from water stored from snowmelt.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong winds were observed across multiple locations in southeast Ohio on February 20th as they accompanied a cold front. The initial burst of winds arrived in the late morning timeframe with the frontal passage, and continued to be breezy to strong through the day as stronger winds from aloft mixed down to the surface. The strongest winds in the area measured that day was reported from an AWOS observation site in the town of Jackson with a 47 mile per hour gust noted around the time of the front's passage. Several trees were blown down in the midst of these stronger winds as a result. High pressure building in from the west helped to ease the stronger winds just before midnight that evening.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.75 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

May 2026 in West Tennessee was a textbook example of weather whiplash. The month began with the region enduring the peak of a grueling, multi-season drought that originally took hold in late 2025. Because a persistent weather pattern had largely cut off moisture from the Gulf of Mexico for months, West Tennessee completely missed its traditional winter and early spring recharge window.||However, the narrative flipped abruptly during the second half of May. A significant atmospheric shift finally broke the dry dome, bringing heavy, consistent rainfall and improving conditions to West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 Extreme Drought conditions improved to D2 Severe Drought by the end of the month. A small, localized area of D3 persisted into June in western portions of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot conditions prevailed across the Panhandles during the week of June 8 through 12. However, the combination of lingering moisture, a dryline and these hot conditions allowed for a few thunderstorms to develop each day during the afternoon and evening. Some of these storms were severe with hail and damaging winds being the main hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm wind gust of 96 mph was measured at the Oklahoma mesonet site located 11 miles northeast of Eva. The site also measured wind gusts of 70mph at 920pm and 58mph at 925pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved through lower Michigan late on the 14th into the early morning hours on the 15th. Very strong winds and 2 tornadoes occurred in the Grand Rapids forecast area. Total of 9 tornadoes were confirmed in Lower Michigan during this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage on the south side of Fine Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate to strong Santa Ana winds set up late in the day on January 8th along coastal slopes and into the valleys of Southern California in the wake of an inside slider low pressure system. The pattern remained favorable for Santa Ana winds through the weekend with strong surface high pressure in place over the intermountain west. Gusts of 60-80+ mph were common along coastal slopes and through the foothills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Edison mesonet station recorded a 69 mph wind gust at Lytle Creek Ridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was split in half and fell on a powerline.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving surface low pressure moving along the Michigan and Wisconsin state line on the 24th brought thunderstorms that caused severe hail and urban flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image shared on social media indicated a flooded intersection at E Broad and Fourth. The time of this flooding was estimated by radar. Broadcast media also reported heavy rainfall caused sewer overflows and forced L'Anse to close the waterfront and beach. Rainfall reports throughout the region ranged from 1 inch to over 3 inches between mesonet stations, Co-OP Observers, CoCoRaHS stations, and public reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms on June 10th brought severe wind gusts and isolated large hail to portions of western Wisconsin throughout the day. The most prolific of these rounds was during the afternoon, where wind gusts as high as 85 mph were reported with a bow echo that clipped southern Grant County and continued eastward across southern Wisconsin. This intense complex that was later classified as a derecho by SPC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree that fell on a house in Mauston. The tree was roughly 2 and a half feet in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter network report of 55 to 60 mph winds, with a few 65 mph gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Schenectady and Saratoga Counties in early March after an ice jam broke loose on the Mohawk River. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. As a direct result of the ice jam flooding, the SUNY Schenectady campus was closed on March 9th with all classes on campus cancelled due to associated parking lots and roadways inundated with low amounts of standing water. Additionally, NWS Albany was made aware that Rosendale Road between Mohawk Road and Niskayuna Road was closed due to flooding from this same ice jam. However, local emergency managers in the area stated that this flooding was more minor compared to the flooding in Saratoga County. Here, the town of Halfmoon sustained more significant impacts with the closure of Riverview Road near Boyack Road. In a recording of a local news report, water from a small stream stemming off the Mohawk River was overrunning a low point in the road to a fairly significant extent. The water was also moving at the time of the broadcast and the reporter noted that it had begun to recede compared to what it had been. Luckily, it only took about 24 hours or so for the flooding to recede from all areas, allowing the aforementioned roadways and the SUNY Schenectady Campus to promptly re-open by the following morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Albany Meteorologists contacted the Schenectady County Warning Point to seek more information about flooding from an ice jam that had been reported on by a local news team. The warning point relayed that Rosendale Road was closed between Mohawk Road and Niskayuna Road due to the same ice jam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of strong winds and light snow just the day prior, many locations saw a second cold front move through the region, producing gusty winds and light snow from the morning of the 18th through the morning of the 19th. Since there was little to no snowpack on the ground, any reductions in visibility depended on how heavy the falling snow was and how strong winds were. Conditions were generally worst in open, rural areas where the snowfall was able to blow around easier.||Winds gusted up to 45 mph in parts of western and southern Minnesota, and generally under an inch of snow fell across the region. Visibilities dropped to 1/4 mile in several locations, though it was often brief due to the showery nature of the snowfall. The snowfall was heaviest before the strongest winds developed, limiting overall impacts from this event.||The strongest measured wind gusts from January 18-19 were:|46 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN.|45 mph at KBDH in Willmar, MN.|44 mph at KAXN in Alexandria, MN.|44 mph at KDXX in Madison, MN.|44 mph at KJYG in St James, MN.|43 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds gusting to 40 mph and scattered snow showers resulted in periodic reductions in visibility as low as a 1/4 mile at times. The worst conditions were during the afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.
A coastal low offshore and upper trough combined with deep arctic air led to significant snowfall across the Carolinas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 31 and ended on February 1, ranging from 7 to 10 inches across the zone, with an isolated area of 10 to 18 inches in the western part of the zone near the state line. County schools were closed the two days following the events. Impacts from the storm were limited.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a strong arctic high pressure system and very dry air resulted in very cold temperatures ranging from zero to 10 degrees above zero on the morning of January 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures ranged form 5 to 10 degrees across Tom Green County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed around midday over the central Nebraska Panhandle. This activity tracked to the east and southeast into the evening hours, producing numerous damaging wind and large hail reports. The greatest damage was at the eastern end of Lake McConaughy. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 81 MPH were reported. Hail up to golf ball size was reported near Imperial.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported from Mpng.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam (PUTN) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado crossed from Macon County into Shelby County just east of Route 51 near Long Grove Creek.  It tracked east, just south of the county line for about 1.8 miles, damaging trees and electrical transmission lines.  The tornado lifted 3 miles northeast of Moweaqua along N 1000 East Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 16th, a Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved from west-southwest to east-northeast across the lower Ohio Valley, providing forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. Thunderstorms were able to feed off of a seasonably high amount of instability, with around 2000 J/kg Mixed-Layer CAPE present in the pre-storm environment. While synoptic scale ridging over the southeast US meant that large scale flow was fairly weak, the MCV provided a mesoscale enhancement to the wind shear profile, with around 30-35 knots of effective shear supporting organized multicell clusters. Scattered strong to severe storms moved along the Ohio River in north central Kentucky, producing several reports of wind damage as well as isolated instances of near-severe sized hail. The most robust storm of the evening produced a 65 mph wind gust as it moved across Oldham and Henry County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down onto River Road near Lockport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low and subsequent coastal low pressure brought heavy snow to northeastern North Carolina from January 31 to February 1, 2026. Heavy snow was focused along the coast with lower amounts with westward extent.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow fell from January 31 to February 1, 2026 across Perquimans County. Event total snowfall amounts ranged from 6-9 across the county. A snowfall total of 9 was received two miles (SW) from Burgess.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree onto a home on Good Hope Road in Ethridge. Several other trees were also downed in the area. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front advancing northward over cold ground helped cause widespread fog to form late on March 7th and early on March 8th. The fog dissipated by mid morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Trenton-Mercer Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on Big Sandy River Road near the underpass, blocking half of the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 2 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass surged into southern Mississippi behind a strong cold front on January 25���26, 2026, resulting in dangerously cold temperatures and wind chills across the region.  Strong cold air advection, driven by a 1040+ mb surface high building southward into Texas and Louisiana, combined with persistent north winds of 10 to 15 mph to produce hazardous conditions.  By the morning of January 27th, air temperatures had fallen into the teens and 20s across southern Mississippi. When combined with strong northerly winds, wind chills dropped into the single digits across southwest Mississippi and values generally ranging from 10 to 15 degrees along the Mississippi Gulf Coast. These conditions persisted for several hours during the early morning, prompting an Extreme Cold Warning for the entire area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local observations showed wind chills dropped into the single digits for several hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems moved over southern California during the mid part of the month of February, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms, strong and gusty winds, and high elevation snow from the 10th thru the 11th, and then again on the 16th thru 18th. This resulted in a few reports of damage due to strong winds from thunderstorms. There were also several reports of flooding/flash flooding due to heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Member of the public reports medium-sized tree snapped in half and landed on their car. Picture provided via social media with wind estimates near 30-40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on Mill Swamp Road in Isle of Wight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were blown down by thunderstorm winds in a swath between northwest of Elkin and the community of Stony Knoll. This included a tree blown down at the 1300 Block of Stanley Mill Road. A power line was reported down along Bronco Trail. A large tree was blown down near the intersection of Highway 268 and Spice Farm Way. Another large tree was down along the 11000 Block of Highway 268. A large tree was reported down near the intersection of Highway 268 and Cedar Forest Drive, while another was blown down near the intersection of Joe Layne Mill Road and Beach Road. A power pole and multiple power lines were blown down near the intersection of CC Camp Road and Highway 268, while another power line was reported down along Highway 601. Multiple large trees were blown down near the intersection of Highway 601 and Highway 268, near the intersection of Highway 268 and Chariot Lane, near the intersection of Highway 268 and Bear Creek Church Road, and along the 400 Block of Roy Stanley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact low pressure system moved through the region from the evening hours of March 12th to the morning on March 13th. As this moved northward, a band of heavy snow moved through Taylor County bringing heavy snow accumulations to the area. Combined with increased winds, this resulted in localized whiteout conditions at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across Taylor County ranged from 6 to 8 inches as snow moved through the region during the evening on March 12th and into the early morning on March 13th. The highest reported snowfall total in the county was in Westboro where 7.7 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th and 19th. On the 19th, a cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms produced widespread lightning (over 2500 strikes), heavy rainfall of 1 to over 2 inches and several reports of flash flooding in western NV from Stagecoach to southeast Reno/Hidden Valley, east Sparks to Lockwood and Spanish Springs. Hail up to 1��� diameter and wind gusts of 60-75+ mph also occurred with these storms as they pushed across northwest and west central NV.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement and public reported flash flooding in Spanish Springs. This included a house flooded on Moonbeam Drive as well as water one to two feet deep at the intersection of Talking Sparrow Drive and Garnet Star Way.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of eastern ND and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening, with very large hail and severe winds reported over parts of eastern ND. The largest hail was the size of softballs in south Fargo, ND.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed photo of 4  inch hail stone next to tape measurer from south Fargo area. Estimated location and time based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts moving through western and central North Dakota combined with a series of short-wave troughs resulted in an extended period of strong winds. The strongest reported wind gust was 74 mph at the Bowman Airport in Bowman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hettinger ASOS reported wind gusts to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed during the afternoon of 6/14 along strong low level convergence associated with a prefrontal trough. Moderate instability with MLCAPE around 1500 J/kg and enhancement from an outflow boundary led to damaging wind gusts in a portion of the line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four pine trees uprooted and additional trees broken near the intersection of Hwy 6 and Blackville Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with large hail fell across portions of southwest Missouri during the morning of March 4th. Additional thunderstorms with large hail fell across southern Missouri during the evening of March 4th. The two rounds of thunderstorms produced a swatch of 2-4 inches of rainfall from Cassville to Springfield to Salem. This rainfall caused localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Buck Road in Christian County was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree was downed across both lanes of Peeled Chestnut Ridge Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gusts of 52-62 mph from near Blanchardville to Monroe. Frequent wind gusts in the 50 mph range across the county. Many branches down and a small number of power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong area of low pressure brings strong front through the region and brought high winds that impacted much of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SD Mesonet recorded wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An widespread area of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall of 2-4 inches in a short period of time during the morning that resulted in flash flooding and some downed trees in Cullman county. Isolated strong storms occurred in the afternoon hours as well. One storm downed a tree in Morgan county, Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At least 6 inches of water was reported flowing over Oliver road by a digital media entity on Oliver road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front brought wind gusts of 45-55 mph to the northwest and far western NV for the afternoon-evening of the 15th, with colder than average temperatures (highs mainly in the 50s) prevailing through the 17th. Most communities in western NV saw sub-freezing temperatures on the morning of the 17th, with a relatively rare Freeze Warning issued in April due to an early start to gardening, agriculture and irrigation resulting from the March heat event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: RAWS CATN2 Catnip Mountain measured a wind gust of 47 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility company reported trees blown down on power lines and causing outages in Belmont and vicinity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured at 2.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent Arctic Front across southern Ontario and western New York began to shift southeasterly during the late evening hours of December 31, 2025 and continued into the early morning hours of January 1, 2026. This potent cold front allowed for a line of snow squalls to form across all of central Pennsylvania, with widespread whiteout conditions are the line of squalls moved through the area. Whiteout conditions were observed at the NWS State College office, along with by multiple spotters in Centre, Mifflin, Blair, and York counties. No accidents or injuries were reported during these snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall was observed at Harrisburg International Airport, with visibility at or below one quarter of a mile for the duration of the snow squall with heavy snow being reported at the airfield in the early morning hours of January 1, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding from heavy rain on Westbound Interstate 80 at Penryn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A hail swath from a mile to 2 miles wide continued from northeast of Marionville and continued to the northeast across far western Christian County. Hail from quarters to baseballs in size fell along a path from northeast of Marionville to north of Billings as a left moving supercell moved to the northeast across the County. Along the storms path, numerous homes, vehicles, businesses, equipment, crops, livestock and other structures were damaged by hail before the storm passed into southwestern Greene County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mature mesoscale convective system (MCS) impacted portions of far northern Oklahoma during the very late evening of the 1st into the early morning hours of the 2nd. Several severe wind gusts were observed across this area during that time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Medford (MEDF) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of May 27th into the morning of the 28th, plenty of atmospheric moisture and lift led to training thunderstorms across the northeastern combined Panhandles. Some flooding eventually occurred in northern Lipscomb County due to the heavy and repeated rainfall. Going into the 29th, moisture and lift continued to lead to thunderstorms, some of which became severe with hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 75 to 80 mph. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One inch hail occurred one mile north of Happy, TX off of Interstate 27. Small  accumulating hail also occurred at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of April, persisting extreme drought (D3) and  exceptional drought (D4) conditions area-wide. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of beneficial rainfall in April continued the Exceptional (D4) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public mPING report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second day of high winds occurred for Northwest Kansas.  The high winds began after 9 AM MT and continued as late as 5:30 PM MT.  The peak gust was 76 MPH reported at the Goodland airport.  The combination of high winds and loose soil led to dust storm conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on Red Willow, Hitchcock, and Thomas counties observing high wind gusts of atleast 58 MPH, Decatur county should have had these winds as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex storm system brought numerous severe thunderstorm winds to northern UT and a flash flooding event to the San Rafael Swell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emery county emergency management reported an ongoing flood and search and rescue  operation in Little Wildhorse Slot Canyon. Water was at least 1 to 2 feet deep with locally deeper water. Rescue was successful with no significant injuries reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall drought conditions did not change across northern and eastern Maine during January. Several storms impacted the region during January bringing mostly snow, though a wintry mix and rain did occasionally occur across mostly Downeast areas. The heaviest snows generally occurred across east-central and Downeast portions of the region. Monthly precipitation totals for January generally ranged from 0.50 to 1.50 inches below normal across northern and eastern Maine. However...with frozen ground preventing soil penetration...soil moisture and groundwater was relatively unchanged during the month. Severe ( D2 ) level drought conditions generally remained unchanged from late December. Moderate ( D1 ) level drought conditions persisted across the remainder of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overall Severe ( D2 ) level drought conditions persisted through January...unchanged from late December.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Repeated rounds of rainfall throughout May significantly improved drought conditions across South Texas and the Coastal Bend. Early-month rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches along the Coastal Bend and 1 to 10 inches across South Texas, with additional rainfall continuing through mid-May. Several storms produced strong winds, hail, and tornado warnings, resulting in localized damage. A more significant rainfall event occurred during the last week of May, when multiple storm systems produced widespread totals of 1 to 12 inches, with localized amounts exceeding 5 inches along portions of the Coastal Bend. The heavy rainfall led to localized creek flooding and more widespread flooding in portions of Refugio County. By month's end, topsoil and subsoil moisture had improved from short to surplus in many locations, substantially alleviating drought impacts and improving rangeland, pasture, and water availability across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 5/26, ending inclusion in Storm Data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around one half of the roof removed from a large church. Some roof material collapsed into the church. Across the street, a pine tree was uprooted. Another pine tree snapped halfway up and landed on a machine shed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees in the Cumberland Furnace area, causing power outages. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms developed into northeastern Oklahoma during the late evening of the 23rd, as a cold front moved into the area. These thunderstorms organized into a line of thunderstorms and moved into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 24th, the strongest of which produced damaging wind. ||Another round of thunderstorms developed along the cold front over east central Oklahoma and west central Arkansas during the afternoon of the 24th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While occasional precipitation events occurred in January 2026, including an impactful winter storm in the late month, most areas saw continued precipitation deficits relative to January normals. Rather widespread severe (or worse) drought conditions continued in areas near and south of the Interstate 40 corridor.

Supercell thunderstorms rolled across the Denver Metro area mid afternoon on June 8th producing up to golf ball sized hail. Isolate severe wind gusts were recorded as well. As the storms progressed east of the Denver their intensity increase. A supercell thunderstorm continued to track eastward, stay south of I-70. Farther north, thunderstorms organized into a broken line, producing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph across far northeast Colorado.

A coastal low rapidly deepened off the coast of Virginia from 1004mb along the Outer Banks on the morning of February 22 to 968mb off the Mid-Atlantic and New England coastline on the morning of February 23. This brought heavy snow and occasional blizzard conditions to the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore from February 22 into February 23.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain changed over the snow during the afternoon of February 22 in Worcester County. Heavy snow and gusty winds lasted from the afternoon of February 22 into the morning of February 23 with occasional blizzard conditions. Snowfall totals ranged from 8 to 16 inches across the county with the highest totals across the northern portion of the county. A maximum report of 16 inches was received in Bishopville. Additionally, winds gusted to 45 to 60 mph across the county with a peak gust to 49 mph at the Salisbury Regional Airport ASOS (KSBY) to the west and a peak gust to 59 mph at the Ocean City Airport ASOS (KOXB). Multiple trees were reported to have fallen throughout the county, including at least one tree on a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large, long-period northwest to northerly swell impacted the Atlantic waters and local passages of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands from February 9 through February 11, 2026. This swell developed over the western Atlantic, maintaining hazardous marine conditions across the region.||Seas built to hazardous levels, with buoy observations indicating wave heights near 9 feet and long periods of 14 to 15 seconds. These conditions generated large breaking waves along north- to northeast-facing coastlines, with surf heights estimated between 10 and 16 feet.||The swell produced dangerous marine and coastal conditions, including life-threatening rip currents, high surf, and minor coastal flooding across exposed coastal areas of Puerto Rico, Culebra, Vieques, and the northern U.S. Virgin Islands. The most significant impacts occurred from February 9 through February 10, with hazardous conditions gradually subsiding by February 11.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coastal flooding occurred near La Palmita Beach in Barceloneta during the afternoon of February 9, 2026. Emergency managers reported that water and debris covered portions of Road 681 due to wave run-up from large swells. The flooding impacted the roadway and required cleanup operations. The event was caused by large breaking waves associated with a long-period northerly swell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

During the last two days of June, a favorable synoptic weather pattern brought extreme heat to portions of northeast Iowa as ample moisture resulted in remarkably high dewpoints. Consequently, heat indices soared well above 100 degrees with numerous locations seeing heat indices of 110 to 115 degrees or even higher in some locations. June 29th was the hottest day but extreme heat persisted into the 30th where heat indices in excess of 100 degrees were still common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme heat moved into the region during the end of June with widespread heat indices over 100 degrees. On June 29th, heat indices ranged from 105 to 111 degrees across the county during the afternoon and early evening. The highest heat index observed in the county was 111 degrees in Decorah. On June 30th, continued heat indices over 100 degrees persisted throughout much of the daytime hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon hours of May 17th, storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of NW Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of trees blown over in Maryville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm moved over Tutuila island on the morning of May 20th. Gusty winds accompanied heavy rainfall. The highest estimated winds are on the western edge of the island where structural damage and flying debris were reported. WFO American Samoa recorded 1.53 inches of rainfall between 4 AM and 5 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee reported a landslide along the main road in Failolo village. Rocks/boulders from the landslide blocked the west bound lane. The landslide was caused by heavy rainfall. The total rainfall is estimated at 2 inches in the area between 4 AM and 6 AM on May 20th. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1.75 inch diameter hail north of Cottage Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours.
