EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.
By mid-February, higher moisture content from a lingering front and locally induced afternoon shower and thunderstorm activity produced periods of heavy rainfall across Puerto Rico.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding over a low-level bridge along PR-372 near the conjunction of Rio Yauco and Rio Duey in Barrio Diego Hernandez Sector Cotui, due to river rise. USGS sensor at Rio Yauco reported action stage level (up to 7.14 feet).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a quasi-stationary front extending across southern Missouri and northwest Tennessee during the afternoon hours of June 13, 2026.  These storms were supported by SBCAPE values of 3000 to 4000 J/kg and 0-6km bulk shear values of around 30 knots. The storms formed into a line by late afternoon, with several reports of damaging winds. Slow-moving storms combined with precipitable water values around 2 inches to produce heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed electric lines occurred in the Nora Drive / Edward Street area of Newbern.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing theta-e, steep mid level lapse rates, strong shear and limited MUCAPE allowed for the development of several thunderstorms which moved from White county to northern portions of Allen county during the morning hours. Additional storms developed in the afternoon. Low freezing levels and the elements noted above resulted in efficient hail producing storms, with one in particular leaving a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path. A few severe level hail stones were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Little Muskingum River at Bloomfield rose above a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest around 22.4 feet that night. The river then slowly receded back below bankfull level the next morning. While the river was out of its banks, flooding of fields next to the river and Route 26 near the intersection with Route 260 took place.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved quickly across central and southeast Wyoming during the middle afternoon to late afternoon hours. Most strong gusty winds were reported with a few severe hail reports. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Camp Creek RAWS site gusted to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record warmth, coupled with little to no rainfall in March, led to rapid expansion of drought conditions across all of western and north central Nebraska. By the end of the month, areas of moderate (D1) drought conditions expanded to severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of March. North Platte saw its 3rd warmest, and Valentine had its warmest March on record. Valentine had its 9th driest and North Platte 19th driest March on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions transitioned to extreme (D3) drought conditions over most of Perkins County by the end of March. Over the northeastern quarter of the county, severe (D2) drought conditions persisted through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually extreme, early-season heat wave impacted central California during the middle of March, setting several monthly heat records across the region. Radiosonde observations from Oakland reported a monthly record for highest 850 mb temperature at 23.4 degrees Celsius, or around 74.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Notably, this temperature would also break the monthly record for April, had it occurred during that month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated time and location of tornado based on reports received from emergency management and radar interpretation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power poles were knocked down throughout the county. Widespread power outages due to downed trees and power poles in Alamo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted Missouri beginning on the morning of January 24th, continuing into January 25th. This storm brought significant snowfall to the region, with many counties receiving 5 or more of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense (130-150 knot) jet streak atop warm and very dry surface conditions fostered a high wind and wildfire episode across the northern Texas Panhandle, Oklahoma Panhandle and portions of northwestern Oklahoma on the 17th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Picture on social media showed water in cars parked along Brownswitch Road in Slidell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: River flooding in northeastern Jackson County was exasperated locally by heavy rainfall during the overnight of the 4th-5th around 2.00 inches, with the East Fork White River later cresting at Seymour in major flood stage on the 5th evening.  On the 6th morning around 700EST, a man in an airboat near Courtland, while attempting to rescue individuals stranded in a submerged vehicle, died after the boat experienced mechanical issues, capsized, and was swept under a bridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low offshore and upper trough combined with deep arctic air led to significant snowfall across the Carolinas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 31 and ended on February 1, ranging from 7 to 10 inches across the county, with an isolated area of 10 to 16 inches of snow near the state line. Impacts from the storm were limited.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported baseball size hail in the areas of Whitewright, Trenton, and Leonard. Numerous homes and cars have windows broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A landslide was reported near the Santo Collazo Waterfall in San Sebastian, next to the intersection of PR-111 and PR-450. PR-450 was partially impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon and evening of Saturday, May 9, 2026, a line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Erie, Northern Ohio, and Northwest Pennsylvania. Within this line, several severe thunderstorms produced marine wind gusts, wind gusts over land, and wind damage over land areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree limb was blown down across Nelson Mosier Road by a thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An outbuilding/shed was partially blown into the roadway at Lee Road 246 and Lee Road 289.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 60 mph was reported near Franklinville Road and Route 176.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked several trees down in Nuremburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts flipped a semi-trailer truck on Interstate 65.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking the road at intersection of Rockdale Road and Heller Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down on Highway 96 between Bronson and Pineland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCS moved out of Kentucky into East Tennessee during the early morning hours of June 28th. This laid out a boundary that acted as a focus for additional shower and thunderstorm development through the late morning hours, resulting in training storms across the central Tennessee valley and numerous reports of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One lane closed on Veterans Blvd, near the Dig'N Zone theme park, due to flood issues.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Madison County decreased from D2 (Severe Drought) to D1 (Moderate Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was stalled over the coastal Mississippi.  At the same time, a weak upper level trough was moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley.  Both of these features tapped into a warm and unstable airmass to produce thunderstorm activity in coastal Mississippi.  These thunderstorms produced some severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on a power line on Go Go Road in the Silver Hill area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stationed across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours allowed for thunderstorm development to form across the Shenandoah Valley during the late morning hours of March 16, 2026 that began to surge towards southern Pennsylvania. Severe thunderstorms in a favorable unstable and highly sheared environment across Virginia and Maryland began to shift into the a more stable and less sheared environment; however, momentum from these thunderstorms allowed for isolated instances of tree damage during the afternoon hours. As the cold front continued to track eastward, slightly more instability was available across eastern Lancaster County during the evening hours, with more readily available lift and moisture, allowing for more robust winds that caused more significant wind damage in eastern Lancaster County. The most notable wind damage came in the form of significant roof damage in New Holland along with significant damage to a barn and a nearby residence near Terre Hill. Multiple trees were also knocked down near Terre Hill and near Gap.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated between 70 and 80 mph caused significant roof damage to a single family home on South Custer Avenue in New Holland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed within the vicinity of a strong mid-upper level shortwave trough and a surface low. One supercell tracked from southeast Minnesota through northeast Iowa and into southwest Wisconsin while maintaining is strength during the late afternoon. The storm evolved into a line as it trtacked through south central Wisconsin during the early evening and produced a swath of damaging winds and three tornadoes.

Most locations saw a dry start and middle of the month before more numerous convective systems impacted parts of the area toward the end of the month. This was especially true across far north-central Oklahoma and near the Red River, with central Oklahoma seeing near- to below-normal monthly rainfall totals. As a result, severe (or worse) drought persisted during the month, with some general category improvement towards the last days of the month.

Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Ohio Valley into the northern Mid-Atlantic region. A mid-level system tracked in from the west and led to numerous showers and storms across the Coastal Plain and Piedmont of Central North Carolina. Numerous wind damage reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near Old Stage Road and Vandora Springs Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon hours of March 10th, supercells brought massive hail to portions of eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail reported near Roe and 71st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Breezy southerly winds shifted to southwesterly later into the evening of the 8th ahead of a cold frontal passage. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours in Western Kentucky. Gusty gradient winds of near and above 40mph developed in portions of Western Kentucky during the evening hours ahead of the storms, generally at sites near the Ohio River.

During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, a line of multicell rain showers and thunderstorms generated sporadic straight-line convective wind damage in Wyandot and Marion Counties to Ashland County as the line persisted generally eastward in northern OH. Behind the line, a cluster of multicell rain showers generated a severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust at the Lorain County Airport ASOS as the cluster of showers persisted generally northeastward. These showers and storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Barn destroyed along County Road 110 on the northwest side of Upper Sandusky. Damage was related to a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources reported a smattering of trees blown down across northeast Buncombe County, from the Woodfin area, across Weaverville to the Dillingham community. Several trees were down across roads, and a barn was damaged by a fallen tree near Weaverville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Bland county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 10th to 20th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Walker Creek, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A classic ice storm setup developed across the Midlands of South Carolina January 25th. Cold air damming at the surface and strong overrunning aloft produced light and moderate freezing across the Central Midlands with sleet predominant in the Northern Midlands. The southern Midlands saw a shorter period of freezing rain and rain. Damage was primarily due to tree and limb damage along with associated hazardous and impassable roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Highway Patrol reported multiple trees and large branches down due to ice accumulation in the cities of Cayce and Chapin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power lines were blown down across Progress Ridge Road near Walker Road in Walker.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Calm winds and clearing skies behind a cold frontal passage resulted in a few hours of dense fog formation near dawn in portions of Southeast Missouri near Cape Girardeau.

On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous hail reports near Bicknell and the surrounding countryside of hail up to 2 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated light rain showers and virga associated with a weak shortwave led to strong wind gusts across parts of North Texas the evening of May 15. Wind gusts around 60 MPH were measured, and trees were blown down in a few locations within the DFW Metroplex.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 68 mph wind was measured off Main St near 121 in The Colony. A station at 30 ft above ground also reported a gust to 78 mph but appears high compared to values throughout the day. Multiple trees also were damaged in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of strong to severe storms became organized as it progressed mostly across the I-20 corridor and surrounding areas in Louisiana. This thunderstorm activity produced numerous reports of wind damage as it was aided in its progression and intensity by an ongoing Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down on Louisiana Highway 568 and on D Sreet in Waterproof.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System moved across the Ohio Valley on the night of June 17th, 2026 and the morning of June 18th, 2026. Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service completed a storm survey and determined that a tornado occurred during the early morning hours on June 18, 2026 in Scott County and Jefferson County Indiana and then crossed the river into Trimble County Kentucky. The tornado was 1000 yards wide and 23.62 miles in length. Maximum winds were |EF2 130 mph.||The tornado first touched down on the northeast side of Austin, Indiana near the community park. Several trees were damaged with twisted tops or brought down entirely in the park. Some fencing and bleacher damage was also observed at the ball fields. The tornado continued across rural portions of Scott county just north of state road 256 with tree damage along the way. The most notable damage started occurring in extreme eastern Scott county north of Wooster along Blanton Road. Drone footage had shown a clear path in the woods of extensive tree damage with several house structures also having damage south of Hardy Lake. High end EF1 winds around 110 mph began here before the tornado crossed into Jefferson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through Delaware. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to Delaware.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees uprooted with some snapped. Irrigation systems damage. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure from Green Bay to Lake Huron, measuring 988mb, produced widespread wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. This resulted in property damage and numerous reports of blown-over semi-trucks throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Automated station KBEH Benton Harbor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Copernicus Sentinel satellite imagery revealed a brief tornado track in an open field around 8 miles southwest of Albert City. The tornado was estimated to touch down near the intersection of 570th Street and 180th Avenue. The tornado tracked northeast across open fields for less than two minutes before lifting southwest of the intersection of 560th Street and 200th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive, long-duration atmospheric river brought copious snowfall and high winds to western Montana.  Some high-elevation areas received a few feet of snow.  Impacts from this storm included power outages and impacts to travel.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wet, heavy snow snapped tree limbs which fell on power lines, causing several power outages in the Missoula and Bitterroot valleys.  Missoula COOP reported 2500 customers without power on the night of March 13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Desdemona Fire reported multiple large tree limbs of 6 to 8 inches in diameter were snapped and broken northeast of the town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surprisingly strong surge of winds impacted far southeast MT, producing gusts up to 64 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Miles City airport gusted to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a large tree on the north side of Armstrong Valley Road in south Murfreesboro. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were in place across portions of Martin, Pitt, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, northern Craven, and Beaufort Counties from mid January to the end of January according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Pitt County from January thirteenth through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low level frontogenesis developed ahead of a cold front, and an upper level shortwave provided lift to create a period of snow as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding observations, most of Gallatin County received 3.5 to 4 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper wave dropping south across the Great Lakes and it's associated cold front brought widespread accumulating snow to the region New Year's Eve and into the new year across the ridges of western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Enhanced orographic lift resulted in higher totals across the Laurel Highlands and eastern West Virginia ridges, with relatively high snow ratios between 18:1 and 21:1. Widespread Advisory level snow was also observed across the region, ranging from 2.5 inches to 5.5 inches outside of the ridges of Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall, generally exceeding advisory criteria but falling short of warning criteria, fell across the county with amounts around 3-6 inches and the highest total of 5.9 inches reported by the public 4 miles northeast of Rowlesburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts across Lake Erie.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station 45204 - Sheffield Buoy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. Temperatures dropped below 32 during the late evening on the 10th, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours on May 11. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Morning lows between 24 and 27 were observed across Lake of the Woods County. The lowest value was at Roosevelt, MN 15 SW HADS site at 11:30 PM CST during the late evening on May 10. KBDE ASOS reported a low of 25 at 5:53 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a travel trailer blown onto its side was shared on social media. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 60 mph near Kennard, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered small to medium branch debris. Some branches were 5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Watonga (WATO) Mesonet observation. Wind gust associated with a probable heat burst event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam County Emergency  Management reported that lightning sparked a  wildfire that was approximately 6.65 acres in  size located along West River Road near Palatka. Time of event was based on lightning strike data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged winter storm affected the Southern Plains on January 23rd through the 25th. Central and eastern Kansas saw all snow for this event. It snowed for 40 straight hours in Wichita. Most locations across central, south central and southeast Kansas picked up between five to a little above nine inches; near Smolan in Saline County measured 9.1 inches for the event.||Extreme cold air spilled south across the Plains with this event.  Nine temperature records were either set or tied during the January 23rd through January 26th time frame. Both Russell and Salina saw low temperatures of -16 with widespread wind chills in the 10 to 20 below zero range. In Wichita, the homeless shelter provided housing for over 365 guests which is above average and near their capacity. There is one unconfirmed fatality of an unhoused individual who didn't seek shelter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding reports as well as reports from within the county, an estimated 7 to 8 inches of snow fell across Woodson County throughout the event. The highest reported snow total was 8 inches in Toronto.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No observations within the county. Estimated maximum wind gusts of 58-62 mph based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree limb at least 12 inches in diameter was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As an upper level low moved through the region, severe thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front that moved through North Dakota. Scattered showers and non-severe thunderstorms were ongoing during the morning before increasing in strength throughout the afternoon. A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind damage reported approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak frontal boundary drifted into southeast Texas well ahead of Tropical Storm Arthur. Heavy rain produced areas of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flood water entered a couple homes near Wildwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm moist air advancing northward over cold ground helped cause widespread fog to form late on March 11th and early on March 12th. The fog dissipated near dawn.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Heritage Field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Rio Grande and Coastal Plains received less than normal precipitation during the month, and the drought worsened or remained unchanged. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down near the 1000 block of Calvert Beach Road.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: UPR Mesonet station UP326 4 miles west of Scottsbluff gusted 68 mph at 11:59 AM on February 25th. This was the first, highest, and final gust recorded for this zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Falfurrias (northeast Brooks County) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 25F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 8.5 hours from 3:15-11:35am CST on Sunday January 25th. Proxy observations from southern Kleberg County suggest that the Sarita-Armstrong area, at minimum, had similar duration of wind chill temperatures during this period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 4 to 8 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 13.6 inches of snow reported at Hesperus 13.3 SSW over a 3 day period. Winds gusted in the 25 to 50 mph range with a peak wind gust of 58 mph at the Durango-La Plata County Airport with visibility down to quarter mile at times in snow squalls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low moved across northern Mexico bringing a strong cold front through South-Central Texas. This resulted in very cold air in the boundary layer with a layer of above freezing air aloft which produced sleet and freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The County EM reported a path of damage near FM 1497 and CR 15600 in the southeast part of the county. Tree damage was observed in a twisted manner and along a convergent path, a shipping container was moved, and a boat dock was displaced out of a pond to the south along the track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees reported down on State Route 800.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Chattahoochee County remained under D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on October 14, 2025, the county sustained 25 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought conditions persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KCVN Airport measured high sustained winds of 40 to 43 mph.

Soon after, on Easter Weekend, the worst drought in 13 years would begin to crack with the start of spring rains, which continued through at least the end of May. ||Still, there were likely notable crop production/harvest losses in the Valley, and cattle herd production losses across the ranchlands, who had the longest duration of D3 and D4 conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down along Hollow Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front brought gale- to storm-force winds in snow showers to the tidal waters of the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay early on New Year's morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down near Stoystown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed on Plant Rd and Renfroe Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a slowly advancing cold front across south-central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and nighttime hours of April 17. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and up to 70 mph wind gusts. Wind damage was also noted across a couple locations across southeast Kansas from these storms.

Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

CZ_NAME: PARADOX VALLEY / LOWER DOLORES RIVER BASIN
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep Pacific trough brought moist southwesterly flow to much of the western CONUS on January 1. A weak upper-level jet streak arrived in coincidence with the surge of moisture, prompting widespread precipitation in western Colorado throughout the morning of the 1st. Strong cold air advection behind the storms rapidly saturated valleys, and areas of dense fog developed during throughout the night and into the morning of January 2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Patchy dense fog developed within Paradox Valley on the morning of January 2. The KAIB AWOS at Hopkins Field in Nucla, Colorado reported brief 1/4-mile visibility from dense fog before sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and early evening on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, extending along the Middle Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across the area, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, extending well into the afternoon and early evening. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. As a result, several damaging wind reports were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed along Highway 29 south of Bradley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak mid level shortwave moved through during the afternoon initiating a few strong storms which produced scattered wind damage reports in western MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Belchertown, several trees were down on Blue Meadow Rd.
