Downeast region saw some snowfall early Tuesday morning, and alongside the warm front, mid-level warm air advection created a prime environment for some sleet development. Precipitation began as snow in the north, freezing rain/sleet in the Central Highlands, and rain Downeast. As the cold front quickly swept through the region, tanking temperatures. and resulting in more mixed precipitation. By the time the system fully moved through the region by Wednesday, roughly, 1/2 to just under 1 inch of sleet fell in Aroostook county. Roughly 0.1 to 0.25 inches of freezing rain fell in southern Aroostook, Piscataquis and northern Penobscot counties. Event continues into April 1st. System resulted in messy travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-2 inches of snowfall and sleet fell during the evening of the 31st. Millinocket ASOS reported a 0.21 inches of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought. Conditions worsened through the month with the county being upgraded to Exceptional (D4) drought on March 17, 2026.  Exceptional drought then continued for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Early in the morning of March 16th, a strong cold front swept through southeast Ohio. Accompanied with this boundary was a broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms. While minor tree damage was observed in Vinton County when the storms passed overhead, a member of the public noted a 60 mile per hour wind gust in Lawrence County in the storm that passed over their home. Additionally, a period of elevated synoptic winds took shape across southeast Ohio after the storms swept through. Peak wind gusts ranging from 36 to 56 miles per hour were observed by several Mesonet and AWOS sites in the area just before sunrise on March 16th. Surface winds decreased quickly heading into the daytime hours amid building high pressure from the west.

A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 3/4 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 20 mph with frequent gusts over 25mph. The 2-day snowfall reports ranged from about 4 to 7 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 7 inches in Elk River. Road conditions became dangerous Saturday night and much of Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires down along Oak Shade Road in Tabernacle. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across southeastern Oklahoma and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the area was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. A tornado, isolated damaging wind, and large hail up to two inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball size hail damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Somerset County averaged 4.13 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.94 inches above normal. The USDM on March 31st had 78% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 22% in Extreme Drought (D3). Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 8 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across southern Illinois, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the afternoon and evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. Areas along and northwest of interstate 57 experienced another interval of dangerous wind chills during the morning and afternoon hours on the 25th while areas to the southeast remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

A Mesoscale Convective System moved across the Ohio Valley on the night of June 17th, 2026 and the morning of June 18th, 2026. Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell and was blocking one lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14 before crossing the Chesapeake Bay and moving into the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore. Isolated damaging wind gusts continued as the storms moved across Maryland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down near the intersection of US-50 and MD-16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||In southeast Ohio, the highest snow amounts, which ranged from around five to ten inches, were observed in Perry, Washington, Athens, Vinton, and Jackson Counties. In addition to a few inches of snow, sleet and freezing rain become more dominant further south. Jackson and Lawrence Counties had the most notable sleet amounts, each coming in with around an inch of accumulation. As for freezing rain, a few tenths of an inch of ice were observed in Lawrence County.

Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.

Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball sized hail was estimated by a photo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought all severe hazards to portions of Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball sized hail reported along Route 58 between Strasburg and Kingsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency managers reported flooding along PR-4417 near Escuela Aquilino Cab��n in Aguada. Floodwaters covered the roadway, making it impassable and creating hazardous travel conditions. No injuries or damage to nearby structures were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Glens Falls ASOS reported a gust of 62 mph via an updated METAR.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across northeast Georgia by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 10 driest on record across the area. Unusually warm weather developing during March and April of 2026 exacerbated drought impacts. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across the Missouri Bootheel.||Thermal profiles across the Missouri Bootheel favored predominantly snow, however, with the development of the surface low, a shallow warm nose aloft overspread the area, causing a changeover to sleet. Poor road conditions continued for nearly two weeks after the storm, causing difficult travel and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow and sleet accumulations of 6 to 8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video of wires down causing a fire on Gully Road in Wading River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed on Mill Creek Rd and also on Highway 5.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cyclone approached the Central Coast on February 10, resulting in the first substantial rainfall in over a month for much of the Bay Area and Central Coast. A Wind Advisory was issued for all of Monterey and San Benito Counties as wind gusts up to 50 mph were expected across the region late on the 10th and into the early morning of the 11th. The orientation of the low favored rainfall for the Santa Cruz and Santa Lucia ranges, where rain totals reached 1-3 inches in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and 2-5 inches in the Santa Lucias.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Mining Ridge rain gauge reported 6.10 inches of rain from 2:30 AM on February 10 to 11:10 PM on February 11.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought continued across portions of East Texas through the first three plus weeks of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. However, widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 2.00+ inches fell across much of Rusk, Gregg, San Augustine, and Sabine Counties between the 19th  and 26th, resulting in a one category improvement to Moderate (D1) drought across these areas by the May 28th release of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2.50-4+ inches across Rusk and Gregg Counties, and between 5-8+ inches across San Augustine and Sabine Counties, which was near to as much as twice the monthly normals. Thus, some improvement to pasture greenup, stock pond levels, and streamflows across area rivers, bayous, and creeks were observed by month's end. ||Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana. Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.
A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.

In May 2026, New Hampshire saw noticeable short-term improvements in drought conditions, though deep groundwater deficits continued to pose a challenge across the state. Soaking rains in mid-May provided widespread relief, particularly across the northern mountains and foothills. Over a single week ending May 19, the coverage of Severe Drought (D2) in New Hampshire dropped significantly from 36% down to 20.5%. The mid-May rain events successfully replenished surface topsoil moisture, restored streamflows, and boosted lake and reservoir levels back toward seasonal baselines. However, extended precipitation deficits over the preceding 90 days, particularly across southern New Hampshire, kept deeper hydrologic systems under stress. Deep groundwater aquifers respond on a much slower, lagging timeframe, meaning the water table remained significantly lower than long-term historical averages for May. Consequently, several groundwater monitoring wells across southern and central New Hampshire continued to record below to much-below normal levels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had 12% of Grafton County in Severe Drought (D2), but by the end of May severe drought was reduced to under 2% (1.79%), with 21% Moderate Drought (D1) and 59% Abnormally Dry (D0).  May rainfall averaged 5.95 inches, well above normal by 2.26���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 11-month period ending May 2026 still ranked as the 8th driest on record, leaving the area with a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours along a frontal boundary situated across central Ohio.

A few isolated to scattered thunderstorm moved east to southeast across far southwest Nebraska during the afternoon hours on the 20th, ahead of deepening High Plains low pressure. Hail up to three-inches in diameter occurred in Hitchcock county, and winds up to 60 mph occurred in Dundy county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report came through Spotter Network.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado had peak intensity of EF1, with estimated peak winds of 95-mph, and impacted the northeastern and eastern outskirts of Mount Gilead. The tornado began along U.S. Route 42, near Home Road, and caused extensive tree damage, which included multiple snapped and uprooted trees. The tornado continued southeastward, crossed Township Road 103, and caused sporadic tree damage. The tornado then crossed OH Route 95, near Township Road 110, and destroyed a 60 foot by 100 foot outbuilding. Debris from this outbuilding were displaced about 100 to 200 yards to the south-southeast by the tornado before the tornado ended. Scattered tree damage and some structural damage associated with straight line convective wind gusts up to 75-mph were found both north and south of the tornado track. Radar data suggest this tornado was associated with a cyclonic mesovortex along the poleward side of the descending rear-inflow jet of a bow echo and the bow echo was embedded within the flanking line of a cyclonic supercell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Northeast Pennsylvania. and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region. With one storm, lightning struck a church and led to a fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds caused a peanut trailer to flip and tree tops were splintered off with damage to an outbuilding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front blasted across VT during the morning hours of February 7th sending temperatures plummeting through the teens into the single numbers by Saturday (2/7) evening on brisk northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts creating dangerous windchill temperatures of 10 to 25 below zero during the afternoon hours. ||Although winds diminished somewhat on the night of the 7th, sub-zero temperatures still accounted for 15 to 30 below wind chills through midday on February 8th with daytime wind chills still 15 to 25 below zero.||This was the 3rd such cold spell within the past month that attributed to the Ice Over of Lake Champlain on February 13th, the first time since 2018.||Arctic high pressure crested across the region on the night of February 8th into the morning hours of February 9th. This allowed temperatures to radiate down to 5 to 20 below zero across VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime temperatures falling to the single digits above zero on Saturday (2/7) combined with northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts created wind chills of 10 to 20 below zero during the daylight hours. ||Saturday night (2/7) - Sunday morning (2/8)...although winds diminished to 5 to 10 mph and gusty at times, actual air temperatures fell to 5 to 10 below zero creating dangerous wind chills of 20 to 30 below zero. During Sunday (2/8) temperatures were 0 to 10 degrees above zero but a persistent wind around 10 mph created wind chills up to 10 below zero. High pressure crested across the region during the overnight into the early morning hours of February 9th, allowing temperatures to fall to 15 to 20 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1.25 inch diameter hail near Sun Prairie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line moved through the Great Lakes region, sparking showers and thunderstorms.

Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms for the first part of the month improved conditions in south central and southeast Kansas to drop the drought status to moderate drought (D1) to even none in portions of Labette and Montgomery counties by the end of the month. The rainfall totals ranged from 1.6 to 10.2 inches with the highest values in Labette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While severe drought conditions (D2) started the month, there were rounds of showers and thunderstorms to improve the status through the month. All but a sliver in a far southern portion of the county improved to moderate drought (D1) in the first week of the month. This sliver dropped to moderate drought on the 21st while the rest of the county further improved to abnormally dry (D0). At the end of the month, the northeast third had their drought status removed completely. There was a range of 4.6 to 10.2 inches of rain that feel in the first 21 days of the month according to CoCoRaHS and cooperative observer reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree fell onto a home along South Arch Road. In addition, additional trees were knocked down along Arch Road, blocking the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached afternoon peaks as high as 108 degrees at Yankton and 106 degrees 10 miles north of Yankton and near Gayville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front pushed into the Mid-South during the morning of June 22, 2026. A weak surface low pressure system tracked along the front and across the Mid-South as the front slowly moved across the area. Meanwhile, an upper level disturbance moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley helped to trigger widespread showers and thunderstorms along the front. Anomalously high precipitable water values of over 2 inches were pooled along the front resulting in heavy rainfall with some places reporting over 6 inches. Several areas experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The intersection of Highway 64 and Fletcher Trace parkway was flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in late February and early March. Large wildfires that began in late February continued into early March, with some additional wildfires beginning in the first few days of March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 10,000 acres in Latimer County, over 2500 acres in Pittsburg County, over 1600 acres in Pushmataha County, and more than 500 acres in Cherokee County and Le Flore Counties.

From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds gusted as high as 53 mph 1 mile west-northwest of Lake Benton and 51 mph 3 miles south of Hendricks. During and after a period of heavy snowfall which totaled 6.0 inches 8 miles southeast of Hendricks, visibility was reduced to near zero at times with blowing snow.  U.S. Highway 14 was closed for a time, with travel not recommended over most roadways during the height of the blizzard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blocked a tree into the road northeast of Marionville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in Plain Dealing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough was moving southeast through southern New Mexico with some mid level moisture available for thunderstorms to develop.  A very dry surface with dew point depressions over 65 degrees allowed for gusty thunderstorm winds to occur.  Blowing dust also developed over the Lordsburg Playa causing the interstate to be closed for a short period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Deming Airport recorded a peak gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A widespread winter storm affected the region from the 23rd and lasting until the afternoon of the 25th. Beginning on the 23rd, an arctic cold front moved through the region during the morning and afternoon. Shortly after the cold air moved into the region, Pacific moisture began to stream over from the southwest resulting in wintry showers. Precipitation initially began as freezing rain at many locations but quickly switched to sleet as the lower levels of the atmosphere cooled. Despite temperatures well below freezing into the single digits by the morning of the 24th, sleet continued to be the dominant precipitation type. A strong warm layer aloft allowed for much of this precipitation to remain as sleet. By the afternoon of the 24th, the warm layer aloft cooled enough to allow mostly snow to fall as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Snowfall continued through the night of the 24th ending late in the afternoon on the 25th. The heaviest amount of snow fell over the western South Plains into the extreme southern Texas Panhandle where totals of six to eight inches were observed. The remainder of the South Plains and Rolling Plains saw between three and six inches of snowfall. Additionally, breezy winds combined with bitterly cold temperatures producing dangerous wind chills. A strong winter storm began Saturday night and continued through Sunday as it passed over an entrenched arctic airmass. A strengthening surface low over the Tennessee Valley combined with upper level dynamics to produce snowfall up to ten inches in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The EMA measured 6 inches of snow at Brooksville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser observed/recorded a brief tornado and observed power flashes. This location is estimated based on his observations and radar data. An NWS storm survey of the area found no damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed the area, with most robust activity occurring in the afternoon and evening of the 23rd and 24th. The majority of the area received one to three inches of rain during this time, with a few pockets between three and four inches.  Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Raleigh, Taylor, and Upshur Counties and led to a mud slide in Kanawha County. A couple of severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines in Logan and Mingo counties the evening of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Valley Falls Road flooded.

A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage occurred and an outbuilding was blown down in Rosemont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low in the Central Plains moved northeast into the Great Lakes late on Sunday the 15th. Ahead of its attendant cold front that passed later in the evening, a low level jet developed in the late morning and moved east. Daytime heating gave added energy to mix the lower levels of the atmosphere and bring strong winds from this feature to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gust to 52 mph was measured at the Union County Airport.

Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An OKC television storm chaser observed and photographed a tornado esimated to be about 6 miles west of Putnam. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Bitterly cold air moved across northern Illinois on January 23rd and January 24th with wind chills between 25 below and 35 below zero.  Wind chills 35 below to 40 below zero occurred across far northern and northwest Illinois.
With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires down along Saylors Pond Road and Meeting House Road. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of South-Central Texas received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to maintenance and improvement in the ongoing drought. Hays County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Bastrop, Travis, and Wilson Counties remained in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 16.7 feet below normal. Lake Travis rose 2.2 feet but was 8.9 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower San Antonio and upper Colorado Rivers.

Hays County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Bastrop, Travis, and Wilson Counties remained in D2. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo on Facebook showing a large tree uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.
Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 13th.

An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree branches/limbs, up to 6 inches in diameter, were blown down. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced an estimated wind gust to 34 knots (39 MPH) near a Tempest station at West Patuxent Basin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 0.75 inches in diameter. Report received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushed across eastern New York during the afternoon hours on June 6, 2026 within the warm sector of a low pressure system. The strongest and most organized thunderstorms moved across Ulster and Dutchess Counties where numerous reports of downed trees and wires occurred. More isolated thunderstorms also produced some downed trees across far northern Washington County and near North Creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed on Route 32 near Rosendale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southern Illinois on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Williamson County, IL on the 26th. Northwest portions of southern Illinois and areas south of route 13 only experienced advisory criteria with values of -9 to -14. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the early morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Alexander, Pulaski, and Massac County, IL where wind chills warmed above -5 the morning of the 26th due to calmer winds.

Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large limbs from 6 to 8 inches of diameter were downed by high winds. .

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Em reports a tree down at fayetteville rd and vaughn rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front draped over the Ohio Valley tracked into the central and southern Appalachians by the late evening and overnight period. Ahead of the front, scattered showers and storms tracked from the North Carolina mountains into the Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the evening hours. Numerous wind damage reports were observed over the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An uprooted tree fell onto a shed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms that moved through Arkansas. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced a number of damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind damaged the roof of a home and snapped large tree limbs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few large trees uprooted or snapped, around Mallard Pond Ct. Time was estimated based off radar and the public report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief tornado touched down IL just east of Illinois Route 4 and just north of Lower Marine Road where it collapsed the overhead doors of a metal building and caused minor roof damage to a double wide manufactured home. The tornado lifted shortly after.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak short wave trough tracked across the higher terrain along the New Mexico/Colorado border during the evening of the 26th. Large scale ascent from this short wave along with low level convergence in a surface pressure trough in eastern New Mexico initiated thunderstorms during the evening hours across eastern New Mexico. This initial thunderstorm activity generated a strong outflow boundary which then moved into the South Plains of West Texas. A very dry lower atmosphere allowed these storms to produce widespread severe wind gusts as they tracked eastward across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle through the early morning hours of the 27th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Anton measured a wind gust of 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary frontal boundary as well as both a Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coast sea breeze combined with plentiful diurnal instability to produce robust thunderstorms across northeast FL during the afternoon and evening hours. Along with isolated severe thunderstorm activity, PWATs around 1.8 inches and slow moving/training convection resulted in very heavy rainfall and localized minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree Reported Down On State Road 11 Near Bunnell. Time Of Event Based On Radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 61 mph was measured at the DuPage Airport.
