EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on County Road 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front set up across central Kansas later in the afternoon and eventually, storms began to develop along it. The strongest storms were mainly across southeast Kansas with damaging wind reported in Montgomery and Labette counties; Parsons Airport had a measured wind gust to 86 mph. As the front slowly tracked to the southeast through the evening, storms became more widespread and trained across the same areas. There was a stronger storm within the activity which produced quarter sized hail in Sedgwick County, but the associated heavy rain was the bigger show. The hardest hit area was the Wichita metro and southern Sedgwick into northern Sumner County where a widespread 4 to 7 inches fell, most of it in a 2 to 3 hour period. Flash flooding reports from Wichita and surrounding areas were plentiful with around 112 reports of stalled vehicles in Wichita alone. Homes along the creeks were also threatened and impacted by flood waters. Basement apartments were evacuated in west Wichita. Just after 10:30 PM KAKE News shared reports on social media from the following intersections of flooded roadways: 13th and Maize, 8th and West, 21st and 295th, Custer and Pawnee, 13th and Rock, Pawnee and Seneca, Central and Tyler. The number of flooded intersections only increased through the next several hours as rain continued. Some of the flooding was due to quickly rising creeks, including the Cowskin in west Wichita, which led to additional street and property flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was damage to an animal shed from strong winds in addition to some broken tree branches in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage was observed along Clearview Heights Road in the Ripley area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Remnant convection from Oklahoma pushed into the bi-state area and strengthened with the help of a potent low-level jet. These renewed thunderstorms were able to cause sporadic wind damage in south-central Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed limbs in Shattuc.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought was observed to begin June across almost all of the Oklahoma Panhandle. Normal to above normal rainfall occurred in the first and last week of the month, and normal to below normal rainfall occurred in the middle of the month across most of the region. The most beneficial rainfall occurred in northern and eastern Beaver county, southern Cimarron, and portions of north-central Texas county. Normal to below normal rainfall was observed elsewhere. Most of this region saw the drought category get reduced between 1 to 3 categories with the only exception being southwestern Beaver county, southeastern Texas county, and most of Cimarron county. Moderate (D1) drought to D4 drought persists across Beaver county, with Severe (D2) to D3 drought elsewhere due to a 1-6 inch rainfall deficit over the previous 180 days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. Several wildfires developed due to the dry grasses, low relative humidity and high wind gusts. One wildfire in Beaver County burned into Kansas and consumed over 200,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak wind gust in Beaver County was 67 mph observed at the mesonet site located one mile south-southwest of Beaver at 1220CST. Other wind gusts around the 60 mph range were observed from about 1100CST until 1500CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC DPS reported a tree down on the roadway at the intersection of Horrell Hill Rd and Crossing Creek Rd. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts.  Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree was reported down in the vicinity of Knox Rd. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported the tornado was first visible in an open field west of 466th Avenue and north of 291st Street. The tornado moved slowly southeast toward a farmstead at the intersection of 466th Avenue and 291st Street where minor tree damage was reported. The primary circulation then broadened as the tornado turned more eastward and at times exhibited smaller brief vortices. Additional minor tree damage occurred before the tornado lifted in the vicinity of 291st Street and 467th Avenue. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 75 mph and an estimated average path width of 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. Storm development occurred both along a quasi-stationary boundary across northern Oklahoma and along an accelerating Pacific Front from far western Oklahoma into western-north Texas. A mix of supercells and a well-developed quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) yielded reports of large to very large hail and wind damage across portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hollis (HOLL) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough approached Georgia on the morning of Sunday, January 18th, drawing Gulf moisture northward into central Georgia. Meanwhile, a cold front brought an influx of colder air into the area. This interaction led to a few hours of snowfall across much of central Georgia on the morning of January 18th. Snowfall accumulations were generally in the 1-2 range across this stretch of the state, though a few spots received near 3 of snow. After a brief period of slowed travel and snowy scenes, afternoon sun brought warmer temperatures which quickly melted the snow, bringing a quick end to this relatively uncommon central Georgia snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain transitioned to snow in the early morning hours of the 18th. Snowfall accumulations of T to 1.5 inches were recorded by mid morning and snowfall ended by late morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down across the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of April, persisting extreme drought (D3) and  exceptional drought (D4) conditions area-wide. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of beneficial rainfall in April continued the Extreme (D3) drought for the rest of the month.

Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds pushing colder air into the area in the wake of an arctic cold front interacting with moisture banked against the western slopes of the Appalachians resulted in a protracted period of snow showers developing near the Tennessee/North Carolina border. The snow showers began developing on the morning of the 22nd, and continued off and on for more than 36 hours before tapering off during the early morning of the 24th. Snowfall totals were heavily dependent upon elevation and exposure to northwest winds, with accumulations of 8-12 inches reported above 3500 feet across Avery County. Totals in the lower elevations were more in the 3 to 6 inch range.
Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Kellys Lane in Richmond County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed western Massachusetts on June 18, 2026. A complex of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and large branches as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Bartlett Avenue in the City of Pittsfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure area and frontal boundary brought a west to east swath of 2 to 5 inches of snow. Slick roads resulted in numerous vehicle slide-offs and accidents on highways and secondary roads.  There were major travel disruptions on the interstates and highway 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulation of 2-4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An occluded area of low pressure traveled across the Great Lakes, NY and New England during the night of February 20th with a new surface low developing off of the Cape cod coast by the early morning hours of February 21st.||Snow overspread VT during the late afternoon and early evening hours, becoming  heavy at times during the evening commute with snowfall rates in excess of 1 inch per hour at times. Snow ended during the early morning hours of February 21st. Snowfall totals across the VT were generally 4 to 9 inches with the heavier totals across the central Green Mountain communities. The main impacts were travel related due to the timing and there were some isolated power outages due to the wet, heavy nature of the snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall across the region was 4 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near average temperatures and precipitation led to little long-term change in drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions eased briefly to moderate (D1) drought around mid-month before returning to severe (D2) late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal trough combined with the daily seabreeze and a second inland trough to produce multiple rounds of shower and thunderstorm activity through the day and into the evening hours on June twenty-seventh. With ample instability and deep layer shear in place some of these thunderstorms became strong to severe in nature bringing a strong and damaging wind threat to the waters mainly north of the Crystal Coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust came in via the KHK Resort XRTH WeatherFlow station as thunderstorms moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed through the evening hours as an upper level low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed in the 1100 block of West Pleasant Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freedom (FREE) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold frontal boundary progressed across the southeastern states on the 23rd of June before slowing progress and nearly stalling over the northeast FL/southeast GA region. Plenty of summer moisture and instability in the vicinity of the boundary resulted in numerous to widespread showers and thunderstorms for several days in a row.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Employee relayed a report from social media of a tree down at the intersection of  Youngerman Circle and Argyle Forest Blvd. Time of damage estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a slowly advancing cold front across south-central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and nighttime hours of April 17. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and up to 70 mph wind gusts. Wind damage was also noted across a couple locations across southeast Kansas from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hailstones were mainly pea to penny size with a couple of quarter size hailstones included.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

Despite occasional precipitation episodes, especially across portions of northern Oklahoma and the eastern Red River Valley during the middle of the month, near to slightly below-average precipitation totals were observed for February 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A number of organized thunderstorm complexes affected eastern Oklahoma during the month of June, which resulted in widespread heavy rainfall across the region. Most of the area received between six and fifteen inches of rain, with as much as around twenty inches occurring locally. This rainfall corresponded to 150 to 450 percent of average monthly rainfall amounts across much of the region during the month. As a result of this abundant, widespread heavy rainfall, severe (D2) drought conditions across portions of Muskogee, Cherokee, and Mayes Counties, and extreme (D3) drought conditions across portions of Choctaw County, improved to abnormally dry (D0) drought conditions or better by the end of the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down into the roadway with lines hanging low near Johnstown Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued lack of rainfall combined with hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 10th drought monitor update, continuing through the rest of the Month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Stonewall Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.

A significant winter storm moved across the state between January 23rd and January 25th. Mixed precipitation was observed with significant accumulations of sleet and snow over the northern two-thirds of the state and freezing rain mixed with sleet over the southern third of the state. A very cold air mass followed this event prolonging accumulations to well beyond a weeks time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mix of sleet and snow accumulated to 5 inches at Point Cedar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of May saw below normal precipitation through the Four Corners region and portions of the central highlands of New Mexico, while areas along the Rio Grande Valley, southwestern, and eastern NM saw near to above normal precipitation. Mean temperatures trended near to slightly above normal through western NM and near to slightly below normal across eastern NM. This led to a modest expansion of extreme drought conditions across western NM and portions of the eastern plains of NM along the TX border. Gaps of severe drought through the northern mountains were filled in. Due to ongoing drought conditions and record low snowpack the previous winter, the Rio Grande dried up through the Albuquerque metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought was introduced to the northern half of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th morning into the early evening, temperatures were as low as -4F, with sustained winds around 10-15 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -23F.  During the 26th late evening into the overnight, temperatures were as low as -3F, with sustained winds around 10-15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.  During the 28th pre-dawn and early morning hours, temperatures were as low as -9, with sustained winds around 5 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions developed in the Ozark Foothills of Southeast Missouri early September due to a very dry August and first half of September. While conditions improved with October rainfall, D2 (Severe Drought) remained in northwestern Carter County and southwestern Ripley County through the end of year and expanded through Wayne and Butler Counties during January. Very dry conditions continued through February with a half inch to an inch of precipitation for the month, around 2.5-3 below normal, and the 2nd driest February in Poplar Bluff. The entirety of winter across Southeast Missouri finished with record low winter precipitation, with 2.44 at Poplar Bluff. By the end of February, roughly half of Carter and Ripley Counties had changed to D3 (Extreme Drought) status. Occurring in between the '25 and '26 growing seasons, impacts from drought in February were very limited. Drought conditions continued into March.

Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. Winds persisted into the midday on January 17, with occasional gusts as high as 35 to 50 mph. Areas of light snowfall generally on the order of a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, and locations mainly near Highway 71 experienced considerable time with visibility near or below one quarter mile with travel not recommended in areas surrounding Windom.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Persistent northwest winds gusted as high as 35 to 44 mph with periods of very light snowfall, which contributed to a prolonged reduction in visibility to one-quarter mile or less. Travel was not recommended by the evening of January 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported golf ball sized hail 7 miles south of Mexia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th into the early morning hours on April 26th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and extreme North Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across parts of extreme North Louisiana in addition to isolated damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Baseball size hail reported along Highway 534 southwest of Homer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to its neighbors across the Mississippi River, West Tennessee spent April 2026 battling a persistent, long-term moisture deficit dating back to July 2025. While central and northern parts of the Midwest received heavy spring rains that broke their droughts, West Tennessee experienced a highly regionalized spring recharge gap. EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions worsened to D3 conditions mid month and persisted into May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of convection earlier in the day, a meso-low moved through far northwest Indiana and southwest Michigan, producing a widespread swath of 45-55+ mph wind gusts. The highest wind gust report was a 70 mph gust that occurred at the South Bend Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snowfall as high as 36 inches in the city of Mackinaw City, MI, with upwards of 2 feet countywide, resulting in impassible roads -- even for many plow trucks, with several reports of plow trucks stuck in the snow. Blizzard conditions reported at the Cheboygan airport, KSLH, on the 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree clipped a passing car and caused minor damage to the vehicle. This occurred along OH Route 281, between Milton and Weston Roads, east of Custar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced reports of damaging winds and large hail across northern Ohio.

A deep low pressure trough moved eastward out of the Great Basin and tracked across eastern Utah into western Colorado, with above normal moisture pulled in ahead of it. This resulted in moderate snowfall for most mountain ranges in eastern Utah and western Colorado with the central and southern Colorado mountains receiving the heavier snowfall as colder air wrapped into the center of the low as it tracked further south over the Four Corners.  This favorable northerly flow on the backside of the low along with colder air resulted in higher snowfall amounts in the Uncompahgre Gorge of the Northwest San Juan Mountains and the valleys upstream from Ouray to Montrose.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 6 to 9 inches of snow fell across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the parish fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th. A 78 year old female died of hypothermia due to exposure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated southeast of Angora Nebraska in eastern Morrill County during the afternoon hours of March 12th.  Aided by west-northwest winds, gusting over 50 MPH, fire raced to the east-southeast. By late evening on March 12th, the fire had tracked some 70 miles across Garden County into southwestern Arthur, far southwestern Grant, and northwestern Keith County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, 642,029 acres were consumed.  The Morrill fire was the largest fire on record in the state of Nebraska. One direct fatality occurred as a result of the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Morrill fire entered northwestern Keith County during the evening hours of March 12th prompting the evacuation of residences and approximately 300 persons on the northwest side of Lake McConaughy. The fire continued and was contained on March 28th. A total of 37,212 acres were consumed in the fire and one outbuilding was destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front interacting with an unseasonably warm early January airmass with temperatures in the lower to middle 60s triggered a couple lines of strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of January 8th.  A few of the storms produced minor wind damage in Tazewell County and toppled two semis further east in Champaign County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown into tree branches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning, afternoon and evening hours of April 26 through April 29 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail and a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to the size of ping-pong balls fell between Purvis and Oak Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex, multi-day weather system moved across the region bringing rounds of wind, snow, and when combined, blizzard conditions. Strong winds aloft brought a round of high winds to the region beginning late on the 11th through the 12th. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station K1HM 6 NNE Fairfield. Blizzard conditions began at 10:56am and ended at 1:156pm MST. Montana Department of Transportation declared emergency travel only on I-15 through Dutton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front approached from the south as multiple shortwaves moved through aloft. A few storms were able to become severe as a decent veering wind profile with sufficient speed shear was available. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees down near Westerleigh on Staten Island.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of a rain/snow/light freezing rain mix which lasted several hours each. A CoCoRaHS observer 9 NNE of Bird Island reported a light coating of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado moved into Atoka County from Johnston County and continued moving east-southeast and then east. Tree and outbuilding damage occurred along Butterfield Crossing Road between Featherstone Road and Overland Trail. Crossing Overland Trail, the tornado turned east-northeast and snapped a few more trees near and west of Park Lane. The tornado dissipated near Boggy Depot Road east of Park Lane.

Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a highly unusual and taxing month for Northeast Arkansas. The state effectively skipped its typical stormy, rainy spring, pushing Mother Nature���s timeline forward by nearly two months into a hot, dry pattern. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down on Florida Court.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong-to-damaging wind gusts from the northwest developed during the morning across the mountains near the Blue Ridge escarpment in the wake of a cold front. Frequent gusts of 50-60 mph, with occasional gusts as high as 65 mph occurred in the lower elevations. Meanwhile, winds gusted as high as 80 mph on exposed peaks and ridgetops. Numerous trees and large tree limbs were blown down throughout the area, with some trees falling on power lines and causing scattered power outages.

Following a six-month respite (since early-September 2025) with no worse than Moderate Drought (D1) assigned to any portion of this 24-county South Central Nebraska area by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM), unfortunately March 2026 brought a steadily worsening drought situation back into the spotlight as much of the area not only spiraled into Severe Drought (D2), but also Extreme Drought (D3). This marked the first D3 within the area in 10 months (since May 2025) and marked the highest areal coverage of D3 in at least 2.5 years (since Sept. 2023). These rapid degradations not only stemmed from an incredibly dry March, but also from the inevitable consequence of cumulative dryness that had been building for six months...as October 2025-March 2026 ranked among the Top-4 driest October-March periods on record across most of the area (see below for more detailed precipitation info).  Breaking down the significant changes in county-level USDM drought categories during March, the month opened with the vast majority of the 24-county domain assigned either D1 (mainly counties along/north of Interstate 80) or Abnormally Dry/D0 (most places south of I-80). Only a small sliver of the area (around 2 percent of it) was void of all drought categories whatsoever...mainly southeast Thayer County. As March unfolded, degradation came swiftly, with portions of several counties designated D2 on the very first USDM issuance of the month, and a steadily expanding introduction of D3 arriving just a few weeks later. As a result, the end-of-March categorical breakdown stood as follows (in order of drought severity): 1) roughly 52% of South Central Nebraska featured D3 (most prevalent within counties along/north of I-80)...2) approximately 32% of real estate contained D1...3) around 15% of the area was in D1 (almost entirely within southern-most counties along the Kansas border)...4) the remaining sliver of the area (far southern Thayer/Nuckolls counties) was allotted D0. ||Turning to the dire precipitation details, and starting with the longer-term dryness (including a pronounced lack of snow) that defined Oct. 2025-March 2026, this six-month stretch registered among the Top-4 driest on record across South Central Nebraska. More specifically, based on a mix of observations from over 100 NWS and NeRAIN/CoCoRaHS observers along with some radar estimation, the majority of the 30-county area (roughly 80% of it) measured merely between 1.65-4.45...only 25-67% of normal. The highest concentration of amounts 2-or-less focused within primarily far northern and western counties, particularly: Dawson, Gosper, Furnas, Valley, Greeley, Buffalo. Citing six-month totals from just a few longtime NWS Cooperative Observer sites, the Canaday Power Plant (near Lexington) incredibly registered just 0.87 (17% of normal...driest on record), Arcadia 2W reported only 1.29 (21% of normal...driest on record) and Elwood 8S tallied just 1.36 (25% of normal...driest on record). At the Tri Cities airports, October-March ranked between the 2nd-4th driest on record, with totals ranging from 1.69 (Kearney) to 2.68 (Hastings). The only part of the area where precipitation amounts were even remotely close to normal (but still below it)...with at least 5...focused within portions of Thayer and Nuckolls counties. Drilling down to March itself, while October-February were dry enough, March truly brought things to a whole other level. In fact, the majority of South Central Nebraska measured somewhere between a paltry trace and 0.27 (essentially zero to 20% of normal). In fact, around 96% of the 24-county area observed LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH NORMAL March precipitation. Among the very driest of the dry, the following NWS stations were just a few of several that received a paltry trace for the month: Cambridge, Elwood 8S, Beaver City and Orleans 2W. In the Tri Cities, the airports registered just 0.12-0.14. Even the wettest parts of the domain were still significantly below normal, including totals of 0.63 at Hebron, 0.36 in St. Paul, and 0.35 at Belgrade. Needless to say, the significant dryness that spanned the end of 2025 into the start of 2026 set the stage for not only a rough start to the 2026 agricultural growing season in South Central Nebraska (meager soil moisture profiles) but also sparked an above-average early-spring wildfire threat. In addition to several smaller fires across the 24-county area, portions of southwestern Dawson County were ravaged by the massive Cottonwood Fire that ignited on March 12th in far southeastern Lincoln County.

Most of the lower elevations remain primarily as rain, but mixing with and changing to snow at times did allow for some light accumulations. Across the higher terrain snowfall and accumulations increased, especially for areas east of Lake Ontario where warning level snowfall amounts were observed. ||Another component of this storm was the winds associated with the system. Several reports of winds reaching 58 to 63 MPH were observed across the Western New York area. ||Notable snowfall reports include: 10.7 inches in Copenhagen, 9.8 inches in Highmarket and 8.0 inches in Constableville. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No observations within the county. Estimated maximum wind gusts of 58-62 mph based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An overall active pattern continued into June 2026 with daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received generally 3 to 8 inches of rain with the highest amounts favoring areas along and near the Tennessee River as well as areas near the Tennessee/Alabama border. It was also these areas that received more than their monthly normal precipitation while other areas continued to run a deficit. Fortunately, these repeated rounds of rain continued to improve drought conditions. For the first time since April 2026, none of Middle Tennessee was in extreme drought. About 11 percent of the area continued to be in severe drought, an improvement from 34 percent in May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from May 2026 improved in June to abnormally dry to moderate drought conditions across Van Buren County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to 5 to 20 below zero with wind chill temperatures of  15 to 35 below zero across northern NY.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures around 10 to 20 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 25 to 35 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached afternoon peaks as high as 109 degrees at Ida Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on February 19th into the morning hours on February 20th, a narrow but potent band of heavy snow moved into portions of west-central Wisconsin bringing snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. The heaviest snowfall totals fell in a narrow corridor in Crawford, Vernon, La Crosse and Monroe counties where 8 to 12 inches of snow fell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This snow band brought snowfall totals of 2 to 5 inches across Trempealeau County. The highest reported snowfall total was in Centerville where 5 inches was measured.

In addition to snowfall, winds and arctic air brought very cold windchills in the -20s across the U.P.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The EF1 tornado with winds up to 95 mph appeared to start just south of County Road 2200 N in Bureau County, where a barn structure sustained roofing damage. The tornado then moved northeastward into LaSalle County, producing damage to trees and farm outbuildings. Several wooden power poles were damaged just southeast of Mendota before a semi truck was blown over on I-39 as the tornado continued northeastward. The tornado then passed near Meriden, causing additional damage to trees and farm outbuildings before dissipating in an open field northwest of Earlville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced gusty winds that produced damaged along with large hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe thunderstorms tracked across portions of central and northeast South Dakota during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 3, generating high winds, large hail, and heavy rainfall.  ||One cluster tracked along the North Dakota border, where a personal weather station in Frederick recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph. These high winds destroyed the football field scoreboard and a storage shed in Frederick, knocked down trees and a radio tower, downed power lines in Hecla, and snapped power poles and flipped an irrigation pivot six miles north of Britton. The city of Britton lost electrical power. Three additional weather stations in Marshall County clocked wind gusts in excess of 60 mph. ||A second storm cluster moved out of eastern South Dakota into the southern Glacial Lakes region. Quarter-sized hail occurred at several locations. Heavy rainfall topping out at 4.40 inches in Clear Lake resulted in water six inches deep running over roads and caused a creek near the golf course to overflow its banks. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 12 to 18 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest amounts were 21 inches in Andover and 14.5 inches in Groveland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused rapid rises along a tributary crossing PR-5516 in Adjuntas. Floodwaters overtopped a bridge located between Selecto Supermarket and the Sweet and Frozen business, making the roadway impassable and disrupting local travel. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.00 to 1.30 inches across the month of February. This maintained D2 conditions for all but far southern Boone county through the month. D2 conditions would end with the March 10th drought monitor update.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed on U.S. Route 44 between Bangall Road and Nine Partners Lane in the Town of Washington. A tree and wires were downed on New York Route 216 between Old New York Route 52 and Phillips Road in East Fishkill. A tree was downed on New York Route 55 east of Old Route 55 in the Town of Pawling. An estimated 7700 people were without power throughout Dutchess County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. The most significant damage came from a surging portion of the line with an embedded supercell that resulted in two tornadoes: 1. an EF-0 tornado which crossed from northeastern Hopkins County into McLean County, and 2. an EF-1 tornado which caused damage from southeast of Rumsey to north of Livermore in McLean County. A swath of straight-line winds accompanied the first tornadic circulation. The tornadoes damaged numerous trees, some electrical lines and power poles, and a few homes and outbuildings. Several other straight-line wind damage reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS damage survey team found an EF-1 tornado, with peak winds of 95mph, occurred north of Livermore in McLean County. The tornado began near KY-138, causing significant loss of roof paneling to a barn. As it traveled a winding path generally eastward, extensive tree damage occurred along the path, including snapped tree trunks and uprooted trees. Two homes suffered significant damage when trees fell onto them. Other homes suffered shingle and fascia damage, and one had a detached garage collapse. A few power poles were damaged. The tornado lifted near the Ohio County line after damaging tree branches on Logsdon Ln.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Simultaneously and ahead (i.e. south) of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward and produced sporadic peak straight-line convective wind gusts of gale-to-storm-force along the OH shore amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. Within the warm and relatively-moist sector south of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward over and near Lake Erie and generated sporadic gale-force peak straight-line convective wind gusts along the OH shore during the predawn hours of the 15th amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Conneaut Light weather station recorded a peak straight-line convective wind gust of 52-mph from a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak ascent atop a very hot/unstable boundary layer fostered clusters of thunderstorms - generally disorganized/multi-cell in nature - from southwestern into north-central Oklahoma on the 29th. Damaging wind gusts and hail were observed with activity throughout the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated wind gust in Marshall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KLVS ASOS measured a peak gust of 58 mph.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Clipper system moved across NY and New England during the evening and overnight hours of February 10-11th to into the Gulf of Maine by the morning of February 11th.||Light to moderate snow spread across VT during the late afternoon and evening hours causing some hazardous travel for evening commute. The steadiest snow exited the region around midnight but more scattered orographic enhancement snow redeveloped around daybreak of the 11th and continued during the day and evening with travel issues the morning and evening commutes in some locations as well. ||Snowfall totals across the region were generally 3 to 5 inches with slightly lower amounts in the Champlain Valley of Addison and Rutland counties with some locally higher amounts in orographic favored higher terrain in central and northern VT with the first round of snow. Additional snowfall during the day and evening hours of February 11th led to an additional 3 to 6 inches along some communities along the western slopes of the Green Mountains. Two-day snowfall totals were generally 3 to 6 inches with locally 8 to 12 inches along western foothills of the central and northern Green Mountains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant snowstorm struck portions of East Tennessee at the end of the month, thanks to strong lift from a deep upper trough diving from north to south. A couple of long term cooperative weather stations saw top 10 snowfalls during this storm. This storm led to 3 confirmed fatalities in East Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell in parts of Polk County, with 3 inches of snow measured near Benton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of rain/freezing rain/snow mix which lasted several hours each. CoCoRaHS observers across the county report a glaze to an eighth of an inch of ice accretion across non-paved surfaces.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms moved across the lower Maryland Eastern Shore in the late afternoon and evening of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. A storm cluster produced a swath of damaging winds in Dorchester County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of damaging wind gusts. A few destructive wind gusts were noted in north-central Virginia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into eastern New York on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of the Hudson Valley into Washington County and the southern Taconics on one or both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms produced some large hail along with downed trees and wires. The Town of Pawling was hardest hit on June 11 as an intense thunderstorm produced hail in excess of 2 inches in some areas and widespread tree damage.
