EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A human triggered avalanche occurred on December 9th in the area of Long Pass in Kittitas county. The avalanche was preceded by a multi day heavy snow event that saw 1 to 2 feet of snow fall in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Northwest Avalanche Center reported an avalanche occurred in Longs Pass when 4 backcountry skiers attempted to descend a south facing slope. Two of four skiers passed away from either injuries sustained from the avalanche or from being buried by avalanche debris. In their report, the Avalanche center suggested that the avalanche failed on a melt-freeze crust from a rain even that occurred earlier in the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front slowly dropping in from the north triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms in an unseasonably warm airmass. A few of the storms produced sporadic damaging wind gusts and large hail, both during the afternoon and with a second wave in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on Saint John's Road/Hickory Hill Road near the intersection with MD-235 Three Notch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed along the 600 block of Lost Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system skirted across the northern combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles early on January 9th and brought rain with a changeover to snow. The heaviest snow produced by this system occurred in Kansas but did bring around three to six inches to eastern Cimarron County and western Texas County. Further south, across the far northwestern Texas Panhandle, areas still received one to two inches of snow from this system. This weather system was located far enough north that the rest of the Texas Panhandle was left dry.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The northern parts of the county observed around one inch of snow, especially around Stratford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather outbreak unfolded across central and north-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening of Friday (4/17). The event was triggered by a surface low-pressure system and cold front across the upper Midwest. ||NWS storm surveys confirmed 2 tornadoes that resulted in structural damage. A tornado formed 3 miles northwest of Glandon around 4:44 PM CDT and tracked into southeast Lincoln County producing EF-1 damage before dissipating around 4:55 PM CDT. Another tornado formed 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle in Marathon County around 4:46 PM CDT and dissipated around 5:03 PM CDT 5 miles southwest of Hogarty. This tornado produced EF-3 damage and destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. ||Beyond the tornadic threat, the storms produced isolated large hail up to half dollar size and damaging winds. Heavy rainfall was another impact, with localized totals ranging from 1 to 4 inches. These torrential downpours caused flash flooding, particularly in Marshfield where 2.65 inches of rain fell and multiple vehicles were reported stranded in deep water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny size hail fell near Athens.  The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent enhanced westerly flow with multiple embedded shortwave troughs brought multiple instances of severe wind gusts and hail to northern Utah as well as flash flooding to Sevier county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1.00 hail in Plymouth, UT via social media. Time and location are approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding throughout southern Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a tree down on the 8900 block of North 400 East Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 9, 2026, scattered thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across portions of eastern Nebraska. A warm, unstable air mass fueled the activity as a surface low deepened and moved eastward into the state. Storms initially developed in central Nebraska before tracking east-northeastward, with peak wind gusts measured between 59 and 70 mph across Boone, Antelope, Butler, and Wayne counties. Storm intensity gradually diminished as the system moved northeastward into the late evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of several trees down in David City, NE with estimated wind gusts of 60 mph. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 0.75 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system made its way into the Bering Sea early Wednesday morning (4/22), bringing widespread snow, mixed precipitation, and strong winds to Western Alaska and portions of the Western/Central Interior. As the low moved inland, a front moving northeast off the low brought predominantly snow to the Seward Peninsula and YK Delta with 2 to 8 of total accumulations. This system was able to support gusty winds up to 60 mph and easily created widespread blowing snow conditions to much of the West Coast. By the time the front made its way into the Interior, a rain/snow mix of around 2 to 6 fell in addition to strong southerly gap winds through both Isabel and Windy Pass. Winds gusted anywhere between 65 to 75 mph through the passes, creating difficult travel conditions along the Parks and Richardson Highway. Effects from this system subsequently diminished by the weekend (4/25 through 4/26), resulting in a steady warming trend as upper level southerly flow set up over the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Hooper Bay AWOS site (PAHP) reported blizzard like conditions beginning at 00:25 AKDT on 4/22 and continued through 08:50 AKDT on 4/22. Blizzard conditions were met at 03:25 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 38 mph winds gusting to 44 mph. A peak observation was reported at 04:38 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 43 mph winds gusting to 48 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low pressure system moved across the region, creating a deformation zone that brought winter weather conditions to the Northern Rockies. The primary synoptic driver of the precipitation was an advancing frontal boundary that moved through the area during the morning and day of Thursday April 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation began as a frontal passage that moved through around 0700MST on April 2, bringing snowfall rates of nearly two inches per hour to the Discovery Ski Area. Snow continued into April 3, resulting in storm total accumulations of ten inches at Discovery and five and a half inches northwest of Anaconda. Roadway conditions deteriorated, leading to significant travel impacts on April 3. At 0239MST, chains were required for towing units on Interstate 90 between mile markers 228 and 241. A crash resulted in a right lane closure on US Highway 12 westbound at mile marker 29.5 at 0305 MST (indirect). Additionally, spun-out semi-trucks forced a right lane closure on Interstate 90 eastbound at mile marker 232 around 0355MST (indirect). At Georgetown Lake, snowfall began around 0600MST on April 2, accompanied by wind gusts near twenty miles per hour and road temperatures dropping to thirty-two degrees, before tapering off by 0300MST on April 3. Snow eventually tapered off at Homestake Pass by 0830MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong north winds affected North and Central Texas the day of March 15 following the passage of a cold front. Wind gusts at times exceeded 55 mph. Unfortunately a fatality occurred on an area lake due to the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The TKI ASOS reported a 61 mph wind gust at 541 PM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into Lower Michigan on June 10 resulting in tens of thousands of power outages statewide from wind damage and down trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires down at Lighthouse Way and 131st street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee reported snowfall totals of sixteen inches near Hubert, North Carolina, with several additional reports from the public, and CoCoRaHS stations reporting between twelve and seventeen inches of snowfall across Onslow County. Snowfall fell between the morning hours on January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Breezy southerly winds shifted to southwesterly later into the evening of the 8th ahead of a cold frontal passage. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the late evening hours in Southwest Indiana. Gusty gradient winds of near and above 40mph developed in portions of Southwest Indiana during the evening ahead of those storms.

Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on IL-29 south of Cedar Hills Dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a dryline and some of these storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced ping pong ball size hail on the north shore of Lake Amistad.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A broken pole occurred on Booster Club Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar sized hail was reported in a mainly rural area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported golf ball sized hail 4 miles north of Rochester.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree on a house on the 100 block of covey trl.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds on a powerline near the end of Sauratown Mountain Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms trained over portions of Barton, Russell, Ellsworth, and Lincoln counties during the afternoon and evening hours of May 17th. Several reports of large hail and flash flooding were received. The largest hail report was near Milberger in Russell County with a size of 2.25 inches in diameter.

A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down along North Fork Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas on the evening of the 14th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of eastern Foard County, producing reports of large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through Spotter Network.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Long-term drought combined with generally dry conditions to provide an environment where any fires that start could spread and linger.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The MM-45 wildfire reached a total acreage of 9600 acres. No deaths or road closures were reported during the incident and no damage to structures occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter at Sims measured 6 inches of snow in 24 hours. The National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center estimated 12 to 24 inches of storm total snow from this storm. Southerly wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph were observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 2.5 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow overspread the western Maine foothills by the afternoon on the 25th. Within an hour or two snow was moderate to heavy at times as an intense band of lift moved into the region. Snowfall rates were one to two inches per hour during the heavy snow. Snow continued overnight into the 26th, with occasional breaks or lighter snowfall before the storm center moved into the Atlantic. Snowfall totals ranged from 14 to 18 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold storm system moved into the region on the 16th and 17th. Winds increased on the 16th with stronger gusts on the 17th. Light rain and snow showers along with much colder conditions followed with highs only in the 50s accompanied the winds on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station 616SE SCE Sherwin Hill East measured a wind gust of 61 mph. Also, mesonet station C3GDP Glider Point measured a wind gust of 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front attendant to a southern Canada low pressure system moved slowly through western and central Virginia, triggering showers and thunderstorms. Bulk shear of around 30kts just east of the Blue Ridge supported damaging wind gusts from a few storms, which resulted in localized tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bogle Field scoreboard at Cave Spring Middle School was blown down by thunderstorm winds, also damaging a nearby fence in the process.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A 985mb low pressure moved through the region. The associated cold front sent temperatures plummeting from the 60s to 70s down into the 20s and 30s. Prior to the cold front, gusty wind of 45 to 50 mph where common, but there were a couple of instances of 55 mph to 60 mph wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at Goshen Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front moved through western Kentucky on the morning of the 30th, bringing cold temperatures down to the teens. Blustery northwest winds caused wind chills to fall around -5 to -7 the night of the 30th into the morning of the 31st. Intervals of dangerous wind chills was variable across the region with northern portions of the Kentucky Purchase and Pennyrile remaining above threshold.

Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 15 to 24 inches fell across the zone with near blizzard conditions at times. Cocorahs observers reported 22.6 inches in Armonk, and 17.0 inches in Shrub Oak. A trained spotter reported 21.5 inches at 2 NNW White Plains with public reports of over 20 inches across the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto a vehicle on Huber Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave brought about windy thunderstorms across much of southern MT. In it's wake, a cold front crossed the area, and strong winds behind the front persisted well into the 14th. Non-convective gusts up to 80 mph were observed, with convective gusts up to 80 mph observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lodge Grass W mesonet gusted to 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large hardwood trees were blown down along Left Freemans Creek Road, Churchville Road, and Freemans Creek Road between Churchville and Camden.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 90 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL WATERS FROM PORT FOURCHON LOUISIANA TO LOWER ATCHAFALAYA RIVER LOUISIANA FROM 20 TO 60 NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station KSPR 55 SW Cocodrie measured a 46mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Numerous damaging wind reports occurred across eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a tree onto a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Additional heavy rainfall along with wet antecedent conditions lead to more flash flooding, some significant, in the Pine Belt region of Mississippi. Several major roads were flooded, as well as homes. Water rescues were conducted in the Seminary area as several cars became stranded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered Keith's Gas Station in Seminary. Two cars went into the ditch nearby. Local residents abandoned cars on roads, with water rescues conducted by the local fire department. Several homes were flooded as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning and afternoon hours of June 22 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on Old Highway 27.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was down near Home Depot entrance.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and stagnant air mass in the wake of a wet snowfall resulted in areas of dense freezing fog late on January 17th and early on January 18th. The fog dissipated before dawn as a cold front moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense freezing fog was observed at Wings Field Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.

A trough stationed over western Pennsylvania during the early morning hours with ample moisture and lift allowed for snowfall to begin across much of western Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of January 24th and the early morning hours of January 25, 2026. Moderate-to-heavy snowfall rates were observed at onset with low-level frontogenesis allowing for a moderate snowfall band across portions of western Pennsylvania prior to sunrise. Ample moisture in place with an approaching area of low pressure from the Lower Ohio River Valley also allowed for snowfall to begin across portions of southeastern Pennsylvania ahead of sunrise on January 25th. The progressive movement of the aforementioned trough and low pressure system allowed for a shorter duration of snowfall than could have occurred, with snowfall gradually tapering off across much of the area by the evening hours of January 26th. Westerly flow in the wake of the system did allow for continued upslope snow showers across the western highlands, which continued to allow for additional accumulations. Much of central Pennsylvania observed heavy snowfall, with Harrisburg International Airport and Williamsport Regional Airport breaking daily snowfall records, which have been tracked since 1888 and 1895, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow began in the early morning January 25 and continued into the evening, with most of Union County seeing 8-12 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Great Lakes region, producing strong thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A barn was blown down along Byrket Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds, gusting to 58 MPH, were reported at the Santa Cruz Island Reservoir.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent cold front ushered a bitterly cold airmass into eastern New York on January 23-24, 2026. The combination of bitterly cold air temperatures (minimum temperatures ranging from -34 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit) and gusty winds (ranging from 25 to nearly 50 mph) made for dangerously cold wind chills or feels-like temperatures. Minimum feels-like temperatures ultimately ranged from about -35 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit across the region with the coldest of these confined to portions of the Southern Adirondacks, Lake George-Saratoga Region, and Mohawk Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -32 degrees Fahrenheit reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1.25 inch diameter hail east of Sun Prairie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening hours of the 20th. A couple of the storms became severe with hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter.

Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF1 tornado touched down just southwest of Fordsville Road east of Tylertown, MS in Wathall County. The worst damage damage was seen just northeast of the touchdown point with light damage to a roof and an area of tree damage with multiple uprooted trees. Light tree damage was noted along the path. It then crossed into Marion County where tree damage was noted near the intersection of Welch Lane and Branton Bay Road. The tornado tracked northeast, closely following Branton Bay Road up to Highway 98. The tornado did some roof damage to Popwell's Family Restaurant on Highway 98. The tornado ended as it crossed Old Highway 24. The maximum winds were estimated at 90 MPH. The total path length across Wathall and Marion counties was around 7 miles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.

The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.
A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing strong winds and dangerous marine conditions as the line moved offshore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XTCY at the Texas Corinthian Yacht Club measured a 38 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

A record-breaking winter storm impacted western Montana as a very cold trough, originating from Siberia, transitioned southeast into the region. This system coincided with an Arctic air mass pushing west toward the Continental Divide. A powerful surface low of 981 millibars broke all-time February sea level pressure records across the Northern Rockies, including a record 985.2 mb at Missoula (previous record 985.5 mb in 1963). The negatively tilted nature of the trough resulted in prolonged heavy snowfall on the morning of the 17th, particularly across northwest Montana. By February 18th, shortwaves embedded in the cyclonic flow produced convective snow showers and squalls overrunning the Arctic boundary in place. This brought isolated flash-freeze and high impact travel to the evening commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall impacted the US-93 and US-2 corridors. Eureka received 5 inches of snow, and a nearby location, southeast of Eureka, reported 7.5 inches of snow. A CoCoRaHS observer in Marion reported 3.8 inches. Arctic air seeped south after midnight, leading to slick roads and a flipped truck reported north of Eureka at 0855MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down along Juniata River Road in Woodbury Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.

High winds caused by pressure differences in the wake of thunderstorms gusted up to 67 mph in Racine and 58 mph in Lafayette County. Outdoor equipment and trailers were moved across a parking lot in Racine, including substantial damage to sheds. Some snapped and uprooted trees also occurred in the Racine area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Batten Airport in Racine recorded a wind gust of 67 mph. Outdoor equipment and trailers were moved across a parking lot of a large retailer, including substantial damage to its sheds. Some snapped and uprooted trees also occurred in the Racine area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree fell on a car on Hwy 21 and Fairgrounds, in Bush.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain over steep terrain resulted in NH-153 in Eaton being reduced down to one lane due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of showers and thunderstorms that had developed along a quasi-stationary front over southern Kansas, moved slowly southward across much of northeastern Oklahoma during the morning and afternoon of the 10th. Locally heavy rainfall amounts of two to three inches in just a few hours occurred across portions of northeastern Oklahoma, which resulted in isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle was stranded in flood water on West 5th Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique snow setup for South Carolina continued into February 1st as a strong coastal low strengthening offshore, while a upper level disturbance shifted over our area. This provided sufficient synoptic and mesoscale lift to continue across portions of northern and eastern SC with unusually high snow to liquid ratios between 15-20 to 1 and highest amounts in the Pee Dee region of SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple measurements across the county from COOP, CoCoRAHS, public, and spotters of between 2 to 5 inches of storm total snowfall with snow accumulating into February 1st. Highest measured amount in the county was 5 inches near Lugoff for storm total.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (105F) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level trough moved into the Rockies on May 18, with southwest flow aloft over the Missouri Ozarks. A cluster of thunderstorms pushed southeast into portions of central Missouri, bringing heavy rainfall and flash flooding to St. Clair, Benton, and Camden counties. Additionally, a low level jet axis extending from the Gulf through eastern Kansas strengthened overnight into May 19 while interacting with the upper level trough and a surface front. As a result, a second line of thunderstorms formed across northern Kansas, moving into Missouri overnight before exiting the state in the late afternoon hours. With the multiple rounds of heavy rainfall, storm total rainfall observations ranged between 3-7 inches across portions of southeast Kansas and the Missouri Ozarks, with 8.20 inches of rainfall measured in Hickory County. This led to multiple road closures reported from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few reports came in of trees down in McDonald County from the morning round of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Chatham Airport ASOS (KCQX) blizzard conditions occurred from 625 AM EST to 530 PM EST. The highest gust was 72 mph at 604 AM EST. Chatham MA (KCQX) observations are not available after 930 am due to ASOS failure, so end time is estimated. The Falmouth Airport ASOS (KFMH) had blizzard conditions from 200 AM EST to 400 PM EST. A reliable observer measured a wind gust of 80 mph in Falmouth.  At the Hyannis Airport ASOS (KHYA) blizzard conditions were reported between 520 AM EST and 530 PM EST. Generally 12-20 inches of snow fell. The highest amount was 21 inches in Forestdale. Cape Cod suffered nearly total power outage for a time, and power outages stretched well into the middle and end of the week.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the night of June 21st, 2026 and into the early morning of June 22nd, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System moved through southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. This system brought multiple lines of storms and some supercells. Several tornadoes occurred along with flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a tree down over the 2800 block of KY 162.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably mild air moved into the region ahead of a strong low pressure system. These conditions, on top of a fairly dry February across western South Dakota allowed a fire to develop northeast of the community of Green Grass and spread rapidly southeast. 991 acres of mostly prairie and pasture were burned in the fire, with a portion of Highway 63 closed due to smoke and the threat of the fire crossing the Highway. ||Winds picked up dramatically with the passage of the low pressure system, with a peak wind gust of 81 mph recorded at the Pierre Regional Airport ASOS. The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.

As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures near of just above 100 degrees and high humidity, a remnant of rainfall associated with tropical moisture as Tropical Storm Arthur began to form, created heat index values estimated to be between 111 and 114, with a peak of 115, in inland Willacy County.  Observed data from Valley International Airport (Harlingen, about 8 miles south of the county line) and Brooks County Airport (near Falfurrias) were used as proxy data for this area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dense fog developed along a vertical column across the center of the CWA including the most of the bigger cities. This started near the end of 3/3 and into the morning of 3/4.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station KLBL Liberal reported quarter-mile visibility in dense fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media picture indicated several large trees branches blown down across Highway 111 north of the city of Hamilton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.

A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto power lines along Wickham Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought significantly worsened across much of eastern Utah and western Colorado during the week between the March 24th US Drought Monitor update and the March 31st update. Nearly every zone in eastern Utah and western Colorado was now experiencing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, or worse.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: With the 3/31 US Drought Monitor update, 100% of Utah Zone 028 - La Sal & Abajo Mountains was under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. No reports of impacts or losses related to drought conditions in the zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While occasional precipitation events occurred in January 2026, including an impactful winter storm in the late month, most areas saw continued precipitation deficits relative to January normals. Rather widespread severe (or worse) drought conditions continued in areas near and south of the Interstate 40 corridor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oklahoma City Will Rogers International Airport (KOKC) observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation continued to lack across much of northwest Iowa with 25 percent to 75 percent of normal during the month for areas west of U.S. Highway 59.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions worsened to severe (D2) very late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Louisiana and Arkansas and produced damaging wind gusts and hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed across northern Catahoula Parish. Some were blocking roads, including at the LA Highway 124 and Tew Lake Road intersection.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This episode is part 1 of 2 from two rounds of severe weather that occurred during the late evening of June 9th into the early morning of June 10th. ||Widespread wind damage occurred across western Minnesota during overnight storms which had moved in from the Dakotas. The strongest wind report was observed in Lac Qui Parle County at 83 mph near Marietta, MN. One tornado was caught on camera overnight near the Kandiyohi and Pope County line, but no damage was reported, leaving its rating as EF-U (Unknown). As the line of storms continued east, wind gusts decreased to 30-40kts in most areas. However, several emergency managers areas reported downed trees within their municipalities. A few downbursts did occur northeast of the Twin Cities metro area, with tree damage being reported from St Paul up towards Shoreview and White Bear Lake and then all the way up to Forest Lake and Chisago City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind gusts downed a dozen trees in Leaf Valley MN or 10 miles NW of Alexandria. The AWOS Station located at Alexandria Airport recorded a 64mph thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

A strong cold front produced a low end squall line of thunderstorms, which in turn produced several reports of damaging winds. After the cold front's passage, a much colder airmass moved in and snow showers developed, leading to light snowfall for much of northeastern Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were felled by severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Extreme Drought (D3) category ended in portions of the Upper Gila River and Aravaipa Valleys. The overall precipitation for Arizona ranking was 28th driest for the period of record for the month of January. Soil moisture readings continued to range between the 30th and 70th percentile ranking for the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: For the month of January, Graham county ranked the 24th driest for the period of record and Greenlee county ranked the 21st driest for the period of record. Soil moisture readings continued to range between the 30th and 70th percentile for the month of January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D3-D4 drought conditions prevailed to start the month of May across southwest and south central Georgia. However, beneficial rain during the month reduced the drought to D2 by the end of the month near a line from Albany to Bainbridge and westward. D3-D4 drought still prevailed farther east across south central Georgia.
Storms moved through SE Texas and produced strong winds and heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported wind damage to a Lowes. Part of the front sign was damaged, though otherwise damage was minor. Winds were estimated a 65 mph using LIRB with a DoD of 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed in the foothills during the morning hours of March 12th. Strong winds spread onto the plains through the day. Extreme high winds occurred north of Fort Collins/Wellington area to the Wyoming/Colorado border. Gusts peaked at 85 to 95 mph. U.S. Highways 287 and 85 as well as I-25 were closed before of the strong winds. There were reports of trees blown down and roof damage in Fort Collins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 70 mph wind gust was reported 3 miles north-northwest of Ketoa and a 66 mph wind gust was reported 11 miles west-northwest of Westplains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of April, persisting extreme drought (D3) and  exceptional drought (D4) conditions area-wide. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in April continued the Extreme (D3) drought. Conditions worsened through the month with the county being upgraded to Exceptional (D4) drought on April 7, 2026. Exceptional drought then continued for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong clipper storm system from the Canadian Rockies moved into our region, producing strong and damaging wind across northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bloomfield CWOP mesonet site (G0525) measured a 71 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to nickel-size along OH Route 61 on the southeast side of Iberia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 12th, the San Juan streamer persisted over the same areas across the San Juan metro area and nearby counties, leaving between 1 and 2 inches of rain during the mid-afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A car was stranded due to flooding waters at Calle Santiago Iglesias.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weatherlink site 10 N selkirk measured 59 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 5F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto the roadway near Valley Green.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof ripped off of Ace Hardware.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of strong to severe storms impacted southeast Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and 70 mph wind gusts which blew over a semi truck in Montgomery County.

CZ_NAME: EAST SLOPES SANGRE DE CRISTO MOUNTAINS
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level disturbance moved across the northern and central Rockies during the day on April 23rd resulting in some strong wind gusts across the Sangre de Cristo Mountains before sunrise before spreading east to the adjacent highlands across northeast and east central NM mid to late morning as daytime mixing commenced. This resulted in a period of high winds at Clines Corners during the late morning hours. These strong winds helped the Tusas Wildfire near Sapello, NM, that started April 22nd, grow to 233 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Tusas Wildfire began along NM Highway 266 between mile markers 3 and 4 west of Sapello, NM. The fire grew northeastward into surrounding hills located in an area surrounded by but not included within the 2022 Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar. The fire grew in a critical fire weather environment April 23rd before coming under control April 24th, burning a total of 233 acres. No structures were reported destroyed or damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail southwest of Richfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of May, D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Issaquena County to Forrest County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Lawrence County decreased from D1 (Moderate Drought) to D0 (Abnormally Dry) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.
