EVENT_NARRATIVE: County 911 center reported that route 956 was closed in the vicinity of Fayette-Neshannock Falls Road because the roadway was flooded in several locations due to an ice jam on Neshannock Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak continued into the first couple days of February. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, as it extends well back into January. For the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Highlands, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For the Shenandoah Valley, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. For the Virginia Piedmont to I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large cedar tree limbs in wind break were broken.  There was damage done to gutters on the house, which may have been due to the limb hitting the gutters.  A small tower for internet was bent over the nearby garage.  A small unanchored grain bin used for storage was blown off the foundation.  An irrigation engine on a stand was tipped over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure moved from the Northern Rockies the morning of the 12th to the Upper Great Lakes the morning of the 13th and deepened as it moved east. This brought heavy snowfall to the region starting the afternoon/evening of the 12th and continued into the morning of the 13th. Snowfall totals of 4 to 8 inches were seen across the area with higher pockets of 7 to 10 inches plus, including a high report of 14 inches in Hovland. Additionally, strong winds off of Lake Superior led to a period of blizzard conditions along the North Shore into the Twin Ports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall across the northern part of the county was heavier than expected with widespread totals of 6 to 9 inches. A high report of 10.3 inches was received from 7 miles west of Hackensack.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 1 inch were reported across McLennan County. The highest sleet and snow totals were reported near Waco and Hewitt.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported that the marginal between PR-100 and El Meson restaurant in Cabo Rojo is being affected by flooding. Around 2.5 inches of rain have fallen in that area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS in Chester measured around 15 inches of heavy snow over this period. The National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center estimates 2 to over 6 feet of heavy snow. Highway 70 was closed at times due to heavy snow. Wind gusts of 35 to 55 mph were observed. Thousands of power outages were reported from downed trees and heavy snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong upper level troughing diving southeastward from central BC toward southern AB/SK resulted in a sharp transition to strong zonal flow aloft across the Northern Rockies April 7. Favorable timing of the system, arriving during the day, allowed for daytime mixing to translate stronger gusts to the surface in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station KMTMONTA17 IngerRanch measured two gusts of 58 mph or greater.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple trees blew down in Williamsport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail was mostly to the size of grapes but a few were to the size of golf balls to hen eggs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak gust to 87 mph was recorded at the KMYP AWOS on Monarch Pass at 3:15 AM MST 2/17. Additional gusts recorded at this sensor were to 72 mph at 5:55 AM MST 2/17, and to 86 mph at 11:55 AM MST 2/17. Gusts at other sensors across the region ranged from 45 mph to 71 mph during the period of highest winds. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities related to this wind event were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were reported down near Crockers Nub Road and Old Bailey Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line was blown down near Brannon Stand and Pine Needles Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Garage door was blown in by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage was reported on Red Brush Trail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across Maryland. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 12 to 16 across Garrett County, with a general 8 to 12 across the remainder of the area aside from southern Maryland where 4-8 was observed. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed across southern Maryland. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state.
A strong upper trough and Arctic high pressure over the Mid-Atlantic combined to produce a period of high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Maryland DOT sensor measured a peak wind gust of 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The continuation of a prolonged period of dense fog occurring every night and every morning across San Joaquin Valley into the first part of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KMCE Merced Airport reported near zero mile visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Cherry Fire ignited around 10:30 a.m. on Friday, June 26, 2026, near Weiss Highway and Cherry Creek in Juab County, Utah. It subsequently merged with the nearby Maple Peak Fire, which had started the night before. Given exceptionally hot, dry, and windy conditions through much of its early life during a PDS Red Flag Warning day, it would go on to grow fast and rapidly through the next few days while exhibiting extreme fire behavior as it grew across portions of Juab, Utah, and Tooele counties (encompassing portions of public zones 101, 102, and 115) eventually reaching the ongoing Iron fire. Thankfully, no structures were harmed with no reported injuries or fatalities. This fire has been contained as of July 9, 2026 and reached a total of 34,252 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Cherry Fire ignited around 10:30 a.m. on Friday, June 26, 2026, near Weiss Highway and Cherry Creek in Juab County, Utah. It subsequently merged with the nearby Maple Peak Fire, which had started the night before. Given exceptionally hot, dry, and windy conditions through much of its early life during a PDS Red Flag Warning day, it would go on to grow fast and rapidly through the next few days while exhibiting extreme fire behavior as it grew across portions of Juab, Utah, and Tooele counties (encompassing portions of public zones 101, 102, and 115) eventually reaching the ongoing Iron fire. Thankfully, no structures were harmed with no reported injuries or fatalities. This fire has been contained as of July 9, 2026 and reached a total of 34,252 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed near Main street and West Street in Argyle. An additional tree was downed on State Route 40 near Argyle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong low pressure area swung through southern Virginia, dragging a cold front across Eastern NC by the evening hours. Ahead of it, bands of thunderstorms formed in the afternoon due to unstable conditions and wind shear in place. Scattered severe wind gusts embedded in some of the storms produced wind damage across the area. There were also several reports of hail up to nickel size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny sized hail fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near normal precipitation in April kept drought conditions mainly in Severe(D2) drought category or better.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe(D2) drought continued for the entire month.  There was only a trace of precipitation recorded by the White Signal Cooperative Observer which was 0.30 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed and moved across western SD and brought strong, damaging wind gusts to the Black Hills. Storms consolidated into a line and produced strong wind gusts further east.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SDOT submitted wind gust report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A robust low pressure system was located off the California coast combined with a high pressure system, produced a tight pressure gradient across the region. Strong winds were observed mainly across Kern County desert.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station SE300 Pigeon Spring (SCE).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A midlevel trough lifting northeast from Arkansas and Mississippi, interacted with a cold front moving in from the north, to cause widespread showers and thunderstorms across East Tennessee from late in the evening on May 29th, through the late morning hours on May 30th. This led to scattered reports of flash flooding across East Tennessee, most notably in the central Tennessee valley and northern Cumberland Plateau areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The right lane of US Highway 411 South by Ridgeway Trail closed for flooding over  roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Area had slow moving thunderstorms producing a radar estimated one to two inches of rain. Soil was already saturated from melting snow. Rain gauges in the area recorded 0.3 to 0.7 inches of rain. The gauges were not in the area impacted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large road washout on Green Hollow Road at MP5, with large boulders in road and mud flowing across road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were down around Skipperville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter-sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lingering stalled front remained in the forecast area 5/23, but a embedded shortwave in the general troughing pattern moved in during the afternoon and evening hours, leading to scattered convection to develop. The environment ahead of this shortwave was characterized by MLCAPE values over 2000 J/kg and effective shear near 30-35 kts. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across the forecast area during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing damaging winds, hail up to golf ball sized, and even a report of a waterspout over Lake Murray in SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement officer reported a tree down with picture of blocking roadway near Cedar Grove Lane and Shady Grove Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front interacting with an unseasonably warm early January airmass with temperatures in the lower to middle 60s triggered a couple lines of strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of January 8th.  A few of the storms produced minor wind damage in Tazewell County and toppled two semis further east in Champaign County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four power poles were snapped along Stringtown Road just southwest of Minier.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another long duration strong wind event hit southeast Wyoming and spanned nearly 3 days. Although the strong winds were more confined to the Interstate 80 and Interstate 25 corridors this time around, very strong winds up to 79 MPH were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four observation sensors reported wind gusts over 58 MPH during the afternoon of March 9th. Peak wind gust was observed at Douglas Airport ASOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough with a cold front swept across Kansas. This brought strong upper-level winds up to 50-60 KTs. As winds mixed down to the surface, very strong winds were recorded up to multiple 67 mph gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station recorded a 64 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The right entrance region of a jet within stronger flow across the northern tier of the U.S. helped to increase convergence by late afternoon and early evening along a cold front working eastward through northwest Iowa.  Mixed-layer instability reached up to 1500-2000 J/kg courtesy of 8C/km mid-level lapse rates with deep-layer shear of 40 to 50 knots. Initially discrete cells produced large hail, with a tendency to evolve toward more linear structures.
Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were downed just south of Fayette Central Elementary School.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of short wave moved across Southeast Texas and produced a few severe storms during late May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were reported down near the south end of Toledo Bend.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a weak surface front/pressure trough across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 26th. This activity produced damaging winds, hail and flooding as it progressed south/southeastward into the early morning of the 27th. Significant damaging winds and hail were noted with a trio of more organized thunderstorms (supercells) during this time impacting areas around Enid, Stillwater, Oklahoma City and Chandler, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee reported a large tree blown down on Vaughn Ridge Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A heathly tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A private weather station measured 4.02 inches of rain in 3 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball sized hail reported east of Westboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe storms developed along a slow moving cold front as it creeped across the area through the afternoon and into the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 2-inch hail along with estimated winds up to 90 mph. Multiple structures were damaged across south-central Kansas due to these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were estimated to be around 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gust was measured by a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 4 miles south of Arlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass that was in place across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and powerlines were were downed between Skeels Road and U.S. Route 33.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An elevated warm front which resulted in warm advection in the mid levels resulted in an accumulating snow across northwestern portions of Southern Connecticut. The first of 2 accumulating snowfalls within 48 hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters reported 5.9 inches at 4 NNW New Fairfield, along with 2.5 inches at 3 WSW Shelton, and 2.5 inches at 3 SSE Weston.  The public reported 3.5 inches at 4 NNW Ridgefield and 2.7 inches at 2 SW Newtown. An emergency manager reported 3.0 inches in Bethel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Ohio Valley into the northern Mid-Atlantic region. A mid-level system tracked in from the west and led to numerous showers and storms across the Coastal Plain and Piedmont of Central North Carolina. Numerous wind damage reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of Piney Grove Church Road and Gum Pond Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low and subsequent coastal low pressure brought heavy snow to northeastern North Carolina from January 31 to February 1, 2026. Heavy snow was focused along the coast with lower amounts with westward extent.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow fell from January 31 to February 1, 2026 across Camden County. Event total snowfall amounts ranged from 5-9 inches. A snowfall total of 8.5 inches was received in Riddle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The largest hailstone was baseball size, although dime to tennis ball size hailstones fell for 10 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms moved across South Florida on April 8, 2026. A mesoscale area of low pressure followed the earlier round of storms producing widespread strong winds across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Elevated Tempest Weather Station E 11 Street near the Port of Palm Beach reported a wind gust of 61 mph at 5:40pm as gusty winds pushed onshore associated with a thunderstorm offshore.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||In southeast Ohio, the highest snow amounts, which ranged from around five to ten inches, were observed in Perry, Washington, Athens, Vinton, and Jackson Counties. In addition to a few inches of snow, sleet and freezing rain become more dominant further south. Jackson and Lawrence Counties had the most notable sleet amounts, each coming in with around an inch of accumulation. As for freezing rain, a few tenths of an inch of ice were observed in Lawrence County.
Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 80 mph touched down near Olesen Drive and Gartner Road and moved northeast across the Huntington Hills and Olesen Estates neighborhoods of Naperville producing a narrow path of 50 to 75 yards of snapped and uprooted trees. The tornado broaden in width while crossing Naper Boulevard and passing an apartment complex, where a roughly 150 yard wide path of extensive tree damage occurred. The tornado turned to the east and ended near Bristol Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were knocked down around the town of Centerville. One occurred along Bridge Branch Road and the other on the Right Fork of Garretts Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Southwest and south-central Georgia started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter emailed a photo of 1.75 inch hail south of Blue Mound.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on Central Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercell thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 10th across portions of central and northeast Kansas. Large hail up to baseball size, damaging winds, and a brief tornado occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received via mPing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down across Long Lane and US 6 near Union Mills.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June brought some drought relief to north Mississippi, but recovery remained limited. Beneficial rainfall helped reduce drought intensity in localized areas, but Extreme and Severe Drought persisted in the southwestern zones, and significant agricultural impacts continued. Sustained and widespread rainfall will be necessary to replenish deeper soil moisture, restore pastures, and substantially reduce the long-term precipitation deficits across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 Extreme Drought persisted across the Tallahatchie tail for the month of June. However, conditions elsewhere improved to D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought conditions by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An inch diameter tree was uprooted by thunderstorm wind gusts. Nearby there was damage to furniture and siding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through eastern Pennsylvania. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 68 MPH gust was measured at Reading Regional Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front passing through the region generated high winds, with 20 weather stations recording a peak wind of 58 mph or greater. A peak wind of 66 mph was measured at the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 13 miles east of Eureka, while the SDDOT RWIS near Ridgeview and the Grand River RAWS both topped out at 65 mph.

Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photograph on social media showed quarter size hail south of Lockney.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued, and worsened across Surry county through April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station measured a wind gust to 77 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather outbreak unfolded across central and north-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening of Friday (4/17). The event was triggered by a surface low-pressure system and cold front across the upper Midwest. ||NWS storm surveys confirmed 2 tornadoes that resulted in structural damage. A tornado formed 3 miles northwest of Glandon around 4:44 PM CDT and tracked into southeast Lincoln County producing EF-1 damage before dissipating around 4:55 PM CDT. Another tornado formed 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle in Marathon County around 4:46 PM CDT and dissipated around 5:03 PM CDT 5 miles southwest of Hogarty. This tornado produced EF-3 damage and destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. ||Beyond the tornadic threat, the storms produced isolated large hail up to half dollar size and damaging winds. Heavy rainfall was another impact, with localized totals ranging from 1 to 4 inches. These torrential downpours caused flash flooding, particularly in Marshfield where 2.65 inches of rain fell and multiple vehicles were reported stranded in deep water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail fell in Hazelhurst.  The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough brought an increase in southerly winds aloft on the 13th. This combined with a strongly unstable atmosphere brought severe thunderstorms producing scattered severe wind gusts across the region. High synoptic wind gusts also accompanied thunderstorms on the 13th and 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station GW0416 Joplin thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of western Massachusetts from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across western Massachusetts from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, declared a state of emergency prior to this event which authorized additional local resources as well as orders for travel restrictions. NWS Albany additionally received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across western Massachusetts. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 15.8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported 2.25 inch diameter hail near Tradinghouse Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported 4-5 downed trees scattered across Franklin County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked down multiple trees and wires along Welsh Run Road and Mercersburg Road approximately 3 miles east-southeast of Claylick.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.

Strong to severe thunderstorms moved northward through Southeastern Arizona the afternoon and evening of June 17th, 2026. These storms caused thunderstorm wind damage causing 8 power poles to be downed and 7,000 customers to be without power in the Tucson Metro and damage to a power transformer that caused a power outage for Tohono O'odham Nation. Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms caused flash flooding in normally dry rivers and washes that resulted in multiple swift water rescues that resulted in 1 fatality and 2 injuries. Additionally, multiple roadways in Cochise County was impassible due to flooding. An estimated penny sized hail was reported on the SW side of Tucson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Swift water rescue reported near Elm St and N Stone Rd. Nearby rainfall gauges recorded between 0.5 and 0.75 inches of rainfall. No injuries or fatalities reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surge of Arctic air invaded East and Northeast Texas during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens and lower 20s by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across East and Northeast Texas from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized inch hail was reported along I-295 near exit 9.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex moved across western and central ND during the evening hours of June 7th. As it moved into to the western part of the Devils Lake Basin a severe wind gust of 59 mph was measured before the complex weakened becoming sub-severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down across County Road 625 about one-half mile west of County Road 627.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind-driven hail up to 2.25 inches in diameter damaged homes, vehicles, outbuildings, and trailers. The hail drifts were up to 2.5 feet deep, and were still evident on the north side of buildings until May 12th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing cold front kicked off isolated severe storms in Central New York. These storms had damaging wind gusts and large hail. A tree fell on two people standing outside of their tent in a campground; both people were injured.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on two people standing at the edge of their tents at the Kittatinny Campground Riverside Area causing injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 2.50 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm produce 2 tornadoes severe hail and wind gusts up to 74 mph.

A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began in Cumberland County during the early morning hours with the heaviest snowfall falling during the evening hours of February 22nd and into the morning hours of February 23rd allowed for slick travel conditions, mainly during the early morning hours of February 23rd, where a tractor trailer overturned on Interstate 81 in Penn Township. There were no injuries reported from this incident; however, the northbound lane of Interstate 81 was closed for a brief period of time. Snowfall amounts in the county ranged from four to six inches across the eastern half of the county, with locally heavier amounts under a heavy snow band that set up in the region. Snowfall became lighter during the late morning hours of February 23rd before tapering off during the afternoon/evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Lost Creek, a tree blew down with lines along the 500 block of Bisetown Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated a 60mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, one storm produced three different EF-1 tornadoes in Lee County near Donnellson.

A major winter storm impacted southern Illinois on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th. Along and south of Route 13 towards Interstate 24, a brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 8 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in areas that experienced mixing. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassable closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in Massac County, IL. Route 3, 127, and 146 in Alexander County, IL were all snow and ice covered, which led to the County Sheriff issuing an Emergency Travel Only Order due to all roads being too dangerous for travel. Interstate 57 in Williamson County, IL also experienced very difficult travel due to the snow while Jefferson County, IL near Mount Vernon had a multi-vehicle pileup that blocked the southbound side during the afternoon hours on the 25th.  The collision near milepost 92 involved seven vehicles, including a jackknifed truck-tractor semi-trailer that led to minor injures and traffic being diverted. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow, especially near Du Quoin in Perry County, IL where most secondary roads were also impassable. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures.

A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of Hutchinson, Roberts, and Hemphill counties were in Exceptional Drought (D3) at the start of the month. Conversely much of Hansford, Ochiltree, and Lipscomb counties started the month in Severe Drought (D2). With a continually growing deficit in rainfall, the cluster of counties that included Hansford, Ochiltree, and the northwestern half of Lipscomb fell into D3. An area of Exceptional Drought (D4) developed over the southeastern half of Lipscomb, all of Hemphill, and the southeastern half of Roberts County. Areas that developed D4 had a 120 day rainfall deficit of 5 to 8 while the areas with D3 had a 4 to 5 deficit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle moved east into southwestern Nebraska during the late evening hours of June 30th. This activity continued into the early morning hours of July 1st tracking across the Sandhills into north central Nebraska.  Strong damaging winds up to 85 MPH were reported at Kingsley Dam.  There were several 60 to 80 MPH wind gusts reported over southwestern Nebraska.

A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold/Wind Chill: KRAS reported wind chills at or below 15 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Extreme Cold Warning criteria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 7.3 inches of snow and up to 2.0 inches of sleet. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm travel east across eastern Arapahoe and Washington Counties, and also clipping far northern Lincoln Counties. Large to very large occurred at times with the largest hail reaching 4.5 inches. Three brief tornadoes were also reported by spotters. No damaged occurred as these tornadoes were over open fields.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms formed ahead of an outflow boundary along the Mississippi River around midday on June 10th.  Some of the stronger cells within the line produced 60mph wind gusts and scattered damage along and north of a Jacksonville to Clinton line through mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few 8 to 10-inch diameter tree limbs were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL WATERS FROM MEXICO BEACH TO APALACHICOLA OUT 20 NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms ahead of a cold front brought several measured gusts of 34 knots or greater along the coast.

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions were in place across most if not all of Jones, northern Craven, and Beaufort Counties into June thirtieth with the size of the severe to extreme drought decreasing to around a quarter or less of the county by the end of the month according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Beaufort County through mid June with Extreme Drought conditions noted across far western portions of the county from June sixteenth onwards to the end of June. The size of the area of severe to extreme drought shrunk to about a quarter of the county mainly along the far western portions of Beaufort County on June thirtieth into the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough stationed over western Pennsylvania during the early morning hours with ample moisture and lift allowed for snowfall to begin across much of western Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of January 24th and the early morning hours of January 25, 2026. Moderate-to-heavy snowfall rates were observed at onset with low-level frontogenesis allowing for a moderate snowfall band across portions of western Pennsylvania prior to sunrise. Ample moisture in place with an approaching area of low pressure from the Lower Ohio River Valley also allowed for snowfall to begin across portions of southeastern Pennsylvania ahead of sunrise on January 25th. The progressive movement of the aforementioned trough and low pressure system allowed for a shorter duration of snowfall than could have occurred, with snowfall gradually tapering off across much of the area by the evening hours of January 26th. Westerly flow in the wake of the system did allow for continued upslope snow showers across the western highlands, which continued to allow for additional accumulations. Much of central Pennsylvania observed heavy snowfall, with Harrisburg International Airport and Williamsport Regional Airport breaking daily snowfall records, which have been tracked since 1888 and 1895, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow began in the late evening of January 24 and continued into the evening of January 25, with most of Dauphin County seeing 7-10 inches of snow and sleet. The highest snowfall total in the county occurred near Middletown, where 12.5 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal moisture moved into the Four Corners from the southwest due to remnant Atmospheric River moisture ahead of a strong closed low pressure system and cold front that brought mountain snow above 9000 feet and valley rain. Temperatures were very warm ahead of this system and fell to below normal levels afterwards with abundant moisture resulting in heavy, wet snow favoring the central and southern mountains with the heaviest accumulations above a foot at the higher elevations where the winds were also the strongest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 10 to 20 inches of snow fell across the area with 19.5 inches of snow reported at Crested Butte 6.2 N. Winds gusted in the 45 to 50 mph range with a peak wind gust of 57 mph at Irwin Guides.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding across north central Kentucky. On April 28th, the system's cold front dropped southeast, bringing a line of thunderstorms through central Kentucky. This produced additional wind damage and multiple small tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were power lines and trees down along Crab Tree Alley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to its neighbors across the Mississippi River, West Tennessee spent April 2026 battling a persistent, long-term moisture deficit dating back to July 2025. While central and northern parts of the Midwest received heavy spring rains that broke their droughts, West Tennessee experienced a highly regionalized spring recharge gap. Abnormally hot temperatures and meager rainfall caused drought conditions to actively worsen across the region during the first half of the month, though patchy late-month systems provided highly localized stabilizing relief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D0 conditions rapidly worsened to D2/D3 by mid month and continued for the rest of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large storm system moved across the Midwest March 15 to the 16th, initially bringing rain and thunderstorms to the area on the morning of the 15th. This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. Local news reported that most areas schools were closed and several Department of Transportation districts reported snow covered road ways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Moline-Quad Cities International Airport ASOS reported several hours of visibilities between 1/2sm and 1 mile from 6:30 PM to 8 AM CST on the 16th. The official NWS observation at the Moline Quad Cities Airport was 7.0 inches. Trained spotter snowfall reports ranged from 5.5 inches 1 mile southwest of Silvis to 7 inches 2 miles north of Rock Island.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 90 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local highway department reported that a tree had been blown down onto powerlines between MM10 and MM12 along KY-1812.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Gusty to strong west downslope winds developed along the east slope of the Front Range Mountains and Foothills during the morning of the 25th. Windy conditions spread east across the plains with gusts of 45 to 55 mph with a few local gusts reaching 65 mph. The strong winds combined very warm and dry conditions fuel two wildfires. One on the north Denver metro area and a second in northern Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wildfire was ignited by a motor vehicle accident at Highway 113 and Logan County Road 66, according to the Logan County Office of Emergency Management. The area is mainly grassland and rough terrain. Strong northwest to north winds fanned the fire burning 3,500 to 4,000 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This episode is part 2 of 2 from two rounds of severe weather that occurred on June 10th. ||Two clusters of storms redeveloped across Minnesota during the early afternoon of June 10th. The first cluster developed over Douglas and Stevens Counties and rapidly intensified as it entered Pope County. This cluster produced golf ball to tennis ball size hail in Glenwood and Villard (Pope). This storm would weaken some as it continued to the NNE into Stearns, Todd, and Morrison Counties where a brief funnel cloud was observed just south of Sobieski (Morrison). ||The second cluster of storms developed farther east across eastern MN along the I-35 corridor. A supercell entered Chisago County and produced quarter size to golf ball size from Wyoming to Center City.

A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mix of public, CoCoRaHS, and trained spotter reports of twelve to eighteen inches of snow was reported across northern Craven County. Snowfall fell between the early afternoon on January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Diurnal convection interacted with a very moist atmosphere across portions of Louisiana. These slow moving storms produced flooding and a report of damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were downed in Lecompte.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms following the Appalachian mountains reorganized later in the afternoon and brought damaging wind gusts to parts of south-central Virginia. Surface heating and mixing resulted in MLCAPE values of 750-1000 J/kg and low level lapse rates of 7-8��C/km. Mid-level lapse rates were not as impressive which may have limited the coverage of severe storms but DCAPE values of 700-900 J/kg contributed to some downed trees in Charlotte and Halifax Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on James D Hagood Highway near its intersection with Bethel/Scottsburg Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of the 30th, a dryline moved back into the Rolling Plains of West Texas allowing for low level moisture to surge into the region. Areas on the caprock saw scattered high based showers and thunderstorms generating severe wind gusts over Lubbock and Floyd Counties. Stronger moisture in the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle allowed for more robust thunderstorms. These storms produced severe wind gusts as well as hail as large as golf ball size in the city of Memphis (Hall County).
