EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms swept over Lake Superior in late June as minor disturbances pivoted around a mid-level ridge over the southeastern CONUS. These disturbances caused multiple incidences of thunderstorm-driven outflow and gusty winds on Lake Superior from the afternoon of the 29th to the early morning hours of the 30th.  A strengthening low level jet and wake lows trailing the thunderstorms resulted in additional periods of gusty winds, above gale force.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm wind gust of 39 kt was observed at the Stannard Rock Lighthouse. Winds above 34 kts lasted for 20 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a tree uprooted was shared on social media. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms developed along a stationary front during the early evening hours of June 28. Storms intensified into the mid evening hours with hail up to the size of base balls being reported over northern Sheridan County. Severe storms continued through 1 AM MDT on June 29th before lifting north into southern South Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report via social media with pictures. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak clipper system moved from the Great Lakes across NY and New England during the night of January 6th through the morning of January 7th. Snowfall developed during the late evening of January 6th and ended across VT around daybreak on January 7th.||Snowfall totals ranged from 1-3 inches across the International border with Canada to 4 to 6 inches across the eastern slopes of Vermont's central and southern Green Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches fell across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressively moist airmass was in place with dew points well into the 60s across north-central Idaho during the afternoon, contributing to high instability. A vigorous shortwave trough pivoted northwestward through the northern Great Basin, providing strong forcing for ascent. This forcing, in conjunction with daytime heating and destabilization along the high terrain, initiated supercell thunderstorms that produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 600 customers were reported without power due to this storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed the area, with most robust activity occurring in the afternoon and evening of the 23rd and 24th. The majority of the area received one to three inches of rain during this time, with a few pockets between three and four inches.  Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Raleigh, Taylor, and Upshur Counties and led to a mud slide in Kanawha County. A couple of severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines in Logan and Mingo counties the evening of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down along Locust Street in Logan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved east across the coastal waters of southeast Louisiana and coastal Mississippi during the morning of January 25th.  A line of showers and thunderstorms developed along and just ahead of the front within a moist and moderately unstable airmass.  As the line progressed eastward, embedded cells within this line produced severe wind gusts at multiple locations of the local marine areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NOS station on Petit Bois Island measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 43 mph or 37 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of active winter weather, much of central Indiana remained entrenched in a cold, arctic air mass as the 19th began. While ambient temperatures were not as deep into the negatives as previous events, a tightening pressure gradient across the region resulted in significantly higher wind speeds, which served as the primary driver for hazardous conditions.||West-northwest winds gusting to around 25-30 mph across central Indiana ushered in the cold by mid-morning on the 19th, with ambient lows holding steady at mainly single digit degrees across the impacted northern and central zones. These intense breezes led to a primary period of criteria wind chills for several counties, including Warren, Montgomery, Clinton, and Tipton. Wind chills fell to -20 to -25 within the 19th 0800-1100 EST period, with the most severe conditions observed in Montgomery County where the combination of single digit air and 25 mph sustained winds produced a -25 wind chill.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures on the morning of the 19th were as low as 4F, while gusty winds were sustained as high as 26 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.5 inches of snow, up to 2.0 inches of sleet, and up to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest ice total in Waushara County was 0.31 inches in Wautoma.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking 1 lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak surface high pressure ridging was centered just to the south of the JAX CWA on both the 26th and 27th, resulting in a west to southwest flow across the region. Sufficient moisture and summertime instability resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms, with some strong to severe storms causing isolated reports of damage across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed Report. Photos shared on social media of uprooted tree falling on a home in the Mandarin area, causing damage to home and AC unit. Time estimated on Radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through western Massachusetts, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Most of this precipitation fell in the form of snow, though some of the highest elevations of the Berkshire Mountains received minimal accumulations of freezing rain and sleet with some lower-lying areas conversely receiving some plain rain. ||The highest accumulations of snow fell across portions of the northern Berkshires where about 4 to 7 inches were recorded. Across lower elevations, about 1 to 3 inches were common. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 2.3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires down along Nicholson Loop Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of a tree down on wires on Hooker Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 2, thunderstorm development was initiated by a weak backdoor cold front moving in from the northeast. The resulting activity was primarily concentrated within and surrounding the DFW Metroplex, leading to instances of marginally severe hail and strong to severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported nickel size hail at The Colony City Hall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined Panhandles were located between low pressure to the north and high pressure to the south. This allowed for late afternoon and evening storms to move from northwest to southeast across the region in a warm, moist and unstable environment. Supercell and multicell clusters of storms developed and affected the central and eastern portions of the Texas Panhandle during the later afternoon and evening hours. Large hail, damaging winds and flooding occurred across the region. The main reports that came out of the Oklahoma Panhandle were related to flash flooding across portions of Beaver County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous county roads were impassable due to widespread flooding in the area with several washed out from just south and southwest of Slapout to the state line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported damage from strong wind gusts in Williston. Power lines are down in the city and there was damage to the top of a tall car dealership sign.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing damaging winds and some hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported a downed tree in the backyard of a residence in Sugar Land.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down on N King Street in Jonestown.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public sent in photos on facebook of trees down in parking lot near intersection of Ridge Ave and Bells Mill Rd.  Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow showers developed through the late morning and afternoon on the 31st. Total snowfall accumulations were light with generally less than 1 inch.

Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: What eventually became Super Typhoon Sinlaku (04W) originally crossed the Date Line at 4N around March 29, with a circulation at 4.2N 179.5E. This circulation would struggle to organize as it drifted westward and the circulation would redevelop south of Kosrae on April 4 near 2N164E.By 0000 UTC on April 6, Invest 90W had formed south-southwest of Pohnpei/southeast of Chuuk near 4.5N 159.8E. By April 8th the new circulation had lifted northwest to a position northeast of Chuuk. At 0200 UTC on April 9th 90W was upgraded from sub-low to Medium by JTWC. Aided by a strong westerly wind burst of 30 to 35kt, by 1800 UTC on the 9th of April a Tropical Cyclone Formation Alert was issued for 90W as it continued to rapidly organize. By 1200 UTC on the April 9, 90W became Tropical Depression (TD) 04W as it drifted slowly west to a position north of Chuuk (roughly 50 miles north). By 0000 UTC on April 10, 04W was upgraded to Tropical Storm (TS) Sinlaku (04W) and was located roughly 70 miles northwest of Chuuk. AT 0000 UTC on the April 10, TS Sinlaku was located at 8.2N 151.2E, at 08:22 UTC, there was a voluntary ship ob of westerly winds at 30 KT at 5.87N 147E., and westerly winds of 35kt at 2.1N  158.1E. By 0000 UTC on the April 11, Sinlaku became a typhoon (TY), nearly stationary about 80 miles northwest of Chuuk. Sinlaku continued to meander in the area as it strengthened northwest of Chuuk, becoming a super typhoon (STY) by 0000 UTC April 12. STY Sinlaku continued to strengthen as it moved north then northwest toward the Marianas. Sinlaku continued to move slowly NW with maximum sustained winds of 175 MPH on the 12th. At 1140 UTC on April 14 the western edge of the eye wall impacted Tinian and Saipan. The wind field continued to expand with Sinlaku, resulting in the maximum sustained wind and maximum gust occurring on April 14th in Guam. Sinlaku continued to move through the Marianas slowly, maintaining TS warning for Guam for 4 days. Sinlaku turned north, then north-northeast, affecting the islands of Alamagan, Pagan and Agrihan in the far northern CNMI. Sinlaku finally moved out of the northern CNMI on April 18. Sinlaku became an extratropical cyclone on April 20, 2026. There were 17 deaths (direct and indirect) and 6 injuries associated with STY Sinlaku. Nine fatalities (7 direct/2 indirect or unknown) and  direct 5 injuries were reported in Chuuk State. For the Mariana Islands, 2 indirect deaths were reported on Guam, while 6 direct deaths and 1 injury was reported in the CNMI. Chuuk State government estimate home and crop damages total around 96 million USD. On Guam, estimate 434.5 million USD damage to public property and 2 million USD for crop losses. Initial estimates from FEMA estimate damage cost exceed 1 billion USD across the CNMI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Super Typhoon Sinlaku passed north of Guam and Rota and passed near or over Tinian and Saipan on April 15. Tropical storm winds started 1900ChST April 13 and ended just before 1300ChST April 16. Strong westerly tropical storm winds were recorded on Guam. The Apra Harbor Tide Gauge recorded a max wind of 58 mph at 1100ChST April 14 with a gust of 74 mph at 0155ChST April 15. Guam International Airport reported sustained winds of 55 mph at 2255ChST April 14 with a max gust of 87 mph at 1542ChST April 14. Pago Bay Tide Gauge reported a max water level of 2.03 feet (MHHW) at 0612ChST April 14. Lowest pressure measure on Guam was 976.0 mb (MSLP) at the Dandan RAWS near Inal��han at 2200ChST April 14.  NWS Storm Survey around Guam saw extensive coastal inundation. On the east side of Guam near Talo'fo'fo, coastal run-up to 15.67 feet was recorded as the likely absolute max, with  5.50 ft and 9.00 ft of coastal run-up measured at Inal��han. On the west side of Guam 9.58 ft to 10.85 feet was measured at Asan, near the War in the Pacific Park. This flooding pushed sand up and across to Route 1 (Marine Corp Drive), along the stretch of road from Asan and northward to near Hag��t��a, the capital of Guam. Ritidian on the northwest tip of Guam saw coastal run-up to 11.20 ft. Two indirect deaths were reported on Guam as an elderly pair were found dead due to carbon monoxide poisoning due to a generator running indoors after the storm passed. Crop damage was estimated to be around 2 million USD and property damage estimated around 434.5 million USD on Guam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed along a trough axis during the evening hours on June 6, resulting in multiple reports of thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust near the intersection of Interstate 40 and U.S. Highway 377.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late day and evening thunderstorms becoming strong in portions of central Wyoming. To the southwest of Cody, nickel sized hail was reported. In Riverton, a strong thunderstorms produced large amounts of hail up to penny size that accumulated a few inches in some locations. Very heavy rain accompanied the hail, with a retired National Weather Service meteorologist reporting 1.40 inches of rain and melted hail in only 30 minutes. As a result, there were numerous reports of minor street flooding and some flooded basements.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported nickel size hail to the southwest of Cody.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clear skies and calm winds following a cold frontal passage allowed for locally dense fog to form over far Southwestern Kentucky late evening on the 21st through the early AM hours of the 22nd. Patches of freezing fog occurred, with icy roads reported in the town of Dublin in far western Graves County. Northerly winds increasing to 4-7mph before dawn brought an end to fog conditions.

A cold front moving across the area combined with a strong jet stream to produce high wind gusts across portions of western and central Wyoming. The highest recorded wind gust was 89 mph at Red Canyon along South Pass. In the lower elevations, wind gusts of 70 mph or greater occurred in Johnson and Natrona Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 63 mph wind gust occurred at the South Big Horn County airport near Greybull.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low moved across northern Mexico bringing a strong cold front through South-Central Texas. This resulted in very cold air in the boundary layer with a layer of above freezing air aloft which produced sleet and freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mix of sleet and freezing rain began during the evening of the 24th. There were some icy patches on Hwy 277 in Eagle Pass along with a light glazing on elevated metal surfaces, overall impacts were insignificant.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A departing high pressure system generated strong southwest winds, with a peak wind gust of 70 mph at the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) station 6 miles south southwest of Peever. Additionally, the SDDOT RWIS 4 miles north of Altamont recorded a peak gust of 68 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS in Summit topped 66 mph. ||These high winds were directly responsible for a grassfire 2 miles west of the town of Gary in Deuel County, which burned approximately 100 acres of pasture and farmland. The high winds also caused intermittent near zero visibility due to blowing dust along a portion of Highway 14 between Ree Heights and the city of Miller. 3 trees collapsed due to the wind stress in the city of Miller as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station near Ree Heights recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph. Due to these high winds and an ongoing dry spell, areas of blowing dust resulted in intermittent near-zero visibility along portions of Highway 14 between Ree Heights and Miller. Additionally, three trees collapsed within the city of Miller due to wind stress.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A water rescue occurred where 5 individuals were saved from a car caught in rising flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong winds with a storm near Olney in Young Country produced scattered wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported a southwest to northeast swath of damage near Olney. Multiple power poles were snapped, roofs and carports were damaged, a short concrete block dividing wall was destroyed, and a silo tipped over onto a truck. Additionally, a resident's bee hives were blown away. Damage was consistent with 80 to 95 mph winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roads around Carson were submerged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening area of showers and thunderstorms in an environment with sufficient instability and shear continued tracking from eastern Ohio into portions of northwestern Pennsylvania during the evening hours of March 26, 2026. The environment across northwestern Pennsylvania was slightly less favorable with respect to instability closer to sunset but still retained a favorable amount of shear for strong-to-severe thunderstorms to continue for a couple of hours after sunset. These thunderstorms produced isolated instances of wind damage in western Warren County before thunderstorms weakened further below severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked multiple trees down on Buckley Road near Tidioute. Multiple power outages were also reported in Tidioute.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona were 2 to 6 degrees above normal with Minor to Moderate HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that heat was a factor in the cause of death for 7 individuals, with 2 having heat as the primary factor and 5 as a secondary factor in their deaths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona was 6 degrees above normal with Moderate HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that heat was a contributing factor the cause of death for an individual in Sierra Vista. A Sierra Vista CWOP recorded a high temperature of 96 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.
On May 16th, storms brought all severe hazards to Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball sized hail was reported in Trenton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were knocked down on Big John Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (105F) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.

A short lived tornado occurred in far northwest Thomas County on the leading edge of one of the storms.

This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.

This tornado is also damaged multiple trees in the area which was confirmed via Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis. The tornado had maximum winds of 80 mph and was on the ground for about 0.4miles with a width of 200 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped south into the region and combined with a warm, moist and unstable airmass to bring isolated showers and thunderstorms to the region on the afternoon and evening of June 13. Storms primarily affected the east and northeast Texas Panhandle with damaging winds and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down and some fell across roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low deepened as it moved through North Dakota, leading to high non-thunderstorm wind gusts. By the early afternoon, the strong winds were producing blowing dust and significantly reduced visibility across western North Dakota, with a Blowing Dust Warning and Blowing Dust Advisory issued for much of western and central North Dakota. Visibility was under one quarter of a mile at times. The strongest wind gust reported was 76 mph near Crosby in Divide County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona were 14 to 18 degrees above normal with Minor to Moderate HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that the cause of death for 3 individuals had heat as a contributing factor. One heat contributed in Tucson and two individuals deaths were heat caused, one in Tucson and one in Sells. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered clusters of thunderstorms developed across the Atlantic coastal waters in the evening hours and moved into portions of the southeast Georgia and southeast South Carolina coast. Several of these thunderstorms became strong enough to produce strong wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS observation site at Edisto Beach State Park measured a 40 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper wave dropping south across the Great Lakes and it's associated cold front brought widespread accumulating snow to the region New Year's Eve and into the new year across the ridges of western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Enhanced orographic lift resulted in higher totals across the Laurel Highlands and eastern West Virginia ridges, with relatively high snow ratios between 18:1 and 21:1. Widespread Advisory level snow was also observed across the region, ranging from 2.5 inches to 5.5 inches outside of the ridges of Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall, generally exceeding advisory criteria but falling short of warning criteria, fell across the county with amounts ranging from 3-5 inches and the highest amount of 5.5 inches reported by the public in Ford City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary with warm air rising just above the surface produced an east-west swath of 1 to 4 inches of snow and a light glaze of ice due to freezing rain over portions of central Wisconsin. Roads became snow covered and slick during the late evening and overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulation of 2 to 3 inches with highest amounts in the northern portion of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front helped force a line of showers and weak thunderstorms that crossed from west to east across East Tennessee. Winds aloft were quite strong, and convective transport in the strongest cells helped bring those winds to the surface in the form of convective downdraft gusts, producing damage and high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An old barn was blown down by powerful thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of streets from Sussex toward Menomonee Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across portions of eastern Nebraska through the month of April. However, there was some slight improvement through the month with only small departures from average precipitation in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were present across Thurston County at the beginning of the month. However, severe drought coverage was reduced to zero early in the month, and the coverage of moderate (D1) drought shrank from around 45 percent at the beginning of the month down to zero, leaving the county in abnormally dry (D0) status.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant area of high pressure with heights reaching around 595 dm over the region allow for several days of all-time record breaking heat, with values as much as 30 degrees or more above the seasonal temperature for the month of March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KSNA ASOS reported new daily maximum high temperature records broken in Santa Ana (John Wayne Airport) of 100F on 3/17, 95F on 3/18, 95F on 3/19, and 95F on 3/20, and 95F on 3/21.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across northern Illinois during the morning of January 14th with a band of heavy snow and snow squalls. Wind gusts were between 40 mph and 50 mph with a few higher gusts, including a gust to 61 mph near Crescent City. Visibility was reported to be near zero in many locations. Snowfall amounts were generally between 1 and 2 inches and with temperatures falling below freezing as the snow began, roads became icy.  Hundreds of vehicle accidents were reported across northern Illinois.

A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flood waters affected a house in 124 Ponce de Leon and nearby areas. Standing water was observed inside the first floor of the house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Wythe county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th to 10th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper level system combined with a stalled frontal boundary extending over portions of southeast Louisiana and coastal Mississippi to produce a period of training thunderstorms over parts of Harrison, Hancock, and Pearl River Counties in coastal Mississippi.  Very high moisture content in the atmosphere and warm air in the mid and upper levels allowed for very high rainfall rates to accompany these training thunderstorms resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooded road on Woodridge Lane 2 miles east of Picayune.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed wires, blocking Old North Groton Road in  Rumney, NH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Bartow, a downed tree blocked portions of WV-28 at Mile Marker 30.0.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down numerous trees down on Goodville Road and Evans Hollow Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic airmass brought very cold temperatures to the entire region Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).  Winds of 15 to 25 mph combined with low temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero brought wind chill values down to 30 to 55 below zero Thursday evening (1/22) through Friday morning (1/23). Temperatures did not warm much Friday afternoon, with daytime highs ranging from 5 to 15 below zero, offering little relief from the cold, with wind chill values at or near extreme cold criteria, even in the afternoon. Plummeting overnight temperatures Friday night (1/23) into Saturday morning (1/24) of 15 to near 40 below zero once again pushed wind chill values down to 30 to near 50 below zero. Temperatures had finally warmed to above extreme cold criteria late Saturday morning (1/24) but remained cold through the weekend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds caused wind chill values to fall to -30 to -44 degrees from early Friday morning (1/23) through Saturday morning (1/24).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down northeast of the intersection of North 1800th Street and East 2000th Avenue about 2 miles north-northwest of Yale at 6:10 AM CDT.  The tornado tracked northeastward, damaging trees and destroying a barn south of the intersection of North 2000th Street and East 2100th Avenue before dissipating at 6:12 AM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.25 inch hail near Decatur from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving shortwave upper level trough followed by a shortwave ridge tracking near the International Border produced a strong surface pressure gradient on the 7th and accompanying strong winds across North-Central MT.  Heading into the 8th, the upper level ridge broke down. This day brought a longer duration of strong sustained winds and widespread strong wind gusts over North-Central MT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous weather stations in the zone measured high wind gusts and a few reported high sustained winds. The highest was at ASOS station KHVR Havre Airport, where they measured a 78 mph wind gust and an average sustained wind of 44 mph between 10:20am to 2:15pm MST. During this time period, the ASOS also consistently had visibility drop to 1 to 3SM due to blowing dust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A traffic light was blown down at the corner of 170th Street and Oak Avenue in Lansing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed ahead of a cold front across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 12. These storms produced damaging winds as they moved east.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down onto Scotchtown Road south of Chiswell Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Hinds County decreased from D2 (Severe Drought) to D1 (Moderate Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High-based showers and thunderstorms produced dry microbursts and several observations of severe wind gusts across western Oklahoma on the evening of the 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Elk City (ELKC) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 4 to 12 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, moderate to heavy at times, developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 6 and 8 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. There was a report of 7.5 inches in Rochester. Roads were snow covered and slick with numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: March 2026 brought significant drought relief to northeast Mississippi. Frequent rainfall and improving hydrologic conditions led to widespread recovery from the drought conditions that developed during late 2025. South and western portions of north Mississippi were not as fortunate as D2 Severe Drought persisted over much of the area. Localized worsening conditions led to D3 Extreme Drought and D4 Exceptional Drought conditions to persist throughout the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions encompassed the entire county at the beginning of the month. Northern portions of the county saw 1 category degradation to D3 Extreme Drought conditions by months end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Alliance Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached a brief afternoon peak as high as 106 degrees near Ponca.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Weather outbreak in southeast Idaho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph wind gust measured at Tom Cat Summit on US Highway 20.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense thunderstorm cluster, exhibiting occasional supercell character, moved from the western suburbs of Oklahoma City, OK southward towards Lawton, OK. In addition to reports of large to very large hail, a concentrated corridor of thunderstorm wind damage occurred on the east and southeast sides of Lawton, OK. This included several observations of significant severe winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported by a broadcast media storm chaser.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of April, persisting extreme drought (D3) and  exceptional drought (D4) conditions area-wide. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of beneficial rainfall in April continued the Extreme (D3) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported quarter sized hail 6 miles south of Four Corners.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A midlevel trough lifting northeast from Arkansas and Mississippi, interacted with a cold front moving in from the north, to cause widespread showers and thunderstorms across East Tennessee from late in the evening on May 29th, through the late morning hours on May 30th. This led to scattered reports of flash flooding across East Tennessee, most notably in the central Tennessee valley and northern Cumberland Plateau areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads impacted by flooding across Loudon County, including Highway 72, Vonore Road, Meadow Road West near Big Hill Road, Highland Avenue, ,and Old Highway 95.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.

A cluster of thunderstorms developed over the Pine Ridge of northwestern Nebraska during the early evening hours of June 4th. As this activity pushed east into Sheridan and Cherry Counties, it strengthened, becoming severe. Severe storms tracked east across northern Cherry County before weakening over Keya Paha, northern Brown and northern Rock Counties. Hail up to quarter size and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported with the strongest storms.
Light snow showers occurred for a few hours during the early morning hours of March 16 2026 across several areas in MS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief snow shower occurred in Philadelphia, with a trace of snow reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe thunderstorms produced small hail and gusty wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Media relayed picture of hail in Three Rivers around nickel size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of heavy precipitation events resulted in record setting and historic flooding on several rivers across northeast Wisconsin from the middle to late part of April. The heavy rainfall especially impacted the Wolf River basin, leading to record setting flooding for the Wolf River at Shiocton and the Wolf River at New London. Record flooding also occurred on other rivers over northeast Wisconsin, including the Embarrass River. ||The river flooding resulted in tremendous disruptions to daily life for those living along and near the Wolf River and Embarrass River. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days. Power and gas were shutoff in these areas as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses. The peak of the flooding along the Wolf River occurred from April 16 through April 21.  Flooding then moved downstream on the Wolf River, impacting the Fremont area. Over 150 homes were affected, with damages estimated over $4 million.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread low-land flooding occurred in Outagamie County, resulting in considerable flood damage along the Wolf River and Embarrass River to 52 homes and $4.6 million of damage. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days.  Power and gas in these areas were shutoff as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a slowly advancing cold front across south-central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and nighttime hours of April 17. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and up to 70 mph wind gusts. Wind damage was also noted across a couple locations across southeast Kansas from these storms.
A weak mid level shortwave system produced scattered thunderstorms, of which an isolated severe storm yielded hail.

A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest sleet total in northern Oconto County was 1.6 inches near Townsend. 0.25 inches of ice was also measured in Mountain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a weak surface front/pressure trough across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 26th. This activity produced damaging winds, hail and flooding as it progressed south/southeastward into the early morning of the 27th. Significant damaging winds and hail were noted with a trio of more organized thunderstorms (supercells) during this time impacting areas around Enid, Stillwater, Oklahoma City and Chandler, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A section of the roadway was washed out due to flooding near the intersection of Southwest 174th Street and Market Road. The event time is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into eastern New York on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of the Hudson Valley into Washington County and the southern Taconics on one or both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms produced some large hail along with downed trees and wires. The Town of Pawling was hardest hit on June 11 as an intense thunderstorm produced hail in excess of 2 inches in some areas and widespread tree damage.

Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. The strongest winds were generally west of the James River Valley where gusts to 60 to 70 mph were common. While areas of light snowfall generally on the order from a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, there were only very spotty and brief instances of visibility below one mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 30 to 36 mph at times with a peak gust of 55 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 5 miles east-southeast of Tyndall and 45 mph at a personal weather station 2 miles south of Scotland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 5F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began in rural far eastern Vernon County where it caused minor damage to a residence and damaged some trees before moving into Juneau County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with occasional severe weather reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were down across Jefferson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trimble County received heavy snow and sleet totaling 7 to 9 inches, in addition to light ice accumulation up to 0.10 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of upper level disturbances pushed through southeast Texas causing multiple days of stormy weather. A pair of severe weather reports were received. Behind the fast paced fronts that caused the unsettled weather, tides fell below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of 1.25 inches was reported from Chester.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D3-D4 drought conditions prevailed to start the month of May across southwest and south central Georgia. However, beneficial rain during the month reduced the drought to D2 by the end of the month near a line from Albany to Bainbridge and westward. D3-D4 drought still prevailed farther east across south central Georgia.
A strong cold front resulted in a few bands of thunderstorms that produced widely scattered instances of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were down around the 800 block of Downing Farm Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, one storm produced three different EF-1 tornadoes in Lee County near Donnellson.

After a morning of showers and overcast clouds on May 13th, clearing skies during the afternoon resulted in strong thunderstorm development across West Virginia. Convection initially developed during the early afternoon west of the Ohio River, then crossed into north-central West Virginia during peak heating hours. This helped to maintain severe strength in some of the storms that crossed through Lewis and Calhoun Counties. Local power outages caused by downed trees and small to large hail were noted in locations north of Route 50, with one lone instance of sub-severe hail taking place in Raleigh County. The broken line of storms tracked east of the forecast area by the evening, bringing the risk for severe weather to an end for the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed trees along Vineyard Drive near Weston resulted in local power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across portions of western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 21st.

An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was uprooted, landing on an adjacent carport, near the intersection of Flood Avenue and Gray Street. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines downed in Caledonia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening surface low crossed northern Maine during the 1st. At the same time...a secondary low developed across the Gulf of Maine and tracked toward Nova Scotia with a trof extending between the lows. Snow developed during the early morning hours of the 1st...persisting into the evening. A meso-scale snow band developed along the trof axis...running across central and coastal portions of Washington county. Localized snow fall rates of up to 4 inches per hour occurred with this band. The greatest storm total snow accumulation occurred with the band...with totals of 8 to 14 inches. Storm totals across Washington county...outside of this band...ranged from 5 to 8 inches. Warning criteria snow accumulations occurred during the late afternoon of the 1st. Storm total snow accumulations of 4 to 6 inches occurred to the north of Washington county across the remainder of eastern Maine along the trof axis. Snow totals tapered to 1 to 2 inches across western portions of the forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Discrete severe thunderstorms developed off of Lake Michigan and tracked southeast producing a few reports of quarter-sized hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo on Facebook showing hailstones ranging from dime to quarter size on SR 19 near the West 700 South.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad scale upper lift led to a complex winter storm across East Tennessee, with onset precipitation of snow transitioning to freezing rain before ending as rain as the temperatures rose through the evening, night, and following morning. This storm led to 7 fatalities in East Tennessee. On the morning of the 25th the strengthening low level jet that was advancing warm air northwards led to a high end mountain wave wind event in portions of the East Tennessee mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inches of snow and an unknown amount of freezing rain fell in Scott County during the two distinct periods of precipitation, with wintry mix in the first bout, then rain, then snow to end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on Klondike Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense low-pressure system tracking through the northern Great Lakes brought damaging winds of 50 to 71 mph to much of southeast Michigan. The strongest gusts were concentrated along and south of the M-59 corridor, where numerous trees and power lines were downed across the Detroit Metro area. Both Detroit City Airport and Ann Arbor Airport recorded peak gusts of 71 mph during the height of the storm. The most intense winds occurred in the afternoon following the passage of a strong cold front, leaving around 200,000 DTE Energy customers without power at the peak of the event. Tragically, the storm claimed the life of a Huntington Woods public works employee, who was struck by a falling tree limb while working to clear a roadway during the evening hours.

Ascent from a 700 mb shortwave within a broad plume of 1000-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported development of thunderstorms on the afternoon of 4/14. Some of those became severe with reports of hail up to ping pong ball sized and uprooted trees from strong wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree uprooted and fallen onto a shed and a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of April 4, 2026. These thunderstorms were initially weak as they tracked through west Middle Tennessee, but they strengthened once east of Nashville. The strongest portion of the line was located in Wilson and Macon counties where several reports of downed trees, utility lines, and minor roofing damage was received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds caused shingles to be blown off a house as well as caused fencing damage on Hunters Village Drive in Lebanon. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with isolated severe weather reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines fell onto three vehicles traveling on Highway 111 South near Broome Circle, blocking the roadway. Live lines on vehicles were reported but no injuries occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Beaufort County 911 Call Center reported a tree down at Charleston Highway and River Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing damaging winds and some hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported a downed fence and damage to a garage door in Sugar Mill.
