EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 8-12 based on nearby automated snow measuring gauges. The highest measurement within the zone was 8.7 from Bethany Beach. Blizzard conditions were confirmed based on nearby photos, videos, and weather station observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees and power lines were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region late on January 24th into early January 25th, followed by a surge of very cold Arctic air at the surface. As this shallow cold air mass advanced southward, it undercut lingering moisture and a warm layer aloft associated with departing precipitation.  During the early morning hours of January 25th, a brief period of freezing rain developed across portions of southeast Louisiana where surface temperatures fell below freezing while rain continued. This resulted in a light glaze of ice, generally less than one quarter inch, primarily on elevated surfaces such as trees and vehicles.  The freezing rain was short-lived, lasting approximately 3 to 6 hours before drier air aloft eroded the precipitation and ended the freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media photos indicated a light glaze of ice, less than 0.25 inches of accumulation, on trees and elevated surfaces. The greatest amount of ice was observed in northwestern portions of the parish with little to no ice in southeastern parts of the parish.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the night of June 21st, 2026 and into the early morning of June 22nd, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System moved through southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. This system brought multiple lines of storms and some supercells. Several tornadoes occurred along with flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Deep water was flowing over Cisco Road and Versailles Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak disturbance moving across the Intermountain West combined with intense daytime heating resulting in scattered high based evaporating showers and dry thunderstorms across western and central New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 13th. These showers resulted in dry microbursts at the Farmington Four Corners Regional Airport and the NMDOT weather station along I-40 at SR6 in Laguna Pueblo. High based shower and thunderstorm activity across western and central New Mexico dissipated around sunset with the loss of daytime heating. Two rounds of high based shower and thunderstorm activity developed across the eastern plains of New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 14th and 15th with dry microbursts in Clayton. High based shower and thunderstorm activity exited east into west Texas and tapered off during the evening hours, with one area of collapsing showers resulting in a heat burst at the Fort Sumner Municipal Airport late on May 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NASA Davis Vantage Pro 2 weather station at Fort Sumner Municipal Airport measured a brief 67 mph wind gust due to a heat burst caused by nearby collapsing showers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2/D3 conditions persisted across the county for the entire month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms affected the area for multiple days ahead of a cold front. Some storms were severe with impacts to trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs were snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The last of three winter storms moved through starting the night of February 19th and lasting through the morning of February 20th.  This was the coldest storm of the three with snow falling lower than the previous two storms.  However, this was another fast moving storm with gusty high winds, so snowfall amounts were difficult to measure and lower than expected.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A COOP Observer reported 5.7 inches of snow at Grand Canyon Village 25 E.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 19th afternoon, an unstable airmass ahead of an approaching surface trough triggered a cluster of severe thunderstorms across central Indiana.  Convection initially intensified over the western and northern portions of the Indianapolis metropolitan area shortly after 1500 EST, capitalizing on strong low-to-mid level wind shear. These storms quickly organized into severe segments that tracked eastward and southward, producing a concentrated swath of damaging straight-line winds across Hendricks, Hamilton, Delaware, and Bartholomew counties before exiting the IND CWA by 1700 EST.||Damaging winds were the primary hazard with this event, resulting in structural damage, power outages, and travel disruptions. Hamilton County was particularly hard hit, where estimated wind gusts up to 55 knots (63 mph) downed multiple utility lines, left a power pole leaning in Noblesville, and knocked a large tree through the roof of a residence.  Transportation infrastructure was also impacted:  in Delaware County, estimated gusts of 55 knots blew over a semi truck on Interstate 69 near mile marker 249.  Earlier in the afternoon, severe gusts in Hendricks County downed several trees, including one that blocked a roadway southwest of Danville.  As the severe weather pushed into south-central Indiana, the KBAK AWOS at Columbus Municipal Airport in Bartholomew County recorded a peak measured wind gust of 52 knots (60 mph).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility pole is leaning from thunderstorm winds at Olio Road and SR38 in Noblesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 and D3 drought conditions continued or developed across mainly the southeastern half of the CWA during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions occurred across the eastern half of Hunt County for the entire month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent hurricane force North Pacific Low moved into the Bering on January 4. This, combined with potent shortwave troughs and cold air advection behind the low allowed for gusty, westerly to southwesterly winds across the Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula. The Eastern Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula saw strong, gusty winds for a time. As the low moved eastward, heavy snowfall and blizzard conditions were observed over the Southwest mainland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bethel ASOS observed blizzard conditions (blowing snow, >35 mph wind gusts, and quarter mile visibility or less) from 11:23 AM to 3:10 PM AKST January 4 with only short breaks in blizzard conditions within that timeframe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 3rd drought monitor update, continuing through the rest of the Month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front draped across Arkansas in tandem with an approaching upper level trough axis would spur multiple days of severe winds, flash flooding, and heavy rain totals for the multi-day event across the state of Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were blown down in the vicinity of Antoine leading to widespread power outages within the town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad southwesterly flow aloft on the eastern side of a western CONUS trough carried several weak disturbances across the central Gulf Coast, while southeasterly low-level flow maintained deep moisture. Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi. A thunderstorm over the local marine areas produced a waterspout near the Interstate 10 Twin Span as well as severe wind gusts at other coastal locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet at Gulfport XGPT measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 49 mph or 43 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A decaying thunderstorm produced isolated wind damage in the northern portions of the city of Florence. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall led to flash flooding in Marshall, Jackson, and Cullman Counties in Northeastern Alabama, flooding roads and causing them to become impassable.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gilley Drive impassable due to flash flooding. Depth of water unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Road 148 was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Cincinnati airport (KCVG) measured a 54 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The bridge on CR30E between 130S and 140S had enough flood water over it that the bridge was blocked by debris and not passable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked wires down on Talhelm Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

A classic winter weather pattern setup across the region with an upper low moving through northwest Mexico while a back door cold front moved into Otero County. Southwest flow aloft ahead of the upper low kept some warm air aloft over the area and the Sacramento Mountains experienced a period of freezing rain before transitioning over to all snow.  This combination of winter weather types caused numerous power outages and over 2 feet of snow in the Cloudcroft area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A meteorologist from Holloman AFB, reported 4 inches of snow in Alamogordo.  Other reports included 4 inches about 2 miles south of La Luz and 5.7 inches about 9 miles north of Alamogordo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Automated Weather Observing System site at Sheldon had frequent sustained winds around 40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.
A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down near Highway 311.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house on CR 417 near Blair, MS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KYTC reported at 654 EST that KY-2013 had been closed due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed north of Gladewater, reported via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Exceptional Drought (D4) to Extreme (D3) on June 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved from Illinois through southwest Michigan and northern Indiana. The line of storms eventually weakened, but prior to this, damaging wind gusts were recorded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of powerlines downed in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary. With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.

During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a 59 mph wind gust 1 mile northwest of Spring Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 26, 2026, a potent cold front tracked across central Indiana, interacting with a warm and unstable airmass to trigger severe storms.  Severe thunderstorms developed rapidly, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across northern central Indiana that downed trees and power lines, leading to over 1,700 power outages as residents dealt with the abrupt onset of hazardous weather.||Significant structural damage was observed, including a destroyed pole barn and a garage roof failure in Clinton County. While the environment supported supercellular rotation and prompted numerous tornado warnings, the only severe modes were straight-line damaging winds and large hail, with reports of 1.5-inch hail in Veedersburg. The convective activity gradually weakened as it progressed south of the I-70 corridor and encountered a more stable airmass, effectively concluding the active weather event for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small tree was snapped by thunderstorm wind gusts near its base.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front passed through Central Alabama on January 17-18. By the early morning of the 18th, rain associated with the front began to transition to snow southeast of Interstate 85. Some areas of Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties received 1-2 inches of snow by 9 AM. By mid-morning, cloud cover cleared, and the snow quickly melted. Impacts to roadways were minimal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One to two inches of snow fell across Barbour County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down onto power lines along Field Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

After a prolonged period of light to moderate rainfall across the two counties, a strong atmospheric river brought heavy rain to the area on January 5th. This resulted in numerous reports of flooding and closed highways, particularly in the two county area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scott Valley Road flooded and closed near Highway 20.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.25 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed on Old National Pike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous social media photos showed hail ranging from golf ball to baseball size in Hallsburg. Significant damage occurred to vehicles with destroyed windshields and large dents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front over the northwestern United States moved across northern Nevada. Strong winds were reported across sections of humboldt county and some of the upper elevated mountain ranges in central Nevada.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS Station (KWMC) Winnemucca Airport, elevation 4301 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens.

An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens. There were numerous social media posts of frozen and burst water pipes across the area.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of East Texas through roughly the first half of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged between 2-4 inches, which was a continuation of below normal rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. However, widespread wetting rains of 1-3+ inches fell across much of Deep East Texas on March 11th, resulting in improvement to moderate drought (D1) in the March 19th issuance of the U.S. Drought Monitor.

An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter measures 88 MPH gust on home weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the afternoon of 4/25, two strong storms both producing severe hail with one producing 2.5 hail. Some severe wind gusts were also reported. A cold front bisected the area and interacted with a shortwave that produced organized convection with low level moisture and deep-layer shear. The shear CAPE available generated numerous reports of severe winds while the steep lapse rates aided in generating severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 1 inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather moved northeast across south-central and southeast Kansas during the evening hours March 10th. These severe thunderstorms produced numerous reports of large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KAKE News relayed the observed wind measurement.

CZ_NAME: TIDAL POTOMAC KEY BRIDGE TO INDIAN HD MD
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced an estimated wind gust to 34 knots (39 MPH) near the ASOS at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (KDCA) adjacent to the tidal Potomac River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front draped over the Ohio Valley tracked into the central and southern Appalachians by the late evening and overnight period. Ahead of the front, scattered showers and storms tracked from the North Carolina mountains into the Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the evening hours. Numerous wind damage reports were observed over the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms formed ahead of an outflow boundary along the Mississippi River around midday on June 10th.  Some of the stronger cells within the line produced 60mph wind gusts and scattered damage along and north of a Jacksonville to Clinton line through mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree branch was blown down on 6 Points Road just west of Juniper Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved across the area and brought heavy snow, especially to the  mountains. The heaviest snow fell in the Tetons, where there were many reports of over a foot of new snow with a maximum amount of 25 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort. Other notable amounts included 20 inches in the Salt and Wyoming Range, 15 inches in the Bighorn Range, 14 inches in the western Wind River Range and 12 inches on Casper Mountain. Lesser amounts fell in the lower elevations. However, in northern Johnson County, a combination of snow and wind gusting to 50 mph brought closures of Interstates 25 and 90 for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to 13 inches of new snow fell along the western slopes of the Bighorns.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting northern to central Maryland during the late afternoon hours with swaths of 60 to 70 mph wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were dozens of trees, branches, and power lines blown down especially in northeastern Washington County near Hagerstown. Approximately 12,000 power outages resulted from the storm damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From late January 22 into January 23, 2026, an arctic front advanced through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, ushering a bitterly cold airmass into the region. Northerly wind gusts of 10 to 15 mph, combined with minimum temperatures of 5 to 12 degrees below zero, produced dangerous wind chill values of 30 to 35 degrees below zero across northeast Nebraska and western Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No observations within the county. Estimated minimum wind chill temperatures of 30 to 33 degrees below zero based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed over the northern panhandle and far southern South Dakota during the early evening hours of June 27th. As this activity tracked east into the late evening and early overnight hours, hail up to the size of golf balls and wind gusts up to 79 MPH were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across Clay county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought was observed at the beginning of the month. Normal to above normal precipitation fell in roughly the first half of the month, followed by normal to below normal precipitation through much of the second half. Overall, normal to above normal precipitation fell in western Deaf Smith and Oldham counties, and central Potter into southern Randall counties. Drier than normal conditions were observed from central Oldham into central Deaf Smith counties. Drought conditions improved across most of this region by 1 category, but Severe (D2) to D3 remains due to a 120-day rainfall deficit of 2 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One large tree was uprooted, and multiple large tree branches were downed in Vienna.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof damage occurred in the Providence community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening of June 11 into the early morning of June 12, a severe thunderstorm complex tracked west to east across Southeast Michigan, producing scattered pockets of damaging straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large trees and wires were reported down across northern Monroe County.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL WATERS FROM OCHLOCKONEE RIVER TO APALACHICOLA FL OUT TO 20 NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois during the afternoon of Sunday, March 15, 2026. The environment was characterized by high shear and weak instability. A line of storms swept across the state, producing scattered wind damage and eight tornadoes within the NWS Central Illinois coverage area.  The tornadoes occurred southeast of the I-72 corridor and all were rated EF-0 or EF-1. No injuries occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small patches of shingles were blown off of a school building.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to 5 to 20 below zero with wind chill temperatures of  15 to 35 below zero across northern NY.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures 5 to 10 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 20 to 35 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Giles county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 10th to 20th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal moisture moved into the Four Corners from the southwest due to remnant Atmospheric River moisture ahead of a strong closed low pressure system and cold front that brought mountain snow above 9000 feet and valley rain. Temperatures were very warm ahead of this system and fell to below normal levels afterwards with abundant moisture resulting in heavy, wet snow favoring the central and southern mountains with the heaviest accumulations above a foot at the higher elevations where the winds were also the strongest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 10 to 15 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 20 inches of snow at Park Reservoir. 15 inches of snow was reported at Skyway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This EF-1 tornado began just south of Union Road Southeast, where it broke some large branches. The tornado continued northeast and crossed Harmon Drive Southeast where it snapped a couple of trees. The tornado also snapped a few trees and caused roof damage to a home along Pleasant Grove Drive. The tornado crossed Highway 84 uprooting a few more trees, before crossing into Lawrence County. The tornado crossed Foster Road where it caused damage to the roof of an outbuilding and ended just east of Foster Road. Max Winds 100 mph. Max width 250 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was water over the bridge with debris causing CR15S between 60E and 70 E to be impassible.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Friona measured severe wind gusts from 1801 CST through 1807 CST. A peak wind gust of 73 mph was measured at 1807 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex setup characterized by moisture overrunning an entrenched wedge of cold air at the surface led to freezing rain and sleet beginning across north Georgia late on the night of January 24 and persisting through much of the day on January 25. Widespread ice accretion of one-tenth to one-quarter inch ice occurred with some areas receiving over a half inch of freezing rain accumulation. ||Significant tree damage and power outages occurred in the worst-affected areas of northeast Georgia, while spotty tree damage and isolated power outages occurred in other areas. Additionally, a layer of sleet occurred in much of northeast Georgia, leading to hazardous roadways. ||The hardest hit areas locally were White County as well as portions of Dawson and Lumpkin counties. The vast majority of the White County lost power with many locations remaining without power for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light rain showers began through the late evening and overnight hours of the 24th. Rain accumulations transitioned over to freezing rain through the early morning of the 25th and continued through the day. The heaviest ice accumulations occurred with the second push of precipitation in the afternoon of the 25th. All precipitation ended Thursday evening with total ice accumulations of 0.1 to 0.25 across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved from the Central Plains to the western Great Lakes the 3rd into the 4th quickly after the previous system. This low tracked more to the south from southern Minnesota into northern Wisconsin. This storm track resulted in heavier snowfall across northern Minnesota and areas of freezing rain across northwest Wisconsin. Ice accumulations across parts of northwest Wisconsin reached into the 0.25 to 0.30 range with a high report of 0.35 in Spooner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain began during the evening of the 3rd and continued through the night along with gusty winds. Upwards of a quarter of an inch of ice accumulation was received by the time rain ended across the far southern part of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.

An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Halliday NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a passing shortwave and a tight pressure gradient brought high wind to the favored southwest flow areas. Wind gusted as highs as 82 mph along Scenic Drive on the south side of Casper. The Natrona County airport had a maximum gust of 63 mph. Along Highway 220 to the southwest of Casper, wind gusts of 61 mph were recorded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were numerous reports of wind gusts over 58 mph in Natrona County, with a maximum gust of 82 mph at Scenic Drive on the south side of Casper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree limbs were blown down on Lemont Road near Central Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Huntingfield Point Mesonet measured a strong wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th morning into the early evening, temperatures were as low as -3F, with sustained winds around 10-15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -22F.  During the 26th late evening into the overnight, temperatures were as low as -2F, with sustained winds around 10-15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.  During the 28th pre-dawn hours, temperatures were as low as -5, with sustained winds around 10 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed on South River Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on Taylor St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of showers and thunderstorms that had developed along a quasi-stationary front over southern Kansas, moved slowly southward across much of northeastern Oklahoma during the morning and afternoon of the 10th. Locally heavy rainfall amounts of two to three inches in just a few hours occurred across portions of northeastern Oklahoma, which resulted in isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of S 289th E Avenue between E 131st Street S and Highway 51 were closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad upper trough was located across the Western United States with west-southwest flow across the Borderland.  An upper level jet of 100 knots was moving into southern New Mexico and combined with an approaching cold front to bring wind gusts up to 88 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Salinas Peak Mesonet site on the White Sands Missile Range recorded a peak gust of 87 mph.  Other sites on the missile range included 71 mph at Jallen Hawk 40, 65 mph at Salt Creek and 62 mph at Denver WIT.  The Truth or Consequences ASOS recorded a peak gust of 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms affected portions of west-central Texas from Crockett County, northeast to Throckmorton County, as well as areas in between.  Severe storms produced large to very large hail as well as a few isolated tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported half dollar sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface high was building into the northern and central Rockies. This high pushed a back door cold front into far west Texas with wind gusts on the back side of it reaching at least 65 mph with several reports of damage in the El Paso area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media post showed sign damage at the El Paso Trading Post 1 mile southeast of Anthony. There was also a fallen tree in an apartment complex along Shadow Mountain Drive in El Paso reported by an off-duty NWS employee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through North Dakota, bringing strong winds to the state. Showers along the front aided in mixing down non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts. The strongest wind gust of 68 mph was reported near Ray in Williams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NDAWN station 12 SSE Ray reported wind gusts up to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and moist trough pushed inland during the middle portion of February, leading to several days of impactful weather. Strong southwesterly flow on the leading edge of the trough resulted in many instances of strong winds and gusts, and moisture was sufficient to begin producing mountain snow more or less throughout the state. The deep nature of the trough then contained sufficient cold air to drop snow levels following a cold frontal passage, bringing snow to many valley floors, areas of scattered snow squalls, and a period of intense snowfall rates to some of the northern mountains. The snowfall resulted in numerous vehicle accidents, road and canyon closures, and avalanches (of which a fatality was reported).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm brought heavy snow and strong winds to the area. Reported snow observations include 47 inches of snow at Alta - Collins (4.7 inches water), 36 inches of snow at Brighton Crest (3.7 inches water), 32 inches of snow at Solitude (3.3 inches water), and 28 inches of snow at Park City Mountain (2.7 inches of water). Additionally, SNOTEL stations including Thaynes Canyon and Mill-D North recorded from 2.2 to 2.4 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 31 to 34 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 103 mph at Arrowhead Summit, 96 mph at Hidden Peak, and 84 mph at Alta - Mt Baldy. A prolonged period of intense snow rates at or in excess of 3 inches per hour along with the strong winds 2/18 resulted in premature closure of area ski resorts, and full closure of both Big Cottonwood Canyon and Little Cottonwood Canyon. Little Cottonwood Canyon remained closed into the following morning for avalanche mitigation. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were also reported in the Cottonwood canyons in addition to Provo Canyon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees and wires downed in Delevan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Taylor County remained in D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout the month of January. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 14, 2025, the county sustained 16 consecutive weeks of D2 conditions as of the end of January. These conditions remained unchanged as the event persisted into February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures between 24 ang 30 were reported across Kittson County. The lowest value of 24 was reported at the Lancaster, ND DOT site at 3:50 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of central and eastern Illinois during the early morning of June 6th producing isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting northern to central Maryland during the late afternoon hours with swaths of 60 to 70 mph wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were over a dozen calls for trees blown down throughout Allegany County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.
A strong cold front moved through south Louisiana during the end of January. This pushed the tides below normal into February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tide at Freshwater Lock fell below -1 foot MLLW for multiple hours. The tide hit a low of -1.84 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a large tree onto Dunwoody Road north of Huntersville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees near Highway 111 and Highway 293. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure from Green Bay to Lake Huron, meausring 988mb, produced widespread wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. This resulted in property damage and numerous reports of blown-over semi-trucks.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines down and roof damage at the Mississinewa High School. KMZZ AWOS recorded wind gusts of 56 to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved into the region, generating thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported hailstones up to the size of hen eggs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, daytime heating pushed temperatures into the upper 80s and lower 90s, combining with surging humidity to drive heat indices near 100��F and create a highly unstable environment with MLCAPE values reaching 2,500 J/kg. Weak low-level convergence initially triggered severe storms over Wayne County, which dropped 1 to 1.25-inch hail across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights. Later in the evening, a destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into southern Lower Michigan, though it steadily weakened as it moved through Southeast Michigan before completely clearing the state by midnight. While the broader system left over 85,000 customers without power statewide, wind damage, downed trees, and power outages within Southeast Michigan remained isolated to scattered, impacting communities primarily along and west of U.S. 23.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of 1 inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small section of northern Dallam and Sherman counties up against the Oklahoma Panhandle started the month of May in Extreme Drought (D3). The rest of Dallam and Sherman, and all of Hartley and Moore, counties started the month in Severe Drought (D2). Around half way through the month all of Dallam, the northwest two thirds of Hartley and just about all of Sherman had degraded to D3. Rain events just started to pick up across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles which spared the area of D2 from D3 until later in the month. By month's end Moore County fell into D3 while a good portion of Dallam, Sherman, and north-central Hartley improved back to D2. The entire area kept a 120 day deficit around 1 to 4. This late into the spring, crop and other agricultural damage had already been done.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across western and central Wyoming and brought a scattering of showers and thunderstorms. With large dew point depressions and supportive upper level dynamics, strong wind gusts occurred across much of central Wyoming. The most widespread high wind gusts were in Johnson County. After the cold front passage, a brief period of high wind driven by a tight pressure gradient and northwest flow brought strong synoptic winds to Johnson County.
