EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires during the middle of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wildfire ignited near Conner-Nelson Rd in Hilliard on the 14th of April, resulting in the evacuation of one residence and a closure of County Road 115 nearby as a result of poor visibility from smoke. The fire grew to 500 acres shortly thereafter. By the evening of the 22nd of April, the fire was almost fully contained and all road closures had been lifted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, one storm produced three different EF-1 tornadoes in Lee County near Donnellson.

Strong to severe thunderstorms developed in advance of a cold front on the morning of March 7th from eastern Oklahoma into western Arkansas. Wind profiles were quite favorable for organized thunderstorms, with moderate deep-layer shear and effective storm-relative helicity near/above 250 m2/s2. Further analysis also indicated a modest increase in MLCAPE overnight into the early morning hours in the pre-frontal warm air regime, as rich low-level moisture was transported into the region from the southwest. Farther south, storms also increased in coverage and intensity across Northeast Texas, within the zone of deep and rich low-level moisture. This led to some intensification of convection prior to the arrival of the approaching cold front, with one thunderstorm producing a tornado near the Prospect community in central Marion County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Early on the morning of March 7th, a severe thunderstorm produced an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 115 mph near the community of Prospect in Northern Marion County, Texas. The tornado initially touched down just west of U.S. Highway 59 where multiple snapped trunks of hardwood trees were noted. As the tornado continued east, it heavily damaged several structures. A residential home west of the highway was damaged by a fallen tree. Next to the home, a barn was completely destroyed, with only the wooden frame remaining. Debris from the barn along with the barn's contents were strewn across the front yard and into the highway median and onto the northbound side of the highway. Just to the east of U.S. Highway 59, another residential home experienced significant damage after being shifted feet away from its foundation. Several large hardwood trees were also uprooted and fell onto a nearby shed. Just north of this home, another home experienced tornado damage. In the backyard of this home, a small shed was completely destroyed, with contents strewn across the yard, along with damage to vehicles. At this residence, a camper was tossed and rolled into another nearby shed, where multiple occupants were thrown about and injured. The tornado continued east/northeast, snapping and uprooting numerous trees before moving into additional residential areas on East Prospect Road. Here, additional damage to several roofs was noted, sheds and barns experienced significant damage, along with major hardwood tree snaps and downed power lines. The tornado weakened as it moved northeast away from East Prospect Road and crossed Scotts Bayou. Some tree damage was found along Hall Road before the tornado then lifted as it moved east along East CC Road and toward the town of Lodi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushed across eastern New York during the afternoon hours on June 6, 2026 within the warm sector of a low pressure system. The strongest and most organized thunderstorms moved across Ulster and Dutchess Counties where numerous reports of downed trees and wires occurred. More isolated thunderstorms also produced some downed trees across far northern Washington County and near North Creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed, one on a house, along Black Point Way in the Town of Putnam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm sector convection ahead of an approaching cold front spawned thunderstorms, some of which were severe. An axis of up to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE nosed up to Pittsburgh metro with strong effective shear as high as 60 knots. Hail and wind damage were reported with up to 1.5 inch hail, a measured 64 mph wind gust at a home weather station, and trees down on wires.

Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Wilcox County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on November 11, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 12 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Pacific weather system crossed western and central Wyoming and brought heavy snow west of the Continental Divide and high wind to the east of the Divide. Notable accumulations fell throughout the western mountains. The highest amount was in the Salt River and Wyoming Ranges where 34 inches of new snow fell at the Spring Creek Divide SNOTEL site. Other notable amounts included 30 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL in Yellowstone National Park, 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL in the Absarokas and 24 inches over Togwotee Pass. High winds occurred along and East of the Divide as well as across Sweetwater County. Some of the more notable wind gusts included 82 mph along South Pass and 81 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell through most of the Absarokas, with the maximum amount of 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a west-east oriented boundary positioned through the Ozarks region of Missouri with low pressure positioned in Southwestern Missouri, a small but potent surging storm line pushed through Carter, Ripley, and Butler Counties mid-afternoon on the 28th. Large hail and winds in excess of 70mph were associated with this bowing segment as it dove east-southeastward from South Central Missouri into the Bootheel. A more intense pocket of wind known as a macroburst produced winds up to 100mph across portions of Ripley County from southeast of Doniphan to south/southwest of Naylor, uprooting dozens of trees and damaging several structures and multiple vehicles.||For the Carter-Ripley-Butler corridor, environmental parameters included: MLCAPE of 1000-2000J/kg, DCAPE of 500J/kg, very strong effective bulk shear of 60-70kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 6-7C/km.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to half-dollar size fell west of Doniphan, accompanied by wind gusts up to 50mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

Behind the northward retreat of a warm front, a cluster of showers moved along and just ahead of a cold front from Virginia into northwest North Carolina during the evening hours. These showers deepened and led to growing clusters of storms, along with one sustained supercell that brought a swath of large hail (0.75 to 1.25) and sporadic power outages and downed trees to the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media report shows 1.25 to 1.5 inch hail in the town of Mebane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall and storms moving over the same locations brought flooding to Wheeler. Water flooded streets with around three to six inches deep in some locations. Water entered a nursing home with fire department having to move residents. Several roads in town and around town were impassable due to flooding including County roads 17 through 20 east of town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours. ||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS KMAE Madera Municipal Airport reported quarter-mile visibility in dense fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system for mid-June brought two rounds of thunderstorm on Wednesday June 17th. The strongest round of storms occurred during the morning hours that brough damaging winds (some significant), heavy rain, and two EF-1 tornadoes occurred in Iowa. One of these tornado was in Linby in Jefferson and the second touched down in far southeast Lee County and moved into Clark County Missouri and then into Warsaw Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility poles and power lines down, the time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, 2026, two distinct rounds of storms impacted northeastern Minnesota. The initial early-morning line of storms brought damaging wind gusts up to 60-65 mph that uprooted trees and knocked out power in a few places. A second round of severe thunderstorms fired up during the afternoon and evening hours, producing localized strong winds, heavy rainfall, and large hail ranging from quarter to half dollar size.

A shortwave advancing through the Ohio Valley and Pennsylvania allowed for a complex of thunderstorms to develop across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours of June 10, 2026. Upscale growth of this complex continued into portions of central Pennsylvania where slightly more moisture and instability was in place, with CAPE values peaking between 2000-3000 J/kg during the afternoon hours across much of the region. Storms largely stayed below severe limits due to the lack of bulk shear; however, some strong-to-severe thunderstorms knocked down trees in northern York County. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall occurred during portions of Mifflin County, where ponding of water occurred due to a slow-moving thunderstorm ahead of this complex with additional rainfall occurring during the afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a large tree across Starview Road south of Manchester.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought snow followed by high winds, warming temperatures and heavy rain to the panhandle January 8th and 9th. A low pressure center developed along a triple point front as it tracked NE across the western Gulf of Alaska on the 9th. The low center deepened to 960mb as it approached the northern Gulf and the frontal system brought a period of high winds to the central and southern panhandle. This system brought with it heavy snow across the north, followed by a significant warm-up, heavy rain, localized flooding due to previous heavy snow blocking drainages, and avalanches. The flooding falls into the advisory level, but the rain was an additional impact due to the added weight of the snow on structures. Disaster declarations were expanded to more communities across the northern panhandle after this storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter's home weather station in Hydaburg measured a peak gust of 65.9mph on the 9th. Times are estimated based on other locations on Prince of Wales and Annette Island. The Hydaburg AWOS was down at the time. Peak wind at the Klawock Airport (39mph) was measured at 551pm. The highest sustained wind measured by the Kasaan FAA webcam was 31mph at 10am.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of March 7th during a period of record warmth. These storms formed a broken line of loosely organized convection west of the area that afternoon ahead of a cold frontal passage. While some of the storms proved to be severe in Ohio, the threat waned quickly as they progressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia that evening. Strong wind gusts were still associated with storms as they swept through the state, which caused isolated tree damage in Wood, Ritchie, and Upshur Counties. Further deterioration of storms took place on the evening of the 7th due to the loss of daytime heating, bringing the severe threat to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Parkersburg, a tree fell onto power lines at the intersection of Neal Street and 4th Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistently dry conditions coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across San Augustine County in East Texas by the final few days of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 1.00-2.00 inches, which was only half or less than the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers developed, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also observed, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to penny-size about three-miles SSW of Chatfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on East Consolidated Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

Several clusters of severe thunderstorms tracked across portions of central and northeast South Dakota during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 3, generating high winds, large hail, and heavy rainfall.  ||One cluster tracked along the North Dakota border, where a personal weather station in Frederick recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph. These high winds destroyed the football field scoreboard and a storage shed in Frederick, knocked down trees and a radio tower, downed power lines in Hecla, and snapped power poles and flipped an irrigation pivot six miles north of Britton. The city of Britton lost electrical power. Three additional weather stations in Marshall County clocked wind gusts in excess of 60 mph. ||A second storm cluster moved out of eastern South Dakota into the southern Glacial Lakes region. Quarter-sized hail occurred at several locations. Heavy rainfall topping out at 4.40 inches in Clear Lake resulted in water six inches deep running over roads and caused a creek near the golf course to overflow its banks. Across central South Dakota, storms produced hail ranging from penny to golf ball size south of Interstate 90.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six inches of water was observed running over and along Parkway Drive on the south side of Clear Lake. Water in the creek had also topped its bank on the southwest side of the road adjacent to the golf course.  A resident in Clear Lake recorded 4.40 inches of moisture with the system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A picture on social media showed 1.5 inch sized hail near Tylertown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex, multi-day winter system brought a sharp divide in impacts across the Northern Rockies. An interesting synoptic pattern set up as an unseasonably cold low pressure parked over the region for several days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Eight inches of snow fell at Garnet Ghost Town. Five inches of snow accumulated in Potomac, and three inches fell in Clinton. Two vehicles had to be towed out after getting stuck attempting to drive to Garnet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall and near-record early-to-mid month heat allowed worsening drought conditions across locations mainly east of Interstate Highway 69C/US 281 across the lower/mid Rio Grande Valley and the Deep South Texas ranchlands in February 2026. Farm and ranch difficulties due to limited forage, water supplies, and heat continued and expanded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover much of northern Hidalgo County, with a remaining area of Severe (D2) in the northeast corner of the area, and another area mainly west of IH-69C west of Linn/San Manuel. The small area west of IH-69C would become D3 on the 17th, while the other D2 area (northeast corner) remained intact.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving Pacific system moved across the Front Range and brought some much needed snowfall to portions of southeast Wyoming. Although widespread accumulations were generally between 2 to 6 inches, some places received locally higher amounts. This was the largest daily snowfall total for Cheyenne during the 2025 and 2026 winter season at the time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Crow Creek SNOTEL in the southern Laramie Range reported a storm total snow accumulation of 8.8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure system sat north of Maine, as a low pressure moved northeast into the region. Favorable cold air damming set up led to temperatures at, or around, freezing throughout the state. Precipitation began to move in late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Warm mid-layer temperatures move in with associated warm front, transitioning snow in the northern regions over to mixed precipitation. Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. A trace - 0.05 inches of freezing rain in the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Downeast region. A trace - 0.75 inches of sleet fell in the Central Highlands region. Sleet fell on top of snowfall, which had resulted in messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in  Northern Somerset. Estimated roughly a T - 0.75 inches of sleet and trace of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms moved through SE Texas and produced strong winds and heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding was reported over portions of northeast Brazoria county. Flash flooding was initially reported by the member of the public, who estimated around 4 inches of standing water in Hillcrest. A storm chaser shared a video on social media showing flooding over portions of Alvin. In the video, extensive inundation can be seen across two residential properties with both homes surrounded by water. One property had water over the front porch, reaching the front door. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Through most of the month of May, drought conditions intensified and expanded across the eastern edge of Montana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado, producing hail as large as 2.75 inches in diameter.

Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees on the north end of Tyrone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail estimated up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms raced out of Illinois in the evening of April 17th. Prior to becoming outflow dominant and weakening east of South Bend, IN, the line of thunderstorms produced one tornado along with instances of damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 18-25. The highest reliable measurement received was 26.5 from Strathmore. Blizzard conditions were confirmed based on nearby photos, videos, and weather station observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.10 to 1.30 inches across the month of February. This maintained D3 conditions across northeastern Clinton county with D2 conditions across the remainder of the county. These drought conditions continued into at least March 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted much of western SD and the eastern Plains. Biggest threat was large hail which was confirmed by numerous chaser reports. Damaging wind gusts were also measured by SD mesonet stations and personal weather stations across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported wind gust at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Northeastern New Jersey. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Northeastern New Jersey with blizzard conditions across the eastern zones.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Northeastern New Jersey. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A heavy snowfall occurred across the zone of mainly 12 to 18 inches. A cocorahs observer reported 14.0 inches in West Milford. The public reported 18.5 inches at 2 NE Wayne and 16.0 inches in Totowa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Butler County Airport (HAO), a gust to 57 mph was recorded. AWOS platforms at Oxford Miami University Airport (KOXD) and Middletown Hook Field (KMWO) measured gusts to 56 and 54 mph, respectively. The CWOP observer in Blue Bell measured a 46 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed in the Wellington area, including Graham Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure (991 millibars) moving across the Upper Midwest lifted a warm front northward into the Altamaha River in southeast Georgia. Deeper moisture surged northward into northern Florida in the wake of the warm frontal passage. This combined with a warm and unstable air mass resulted in scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developing in the afternoon into evening along the inland moving sea breezes mainly south of the I-10 corridor. Cool mid-level temperatures, steep lapse rates and ML CAPE values in excess of 2,000 j/kg caused strong storms to briefly severe to develop in the late afternoon into the evening hours. The Storm Prediction Center had a Marginal (level 1 out of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorm development across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported Marion County firefighters were called to a house fire on Southwest 115th Street around 8:19 p.m. The 911 caller told them the home was struck by lightning and the attic was filling with smoke. The roof caught on fire and quickly destroyed much of the inside of the home. The lightning caused a large hole in the roof. The family has been displaced. No injuries or fatalities.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another low pressure passed through the Upper Great Lakes late on the 3rd through the 4th, bringing mixed wintry precipitation with ice storm conditions observed in some locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS station KCMX Houghton County Memorial Airport reported 0.14 inches of ice accumulation. Additionally, snow and sleet reports around the area were 1 to 4 inches. Key impacts: slick roads, travel delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media video showed Puente El Coqui in Sector Maldonado Barrio Jaguas in Penuelas impassable due to Rio Jaguas (Guayanes).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust at the Chanute Martin Johnson Airport ASOS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front pushed into the Mid-South during the morning of June 22, 2026. A weak surface low pressure system tracked along the front and across the Mid-South as the front slowly moved across the area. Meanwhile, an upper level disturbance moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley helped to trigger widespread showers and thunderstorms along the front. Anomalously high precipitable water values of over 2 inches were pooled along the front resulting in heavy rainfall with some places reporting over 6 inches. Several areas experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Car was stuck in water at gas station in Caraway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions continued into early January across southern portions of Central Alabama. Several inches of rainfall on January 9-10 greatly reduced drought conditions in southwestern counties. Drought expanded across the southeast in areas that received less rainfall during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Macon County began January in Severe (D2) drought. Eastern and central parts of the county were upgraded to Extreme (D3) by the third week of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system from the west moved over Maine, late on 02/10 into 02/11. Occluded front moves over the state, bringing precipitation in the form of snow from west to southeast. Low began to slow down over eastern Maine, and alongside a surface low developing, heaviest snowfall occurred over eastern Maine. Warning criteria snowfall occurred in central and costal Washington county, with accumulations around 7-9 inches during the afternoon of the 11th. Storm total accumulations around 6-8 inches in southern Aroostook. Northern and eastern Aroostook, alongside Hancock county, had accumulations around 3-5 inches. The rest of the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Bangor region received about 2-4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 3 to 5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -50F. ||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F. ||The lowest wind chills were:|-50F at AXN in Alexandria, MN.|-49F at STC in St Cloud, MN.|-49F at OWA in Owatonna, MN.|-49F at GHW in Glenwood, MN.|-47F at MSP in the Twin Cities, MN.|-47F at BDH in Willmar, MN.|-47F at CFE in Buffalo, MN.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limb downed by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 conditions at the start of the month for much of the county remained in a steady state before heavy rains began to trim the D3 back down on the March 10th issuance and weekly afterwards through the end of the month. D3 drought ended on the 10th with D2 drought ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 5 to 7 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally dry spring led to expansion of ongoing drought conditions across Central Alabama during the month of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Autauga County was upgraded to Severe (D2) drought in late April, with most of the county subsequently upgraded to Extreme (D3) conditions at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds caused structural damage to a barn and downed several trees in the Cumberland City area. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms tracked across north central and northeast Colorado with wind gusts up to 68 mph and hail up to one inch in diameter.

Dense fog continued until the early to mid-morning hours. Many locations reported low temperatures slightly below freezing but no reports were made of freezing fog development.

Severe storms moved across SE Arkansas during the late evening hours of April 28, 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail. One of these storms produced a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported multiple trees and powerlines down along Highway 133.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems affect portions of northern Nevada the first half of the week, bringing in high winds and much needed snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough stationed over western Pennsylvania during the early morning hours with ample moisture and lift allowed for snowfall to begin across much of western Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of January 24th and the early morning hours of January 25, 2026. Moderate-to-heavy snowfall rates were observed at onset with low-level frontogenesis allowing for a moderate snowfall band across portions of western Pennsylvania prior to sunrise. Ample moisture in place with an approaching area of low pressure from the Lower Ohio River Valley also allowed for snowfall to begin across portions of southeastern Pennsylvania ahead of sunrise on January 25th. The progressive movement of the aforementioned trough and low pressure system allowed for a shorter duration of snowfall than could have occurred, with snowfall gradually tapering off across much of the area by the evening hours of January 26th. Westerly flow in the wake of the system did allow for continued upslope snow showers across the western highlands, which continued to allow for additional accumulations. Much of central Pennsylvania observed heavy snowfall, with Harrisburg International Airport and Williamsport Regional Airport breaking daily snowfall records, which have been tracked since 1888 and 1895, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow began in the early morning January 25 and continued into the evening, with most of Southern Centre County seeing 8-12 inches of snow. The highest snowfall total in the area occurred near Port Matilda, where 15.5 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and moist trough pushed inland during the middle portion of February, leading to several days of impactful weather. Strong southwesterly flow on the leading edge of the trough resulted in many instances of strong winds and gusts, and moisture was sufficient to begin producing mountain snow more or less throughout the state. The deep nature of the trough then contained sufficient cold air to drop snow levels following a cold frontal passage, bringing snow to many valley floors, areas of scattered snow squalls, and a period of intense snowfall rates to some of the northern mountains. The snowfall resulted in numerous vehicle accidents, road and canyon closures, and avalanches (of which a fatality was reported).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm brought heavy snow and strong winds to the area. Reported snow observations include 27 inches of snow in the Logan Mountains (3.1 inches water), 23 inches of snow at Powder Mountain (2.5 inches water), and 18 inches of snow at Snowbasin - Base (1.9 inches of water). Additionally, several SNOTEL stations including Lightning Ridge, Ben Lomond Peak, and Monte Cristo recorded from 1.6 to 2.7 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 21 to 37 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 97 mph at Snowbasin - Straw Top, 78 mph at Snowbasin - Strawberry Tower 15, and 76 mph at Ogden Peak. Inclement conditions also resulted in widespread winter driving conditions along higher elevation routes. Examples include a multi-vehicle pileup on I-80 near the Wyoming border, closure of Sardine Canyon for road snow mitigation, and numerous accidents and slide-offs on I-80 through Parleys Canyon. Incidences of additional accidents and slide-offs are noted elsewhere through the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary boundary hovered over central Ohio, northern West Virginia, and southern Pennsylvania on June 27th and 28th, but eventually sank south of the area early on the morning of the 29th. ||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued to develop along and south of the front, depositing one to three inches of rain across much of the area. While the heaviest rain amounts fell in the southern coal fields, soils to the north had already been compromised by prior rounds of precipitation. Thus, an inch to an inch-and-a-half of rain was enough to spawn some flooding on roads in Harrison, Barbour, and Randolph counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was observed on Canfield Hollow Road.

Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For far western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. Along and east of I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Stalled vehicles at US Highway 90 and Debuys Road between Biloxi and Gulfport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms affected the combined Panhandles each afternoon and evening in the early parts of June. With enough moisture, instability and sources to provide atmospheric lift, these storms were able to become severe each day and bring large hail to the region. A few instances of damaging winds and flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water covered roads and some roads were impassable with fast flowing water about one mile east of Wellington. A large tree branch was swept away in a bar ditch from fast flowing water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface boundary was in the vicinity of the combined Panhandles through the afternoon and evening hours of June 29th. This combined with daytime heating, ample instability and enough dry air in the higher levels of the atmosphere to bring scattered showers and thunderstorms to the region. Some of these storms intensified to be severe with damaging winds being the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A crop pivot was blown over and appeared to be a total loss.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe storms over southwest Georgia resulted in wind damage and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down across the entire roadway at Old Berlin Road and Horseshoe Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An occluded area of low pressure traveled across the Great Lakes, NY and New England during the night of February 20th with a new surface low developing off of the Cape cod coast by the early morning hours of February 21st.||Snow overspread northern NY during the afternoon hours and quickly became heavy at times during the late afternoon and evening hours with snowfall rates in excess of 1 inch per hour at times. Snow ended during the early overnight hours of February 21st. Snowfall totals across the region ranged from 3 to 5 inches across St. Lawrence county to 5 to 9 inches across the rest of northern NY. Impacts were generally travel related due to the timing of the heavuest snowfall during the evneing commute.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pickardville NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were photos of multiple large trees down on Gillis Falls Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of strong thunderstorms shifted into northwest Alabama during the late afternoon and early evening hours.  The storms produced strong and gusty winds knocking down a few trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down blocking one lane at CR 69.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

A historic and complex winter storm moved into western Wisconsin during the late evening hours on March 14th and continued through the morning on March 16th. Along the I-90 corridor, a period of heavy sleet manifested for the morning hours which was accompanied by thunder at times before switching to snow by late morning. North of I-90, a band of heavy snow set up during the morning hours on March 15th resulting in rapid snowfall accumulations with locations receiving upwards of 18 to 26 inches of snow. As the evening approached on March 15th, a secondary round of snow moved into the area with increasing winds leading to localized whiteout conditions at times before the winter storm exited the area towards daybreak. Numerous vehicles were stranded on I-94 as a result of the heavy snow near Osseo, WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This winter storm brought heavy snowfall to Trempealeau County with snowfall totals ranging from 8 to 25 inches. The highest snowfall total report in the county was in Strum where 25 inches of snow was measured. Additionally, the heavy snowfall totals resulted in numerous vehicles becoming stranded on Interstate 94 near Osseo resulting in a closure of the interstate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -3 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -22 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning.||While individual event narratives are not included for Clay County, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of mainly sleet and some snow during this event, producing 1 to 4 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (4 inches) was reported near Quanah. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a large tree uprooted and on powerlines. Wind speed estimated from radar data, nearby observations, and damage.
