EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple offshore-moving thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Patrick Space Force Base measured a peak wind gust of 41 knots from the southwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure system passing from the Northern Rockies through the Northern Plains resulted in snow developing, with heavy snow over portions of southwest and south central North Dakota. The greatest snow report of ten inches occurred at Gladstone in Stark County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Solen received six inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ROSEBUD mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 61 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through southern New England during the late afternoon and evening. While the bulk of the severe weather remained in northern New England some wind damage was reported in northern MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Winchendon, numerous trees were down in the Winchendon area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona near to 4 degrees above normal with Minor to Moderate HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that heat was a factor in the cause of death for 5 individuals, with 2 having heat as the primary factor and 3 as a secondary factor in their deaths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona was near normal with Minor HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that heat was a primary factor in the death of an individual and contributing factor in the death of an individual in Tucson. Tucson International Airport ASOS recorded a high temperature of 99 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.

A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of the central to eastern part of the county received 4 to 5 of snow. However, the storm set up a heavier band of 6 to 7 of snow along and north of the Highway 60 corridor. The lowest snowfall measured was around 1.5 inches in Booker.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The incredible stretch of severe weather continued on Wednesday June 10th with more severe storms and a few small tornadoes across Dickinson county.  The storms also dumped  more flooding rains across parts of Kansas that were already saturated from days of torrential rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread flooding is occurring on multiple roadways throughout Abilene.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the North Carolina mountains during the evening of the 24th, beginning as a mix of sleet and snow. The precipitation quickly transitioned to all sleet before mixing with freezing rain during the early morning hours of the 25th. Mostly freezing rain fell during the daylight hours before the wintry precip ended late in the afternoon. Total sleet and snow accumulations generally ranged from 0.5-1.0 inch, with around 0.25 inch falling on top of that. Unusually cold temperatures following the event resulted in several days of travel difficulties.

A large south swell brought dangerous surf of 10 to 15 feet with occasionally higher sets. This swell created numerous hazards and impacts to south facing shores of each island including coastal over wash, harbor surges, and powerful shoreline currents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 22 foot boat capsized in high surf off of the waters of Aina Haina. The boat was carrying 5 passengers, all of those 5 were rescued with one passenger taken to the hospital in serious condition.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A windy day was observed on February 20th across northeast Kentucky in response to a cold front and strong winds mixing down in its wake. The front itself passed through around midday and unveiled a gusty afternoon and evening before winds settled down after sunset. A gust of 40 knots was measured at the Boyd County Emergency Operations Center in Ashland during the early afternoon. Multiple downed trees were noted that afternoon across portions of Greenup and Boyd Counties as a result of the strong winds.

A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS station KRAW in Warsaw, measured a 62mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably warm and humid airmass developed across central Illinois on March 26, 2026, with some locations recording record high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s. Dewpoints also surged into the lower 60s. As a cold front approached during the evening, scattered to widespread strong to severe storms developed along and ahead of the front, primarily in areas north of I-70. These storms produced hail as large as golf balls, as well as a few wind damage reports.

A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gause Boulevard in Slidell impassable due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station 5 NNW Ash Valley KKSRUSHC14 recorded a wind gust of 52 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of dry, Arctic conditions across Central Alaska, a potent weather shift occurred on Thursday, January 15. A strong low-pressure system entering the North Pacific coupled with high pressure over Western Canada to funnel a stream of warm, moist air into the region. As the associated warm front tracked north over the Alaska Range, it produced heavy snowfall and high winds, resulting in widespread blizzard conditions. Simultaneously, strong winds to the west triggered blizzards along the West Coast. In the wake of the front, colder air returned alongside a series of upper-level disturbances. By Friday and Saturday (January 16���17), these systems produced additional heavy snowfall across the Interior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Steady snow fell throughout the day on January 16th with heavy snowfall and visibilities dropping to 1/4 mile or less during the afternoon hours. Nearby the Dahl Creek SNOTEL (DHLA2) reported a 10 inch increase in snow depth throughout the day of January 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along a slowly advancing cold front across south-central and southeast Kansas during the afternoon and nighttime hours of April 17. Storms produced up to golf ball sized hail and up to 70 mph wind gusts. Wind damage was also noted across a couple locations across southeast Kansas from these storms.

A stationary front draped across Arkansas in tandem with an approaching upper level trough axis would spur multiple days of severe winds, flash flooding, and heavy rain totals for the multi-day event across the state of Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous low water crossings flooded across parts of northern Faulkner County and southern Van Buren County, especially in the community of Guy. The nearby COOP observer at Damascus recorded storm total rainfall of 4.14 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the North Carolina mountains during the evening of the 24th, beginning as a mix of sleet and snow. The precipitation quickly transitioned to all sleet before mixing with freezing rain during the early morning hours of the 25th. Mostly freezing rain fell during the daylight hours before the wintry precip ended late in the afternoon. Total sleet and snow accumulations generally ranged from 0.5-1.0 inch, with around 0.25 inch falling on top of that. Unusually cold temperatures following the event resulted in several days of travel difficulties.

The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong northeast winds and heavy snow arrived at St Lawrence Island early on the 13th and continued throughout the day and into the wee hours of the next morning. By early afternoon the Gambell AWOS (PAGM) was reporting wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and a visibility at or below 1/4 mile due to blowing snow. These blizzard conditions continued into the evening hours with strong winds continuing to produce near blizzard conditions well into the overnight hours before the winds finally weakened a bit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold upper level trough along with deep moisture and southeasterly winds allowed heavy rainfall to develop over the Koolau mountain range of Oahu, over Kauai, and over windward portions of Maui. On Oahu, the heavy rain developed and remained persistent for several hours, which led to flooding and flash flooding over the eastern and northern portions of the island. Particularly the Koolau Mountain Range was impacted. Portions of Maui and Kauai also experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain began falling over the Koolau mountain range early in the morning and became anchored through most of the day. Widespread flooding occurred over much of the Koolau Mountains and eastern areas of Oahu. The following event summary includes a list of impacts that the flooding caused. A man in Kaneohe reported forty inches of water in his backyard with twenty inches of water in his house along the Keeahala Stream. The Kokokahi Gymnasium was reportedly flooded according to the broadcast media. Flood waters reportedly inundated homes in the neighborhoods bordered by the Likelike and Kamehameha Highways downstream of the Hoomaluhia Botanical Gardens. A business was flooded on Kamehameha Highway at the confluence of Opaeula Stream and Helemano Stream. The Likelike off ramp from the H3 Kaneohe-bound was closed due to flooding, and cars were flooded up to their windows. As a result, residents had to be rescued from their vehicles. A family on Kaneohe Bay Drive reported that rapid flood waters washed away the stairs leading up to their home. According to the City and County of Honolulu, a wastewater spill at the Ahuimanu Preliminary Treatment Facility occurred due to heavy rainfall and resulting inflow and infiltration into the wastewater system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions continued into early January across southern portions of Central Alabama. Several inches of rainfall on January 9-10 greatly reduced drought conditions in southwestern counties. Drought expanded across the southeast in areas that received less rainfall during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Perry County began January in Severe (D2) drought conditions, which was downgraded to Moderate (D1) following several inches of rain on January 9-10.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass that was in place across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant wind damage occurred at a farm on County Road 13. Two grain bins were completely destroyed and another one was partially damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image of a large tree snapped in half was shared on social media. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong southerly winds caused a tree to fall across the roadway on Fish Trap Road before Old Chisholm Creek Road in western Lawrence County. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a slow-moving cold front. Some of these storms produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced golf ball size hail off Spur 406 on the north side of Lake Amistad.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a large tree onto a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Waves of thunderstorms passed through Central Alabama from April 28 into April 29, affecting predominantly northwestern Central Alabama. A few instances of hail and wind damage occurred from the morning to the evening of April 28 across Marion, Winston, and Lamar counties, with a couple more areas of wind damage reported in Fayette and Walker counties just after midnight. The next evening, a localized area of tree damage occurred in Irondale in Jefferson County, which included a couple trees falling onto homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed across western Marion County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. Training along the boundary mostly resulted in a flash flooding threat, though moisture pooling ahead of the front supported MLCAPE values reaching 1000 J/kg, and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported some storm organization for a damaging wind and embedded tornado threat with locally backed surface wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Storm Survey confirms an EF-1 tornado with maximum wind of 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down at 500 CR 1375 blocking the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Smyth county in early April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Holston River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure tracked across the Northern Plains, leading to moisture advection and isolated severe thunderstorms across central North Dakota. Supercells developed during the evening hours, continuing until the late evening. The strongest wind gust report was near Minot Air Force Base in Ward County, where a trained spotter reported wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. The largest hail occurred in McHenry County, with hail of 2 inches in diameter observed near Velva and Drake. A tornado was observed approximately 4 miles east-southeast of Riverdale in McLean County around 9 PM CDT. There was no known damage from this tornado, therefore there is no estimated wind speed and it is assigned a rating of EF-Unknown per NWS policy.

A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. A swath of 1 to 1.75 inch hailstones were observed from Putnam and Logan Counties over to Kanawha and Clay Counties. The severe risk subsided as the sun began to set for the evening and the cold front began its passage through the forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage in the area of Lynn Hollow resulted in approximately 60 homes to be without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong southerly winds led to multiple impacts across east Honolulu. A roof was blown off a house on Aipo Street, and multiple trees were blown over across many different roads, some blocking traffic. Another roof was blown off in Hawaii Kai.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions improved to moderate (D1) late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful, but rather moisture starved low pressure system moved across the Northern Plains March 12-13. Widespread high winds raced across the region late on the 12th and into the early overnight of the 13th with gusts ranging from 58 to 78 mph behind a strong cold front. With little to no snow on the ground, there were no significant reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 49 mph at times, with gusts as high as 69 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Parker.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 40 to 50 mph wind gusts across VT. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across VT during the early morning hours of March 17th a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts that resulted in several reports of tree limbs/trees on utility lines causing 15,000 customers without power, mainly across the spine of the Green Mountains eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in the 40-50 mph from the west with the passage of the sharp cold front during the early morning hours. Several wind gusts in excess of 40 mph from the south on March 16th with no to little impacts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of March with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across far south Miami-Dade County in March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread showers and storms developed across south-central and southeast Kansas during the morning hours of June 18th. These storms continued to fester across southern Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours. While no damaging wind was reported, the strongest of these storms produced quarter to golf ball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter to golf ball size hail fell in Harper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported that a roof was blown off of a single wide trailer. Nearby, a ship measured a gust to 68 knots (78 miles per hour).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds ripped a section of roof panels from a large outbuilding.  An irrigation pivot was also tipped eastward.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of showers and thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the morning and afternoon of the 6th, as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Locally heavy rainfall from this activity resulted in some flash flooding in Creek, Tulsa, and Okmulgee Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of Hackberry Road and the E 260 Road were washed out east of Dewar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions originally just in Jackson/Dekalb Counties to start the month expanded for the month of April to include all of NWS Huntsville's County Warning Area including 11 counties in AL and 3 in Southern Middle TN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions introduced and expanded through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across portions of eastern Nebraska through the month of April. However, there was some slight improvement through the month with only small departures from average precipitation in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions were present across Platte County at the beginning of the month, but conditions improved steadily throughout April. Extreme drought coverage was removed completely by the end of the month, while the coverage of severe (D2) drought shrank from nearly 99 percent at the beginning of the month down to around 11 percent. The cooperative observer at Columbus 3 NE recorded 2.85 inches of precipitation, 0.08 inches below average. The CoCoRaHS observer at Humphrey 5.7 SSW recorded 2.83 inches of precipitation, 0.08 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds uprooted a few trees onto a fence along Sinking Creek Road southwest of Shelbyville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around 3 to 5 inches of snow fell from Saturday night into Sunday morning. The highest report was 4.3 inches in Chokio. The snow was heavy at times, impacting visibility and driving conditions Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media video showed several vehicles stalled in flood waters on West Crosby Rd  near I-35E in Dallas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions redeveloped during the middle of January and continued into February.

A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dozens of trees uprooted or snapped.
