EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above normal temperatures and minimal precipitation continuing from late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of southeast AR. Through the month of June, D3 (Extreme Drought) and D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions expanded to affect Ashely and Chicot Counties as depicted on the U.S Drought Monitor. Average temperatures for the month ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal, and several daily temperature records were set especially late in the month. Observed precipitation values ranged from 50 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 10 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Chicot County intensified from D3 (Extreme Drought) to D4 (Exceptional Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful and expansive storm system brought widespread heavy wintry precipitation across nearly two thirds of the width of North America, stretching from the southern Rockies and southern Plains, across portions of the Midwest, Deep South, and Southeast, into the Mid-Atlantic and New England. For the Mid-Atlantic region, this was an overrunning precipitation event, with a very cold and dry, arctic airmass in place ahead of the storm. The main low pressure center passed offshore just to the south of the forecast area.||Precipitation began as all snow across the local region during the very early morning hours of January 25th. A transition to sleet occurred from south to north after dawn, reaching as far north as the I-78 to I-80 corridors by the evening before precipitation ended. Some freezing rain occurred across the coastal plain of New Jersey and Delmarva during the afternoon and evening hours. Temperatures warmed above freezing across far southern New Jersey and southern Delaware where the marine front moved inland, resulting in a period of rain before precipitation ended. The marine front remained south and east of the I-95 to I-195 corridors. North of the front (along and north of the I-95 to I-195 corridors, including much of the Philadelphia metropolitan area, central and northern Delmarva) into the I-78 corridor, temperatures remained in the 10s (and even single digits near the I-78 corridor) when snow changed to sleet. Total sleet accumulations between 1-3 were reported in this region, on top of approximately 5-10 of snow. North of the I-78 corridor, precipitation remained mostly all snow, where near a foot or more of accumulations were reported, though at least some mixing of sleet was reported as far north as I-80.||The snow and sleet proved very challenging to remove following the storm due to the weight and density of the ice-capped snowpack and below freezing temperatures. At least 3 fatalities related to snow removal occurred in the Lehigh Valley. Snow removal took a few days in some places. Untreated or unplowed pavement remained covered in snow and/or ice for one to two weeks following the storm.||A 17 day period of largely well below freezing temperatures began the day before this storm on January 24th and continued through February 9th. This was one of the coldest  17 day periods in several decades for much of the region at the time. Mean temperatures in the period ranged from the mid 10s to low 20s. The extreme cold preserved the ice-capped, glacier-like snowpack for approximately 3 to 4 weeks following the storm. The snowpack remained across the entire region until about the third week of February, before melting away completely in most areas due to light rainfall and low temperatures remaining above freezing for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow and sleet accumulation totals ranged from 5-10 from south to north. The highest report received was 10.3 in Point Pleasant Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East Texas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-1.75 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded farther southeast from Red River, Franklin, and Titus Counties to start the month into Western Bowie, Morris, and Camp Counties.

A fairly typical summertime pulse environment took shape the afternoon and evening of 5/24 with PWAT's between 1.80-2.0 and MLCAPE values over 1500 J/kg. This led to scattered convective development across the forecast area, but with weak mean 800-300mb flow, storm motions were under 10-15kts. As a result, strong thunderstorms persisted over Sardis GA for nearly 2 hours with efficient rain rates, causing flash flooding south of Sardis.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Burke County dispatch reported that the 15100 block of Hwy 23 was flooded with water  covering both lanes.

CZ_NAME: DEL NORTE VICINITY / NORTHERN SAN LUIS VALLEY BELOW 8500 FT
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough came through Colorado early in the month, bringing widespread moderate snowfall to the area, mainly along the mountains-plains interface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 4.3 inches of snow measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down at Brighton-Clopton Road and Shady Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought conditions across Houston County from April 2026 improved to severe drought in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in gusty winds and light snow from the morning of the 16th through the afternoon of the 17th. Since there was little to no snowpack on the ground, any reductions in visibility depended on how heavy the falling snow was and how strong winds were. Conditions were generally worst in open, rural areas where the snowfall was able to blow around easier.||Winds gusted over 40 mph in parts of western and southern Minnesota, and generally under an inch of snow fell across the region. Visibilities dropped to 1/4 mile in several locations, though it was often brief due to the showery nature of the snowfall. Two counties, Stevens and Watonwan, experienced blizzard conditions, with prolonged reductions in visibility at or below 1/4 mile and very strong winds.||The strongest measured wind gusts from January 16-17 were:|44 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.|43 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN|43 mph at KRWF in Redwood Falls, MN.|43 mph at KJYG in St James, MN.|41 mph at KBBB in Benson, MN.|39 mph at KBDH in Willmar, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds gusting to 40 mph and scattered snow showers resulted in periodic reductions in visibility as low as 3/4 miles at times, though generally around 2 to 3 miles. Total snow accumulation was under an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado track and timing are based on videos from two different storm chasers as well as damage reported by personnel with the Elmore Fire Department. The tornado mostly moved over open fields, but toward the end, it hit a farm, taking tin off a shed and blowing in garage doors. Trees were also broken. The maximum wind speed was estimated at 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong trough moving into the Rockies created a long duration high wind event across most of southeast Wyoming and parts of western Nebraska. A strong sea level pressure gradient lead to strengthening winds aloft, with strong subsidence and mountain waves helping get these strong winds down to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 62 MPH was observed at the Gun Barrel WYDOT sensor along US-85 at 12:06 AM MST on 4/23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong trough of low pressure over the Pacific Northwest brought high gradient winds to the southern Great Basin and southern Nevada.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds were recorded at a Nevada Department of Transportation roadside mesonet sensor. The sensor ceased reporting at 1824 PST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system in the Gulf of Alaska pushed a strong frontal boundary northward into central Alaska bringing widespread snowfall and blizzard conditions. Winds strengthened ahead of the front, producing gusty winds through Alaska Range Passes and Dalton Highway Summits. Snowfall moved through the Interior from southeast to northwest, with the highest accumulations across the Alaska Range. Blizzard conditions developed in areas where falling snow and gusty winds were present. Effects from this storm were seen as far south as the Alaska Range, to as far north as the central/eastern Brooks Range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Vitus (Energy Company) employee reported whiteout conditions with drifting and blowing snow at 07:58L on 1/11/26. They also estimated approximately 8 inches of snow had fallen, but couldn't verify because of the on-going blowing snow conditions. A DOT report at 07:53L on 1/11/26 later estimated as much as 12 inches of snow had fallen in and around Cantwell, with heavy blowing/drifting snow and gusty winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon and early evening hours of June 24th. As activity moved to the east and southeast, storms became severe with strong winds and large hail. Hail up to the size of baseballs was reported near Wauneta and wind gusts up to 77 MPH were reported near Grant. Thunderstorm wind damage, with winds estimated at 80 MPH overturned multiple pivots and damaged buildings south of Madrid.

A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Manager of the Road Maintenance Division of Public Works reported a landslide that occurred in Faga'itua Village. The manager said that the village road next to where the landslide occurred was completely blocked. They were unable to clear the property until the morning of the 19th. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Newly installed wooden play set broken and rolled 10 yards. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved through north central and northeast South Dakota late on June 27 into the early morning of June 28, generating isolated pockets of high winds. A personal weather station in northeast Aberdeen and the South Dakota State University mesonet station seven miles south of Claremont both recorded peak wind gusts of 70 mph.

A multi-phased system brought a combination of system and lake enhanced snow to northwest and portions of north central Indiana Saturday night into early Sunday morning followed by more organized lake effect snow showers late Sunday into Monday. This prolonged snow event coupled with gusty north to northwest winds lead to hazardous travel conditions and numerous slide-offs and accidents across favored lake effect snow region across northwest and north central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of system and lake enhanced snow Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by a more organized lake effect snow phase Sunday afternoon through midday Monday. Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 2 to 5 inches. A report of 3.3 inches of snow was received 4.4 miles east southeast of Wanatah, IN.  In addition to the snow, north to northwest winds gusting to 30 to 35 mph resulted in some blowing and drifting snow along with periods of reduced visibilities. Numerous slide-offs were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms fired along a stalled frontal boundary throughout the day, resulting in localized heavy rainfall and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported over State Route 726, near Shurley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree blocked Glendale Road in Cairo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A low spot on Kincheloe Road northwest of Jane Lew flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KLVS ASOS measured a 64 mph wind gust from outflow enhanced by a nearby decaying convective showers and thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a quasi-stationary front extending across southern Missouri and northwest Tennessee during the afternoon hours of June 13, 2026.  These storms were supported by SBCAPE values of 3000 to 4000 J/kg and 0-6km bulk shear values of around 30 knots. The storms formed into a line by late afternoon, with several reports of damaging winds. Slow-moving storms combined with precipitable water values around 2 inches to produce heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and minor building damage reported in downtown Sharon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree and power lines, partially blocking the roadway at the intersection of Highway 8 and County Road 35.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deepening surface low pressure system was centered over Illinois and an attendant cold front extended south-southwestward sweeping from west to east across Arkansas during the afternoon and evening hours of March 15, 2026. Multiple severe thunderstorms developed in a well-defined warm sector positioned across the state where storms matured and quickly became severe producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Union Pacific Railroad Weather Station measured a wind gust of 77 mph near Minturn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad upper level low centered offshore from northern California produced numerous thunderstorms in southern Oregon. One long-lived thunderstorm produced damaging winds across a portion of Jackson and Josephine counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced strong winds in Grants Pass. Damage included a tree falling on and damaging a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front brough a messy line of convection to western and central Massachusetts Tuesday evening which caused some limited wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Buckland, a tree was downed on East Buckland Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex over Central Texas sent an outflow boundary into the conditionally unstable, moist airmass over South-Central Texas. This boundary generated thunderstorms that produced locally heavy rain leading to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. In Johnson City, low water crossings on W. Pecan Dr. and E. Ash Dr. at Town Creek were closed due to water over the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The southern stream of the jet remained over the area for multiple days driving a series of short waves across the region. This resulted in a few days of unsettled weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto a home on Wren Street in Morgan City. No injuries occurred. A tree was also downed on Fig Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across eastern North Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NDAWN station at Lisbon 2W consistently reported wind chills -40 or lower from the evening of January 22 through the early morning hours of January 23. The lowest wind chill value during this period at the station was -44.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.

An area of thunderstorms produced a bolt of lightning, striking a residence in the Townsend area.  The lightning caused a fire and produced extensive damage to the home, estimated to be around $100,000.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A bolt of lightning struck a residence in the Townsend area, which started a fire and produced extensive damage to the home, estimated to be around $100,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-day period of frigid conditions continued into the beginning of February across much of southern Vermont. Wind chill values during the morning hours on February 1 dropped to as low as 10 to 30 degrees below zero for most areas.

An unsettled weather pattern unfolded across the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians for the start of June amid a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity. This combination allowed for daily storm initiation across the Midwest that eventually tracked into Ohio and northern West Virginia. On June 6th and 7th, storms tracking into the area reached Harrison and Taylor Counties late in the evening and caused tree and power line damage before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Grafton, a tree blew down onto Addison Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down on Cherry Springs Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blew down near the intersection of East Belvedere Avenue and The Almeda.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.
Showers and thunderstorms popped up and developed over a very hot and humid airmass. A few strong to severe thunderstorms were mixed in, producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down on Branin Road in Medford. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of Hutchinson, Roberts, and Hemphill counties were in Exceptional Drought (D3) at the start of the month. Conversely much of Hansford, Ochiltree, and Lipscomb counties started the month in Severe Drought (D2). With a continually growing deficit in rainfall, the cluster of counties that included Hansford, Ochiltree, and the northwestern half of Lipscomb fell into D3. An area of Exceptional Drought (D4) developed over the southeastern half of Lipscomb, all of Hemphill, and the southeastern half of Roberts County. Areas that developed D4 had a 120 day rainfall deficit of 5 to 8 while the areas with D3 had a 4 to 5 deficit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and Wires down blocking all lakes near Jogee Rd and Mt Orange Rd in Wawayanda  Orange County.

CZ_NAME: OUTER SAGINAW BAY SW OF ALABASTER TO PORT AUSTIN MI TO INNER SAGINAW BAY
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms moving through Saginaw Bay and southern Lake Huron produced wind gusts around 50 knots.

A low amplitude shortwave and accompanying 40 kt speed max approached the Mid-South and allowed lapse rates to steepen above 7 C/km. Ahead of this activity, the Mid-South housed around 750 J/kg of SBCAPE and bulk shear in excess of 45 kts. Small, organized clusters impacted the Mid-South in the late afternoon and brought damaging winds and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree was downed and is blocking the roadway, just south of Pocahontas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornado damage occurred along Gobblers Knob Road, where some trees were damaged. Additional damage was found on Seeley Road, where large tree limbs were knocked down. The tornado moved east, producing more tree damage along Johnson Fork Road. The tornado strengthened as it moved into Drewersburg, producing more significant tree damage along Welsh Drive and Drewersburg Road. One single family home along Welsh Road had its roof completely lifted off with collapse of some exterior walls.||Winds that produced this damage were estimated to be around 125 mph, which corresponds to an EF-2 rating on the Enhanced Fujita Scale. The tornado continued east, where a roof was lifted off of a home on Drewersburg Road.||The tornado curved southeast as it moved onto State Line Road, blowing some large tree limbs down. The tornado weakened to EF-0 intensity as it moved into Butler County, Ohio, at 0030EST, about a half mile north of Drewersburg.  The tornado continued southeast into Butler County, Ohio, before dissipating at 0033EST near Schradin Road, five miles northeast of Harrison, Ohio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A one foot-diameter tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mesonet platform 3 miles southwest of Maysville measured a gust to 49 mph. The AWOS at the Fleming-Mason airport (KFGX) measured a gust to 47 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across northeastern Minnesota on the afternoon of the 17th. As the storms moved across northwest Wisconsin, they transitioned from mainly hail producing storms to wind producing storms. Multiple reports of tree damage were received from Bayfield, Washburn, Ashland, and Sawyer counties with a roof being removed from a building in Hayward. A gust of 68 mph was recorded near Minong. A few large hail reports were received as well, mainly across Sawyer and Price counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported quarter size hail about 5 miles west of Park Falls near the animal rescue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

A deepening surface low pressure system was centered over Illinois and an attendant cold front extended south-southwestward sweeping from west to east across Arkansas during the afternoon and evening hours of March 15, 2026. Multiple severe thunderstorms developed in a well-defined warm sector positioned across the state where storms matured and quickly became severe producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were knocked down near the community of Strawberry.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed along and east of a dryline across east central Kansas late afternoon on April 13th.  The storms produced very large hail to the size of baseballs and also a strong tornado in Franklin County and a brief weak tornado in Osage County.  3 injuries were reported due to the Franklin County tornado none serious.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emporia city manager reported quarter to half dollar size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 12-17. The highest reliable measurement received was 17.2 from Somers Point. Blizzard conditions were confirmed based on nearby photos, videos, and weather station observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree reported down on culp lake rd near the intersection with bailey rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level anomalous ridge over the east coast funneled in well above normal temperatures and moisture on southwest flow across New Hampshire for Mid-April.  A pre-frontal trough pushed into New Hampshire by the evening creating a catalyst for thunderstorm development, with a line of storms pushing through Southern New Hampshire.  A few of these storms became severe, bringing gusty winds and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed trees and powerlines in Hollis, blocking Dow Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf balls in size were reported on the southern edge of town. some minor damage to roofs and vehicles occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blackwell (BLAC) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across portions of the far southeastern portions of the CWA in Oregon and southern Howell Counties. Through the month the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southern Missouri shrank significantly. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri continued to experience (D3) Drought conditions. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, only small areas of Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service employee reported moving water over the I-35 Frontage Road near County Road 248 between Sanger and Valley View.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL WATERS FROM OKALOOSA-WALTON COUNTY LINE TO MEXICO BEACH OUT 20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong thunderstorms moved across the western coastal waters with reports of waterspouts and a measured wind gust of 43 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A waterspout was captured on video near the Majestic Sun Condos.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated thunderstorm wind speeds up around 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts associated with the coastal system knocked down a tree onto power lines that was then knocked down onto a PennDOT truck on State Route 287 in Delmar Township. No injuries were reported from this incident; however, the roadway was closed during the early morning hours of February 23, 2026. Gusty winds began during the late evening hours of February 22nd and continued into the mid-morning hours of February 23rd, where highest estimated wind gusts were 45 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of North Louisiana along with a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported near Spring Ridge just west of Keithville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. Cost of debris cleanup in Hyde county alone topped out at 1.4 million dollars. ||Electrical infrastructure was severely disrupted, causing $2.4 million in utility distribution damage across Hyde and Hand counties. Power was knocked out to 1,072 residents in Hyde County (94% of the county). Power generation was heavily impacted; at least 20 wind turbines were damaged or destroyed at the Triple H and North Bend wind farms, with replacement costs estimated at $50 million.||Day County suffered extensive damage, particularly around Andover, where straight-line wind speeds reached 100 mph. Extensive tree stands were leveled, grain bins dented, and buildings damaged at the Andover Threshing Grounds. Day County power damage reached $18,000, leaving 487 residents without electricity. A brief EFU tornado was confirmed near Andover.||Even as the storm system departed, wrap around high winds caused additional tree damage in areas that had just missed out on thunderstorm wind damage, with several trees and limbs down in parts of Aberdeen, and a peak wind gust measured on a personal weather station of 88 mph in the town of Westport (Brown county).||Governor Rhoden requested a Presidential Disaster Declaration to assist with damage cleanup and repairs for Hyde, Hand, Hughes, Buffalo and Stanley counties including Lower Brule and Crow Creek reservations.

An upper-level trough moving through the region combined with cooling temperatures aloft and daytime heating to facilitate shower and thunderstorm activity. A shower was strong enough to produce a cold-air funnel along the coast in addition to a short lived thunderstorm producing strong outflow winds in southwest Washington.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An unusually intense storm was able to generate a strong downdraft despite limited environmental support, which resulted in a narrow damage swath in Meadow Glade, WA in Clark County. NWS Portland conducted a damage survey in the affected area on Sunday, June 7. NWS storm surveyors found a small area at the  west end of the storm track which experienced heavier damage,  including a metal roof peeled back from an outbuilding and  multiple hardwood trees with trunks snapped multiple feet above  ground level. These damage indicators suggest a maximum wind speed  of just over 90 mph. As the storm moved east, associated wind  speeds weakened, producing minor damage including small downed or  broken tree limbs, lifted roof shingles, and damaged fences,  corresponding to wind speeds of 50-65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced a low end squall line of thunderstorms, which in turn produced several reports of damaging winds. After the cold front's passage, a much colder airmass moved in and snow showers developed, leading to light snowfall for much of northeastern Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm mountain winds first exceeded high wind criteria at the 11 pm observation with 61 mph, reached a peak of 77 mph at the 2 am observation, and at 3 am receded to 72 mph. At 5 AM the final observation above high wind criteria was observed at 72 mph. At 6 AM the next observation fell to 55 mph, and by 9 AM the winds had consistently fallen below advisory criteria. These observations were at the Cove Mountain Fire Tower.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure tracked through the Great Lakes on March 10th through the 11th, bringing widespread precipitation to much of the U.P.  Freezing rain was mixed in over the far southern U.P.  The main impacts were school closures and delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Difficult travel conditions from widespread snowfall resulted in multiple school districts closing schools on 3/11 including Marquette and Gwinn schools. Key impacts: travel delays, school closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A hail swath from a mile to 3 miles wide began southwest of Republic and continued to the northeast across Greene County. Hail from quarters to 4.75 inches in size fell along a path from Republic to northwestern Springfield to Fair Grove as an intensifying left moving supercell moved to the northeast across the County. Along the storms path, numerous homes, vehicles, businesses, equipment, crops, livestock and other structures were damaged by hail before the storm passed into northwestern Webster County.  ||As the storm moved across northwestern Springfield, it moved over the Springfield-Branson National Airport where 4 commuter jets, two cargo jets and up to 25 general aviation aircraft were on the TARMAC. Over 1200 vehicles were in the short and long term parking lot. The storm them moved over the Springfield Zoo killing an Emu and injuring another. At least two dozen people were injured by hail by being outside during the hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record warmth, coupled with little to no rainfall in March, led to rapid expansion of drought conditions across all of western and north central Nebraska. By the end of the month, areas of moderate (D1) drought conditions expanded to severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of March. North Platte saw its 3rd warmest, and Valentine had its warmest March on record. Valentine had its 9th driest and North Platte 19th driest March on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions, transitioned to extreme (D3) drought conditions over the eastern quarter of Boyd County by the end of March. Over the remainder of the county, moderate (D1) drought conditions transitioned to severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down at dividend drive near falcon drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two back to back winter storm systems impacted northern and central NM with the first from late January 7th through the morning of January 8th with the second colder system crossing the state late January 8th through the afternoon of January 9th. The first storm brought snow to mainly the mountains and nearby highlands, with valley and plains locations receiving mainly rain. Gusty west winds were observed across the central highlands midday on January 8th between the two storm systems with a peak wind gust of 65 mph at a Ziamet station southeast of Vaughn. The second storm system approached the state during the afternoon hours of January 8th with western New Mexico impacted by a band of snow on the leading edge of the storm. This band of snow moved into the middle Rio Grande Valley during the evening. This band contained a convective storm with large hail and graupel across the Albuquerque metro area. Accumulating graupel and hail forced the closure of I-40 west of Albuquerque with one inch diameter hail and graupel observed at the National Weather Service office. As the core of the system moved into western NM the night of January 8th and early morning of January 9th, a wraparound snow band brought moderate to heavy snow across northwest and north-central NM, including Farmington, Taos, and Santa Fe. Moderate to heavy snow then shifted to northeast NM on the north side of the storm during the morning and midday hours of January 9th. North wind gusts of up to 45 mph resulted in blowing snow and near whiteout conditions and the temporary closures of I-25 at Raton Pass and U.S. Highway 64/87 between Raton and Clayton. Snow across northeast NM tapered off during the early evening hours as the system exited into the central Great Plains. A lingering band of snow across Espanola, Los Alamos, Santa Fe, and Glorieta brought some light snow during the evening hours of January 9th before skies finally cleared up and temperatures plummeted overnight.||In the end, snowfall amounts of 2 to 6 inches were observed across lower elevations of northwest and north central New Mexico, 4 to 7 inches across the Jemez and Tusas Mountains with an estimated 10 inches at the Bateman SNOTEL site in the southern Tusas Mountains. The Sangre de Cristo Mountains observed 1 to 2 feet of snow with the higher end of this range observed at Ski Santa Fe and the Santa Fe SNOTEL site. The eastern foothills of the Albuquerque Metro observed 1 to 2 inches of a snow and graupel mix and the Sandia and Manzano Mountains observing around 5 to 9 inches of snow with locally a foot on the Sandia Crest. The west-central and southwest mountains observed around 3 to 5 inches of snow with locally up to an estimated 16 inches at Whitewater Baldy Peak. Finally, the Ruidoso area observed around 1 to 4 inches of snow with 10 inches at Sierra Blanca Peak and Ski Apache.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bernalillo County Sherriff Office reported the closure of I-40 at mile marker 140 west of Albuquerque to be closed from accumulating graupel/hail on the highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked a couple trees down on roadway in Tyrone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted southern Illinois on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th. Along and south of Route 13 towards Interstate 24, a brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 8 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in areas that experienced mixing. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassable closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in Massac County, IL. Route 3, 127, and 146 in Alexander County, IL were all snow and ice covered, which led to the County Sheriff issuing an Emergency Travel Only Order due to all roads being too dangerous for travel. Interstate 57 in Williamson County, IL also experienced very difficult travel due to the snow while Jefferson County, IL near Mount Vernon had a multi-vehicle pileup that blocked the southbound side during the afternoon hours on the 25th.  The collision near milepost 92 involved seven vehicles, including a jackknifed truck-tractor semi-trailer that led to minor injures and traffic being diverted. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow, especially near Du Quoin in Perry County, IL where most secondary roads were also impassable. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures.

An arctic cold front brought widespread lake effect snow and strong winds to the north-central U.P.  Winds were strongest near the lakeshore where blizzard conditions were observed at times.  Lake ice along the shorelines contributed to a long fetch for blowing snow, contributing to a multi-vehicle accident on M-28 in Alger County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS station KP53 Munising Lakeshore reported wind gusts in excess of 35 mph from 11 AM to 8 PM Eastern on the 6th, with webcams supporting low visibility. Key impacts: School closures, road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic cold front quickly moved across southern Wisconsin during the early morning hours, bringing a burst of moderate to heavy snow to the many locations along and east of Interstate 39. While snow accumulation was minimal, the brief moderate to heavy snowfall rates combined with gusty winds to significantly reduce visibilities. With high temperatures in the 50s the day prior, flash freezing of roadways also occurred. Significant morning commute impacts occurred as a result of the conditions, with numerous crashes reported on across the impacted area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulation generally an inch or less countywide; numerous reported crashes on roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved along the US Highway 54 corridor during the late evening of March 10th. Damaging winds occurred along this line of storms with damage to trees and structures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down over the roadway along Commercial street and Niangua street in Warsaw.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on Petree Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media shared on social media a report from floodwaters along PR-3 in direction to Tropical Beach in barrio Hucares in Naguabo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Altus (ALTU) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utah DOT reported that a semi truck was blown over on I-80 near mile post 77 along I-80, most likely as a result of outflow winds associated with an area of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: First responders performed a water rescue successfully after a motorist drove into flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous powerlines fell near Moyock middle school.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clearing skies and light winds under high pressure, along with lingering low-level moisture, allowed for widespread dense fog formation to develop late evening across Western Kentucky. Dense fog continued until the mid-morning hours. Many locations reported low temperatures slightly below freezing but no reports were made of freezing fog development.

CZ_NAME: BOULDER & JEFFERSON COUNTIES BELOW 6000 FEET / W BROOMFIELD COUNTY
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow fell in the higher foothills (above 7500 feet) and mountains of northern Colorado at times during May 18th and early on the 19th. 4 to 12 inches of snowfall were common with heavier snow over the mountains of Rocky Mountain National Park and nearby mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports from CoCoRaHS ranged from 3 to 9 inches across the zone. The Estes Park area received 5 to 8 inches according to reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak wind gust in Sherman County was 63 mph and this was observed at the mesonet site located nine miles north-northeast of Sunray at 1251CST. Gusts greater than 58 mph were observed in the county from about 1100CST through 1400CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was downed on Cedar Grove Court near Clough Pike and Taylor Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in Badin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Highlands, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For the Shenandoah Valley, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. For the Virginia Piedmont to I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.
Early summer southwesterly flow combined with the effects of the Atlantic Sea breeze resulted in numerous thunderstorms over northeast FL.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds resulted in a downed tree south of Jasper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system over the Pacific Coast pushed into the western CONUS which produced spring and winter weather. Nevada experienced strong gusty winds across the state with tightening pressure gradients ahead of the storm front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds greater than 58 mph caused an electrical pole to snap. This resulted in electrical lines falling on four cattle and one horse, electrocuting them. This was a total loss of resources.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second round of high winds and snow showers created hazardous travel conditions across northeast South Dakota. Although snow accumulations were minor, totaling only 2 inches or less, the light snow led to slick roads and intermittent near-blizzard conditions. These conditions resulted in several accidents, including a vehicle rollover on Interstate 90 near Vivian and a jackknifed semi-trailer on Highway 12 west of Aberdeen. The highest wind gust of 63 mph was recorded by South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet stations near Roscoe and Bowdle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Day County Sheriff reported blizzard conditions and advised against travel. The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Andover recorded a peak gust of 43 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Part of Banfield Brook overflowed onto Bergdorf Drive in Madison resulting in the road  closure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. On May 18th, storms which initially developed as scattered cells over southern Illinois merged into a line across southern Indiana. This line of storms had a modest amount of instability and vertical wind shear to support it, with temperatures in the upper 80s and dewpoint temperatures in the upper 60s supporting 1500-2000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Scattered wind damage was observed across southern Indiana, with the greatest concentration of damage occurring in Dubois and Washington County, where several trees were blown down. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms later in the evening would also lead to a few occurrences of flash flooding, especially along tributaries of the Blue River in Washington County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down along Indiana State Road 160 near its intersections with Franklin School Road and Conway Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported 1.75 inch hail in Emory.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early evening hours on the 21st, a few clusters of thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of northwest Kansas. Hail up to one inch in diameter occurred in Thomas County, and wind gusts up to 70 mph occurred in Wichita County, downing numerous power poles.  A short lived tornado occurred in far northwest Thomas County on the leading edge of one of the storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Tribune/Greeley County Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds caused roof damage to a barn. Additionally, several power poles were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal moisture moved into the Four Corners from the southwest due to remnant Atmospheric River moisture ahead of a strong closed low pressure system and cold front that brought mountain snow above 9000 feet and valley rain. Temperatures were very warm ahead of this system and fell to below normal levels afterwards with abundant moisture resulting in heavy, wet snow favoring the central and southern mountains with the heaviest accumulations above a foot at the higher elevations where the winds were also the strongest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 3 to 10 inches of snow fell across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

A deep upper-level low moved across northern Mexico bringing a strong cold front through South-Central Texas. This resulted in very cold air in the boundary layer with a layer of above freezing air aloft which produced sleet and freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind chill temperature in Rocksprings dropped to 1 degree.

In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 3.39 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.57 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 28% in Extreme Drought (D3) and 72% in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). By the end of April the extreme drought had been eliminated, shifting to moderate drought which now represented 100% of the county. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 12 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
