EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread, slow-moving showers and storms trained over the same areas and resulted in locally heavy rainfall and scattered flash flooding across central and eastern Virginia on May 25.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported near the intersection of Maury Street and Commerce Road via Waze.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.

Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and embedded thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the late morning and early afternoon of April 27th.  On the back side of this precipitation, a wake low developed, producing wind gusts between 50 and 70 mph, which blew down trees, tree limbs and power lines.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across east central Illinois during the evening of April 27th producing isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports of downed trees and tree limbs came out of central and east-central DuPage County, namely along a corridor extending from Wheaton to Villa Park. At least one large tree was uprooted in Villa Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 6th afternoon to early evening, a moist column combined with dynamic lift from an approaching cool front to produce numerous to widespread training thunderstorms over northern portions of central Indiana.  While most cells were generally sub-severe, isolated damaging winds were most organized in Warren County and most intense at the Muncie airport.  More noteworthy was the quasi-parallel nature of the approaching boundary to the moist conveyor's axis, which produced multiple roudns of heavy rain over several zones, and considerable flash flooding in portions of Warren County and Fountain County where up to an estimated 7.00 inches of rain fell. This severe weather event would be the first of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak gust from thunderstorm winds at KMIE Delaware County Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 1.72 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.68 inches below normal, marking the 5th driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 92% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). It was the driest June through February stretch on record, approximately 11 inches below normal for that 9 month period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 50 to 70 mph wind gusts across northern NY that resulted in several reports of tree limbs or trees in utility lines and several thousand power outages across northern NY. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across northern NY just prior to midnight on the 16-17th with a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts and some additional damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gusts in excess of 55 mph for several locations with reports of downed tree limbs/trees onto utility lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
Strong cold air advection in wake of a passing cold front led to gusty wind conditions capable of producing damage across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree down and blocking one lane near the intersection of Zion Road and Coolers Dairy Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on County Road 700 North by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 80 in Eastwood was flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were downed in Mayfield as storms moved through the city.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 4.5 inches of snow, up to 5.0 inches of sleet, and up to a trace of freezing rain. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms swept over Lake Superior in late June as minor disturbances pivoted around a mid-level ridge over the southeastern CONUS. These disturbances caused multiple incidences of thunderstorm-driven outflow and gusty winds on Lake Superior from the afternoon of the 29th to the early morning hours of the 30th.  A strengthening low level jet and wake lows trailing the thunderstorms resulted in additional periods of gusty winds, above gale force.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Great Lakes Observing System weather station BIGM4 at Big Bay Harbor observed a wind gust of 34 kt. This was outflow from an approaching thunderstorm. Nearby, a public observation of an estimated wind speed of 43 kt was reported. This estimate was based on the minor tree damage in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dryline pushed west towards the Rio Grande Valley and a subtle upper level disturbance in southwest flow helped to trigger severe thunderstorms with strong winds and heavy rain. Almost 2 inches of rain was reported with some of these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A series of trees and power lines were downed on Little Road near La Union.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant ice accumulation was observed across the county with a range from 0.5 inch to 1 inch. Extensive damage was observed to to trees and power lines. Many roads were blocked due to fallen trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois during the afternoon of Sunday, March 15, 2026. The environment was characterized by high shear and weak instability. A line of storms swept across the state, producing scattered wind damage and eight tornadoes within the NWS Central Illinois coverage area.  The tornadoes occurred southeast of the I-72 corridor and all were rated EF-0 or EF-1. No injuries occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A six-foot tall wooden fence had several fence lengths blown down by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -50F. ||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F. ||The lowest wind chills were:|-50F at AXN in Alexandria, MN.|-49F at STC in St Cloud, MN.|-49F at OWA in Owatonna, MN.|-49F at GHW in Glenwood, MN.|-47F at MSP in the Twin Cities, MN.|-47F at BDH in Willmar, MN.|-47F at CFE in Buffalo, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLXL reported wind gusts as high as 30 mph during the early evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -25F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -45F at 7:30PM on the 22nd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave of low pressure along a stationary front resulted in strong to severe thunderstorms tracking east across southern WI during the late evening and overnight  hours.  A tornado was documented in far southwest Wisconsin with other tree damage noted due to high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of downed trees, some on power lines in Dodgeville. Also a measured wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For far western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. Along and east of I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

A line of severe storms developed in north central Kansas during the mid afternoon on 4/26 and tracked eastward through northeast Kansas, producing large hail to ping pong ball size and wind gusts estimated to around 70 mph. Clusters of late evening severe storms impacted much of northeast Kansas through the early morning of 04/27. Large hail to Golfball size and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported. Flash flooding also occurred in Shawnee, Jefferson, and Douglas counties as in upwards of 5 inches of rain fell.
Scattered thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts on Lake Erie.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Buoy station HHL01 Huron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stalled across the region while multiple short waves moved overhead. This produce multiple days of unsettled weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple roads in Basile were flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 80 mph, knocked down numerous large trees and wires in and around Somerset. This includes multiple trees and wires down on North Center Avenue on the north end of Somerset that blocked traffic for multiple hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved from the Central Plains to north of Lake Huron on the 2nd into the 3rd. Snowfall was heavier than expected due to temperatures being slightly cooler than forecast. This lead to snowfall totals of 3 to 7 inches across the area with a high report of 7.9 inches near Finland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall was heavier than expected across the central portion of the county with a few locations reaching 6 inches. A high report of 6.2 inches was received from 12 miles south-southwest of Hibbing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on January 22nd and morning on January 23rd, an arctic airmass moved into the Upper Midwest resulting in dangerously cold temperatures across the region. Many locations saw low temperatures colder than 20 degrees below zero with widespread wind chills ranging between 35 to 55 degrees below zero across northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beginning late on January 22nd and into the morning hours of January 23rd, a period of extreme cold moved into the region bringing dangerously cold wind chills. In Chickasaw County, wind chills ranged from around 35 to 45 degrees below zero with the coldest observed wind chill in the county being 45 degrees below zero in New Hampton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: South Carolina Highway Patrol reported a tree down on Confederate Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing storm system brought localized high winds to Owens Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet site near Bishop briefly recorded high winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper level disturbance moved over the area from morning into the afternoon hours. Lift from this feature along with a very moist atmosphere created scattered thunderstorms across the region. Although most storms brought brief heavy rainfall, a couple of storms became severe producing severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Jayton measured severe wind gusts from 1412 CST through 1413 CST. A peak gust of 62 mph was measured at 1413 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

Anomalous cold air settled into the eastern US for late January, with the coldest period for the Upper Great Lakes from the night of Jan 22nd through the morning of the 24th. Actual air temperatures struggling to break 0 degrees Fahrenheit, combined with winds gusting as high as 15-25mph at times, resulted in extreme cold apparent temperatures of -15 to -25F, and -25 to -35F during the overnight hours on the 22nd into the 23rd, and the 23rd into the 24th. The 23rd into the 24th was the coldest of the two nights. Strong gusty winds and some snowfall resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow, reducing visibilities to whiteout conditions at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Apparent temperatures at KMCD, Mackinac Island AWOS, as low as -34F on the night of the 22nd-23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of sleet and snow during this event, producing 2 to 5 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (5 inches) was reported near Durant. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: State official reported water over Rodi Road.

A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached a brief afternoon peak as high as 108 degrees near Arlington and 103 degrees near DeSmet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system passed through the Pacific Northwest and over the Northern Rockies into the Northern Plains. This system brought heavy snow primarily to the southern half of North Dakota, with the heaviest snow generally south of Interstate 94. The greatest snow amount reported was 16 inches at Napoleon in Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Locations near New England received nine inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gust was measured by a personal weather station at Lake Henry Campground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aiken County EM reported power pole snapped on power line at Powderhouse Rd at Longford St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a passing cold front and a strong jet stream overhead brought high winds to western and central Wyoming for the third time in as many days. The highest winds occurred in the mountains. Mount Coffin in the Salt and Wyoming Range registered a maximum wind gust of 141 mph. Along South Pass in the Wind River Mountains, the maximum gust was 111 mph. The high wind resulted in roads closing to high profile vehicles for several hours, impacting transportation. The passing cold front was accompanied by a period of moderate to heavy snow that further hampered transportation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High wind occurred in portions of Natrona County. Some notable gusts included 76 mph at Scenic Drive and 67 mph at the Natrona County airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed on CR 84 and CR 86 in Calera.
