EVENT_NARRATIVE: An 85 mph wind gust was recorded at the Juniper Interchange on interstate 84.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain caused significant impacts near Corbin, where the public reported an estimated 0.31 inches of ice accretion at 1305EST on the 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, 2026, two distinct rounds of storms impacted northeastern Minnesota. The initial early-morning line of storms brought damaging wind gusts up to 60-65 mph that uprooted trees and knocked out power in a few places. A second round of severe thunderstorms fired up during the afternoon and evening hours, producing localized strong winds, heavy rainfall, and large hail ranging from quarter to half dollar size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several nickel to quarter-sized with a few half dollar-sized.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous hailstones measuring 2 inches to 4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing shortwave generated showers and thunderstorms across the upper Ohio Valley in the evening of the 24th. Some training of the storms resulted in higher amounts approaching 3 inches, which resulted in some isolated flash flooding in Ohio, West Virginia, and western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported flooding on Weir Avenue in Weirton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with a gusts to around 60 mph occurred across west central, southwest, and central Nebraska during the early morning hours until the early afternoon hours on March 15th. Peak wind gusts reached 60 mph or higher at the Imperial, Broken Bow and North Platte ASOS stations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts to around 50 mph or higher were common across Logan County during the morning hours into the mid afternoon hours. The nearby North Platte ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 1107 am CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three trees were downed in the Hokes Bluff area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm system impacted the State of Tennessee starting late Friday, January 23 and continuing into Sunday, January 25, 2026. Cold air moved into Tennessee Friday evening, setting the stage for winter weather through the weekend. This cold air along with a potent storm system resulted in primarily snow Friday night into Saturday morning. However, as warm air aloft moved north into Tennessee, this changed the precipitation from snow to sleet and then finally to freezing rain Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon. By the time precipitation came to an end, snow accumulations were highest across northwest Middle Tennessee where generally 3 to 5 inches were measured. A swath of ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inches was reported from Wayne County northeast through Nashville and to the Tennessee/Kentucky border. Locally higher amounts over one half inch were reported around the Nashville metro area.||These accumulations caused widespread, crippling damage in the form of broken and downed trees and power lines, dangerous to impossible travel conditions, and hundreds of thousands of power outages. Nashville Electric Service (NES) alone reported 230,000 customers without power which is the largest number of outages at one time NES has ever experienced. ||The other major impact from this winter storm was frigid temperatures. Cold air already in place over the weekend was reinforced Sunday night as arctic air moved into Tennessee behind this winter storm. The coldest temperature readings were recorded Monday and Tuesday mornings with widespread readings in the single digits and wind chills below zero. With these very cold temperatures, impacts were felt long after the precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mixture of snow, sleet, and ice impacted Stewart County during the early morning hours of January 24th into the afternoon of January 25th. A variety of reporting sources measured snow accumulations of 3 to 5 inches with ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.35 inches. This led to several reports of treacherous travel and downed powerlines, trees, and tree branches. Total power outages were 1,039 customers across Stewart County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Antecedent arctic air mass on the 29th, combined with radiational cooling and a light wind going into the morning of the 30th, led another chilly night, with some sites dropping into the -20 to -30F range for apparent temperatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill of -21F measured at Rexton RAWS site in the northern portion of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several reports of trees blocking roadways across Cumberland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the very early morning of March 11th, a QLCS pushed through northeastern Missouri and caused wind damage to several structures as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree. The tree fell onto a home in Leadwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold air settled into South Florida behind a strong cold front which allow temperatures to drop below freezing over portions of the area on the nights of February 1st and 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing temperatures between 25 to 32 degrees occurred with a duration of 4 or more hours in some areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 100-foot tall tree that had no previous damage was downed. Multiple other smaller trees were down as well. Branches were found speared into the ground after the storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued in Pittsylvania county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 10th to 20th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced wide spread wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph across east central Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: St. Lucie County International Airport measured a peak wind gust of 52 knots from the west.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media outlet in Cullman County reported photo of flash flooding along CR 1727.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread and consistent rainfall following a pattern change in mid-May led to reductions in drought severity across Central Alabama from late May into early June. As two-month rainfall totals heading into June were near or above average, along with recovery in stream flows around the state, Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Central Alabama during the first week of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lingering Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Bullock County in early June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread storms developed across central Virginia in the afternoon of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. Upscale growth into a few storm clusters produced swaths of damaging winds across central Virginia, eventually progressing eastward toward eastern Virginia in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 call center reported a damaged power line on King William Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in a few bands of thunderstorms that produced widely scattered instances of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees blew down in eastern Howard County in  Ellicott City, Scaggsville, Ilchester, and Columbia, including one onto a car on Scarecrow Court in Columbia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough brought an increase in southerly winds aloft on the 13th. This combined with a strongly unstable atmosphere brought severe thunderstorms producing scattered severe wind gusts across the region. High synoptic wind gusts also accompanied thunderstorms on the 13th and 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Montana Mesonet Big Sandy SE thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and wires down around Princeton. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching frontal boundary to the Natural State at the beginning of the episode would become a stationary boundary as the upper level flow pattern would begin as an approaching positively-tilted trough axis which would become an omega block and lock the mesoscale feature of the stationary boundary in position across Arkansas leading to a multiple day period of severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A creek in Batavia overflowed its banks leading to widespread flooding along Arkansas Highway 392 in the vicinity of the Batavia Assembly of God Church.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low offshore and upper trough combined with deep arctic air led to significant snowfall across the Carolinas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 31 and ended on February 1, ranging from 5 to 7 inches across the county. County offices were closed the day after the event, with schools closed for two days. Impacts from the storm were limited.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front swept southward across eastern Colorado during the evening of January 15th, with it bringing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph. Winds subsided overnight, but became strong again during morning and afternoon hours of January 16th. A few power poles came down in Larimer County. Several miles of I-25 north of Fort Collins to the WY state line was closed to all traffic and US 85 north of Greeley to the WY line was closed to all traffic as well. A grass fire (about 500 acres) occurred along I-76 in Sedgwick county south of Sedgwick. Mandatory evacuations south of I-76 and east of HWY 59 lasted about hour before the fire was contained.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weather station in Byers reported a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most of this region was in Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought to begin June. Normal to well above normal precipitation was observed through most of the June except for a dry middle of the month. Well above normal precipitation was observed for the month across eastern portions of this region, while normal to below normal precipitation was observed elsewhere. The drought category improved this month but areas of D2 to D3 persist due to a 2-6 inch 120 day rainfall deficit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather pattern in the upper atmosphere favored the development of showers and thunderstorms across the local area. At the surface, a stalled frontal boundary stretched from west to east near the I-10 corridor and provided a focus for repeated thunderstorm development. Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of coastal Mississippi over the two-day period and resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads on Keesler Air Force Base are impassible.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rain across parts of central Illinois from the evening of June 10th into the pre-dawn hours of June 11th.  Rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches were common, with some locations exceeding 3.50.  Excessive rainfall rates associated with strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of June 10th resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding across Knox, Peoria, Tazewell, McLean, and Sangamon counties.  In addition, sharp rises on area creeks and streams led to overland flooding in a few spots...most notably on the north side of Lexington in McLean County.  The flood waters gradually receded after sunrise on June 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle stalled in waist-deep water on a roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo on Facebook shows a hailstone that measured 1.75 inches.  This stone reported fell between Mendon and Three Rivers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: MNDOT RWIS sites reported visibilities at or below 1/4 mile for several hours as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 35 mph. The 2-day snowfall estimates ranged from about 6 to 9 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 9 inches in Wells. The DOT issued a travel advisory on Sunday due to the blizzard conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached a brief afternoon peak as high as 106 degrees near Round Lake, 102 degrees near Lakefield, and 100 degrees at Jackson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the midday of the 17th, west-southwesterly winds began gusting up to close to 70 MPH ahead of a cold front.  Behind the front high winds continued.  The west-southwesterly winds did loft dirt into the air, causing widespread visibilities to drop to around 1-2 miles with isolated pockets of intense plumes leading to brownout conditions. One such location was at mile marker 66 on I-70 where a two vehicle accident occurred, causing one fatality.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported brownout conditions along Highway 83 south of Oakley in various locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak gust to 59 mph occurred at 10:10 PM MST 2/16 at the Hole N The Rock mesonet site, south of Moab, UT. An additional gust to 59 mph occurred at the Hole N The Rock site at 1:20 AM MST 2/17, with a gust to 58 mph at the US-191 at MP 104 Flat Iron Utah Department of Transportation site at 3:30 AM MST 2/17. Other gusts at various sensors around the zone ranged from 45 mph to 55 mph during the period of highest winds. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities associated with this high wind event were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid air to the south of a warm frontal boundary spawned heavy rain producing thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Storms repeatedly moving over the same regions produced pockets of 3 to 4 inches of rain which triggered areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water reported over West Lake Road in many locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 16th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delete.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid-day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||With soils already saturated from previous rainfall, the additional one to three inches of rain that fell over southeast Ohio prompted more flooded roads in Gallia and minor flooding on portions of Duck Creek, the Muskingum River and Little Muskingum River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto Zion Road Northwest near Somerset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.

A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet accumulation less than 1/2 inch, followed by 1/4 inch of ice across the northern and western part of Itawamba County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass overspread the southern Appalachians in the wake of a strong cold front throughout the 26th and 27th. Widespread air temperatures in the single digits combined with gusty northwest winds to produce wind chill values of 5 to 10 below in the valleys. Temperatures near or below zero combined with generally stronger winds to yield wind chills of 15 to 25 below above 4000 feet.

A strong upper trough approached Georgia on the morning of Sunday, January 18th, drawing Gulf moisture northward into central Georgia. Meanwhile, a cold front brought an influx of colder air into the area. This interaction led to a few hours of snowfall across much of central Georgia on the morning of January 18th. Snowfall accumulations were generally in the 1-2 range across this stretch of the state, though a few spots received near 3 of snow. After a brief period of slowed travel and snowy scenes, afternoon sun brought warmer temperatures which quickly melted the snow, bringing a quick end to this relatively uncommon central Georgia snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain transitioned to snowfall in the early morning hours of the 18th. Snowfall accumulations reached T to 1.5 inches across the county. Any remnant snow showers tapered off by late morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The East Fork White River, rising amid moderate flood stage at Shoals, inundated Sprout Springs Road, which swept an elderly man's truck off the road on the 9th, and while the vehicle's passenger was later rescued from a tree vine, search efforts continued for the man through following days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into central NY, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on a house on Caroline Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to 5 to 20 below zero with wind chill temperatures of  15 to 35 below zero across northern NY.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures around 10 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 20 to 30 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

CZ_NAME: MOUTH OF CHESAPEAKE BAY FROM NEW POINT COMFORT TO LITTLE CREEK, VA
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow sensor at 3rd Island reported a wind gust of 37 knots (43 miles per hour).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into eastern New York on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of the Hudson Valley into Washington County and the southern Taconics on one or both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms produced some large hail along with downed trees and wires. The Town of Pawling was hardest hit on June 11 as an intense thunderstorm produced hail in excess of 2 inches in some areas and widespread tree damage.

Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments. It's along those stronger segments where multiple marine locations were impacted by severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet at Ship Island XHSHI measured a wind gust of 50 mph or 43 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant snowfall occurred across the region, with as much as 2 feet of snow in spots, along with significant blowing and drifting. Road cleanup continued well into the 17th. County offices were closed through the 17th due to conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image of a caliper-measured hailstone was shared on social media. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the first segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado developed over the southern portion of Inola, and moved northeast across the east side of town. One home had a portion of the roof blown off, and a number of other homes received minor damage. Many large limbs were snapped from trees. The tornado then moved northeast across the E 595 Road, where the roof of a home was damaged and trees were blown down. It uprooted trees as it moved across the E 590 Road, crossed Highway 412, and blew a portion of the roof from a home on the E 580 Road. The tornado moved into Mayes County near the E 580 Road. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 100 to 105 mph. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous 6 to 8 inch diameter limbs downed,  a couple of uprooted pines between Wall Lake  and the Greenlawn Cemetery areas near  Orland, IN.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to June 28th, pulses in the southwesterly flow aloft coupled with upslope flow yielded shower and thunderstorm development, starting in the higher terrain and spreading northeastward towards the Trans-Pecos and Permian Basin. A few storms produced severe downburst winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire chief reported significant flash flooding along Hwy 170. A high water rescue was performed under the Terlingua Creek Bridge. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar. The cost of damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 5F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees and power lines blew down across Stuarts Draft area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power pole was knocked down in the 500 block of Nelson Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding across eastern Nebraska. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||Sinitially presenting a significant large hail threat before transitioning into a destructive wind event. Through the early to mid-evening hours, widespread hail ranging from quarter (1.00 inch) to baseball (2.75 inches) size bombarded Platte, Saline, Seward, Gage, Lancaster, and Jefferson counties. The most intense hail occurred in Jefferson and Saline counties, highlighted by 2.75-inch hailstones measured near Plymouth and 2.50-inch hailstones reported near De Witt.||As the storms progressed into the late evening and early morning hours of May 17, the primary hazard shifted to severe and damaging straight-line winds. Jefferson County absorbed the brunt of this impact, with multiple mesonet stations and emergency management officials measuring extreme wind gusts between 75 and 88 mph in and around Fairbury. These intense winds caused significant impacts, including downed trees, widespread power outages, and near-zero visibility. The line of storms maintained severe intensity as it pushed eastward, producing gusts in excess of 60 mph across Gage and Richardson counties before eventually clearing the region.||In addition to the severe weather, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall brought flash flooding to southeast Nebraska, primarily impacting Gage, Johnson, Jefferson, and Saline counties. Widespread precipitation totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the region, with localized maximums of 5.80 to 7.00 inches concentrated in Gage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 79 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure from Green Bay to Lake Huron, measuring 988mb, produced widespread wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. This resulted in property damage and numerous reports of blown-over semi-trucks.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Automated stations reported wind gusts of 54 mph to 77 mph. 77 mph wind gust was recorded at a mesonet station in Van Wert. Multiple semi trucks were blown over and power poles were downed in multiple locations. Blowing dust reduced visibility to 1/4 mile or less, prompting a blowing dust advisory.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Giles county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass persisted across eastern New York during the early morning hours on February 2, 2026. The combination of cold temperatures and a lingering breeze resulted in some wind chill values (or feels-like temperatures) to reach 10 to 25 degrees below zero, though coverage was not as widespread as previous days.

A deepening low-pressure system located across the western Canadian Prairies moved into Manitoba on April 23rd, 2026. A surface cold front associated with this low was stretched across Minnesota. This aided the development of showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. A few stronger storms did produce large hail measuring quarter size (Freeborn Co.) and half-dollar size (Meeker Co.). Additionally, in southern Minnesota, the AWOS station located in Albert Lea measured a 62-mph wind gust.

Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over southeast Louisiana, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D3 to include St Tammany, southern Tangipahoa, and St James Parishes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 to D3 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of East Feliciana Parish according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.

A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down off of Old County Home Road in the Dobson Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Terrell Volunteer Fire Department reported flooding in Terrell, with vehicles stuck in high water near the intersection of Texas Highway 34 and High Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dense fog developed along a vertical column across the center of the CWA including the most of the bigger cities. This started near the end of 3/3 and into the morning of 3/4.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station KTQK Scott City reporting quarter-mile visibility in dense fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust from a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rare strong and damaging downslope wind event started in the early morning hours of March 12th and continued through March 13th. Intense mountain wave activity was also a contributing factor to widespread wind gusts between 80 to 110 MPH across southeast Wyoming. Numerous reports of tree damage, power outages, and property damage including flipped over sixteen-wheeler tractor trailer trucks were reported to WYDOT and the National Weather Service. Areas of blowing dust also resulted in lower visibility on area roadways, which added to the already difficult travel scenario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most observation sites in eastern Platte County reported wind gusts over 58 MPH. The public reported and sent a photo of an uprooted tree and several downed power lines in Wheatland Wyoming. Peak gust of 76 MPH was measured at the Coleman WYDOT site north of Wheatland while Wheatland Airfield measured a gust of 63 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at Lone Star Road and Hahn Road and Old Highway 99 from Delevan to Maxwell Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.

Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Worcester Airport ASOS (KORH) blizzard conditions occurred from 245 AM EST to 940 AM EST. The strongest gust was 59 mph at 1108 AM EST. Generally 12-17 inches of snow fell. The highest amount was 19.5 inches in Milford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding across north central Kentucky. On April 28th, the system's cold front dropped southeast, bringing a line of thunderstorms through central Kentucky. This produced additional wind damage and multiple small tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking the road near the intersection of Defries Road and Davis Bend Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The end of January rounded out with accumulating snow showers across southwestern Virginia in response to a passing low pressure system. The center of this disturbance intensified over the Carolinas on January 30th, pulling an abundance of moisture up from the south. Colder air ushered in from the north set the stage for precipitation to fall as snow as this event got underway on the morning of the 30th. The track of the storm kept the bulk of measurable snow contained within the southern coalfields and eastward into the Mid-Atlantic region before wrapping up by the later half of the day on January 31st. For Buchanan and Dickenson Counties, six to seven inches of snow fell across the highest elevations and between three to five inches for the lower elevations.
Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the Gulf waters and bays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XGAL Galveston Bay measured a 39 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to June 10th, upslope flow led to thunderstorm development in and around the higher terrain, particularly the Davis Mountains. A couple of storms became severe, producing damaging winds. Flash flooding was also reported in Pecos.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pecos Fire Department reported a tree uprooted on 7th and Hackberry Street. The total time of occurrence, cost of damages, and maximum wind gust are estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

Yet another in a week of extremely strong winds occurred with the strongest wind day with a peak of 89 mph at East Butte and several gusts over 70 mph throughout the state.  Interstate 15 was pre-emptively closed from Shelley to north of Idaho Falls in anticipation of the extreme event.  It was a widespread event with some damage and power outages occurring as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 73 mph wind gust was recorded at Mount Baird 6 miles east northeast of Palisades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lightning damaged two homes in North Carolina during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down in Columbus County. No additional information was available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal April rainfall upstream along the Ohio River from East Central Missouri and Central Illinois to Iowa/Wisconsin resulted in river levels on the Mississippi River rising into minor flood at Chester and Cape Girardeau to end the month, with minor flooding continuing into May. Impacts were limited to bottomland agricultural areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor flooding began at the end of April along the Mississippi River near Chester, with limited impacts to low-lying agricultural areas. Flooding continued into May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front brought two rounds of showers and thunderstorms to South-Central Texas. As the front moved southward it produced a few storms with large hail. The next morning it moved back northward as a warm front and produced heavy rain that led to minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flooding in southeastern San Antonio. A few low water crossings were closed in the vicinity of the intersection of I-37 and I-410.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into Lower Michigan on June 10 resulting in tens of thousands of power outages statewide from wind damage and down trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees across several roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly sinking cold front provided lift for thunderstorm development during the evening hours across north Mississippi. Partial clearing of skies prior to the frontal arrival resulted in moderate destabilization. Climatologically, February is cooler, which increases confidence in very cold air aloft. The lift from the front, an unstable environment, and cold air aloft raised a primary concern for large hail. Elevated MUCAPE values (up to 1500 J/kg) and steep lapse rates resulted in hail up to golf ball size to occur.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small tent greenhouse was damaged near Etta.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree which blocked a roadway in Hendersonville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Mulberry Road in Richmond County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light snow showers occurred for a few hours during the early morning hours of March 16 2026 across several areas in MS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS employee reported light snow showers in the Byram area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to quarter size fell in northwestern portions of Carbondale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bowbells NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.

An intense thunderstorm cluster, exhibiting occasional supercell character, moved from the western suburbs of Oklahoma City, OK southward towards Lawton, OK. In addition to reports of large to very large hail, a concentrated corridor of thunderstorm wind damage occurred on the east and southeast sides of Lawton, OK. This included several observations of significant severe winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Relayed images show portions of a church's brick siding blown off. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather system resulted in a light wintry mix of precipitation during the afternoon of January 4th. Surface temperatures were about 5 to 10 degrees below freezing, under a slightly warmer air mass just above the surface. This resulted in a few hours of light freezing rain or drizzle, and ultimately light ice accretion, creating slick surfaces for a number of counties. The farther north, the airmass was cooler just above the surface, resulting in more snow mixing in with any freezing precipitation. This limited impacts for Polk, Barron, and Rusk counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at KRNH reported two hours of a mixture of snow and light freezing precipitation during the afternoon. CoCoRaHS observers reported a glaze of ice near Knapp and Hudson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Seven tenths of an inch of sleet fell, along with trace accumulations of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow accumulation generally ranging from 12 to 14 inches was reported across the county with the highest total of 16 inches reported by the public in Oakland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning of March 11th, a QLCS pushed through portions of southern Illinois. The QLCS caused thunderstorm wind damage as it passed and produced 4 tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree limb which damaged a mobile home. They also broke 2 power poles near the intersection of Route 154 and Plum Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A system brought locally heavy snow and strong winds ranging from 45 to 55 mph to northeast South Dakota. Due to deteriorating conditions on March 14th, Interstate 29 north of Watertown and several highways across the northeast and north central parts of the state were closed. The COOP observer 1 mile southwest of Clear Lake recorded 8 inches of snow, while the CoCoRaHS observer in La Bolt measured a total of 6.2 inches.||Falling snow ended before the winds increased, resulting in only intermittent, short-lived blizzard conditions.  The Andover COOP and a CoCoRaHS observer 6 miles southwest of Gary reported near-blizzard conditions at the time of their observations.

Arctic high pressure brought another surge of cold air to the region late Sunday night (1/25) into Monday morning (1/26). A few locations across north-central Wisconsin once again dropped to extreme cold criteria Monday morning (1/26) as cold temperatures of 20 to 30 below zero and light westerly winds of 5 to 10 mph pushed wind chill values down to 35 to nearly 40 below zero.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of cold temperatures and light winds caused wind chill values to fall to -35 to -39 degrees Monday morning (1/26).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power pole broke and was leaning over Bandana Road. At the peak of storm outages, approximately 8% of Ballard County was without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions worsened to Extreme (D3) conditions late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A fallen tree blocked Highway 58 near the intersection of Landfill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to nickel-size about one-mile east of Tallmadge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS site KBDR at Bridgeport Airport measured a 45 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of April 29th, a cluster of thunderstorms worked their way through West Virginia amid a passing cold front. Storms mainly exuded moments of damaging wind gusts, with the exception of one that passed over Fayette County. This storm produced an EF1 tornado that traveled 5 miles from Pine Grove over to the community of Lookout. While the tornado was on the ground, extensive tree damage was observed, along with minor roof damage to a few structures in its path. Convection quickly progressed eastward into the Greenbrier Valley that evening as the front made southeastward progress through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF1 tornado began between US 19 and Whispering Pines Lanes in the Pine Grove community of Fayette County. The tornado skipped along in an east-southeasterly direction with the damage path ending near the intersection of Mountain Vista Drive and US 60 in the Lookout community. Tree damage was extensive along Edmond Road and between Lansing Edmond Road and US 60 with the trunks of some healthy mature hardwood trees snapped in both locations and many trees uprooted. Only some minor roof damage occurred to a couple structures in the tornado's path.||This is the fifth documented tornado to occur in Fayette County since 1961, and the first since 2024. This tornado crossed US 60 a mere 1.9 miles south of where an EF2 tornado crossed on April 2nd, 2024.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.
A cold front brought severe weather, heavy rain, and flash flooding to southeast Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down along Sanitary Dairy Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Madill (MADI) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.
Strong low-level flow ahead of an eastward advancing front combined with scattered showers to produce sporadic high winds across southeast South Dakota on May 14.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds briefly reached 40 mph, with gusts as high as 58 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Dell Rapids.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL WATERS FROM SOUTHWEST PASS OF THE MISSISSIPPI RIVER TO PORT FOURCHON LOUISIANA OUT 20 NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Buoy station GISL1 Grand Isle, LA measured a wind gust of 42mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 23rd with sub-zero temperatures (5 to 20 below zero) and brisk winds to create dangerous wind chills of 20 to 40 below zero across the region for the overnight of January 23rd into the morning hours of January 24th. Very strong arctic high pressure across the region during the night of January 24th allowed for more sub-zero temperatures (10 to 20 below zero) across the region but winds were calm or light.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures of 5 to 10 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 15 to 30 below zero during the night of January 23rd into the morning hours of January 24th. Morning low temperatures on January 25th were 5 to 15 below zero with light winds creating colder wind chill values.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and weak thunderstorms generated high winds across portions of central and north central South Dakota from the afternoon of April 22nd into the early morning hours of April 23rd. A peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at the Sand Lake RAWS 13 miles east northeast of Eureka, and at the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles north of Reliance. Winds were strong enough 5 miles east of Pollock to flatten a 10 by 10 outbuilding and gazebo, and power poles were snapped 6 miles north northeast of Eureka, with a loss of power to 615 customers. Power outages were also reported in Walworth county to 108 customers. The lightning overnight sparked a 30 acre fire near the town of Barnard in Brown county.

A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.
