Severe to extreme drought conditions covered much of East Texas and eastern Central Texas throughout the month of April 2026, though minor improvements occurred during the latter half of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions covered Robertson County for all of April 2026, along with a few instances of Extreme Drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions persisted across parts of northeastern Minnesota during the month of February. A slight reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought was realized with the update on the 24th, but no significant chances were observed. Precipitation for the month was around 0.25 to 0.75 inches below normal in the western portion of the D2 Severe Drought area with 0.5 to 1 inches above normal in the eastern portion where the reduction in area occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought covered the northern 2/3rds of the county during the month of February. No changes in drought category were observed over the course of the month. Precipitation for the month was 0.25 to 0.50 inches above normal, highest in the far northeastern corner of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.

During the late afternoon and evening hours on May 27th, a cluster of strong to severe storms produced up to quarter sized hail across portions of Clark and Jackson counties. Additionally, some instances of tree damage due to straight-line winds were noted in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported quarter sized hail in Black River Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours.||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Super patchy dense fog along Highway 198 near 9 & 10 ave. Vis down to 50 feet. |Widespread dense fog of less than 300 feet from Kings/Tulare Co line to 9 ave on 198.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped into the area after a prolonged period of humid conditions. A few bands/clusters of thunderstorms developed resulting in several damaging wind gusts and sporadic large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a call for trees down near the intersection of Elys Frd Road and Yellow Bottom Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 8th, 2026, storms brought severe weather to portions of Bates County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree and power pole downed at College and Maple.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across northwest and west central Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NDAWN station Ottertail 1SW reported frequent wind chill values -40 or lower from the early afternoon on January 22 through the morning of January 23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of multiple trees down in Tabor, IA. Wind speeds were estimated at 60-70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Discrete severe thunderstorms developed off of Lake Michigan, tracked southeast, and congealed into multicell clusters. Along the way, storms produced quarter-sized hail. Most reports of quarter-size hail came from Putnam County, Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Range of hail sizes, largest stones nickel to quarter sized.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The town of Atlas has multiple uprooted trees in multiple directions down with telephone pole snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A boundary set up across eastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania allowed for ample lift ahead of the cold frontal passage given sufficient instability and ample shear in place across the region during the afternoon and evening hours of March 31, 2026. These thunderstorms began to develop across western Ohio and gradually developed stronger as they continued tracking across central and eastern Ohio and into portions of western Pennsylvania. This line of thunderstorms along the boundary caused multiple instances of tree damage across Warren and McKean counties with no injuries reported despite all of the tree damage. A secondary surge of thunderstorms later in the evening allowed for a tree to get knocked down in Clearfield County, with no injuries reported from this incident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down across Route 59 in Smethport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted the Ozarks region from January 23���25, 2026, bringing significant snow, ice, record-breaking cold to southwestern Missouri and far southeastern Kansas. The event, which peaked between Saturday, Jan 24, and Sunday, Jan 25, resulted in double-digit snowfall totals in some areas and widespread, dangerous travel conditions. Heaviest snowfall occurred near the Missouri-Arkansas border, with many locations receiving over 6 inches of snow. Some areas recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall with the highest amounts occurring along the Arkansas State line as bands of heavy snow developed. Roads and highways were severely impacted, with partial to full coverage reported across the region, including I-44 and I-49, making travel difficult or dangerous. Numerous crashes were reported with significant portions of I-44 experiencing closures, accidents, and hazardous conditions, particularly in Southwestern Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began to push into the County during the late evening hours of January 23 as the first round of snow that would continue into January 25th. Moderate to heavy snowfall then occurred during through the day January 24 and into midday January 25th. Between 4-7 inches of snow were reported across the County, causing multiple schools to close. Additionally, Interstate 49 was reported covered and partially closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Areas of drought impacting portions of central and south central Kansas persisted through much of the month. A degradation in the conditions occurred in Barton, McPherson and Rice counties with a classification of the extreme category (D3) beginning on May 5th. Northern Reno County was included in the degradation to D3 with a brief improvement following some rain for about a week before returning back to it by the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: West central to southeast portions of the county entered the month in severe drought (D2) status. While southern portions of the county remained there through the month, west central portions of the county improved to moderate drought (D1) status after rounds of storms moved through from the 17th-18th with observations in the area ranging from nearly two to over five inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level disturbance interacting with an unseasonably warm and humid airmass triggered a line of thunderstorms in the Illinois River Valley during the late afternoon of March 6th.  As the line progressed eastward, a few of the stronger cells produced marginally severe hail and a few reports of minor wind damage.  A second line of convection formed near the Mississippi River later in the evening and produced a couple wind and hail reports in Fulton County toward midnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A grain bin, tree, small sheds, playground set, garage door, and soffit were damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.||In addition, locally repeated heavy rainfall produced some urban flash flooding in Rock Valley.

A moist and stagnant air mass in the wake of a wet snowfall resulted in areas of dense freezing fog late on January 17th and early on January 18th. The fog dissipated before dawn as a cold front moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense freezing fog was observed at Somerset Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper low was moving into the Pacific Northwest with a 160+ knot jet moving into the Southern Rockies. Southwest winds ahead of an associated cold front gusted over 60 mph in many areas with a peak gust of 98 mph recorded.  These winds brought blowing dust to the region with visibilities reduced to near zero around Deming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Truth or Consequences Airport ASOS reported a peak gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm rainfall up to 2.50 inches in under 1.5 hours produced flash flooding, stranding cars in northeastern Sullivan County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall during February combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in continuing Extreme Drought (D3) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercell thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 10th across portions of central and northeast Kansas. Large hail up to baseball size, damaging winds, and a brief tornado occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was caught on video just north of Nickerson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upslope snow developed behind a departing low pressure system. This resulted in a general two to four inches of snow. Winds gusted upwards of 50 mph resulting in significant blowing and drifting of snow. The greatest amounts were west of Keyser's Ridge.

An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree knocked down a power line along County Road 16 in south Buckhannon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kennebec County averaged 1.48 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.72 inches below normal, making the 2nd driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level disturbance rotated through cyclonic northwest flow established over the Northern Plains. Scattered storms developed along a weak surface convergence boundary with minimal MLCAPE around 500 J/kg during the afternoon, but managed to yield an isolated damaging wind gust in southeast South Dakota and isolated large hail in southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gust was measured by the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site north of Wolsey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. The strongest winds were generally closest to the Missouri River where a wind gust up to 58 mph occurred near Sioux City. While areas of light snowfall generally less than one-half inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, there were only very spotty and brief instances of visibility in falling and blowing snow below one mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 30 to 35 mph at times with a gust as high as 49 mph at an Automated Weather Observing System site in Le Mars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread storms developed across central Virginia in the afternoon of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. Upscale growth into a few storm clusters produced swaths of damaging winds across central Virginia, eventually progressing eastward toward eastern Virginia in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 call center reported a tree down on I-64 blocking one lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Difluence ahead of an incoming shortwave interacted with ample moisture across west Texas and southeast New Mexico, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop across the area during the morning of the 26th. The biggest issue during the morning was training thunderstorms which, combined with heavy rainfall, yielded flash flooding for numerous locations. Later that evening, storms redeveloped in southeast New Mexico and moved into portions of west Texas. Large hail and strong winds were observed with these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of street flooding at the intersection of Hwy 158 and I-20. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated from radar. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooded roadways with numerous roads closed around Hume.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds occurred over the mountains and spread down into the surrounding lower elevations, with gusts up to 72 in the higher elevations, and up to 64 mph in the lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Yellowstone River Bridge gusted to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous videos from storm chasers documented a satellite tornado partially rotating around the Braman tornado approximately 5 miles west-southwest of Braman. The path is estimated but likely occurred east of 124th Street moving southwest then southeast crossing Earth Road. If this tornado produced damage, it was indistinguishable from damage caused by the Braman tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: EM relayed public report of 70 mph wind gust near Gilman City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rounds of showers and thunderstorms improved drought conditions across central Kansas early in the month. A couple areas went from severe drought (D2) to none. By the end of the of the month, remaining counties or portions of counties improved to moderate drought and abnormally dry categories. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 4.5 inches to around 15 inches in the drought stricken areas with the highest amounts across south central Kansas. These values were 7 to nearly 9 inches above seasonal normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the northwest corner to start the month, there was an area of extreme drought (D3) with severe drought (D2) from west central to the northeast corner of the county. Multiple rounds of showers and storms improved the northwest corner to D2 on the 2nd then further to moderate drought (D1) on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on the morning of the 31st and continued into the afternoon. Total snowfall across the county was 3 to 6 inches with a narrow band of heaviest snowfall stretching north to south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 16th, a Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved from west-southwest to east-northeast across the lower Ohio Valley, providing forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. Thunderstorms were able to feed off of a seasonably high amount of instability, with around 2000 J/kg Mixed-Layer CAPE present in the pre-storm environment. While synoptic scale ridging over the southeast US meant that large scale flow was fairly weak, the MCV provided a mesoscale enhancement to the wind shear profile, with around 30-35 knots of effective shear supporting organized multicell clusters. Scattered strong to severe storms moved along the Ohio River in north central Kentucky, producing several reports of wind damage as well as isolated instances of near-severe sized hail. The most robust storm of the evening produced a 65 mph wind gust as it moved across Oldham and Henry County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oldham County Kentucky Mesonet site LGRN measured a 65 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall in March continued the Extreme (D3) drought. Conditions worsened through the month with the county being upgraded to Exceptional (D4) drought on March 24, 2026.  Exceptional drought then continued for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

A winter storm impacted much of southeast Georgia with significant snow accumulations and very cold wind chill temperatures. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type. Rain quickly transitioned to snow during the afternoon hours, which continued into the evening before ending. Most of the snow accumulation impacted areas along and north of Interstate 16, with the highest amounts reported across Screven, Bulloch, and Effingham counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. The wind chill temperature first fell below 10 degrees at the Reidsville Airport (KRVJ) at 20:35 EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief EF0 tornado with estimated peak winds of 85-mph impacted the Apple Creek area. The tornado began just west of Honeytown Road, impacted three residential properties as it moved eastward, and then ended just east of the road. The tornado uprooted and snapped trees, and caused some large tree branches to be impaled into the ground. A carport awning was lofted across a home and knocked over a TV antenna, which caused the chimney to collapse onto the roof. Additional impacts included a blown-down fence, roof damage, and damage to an external propane tank at other residences.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southwest Minnesota during the morning and early afternoon of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 49 mph with gusts as high as 65 mph were reported across the area. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 44 mph at times at a Minnesota Department of Transportation site near Hendricks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trailer on concrete blocks was tipped over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree reported down along Route 949.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The city of Salado reported several roads were flooded and closed, including the bridge on  Southridge Drive, the bridge on Chisholm Trail, the low water crossings on De Grumman  and Chaparral, and Chisholm Trail near Elizabeth Circle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.

An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 3.0 inches of snow, up to 3.5 inches of sleet, and up to a trace of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event which produced two rounds of precipitation. The first round produced mixed precipitation across the county. The second round fell as mostly wet heavy snow that melted on contact with the ground. Snow accumulations amounted to an inch or less across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intense daytime heating resulted in the development of a dust devil in a Rio Rancho neighborhood during the mid afternoon. Video shared by local media showed the dust devil resulted in some minor damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video submitted to media shows a vigorous dust devil lofting a full size trampoline more than 50 feet into the air and destroying the roof of a mobile home. Thankfully, no injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary from northeast Nebraska into northwest Iowa focused development of scattered thunderstorms during the late afternoon and very early evening.  Storms fired and intensified with elevated instability above a stratus layer around 1000-1500 J/kg and 40-50 knots of effective shear.  Stronger and more organized cells produced large hail up to golf ball size.

Severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning, afternoon and evening hours of April 26 through April 29 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail and a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto a mobile home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Buoy station RTAT2 in Port Aransas, TX measured gusts up to 50 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first in a series of strong winter storms impacted the eastern Sierra from the 16th to 17th. In this two day period, upwards of 2 to 4 feet of snow fell, and was accompanied by winds upwards of 80-100 mph. Donner Pass, along with other mountain passes, was closed for over a day. The greatest overall impacts occurred on the 17th when heavy snow of 4-10 inches occurred across the main urban areas of far western NV, and higher amounts between 12-18 inches from bands of heavy Lake Tahoe-enhanced snow between Carson City and Washoe Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook post estimated 4 inches of snow in Silver Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and power lines down approximately 2 to 3 miles south of Bethesda.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th. This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia on the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeastward the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||Severe thunderstorms produced strong winds during this time, which downed trees and caused power outages across portions of northeast Kentucky on the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down in the central part of the county, including along Allcorn Road and Brushy Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Numerous damaging wind reports occurred across eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down power lines in Shady Point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 59 mph at Fond du Lac Airport. Many branches down throughout the county, and a small number of customers without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening upper level system crossed the area February 7, spawning deepening low pressure offshore. An Arctic front brought strong winds and cold temperatures to the region as strong high pressure to the north built into the Mid-Atlantic.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 call center reported portions of a roof were blown off of a residence on Market Street in Vienna, MD.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of the tornado was found on Landings Way where several trees were snapped at their trunks. Farther east, along Oakbrook Road near Pleasant Valley Road, additional tree damage was found along with minor damage to building fascia. The tornado proceeded east through residential areas of Oakbrook near Sentry Drive and Thunder Ridge Drive where a few larger hardwood trees were snapped and minor roof damage was noted. ||The tornado progressed east, uprooting trees and snapping tree trunks along Hopeful Road, Surfwood Drive, and Rosetta Drive. The tornado then crossed Interstate 71/75 where it lifted a portion of the roof of one commercial building and caused additional roof damage to a second building. A large power pole was snapped near the intersection of U.S. Route 42 and Dream Street and a local business had its sign destroyed. This is where the tornado is estimated to have reached peak intensity, with winds around 100 mph. ||The tornado then continued east into additional residential areas. Large tree limbs were downed along Hollywood Drive and there were numerous trees and large branches down along Ann Street, Lee Street, and Julia Avenue. The home near Ann Street had a large tree fall onto it, causing minor roof damage. ||The tornado continued southeast, crossing into Kenton County, at 2343EST, just southeast of Florence. The tornado continued southeast in Kenton County before dissipating at 2346EST, along Tallwood Circle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwesterly flow in the wake of a low pressure system stationed over the northern Atlantic allowed for snow showers to generate during the morning hours of January 19, 2026. Subsidence ahead of a surface trough allowed for some clearing ahead of the snow showers, allowing for meager instability in an environment with ample lift to allow for snow squalls for form during the early afternoon hours. Multiple snow squalls were observed across the western half of Pennsylvania, allowing for near-zero visibility and snowfall accumulating on roadways in these squalls. No injuries or accidents were reported during these squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. The PennDOT RWIS station on State Route 6 near Coudersport reported visibility below one quarter of a mile in heavy snow as a snow squall moved through.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were downed along Peter Hoover Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front brought several reports of wind damage to portions of northwest Florida and southern Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree and numerous branches were blown down in the Wetumpka community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of the 15th, a very strong cold front moved through the region bringing severe wind speeds across the area. Surface winds began to increase around 0800 to 0900 CST in the extreme southern Texas Panhandle spreading into the Rolling Plains and South Plains by 1000 CST. Winds peaked around mid-day and then decreased through the remainder of the afternoon. Areas across the southern South Plains and southern Rolling Plains did not quite reach high wind criteria due to this area being more displaced from the stronger winds aloft.||High wind gusts from Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites are listed below:||69 mph at Memphis (Hall County),|67 mph at Childress (Childress County),|63 mph at Lesley (Hall County),|62 mph at Muleshoe (Bailey County),|61 mph at Turkey (Hall County),|59 mph at Caprock Canyons State Park (Briscoe County),|59 mph at Tulia (Swisher County),|58 mph at Guthrie (King County), and|58 mph at Silverton (Briscoe County).||High wind reports from Automated Surface Observing Systems (ASOS) are listed below:||61 mph at Childress Municipal Airport (Childress County), and|60 mph at Lubbock International Airport (Lubbock County).||Sustained high winds of 40 mph or greater were observed by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites below:||46 mph at Dimmitt (Castro County),|46 mph at Hackberry (Cottle County),|44 mph at Earth (Lamb County),|44 mph at Aiken (Hale County),|43 mph at Abernathy (Hale County),|43 mph at Olton (Lamb County),|42 mph at White River Lake (Crosby County),|42 mph at Paducah (Cottle County),|42 mph at Friona (Parmer County),|42 mph at Levelland (Hockley County),|42 mph at McAdoo (Dickens County),|42 mph at Anton (Hockley County),|42 mph at Matador (Motley County),|41 mph at South Plains (Floyd County),|41 mph at Roaring Springs (Motley County), and|41 mph at Hart (Castro County).

A large scale spring storm brough a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at a mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in west-central Wisconsin, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by WISDOT for the majority of western WI, including the temporary closure of I-94 south of Eau Claire.||The highest snowfall reports were:|20.5 inches near Augusta, WI (Eau Claire).|19.0 inches in Pepin, WI (Pepin).|18.5 inches in Durand, WI (Pepin).|16.0 inches in Cadott, WI (Chippewa).|15.2 inches 7 miles S of Altoona, WI (Eau Claire).|15.0 inches in Lund, WI (Pepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 1 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 30 mph. The 2-day snowfall reports ranged from about 8 to 12 inches throughout the county, with the highest reports being 11 inches from Roberts. The DOT issued a travel advisory on Sunday due to the winter storm conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The decaying northern edge of the line that produced widespread, destructive damage in Somerset County also knocked down trees and limbs in Westmont. This portion of the line had weakened significantly, with wind gusts estimated near 50 mph during the time of the damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size in Williamstown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees and power lines were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Alberta Clipper brought a period of moderate snow during the afternoon and early evening hours of February 6th. This tapered to light snow through the evening. Between 11 PM February 6th and 2 AM February 7th, a potent snow squall moved through along an Arctic Front. This reduced visibilities below one quarter of a mile, wind gusts to 50 mph, and quick accumulations near 1-2 in about 30 minutes. By the time the snow ended, total accumulations of 4 to 7 were observed. Winds gusted to 50 mph through the day of February 7th resulting in significant blowing and drifting of snow. Several roads were reported drifted shut.

Shortwave ascent and forcing out ahead of a cold front supported scattered thunderstorms in northwestern Pennsylvania in the afternoon hours. Sufficient MLCAPE values of 500-1000 J/kg and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported a few instances of tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down into power lines near Peffer Road and Long Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on January 22nd and morning on January 23rd, an arctic airmass moved into the Upper Midwest resulting in dangerously cold temperatures across the region. Many locations saw low temperatures colder than 20 degrees below zero with widespread wind chills ranging between 30 to 55 degrees below zero across western Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme cold moved into the region beginning on January 22nd and continued into January 23rd. During this period extremely cold wind chills of around 40 to 55 degrees below occurred in Taylor County with the coldest observed wind chill being 52 degrees below zero at Medford Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong low pressure area swung through southern Virginia, dragging a cold front across Eastern NC by the evening hours. Ahead of it, bands of thunderstorms formed in the afternoon due to unstable conditions and wind shear in place. Scattered severe wind gusts embedded in some of the storms produced wind damage across the area. There were also several reports of hail up to nickel size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Washington County 911 center reported a tree down along Old Roper Rd in Plymouth. The time was estimated based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Facebook photos and local emergency management reported hail between golf ball to tennis ball size fell in Brock.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 71 mph wind gust was recorded at Sweetzer Summit mesonet station on interstate 84.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front brought high winds to much of southeast Idaho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small metal greenhouse was broken in half by the wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS damage survey found that a microburst occurred in Brogue on the evening of June 14th, 2026. Maximum winds were estimated to be between 80 and 90 mph and damage was concentrated along Forry Road in Chanceford Township. Around 10 trees were snapped, one of which fell onto a parked car. One home also sustained damage to roof shingles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. Despite the rain Hays, Medina, and Travis Counties stayed in D3 and Blanco and Williamson stayed in D2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. Despite the rain Hays, Medina, and Travis Counties stayed in D3 and Blanco and Williamson stayed in D2. |The Edwards Aquifer level rose 12.6 feet but was still 26.2 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 0.2 feet but was 16.8 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in March and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.2 feet and was 69.1 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped 0.2 feet and was 87.4 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina River; below normal on the Blanco River; and below normal to normal on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northeast Illinois during the late evening of June 13th into the early morning of June 14th, producing isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large trees were blown down and uprooted near Burnham Avenue between 154th and 158th Streets.  Some of the trees fell onto homes.  One massive tree was uprooted and fell onto a house near 156th Street and Green Bay Avenue trapping a woman inside her house.  She was transported to a local hospital.  Tree limbs and power lines were also blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into eastern New York on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of the Hudson Valley into Washington County and the southern Taconics on one or both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms produced some large hail along with downed trees and wires. The Town of Pawling was hardest hit on June 11 as an intense thunderstorm produced hail in excess of 2 inches in some areas and widespread tree damage.
Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across much of East Texas throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-5 inches, with isolated higher amounts across Northeast Texas, which remained near to 50% of their normal monthly rainfall. Even with the rains, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

Strong low pressure (991 millibars) moving across the Upper Midwest lifted a warm front northward into the Altamaha River in southeast Georgia. Deeper moisture surged northward into northern Florida in the wake of the warm frontal passage. This combined with a warm and unstable air mass resulted in scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developing in the afternoon into evening along the inland moving sea breezes mainly south of the I-10 corridor. Cool mid-level temperatures, steep lapse rates and ML CAPE values in excess of 2,000 j/kg caused strong storms to briefly severe to develop in the late afternoon into the evening hours. The Storm Prediction Center had a Marginal (level 1 out of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorm development across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power Lines Down Due To Thunderstorm Winds,  Time Estimated From Radar. Mesonet station 1334W 1.6 E Palm Coast (WEATHERSTEM) measured a gust of 49 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. In southern Michigan, damaging wind gusts occurred downing trees, some onto houses. Powerlines were reported to be down in multiple areas as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and utility pole down onto a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass setup over southern Wisconsin in late June.  Low temperatures struggled to get into the 70s while high temperatures in the 90s combined with high dew points led to heat indices reaching the 105F-110F range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak heat index:|106F Janesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Smaller areas of above normal precipitation led to improvement in the drought status toward the Highway 14 corridor but continued below normal precipitation worsened drought conditions in a few locations closer to the Missouri River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions intensified to extreme (D3) during mid to late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were reported down in Rimersburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lingering stalled front remained in the forecast area 5/23, but a embedded shortwave in the general troughing pattern moved in during the afternoon and evening hours, leading to scattered convection to develop. The environment ahead of this shortwave was characterized by MLCAPE values over 2000 J/kg and effective shear near 30-35 kts. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across the forecast area during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing damaging winds, hail up to golf ball sized, and even a report of a waterspout over Lake Murray in SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public shared image via social media of flooded intersection at Hearthwood Cir and W Shady Grove Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Candler County Emergency Management reported a residential fire due to a lightning strike in the 9500 block of Hiawatha Road. The structure is considered a possible total loss due to the fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant short-term drought relief was observed across Maine in May 2026, highlighted by a mid-May soaking rain that markedly improved drought categories in the mountains and foothills. In the single week ending May 19, the state's Severe Drought (D2) coverage fell from 11% to 2.2%. While this spring precipitation effectively mitigated immediate agricultural and hydrological impacts���replenishing topsoil moisture, restoring streamflows, and bringing surface water storage like lakes and reservoirs back to near-normal seasonal baselines���long-term deficits endure. Deep groundwater aquifers are slower to react, leaving deep water table levels substantially below historical averages due to these ongoing groundwater deficits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had 31% of Somerset County in Severe Drought (D2), but by the end of May severe drought was eliminated (0%), with 98% transitioning to Moderate Drought (D1) and 2% Abnormally Dry (D0). May rainfall averaged 4.32 inches, above normal by 0.86���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 12-month period ending May 2026 still ranked as the 11th driest on record, leaving the area with a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a transition over to snow during the afternoon on March 15th, a secondary round of snow moved into northeast Iowa with winds increasing to 30 to 40 mph. Coupled with visibility reductions to 1/4 mile or less at times during the evening and overnight hours, this resulted in a period of blizzard conditions across northeast Iowa. Snowfall amounts remained on the lighter side with amounts ranging from 2 to 5 inches across northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of falling snow and gusty winds resulted in near-whiteout conditions at times across Clayton County during the afternoon hours on the 15th through the morning on the 16th. Additionally, snowfall totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the county with the highest total reported being 1 mile east-northeast of Volga where 4 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds near the intersection of Brookfall Dairy Road and Poplar Springs Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station measured a wind gust to 72 mph with some damage to shingles and siding on a residence.  Wind-driven hail also knocked out windows on a camper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front moved through southern Illinois on the morning of the 30th, bringing cold temperatures down to the teens. Blustery northwest winds caused wind chills to fall around -5 to -7. Intervals of dangerous wind chills were variable across the region during the morning hours on the 30th and 31st with the far southern counties remaining above threshold.

A strong surge of Arctic air invaded Southwest Arkansas during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across Southwest Arkansas from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds gusted as high as 53 mph at North Sioux City. During and after a period of snowfall which totaled 1.6 inches near Jefferson and 1.0 inches 10 miles north-northeast of Elk Point, visibility was reduced to one-quarter mile or less at times with blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southwest Indiana on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Vanderburgh County, IN on the 26th. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th with wind chill values warming above -5.

Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were down in Scammon due to  thunderstorm winds.
