EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across South-Central Texas on the evening of May 10, encountering an unstable airmass and producing a line of strong to severe storms with damaging wind gusts and some severe hail. Most of the  observed wind damage occurred in the Austin area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A CoCoRaHS observer observed a 58 mph wind gust shortly before the arrival of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dickinson ASOS reported wind gusts to 75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning of June 7th, training thunderstorms caused flooding across nearly the entire southern half of Boone County. Most of the flooding consisted of inches of water over roadways and flooded creeks. That afternoon through evening, additional thunderstorms exacerbated the problem, creating even more dangerous conditions through the morning of the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to 5 inches of rain fell in Franklin County, resulting in flash flooding in Sullivan. Water flowed over Highway 85 near Deer Path Crossing and North and South Road. There were also several photos of standing water in residential areas of town. Impacts streets include Mervin, Blair, and Fisher and other unnamed roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D3) developed and intensified across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area during February 2026, driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Early in the month, only isolated areas of severe drought (D2) were present across the northwestern parts of the region, but conditions steadily worsened as rainfall remained below normal, with precipitation deficits of roughly 2 to 4 inches observed across much of the region by the end of February. As a result, D2 drought expanded significantly across southern and southwestern portions of the forecast area, while pockets of extreme drought (D3) developed, particularly near coastal Louisiana. By late February, over 30 percent of the area was classified in D2 drought and more than 10 percent in D3, reflecting a rapid degradation in soil moisture and hydrologic conditions. The expansion of drought was most pronounced south of the Interstate 10 corridor, while areas farther north experienced more gradual degradation, generally remaining in D0 to D1 conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Prolonged D2 drought persisted in portions of Lafourche Parish from February 17th through the end of the month according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct clusters of severe thunderstorms impacted central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon and evening of June 4. In the northeast, severe storms generated large hail up to golf ball size five miles south-southeast of Cottonwood Lake and nine miles southeast of Tulare. The Huron Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) 12 miles east-southeast of Sunshine Bible Academy recorded a peak wind gust of 86 mph.||A separate cluster of storms tracked through mainly central and south central South Dakota producing peak wind gusts of 71 mph and 68 mph at the South Dakota Department of Transportation Road Weather Information System (RWIS) stations six miles southwest of the Joe Creek Recreation Area and nine miles north-northwest of Vivian, respectively.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over western Kentucky allowed for clear skies and calm winds the morning of the 27th. Residual low-level moisture from a cold front that sagged south the previous day supported areas of dense fog during the early morning hours.
Multiple thunderstorms produced severe conditions along the Brevard and Volusia County coasts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: USSF wind sensor on tower 110 (NW Sensor) measured a peak wind gust of 58 knots from the northwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Media report of large tree snapped in half near New Carlisle in St. Joseph County in  Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms organized into a squall line and moved eastward into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 15th. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 16th, storms brought all severe hazards to Missouri.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong short wave moved across the region creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across southeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed onto a home and onto power lines around Silsbee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 Call Center reported a landslide near PR-1 and Camino Dolores Cruz, close to Perfect Cleaning Services, affecting mainly a residential area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved through north central and northeast South Dakota late on June 27 into the early morning of June 28, generating isolated pockets of high winds. A personal weather station in northeast Aberdeen and the South Dakota State University mesonet station seven miles south of Claremont both recorded peak wind gusts of 70 mph.

Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across portions of Northwest Louisiana through the month of June, although some improvement to drought was observed during the latter half of the month as widespread 5-10+ inches of rain fell across these areas. While some of the rain was excessive and resulted in flash flooding at times, improvement to soil moisture as well as streamflow was observed across Bossier, Webster, Claiborne, Red River, and Natchitoches Parishes, with ag producers reporting improvement to stock pond levels and greenup of pastures. Beneficial rain continued into the first half of July, with additional improvement to drought conditions observed.

Mostly near to above average precipitation supported steadily improving drought conditions across far southwest Nebraska, especially for Dundy County very early in the month, and by mid to late June for Hitchcock and Red Willow counties. Near to below average precipitation prevailed across portions of Red Willow County where drought persisted the longest. D2 Severe Drought only persisted through the 1st for Dundy County, with D2 Severe Drought to D4 Exceptional Drought persisting through mid to late June for the northeast half of Hitchcock County, and through the entire month for all of Red Willow County. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about two inches over northern Red Willow county, to a whopping ten inches over northwest Hitchcock county. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and three-quarters of an inch over western Dundy county, to about three and one-half inches over eastern Red Willow county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about three inches to just over seven inches (near normal to about four inches above average), highest over far northeast portions of the county. Normal monthly precipitation across the county is near and either side of three inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was observed at State Route 349 and Lake Alma Road, and State Route 160 was closed due to flooding between South Buffalo Street and State Route 324. During the afternoon of the 4th, a vehicle was observed in water up to the windows at the intersection of State Routes 160 and 349.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm and moist air mass moving northward into the region resulted in areas of dense fog before dawn on April 10th. The fog dissipated by mid morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Delaware Coastal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Southwest and south-central Georgia started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.
A coastal low offshore and upper trough combined with deep arctic air led to significant snowfall across the Carolinas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 31 and ended on February 1, ranging from 9 to 11 inches across the zone. Impacts from the storm were limited.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions across Williamson County from April 2026 improved to moderate drought in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced severe hail along the Volusia County coastline.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed a video of penny to quarter size hail from a resident in Port Orange off of Old Sunbeam Dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall drought conditions did not change across northern and eastern Maine during January. Several storms impacted the region during January bringing mostly snow, though a wintry mix and rain did occasionally occur across mostly Downeast areas. The heaviest snows generally occurred across east-central and Downeast portions of the region. Monthly precipitation totals for January generally ranged from 0.50 to 1.50 inches below normal across northern and eastern Maine. However...with frozen ground preventing soil penetration...soil moisture and groundwater was relatively unchanged during the month. Severe ( D2 ) level drought conditions generally remained unchanged from late December. Moderate ( D1 ) level drought conditions persisted across the remainder of the region.

A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hardwood tree branches broken (1-3 inch diameter).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cutoff low moved in from the northwest and pulled deep tropical moisture from the south over the Hawaiian islands. This led to the development of prolonged slow moving heavy rain and thunderstorms. The heavy rain and thunderstorms caused catastrophic flooding over Oahu's North Shore and Manoa Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 800 pm HST, a mesoscale convective system was observed moving over the Kauai Channel towards Oahu. At around 900 pm HST, this mesoscale convective system moved over the west side of Oahu, then the Northern half of Oahu, and began to deliver large amounts of heavy rain. Due to the slow moving nature of this weather system, enormous rain amounts accumulated in a very short time frame. At approximately 1000 pm HST, stream levels rose above flood thresholds and reservoirs filled up. From 1100 pm HST to 200 AM HST, a massive flood wave surged through the North Shore. Multiple roads became impassable across Northern Oahu, Haleiwa became completely cut off, and multiple homes and many cars got swept away in flood waters. Many homes and cars that were not washed away were heavily damaged beyond use or habitation. Businesses were also flooded, and an ambulance was reportedly lost due to the rising flood waters. With the help of police officers, the crew escaped the ambulance through the side window. There were over 200 rescues by first responders and residents, these rescues included rescues from police, fire, national guard, and lifeguards. 10 people were taken to the ER with non critical hypothermia due to prolonged exposure to the flood waters. Much of the destruction and rescues were reported in Waialua and Haleiwa. However the damage spread to the northeast section of Oahu where multiple homes were inundated with flood waters.  Over 171 million dollars in damages were reported across Oahu's public schools from the Department of Education and officials put the total costs of the storm island wide above 1 billion dollars .

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported flooding in the slow lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted southeast Georgia on January 31st, ushering a very cold airmass into the area as deepening low pressure shifted off the Southeast Coast on February 1st. Snow accumulation ended by midnight on January 31st, but very cold wind chill temperatures persisted in wake of the low through morning hours on February 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. A wind chill temperature of 10 degrees or less was ongoing at the Reidsville Municipal Airport at 12 AM EST and first fell to 10 degrees or less at the UGA Weather Network site in Glennville (UGA88) at 130 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing across numerous low-lying country roads in central and southern Effingham County.  Debris from nearby farm fields was washed onto a few roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported tennis ball sized hail in Millston. The report was relayed via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down near the intersection of McCoysville Road and Quarry Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two batches of strong thunderstorms pushed through north Alabama on the 20th, including one during the midday into early afternoon, and another during the late afternoon evening. The storms produced gusty winds and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs were snapped at 1704 McCurdy Loop Road E.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions across much of central Pennsylvania persisted throughout the late fall and early winter months, allowing for severe drought to form across portions of southern and eastern Pennsylvania in January 2026. Multiple counties across central Pennsylvania were put under a Drought Watch by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, with Fulton County being put under a Drought Warning. Multiple instances of voluntary water reductions were put throughout central Pennsylvania, with two boroughs and a township in Schuylkill County put under a mandatory water conservation notice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 (severe) drought conditions began across southern Fulton County on January 13, 2026 with dry conditions continuing through the end of January 2026. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection issued a Drought Warning for Fulton County on January 8th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful upper level storm system that spread eastward from the Intermountain West brought widespread high winds, blowing dust, and a few wildfires on the morning and afternoon of the 17th. Thick high level cloud cover early in the day initially prevented strong winds from developing. However, these clouds began to thin out and clear by late in the morning from west to east. This allowed surface winds to quickly ramp up where clearing occurred. Most observed severe wind gusts were between 58 and 65 mph, however, the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Olton measured a wind gust of 77 mph. These strong winds also lofted copious amounts of dust into the atmosphere which reduced visibility across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle. Observed visibilities dropped as low as one half mile at times. The strong winds and dry conditions also brought favorable wildfire conditions. Several wildfires started across the region with one igniting near Plainview known as the Arbor fire. A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Concho Valley and Northern Edwards Plateau. Also, a lightning strike destroyed a hotel in Brady.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was golf ball size hail reported on County Road 404, south of I-10.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of  west central and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening period, with very large hail and severe winds reported. One supercell produced 3 inch hail in Moorhead, MN. One EF-0 tornado developed with a supercell in Clay County 6 miles northwest of Hawley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree uprooted between West 44th and West 45th street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
High winds impacted much of Montana. However, it was spotty if the high winds made it down to the surface, with a few counties not seeing gusts at or above 58 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reed Point SE gusted to 64 mph. Busteed gusted to 59mph, and Molt S gusted to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems moved over southern California during the mid part of the month of February, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms, strong and gusty winds, and high elevation snow from the 10th thru the 11th, and then again on the 16th thru 18th. This resulted in a few reports of damage due to strong winds from thunderstorms. There were also several reports of flooding/flash flooding due to heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Fire reports a tree went through a roof on dawn drive. Estimated wind gusts in  the area near 50-55 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The time was estimated from radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.
The combination of a strong arctic high pressure system and very dry air resulted in very cold temperatures ranging from zero to 10 degrees above zero on the morning of January 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures ranged form 5 to 10 degrees across Callahan County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees and wires downed in New Albion.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak disturbance within a buoyant environment forced thunderstorms that caused damaging severe winds in Michigan's Upper Peninsula on the 29th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported to have fallen from thunderstorm winds in the Toivola area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brownsville/South Padre Island International Airport  (BRO) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 6 hours from 4:35-10:20am CST on Sunday January 25th. Harlingen/Valley International Airport (HRL) recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 11.5 hours from 11:25pm (Jan 24th) to 10:40am CST January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portion of east-central and northeast Nebraska during March. Monthly precipitation totals were generally 0.5 to 1.5 inches below average.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A D3 (Extreme) drought was introduced across the northeastern portion of the county on March 3. Through the remainder of the month, D3 drought conditions expanded to encompass nearly the entire county. The cooperative observer near Oakdale, Nebraska recorded 0.30 inches of precipitation for the month, which was 1.17 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large storm system moved across the Midwest March 15 to the 16th, initially bringing rain and thunderstorms to the area on the morning of the 15th. This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. Local news reported that most areas schools were closed and several Department of Transportation districts reported snow covered road  ways. Interstate 80 was closed during the night of March 15 west of Iowa City all the way to the Nebraska/Iowa border.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter snowfall reports ranged from 7.5 inches 3 miles north northeast of Clinton to 8.5 inches in Charlotte. Winds begin gusting over 35 MPH at 3 AM when visibilities drop to a 1/2sm with falling and blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated Extreme (D3) to widespread Severe (D2) drought continued across Southwest Arkansas through the first half of June, before tapering back to Severe (D2) drought as appreciable rainfall helped to ease drought conditions. June monthly rainfall totals ranged significantly from 5-10 inches across Southwest Arkansas with isolated lesser amounts in parts of Union County, generally near and northeast of El Dorado. As a result, drought conditions continued to improve throughout the month with the additional rainfall. Despite the improvement, all of this rainfall was not enough to completely erode the severe drought across the vast majority of Southwest Arkansas, which persisted through the end of the month.

A surface low tracking eastward across the Midwest dragged a cold front south into Texas and east toward the Mid-South by the morning of March 11. Delayed arrival of the frontal boundary allowed diurnal instability to increase, interacting with 40 knots of bulk shear. As the front swept swiftly across the region, it triggered severe thunderstorms capable of producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A billboard was damaged along with some downed trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across much of Northeast Texas through the month of June, although some improvement to drought was observed as widespread 3-8+ inches of rain fell across these areas, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 12 inches falling across much of Red River and Western Bowie Counties. While some of the rain was excessive and resulted in flash flooding at times, improvement to soil moisture as well as streamflow was observed across much of Northeast Texas, with ag producers reporting improvement to stock pond levels and greenup of pastures. Beneficial rain continued into the first half of July, with additional improvement to drought conditions observed.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limbs were knocked down onto power  lines at 2657 AL Highway 65. Time was estimated  by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of April 30th, locally induced showers with isolated thunderstorms developed over portions of the interior and north-central PR and steered by southeasterly winds towards the western half. This resulted in urban and small stream flooding, as well as isolated flash flooding, over sectors of interior to western PR including Hormigueros through the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency managers reported flooding along Calle Mirtos in Valle Hermoso Arriba, Hormigueros. They stated that a sewer overflowed, causing problems at one house where water entered the first floor. Based on radar estimates, around 2 inches of rain fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reports trees down along Briar Patch Cemetery Rd and Neal Rd east of Amite City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles were snapped and irrigation pivots flipped by thunderstorm wind gusts near the intersection of 276th Street and 456th Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid air to the south of a warm frontal boundary spawned heavy rain producing thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Storms repeatedly moving over the same regions produced pockets of 3 to 4 inches of rain which triggered areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Officials reported that Kellogg Road had to be closed due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of June saw overall above normal temperatures and a mixed bag of precipitation with some areas seeing above normal precipitation and others below normal precipitation. This is very reflective of the early summer thunderstorm activity that saw daily rounds of thunderstorms pass over some areas repeatedly, while missing other areas entirely. As a result, most of New Mexico saw no change in drought conditions while around a quarter to a third of the state saw either a 1 class degradation or improvement in drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought persisted over the far western and far eastern portions of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: House roof damaged along County Route 64, east of Township Road 96, on the southwest side of Upper Sandusky.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photos shared via social media showed downed power poles and trees in Bonfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The incredible stretch of severe weather continued on Wednesday June 10th with more severe storms and a few small tornadoes across Dickinson county.  The storms also dumped  more flooding rains across parts of Kansas that were already saturated from days of torrential rainfall.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain across portions of Pickett and Fentress counties on June 28, 2026. An estimated five to seven inches fell across the area from Byrdstown to Jamestown which caused flash flooding. The Wolf River near Byrdstown crested to 15.29 inches, the second highest crest of record. Roadways along the river and nearby creeks were inundated with water and rendered impassable. One home in Byrdstown also reported being inundated with water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 5 to 7 inches of rain in the Jamestown area caused flash flooding. Portions of Lawson Street along Rockcastle Creek in Jamestown were inundated with water and impassable. Damages are unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Wilmington Air Park (KILN).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.

Behind the northward retreat of a warm front, a cluster of showers moved along and just ahead of a cold front from Virginia into northwest North Carolina during the evening hours. These showers deepened and led to growing clusters of storms, along with one sustained supercell that brought a swath of large hail (0.75 to 1.25) and sporadic power outages and downed trees to the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One hundred power outages from trees down on power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in a wildfire developing across northeast Florida. High dispersions and gusty winds at the end of March especially assisted in the spreading of the new wildfire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 23rd, Alachua County Sheriff's Office reported that a small brush fire that ignited near S County Road 325 near Cross Creek. This fire quickly grew in size to 134 acres by the end of the month thanks to very favorable fire weather conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of far northern Illinois during the evening of April 14th producing large hail, wind damage.  Flash flooding also occurred in parts of the Chicago metro area.
A front moving through brought a squall line through western Massachusetts and into central Massachusetts producing pockets of damaging winds which downed several trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Greenfield, a tree was downed at the intersection of Meridian St. and Colorado Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds caused by pressure differences in the wake of showers and thunderstorms gusted up to 77 mph in Milwaukee. Numerous trees were downed along with structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 77 mph at General Mitchell International Airport. The city of Milwaukee received more than 200 calls for downed trees and branches. Many reports of trees landing on homes, vehicles, and roads. Similar reports also in the suburbs of Milwaukee County. More than 50 percent of the roof torn off a warehouse building in the Port of Milwaukee.  Approximately 51,000 We Energies customers were without power due to downed powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For far western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. Along and east of I-95, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued to burn into June. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May helped the final containment of local ongoing wildfires in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 18th of April, the Pineland Road fire ignited over southern Clinch County, rapidly growing to 2500 acres and into Echols county by the 19th of April due to favorable conditions. Per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC), the fire was 98% contained on June 3rd. The fire became 100% contained on June 10th.  The estimated total cost of the wildfire was around $14-15 million.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms produced isolated large hail and localized flash flooding across the eastern half of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size and slightly larger hail with the 1st round, then the second round was about  dime size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front moved across the area during the evening hours of January 15th. Strong winds continued overnight and into the following day. Numerous power outages, damages, and road closures were reported with the abnormally strong northwest winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 75 MPH was observed at the KSNY sensor at 6:48 PM MST on 1/15. Multiple sensors across the county recorded strong wind gusts over 60 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid and upper level jet at the base of a disturbance over the western U.S. moved over New Mexico during the day April 26th. Deep daytime mixing tapped into these stronger winds aloft by mid morning resulting in strong to high wind gusts across much of central and eastern New Mexico. Very dry antecedent conditions resulted in areas of blowing dust and reduced visibility across central and southern NM. Some showers were observed across northwest and north central New Mexico with one of these showers resulting in a brief 59 mph wind gust at Gallup Municipal Airport. Winds tapered off during the late evening and overnight hours as stronger winds aloft slowly exited east of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station near Dora measured high wind gusts up to 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms moved eastward into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening as they organized into a squall line. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down power poles southeast of Bixby.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1 inch in diameter near Lincoln, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the last two days of June, a favorable synoptic weather pattern brought extreme heat to western Wisconsin as ample moisture resulted in remarkably high dewpoints. Consequently, heat indices soared well above 100 degrees with numerous locations seeing heat indices of 105 to 115 degrees. June 29th was the hottest day, but extreme heat persisted into the 30th for areas south of Interstate 90 where heat indices in excess of 100 degrees were still common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme heat moved into the region during the end of June with widespread heat indices over 100 degrees. On June 29th, heat indices ranged from 105 to 112 degrees across the county during the afternoon and early evening. The highest heat index observed in the county was 112 degrees in Soldiers Grove. On June 30th, continued heat indices over 100 degrees persisted throughout much of the daytime hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado first touched down west of Bryant Hill Road and moved|through a large pecan orchard snapping and uprooting numerous|trees.  The tornado moved across Bryant Hill Road and very rapidly reached max intensity as it approached Sleepy Hollow Road.  JGX radar data also confirms the presence of very strong velocities in the area near Sleepy Hollow Road as well.  The|tornado struck a mobile home community on the west side of Sleepy Hollow Road destroying 4 mobile homes, overturning a home and damaging several others.  One of the residents of a home was thrown approximately 40 feet from one of the destroyed homes.  In another home, there were 2 injuries as a result of the home being|flipped over and destroyed.  The overturned mobile home remained intact, however the anchors which were concreted into the ground were pulled out of the ground and hanging from the frame.  Numerous trees nearby the community and across the street were snapped.  The combination of the damage to the mobile homes and the scope of the tree damage nearby are consistent with high end EF1 to low end EF2 and the basis of the low end EF2 rating for this storm.  The tornado continued east toward Hwy 49 snapping and uprooting trees.  Two large silos had their tops ripped off with bricks and debris strewn all around the area near the silos.  The tornado crossed Hwy 49 snapping and uprooting trees in a pecan orchard and flipping 3 sections of a center pivot.  As|the storm continued east, a weakening trend was noted both on radar and the corresponding damage on the ground with mostly sporadic tree damage across Vegetable Road, County Rd 123 and County road 116.  The tornado lifted north of Juice plant road just east of County Road 116.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size about one-mile northwest of Barberton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree snapped and fell onto a truck destroying the vehicle in Green Cove Springs. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens.

A dry spring continued across Middle Tennessee during April 2026. Precipitation amounts were generally 3 to 5 inches across with most of this rain recorded during the last week of the month. While these rain amounts were higher compared to the past couple months, it was still below normal for the month. Drought conditions worsened through the month of April. By the end of the month, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least severe drought with about 38 percent of this classified as extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Abnormally dry to moderate drought conditions from March 2026 worsened in April with severe drought conditions developing across Grundy County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong low pressure area swung through southern Virginia, dragging a cold front across Eastern NC by the evening hours. Ahead of it, bands of thunderstorms formed in the afternoon due to unstable conditions and wind shear in place. Scattered severe wind gusts embedded in some of the storms produced wind damage across the area. There were also several reports of hail up to nickel size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tideland EMC reports over 770 outages along and off of Florence Rd due to trees and  powerlines down damaging equipment.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system for mid-June brought two rounds of thunderstorm on Wednesday June 17th. The strongest round of storms occurred during the morning hours that brough damaging winds (some significant), heavy rain, and two EF-1 tornadoes in Illinois which occurred in Monmouth and Warsaw. |Many trees fell and power lines were damaged, along with several reports of flash flooding. There were also 4-5 train cars that were pushed off the railroad just south of Monmouth, IL in Warren County due to significant straight-line winds (estimated near 100 mph). Additional train cars derailed as a result of these cars being blown off.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief EF1 tornado uniquely tracked across three states. This developed just inside Lee County, Iowa, with peak winds of 105 mph, and tracked southeast through Clark County, Missouri. It then continued across the Mississippi River into Hancock County, Illinois, impacting northern parts of Warsaw damaging primarily trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front advancing northward over cold ground helped cause widespread fog to form late on March 7th and early on March 8th. The fog dissipated by mid morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Wilmington Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four trees were blown down along Columbia Ave and the roof of a trailer was damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down in the 5600 block of West Falls Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees across Rohrerstown and Millersville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began along Highway 43 in Mount Pleasant. Many trees were uprooted or had broken limbs along the highway and Interstate. A few homes and barns had metal roofing blown off. The tornado continued northeast into Columbia, impacting neighborhoods and Columbia State Community College. Tree damage was noted frequently. Structural damage to homes was also noted, mainly to vinyl siding, shingles, and metal fascia. There was one building on Columbia State Community College that sustained roof damage as well as fencing on the ball fields. Next in the damage path was an industrial area along the Duck River. Many trees were uprooted, snapped, or sustained many broken branches. Several buildings lost metal roofing, and one larger metal building system had a portion of the south facing wall caved in. The tornado then moved back into residential areas, causing occasional trees down or branches broken, shingle damage, and damage to vinyl siding. The tornado ended along Green Mills Road in northern Maury County, just prior to reaching Spring Hill. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station measured a wind gust to 65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.

A strong upper level low pressure system passed through the Pacific Northwest and over the Northern Rockies into the Northern Plains. This system brought heavy snow primarily to the southern half of North Dakota, with the heaviest snow generally south of Interstate 94. The greatest snow amount reported was 16 inches at Napoleon in Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Haynes received seven inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting the eastern West Virginia panhandle during the late afternoon hours with damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree blew down in the 1400 block of Shepherd Grade Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low-level flow ahead of an eastward advancing front combined with scattered showers to produce sporadic high winds across southeast South Dakota on May 14.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 45 mph at times, with gusts as high as 59 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Tripp.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved along the US Highway 54 corridor during the late evening of March 10th. Damaging winds occurred along this line of storms with damage to trees and structures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed off of south Marvin Road in Versailles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several inches of water covered a portion of Circular Street in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to Zero to 15 below zero across much of VT with wind chill temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero across much of VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures around 5 to 15 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 15 to 25 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Great Lakes region, producing strong thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power poles were downed across State Route 274.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed utility poles between Hartmann Drive and Hunters Village Drive in Lebanon. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The incredible stretch of severe weather continued on Wednesday June 10th with more severe storms and a few small tornadoes across Dickinson county.  The storms also dumped  more flooding rains across parts of Kansas that were already saturated from days of torrential rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread flooding occurring on roadways throughout Wamego.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow but heavy band of snow focused along the Interstate 94 corridor between the cities of Madison and Milwaukee on the evening of January 16. Periods of 0.5 to 1.0+ inch per hour snowfall rates within the snow band resulted in generally 2 to 5 inches of accumulation in locations impacted by the snow band. A few locally higher totals approaching 6 inches were reported in western portions of Milwaukee County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 2 to 4 inches of accumulation observed countywide, with locally higher totals over 5 inches in western portions of the county. Highest accumulation of 6.3 inches observed in Wauwatosa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Great Lakes region, producing strong thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power poles were downed onto Boundary Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across South-Central Texas on the evening of May 10, encountering an unstable airmass and producing a line of strong to severe storms with damaging wind gusts and some severe hail. Most of the  observed wind damage occurred in the Austin area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 56 kt gust was recorded by the ASOS at Austin-Bergstrom International Airport from a line of severe thunderstorms.
