After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pulaski County dispatch reported multiple trees blown down along KY-192 near the Ruth community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The breakdown of an upper-level ridge brought increased wind speeds aloft. These winds mixed to the surface along the Rocky Mountain Front on the morning of the 16th, spreading out to mainly the North-Central plains by the afternoon. The peak winds occurred on the morning of the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station GW0718 Joplin 25nnw measured a 70 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storm systems continued to bring rain to Northwest California in early January. Persistent south winds resulted in over 1.5 feet of storm surge along the coast resulting in inundation of many homes in the King Salmon area. The south winds also caused isolated power outages and a few downed trees. Flooding was generally restricted to the typical flooding locations around Humboldt Bay.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down blocking Highway 254 in the Myers Flat area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts across Lake Erie.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station FAI01 - Fairport Harbor Lighthouse.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms develop during the afternoon hours across northwest MN, with reports of severe hail and several reports of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photos received of multiple 2 inch hailstones, with many more around a golf ball in size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions were in place across most if not all of Martin, Pitt, Greene, Lenoir, and Duplin Counties through the entire month of June according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Lenoir County through mid June with Extreme Drought conditions noted from June sixteenth onwards to the end of June across the entire County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected portions of Hancock and Pearl River Counties from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video of an overflowing Bayou La Terre near Kiln Delisle Rd with water just below the  bridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power lines were reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Little to no rainfall and a mixture of heat followed by cold and generally dry weather, including a hard freeze toward the end of January combined to steadily worsen drought conditions across northern Hidalgo, Jim Hogg, Brooks, Starr, and Zapata County.  Coverage of Extreme Drought increased to more than 70% of these areas by the 13th, which continued through month's end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: By mid month, Extreme (D3) Drought conditions expanded southeastward to encompass much of Brooks County with the exception of the southeastern part of the county, which remained under Severe (D2) Drought. These conditions of D2 Drought over the southeastern parts of the county and D3 Drought over much of Brooks County remained in place through the remainder of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bowman Airport AWOS reported wind gusts up to 69 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Bedford Airport ASOS (KBED) blizzard conditions occurred from 6:30 AM EST to 9:45 AM EST. The highest gust was 49 mph at 1051 AM EST. Generally 8 to 12 inches of snow fell. The highest amount was 17 inches in Concord.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 1700 residents were without power due to tree damage. There were several concentrated areas of outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Northeastern New Jersey. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Northeastern New Jersey with blizzard conditions across the eastern zones.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Northeastern New Jersey. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A heavy snowfall of mainly 15 to 24 inches fell with near blizzard conditions occurring at times across the zone. Trained spotters reported 15.2 inches in Fair Lawn before the accumulating snow ended, and 17.9 inches at 1 WSW Wallington. A cocorahs observer reported 17.0 inches in Fair Lawn also before the accumulating snow ended.  Their were numerous public reports around and just above 20 inches across the zone with 2 NW Ramsey reporting 20.1 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of snow and sleet during this event, producing 4 to 8 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (8 inches) was reported near Shawnee. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant snowstorm struck portions of East Tennessee at the end of the month, thanks to strong lift from a deep upper trough diving from north to south. A couple of long term cooperative weather stations saw top 10 snowfalls during this storm. This storm led to 3 confirmed fatalities in East Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow was observed in Roane County, with 3.5 inches of snow measured in Kingston and 2.5 inches of snow measured in the town of Rockwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.
Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Gunnison Ridge mesonet station recorded an initial peak wind gust of 73 mph, followed by an additional gust of 59 mph, as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed southeast through the region during the day, starting near daybreak. Snow quickly tapered off from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and was banded in nature within the northwest-southeast axis.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS employee 2 miles west of Bellbrook measured 3 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Prolonged drought, very dry fuels due to recent cold weather, and a lack of recent wetting rainfall contributed to fire weather conditions capable of supporting rapid fire spread during the month of February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Boundary Rd Fire reached 2173 acres on February 11, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down along Ancil Cox Road on the southwest side of Centreville near Griffin Lane. A few trees were downed here, with at least one of them taking down a powerline. The tornado tracked northeast, generally paralleling Ancil Cox Road until reaching the intersection with Old Highway 33. The most significant damage occurred near this intersection, where approximately a dozen trees were uprooted or snapped which supports the 90 mph wind rating. Beyond this point, the tornado continued northeastward producing sporadic tree and limb damage along its path. The final accessible point of the tornado���s track was near Centerville Academy. Minor damage was observed on campus, including a downed light pole, partial roof uplift on a metal building, and a baseball pitching backstop that was thrown approximately 250 feet into a chain-link fence. The tornado continued northeast beyond Lower Centreville Rd where additional minor tree damage was identified. The tornado evidently lifted over inaccessible areas to the survey team prior to reaching Hwy 48.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing damaging winds and some hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported that multiple trees were downed, and various sheds were overturned or blown away in El Campo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.

Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds partially tore the roof off of the Salon Estellar in Barry County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving thunderstorm cluster impacted portions of western-north Texas during the predawn to mid-morning hours on the 7th. Combined with rich boundary layer moisture and occasional back-building convection, scattered instances of flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dispatch reported roadways closed and high-water rescues due to flooding in Wichita Falls. The location and event time are approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from pea to quarter size covered the ground on the south side of Tyler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving and narrow snow band brought remarkably heavy snowfall rates to much of northeast Iowa during the late evening hours on February 19th through the morning on February 20th. Some locations likely received snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the overnight hours with the highest totals being in a narrow band through portions of Floyd, Chickasaw, Winneshiek, Fayette and Allamakee counties where 12 to 16 inches of snow fell. Widespread totals in excess of 6 inches were noted across much of northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This snow band brought heavy snow to Allamakee County with snowfall totals ranging from 8 to 13 inches. The highest reported snowfall total in the county was in Waukon where 13 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the early to mid afternoon of March 1st, north of a warm front as an upper level disturbance approached the region. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to quarter size.

On March 26, 2026, a potent cold front tracked across central Indiana, interacting with a warm and unstable airmass to trigger severe storms.  Severe thunderstorms developed rapidly, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across northern central Indiana that downed trees and power lines, leading to over 1,700 power outages as residents dealt with the abrupt onset of hazardous weather.||Significant structural damage was observed, including a destroyed pole barn and a garage roof failure in Clinton County. While the environment supported supercellular rotation and prompted numerous tornado warnings, the only severe modes were straight-line damaging winds and large hail, with reports of 1.5-inch hail in Veedersburg. The convective activity gradually weakened as it progressed south of the I-70 corridor and encountered a more stable airmass, effectively concluding the active weather event for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A pole barn and trees were damaged by thunderstorm wind gusts. Nearby a garage roof was blown off and a fence was blown down. Numerous pictures showed visibility greatly reduced by dust from the strong winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.
A small area of low pressure along a strong cold front lead to strong thunderstorm winds in Northeast South Carolina, Southeast North Carolina, and the adjacent coastal waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reports several trees down in the western part of the county. One tree also fell on a car on US Highway 177 S.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough lifted northeast from the Ohio Valley into the lower Great Lakes during the evening of June 9, 2026 through the early morning hours of June 10, 2026. Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a nearly stationary front in southern lower Michigan and intensified across northern Ohio with the approach of the shortwave late in the evening. Thunderstorms with intense rainfall rates slowly moved east across Sandusky County, Ohio with PWAT values near 2 inches and weak deep layer shear. Total rainfall amounts of 2.5 to 4 inches fell across Sandusky County, Ohio over a two to three hour period, with instantaneous rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding closed multiple roads due to creeks/streams overflowing their banks and flowing across the roadways. Locations include CR-260 at Pickerel Creek and US-6 between CR-260 and CR-268.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper level storm moved into the western U.S. early on February 17th with a lead disturbance moving over the Four Corners and Intermountain West. Strong mid and upper level winds at the base of this shortwave moved over New Mexico during this time. The Pacific cold front associated with this disturbance moved across the state during the morning hours of the day resulting in brief high wind gusts at several sites along and west of the central mountain chain coinciding with a period of rain and snow west of the Rio Grande Valley and the north central mountains. A peak gust of 84 mph was measured at Kachina Peak within the Taos Ski Valley, while two reports of downed trees with one knocking out a power line came in from Ruidoso. Subsidence behind the cold front allowed stronger winds aloft to translate down the surface resulting in an extended period of high winds along and east of the central mountain chain. High winds tapered off during the late afternoon and evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The RAWS station at Mills Canyon measured a brief high wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A subtle mid-level shortwave trough began to traverse the Mid-South in the late morning hours. A combination of adequate daytime heating, surface dewpoints in the low 60s, around 1200 J/kg of SBCAPE, about 35 kts of effective shear, and elevated surface and mid-level lapse rates was in place heading into the afternoon hours. This translated into an environment that was conducive for rapid convective development capable of producing damaging winds and large hail up to 2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were reported down in the South Fulton area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report and photos of a large tree trunk snapped. Wind gust estimated from radar data, nearby observations and damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May 2026 was a month of dramatic, high-stakes climatic shifts for North Mississippi. The month began with the region locked in the grip of a multi-season moisture deficit that peaked in intensity by mid-month. For the first few weeks, an aggressive early-summer evaporation engine baked the region's topsoil, threatening to derail the spring planting season entirely.||However, the final third of the month brought a significant and much-needed atmospheric pattern shift. A series of massive storm complexes pushed heavy convective rainfall across the Deep South, breaking the multi-month dry spell. While these late-May deluges stabilized crashing topsoil moisture, climatologists quickly warned that the rain fell too fast to fully heal the deeply depleted subsoil and groundwater reserves.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions persisted across portions of the county through the entire month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface boundary kicked off a marginal line of thunderstorms that produced sporadic wind damage across central and eastern MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Norfolk, wires were down on Cleveland St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep surface low pressure over the Northern Plains caused high winds across western Nebraska during the morning hours into the afternoon hours on March 12th. Strong westerly winds as high as 40 to 50 mph with gusts near 70 mph occurred. The highest wind gust recorded was 69 mph at a mesonet site near Lewellen.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Westerly winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts around 60 mph occurred across eastern Cherry County during the late morning hours into the evening hours. The Valentine ASOS  recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph at 450 pm CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down along Tidewater Trail near Occupacia Road and Hunters Hill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front was accompanied by a narrow band of heavier squalls embedded within a larger area of light to moderate stratiform rain. These squalls resulted in several gale-force wind gusts as the front crossed the waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 36 knots (41 MPH) was measured by the Saunders Point Light WeatherFlow sensor (XMTR).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme thunderstorm rainfall up to 5.00-6.00 inches in under 4 hours from east of Sullivan to south of Bloomfield, produced flash flooding in Linton, Lyons and Switz City.  In Linton, vehicles stalled out, a child swept away by water was rescued, and railroad ties floated through town.  Additionally, a culvert was washed out in Greene County on County Road 475 West, while Indiana Route 54 was flooded out in Sullivan County east of Sullivan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening hours of the 10th and early morning hours of the 11th, ahead of a dry line to the west and a cold front to the north, as an upper level disturbance moved into the area. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind damaged outbuildings and rolled over horse trailers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms dropped southeast into southern middle Tennessee and north Alabama during the afternoon and early evening hours.  Damaging winds were reported in northwest Alabama including the Shoals metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees own along CR 24 near St. Florian near the railroad tracks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second of three winter storms moved in on the morning of February 18th and departed quickly on the night of February 18th.  This was a colder storm with more snow than the previous one, however, the bigger impact was the high winds.  This storm caused near blizzard conditions at times as well as blowing and drifting snow and lower snowfall amounts than expected.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 63 mph was measured at the I-40 @ Lupton DOT Site (AZT07).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold Warning Criteria (Wind chills at or below 15F) was reached Baffin Bay (Texas Coastal Ocean Observation Network, TCOON) at around 5 AM, continuing through 9 AM.  Values bottomed out at 13F around 9 AM at the site, on the Kenedy/Kleberg County line.  Slightly lower durations were noted at TCOON Rincon del San Jose (6 to 9 AM). Proxy observations with Falfurrias/Brooks Co. Airport suggested the duration, with likely low values between 13 and 15F from Armstrong to Sarita.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed over the upper Ohio Valley along a passing cold front on the afternoon of January 14th. As temperatures cooled across the Western and north Central New York areas, rain mixed with and then changed to snow. Snow continued across much of the Buffalo forecast area through the day on Thursday January 15th as the surface low tracked from Northwestern Pennsylvania to Central New York. Cold air filtering into the region, along with mid-level troughs over the region helped increase lake enhancement off of both Lake Erie and Ontario. The snow finally tapered off later in the day on January 15th as drier air and a ridge built into the region. While snowfall amounts weren't overly impressive by Buffalo standards, the widespread nature of the snowfall did cause more disruptions to daily activities than snow from a lake effect event with similar amounts. ||While most snowfall ranged from six to ten inches across most of the Buffalo forecast area, there were some larger amounts closer to the foot and a half to two foot mark where lake enhancement really increased snow rates. Notable snowfall amounts from around the Buffalo forecast area include: 21.6 inches in Eden, 17.0 inches in North Boston, 16.0 inches in West Falls, 16.0 inches in Newfane, 13.3 inches in North Tonawanda, 12.1 inches in Lockport, 9.5 inches in Perrysburg, 9.4 inches in Mexico, 9.0 inches in Hamlin and 9.0 inches in Cassadaga.

A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at Tobacco Road and Lamont Norwood Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of substantial rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of June with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across Metro Miami-Dade County in the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A picture of a hailstone compared with a quarter was received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large tree branches were downed in and near Garfield Park. A small tree was also uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto power lines along Ashton Upton Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Deputy reported wind gusts up to 60 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front from the northwest maintained their strength to deliver damaging wind gusts resulting in downed trees and power lines across southeast West Virginia. In spite of the early morning hours, there was Effective Bulk Shear of 30-40 kts and a few hundred MLCAPE to keep the system alive. These storms dissipated after crossing the Appalachian mountains and encountering relatively stable air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down blocking one lane of traffic near the intersection of New Hope and Surface Hill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.10 inches across the month of February. This maintained D2 conditions across portions of Randolph county with D3 conditions in the far northwest. These drought conditions continued into at least March 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree was blown down along Peeled Chestnut Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal moisture ahead of a strong cold front that pushed southward across the western Colorado Divide resulted in light to moderate snowfall accumulations across the western Colorado mountains along the Divide with locally heavier accumulations and rates. Better snowfall accumulations and impacts occurred above 9000 feet with some gusty winds to 50 mph at higher elevations along the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 3 to 6 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts of 12 to 15 inches of snow at Upper San Juan and Wolf Creek Summit on the eastern portions of the Southwest San Juan Mountains. Wind gusts were in the 45 to 50 mph towards the latter portion of the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills at or below zero were observed across Hunt County between January 24th and January 27th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 45 mph with Newark ASOS reporting a 54 mph gust at 3:07 am, and Bayonne mesonet reporting a 53 mph gust at 2:47 am, and JFK ASOS reporting a 62 mph gust at 5:17 am; and frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at surrounding ASOS stations. The college of Staten Island NYSM station reported a 58 mph gust at 1:05 am. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged from mainly 21 to 29 inches across the zone via mainly public reports, along with a Cocorahs report.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTBZH Bozeman Pass measured a 62 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the day on June 6, 2026, a shortwave moved across Lake Erie into Northwestern Pennsylvania. The region had ample warm air advection through the majority of the morning as temperatures and dew points reached into the upper 70s and mid 60s, respectively. ML CAPE rose to around 1000 J/kg and with effective shear of around 30 knots allowed for thunderstorms to generate severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of trees down on Adamsville Road near Pickasaw Lane southeast of Conneaut Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Neshoba County decreased from D1 (Moderate Drought) to D0 (Abnormally Dry) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite episodic rounds of precipitation throughout the month, above-normal temperatures and prolonged stretches of mostly dry weather continued to maintain severe (or worse) drought conditions across portions of northern, central and western Oklahoma.

During the morning of the 8th, a shortwave and upper-level jet max began to move over west Texas and southeast New Mexico while a surface cyclone strengthened over the Oklahoma Panhandle. As the jet max moved overhead, very strong to high winds developed in the higher terrain (namely the Guadalupe and Davis Mountains), as well as the surrounding foothills. Gusts up to 80-90 mph were observed in the Guadalupe Mountains and at Carlsbad Caverns National Park.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station 164 Carlsbad Caverns NP measured numerous high wind gusts, including a gust to 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between large air masses funneled strong and severe winds through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple observations in Petroleum County recorded wind gusts in excess of 57 mph, the strongest of which was 65 mph, measured at the War Horse NW Montana Climate Office mesonet site (WRHM8).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. Water levels on Lake Springfield were below normal. However, well above normal precipitation occurred during March. The official observation for Springfield measured 7.15 inches of precipitation, which was 4.04 inches above normal.  By mid-March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Sangamon County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass persisted across eastern New York during the early morning hours on February 2, 2026. The combination of cold temperatures and a lingering breeze resulted in some wind chill values (or feels-like temperatures) to reach 10 to 25 degrees below zero, though coverage was not as widespread as previous days.

On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 81 mph along with tree branches (6 to 8 inches in diameter) down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent enhanced westerly flow with multiple embedded shortwave troughs brought multiple instances of severe wind gusts and hail to northern Utah as well as flash flooding to Sevier county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station VRH Vernon Hill recorded a thunderstorm wind gust to 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal system brought widespread light to moderate snowfall accumulations to the area. Total snowfall amounts ranged from a light coating to 1 near the coast to 1-4 farther inland. Temperatures near freezing during daytime snowfall fell well below freezing overnight, resulting in slippery road conditions in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 1-3. The highest reported amount was 3.5 in Pitman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) interacted with a sheared and unstable environment to produce numerous supercells in southeast Illinois on June 21st.  13 tornadoes were documented, the strongest being two EF-2 tornadoes near Newton.  Storms training over the same areas led to widespread heavy rainfall and several occurrences of flash flooding.
A coastal low offshore and upper trough combined with deep arctic air led to significant snowfall across the Carolinas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 30 and ended on February 1, ranging from 5 to 9 inches across the county. Government offices closed day after the storm with remote learning at county schools. Impacts from the storm were limited.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees blew down in Prince George's County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact short-wave within northwest flow aloft moved across the Northern Plains late February 27 into February 28. Mid-level frontogenesis and sufficient moisture resulted in a narrow band of light to moderate snow mainly along and north of a De Smet, SD to Windom, MN line. These areas received 1-5 inches of snow. Winds were light during the snowfall, limiting blowing and drifting.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 4.7 inches 6.5 miles north-northwest of Brookings, 4.0 inches 2.2 miles south-southeast of Astoria and 1.6 miles south of Brookings, and 3.8 inches in Aurora.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong trough of low pressure over the Pacific Northwest brought high gradient winds to  Inyo County and the deserts of southeastern California.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained wind of 40mph+ was also observed for an extended period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active weather pattern brought rounds of rain, mountain snow and gusty southerly winds from January 1st through January 5th. There were numerous flooding reports from moderate to heavy rain, along with some reports of mud and rock slides in the foothills. Ski resorts, Caltrans and the UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 1 to 4 feet of heavy snow in the mountains. There was one fatality of a hiker who had gone missing with these storms. Gusty southerly winds of 35 to 50 mph were also observed at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sacramento Metropolitan Fire rescued a drive who got stuck driving through two feet of water in the roadway at Kiefer Boulevard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Daytime heating combined with mid level moisture under an upper high over New Mexico resulted in high based showers and storms across the higher terrain and nearby lower elevations across central New Mexico during the afternoon and early evening hours on May 24th. One decaying thunderstorm resulted in a severe wind gust at Raton Crews Municipal Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A decaying thunderstorm resulted in a 58 mph wind gust at Raton Crews Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall and snowmelt resulted in flooding across the south-central U.P.  Many roads were flooded and several closed.  The flooding also caused damage at the Escanaba Airport (KESC) due to standing water on the runways and power failure. Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th for Menominee and Marquette counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Road Commission reported that water over the road caused County Road 577 in Vulcan to be closed on the 15th. Video on social media showed a railroad track washout near Sagola on the 17th. Damage estimates were minimal and considered part of routine maintenance.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 9, 2026, scattered thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across portions of eastern Nebraska. A warm, unstable air mass fueled the activity as a surface low deepened and moved eastward into the state. Storms initially developed in central Nebraska before tracking east-northeastward, with peak wind gusts measured between 59 and 70 mph across Boone, Antelope, Butler, and Wayne counties. Storm intensity gradually diminished as the system moved northeastward into the late evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 67 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level disturbance moving through the region brought strong winds aloft. These stronger winds were able to mix down to the surface mostly along the Rocky Mountain Front, with isolated strong winds across the North-Central MT plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTM73 Ledger N Mda measured a 61 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Areas of dense fog developed overnight from near Poplar Bluff to Cape Girardeau under clear skies and calm winds. Towards sunrise, southerly winds picked up in the warm sector and advection fog spread across Southeast Missouri through mid-morning as dew points surged to over 50 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry system brought light to moderate snowfall to portions of the region along and especially north and west of I-95. Generally a widespread 1-4 of snowfall occurred in this area between the morning and early afternoon hours, though some localized higher amounts were reported near and north of I-78. Snowfall rates of 0.5-1 per hour caused some travel disruptions to the area. Brief snowfall changed to rain with limited accumulations southeast of I-95.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another shortwave crossed Wyoming and brought another round of strong to severe thunderstorms, primarily impacting Natrona County but also portions of Fremont and Park County. A line of thunderstorms moved through Fremont and Natrona Counties bringing high wind. The highest wind gust reported was 67 mph at Scenic Drive on the south side of Casper. North of Jeffrey City, there was a brief QLCS tornado. The tornado remained over open country and caused no known damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail to the size of baseballs was reported in a mainly rural area. A few homes and vehicles  suffered damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact short-wave within northwest flow aloft moved across the Northern Plains late February 27 into February 28. Mid-level frontogenesis and sufficient moisture resulted in a narrow band of light to moderate snow mainly along and north of a De Smet, SD to Windom, MN line. These areas received 1-4 inches of snow, with a few locations exceeding 5 inches. Winds were light during the snowfall, limiting blowing and drifting.
