EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Marine Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the bays and gulf waters. A waterspout was also sighted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public report of a brief water spout about a mile out from 52nd Street over the Gulf.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surge of Arctic air invaded Southwest Arkansas during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across Southwest Arkansas from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.

The dryline pushed west towards the Rio Grande Valley and a subtle upper level disturbance in southwest flow helped to trigger severe thunderstorms with strong winds and heavy rain. Almost 2 inches of rain was reported with some of these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video showed significant arroyo flooding in Picacho Hills which impacted a horse farm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Treutlen County remained under D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on November 4, 2025, the county experienced a very brief period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in late January. By the end of February, conditions intensified to D3.  In total, the county sustained 18 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry system brought light to moderate snowfall to portions of the region along and especially north and west of I-95. Generally a widespread 1-4 of snowfall occurred in this area between the morning and early afternoon hours, though some localized higher amounts were reported near and north of I-78. Snowfall rates of 0.5-1 per hour caused some travel disruptions to the area. Brief snowfall changed to rain with limited accumulations southeast of I-95.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 3-4. The highest reported amount was 4.5 in Milford Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Springfield-Beckley Airport (KSGH).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds caused numerous downed trees and powerlines, which caused about 3,000 customers to lose power in Wilson County. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 3 to 6 inches of snow fell across the area with 6.3 inches reported at Basalt 5.8 E. Winds gusted in the 25 to 35 mph range at the onset with a peak wind gust of 37 mph at Eagle County Regional Airport with a visibility of 0 miles due to a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees down with estimated wind of 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions under high pressure led to a typical summertime environment capable of supporting strong pulse-type thunderstorms and dangerous lightning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dorchester County Emergency Management reported a house struck by lightning and smoking in the 100 Block of Curico Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level trough dragged a cold front through the Mid-Atlantic and brought scattered thunderstorms to the forecast area. Inverted V-profiles in the weather sounding and high DCAPE values (>1000 J/kg) supported conditions favorable for damaging wind gusts in the form of wet microbursts with these storms. Severe weather potential was limited due to lackluster dew points and absence of wind shear. Nevertheless, several trees were reported down with almost half of them in Buckingham County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While the main thunderstorm was not close to the event, outflow gusts from a thunderstorm along the NC/VA border are suspected of blowing down a large tree branch in the community of Turbeville. This branch smashed through a windshield of SUV travelling on US 58 between Wilkins Road and Turbeville Road. The driver of the SUV did not sustain any injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall amounts that occurred were 2.1 inches to the north-northwest of Farnsworth and an estimated three inches around Perryton. Then than two inches occurred in the western part of the county. A few high amounts may have occurred closer to the Lipscomb county line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, above normal precipitation occurred across the region during March. By late March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Mason County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed north of a warm front during the afternoon hours on Sunday (5/17).  The strongest storms produced hail up to penny size and damaging winds across east-central Wisconsin, causing over $100,000 worth of damage in Two Rivers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged a barn near Shoto. The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado occurred about one mile northeast of Iantha, Missouri. The tornado overturned portions of irrigation pivots and destroyed an outbuilding. Roofing components from the outbuilding were spread over one mile a way. Several power poles were broken as well. Tree limbs were also downed by the tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down at 29th and Roanoke.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought persisted in January and continued into February.

Severe storms triggered by a potent weather system swept through far southeastern Kansas, bringing destructive winds and large hail. These storms were part of a 15-hour severe weather outbreak that impacted central and eastern Kansas finally moving into Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF1 Tornado with estimated wind speeds of 105 mph touched down near the northeast portion of Hallowell before tracking 4.37 miles to the east. The tornado uprooted or snapped several trees, overturned several empty railcars, caused significant damaged to several grain bins, destroyed multiple outbuildings and snapped or broke numerous power poles and downed power lines.  The tornado track ended approximately 1.25 miles east of Sherwin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure passing through Ontario dragged a strong cold front west to east across the region in the afternoon hours. Boundary orthogonal bands of snow squalls developed ahead of the front with steep low level lapse rates and non-zero surface-based CAPE. The result was a widespread area of snow bands reducing visibility to a quarter mile or less with gusty wind greater than 35 mph and rapid accumulation on roadways resulting in at least one highway accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS report of whiteout conditions with zero visibility in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A barn collapsed while being occupied by 30 to 40 cattle. Some deceased cattle reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe storms developed over portions of SE Texas. These storms produced extensive damage to utility lines across Jackson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An emergency manager reported that there were multiple downed wires and broken crossarms along FM530. Live wires left on the ground reportedly killed a cow the next morning after the storms past. Winds estimated at 100 mph from ETL with a DoD of 2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was measured at Iowa Road Weather Mesonet station RIGI4 near Ida Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough and Arctic high pressure over the Mid-Atlantic combined to produce a period of high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Maryland DOT sensor on MD-054 measured a peak wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Numerous damaging wind reports occurred across eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind snapped numerous large tree limbs on the north side of McAlester.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Wyoming as a strong cold front moved across the state. Several areas had multiple lines move through the same region during the event. Severe Thunderstorm Watch was in effect for most of the afternoon through the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WYDOT sensor 1.5 miles east of Sinclair.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts across Lake Erie.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured gust from 45207 - Fairport Harbor Buoy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Continued dryness in May, led to deterioration of drought conditions for much of western and north central Nebraska. There was one pocket of drought improvement across far southwestern Nebraska. By the end of May, 87 percent of western and north central Nebraska was in extreme (D3) or exceptional (D4) drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted through the end of May across the northern third of Frontier County. Over the remainder of the county, extreme (D3) drought deteriorated to exceptional (D4) drought conditions by the end of the month. The cooperative observer at Curtis reported 3.87 inches of precipitation for May. This was 0.18 inches above the normal of 3.69 inches. The cooperative observer at Eustis 2NW reported 2.99 inches of precipitation for the month of May. This was 0.59 inches below the normal of 3.58 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another shot of Arctic Air spilled in February 7th through February 9th. For the mountains, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For the Shenandoah Valley and portions of Northern Virginia, minimum wind chills of -5 to -20F were observed. Areas in central Virginia saw minimum wind chills around 0F. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southern Connecticut. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southern Connecticut, with blizzard conditions across the southern coastal zones, along with Northern Fairfield County.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southern Connecticut. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 35 mph and 1/4 mile visibility or less was reported at Danbury ASOS. SNowfall reported across the zone ranged from mainly 12 to 22 inches via the public, emergency management, trained spotters, Cocorahs, and Amateur radio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas.  Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was high water over 6th Street near Clay Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stationed across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours allowed for thunderstorm development to form across the Shenandoah Valley during the late morning hours of March 16, 2026 that began to surge towards southern Pennsylvania. Severe thunderstorms in a favorable unstable and highly sheared environment across Virginia and Maryland began to shift into the a more stable and less sheared environment; however, momentum from these thunderstorms allowed for isolated instances of tree damage during the afternoon hours. As the cold front continued to track eastward, slightly more instability was available across eastern Lancaster County during the evening hours, with more readily available lift and moisture, allowing for more robust winds that caused more significant wind damage in eastern Lancaster County. The most notable wind damage came in the form of significant roof damage in New Holland along with significant damage to a barn and a nearby residence near Terre Hill. Multiple trees were also knocked down near Terre Hill and near Gap.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated between 70 and 80 mph caused significant damage to a barn as well as to a house near Terre Hill. Multiple trees were also knocked down in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large cyclonic trough occupying the eastern third of the US was the instigating force behind snow showers and northwest orographic snow. This snow resulted in light snowfall across portions of southwestern Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow fell in Russell County, with 2.5 inches of snow measured in Lebanon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With low pressure strengthening and tracking northeastward towards Chicago, the Quad State region experienced breezy southerly to southeasterly winds throughout the daytime hours. Spotty wind gusts to 40+mph were observed in Southeast Missouri, with the strongest gust measured 49mph at the Cape Girardeau Regional Airport's ASOS site. Showers and a few thunderstorms moved eastward across Southeast Missouri during the late afternoon hours.

A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in wind damage and a large number of power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by personal weather station. Scattered power outages in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad upper trough was located across the Western United States with west-southwest flow across the Borderland.  An upper level jet of 100 knots was moving into southern New Mexico and combined with an approaching cold front to bring wind gusts up to 88 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak gust of 88 mph was recorded on San Augustin Pass.  Other gusts recorded across the White Sands Missile Range included 68 mph at Delta Clipper, 62 mph at Brillo West and 60 mph at Pony.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong short wave moved across the region creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across southeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An outdoor play area was destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down onto Pine Grove Road in Bethel Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 3-5, though the far southern portion of the county experienced closer to 6-7. The highest reliable measurement received was 7.3 from Salisbury Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall and near-record early-to-mid month heat allowed worsening drought conditions across locations mainly east of Interstate Highway 69C/US 281 across the lower/mid Rio Grande Valley and the Deep South Texas ranchlands in February 2026. Farm and ranch difficulties due to limited forage, water supplies, and heat continued and expanded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought expanded to the Cameron County barrier island, including Boca Chica Beach, South Padre Island, and the county beaches a few miles north, from February 10th through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic airmass brought very cold temperatures to the entire region Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).  Winds of 15 to 25 mph combined with low temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero brought wind chill values down to 30 to 55 below zero Thursday evening (1/22) through Friday morning (1/23). Temperatures did not warm much Friday afternoon, with daytime highs ranging from 5 to 15 below zero, offering little relief from the cold, with wind chill values at or near extreme cold criteria, even in the afternoon. Plummeting overnight temperatures Friday night (1/23) into Saturday morning (1/24) of 15 to near 40 below zero once again pushed wind chill values down to 30 to near 50 below zero. Temperatures had finally warmed to above extreme cold criteria late Saturday morning (1/24) but remained cold through the weekend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds caused wind chill values to fall to -35 to -43 degrees from early Friday morning (1/23) through Saturday morning (1/24).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An home's roof was damaged about three-miles NNE of Vienna and portions of the roof landed in a nearby cornfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down and across Highway 52 at Exit 27.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe storms developed across north-central Kansas on the evening of May 16. The first was a cluster of supercells that produced large to very large hail and isolated strong winds, while the second was a line of storms that mostly produced damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of quarter size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley on the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A band of precipitation moved into southeast Ohio on the night of the 21st and then continued east across the Ohio River early on the morning of the 22nd. Isolated to scattered showers and a few strong thunderstorms continued to progress across the area during the day, then precipitation tapered off following the frontal passage late in the day. Showers and storms generally produced pockets of one to one and a half inches of rain accumulation, however training storms did lead to a strip of two to three inches in eastern Washington County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down onto State Route 93 and Old State Route 75 near the Old Ford Garage and Old High School track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the county fell as low as 0 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed a large tree uprooted or snapped near 99th Street and Cicero Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite drought improvement noted in February 2026, conditions deteriorated in March due to an abnormally dry month. Rainfall deficits for the month were over 3 inches with the least amount of rain measured across northwest Middle Tennessee. Clarksville in particular only measured 0.86 inches of rain during the entire month of March which was 3.46 inches below normal. By the end of March, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least the abnormally dry category. About 57 percent of the area was in at least moderate drought with about 7 percent of this area in severe drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions developed across Perry County in March 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Screven County Warning Point reported a tree down at the 5800 Block of Newington Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms tracked across north central and northeast Colorado with wind gusts up to 68 mph and hail up to one inch in diameter.

Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began near Farm Road 1078, just to the northwest of Butterfield. NWS ground surveys concluded that the tornado path tracked to the east across Highway 37. A couple of old wooden power poles snapped or were brought down along Highway 37. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Sentinel 2 satellite data analysis revealed that the tornado continued to the northeast, crossing State Highway U, producing an intermittent path of tree damage about 6.6 miles long. Satellite data revealed the tornado was 350 yards at its widest point with estimated max winds of 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. A moderate risk for severe weather covered most of Southern Illinois for the evening hours.||A few late afternoon cells tracking northeastward produced hail in Edwards/Wabash Counties. For the storms arriving from the west during the evening, wind damage became the primary hazard for Southern Illinois. The highest concentration of damage south of Herrin and north of Marion in Williamson County, with damage to multiple homes in both locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A powerful thunderstorm moving eastward caused tree limbs to be down along with minor roof damage to homes and an outbuilding in the Forest Park neighborhood of Herrin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limb snapped by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of northwestern Arkansas experienced above average precipitation during April, with the exception of Carroll County, and portions of Crawford and Franklin Counties. In general, four to ten inches of rain fell across the region, which corresponded to as much as 150 to 200 percent above monthly average precipitation amounts. Much of Carroll County, and portions of Crawford and Franklin Counties received between four and five inches of rain during the month, which corresponded to only 75 to 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Carroll and Madison Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A Pacific weather system crossed western and central Wyoming and brought heavy snow west of the Continental Divide and high wind to the east of the Divide. Notable accumulations fell throughout the western mountains. The highest amount was in the Salt River and Wyoming Ranges where 34 inches of new snow fell at the Spring Creek Divide SNOTEL site. Other notable amounts included 30 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL in Yellowstone National Park, 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL in the Absarokas and 24 inches over Togwotee Pass. High winds occurred along and East of the Divide as well as across Sweetwater County. Some of the more notable wind gusts included 82 mph along South Pass and 81 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High wind occurred in portions of Natrona County. The highest wind gust recorded was 74 mph at Scenic Drive on the south side of Casper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong complex of storms, or a mesoscale convective system, tracked through eastern New York from northwest to southeast in the afternoon through the early evening of June 30th, 2026. Strong to damaging wind gusts caused widespread tree and powerline damage as numerous bowing segments cycled through the main line. Numerous reports of wind damage were relayed to NWS Albany from 911 call centers and local law enforcement in Herkimer, Hamilton, Fulton, Montgomery, Saratoga, Schenectady, Albany, Rensselaer, and Columbia Counties. However, particularly hit hard was Montgomery County where extensive tree and wire damage was reported across portions of Fonda and Fultonville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local law enforcement reported multiple trees down on Clamsteam Rd in Halfmoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of below-normal rainfall led to the development of severe drought (D2) conditions across portions of Pointe Coupee Parish. Rainfall deficits began in mid December and were not able to recover despite receiving a few inches of rain through January.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The extreme northern portion of the parish was in D2 drought for the entire month of January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Upson County remained in D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout the month of January. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 7, 2025, the county sustained 17 consecutive weeks of D2 conditions as of the end of January. These conditions remained unchanged as the event persisted into February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Finley, ND NDAWN observed a low temperature of 30 degrees at 5:25 AM CST and Hope, ND NDAWN observed at low temperatures of 30 degrees at 5:30 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on power lines in the 100 block of Reid Road as well as low hanging power lines at 2200 Shenandoah.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued through the month of May. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May which helped in the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pace CT wildfire near Interlachen continued through most of May at 343.35 acres with 85% containment. Due to beneficial rain through the month, the Florida Forest Service updated the containment to 90% on May 29th. The fire continued to burn through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -50F. ||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F. ||The lowest wind chills were:|-50F at AXN in Alexandria, MN.|-49F at STC in St Cloud, MN.|-49F at OWA in Owatonna, MN.|-49F at GHW in Glenwood, MN.|-47F at MSP in the Twin Cities, MN.|-47F at BDH in Willmar, MN.|-47F at CFE in Buffalo, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLJF reported wind gusts as high as 25 mph during the early evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -20F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -47F at 11PM on the 22nd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of a large tree on home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southeastward moving cold front sparked thunderstorms in the afternoon and evening. Good moisture return for March pushed dew points above 60 degrees with air temperatures in the mid 70s. A 1000-1500 J/kg MUCAPE gradient nosing in from the west with potent EBWD values of 50-60 knots supported severe thunderstorms with large hail up to golf ball size, sporadic wind damage, and urban flooding with training storms.
Drought continued across parts of the area through June, especially in the eastern zones.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: To begin the month, all but the eastern edge of Sheridan County was in at least D2 drought conditions, with D3 drought conditions arriving in the south-central portion of the county. On the last day of the month, drought impacts lessened to include only D2 drought conditions in that south-central portion of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall continuing into February combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 3rd drought monitor update. These conditions continued throughout the month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
A line of severe storms that produced widespread wind damage in Alabama moved into the Florida panhandle and gradually weakened but not before producing a few more reports of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were down over roadway near Greenwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening hours on the 22nd, a couple clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of east-central and northeast Colorado. Yuma County was hit especially hard, with 81 mph winds and four inch diameter hail reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report came through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle was inundated by floodwaters in Springfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down on Piedmont Estates Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry weather continued on February 18th and 19th. Winds were gusty but remained below high wind thresholds. Southwesterly sustained winds of 25-35mph occurred with gusts up to 45 or 55mph. However, given the dry fuels and low relative humidity, this allowed for additional wildfires to develop across portions of the Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Canadian River Bridge Fire occurred about five miles north of Borger, just off of Highway 136 at the Canadian River. This fire burned 428 acres and was caused by welding equipment use.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.

A midlevel trough lifting northeast from Arkansas and Mississippi, interacted with a cold front moving in from the north, to cause widespread showers and thunderstorms across East Tennessee from late in the evening on May 29th, through the late morning hours on May 30th. This led to scattered reports of flash flooding across East Tennessee, most notably in the central Tennessee valley and northern Cumberland Plateau areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 7700 block of the New River Highway, northeast of Petros, was washed away due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening hours on June 19th, a couple of severe storms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts and two brief tornadoes. One of these storms trekked through Trempealeau County where it produced golf ball sized hail in Osseo as well as a weak EF-0 tornado which resulted in minor damage. An additional tornado was documented in Jackson County, but no damage was verified which resulted in an EF-U rating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree down on Highway 37 in Tell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant snowstorm struck portions of East Tennessee at the end of the month, thanks to strong lift from a deep upper trough diving from north to south. A couple of long term cooperative weather stations saw top 10 snowfalls during this storm. This storm led to 3 confirmed fatalities in East Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell in Meigs County, with 3.5 inches of snow measured near Ten Mile, Tennessee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous tree limbs were blown down.

CZ_NAME: COASTAL NORTH BAY INCLUDING POINT REYES NATIONAL SEASHORE
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video posted on social media showed the beach along Seadrift Road completely submerged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rain and mountain snow showers moved across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening of May 4th. Widespread snow then formed over the mountains and northern foothills during the early morning hours of May 5th and continued for most of the day. Across the lower elevations (below 6000 feet), precipitation type was mainly rain through the morning of the 5th and slowly began to turn over to snow during the afternoon. Snow then continued through the night of the 5th and early morning hours of the 6th. The heaviest snow occurred across the foothills and mountains of Boulder and Larimer Counties where 18 to 36 inches of snow fell. Areas west of I-25 to the base of the foothills received 4 to 12 inches, heaviest near the foothills. Main impact was broken tree branches on deciduous trees, some of which fell on powerlines leading to sparse power outages. Power outages topped 50,000 overnight the 5th and early morning the 6th. Denver International Airport (DIA) had over 700 flight delays and 40 cancellations for May 5th and May 6th. Numerous schools were closed on May 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRahs and trained spotters reported 4 to 8 inches of snow. The heavy wet snow led to many broken tree branches and limbs, a few of which fell onto vehicles and homes. Broken branches also fell onto powerlines, leading to some power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires during the middle of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wildfire near Sanderson quickly grew to 500-600 acres during the 12th of April, also prompting 4 evacuations near Doyle Williams Road. These evacuations were then lifted on the 13th of April. There are little details known beyond this date, however it is likely the wildfire continued to burn through the end of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hebron NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front shifted winds out of the northwest, increasing gusts to around 30 to 45 mph across the region. At the same time, 1/2 to 2 inches of light fluffy snow fell across the entire region. The strongest wind gusts and greatest snow amounts were measured across southwest and southern MN during the afternoon and evening, resulting in occasional periods of near-blizzard conditions with visibilities as low as 1/2 to 1/4 mile.||The strongest measured wind gusts on January 21 were:|42 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.|41 mph at KCNB in Canby, MN.|40 mph at KSTP in St Paul, MN.|39 mph at KMIC in Crystal, MN.|39 mph at KRWF in Redwood Falls, MN.|38 mph at KFRM in Fairmont, MN.|38 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of very strong winds and light snow showers resulted in reduced visibility from blowing snow. Occasional near blizzard conditions were reported at the height of the storm. The AWOS at KOVL noted visibility as low as 1/2 mile and wind gusts between 30 to 40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 2.25 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down on Lincoln Boulevard near Everett McKinley Dirksen Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a 73 MPH wind gust from a home weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dryline set up over central portions of the Permian Basin, extending southward towards the Big Bend. A nearby shortwave encouraged thunderstorm development east of this dryline. A couple of thunderstorms produced severe winds in the Permian Basin. Meanwhile, strong winds aloft coupled with the passage of a Pacific front allowed for high winds in the Guadalupe Mountains and in far northern portions of Lea County in SE New Mexico.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station at 2 SW Tatum measured a brief period of high winds, including gusts up to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall reports from the public, trained spotters, and CoCoRaHs data showed between two and eleven inches of snowfall fell across the Northern Outer Banks. Snowfall amounts above three inches fell mainly north of Roanoke Island and Whalebone NC. Snowfall fell between the afternoon of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the community of Pike, one tree was blown down along Glendale Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An occluded area of low pressure traveled across the Great Lakes, NY and New England during the night of February 20th with a new surface low developing off of the Cape cod coast by the early morning hours of February 21st.||Snow overspread northern NY during the afternoon hours and quickly became heavy at times during the late afternoon and evening hours with snowfall rates in excess of 1 inch per hour at times. Snow ended during the early overnight hours of February 21st. Snowfall totals across the region ranged from 3 to 5 inches across St. Lawrence county to 5 to 9 inches across the rest of northern NY. Impacts were generally travel related due to the timing of the heavuest snowfall during the evneing commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across the area were 4 to 5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A system brought strong winds to the region, with a band of snow across the northeast South Dakota. This resulted in blizzard conditions with widespread travel impacts from the early morning through the afternoon of February 18. ||Peak winds associated with the system included a gust measuring 72 mph by a mesonet station owned by a trained spotter in Faulkton, a 71 mph gust recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 4 miles north of Altamont (Deuel county) and a 67 mph gusts measured by the SDDOT RWIS 7 miles east of Clark. 47 additional weather stations would record a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. ||The Andover and Westport COOP observers reported blizzard or ground blizzard conditions at the time of their observations.||Not much overall snowfall occurred with the system, but within the band snowfall averaged about 4 inches with the COOP observers in Westport and Clark reporting a total of 4.1 and 4.0 inches of snowfall respectively. Additionally, the National Weather Service office just outside the Aberdeen Regional Airport measured 3.7 inches.
