EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent cold front ushered a bitterly cold airmass into northwest Connecticut on January 23-24, 2026. The combination of bitterly cold air temperatures (minimum temperatures ranging from -6 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit) and gusty winds (ranging from 25 to 35 mph) made for dangerously cold wind chills or feels-like temperatures. Minimum feels-like temperatures ultimately ranged from about -25 to -12 degrees Fahrenheit across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -6 degrees Fahrenheit reported along with a minimum wind chill of -25 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana.  Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Braman Tornado: Numerous spotters and chasers observed this tornado develop in western Kay County. The initial damage occurred near 140th Street and Earth Road where a tree was uprooted and a farm house suffered roof damage. The tornado continued generally east breaking a power pole on 124th Street south of Earth Road and destroying a barn and damaging more power poles and trees near Earth Road east of 124th Street. The first of two satellite tornadoes developed in this area near Earth Road between 124th and 108th. The primary tornado moved north, then looped back around to an easterly movement as the motion of both the primary tornado and the satellite tornado was influenced by the Fujiwhara effect.||As the primary tornado moved east-northeast after this interaction, a barn was destroyed along Earth Road east of 108th Street, and a number of trees and power poles were damaged along 76th Street near Fork Road. As the tornado was crossing the Chickaskia River, a second satellite tornado developed and rotated around this primary tornado. The tornado continued east snapping power poles along 60th Street, and destroying two barns and more power poles along 44th Street just south of the city limits of Braman. The survey and mobile radar data from the Doppler on Wheels project show that the tornado made another loop just southeast of Braman and east of US-177, then moved southeast damaging trees along Fork Road east of 29th Street before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado with 0.49 miles path length, and path width of 85 yards moved through portions of Bartholomew County. The tornado began east of US Highway 31 and continued northeast through a tree line and into a corn field. A convergent wind pattern was noted.  Peak winds were 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

The last of three winter storms moved through starting the night of February 19th and lasting through the morning of February 20th.  This was the coldest storm of the three with snow falling lower than the previous two storms.  However, this was another fast moving storm with gusty high winds, so snowfall amounts were difficult to measure and lower than expected.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported, via photos on Facebook, 6.5 inches of snow measured at 2 SSW Fredonia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens.

Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on power lines at the intersection of Ash and Hemlock Streets.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mesoscale convective system of thunderstorms dropped southward out of Ontario into Central NY, moving into an unusually unstable and sufficiently sheared environment. This supported severe thunderstorms with widespread damaging winds, an isolated EF1 tornado, and hail. Heavy rainfall also occurred as deep moisture surged northward from the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds brought multiple trees down in Downsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused a creek to overflow in Sector Paracaochero near Camino Los Cruces in San Juan. Flash floodwaters inundated two residential units near Aceros de Am��rica, resulting in flood damage to the affected properties. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought all severe hazards to portions of Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail report north of Coffey on Route 13, resulting in an vehicular accident injuring one person.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Virginia on April 5, 2026. A weak surface low along the cold front helped produce a line of severe storms across southeast Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS station (KNGU) in Norfolk measured a gust to 61 miles per hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a west-east oriented boundary positioned through the Ozarks region of Missouri with low pressure positioned in Southwestern Missouri, a small but potent surging storm line pushed through Carter, Ripley, and Butler Counties mid-afternoon on the 28th. Large hail and winds in excess of 70mph were associated with this bowing segment as it dove east-southeastward from South Central Missouri into the Bootheel. A more intense pocket of wind known as a macroburst produced winds up to 100mph across portions of Ripley County from southeast of Doniphan to south/southwest of Naylor, uprooting dozens of trees and damaging several structures and multiple vehicles.||For the Carter-Ripley-Butler corridor, environmental parameters included: MLCAPE of 1000-2000J/kg, DCAPE of 500J/kg, very strong effective bulk shear of 60-70kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 6-7C/km.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dozens of trees were downed and a power line was snapped along/near MO-21 south of US-60 as a thunderstorm line moved eastward through Carter County. Report submitted via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved east toward the area that helped to produce severe thundertorms over a good portion of the CWA. Flooding also occurred in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported (via Facebook) hail up to the size of ping pong balls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated winds developed across South Texas as a progressive MCS evolved along a stationary front. Ahead of the front, a very moist and unstable air mass was in place, characterized by surface dewpoints near 70��F and extreme instability with MLCAPE values of 3,000-4,500 J/kg. Steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate deep-layer wind shear supported organized thunderstorms capable of high winds. During the overnight hours, clusters of thunderstorms interacted with multiple outflow boundaries, enhancing localized wind production. The moist environment and persistent southerly inflow helped sustain the convective system as it pushed southeastward across the region, producing broad areas of 30-40 kt winds with isolated severe gusts exceeding 50 kt.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MIST2 located 8 miles southeast of Aransas Pass measured gusts up to 48 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Maryland State Highway Administration reported multiple trees down around Ripley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex of thunderstorms developed across portions of north-central Kansas during the late afternoon hours of June 8th. These thunderstorms rapidly intensified and moved south and southeast across the I-70 corridor. Widespread wind damage occurred across portions of Lincoln, Ellsworth, Saline, McPherson, Marion, and Chase counties. In fact, a wind gust of 113 mph was measured at the Salina Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report of a semi flipped over at mile marker 255. The time was estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated thunderstorms developed north of a warm front Thursday night (3/30) across central Wisconsin and east-central Wisconsin. These storms tracked eastward across the region through the early morning hours on Friday (3/31).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to golf ball size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail fell near Ashwaubenon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-80 at MP 40 Knolls mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 67 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe on Thursday March Twelfth reaching the Coastal Plain by Thursday morning and then tracking across the area waters Thursday afternoon. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of rain and thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east across the area. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place some of these storms became strong in nature bringing damaging wind gusts to the inland rivers and sounds as well as the coastal waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weather station at Washington Airport (OCW) recorded a 50 mph wind gust as thunderstorms moved through the area. Report came in via WeatherFlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercells developed and moved into north central Kansas in the late afternoon period. Hazards reported were initially large hail to 2 inches in diameter before the convection formed into a line, tracking southeast during the evening hours. The storms produced winds around 70 mph and heavy rainfall amounts to 3.5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Also reported quarter size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a tree across a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across the North Carolina  Piedmont and foothills continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.
Dry conditions persisted across the tri-state area through April and into May with D3-D4 drought continuing.
Thunderstorms produced hail over parts of Lenawee and Monroe counties, up to 1 inch in diameter.
A hailstorm moves through south Houston overnight from the 30th of April into the early morning hours of May 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A news station published a story sharing information regarding damage to schools in Alvin. The story mentioned that Alvin ISD superintendent reported roof damage to Mary Marek Elementary School, likely caused by a robust hailstorm that moved over the school. Leaks in the roof caused water damage, resulting in the school closing in the final days of the 2026 school year. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down at the intersection of Ridge Road and Lara Road in Heathsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought very large hail and damaging wind gusts to portions of far eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Softball sized hail (4 inch) reported on north side of Paola.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few isolated thunderstorms moved east across Yuma county during the afternoon hours on the 20th, ahead of deepening High Plains low pressure. Hail up to golfball size and winds to 66 mph were reported across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across Central and Northern New Hampshire. Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 0%, D2 - 41%, D1 - 36%. January brought little relief to New Hampshire's drought conditions in these areas, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge. January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas around 75% of normal range. Snowfall remained below normal outside of the White Mountains, snow water equivalent remained below normal for all areas except the immediate coast. Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins. Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the north slopes of the White Mountains for the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought remained in a steady state at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The incredible stretch of severe weather continued on Wednesday June 10th with more severe storms and a few small tornadoes across Dickinson county.  The storms also dumped  more flooding rains across parts of Kansas that were already saturated from days of torrential rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: By mid-February, higher moisture content from a lingering front and locally induced afternoon shower and thunderstorm activity produced periods of heavy rainfall across Puerto Rico.

Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest sleet total in Langlade County was 1 inch in Antigo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rain and mountain snow showers moved across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening of May 4th. Widespread snow then formed over the mountains and northern foothills during the early morning hours of May 5th and continued for most of the day. Across the lower elevations (below 6000 feet), precipitation type was mainly rain through the morning of the 5th and slowly began to turn over to snow during the afternoon. Snow then continued through the night of the 5th and early morning hours of the 6th. The heaviest snow occurred across the foothills and mountains of Boulder and Larimer Counties where 18 to 36 inches of snow fell. Areas west of I-25 to the base of the foothills received 4 to 12 inches, heaviest near the foothills. Main impact was broken tree branches on deciduous trees, some of which fell on powerlines leading to sparse power outages. Power outages topped 50,000 overnight the 5th and early morning the 6th. Denver International Airport (DIA) had over 700 flight delays and 40 cancellations for May 5th and May 6th. Numerous schools were closed on May 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports indicated 6 to 15 inches of snow fell across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Standing water reported at the intersection of Texas State Highway 188 and County Road  85. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm developing ahead of a cold front moved south out of South Carolina into the northeast Georgia Piedmont during the afternoon. The storm produced a swath of damaging wind gusts from the western shore of Lake Hartwell into eastern Elbert County.

At least one outbuilding received roof damage near the Elbert County line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Botetourt county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th to 10th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Gregg, Smith, and Upshur Counties in East Texas by late March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged between 2-4 inches, which was a continuation of below normal rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) drought expanded across more of East Texas by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to penny-size about 1.5-miles NNW of Nankin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 85 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.  At one point, there were around 600 customers without power due to downed lines and poles in parts of Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the Minnesota Road Weather Information System site near Lakefield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching cold front triggered clusters of strong thunderstorms across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 24th.  One of the southernmost storms tracked across Woodford County, resulting in 60mph wind gusts and minor urban flooding.
Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on a property just east of Clarks Creek where several trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado would continue east towards Baton Rouge Road, where several more hardwood trees had large branches broken off, with tree debris thrown onto both sides of the road. Additionally, a barn was completely destroyed in the same area. Sporadic tree damage continued along Baton Rouge Road, eventually leading to another barn where the walls completely collapsed and the roof was blown off. The damage to these outbuildings was consistent with |EF-1 damage, with maximum winds around 90 mph. Just a bit farther down the road, another outbuilding had its sheet metal roof completely ripped off, with pieces of sheet metal thrown about 50 yards into the nearby field. Some of the siding was also peeled off. ||The damage continued along portions of Baton Rouge Road, with extensive tree damage noted leading up to the intersection of Interstate 75. Most of the tree damage was primarily large branches that were broken off, but there was one hardwood tree that was uprooted. Just east of Interstate 75, additional tree and power pole damage occurred. ||The area of most concentrated damage occurred in several neighborhoods just east of U.S. Route 25. On Ridgelea Drive, there were multiple large, healthy trees that were uprooted and/or snapped at the base. On Humes Ridge Road, more large trees and wooden power poles were snapped. The most significant damage occurred near the end of the tornadic path on Waterworks Road, where a standalone, multi-car garage had the majority of its roof ripped off. Multiple sections of the garage had significant loss of its cinder block exterior walls, as well as some minor damage to the interior walls between car ports. Debris from the garage was spread out into the nearby field. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding. 5.11 inches of rain was measured in Marshall in Central Harrison County from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several high water rescues were reported in Marshall, with one house flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering 100% of Utah Zone 025 - Tavaputs Plateau. These drought conditions remained unchanged through the end of the month. Drought impacts at this point are limited to poor winter snowpack conditions. There is increasing concern over the impact of the drought on the upcoming summer wildfire season. Additionally, there is concern over water availability for farming and ranching in the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought improvements continued through mid April thanks to additional beneficial rains that fell between the 10th and 12th. A remnant pocket of D4 (Exceptional) Drought in northern Jim Hogg improved to D3 (Extreme), with mainly D2 Drought conditions replacing most of the D3 areas, with only small pockets of D3 over parts of Zapata, Jim Hogg, Brooks, and Cameron Counties.  On the 14th, D3 areas shrunk to just 10.26% of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most of Brooks County had improved to Severe (D2) Drought conditions with a pocket of Extreme (D3) Drought over extreme northwestern Brooks County during the April 14-20 timeframe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought. Introduction of D4 on 2/24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large limbs down and and power lines down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Warren County in early to mid March after an ice jam broke loose on the Hudson River from the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. According to these sources, water and large chunks of ice flowed rapidly downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In Thurman, portions of River Road became inundated, specifically near The Glen Bridge, by both rapidly flowing water and large pieces of ice. This lead to the closure of the road for several days. In Warrensburg, portions of the Warren County Fish Hatchery also became inundated with some water and ice from a nearby branch of the Hudson River. Additionally, Cronin's Golf Course, which lies right along the Hudson River, became inundated with significant amounts of water. Areal drone images from a local news outlet showed what appears to be the entire golf course covered in water and ice. Due to the substantial nature of this ice jam, flooding impacted these areas for several days after the initial onset.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Warren County Emergency Managers, with the help of local broadcast media partners, reported that at 10 A.M. on Thursday, March 12th, an ice jam that had accumulated near the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg, NY broke free and rapidly flowed downstream. Large chunks of ice were swiftly carried downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In the town of Warrensburg, portions of the Warren County Fish Hatchery become inundated with large pieces of ice and water from a nearby branch off the Hudson River. The ice jam flooding impacted some of the facility's land for several days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from severe drought to moderate drought as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 100th to 200th percentile across much of SE West Virginia. Rainfall totals over the past 30 days ranged from 5.0 to 8.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to near normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Both Mercer and Monroe counties continued to remain in Severe drought as portions of those counties received rainfall totals closer to 3-4 inches over the 30 day period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Monroe county by late June after repeated rounds of rainfall during the month of June. The previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 20th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Greenbrier River, which was observed to be below the 75th to 90th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oldham and Deaf Smith counties started the month of May in Severe Drought (D2), as well as the western halves of Potter and Randall counties. The eastern halves of Potter and Randall counties started the month in Extreme Drought (D3). A continued trend of a dry spring brought on a 120 day deficit around 2 to 4 by month's end. This allowed the areas of D2 to degrade to D3. Parts of far eastern Randall County went from D3 to Exceptional Drought (D4). The drought conditions not only hurt crops but led to some bad wildfires in these counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A convective complex moved through the region during the day on June 21st. Though it remained sub-severe for most of its life, the complex did intensify in south-central Illinois where it produced tornadoes, wind damage, and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey found very clear tornadic damage (EF-1) east of Kinmundy, with supporting video showing a multi-vortex tornado in that location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few power poles were downed on Waesch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over one thousand homes were without power as a result of nearby downed trees and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 4th, ahead of a cold front moving into the region. The thunderstorms continued to affect the area through the early morning hours of the 5th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to golf ball size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hail up to golf ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

Another shortwave crossed Wyoming and brought another round of strong to severe thunderstorms, primarily impacting Natrona County but also portions of Fremont and Park County. A line of thunderstorms moved through Fremont and Natrona Counties bringing high wind. The highest wind gust reported was 67 mph at Scenic Drive on the south side of Casper. In northern Natrona County, quarter sized hail was reported to south of Midwest. In Park County, there was a report of nickel size hail to the southeast of Cody. North of Jeffrey City, there was a brief QLCS tornado. The tornado remained over open country and caused no known damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 63 mph wind gust was recorded at the Camp Creek RAWS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS survey team concluded that an EF-1 tornado tracked from the corner of Afton St and Richmond Ave towards Dixie Ave in Houma. A truck was tossed 30 feet and sustained significant damage. Multiple snapped and uprooted trees were observed. Several homes sustained a partial loss of their roofs. One home had a collapsed carport. Time estimated by radar.

CZ_NAME: DULUTH MN TO PT WING WI
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary boundary was draped across western Lake Superior on the afternoon of the 23rd and led to the development of thunderstorms across the region. Storms were mainly sub-severe, but one storm was stronger and produced a wind gust of 42 knots at Port Wing.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gust of 48 mph was recorded by the PNGW3 Port Wing GLOS station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees and wires near Custer City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across eastern Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through northwest Kansas on the evening of the 15th. Multiple wind gusts ranging from 58 mph - 63 mph were recorded. Multiple reports of blowing dust with less than 1/2 - 1/4 mile visibility reported. A wildfire was detected via satellite and confirmed with local emergency management.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Colby Airport AWOS reported a gust of 56 mph. The mesonet station at 2 ENE Colby reported a gust of 63 mph. An emergency manager reported a semi blown over along I-70 near Brewster.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree fell on a home causing moderate damage with additional large limbs down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was uprooted on West Cox Road near Cayce Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Modest shear and instability associated with an approaching frontal boundary resulted in a line of pre frontal thunderstorms moving across interior southeast GA during the morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of trees and powerlines down across the area. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell on powerlines in Victor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fosston, ND Airport AWOS observed a low temperature of 28 at 5:20 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large limbs were reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 600 residents were without power due to storm damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) swept across portions of central, southern and eastern Oklahoma on the morning of the 8th. This convective system was tied to the passage of a compact upper wave across the region, resulting in very strong wind fields within a weakly unstable boundary layer. In addition to sporadic pockets of thunderstorm wind damage, and generally sub-severe hail, a few tornadoes occurred in a corridor from near Purcell, OK to Shawnee, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is a continuation of the Purcell tornado that moved into Cleveland County from McClain County. After crossing the Canadian River into Cleveland County, the tornado damaged and outbuilding near Moffatt Road. Otherwise, damage to tree branches was noted along U.S. Highway 77 north of Lexington, and northeast of 84th Street and York Road where the tornado likely dissipated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.

Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in several area rivers reaching flood stage. Some rivers reached moderate to major flood stage, with the Lemonwier River at New Lisbon approaching its flood of record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in the Yellow River at Necedah rising into flood stage during the afternoon hours on April 15th. The river then crested in major flood stage during the late evening hours on April 16th before falling below flood stage during the morning hours on April 22nd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moisture associated with Tropical Storm Arthur approached Central Alabama on June 17 into June 18. On June 17, several showers and low-topped supercells developed over southeastern Central Alabama. One cell produced a well-defined funnel cloud in southeastern Lowndes County that was caught in at least two videos posted to social media. The next day, heavy rainfall near Chalkville led to a portion of Sweeny Hollow Rd being flooded.||In the wake of the remnants of Arthur passing through Central Alabama on June 18, a cold front entered the area and became stalled. On June 19, heavy rainfall became concentrated along a boundary along and south of the U.S. 80 corridor, leading to flooding issues in Pike and Lowndes counties. By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media videos showed a well-defined funnel cloud southeast of Letohatchee. No contact with the ground was evident via radar and no ground reports were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak mid level shortwave moved through during the afternoon initiating a few strong storms which produced scattered wind damage reports in western MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Southwick, a tree was downed onto Eden Hill Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front and led to a 59 mph wind gust in northern Hitchcock county and a 60 mph wind gust in Red Willow county at the McCook Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph wind gust was recorded at Ambient Weather Station site Weather_Station_Hock.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front moved through the region during the evening of the 17th. The strongest winds were observed across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle where several severe wind gusts were recorded.||High wind gusts (non-thunderstorms) from Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites are listed below:||64 mph at Lesley (Hall County),|62 mph at Memphis (Hall County),|62 mph at Earth (Lamb County),|58 mph at Guthrie (King County), and|58 mph at White River Lake (Crosby County).
Showers and thunderstorms fired along a stalled frontal boundary throughout the day, resulting in localized heavy rainfall and flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few widely scattered thunderstorms produced localized gale-force winds associated with an upper-level low during the morning to midday hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts of up to 40 knots (46 MPH) were measured by a Tempest station on Beach Side Drive adjacent to the Chesapeake Bay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines downed on Blade Loop Road near Windmill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front slowly moved south into the region on April 29th while a warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place across southwest Mississippi. Thunderstorms developed along and ahead of the front during the afternoon hours, then became increasingly influenced by storm outflow as they moved south faster than the front itself. The strongest storms produced a mix of large hail and damaging wind across portions of southwest Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Management reports a tree down in roadway and powerline down near Carriere.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent Arctic Front across southern Ontario and western New York began to shift southeasterly during the late evening hours of December 31, 2025 and continued into the early morning hours of January 1, 2026. This potent cold front allowed for a line of snow squalls to form across all of central Pennsylvania, with widespread whiteout conditions are the line of squalls moved through the area. Whiteout conditions were observed at the NWS State College office, along with by multiple spotters in Centre, Mifflin, Blair, and York counties. No accidents or injuries were reported during these snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall brought visibility less than one quarter of a mile with heavy snow observed on Interstate 80 near Penfield. Heavy snowfall allowed for quick accumulation on the roadway in a span of 10 to 15 minutes. Winds were observed to gust near 20 to 25 mph as the snow squall moved through the location during the early morning hours of January 1, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 40 to 50 mph wind gusts across VT. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across VT during the early morning hours of March 17th a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts that resulted in several reports of tree limbs/trees on utility lines causing 15,000 customers without power, mainly across the spine of the Green Mountains eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in the 40-50 mph from the west with the passage of the sharp cold front during the early morning hours with scattered tree damage and isolated to scattered power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coastal flooding due to high tides was reported at 2nd St and Irwin St in San Rafael.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of snow set up across northeast South Dakota on the morning of February 28th. 8.3 inches of fluffy light snow was measured 4 miles north of Bristol, with 6.1 inches in Doland. Observers in Chelsea, Columbia, Garden City and 2 miles north of the Hamlin Education Center all submitted 6 inches of total snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two miles north of the Hamlin Education Center, the public reported a total snowfall of 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressively moist airmass was in place with dew points well into the 60s across north-central Idaho during the afternoon, contributing to high instability. A vigorous shortwave trough pivoted northwestward through the northern Great Basin, providing strong forcing for ascent. This forcing, in conjunction with daytime heating and destabilization along the high terrain, initiated supercell thunderstorms that produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The fire department relayed that a house was flooded with children reportedly trapped in Lott.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced across the North Carolina and Virginia Piedmonts in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions were introduced to Botetourt county in early January after the previous two months of November and December recorded precipitation totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November and December, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 6th of January. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James river, which was observed to be below the 25th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stationed across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours allowed for thunderstorm development to form across the Shenandoah Valley during the late morning hours of March 16, 2026 that began to surge towards southern Pennsylvania. Severe thunderstorms in a favorable unstable and highly sheared environment across Virginia and Maryland began to shift into the a more stable and less sheared environment; however, momentum from these thunderstorms allowed for isolated instances of tree damage during the afternoon hours. As the cold front continued to track eastward, slightly more instability was available across eastern Lancaster County during the evening hours, with more readily available lift and moisture, allowing for more robust winds that caused more significant wind damage in eastern Lancaster County. The most notable wind damage came in the form of significant roof damage in New Holland along with significant damage to a barn and a nearby residence near Terre Hill. Multiple trees were also knocked down near Terre Hill and near Gap.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto wires approximately 2 miles southeast of McElhattan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storms system passing to our north resulted in a decaying mesoscale convective system moving across the area late in the night from May 17 into the 18th. Part of the this system re-intensified over eastern Iowa producing isolated damaging wind gusts and large hail up to the size of a half dollar.

Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana.  Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.
