EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of quick-moving low topped convection developed ahead of a cold front and produce damaging wind gusts over the waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS site at JFK Airport measured a 63 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front moving through brought a squall line through western Massachusetts and into central Massachusetts producing pockets of damaging winds which downed several trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near Hawley, a small tree was downed on Massachusetts Rt. 8A.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Moderate (D1) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas but limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to develop across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought expanding leaving Severe (D2) drought, Moderate (D1) drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines downed in the town of Cold Spring.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

A strong winter storm impacted the region from the 3rd to the 5th of January. This produced between 1 to 2 feet of snow in the Tahoe Basin with 2 to 4 feet for the higher elevations. This system also produced winds upwards of 90 mph on the ridges, with gusts commonly upwards of 55 mph elsewhere.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A group of snowmobilers triggered an avalanche near Johnson Peak and Castle Peak north of Truckee. One snowmobiler was fully buried and killed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused flowing water over the road at W US Highway 160  at N Farm Road 115.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of May with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across mainland Monroe County in the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 5.8 inches were reported across Grayson County, along with reports of freezing rain accumulations up to 0.2 inches. The highest sleet and snow total was reported northwest of Van Alstyne.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, D2 (Severe Drought) conditions were introduced to Madison County in early January. After initially reaching the D2 (Severe) threshold early in the month, the county degraded further to D3 (Extreme) by January 20. In total, the county sustained four weeks of D2 or worse conditions through January 31, with D3 conditions persisting into February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.

Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto Plank Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated, late season high winds event occurred in the Bordeaux and Arlington/Elk Mountain wind prones across southeast Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WYDOT Mesonet station KBRX 9 miles south of Wheatland gusted 58 mph at 7:19 AM on May 31st. This was the first and highest gust recorded for this zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.

Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kansas Forest Service reported the Andrew Lane fire began in Seward County before spreading into nearby Meade County. The exact acreage in Seward County is unknown, but the fire burned a total of 7,217 acres. The fire began on February 17, and was controlled by February 20. No structures were threatened from this fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms produced strong winds across portions of central, north central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon of June 15th. A peak wind gust of 69 mph was recorded on the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 5 miles west of Seneca (Potter county), with a 68 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT mesonet station in Waubay (Day county). Rapidly decaying showers also generated strong winds in Lyman and Buffalo counties, with a 66 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT station 5 miles north of Reliance and a 64 mph gust on the SDDOT station 3 miles north of Gann Valley.

In response to a powerful upper-level trough barreling into the Central Plains, digging further south and deepening in the process, an area of low pressure at the surface also strengthened as it shifted east across Kansas and eventually into Illinois by the end of the day on the 15th. The accompanying surface cold front and resulting strong pressure gradient allowed legitimate High Wind criteria conditions to overtake the entire forecast area, with sustained winds commonly 35-45 MPH with gusts 55-65 MPH, and even a few localized 70+ MPH gusts. The brunt of the highest wind gusts occurred mainly during the 10AM-4PM CDT timeframe, with reports more scattered in nature outside of that period. Across south central Nebraska, some of the highest gusts included the following: 74 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located two miles west of Doniphan; 71 MPH, measured by the Hastings Airport ASOS; 67, measured by mesonet stations located three miles north-northeast of Kearney  as well as seven miles west-southwest of Ragan; 66 MPH, measured by the Grand Island Central Nebraska Regional Airport ASOS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained speeds near 40 MPH and wind gusts exceeding 50 MPH were common throughout the day. The peak measured wind gust was 71 MPH, measured the Hastings Airport ASOS. Additional gusts between 59 and 69 MPH were also measured by the Hastings Airport ASOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated severe storm over Dale county resulted in a few trees down blocking roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down and blocking County Road 64.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, sparking thunderstorms in a moist airmass. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sugar Creek was out of its banks, resulting in about a foot of water flowing over Bush Road NW.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down near the intersection academy avenue and joiner street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of intense damaging winds, associated with a quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) mesovortex, impacted areas from southwest to just north of Marietta. Numerous power poles and trees were damaged along Shady Dale and McGehee Roads southwest of town. Several tractor-trailers were blown over along Interstate 35. The most significant damage occurred near the corner of West Creek Street and South 7th Avenue, where a home lost a significant portion of its roof, causing two exterior walls to collapse. Several businesses near Oklahoma Highway 32 and U.S. Highway 77 had varying degrees of roof damage. Intermittent damage to trees and power poles was also noted in Marietta. The wind path and event time are estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado, producing hail as large as 2.75 inches in diameter.

A sharpening High Plains dryline, in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest, spawned scattered thunderstorms across western to northwest Kansas during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 30th. Storms moved north to northeast. A measured wind gust to 68 mph and half-dollar sized hail both occurred in Norton County. Additionally, portions of Graham County received dime to nickel sized hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Norton Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Roanoke county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th to 10th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Roanoke River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.

Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Comal County saw the greatest improvement going from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought. Kendall, Kinney, and Val Verde improved from Severe (D2) Drought to D1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Comal County saw the greatest improvement going from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought. Kendall, Kinney, and Val Verde improved from Severe (D2) Drought to D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sheppard Air Force Base/Wichita Falls Municipal Airport (KSPS) observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.
Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Long County Warning Point reported a tree down on Georgia Highway 57 near the intersection with Poole Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power line damage was observed along Guardian Road in Tennerton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong southwesterly flow ahead of a cold front brought hot humid air northward into the region. The front's passage heralded the end of the heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The heat index at Monmouth Executive Airport reached 108 degrees on June 11th and 107 degrees on June 12th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong area of low pressure brings strong front through the region and brought high winds that impacted much of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant, non-thunderstorm wind event, occurred on March 13th resultant of a strong pressure gradient with cold front passage, mixing into strong wind aloft, and a sting jet. Areawide measured gusts of 50 mph or greater were common with numerous measured from 60-70 mph and as high as 75 mph. Widespread tree and structural damage was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesowest site 5 miles east of Canaan Heights measured 61 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree at a residence near Hall Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into an warm and unstable airmass primarily west of I-95. This resulted in bands of showers and thunderstorms that produced localized damaging wind and spotty large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a call for a tree blown down in Williamsport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down in the community of Pinnacle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across southern Illinois, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the afternoon and evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. Areas along and northwest of interstate 57 experienced another interval of dangerous wind chills during the morning and afternoon hours on the 25th while areas to the southeast remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

An upper low and subsequent coastal low pressure brought heavy snow to northeastern North Carolina from January 31 to February 1, 2026. Heavy snow was focused along the coast with lower amounts with westward extent.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow fell from January 31 to February 1, 2026 across Northampton County. Snowfall totals ranged from 4-6 across the county. Several reports of 4 were received with 5.5 reported from just east of the county line in Murfreesboro, NC.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a strong cold front passage with a elevated LLJ in the 50-60 kt range overhead, some of these gusty winds mixed down to the surface. This led to wind gusts peaking at or above 58 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KCRP Corpus Christi gusted to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Discrete thunderstorms in southeast Oklahoma congealed into a mesoscale convective complex as they moved southeast into northern Louisiana early morning of May 9th. The system consisted of clusters and linear segments moving rapidly eastward, while localized cell mergers and brief training occurred within the broader complex. The storms produced widespread severe wind gusts over local coastal waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet station XLKF Lakefront Airport measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 71 mph or 62 kts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted through the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station 2 N Dodge City KKSDODGE57 recorded several instances of high winds, peaking at 56 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree fell across Deer Park Ave in North Babylon blocking road. Time estimated  by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle moved east into southwestern Nebraska during the late evening hours of June 30th. This activity continued into the early morning hours of July 1st tracking across the Sandhills into north central Nebraska.  Strong damaging winds up to 85 MPH were reported at Kingsley Dam.  There were several 60 to 80 MPH wind gusts reported over southwestern Nebraska.

A major winter storm that brought Evansville's 2nd largest snowstorm on record impacted southwest Indiana on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing around midday. After a brief lull overnight, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued into the morning hours of the 25th. A brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the early evening hours. Between 7 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in Spencer County, IN where the greatest mixing had fallen. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Emergency dispatchers fielded 653 calls in Vanderburgh County, IN with deputies and firefighters responding to dozens of traffic accidents and medical emergencies. Near Evansville at Boeke and Vogel, a 52 year old woman who was driving under the influence was stuck in the snow with a tire coming off the rim of their car during the early morning hours of the 25th. Gibson County, IN issued an Emergency Declaration in line with the state of Indiana, in addition to a travel warning. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow that led to travel becoming extremely dangerous. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, government closures.

The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Cobb County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 7, 2025, the county experienced a period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in February. In total, the county sustained approximately 15 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Waves of thunderstorms passed through Central Alabama from April 28 into April 29, affecting predominantly northwestern Central Alabama. A few instances of hail and wind damage occurred from the morning to the evening of April 28 across Marion, Winston, and Lamar counties, with a couple more areas of wind damage reported in Fayette and Walker counties just after midnight. The next evening, a localized area of tree damage occurred in Irondale in Jefferson County, which included a couple trees falling onto homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were knocked down around a cul-de-sac on Stonehenge Place and the neighboring street Wimbledon Ct, with a couple falling on homes and one falling through a fence. Power lines were knocked down as well, with power outages noted in the area by 10 pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The emergency manager relayed a report of a downed tree at braswell mountain road and  brushy mountain road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 1 fell in Bosque County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather moved northeast across south-central and southeast Kansas during the evening hours March 10th. These severe thunderstorms produced numerous reports of large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimated winds of 50 to 60 mph with pea sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry system brought light to moderate snowfall to portions of the region along and especially north and west of I-95. Generally a widespread 1-4 of snowfall occurred in this area between the morning and early afternoon hours, though some localized higher amounts were reported near and north of I-78. Snowfall rates of 0.5-1 per hour caused some travel disruptions to the area. Brief snowfall changed to rain with limited accumulations southeast of I-95.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 1.5-3. The highest reported amount was 3.5 in Warwick Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree limbs were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow showers and flurried developed in the morning hours of the 31st. Briefly heavy snow in the afternoon resulted in some spotty accumulations. Snowfall accumulations ranged from 0.5 to 2 inches across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree along Old Courthouse Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An area of mainly sporadic tree damage was|found across Kokomo from near Berkley Road, along and near west|Sycamore street, to Crown Point Cemetery. Additional Tree damage|was found along east Sycamore street, near Wildcat Creek.||All of this damage was found to be due to straight line winds, as|all damage was blown down in a east to east-northeast direction.|Wind gust that caused the damage are estimated to be in the 80-90|MPH range with a peak gust of 95 MPH possible.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed across Highway 147 South near the Angelina County line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the community of Andrew, a downed tree was observed near Ridgeview Nellis Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and power line damage was observed along Bonds Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three power poles downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was blown down near Dan Ray Tires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Minnesota Road Weather Information System site near Mountain Lake had frequent sustained winds from 40 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms organized over southwest Kentucky during the early morning hours of June 1, 2026. These storms moved south into West Tennessee and along the Tennessee River into northeast Mississippi during the morning hours. The storms fed on strong instability and adequate deep-layer shear to produce isolated wind damage and large hail. This first round of storms left behind an outflow boundary extending from eastern Arkansas across the Memphis metropolitan area into north Mississippi. Storms ignited along this boundary during the late afternoon and evening hours, fueled by strong instability and an upper-level trough overspreading the region. There were several additional reports of large hail and damaging.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were knocked down on Highway 54 north of Greenfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms develop during the afternoon hours across northwest MN, with reports of severe hail and several reports of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 2 inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gusts of 46 mph in Pardeeville and near WI Dells, but may have reached 50 mph over southern Columbia County. Branches down and a small number of power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts downed trees and powerlines in the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: February 18th, brought strong west-southwest winds and extremely dry conditions across much of the area. This along with dead/dormant grasses, resulted in several field and brush fires spreading out of control reported by emergency management.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Iowa City Municipal Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 53 knots at 316 PM local time, within a period of gusts to near 50 kts between 2 PM to 4 PM.  Around that time, the humidity was reported around 13% by the airport. This strong wind helped create a significant wildfire in Johnson County, between Coralville and Iowa City that could be seen on satellite and was reported by emergency management.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Shawnee (SHAW) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm produced quarter-sized hail near Carlisle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front was approaching the region during the evening of May 3rd. Concurrently, a low-level jet was ramping up in the area. This resulted in the development of thunderstorms, some of which became severe. One of these thunderstorms produced large hail in Warren and Lincoln Counties.

Exceptional (D2) Drought shrunk in coverage on April 21, 2026, with a small pocket of Extreme (D3) conditions holding on across the Brush Country. D2 conditions covered just 56% of the area, with D3 only covering 2.17% of the region - down from nearly 95% (D3 and Exceptional, D4 combined) to begin the month. Additional rainfall, mainly on April 18th, as well as a period of much below average temperatures and light rain/drizzle, helped the cause.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A southern fifth of Brooks County remained under Severe (D2) Drought conditions during the April 21-30 timeframe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 85 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.  At one point, there were around 600 customers without power due to downed lines and poles in parts of Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blew down along Thomas Jefferson Parkway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 35 to 55 mph with gusts as high as 75 mph across southeast South Dakota. When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches north of Highway 18, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and very brief blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds were sustained from 30 to 39 mph with gusts as high as 53 mph near Howard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather moved northeast across south-central and southeast Kansas during the evening hours March 10th. These severe thunderstorms produced numerous reports of large hail and damaging winds.

Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm chaser report of a large tree down in Friend, NE. Wind speeds estimated at 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Waves of thunderstorms passed through Central Alabama from April 28 into April 29, affecting predominantly northwestern Central Alabama. A few instances of hail and wind damage occurred from the morning to the evening of April 28 across Marion, Winston, and Lamar counties, with a couple more areas of wind damage reported in Fayette and Walker counties just after midnight. The next evening, a localized area of tree damage occurred in Irondale in Jefferson County, which included a couple trees falling onto homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At Guthrie Smith Park, a tin roof was blown off a two-story concession stand, with numerous concrete cinder blocks blown off the second story as well. Elsewhere in the park, metal fencing was damaged, bleachers were overturned, and a few trees were downed. Playground equipment and batting nets were also damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm moved across the state between January 23rd and January 25th. Mixed precipitation was observed with significant accumulations of sleet and snow over the northern two-thirds of the state and freezing rain mixed with sleet over the southern third of the state. A very cold air mass followed this event prolonging accumulations to well beyond a weeks time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy accumulation of mostly sleet led to the collapse of the roof portion of a large storage shed for the Saline County Road Department.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto power lines near Perry, Ohio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. Cost of debris cleanup in Hyde county alone topped out at 1.4 million dollars. ||Electrical infrastructure was severely disrupted, causing $2.4 million in utility distribution damage across Hyde and Hand counties. Power was knocked out to 1,072 residents in Hyde County (94% of the county). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Inland Northwest region was impacted by two winter storm systems during February 16 through 19. A cold front brought lower snow levels to the valley floors. This storm was followed by a warm and moist weather system from California. While most locations had 1 to 3 inches, a few locations received 4 to 6 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported 5.5 inches 2 miles northwest of Pullman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mercer County reported significant ice accumulation of 0.50 to 0.75 inches. This ice accumulation resulted in numerous instances of tree damage. Mercer County also received 2 to 3 inches of snow and sleet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island. In Connecticut winds were generally lighter and not damaging with snowfall amounts in the 8 to 20 inch range. The highest amounts in Connecticut were in the eastern part of the state. Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 18 to 24 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest reports included 27.7 inches in Killingly and 27 inches in Wauregan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Large scale upper level troughing with two separate embedded upper level lows progressed across the region late June. The colder core, which actually ended up being the southern of the two, moved across Southwest Montana and resulted in snow levels falling to below 6,000ft at times as heaviest precipitation moved over the area. Heavy snow developed near and above pass level in northwest Beaverhead County, resulting in nearly 2 feet of snow near the peaks close to the ID border.||Meanwhile further north under the second upper low, a strong surface low ended up developing near the Hi-Line, which resulted in strong winds in a few zones before the surface low filled/weakened. ||Strong upper level support further north resulted in widespread heavy rains, with additional upslope forcing along the Rocky Mountain Front, which resulted in some flooding in Glacier NP June 29.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KHVR Havre Airport measured a 70 mph gust. Other sensors in this zone that measured a 58+ mph gust include EW1937 Goldstone and FW1664 Hingham.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down near the intersection of North Washington and Hudson Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through North Dakota, bringing strong winds to the state. Showers along the front aided in mixing down non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts. The strongest wind gust of 68 mph was reported near Ray in Williams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Williston Airport ASOS reported wind gusts to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.

Persistent drought continued into February in northern and central Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of February was 21 inches at the Caribou office, gradually increasing to 26 inches by February 24th. All climate sites recorded below average precipitation, with generally 1.5 - 2.0 inch deficits. At the end of January, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In February,  drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Coastal Hancock led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late January and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The city of Seymour had some street flooding due to heavy rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An occluded area of low pressure traveled across the Great Lakes, NY and New England during the night of February 20th with a new surface low developing off of the Cape cod coast by the early morning hours of February 21st.||Snow overspread northern NY during the afternoon hours and quickly became heavy at times during the late afternoon and evening hours with snowfall rates in excess of 1 inch per hour at times. Snow ended during the early overnight hours of February 21st. Snowfall totals across the region ranged from 3 to 5 inches across St. Lawrence county to 5 to 9 inches across the rest of northern NY. Impacts were generally travel related due to the timing of the heavuest snowfall during the evneing commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across the area were 4 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) swept across portions of central, southern and eastern Oklahoma on the morning of the 8th. This convective system was tied to the passage of a compact upper wave across the region, resulting in very strong wind fields within a weakly unstable boundary layer. In addition to sporadic pockets of thunderstorm wind damage, and generally sub-severe hail, a few tornadoes occurred in a corridor from near Purcell, OK to Shawnee, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of damaging winds occurred from just east of Union City to near the intersection of Southwest 44th Street and Banner Road. Several large outbuildings lost metal roof decking and trees were damaged. Both the wind path and event time are estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -40F were observed on the 23rd and 24th, and as low as -30F on the 25th and 26th. Key impacts: school and business closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite occasional precipitation episodes, especially across portions of northern Oklahoma and the eastern Red River Valley during the middle of the month, near to slightly below-average precipitation totals were observed for February 2026. This led to continued and slowly expanding drought in areas along and south of Interstate 40 in Oklahoma and adjacent western-north Texas.

Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.
