EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May started with severe drought (D2) present across much of eastern WV, including: Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and most of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Moderate drought (D1) also persisted across most of western and north-central WV, with the exception of Pleasants, Wood, northwest Jackson, northern Mason, western Ritchie, western Tyler, and western Wirt counties where conditions were merely abnormally dry (D0). Only minimal changes to D0 and D1 occurred in the second week of the month. D2, however, spread out across all of Boone and Kanawha counties; most of Lincoln, Logan, and Putnam counties; and portions of eastern Cabell, southern Jackson, southern Roane, and eastern Wayne counties. Conditions worsened even more the following week, as D2 engulfed most of southern, central, and eastern West Virginia, and a sliver of extreme drought (D3) crept into eastern McDowell, southeast Raleigh, and eastern Wyoming counties. Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth. Fortunately, enough precipitation fell at the end of the month to eradicate D3 and confine D2 to mainly Boone, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Nicholas, Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Raleigh, Webster, Wyoming, southern Braxton, eastern Lincoln, southern Roane, and southern Wayne. D1 improved to D0 in southern Tyler, Doddridge, northern Harrison, northern Taylor, part of northern Barbour, Ritchie, Wirt, northwest Gilmer, northern Calhoun, northern Roane, northern Jackson, northwest Mason, northwest Cabell, and part of northern Wayne. Meanwhile, drought was completely eliminated from counties, or at least portions of counties, bordering the Ohio River.||Generally less than an inch of rain fell during the first week of May. Around an inch or less accumulated during the second week. During the third week of the month, much of the area received around an inch and a half or less of rain, though a strip of up to two inches fell along the Ohio River. More substantial precipitation occurred at the end of the month, when one to three inches of rain fell to the south of I-64 and one and a half to over four inches fell to the north of I-64. Highest amounts were observed across portions of Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Taylor, Randolph, and Upshur counties. Multiple rounds of rain during this time finally allowed for significant improvement to drought conditions, particularly across the northern and western part of the state.||The six climate sites in West Virginia were evenly split between above and below normal total precipitation for the month, with Beckley, Charleston, and Elkins on the below normal side and Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg on the above normal side. On the 22nd, Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg each received enough rain to break their existing daily precipitation records. Beckley was also able to tie a standing daily precipitation record on the 24th of the month.

From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.

Nine homeless people and dog were rescued in the Manoa-Palolo Stream near Kaimuki High School due to rapidly rising stream levels. Pearl Highlands shopping center also had flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station Berman Storm Water - KFLJACKS5112 measured 2.36 inches of rainfall between 9:09pm to 10:15pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With low pressure strengthening and tracking northeastward towards Chicago, the Quad State region experienced breezy southerly to southeasterly winds throughout the daytime hours. Spotty wind gusts to 40+mph were observed in Southern Illinois, with the strongest gust measured 48mph at the KMDH ASOS site northwest of Carbondale. Showers and a few thunderstorms moved eastward across Southern Illinois during the late afternoon hours.

An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oklahoma City Will Rogers International Airport (KOKC) observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 5 to 6 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.

Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on Sycamore Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources reported golf ball to baseball sized hail was falling in Dublin for nearly 10 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on Farmington Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A car was stranded due to flooding waters at the intersection of PR-114 and PR-319, near km 1.5.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A portion of a high-rise apartment complex's roof was blown-off along Park Fulton Oval in Cleveland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple segments of heavy showers and a few thunderstorms moved across north Alabama during the evening hours.  One segment moved northeast during the late evening from central into northeast Alabama which exhibited a bow echo. This resulted in a power pole being snapped and trees being knocked down in Jackson and Marshall Counties.  A couple of trees were also knocked down blocking roads in Lauderdale and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 50 Clemons Road, a tree was knocked down into the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook report relayed 2 inch hail in Grand Saline.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of heavy rainfall occurred across portions of north central Kansas on 4/10 and 4/11. This resulted in up to 11 inches of rainfall across portions of Marshall county by the early morning hours on 4/11. Roads were closed in the area and several people were stranded at a campground.  Later in the afternoon, additional severe storms caused large hail to around a half dollar size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Nemaha River is out of its banks and 146th street is closed west of highway 63.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mixed precipitation briefly swept through southeast Ohio on March 2nd in the midst of a passing disturbance. These showers arrived into the area just before dawn when temperatures were still below freezing, keeping hydrometeors as wintry precipitation before fully transitioning over to rain in the afternoon. Local members of the public noted freezing rain during the morning, causing a glaze of ice to form along cars. Additionally, a cooperative observer in Perry County measured an inch of snow during this brief stint of winter weather.

A cold front passing through the region generated high winds, with 20 weather stations recording a peak wind of 58 mph or greater. A peak wind of 66 mph was measured at the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 13 miles east of Eureka, while the SDDOT RWIS near Ridgeview and the Grand River RAWS both topped out at 65 mph.

During the morning of June 7th, training thunderstorms caused flooding across nearly the entire southern half of Boone County. Most of the flooding consisted of inches of water over roadways and flooded creeks. That afternoon through evening, additional thunderstorms exacerbated the problem, creating even more dangerous conditions through the morning of the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were numerous reports of flash flooding between California and High Point, including flooded yards and roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near normal precipitation in April kept drought conditions mainly in Severe(D2) drought category or better.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The drought conditions across the zone ranged from Severe(D2) west to Abnormally Dry(D0) over the southeast. The Deming Airport reported a trace of precipitation which was 0.21 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Leflore County intensified from D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooded roads across the county. Total rainfall for the event was around 3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief EF-0 tornado dropped from locally lower ceilings within a bookend vortex embedded in the QLCS near Cecil Harden Lake, 1.3 miles southeast of the Hollandsburg community.  The bookend vortex crossed the lake, spawning the weak spin-up one-quarter mile south of the lake's southeastern shoreline;  along its 900-foot track, the tornado then crossed residential roads East Mallard Drive and South Ebert Drive, before ending 400 feet south of the lake's shore.||Drone imagery showed clear convergence of downed trees in a grove between Meadows Lane and Mallard Drive;  30 to 40 additional trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path.  Incident structural damage was limited to minor siding loss.  The tornado's damage was mainly vegetation, with peak ind gusts of 85 mph for the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds caused a tree to fall on a house in White Bluff which caused a gas leak on Johnny Hall Road. No injuries were reported. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Great Lakes region, producing strong thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A property sustained minor roof damage and also had multiple trees uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms moved across lower Michigan late on April 13th into the early morning hours of April 14th.  Large hail was common with limited damaging winds. Moderate to heavy rain occurred along with some localized inconvenient flooding with one to three inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Gordon County entered January under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Following a period of improvement, the county saw a reduction in drought intensity, officially falling below the D2 drought thresholds on January 12. This event, which originally reached the D2 threshold on December 30, 2025, peaked in both spatial extent and intensity on the same day. In total, the county sustained two weeks of D2 conditions during this brief event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms took place during the afternoon and evening hours on the 22nd. A remnant mesoscale convective vortex, or MCV, crossed across Arkansas, Tennessee, and portions of Alabama and Georgia. Ahead of the MCV, strengthening winds aloft helped fuel thunderstorms. First round was of storms produced only isolated wind damage. Second round presented a strongly bowed cluster of storms which produced significant wind damage in portions of southeastern Tennessee, primarily in Hamilton County. Damages were north of at least $2 million.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree blown down by severe thunderstorm wind gusts along Highway 68.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof damaged at Hidden Lakes and numerous trees downed at and near Hidden Lakes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This weak tornado touched down near Highway 43 and Matlock Road in eastern Madison county and tracked 4.6 miles and dissipated at Red Dog Road in western Leake County. Tree damage, from a handful of uprooted trees, were the main damage at the very beginning of the path. It crossed into Leake County at Forest Grove Road. The remaining damage was mostly small and large limbs blown down along Red Dog Road and the Natchez Trace. One large limb downed a power line. The total path length across Madison and Leake counties was 4.6 miles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed and moved into northern New Jersey, producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees and wires down in Morristown. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought sleet/snow to much of west central Texas. Some freezing rain resulted in a light glaze of ice across the Northwest Hill Country. The snow/sleet amounts ranged from 1 to 4 inches across the northern 2/3 of the area. The winter storm caused disruptions to travel and one fatality due to an accident on Interstate 10 east of Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 2 to 4 inches of snow/sleet across Coke County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed ahead of a cold front across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 12. These storms produced damaging winds as they moved east.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees fell down onto Woodford Road in Woodford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend, persistent dry conditions through late January led to worsening drought and critically low soil moisture, limiting agricultural progress and stressing rangeland. Periods of unseasonably warm weather were followed by hard freezes and a winter storm, though precipitation was generally limited, with only modest rainfall of up to around an inch in parts of the Coastal Bend providing minor short-term improvement to soil moisture. Producers largely completed field preparation but delayed spring planting due to insufficient moisture for germination. Winter pastures and forage growth struggled under the dry conditions, resulting in poor to fair range conditions and increased reliance on hay and supplemental feed for livestock. While citrus and cool-season vegetable harvests continued, drought stress remained a concern for crop development and pasture recovery, and additional rainfall will be needed to improve soil moisture and support the upcoming planting season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms that developed produced wind gusts across Campbell county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Additional peak wind gust measured on personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gusts of 57-62 from near Platteville to Darlington. Frequent wind gusts in the 50 mph range across the county. Many branches down and a small number of power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree limb was knocked down and a small tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down at the intersection of Slocum Boulevard and McCraken Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree fell onto power lines in Churchville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms that moved through Arkansas. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced a number of damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oklahoma Mesonet station near Burbank measured thunderstorm wind gusts up to 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the 5 above to 2 below zero range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped as low as 1 above zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo was received of aspen trees on a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm moved across a portion of northeast Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto an outbuilding on Rocky Ridge Lane near Jolly Ridge Road and Oakridge Circle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous social media videos depicting street flooding throughout the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front interacting with an unseasonably warm early January airmass with temperatures in the lower to middle 60s triggered a couple lines of strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of January 8th.  A few of the storms produced minor wind damage in Tazewell County and toppled two semis further east in Champaign County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A light pole was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large northeast swell brought waves in excess of twenty five feet over north facing areas of the Big Island. This led to localized coastal flooding impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bayfront Highway was closed due to the high surf. The alternate, Kamehameha Hwy, had one lane closed in each direction in the vicinity of Bishop St. due to ponding water on the roadway from high surf. Several beachfront parks were closed as well due to high surf such as Kolekole and Keaukaha beach park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were snapped and uprooted in the Ellis Ridge and Chenoweth Creek area. One tree fell and damaged a shed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds across northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large trees were blown down on power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours in north Alabama. A couple of these storms moved northeast into southern middle Tennessee during the evening hours producing large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported and confirmed by EMA via video and photos in southwest Lincoln County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak continued into the first couple days of February. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, as it extends well back into January. For portions of western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. For the I-95 corridor, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

A slow moving upper level disturbance over northern Mexico and the Desert Southwest combined with moist surface southeast flow resulting in thunderstorm development across central and eastern New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours. Some storms resulted in severe hail at Chacon, severe thunderstorm wind gusts near Sumner Lake and Endee on June 2nd and some burn scar flash flooding in Ruidoso on June 3rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter along State Highway 4 at mile marker 40 near the Valles Caldera Preserve entry observed penny size hail with overall accumulations just under an inch deep from a strong thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed trees along Saunders Ferry Road in Hendersonville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level shortwave moved over Wyoming, accompanied by a jet streak. The surface dew points remained low, resulting in large dew point depressions. The result was many severe thunderstorms that produced wind gusts in excess of 58 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts as high as 66 mph were reported east of Pinedale. In Pinedale, there was a small cinder block structure that was under renovation with many of the interior walls and roof removed by construction crews. The building was open to the weather, and this wind event blew down the remaining exterior walls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong upper level troughing diving southeastward from central BC toward southern AB/SK resulted in a sharp transition to strong zonal flow aloft across the Northern Rockies April 7. Favorable timing of the system, arriving during the day, allowed for daytime mixing to translate stronger gusts to the surface in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: RAWS station WRSM8 Wise River measured a gust of 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-wave severe event unfolded from the afternoon of January 9 through the morning of January 10. While the first wave featured no severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall over Birmingham led to numerous flooding issues. Early the next morning, additional heavy rainfall led to more flooding issues in parts of Jefferson, Shelby, and St. Clair counties. A bowing line segment moved across Marengo, Dallas, Autauga, Elmore, Montgomery, and Lee counties, with scattered instances of wind damage. In addition, a cell in advance of the main QLCS produced an EF-0 tornado in northern Cleburne County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees and power lines were downed around Pell City, including Cook Springs Rd, Mountain Top Loop Rd, Wolf Creek Rd, and Old Coal City Rd at Florida Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds in Eagle Rock near Ball Park Road. Four homes experienced some structural damage from fallen trees, and one vehicle was entirely crushed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Municipal police closed vehicular passage at Conde de Caspe (N 59) bridge due to Rio Culebrinas (river) overflowing its banks. The nearby Torres Pino street is completely inundated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large cyclonic trough occupying the eastern third of the US was the instigating force behind snow showers and northwest orographic snow. This snow resulted in light snow at lower elevations, with several inches of accumulating snow at higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow yielded 1 inch of accumulation on the southwestern edge of Hancock County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex of thunderstorms developed across portions of north-central Kansas during the late afternoon hours of June 8th. These thunderstorms rapidly intensified and moved south and southeast across the I-70 corridor. Widespread wind damage occurred across portions of Lincoln, Ellsworth, Saline, McPherson, Marion, and Chase counties. In fact, a wind gust of 113 mph was measured at the Salina Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report of several trees down in Durham. Time was estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions,  Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural  activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred, despite a significant snow event, which produced little changed in drought conditions through the month leaving Severe (D2) and Moderate (D1) drought along with Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on MD-109 Old Hundred Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of May saw below normal precipitation through the Four Corners region and portions of the central highlands of New Mexico, while areas along the Rio Grande Valley, southwestern, and eastern NM saw near to above normal precipitation. Mean temperatures trended near to slightly above normal through western NM and near to slightly below normal across eastern NM. This led to a modest expansion of extreme drought conditions across western NM and portions of the eastern plains of NM along the TX border. Gaps of severe drought through the northern mountains were filled in. Due to ongoing drought conditions and record low snowpack the previous winter, the Rio Grande dried up through the Albuquerque metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme and severe drought persisted over the northern and southern portions of the zone respectively.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

Thunderstorms moved east and southeast into eastern Oklahoma during the morning and early afternoon of the 24th. Locally heavy rainfall occurred in some places, which resulted in isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of E 91st Street S were flooded near S 145th East Avenue, and several vehicles were stranded in the flood water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported 1.5 inch hail south of Cockrell Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large branches blew down near the intersection of Key Street and North Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong trough moving into the Rockies created a long duration high wind event across most of southeast Wyoming and parts of western Nebraska. A strong sea level pressure gradient lead to strengthening winds aloft, with strong subsidence and mountain waves helping get these strong winds down to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent gust of 50 to 60 MPH were recorded in the Laramie Valley. A maximum gust of 68 MPH from the Quealy Dome WYDOT sensor along Interstate 80 was recorded at 6:46 AM MDT on 4/23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: North Sand Branch left its banks and flooded North Sand Branch Road. On Upper Rock Creek Road, a house and yard flooded, the road flooded, and flood waters were strong enough to push an SUV. McDowell Hollow Road was closed due to flash flooding. Sections of Route 3 between Whitesville and Glen Daniel also flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Southeast Michigan during the late afternoon and early evening of April 4. This triggered two lines of thunderstorms that caused pockets of damage south of I-94. The most significant storm occurred in Wayne County, producing an EF-1 tornado in Van Buren Township. The system also dumped 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some areas seeing up to 4 inches. Because the region had already received 3 to 5 inches over the previous five days, these additional downpours caused the Tittabawassee, Clinton, and Flint rivers to overflow. In addition, significant localized flooding occurred on already saturated ground, with the hardest-hit area being northwest Oakland County, specifically in and around Holly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Metal tower attached to the north side and on top of the grain elevators blown east and collapsed on the train tracks in front of the grain elevators. Tarp roofing damage also noted across the street on Lynch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLAF ASOS measured a 53 kt thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm temperatures, very low humidity, breezy southwesterly winds and dry fuels combined to create conditions favorable for fire starts and spread across Oklahoma on the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 41 Road Fire burned 341 acres across far western Woodward County, northeast of Quinlan. The fire also likely burned into portions of far northwestern Major County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall totals across northern Oconto County included 29 inches near Hayes and 26 inches in Mountain.  In addition, winds gusting to 40 to 50 mph caused blizzard conditions on Monday March 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary, training storm sat over southeast MA and RI and dropped 4+ inches of rain causing flash flooding. Several roads were flooded with cars submerged.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several vehicles were submerged in floodwaters on Plymouth Ave in Fall River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Repeated rounds of rainfall throughout May significantly improved drought conditions across South Texas and the Coastal Bend. Early-month rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches along the Coastal Bend and 1 to 10 inches across South Texas, with additional rainfall continuing through mid-May. Several storms produced strong winds, hail, and tornado warnings, resulting in localized damage. A more significant rainfall event occurred during the last week of May, when multiple storm systems produced widespread totals of 1 to 12 inches, with localized amounts exceeding 5 inches along portions of the Coastal Bend. The heavy rainfall led to localized creek flooding and more widespread flooding in portions of Refugio County. By month's end, topsoil and subsoil moisture had improved from short to surplus in many locations, substantially alleviating drought impacts and improving rangeland, pasture, and water availability across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 5/26, ending inclusion in Storm Data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down at Kent Street and Sidney Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast Georgia with significant snow accumulations and very cold wind chill temperatures. An area of low pressure shifted off the Southeast coast while deepening, ushering in a very cold air mass across the region. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type. Rain quickly transitioned to snow during the afternoon hours, which continued into the evening before ending. Most of the snow accumulation impacted areas along and north of Interstate 16, with the highest amounts reported across Screven, Bulloch, and Effingham counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. The wind chill temperature first fell below 10 degrees at the Claxton Airport (KCWV) at 20:35 EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 6 to 8 inches of snow across Champaign County...including 7.6 inches in Ogden.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the 5 above to 1 above zero range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind chill temperature dropped as low as 1 degree above zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding. 5.11 inches of rain was measured in Marshall in Central Harrison County from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several cars were stalled in high water on King Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 100-mph impacted the Chesterland area. Radar data indicate this was a rare anticyclonic tornado. The tornado began just northeast of the intersection of Watt Road and Fairmount Road, where a large barn had its roof collapse. As the tornado moved generally eastward, it downed several large pine trees onto a house along Fairmount Road, about halfway between Watt and Sperry Roads, but there was no obvious damage to the home. A power pole was snapped in half at this same location. Farther east along Fairmount Road, the tornado downed additional large pine trees. One of the trees fell onto a home and caused some roof and gutter damage. The tornado ended soon thereafter, just west-northwest of the intersection of Fairmount and Rockhaven Roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of several trees, power lines and power poles downed across Cherry Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.

For the second time in a week, a winter storm impacted the Piedmont and foothills of South Carolina as an area of low pressure intensified across the Deep South. In this case, the bulk of the precipitation fell as snow. Snow began falling during the pre-dawn hours of the 31st and continued through much of the day. By the time the snow tapered off during the evening, 4 to 7 inches were reported across much of the area, with locally higher amounts east of I-77.

A line of strong thunderstorms moved across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois and produced 50+ mph winds, causing some areas of damage to trees, roofs, and a few outbuildings.  The line of very gradually fading storms produced surges of straight-line wind damage. These were most pronounced to the immediate south of mesovortices (small scale circulations within the thunderstorm line that can in themselves result in tornadoes). Based on the nature of damage, observations, and radar, these reflect 65-80 mph wind gusts.||Two main areas of damage that experienced enhanced wind surges were:  1.) Kalona, IA (Washington Co)  and 2.) the east-southeast side of Iowa City (Johnson County).||A third area of isolated wind damage from Miles to Sabula, IA (Jackson County) was a little different in that it was much more of an outflow surging from decaying storms, but again straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 40 by 90 feet shed was destroyed. Trees damaged in town. The time was estimated using radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree in roadway blocking all lanes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions developed across northern Illinois on June 29th and continued on June 30th as well into early July. Peak heat index values ranged from 100 to 105 for most areas on both days with high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s.
A few pop up thunderstorms developed in the afternoon over Delaware, producing damaging wind gusts and frequent lightning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A utility pole struck by lightning. Pole needs to be replaced. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down at Leon Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong ridge of high pressure set up across much of the western United States and brought an long period of record breaking warmth. The most impressive stretch was from March 18 through March 21. In total, 71 new daily record high temperatures were set out of a possible 126 high temperatures at RIW CLI sites (longer term climate sites), greater than half of the daily highs. Every location was at least 10 degrees above normal through the period. Every location had their all time warmest period for these two weeks, with three locations; the Riverton Airport, the Sweetwater County airport near Rock Springs, and the Lander airport; more than 8 degrees above the previous warmest period. All locations set their all time high temperature March multiple times in this stretch. Six locations had their earliest 80 degree high temperature, with four stations having their first 80 degree or greater March high temperatures in station history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Lander airport experienced record warmth for most of the second half of March. Daily average temperatures from March 17 though March 30 were more than 17 degrees above seasonal normals, with every day above normal. Nine days were more thn 15 degrees above normal. Nine daily record high temperatures were set, including five days in a row from March 17 to March 21. The old monthly high temperature of 76 degrees was broken four times, including three days in a row from March 19 to 21. There were three days of highs in the 80s, the first three in station history. The high of 80 degrees on March 19 was the earliest 80 degree temperature by 22 days. Records at Lander date back to 1892.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. This MCS moved across southeast Louisiana late that night into the early morning hours of April 25th, producing scattered damaging wind gusts. Several reports of thunderstorm wind damage occurred across the area, mainly from downed trees and large limbs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A comment on a facebook post by local broadcast media showed a tree downed by thunderstorm winds in Central.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 26th an approaching cold front associated with an upper level shortwave trough brought strong shear and modest mid level instability to New Hampshire.  Daytime heating was near seasonable norms, but still enough to create amble low level instability as highs reached the lower 80s.  A few long track storms created a swath of hail and wind damage from Sullivan to Rockingham Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds gusted up to 65 mph in South Hampton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary cold front from an associated upper-level low pressure system tracking from the Ohio Valley allowed for snow shower development during the morning hours of January 11th. Clear skies with cold advection aloft allowed for meager, but sufficient, instability across the western half of Pennsylvania in an environment of ample lift and moisture to produce snow squalls. These snow squalls produced multiple instances of visibility below one-quarter of a mile, with multiple accidents with one reported on US Route 6 in McKean County and another accident on US Route 322 near Port Matilda. No injuries were reported from these accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall moved across Cambria County on the morning of January 11, 2026. The ASOS at the John Murtha Johnstown Cambria County Airport reported a visibility drop to one quarter of a mile in heavy snow as the squall moved through.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds, gusting to 60 MPH, were reported at the Shepard Mesa Road sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

A surface low lifted into the central US with a deformation zone setting up across central Iowa, resulting in a band of heavy snow bisecting the state. Light precipitation fell ahead of the main deformation zone, however dry air and warm temperatures meant this largely fell as rain to start. The main deformation zone set up across Iowa in the afternoon with rain transitioning over to snow and temperatures fell. Heaviest snow fell through the overnight with rates over one inch per hour at times. Snow tapered off quickly through the morning hours. Roads across central Iowa were snow covered with impacts to the morning commute on the 20th, including an accident with injury. Operations were also paused overnight at the Des Moines airport.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from October 2025 through the first week of January 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Desoto, Red River, Grant, and La Salle Parishes in North Louisiana from the second week of January through the end of the month. During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 5-8 inches, which was only 25-30% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also noted especially as lower humidities to end the year accelerated the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.
Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.
Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down along the intersection of I-64 and Parham Road near mile marker 181.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed across the city of Jacksonville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in western Maryland across Garrett and western Allegany counties where 3 to upwards of 15 inches of snow fell. A secondary max associated with an inverted trough was observed from the Catoctins down to northern Montgomery county where 3 to 8 inches fell. Upwards of 12 inches were observed across the Catoctins. Another max of 3 to 6 inches was observed across Calvert and St. Mary's counties. The final max was Carroll to Cecil counties where 4 to 9 inches fell. Elsewhere across the DC and Baltimore metro, there was a relative minimum of 2 to 4 inches.
