Very little snow fell across eastern Allegany into far western Washington County.
Immediately following the strong winds, snow enveloped much of the state. Many areas saw 6 to 15 inches of snow across the lower elevations, much higher in the mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received 8 to 14 inches across multiple locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 30 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 55 to 65 mph across southwest Minnesota.  When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted as high as 64 mph at Beaver Creek and 49 mph at Luverne. These winds combined with periods of light snowfall which totaled around 1 inch to produce visibility briefly as low as one-quarter to one-half mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on March 14th, a narrow band of snow developed across portions of southeast MN with snowfall rates rapidly increasing through the early morning hours on March 15th. Near I-90, a band of heavy sleet occurred that transitioned over to snow near daybreak. Overall, snowfall totals of over a foot were noted in Winona, Olmsted, Dodge and Wabasha counties with even amounts over 18 inches in Wabasha County. After a brief lull during the late morning, a secondary round of snow moved in for the afternoon and into the overnight hours on March 15th bringing additional accumulations accompanied with gusty winds which resulted in localized whiteout conditions. One vehicle accident occurred in Winona County after the snow departed on March 16th resulting in 3 non-life threatening injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This winter storm brought snowfall totals ranging from 16 to 25 inches across Wabasha County. The highest reported snowfall total in the county was in Kellogg where 25 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure moved into the Great Lakes on March 16th and into northern Quebec Canada by the morning of March 17th. This storm brought blizzard conditions across the MN,WI and the western Great Lakes while the sharp cold front brought severe weather outbreaks from TX/OK eastward to the Atlantic coast.||Strong southerly winds, ahead of the low pressure, during the early morning hours of March 16th brought 40 to 50 mph wind gusts across VT. A sharp cold front associated with the strong low pressure moved across VT during the early morning hours of March 17th a short duration of 40-50+ mph wind gusts that resulted in several reports of tree limbs/trees on utility lines causing 15,000 customers without power, mainly across the spine of the Green Mountains eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in the 40-50 mph with the passage of the sharp cold front during the early morning hours. Some isolated to scattered power outages reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist air mass north of a stalled warm front resulted in widespread dense fog late on January 6th and early on January 7th. The fog dissipated after sunrise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Trenton-Mercer Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. The rate of falling and blowing snow reduced visibility to whiteout conditions, making many roadways impassible. Snow lingered for several hours before finally dissipating the afternoon of the following day. Storm total snowfall ranged between a few inches up to 9.5 inches.||The highest measured snowfall totals from this event are:|9.5 inches ENE of Prior Lake (Scott)|8.5 inches in Shorewood (Hennepin)|7.7 inches in Waconia (Carver)|7.0 inches 1 E of Granite Falls (Chippewa)|7.0 inches 3 SSW of Elko New Market (Rice).||The strongest wind gusts measured from this event were: |50 mph at Canby Municipal Airport (Yellow Medicine)|48 mph at Redwood Falls Municipal Airport (Redwood)|48 mph at New Ulm Municipal Airport (Brown)|44 mph at Mankato Regional Airport (Blue Earth).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall with rates near one inch per hour produced 6 to 9 inches across the county. CoCoRaHS observers in Victoria measured 7.7 inches, 7.5 inches in Chanhassen, and 7.0 inches in Excelsior.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in wind damage and a large number of power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Maple tree down and golf cart blown over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

The area was the western periphery of a broad area of high pressure.  A sea breeze boundary moved inland and encountered a warm and unstable airmass resulting in thunderstorm development.  A thunderstorm in Jackson County produced severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed over Valley Forge Rd. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Easterly flow and a moist air mass under high pressure allowed areas of dense fog to form late on June 28th and early on June 29th. The fog dissipated shortly after sunrise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Brandywine Regional Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather system moved into Wyoming and mixed strong winds aloft down to the surface, bringing high wind to much of central Wyoming. The highest wind occurred in the mountains, with a maximum wind gust of 95 mph at Red Canyon over South Pass in the Wind River Range. In the lower elevations, some notable wind gusts included 74 mph at the Lander Airport, 75 mph at Twenty Mile Hill to the north of Casper, 75 mph in Clark, and 69 mph near Buffalo.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High wind occurred in southern Johnson County. The maximum wind gust recorded was 71 mph at Tisdale Mountain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed western Massachusetts during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the morning and afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 46 mph wind gust at the Pittsfield Municipal Airport.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 15 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 30 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as low as 10 degrees below zero) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 25 degrees below zero.
Scattered severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds across northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power lines and poles were blown down on Weis  Road. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The western edge of an area of low clouds descended to the ground, creating an area of dense fog, for some locations east of MT-Highway 24.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Poplar airport AWOS (KPO1) reported visibility of 1/2 mile or less for 7 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in the Piedmont of Virginia. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at the 10000 Block of River Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported quarter sized hail 2 miles south-southeast of Wabasha.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Storm Survey determined an EF-1 tornado occurred along Holly Road with estimated maximum wind speeds of 90 to 100 mph. A narrow path of damage began shortly beyond the intersection of Route 404 and Holly Road and continued east towards the intersection of Holly Road and Central Avenue. The damage path began at two residences. One residence had minor roof damage. At the other residence, the roof of a barn was blown off along with all walls collapsed. Debris from the barn was thrown over a quarter mile away into open fields. There was a horse trailer that was thrown across the yard and flipped multiple times. Multiple windows on the first floor of the house were blown out. Significant tree damage was then observed beyond both of these properties as multiple large softwood trees were uprooted with large branches also snapped. Damage continued to the east with multiple large tree branches snapped in a more wooded area. Near the intersection with Central Avenue, the damage ended with multiple trees snapped or uprooted in this area marking the end of the damage path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Straight-line winds ripped shingles off a house on CR 604.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 5 to 7 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered tree limbs were blown down along County Road 300 S. Some roof shingles were blown off of a house and a few roof panels were blown off of a barn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed along a trough axis during the evening hours on June 6, resulting in multiple reports of thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree was blown into wires with wires sparking.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably warm and humid airmass developed across central Illinois on March 26, 2026, with some locations recording record high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s. Dewpoints also surged into the lower 60s. As a cold front approached during the evening, scattered to widespread strong to severe storms developed along and ahead of the front, primarily in areas north of I-70. These storms produced hail as large as golf balls, as well as a few wind damage reports.

The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, D2 (Severe Drought) conditions returned to Monroe County on January 13. This degradation followed a brief mid-winter reprieve, which had interrupted an initial four-week period of Severe Drought that began on November 18. By the end of January, the county had recorded a cumulative total of seven weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the drought���s inception in the fall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed along an Arctic front crossing the region late on the 15th. The low tracked from southern Piscataquis county to northern Washington county exiting across New Brunswick during the morning of the 16th. Snow developed to the north of the low track during the early morning hours of the 16th...persisting into the afternoon. The greatest snow accumulations occurred across northern portions of Aroostook county where total snow accumulations generally ranged from 4 to 6 inches...locally up to around 8 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 6 inches north...to 2 to 4 inches south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking all of Old Dairy Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms tracked across north central and northeast Colorado with wind gusts up to 68 mph and hail up to one inch in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was from mPing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Remnants from Tropical Storm Arthur produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding, including some significant flash flooding, across portions of central and southern Mississippi. Multiple roads were flooded in the area and several cars had become stranded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A foot of water was over Smith County Roads 131A and 514A north of White Oak.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Corn stripped and laid flat. Small shed destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball-size in Kipton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed power lines all over Centralia. Power poles and trees sustained damage as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm moved across Hopkinsville with the highest concentration of damage located near 10th and 12th St. A roof was blown off a garage. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St. Shingles of a roof were blown off. Several more homes had more minor roof or siding damage. Power poles were downed including on Belmont St. Numerous trees were damaged or downed including on 9th St and 68/80. Wires were downed on McLean Ave and Hope St. Emergency management, trained spotters, law enforcement, and broadcast media provided numerous reports for this part of the city.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of rain/freezing rain/snow mix which lasted several hours each. A CoCoRaHS observer in Henderson reported a light dusting of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening of Thursday March 5th, a supercell thunderstorm tracked out of northern Oklahoma and into southern Kansas. As the storm crossed into Kansas, the rotation strengthened and eventually produced a couple of tornadoes over western Sumner County. One tornado damaged a few farm outbuildings, multiple trees and overturned a pumpjack. It was rated an EF-2. The other tornado damaged farm outbuildings and utility poles. Thankfully there were no injuries or fatalities. The storm produced damaging straightline winds as well. ||Additional storms developed across central Kansas with up to nickel to quarter sized hail reported. There were storms with winds around 60 mph as well including one that damaged a cedar tree.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report of a large eastern red cedar tree was snapped at six feet above the ground. The time is estimated from radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 19th afternoon, an unstable airmass ahead of an approaching surface trough triggered a cluster of severe thunderstorms across central Indiana.  Convection initially intensified over the western and northern portions of the Indianapolis metropolitan area shortly after 1500 EST, capitalizing on strong low-to-mid level wind shear. These storms quickly organized into severe segments that tracked eastward and southward, producing a concentrated swath of damaging straight-line winds across Hendricks, Hamilton, Delaware, and Bartholomew counties before exiting the IND CWA by 1700 EST.||Damaging winds were the primary hazard with this event, resulting in structural damage, power outages, and travel disruptions. Hamilton County was particularly hard hit, where estimated wind gusts up to 55 knots (63 mph) downed multiple utility lines, left a power pole leaning in Noblesville, and knocked a large tree through the roof of a residence.  Transportation infrastructure was also impacted:  in Delaware County, estimated gusts of 55 knots blew over a semi truck on Interstate 69 near mile marker 249.  Earlier in the afternoon, severe gusts in Hendricks County downed several trees, including one that blocked a roadway southwest of Danville.  As the severe weather pushed into south-central Indiana, the KBAK AWOS at Columbus Municipal Airport in Bartholomew County recorded a peak measured wind gust of 52 knots (60 mph).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility lines were blown down by thunderstorm winds. Nearby there were additional utility lines downed on Westfield Blvd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intensifying low pressure  tracked across the southern Gulf Of Maine and east of Nova Scotia from the 25th into the 26th...exiting northeast of Nova Scotia during the early morning hours of the 27th. A Norlun style trof extended back across the forecast area from the ocean low helping prolong the snow. Snow developed through the evening of the 25th. Snow...heavy at times...then persisted through the 26th into the early morning hours of the 27th. Snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour at times occurred during the 26th. Warning criteria snow accumulations were achieved through the morning hours of the 26th.  Snow totals across coastal and interior Downeast portions of the region generally ranged from 12 to 18 inches with local totals up to around 20 inches. Accumulations across east-central portions of the region generally ranged from 8 to 12 inches with local totals up to around 16 inches across southern Piscataquis county. Snow totals steadily diminished northward across the remainder of the region tapering to 2 to 4 inches across the Saint John Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 12 to 18 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked down trees and wires along Long Level Road in Lower Windsor Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low-pressure system lifting northeast through northern Illinois brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the late evening on Friday (4/03) through the morning on Saturday (4/04). Around 1 inch of sleet fell across far north-central Wisconsin with one quarter of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across portions of central and north-central Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest sleet total in Vilas County was 1 inch in Eagle River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An area of damage was surveyed along John C Martin Rd to the south of Clayton and the damage was determined to be the result of a brief, EF0 tornado. The tornado touched down just east of a couple chicken houses where it damaged the roof of a metal outbuilding and ejected pieces of tin into a nearby field. The tornado continued east a short distance through the field then it crossed John C Martin Rd where multiple softwood trees were snapped and uprooted at the intersection of Hovey Rd and John C Martin Rd. A house across the street lost a few shingles and most of the windows were blown out on the front of the home. Several trees in the yard were snapped or uprooted. The tornado quickly weakened as it continued east-southeast into an open field where several large branches were snapped along a tree line then the tornado dissipated shortly after.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 7 miles east of Wagner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the region Wednesday and Thursday that brought heavy rain, damaging wind, and several brief tornadoes to eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO.  The more widespread wind damage occurred Wednesday afternoon June 10th from a derecho that developed in eastern Iowa and moved east. This downed trees, power lines primarily along and north of I-80. The more significant winds between 70-80 mph winds were seen north of the Hwy 20 corridor. A second round of storms later on produced isolated wind damage, including some damage north of Geneseo, IL that was due to straight-line winds.

On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding across north central Kentucky. On April 28th, the system's cold front dropped southeast, bringing a line of thunderstorms through central Kentucky. This produced additional wind damage and multiple small tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado briefly touched down and affected all trees in sparsely populated locations of western Ohio County. The tornado touched down just south of Locks Road and did tree damage along a nearly 2 mile track through the Rough River Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant, non-thunderstorm wind event, occurred on March 13th resultant of a strong pressure gradient with cold front passage, mixing into strong wind aloft, and a sting jet. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing shortwave generated showers and thunderstorms across the upper Ohio Valley in the evening of the 24th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms moved over the marine area and produced gusty winds.

A potent Arctic Front across southern Ontario and western New York began to shift southeasterly during the late evening hours of December 31, 2025 and continued into the early morning hours of January 1, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on White Post Road near US-340.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.

Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees blew down near Chesapeake Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow overspread the western Maine foothills by the afternoon on the 25th. Within an hour or two snow was moderate to heavy at times as an intense band of lift moved into the region. Snowfall rates were one to two inches per hour during the heavy snow. Snow continued overnight into the 26th, with occasional breaks or lighter snowfall before the storm center moved into the Atlantic. Snowfall totals ranged from 14 to 20 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.
High winds occurred over the mountains and spread down into the surrounding lower elevations, with gusts up to 72 in the higher elevations, and up to 64 mph in the lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KILO gusted to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unsettled weather pattern unfolded across the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians for the start of June amid a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity. This combination allowed for daily storm initiation across the Midwest that eventually tracked into Ohio and northern West Virginia. On June 6th and 7th, storms tracking into the area reached Harrison and Taylor Counties late in the evening and caused tree and power line damage before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed along Traders Avenue in Clarksburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful upper level storm system that spread eastward from the Intermountain West brought widespread high winds, blowing dust, and a few wildfires on the morning and afternoon of the 17th. Thick high level cloud cover early in the day initially prevented strong winds from developing. However, these clouds began to thin out and clear by late in the morning from west to east. This allowed surface winds to quickly ramp up where clearing occurred. Most observed severe wind gusts were between 58 and 65 mph, however, the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Olton measured a wind gust of 77 mph. These strong winds also lofted copious amounts of dust into the atmosphere which reduced visibility across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle. Observed visibilities dropped as low as one half mile at times. The strong winds and dry conditions also brought favorable wildfire conditions. Several wildfires started across the region with one igniting near Plainview known as the Arbor fire. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills dropped below 0 degrees across the county between Saturday evening and Tuesday morning, January 24th through 27th. The lowest wind chill of -1 was recorded at TWDB observation site north of Glen Rose the morning of January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, daytime heating pushed temperatures into the upper 80s and lower 90s, combining with surging humidity to drive heat indices near 100��F and create a highly unstable environment with MLCAPE values reaching 2,500 J/kg. Weak low-level convergence initially triggered severe storms over Wayne County, which dropped 1 to 1.25-inch hail across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights. Later in the evening, a destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into southern Lower Michigan, though it steadily weakened as it moved through Southeast Michigan before completely clearing the state by midnight. While the broader system left over 85,000 customers without power statewide, wind damage, downed trees, and power outages within Southeast Michigan remained isolated to scattered, impacting communities primarily along and west of U.S. 23.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree limbs were reported down.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across almost all of Jones County from March fist through March third.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 3rd-5th, rain and mountain snow fell due to atmospheric rivers passing over the region. On the 3rd, precipitation reached near one inch in the San Joaquin Valley, mainly southern portions. Other valley locations received around 0.25 inch to just over 0.50 inch. Lesser amounts occurred in the Central Valley during the 4th-5th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A semi-truck was blown over near the  I-74/I-55 interchange.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota and then western Wisconsin saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moved through the area, covering the ground completely at times.||The second round of storms followed about 30 to 60 minutes behind and produced scattered wind damage to trees and a few power lines. The very southern portion of Eau Claire County saw a highly visible funnel cloud near Osseo, which briefly touched down on the west side of town near the Merchants Baseball Field off US Highway 10. This tornado falls within NWS La Crosse's forecast jurisdiction, and more detail on the tornado can be found there.

Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall during February combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in continuing Extreme Drought (D3) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A messy mix of wintry precipitation fell across Magoffin County. An NWS employee estimated 0.5 inch of flat ice accretion along the Mountain Parkway with particularly heavy loading noted near MM 70.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across the Upstate and Piedmont of South Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal. Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, as May rainfall wound up 150 to 200% of normal. Some locations across the lower Piedmont received around 300% of normal May rainfall. Drought category was reduced to moderate-to-severe across the area by the start of June.

An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along Kelly Mountain Road near the Elkins airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: K4V9 AWOS measure wind gust of 63 mph near Neligh, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds peeled metal roofing off a barn near Ethridge. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted the Ozarks region from January 23���25, 2026, bringing significant snow, ice, record-breaking cold to southwestern Missouri and far southeastern Kansas. The event, which peaked between Saturday, Jan 24, and Sunday, Jan 25, resulted in double-digit snowfall totals in some areas and widespread, dangerous travel conditions. Heaviest snowfall occurred near the Missouri-Arkansas border, with many locations receiving over 6 inches of snow. Some areas recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall with the highest amounts occurring along the Arkansas State line as bands of heavy snow developed. Roads and highways were severely impacted, with partial to full coverage reported across the region, including I-44 and I-49, making travel difficult or dangerous. Numerous crashes were reported with significant portions of I-44 experiencing closures, accidents, and hazardous conditions, particularly in Southwestern Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began to push into the County during the late evening hours of January 23 as the first round of snow that would continue into January 25th. Moderate to heavy snowfall then occurred during through the day January 24 and into midday January 25th. Between 3-6 inches of snow were reported across the County, causing multiple schools to close. Additionally, Interstate 49 was reported covered and partially closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated severe storm developed on Saturday on the fourth of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm spotter reported damage along Rio Grande Boulevard between Deacon Drive and Ponderosa Drive. Large, healthy trees were uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near West Rowan Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary cold front from an associated upper-level low pressure system tracking from the Ohio Valley allowed for snow shower development during the morning hours of January 11th. Clear skies with cold advection aloft allowed for meager, but sufficient, instability across the western half of Pennsylvania in an environment of ample lift and moisture to produce snow squalls. These snow squalls produced multiple instances of visibility below one-quarter of a mile, with multiple accidents with one reported on US Route 6 in McKean County and another accident on US Route 322 near Port Matilda. No injuries were reported from these accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. The ASOS at the Clearfield Lawrence Township Airport reported visibility of one quarter mile in heavy snow as a snow squall moved through. Wind gusts of 25 mph were also observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough approached Georgia on the morning of Sunday, January 18th, drawing Gulf moisture northward into central Georgia. Meanwhile, a cold front brought an influx of colder air into the area. This interaction led to a few hours of snowfall across much of central Georgia on the morning of January 18th. Snowfall accumulations were generally in the 1-2 range across this stretch of the state, though a few spots received near 3 of snow. After a brief period of slowed travel and snowy scenes, afternoon sun brought warmer temperatures which quickly melted the snow, bringing a quick end to this relatively uncommon central Georgia snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain transitioned to snowfall in the morning hours of the 18th. Snowfall accumulations of T to 2 inches were reported across the county by the late morning. Snowfall ended by late morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow began to fall across central Kansas Friday night January 23rd and continued to fall through the 24th before ending early Sunday morning on the 25th.  Despite the long duration of snow most areas received modest amounts ranging from 5 to 8 inches. Air temperatures were unusually cold in the 0 to 5 above range making the snow very dry and powdery.  Winds were not strong with this event mainly staying in the 5 to 15 mph range so widespread blowing and drifting was not a widespread problem.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS report of 8.0 inches measured at KS-OT-2 7 miles northeast of Ada and 7.5 inches measured at KS-OT-17 7 miles northwest of Minneapolis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistently dry conditions coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of Miller and Lafayette Counties in Southwest Arkansas by the third week of February, which persisted through the end of the month. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-1.25 inches, which was near or less than a quarter of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers developed, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also observed, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An ejecting shortwave trough passed over the region during the second week of January, leading to quickly accumulating snow for the mountains and a rain/snow mix for the eastern plains of Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 8.0 inches of snow measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds in the community of Draper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down several trees in the South Los Angeles area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported at PR-936 in Las Torres, particularly over a low level crossing over a local creek. The crossing was briefly impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe thunderstorms produced flooding and marginally severe hail in the early morning of April 15th across far northern Illinois.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of northern Illinois during the evening of April 15th producing localized wind damage, hail and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few inches of standing water on the road were reported in Winthrop Harbor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball-size about two-miles south of Maple Heights.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along Mellon Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported 1 inch hail in Lake Worth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms, a tornado and flash flooding occurred during the evening of June 21, lasting into the morning of June 22.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree on Dead end lane near Pineville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of rain/drizzle/freezing drizzle mix which lasted several hours each. CoCoRaHS observers across the county reported a light glaze of ice accretion on non-paved surfaces.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms moving across north central and northeast South Dakota generated high winds from the evening of June 7th into the early morning hours of June 8th. The South Dakota State University mesonet station 1 mile southwest of Timber Lake recorded a peak wind gust of 65 mph, while the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet stations 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake and 2 miles north of Herreid peaked at 64 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated thunderstorm winds topped out at about 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Stevens Run Road was impassible near the intersection with Hastings Run Road due to high water from Elk Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported flooding across all lanes, with water being thrown up as vehicles slam on breaks and swerve.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary boundary hovered over central Ohio, northern West Virginia, and southern Pennsylvania on June 27th and 28th, but eventually sank south of the area early on the morning of the 29th. ||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued to develop along and south of the front, depositing one to three inches of rain across much of the area. While the heaviest rain amounts fell in the southern coal fields, soils to the north had already been compromised by prior rounds of precipitation. Thus, an inch to an inch-and-a-half of rain was enough to spawn some flooding on roads in Harrison, Barbour, and Randolph counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was observed over Union Road at Reeves Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gust of 58 mph was recorded at Montgomery Dannelly Field at 4:55 pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deepening surface low pressure system was centered over Illinois and an attendant cold front extended south-southwestward sweeping from west to east across Arkansas during the afternoon and evening hours of March 15, 2026. Multiple severe thunderstorms developed in a well-defined warm sector positioned across the state where storms matured and quickly became severe producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple power poles fell in the vicinity of Sedgwick.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected New Orleans from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Intersection of Oak St and Eagle St flooded according to Streetwise NOLA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 19th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the Ohio River, with storms moving from southwest to northeast across northern Kentucky and southern Indiana. While effective bulk shear was relatively unsupportive of organized convection around 20 knots, a few stronger cores were able to develop thanks to 2000-2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. These stronger cells were able to produce a few instances of wind damage vai downed trees as well as near-severe level hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down, blocking Rose Island Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed ahead of a cold front across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 12. These storms produced damaging winds as they moved east.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and powerlines were reported down across far western Louisa County, particularly near Troy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads were flooded in the southern portion of the county.
