EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front was accompanied by a narrow band of heavier squalls embedded within a larger area of light to moderate stratiform rain. These squalls resulted in several gale-force wind gusts as the front crossed the waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A squall produced an estimated wind gust to 34 knots (39 MPH) near the AWOS at Martin State Airport (KMTN) adjacent to the Chesapeake Bay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 (Severe) to D4 (Exceptional) Drought conditions remained in place across all of the Lower Rio Grande Valley/Deep South Texas ranchlands into early April, with 94.59% of the region in Extreme (Level 3 of 4) to Exceptional (Level 4 of 4), and 54.79% Exceptional Drought.  This was the highest coverage of Extreme to Exceptional Drought in the region since April 2013.  There was notable crop and livestock production reductions and loss into early April; these values will be provided once received.||Widespread rains finally arrived on April 4 and 5, and would begin the process of gradual drought improvements starting on April 7 which would continue through the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions persisted from April 1 to April 6 across western Inland Kenedy County. D3(Extreme Drought) conditions persisted across central and eastern Inland Kenedy County. D2 (Severe Drought) conditions persisted across extreme northeastern and extreme south-central Inland Kenedy County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down along Interstate 95 at mile marker 123.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KGNV Gainesville measured a peak gust of 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic storm system brough gusty northwest winds to many locations across northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The BLM Terry Montana Climate Office agrimet site (MTM29) measured a 62 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree brought down power lines along County Road 20.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread showers and storms pressed through southeast Ohio on the first day of April ahead of a cold frontal passage. Strong to severe thunderstorms were first noted shortly after midday along the border of Kentucky and West Virginia, with more quickly infiltrating Ohio by peak heating hours. Storms grew strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts, 1 to 1.5 inch hail stones, and heavy downpours. Aside from numerous reports of large hail across Washington County, downed trees and power lines were observed, along with an isolated instance of flash flooding in Marietta. Storms pressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia by the middle of the evening, bringing the severe weather threat to an end for southeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous downed trees were observed in the Marietta area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe storms developed along a slow moving cold front as it creeped across the area through the afternoon and into the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 2-inch hail along with estimated winds up to 90 mph. Multiple structures were damaged across south-central Kansas due to these storms.

Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 28 to 35 inches of snow fell. One of the highest reports was 33.5 inches in Coventry. Winds gusted 50-60 mph which caused some power outages. So much snow fell that travel became nearly impossible for much of the day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent enhanced westerly flow with multiple embedded shortwave troughs brought multiple instances of severe wind gusts and hail to northern Utah as well as flash flooding to Sevier county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station UTJPS Johnsons Pass recorded a thunderstorm wind gust to 61 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system passed north of the area through the day, setting up a strong pressure gradient across the state. Conditions were very dry, allowing for very deep mixing. A wind advisory and a red flag warning were in effect for the day and widespread gusts of 45-55 mph from the I-80 corridor north to the Iowa Minnesota border. A couple gusts of 58 and 59 mph were also reported. In the strong winds one semi also tipped over on I-35 near Mason City. Winds at the time of the accident were gusting around 45 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gust of 58 mph at KEBS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Pacific weather system crossed western and central Wyoming and brought heavy snow west of the Continental Divide and high wind to the east of the Divide. Notable accumulations fell throughout the western mountains. The highest amount was in the Salt River and Wyoming Ranges where 34 inches of new snow fell at the Spring Creek Divide SNOTEL site. Other notable amounts included 30 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL in Yellowstone National Park, 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL in the Absarokas and 24 inches over Togwotee Pass. High winds occurred along and East of the Divide as well as across Sweetwater County. Some of the more notable wind gusts included 82 mph along South Pass and 81 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Along the Chief Joseph Highway there were several hours of wind gusts over 75 mph, with a maximum wind gust of 81 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of flash flooding occurred throughout Southeast Texas over the course of several days, leading up to Tropical storm Arthur.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported that South Roosevelt Avenue between Plum Grove Road and East Houston Street was underwater and closed. New Salem Road was also reported to be underwater and closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A system brought strong winds to the region, with a band of snow across the northeast South Dakota. This resulted in blizzard conditions with widespread travel impacts from the early morning through the afternoon of February 18. ||Peak winds associated with the system included a gust measuring 72 mph by a mesonet station owned by a trained spotter in Faulkton, a 71 mph gust recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 4 miles north of Altamont (Deuel county) and a 67 mph gusts measured by the SDDOT RWIS 7 miles east of Clark. 47 additional weather stations would record a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. ||The Andover and Westport COOP observers reported blizzard or ground blizzard conditions at the time of their observations.||Not much overall snowfall occurred with the system, but within the band snowfall averaged about 4 inches with the COOP observers in Westport and Clark reporting a total of 4.1 and 4.0 inches of snowfall respectively. Additionally, the National Weather Service office just outside the Aberdeen Regional Airport measured 3.7 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles east of Orient recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph at 337 am. Later that morning, at approximately 10 am, high winds were responsible for blowing a trailer off a truck on Highway 45, 8 miles southeast of Polo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media photo indicated a carport destroyed on County Coad 514 south of Mansfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down in New Kent County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with large hail fell across portions of southwest Missouri during the morning of March 4th. Additional thunderstorms with large hail fell across southern Missouri during the evening of March 4th. The two rounds of thunderstorms produced a swatch of 2-4 inches of rainfall from Cassville to Springfield to Salem. This rainfall caused localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail to the size of half dollars fell northwest of Turners.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter mile swath of tree and powerline damage on Water Wells Road in Alfred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front advancing northward over cold ground helped cause widespread fog to form late on March 7th and early on March 8th. The fog dissipated by mid morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Monmouth Executive Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SC Highway Patrol reported a tree down across Boney Rd north of Blythewood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Additional heavy rainfall along with wet antecedent conditions lead to more flash flooding, some significant, in the Pine Belt region of Mississippi. Several major roads were flooded, as well as homes. Water rescues were conducted in the Seminary area as several cars became stranded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was over a bridge at Old Watermill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening upper level trough across CA and vicinity sent an embedded wave northeastward toward the Northern Rockies Feb 17, which resulted in surface low pressure developing and moving across Southwest Montana. This resulted in a strong cold front progressing through the area, bringing brief snow squalls, synoptic high winds, localized impactful snow, and very cold wind chills to various portions of the region into Feb 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KCTB Cut Bank Airport measured a few gusts of 58 mph or greater, including a peak gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of  west central and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening period, with very large hail and severe winds reported. One supercell produced 3 inch hail in Moorhead, MN. One EF-0 tornado developed with a supercell in Clay County 6 miles northwest of Hawley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of measured hail of 2 inches in Dilworth, MN.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (105) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system entered the Bering Sea to start the month of May. With a cold Arctic high pressure system over the Beaufort Sea, strong south and southwesterly winds developed from Alaska's West Coast eastwards toward the Alaska Range. Along the West Coast, the winds combined with light to moderate snow to create blizzard conditions, while the Alaska Range passes saw damaging wind gusts to start the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Point Lay AWOS (PPIZ) reported just shy of 12 hours of blizzard conditions with wind gusts as high as 39 mph and visibility levels dropping to or just below 1/4 mile in blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter measured a 66-mph peak straight-line convective wind gust from a line of thunderstorms about one-mile NNW of Martin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-afternoon thunderstorms both in broken line segments and single cells developed along and ahead of a cold front. Marginal effective shear values up to 30 knots and MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg supported severe thunderstorms producing both wind and hail. Wind was primarily confined to northern West Virginia along a DCAPE gradient of 600-700 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates up to 6.5 C/km and up to 300 J/kg of hail growth zone CAPE supported numerous reports of quarter size within storms across western Pennsylvania.

A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter measured a 61 mph wind gust with a Tempest weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over southeast Louisiana, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D3 to include St Tammany, southern Tangipahoa, and St James Parishes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of West Feliciana Parish according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A post on social media reported  that 5 head of cattle were found deceased  beneath a tree that was struck by lightning  in the vicinity of Orange Lake in northern  Marion County late on Saturday night. Time  of event based on lightning data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June saw repeated episodes of heavy rainfall interrupted by periods of dangerous heat. Weekly rainfall commonly ranged from 2 to over 8 inches, with localized flooding, saturated soils, and standing water occurring throughout the month. A tropical system during the third week of June produced another round of widespread heavy rain that further improved soil moisture, replenished stock tanks, and significantly improved pasture and rangeland conditions. These wet conditions repeatedly delayed hay harvest and other field operations. Despite the abundant rainfall, temperatures frequently reached or exceeded 100��F, with heat index values climbing to 105-110��F in some areas. By the final week of June, the first extended dry period in a while allowed fields to begin drying and agricultural activities to resume while drought conditions remained substantially improved due to the month's persistent rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 6/2, ending inclusion in Storm Data.
