Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a ruler-measured hailstone was shared on social media. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A microburst overturned a large box storage container. A restaurant sign was blown down. Ten large trees were uprooted. Between 50 to 70 large tree limbs were snapped off and blown down onto roods and powerlines. Peak wind gusts were estimated up to 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of trees were down along Highway 71.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported golf ball sized hail 5 miles south of Bryson on FM 1191.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 59 mph near Oakland, NE. KTQE ASOS measured wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.

The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.
A strong short wave moved across the region creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across southeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto FM 252.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow showers developed of and on throughout the day on the 31st. Total snowfall across the county ranged from 0 to 1 inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A moist onshore flow above the existing snow pack ahead of an advancing warm front resulted in widespread dense fog late on February 17th and early on February 18th. The fog dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Wings Field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fast flowing water was reported over Farm Road 53.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local media reported that heavy rainfall during the afternoon of the 18th caused multiple flooded homes in Ottoville village. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered buildings on the campus of Northwest Louisiana Technical Community College on North Market Steet.

Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions developed across northern Illinois on June 29th and continued on June 30th as well into early July. Peak heat index values ranged from 100 to 105 for most areas on both days with high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s.

Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across northeastern Minnesota on the afternoon of the 17th. As the storms moved across northwest Wisconsin, they transitioned from mainly hail producing storms to wind producing storms. Multiple reports of tree damage were received from Bayfield, Washburn, Ashland, and Sawyer counties with a roof being removed from a building in Hayward. A gust of 68 mph was recorded near Minong. A few large hail reports were received as well, mainly across Sawyer and Price counties.

At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball-size about two-miles northwest of Bainbridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions across Smith County from April 2026 improved to moderate drought in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall and snowmelt resulted in flooding across the south-central U.P.  Many roads were flooded and several closed.  The flooding also caused damage at the Escanaba Airport (KESC) due to standing water on the runways and power failure. Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th for Menominee and Marquette counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County emergency management reported 20 to 30 roads flooded by 9:45 AM on the 12th, with significant flooding of the US-2 rail underpass in Powers as well as much of the surrounding town and the nearby town of Wilson. On the 13th, railroad tracks in Faithorn were washed out. In the overnight of the 13th into the 14th, County Road 563 washed out at Wilson Creek. One water rescue was performed in Harris Township on the 14th.Due to the severity of the flooding, a Disaster Declaration Request was approved by the president on June 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid air to the south of a warm frontal boundary spawned heavy rain producing thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Storms repeatedly moving over the same regions produced pockets of 3 to 4 inches of rain which triggered areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Officials reported numerous roads flooded throughout the Town of Lansing along with some homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 27, a line of severe storms moved into west-central Indiana, becoming a more organized QLCS. A few sporadic wind damage reports and a few measured 60-70 mph wind gusts occurred in Cass, Grant, and Blackford counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of damage east of Eastbrook. Damage to a shed and fence at one home and a window blown out at another. A barn in the area also has damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved east through Middle Tennessee during the evening of April 16, 2026. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms, particularly along a powerful gust front that was produced. Numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines as well as structural damage was received across Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed numerous trees in Hickman County which caused power outages. Roof damage was also reported. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from quarter (1.00) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, a storm near Kewanee Illinois in Henry County produced a funnel cloud.

Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph, knocked down multiple trees between Ankeny and Edie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals between 1.2 and 3 inches were reported across Henderson County. The highest sleet and snow totals were reported in Brownsboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 61 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet on Ship Island XSHI measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 43 mph or 37 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down in Rostraver Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold air in the wake of a winter storm that brought widespread snowfall to central Pennsylvania allowed for many locations to experience a prolonged period of cold weather beginning on January 27th and continuing into January 31, 2026. Cold air in the wake of the winter system allowed for a period of much cooler than average temperatures with gusty winds also allowing for dangerously cold wind chills across western Pennsylvania January 26th and into January 27th. High pressure in the wake of an Arctic Front passage on January 30th allowed for bitterly cold temperatures to continue into January 31st, especially across western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme cold impacted Somerset County on the morning of January 31, with most of the county seeing wind chill values ranging from -15 to -25 degrees. The coldest wind chill of -30 degrees was observed at the Somerset Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow but heavy band of snow developed near the Wisconsin-Illinois border during the evening hours. Enhanced hourly snowfall rates within the snow band led to snow accumulations of 2 to 4 inches, with locally higher totals. Overlapping with the evening commute, the snowfall led to slippery road conditions. Winds became gusty after the snow ended, leading to blowing snow and reduced visibilities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between 2 to 4 inches of snow observed countywide. Highest total of 3.5 inches observed in New Glarus.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours of April 25th. Several reports of large hail were received with the largest being golf ball sized.
Strong pressure gradients caused high winds to develop in some of the southeast Wyoming wind prones.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent gust of 50 to 55 MPH were recorded along Interstate 80 from WYDOT sensors. A maximum gust of 63 MPH from a WYDOT sensor at Foote Creek was recorded at 5:56 AM MST on 1/13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

As southwest winds brought warm temperatures and moisture to the region, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed and worked east through the Lower Ohio Valley, resulting in flash flooding and a single report of wind damage across central Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A culvert washed out and asphalt cracked on Springtown Rd near Loretto.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough pattern moved into the area on the 18th and 19th. On the 19th, a cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms produced widespread lightning (over 2500 strikes), heavy rainfall of 1 to over 2 inches and several reports of flash flooding in western NV from Stagecoach to southeast Reno/Hidden Valley, east Sparks to Lockwood and Spanish Springs. Hail up to 1��� diameter and wind gusts of 60-75+ mph also occurred with these storms as they pushed across northwest and west central NV.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported by the fire department in Stagecoach, NV. This has caused muddy flood waters and debris to cover US-50 as well as streets in surrounding neighborhoods. A mesonet station in Stagecoach, EW-1922, measured 1.12 inches of rain with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms associated with an upper trough and Pacific cold front pushed through North and Central Texas on February 14. Storms were mostly below severe thresholds, but a few became strong enough to produce wind damage and isolated instances of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook photo showed a tree was snapped in the backyard of a home near I-35E and Wheatland Road just north of I-20.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported quarter sized 3 miles north of Romance.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported a large tree down on the roof of a home on Parish Parc Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed along an outflow boundary well ahead of a slow-moving cold front during the early morning of May 16th.  Due to a dry sub-cloud environment, the cells were able to produce damaging wind gusts of 60-80mph north of a Galesburg to Minonk line.  Later in the morning, a collapsing shower resulted in downburst winds of around 80mph and widespread damage across western parts of Jacksonville in Morgan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 by 120 foot pole barn was completely destroyed near the intersection of County Road 650 North and County Road 550 East.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad scale upper lift led to a complex winter storm across East Tennessee, with onset precipitation of snow transitioning to freezing rain before ending as rain as the temperatures rose through the evening, night, and following morning. This storm led to 7 fatalities in East Tennessee. On the morning of the 25th the strengthening low level jet that was advancing warm air northwards led to a high end mountain wave wind event in portions of the East Tennessee mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain accumulated on outdoor surfaces, of at least 0.15 inches, included on powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation was only 25 to 50 percent of normal across most of southeast South Dakota, and a low as 10 to 25 percent of normal in south central South Dakota during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions intensified to severe (D2) by mid month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through New Jersey producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large trees were blown down in the vicinity of Mill Lane near Columbus. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed just west of N Yale Avenue and north of E 76th Street N. It uprooted a tree as it crossed N Yale Avenue and moved northeast across a neighborhood on E 82nd Street N. Several homes were damaged, light poles were blown down, and large tree limbs were snapped. The tornado blew down power poles and snapped large tree limbs as it crossed E 86th Street N. Outbuildings were damaged and large tree limbs were snapped by the tornado as it crossed N Hudson Avenue, and then crossed N Sheridan Avenue, where it dissipated. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 90 to 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained weather spotter reported thunderstorm wind damage in the city of Hebron. Power out in the city of Hebron. Numerous branches and trees down, with lots of debris around town. Estimated winds at 80 to 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms moved across MS during the afternoon/evening hours of March 15 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple powerlines were blown due to strong thunderstorm winds along Hwy 8.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix changed over to snow as temperatures plunged well below freezing behind an arctic front. This created an icy flash freeze environment under a half inch to two inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front moved through with a mixture of sleet and rain changing to a period of snow. Snow accumulations were generally an inch or two at best. However, the cold air rushing in with the front and snow allowed the wet pavement to freeze in the afternoon and early evening. This resulted in reports of slide-offs and accidents across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in a few bands of thunderstorms that produced widely scattered instances of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees blew down including one that impacted a house and a car in northwest Baltimore.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak dryline formed during the day of the 30th and mixed eastward to the edge of the caprock. Convergence along the dryline, a weak short wave trough, and very hot temperatures contributed to convective initiation by mid-afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains. Storms repeatedly trained over Hall County producing intermittent severe winds gusts near Lesley (Hall County) for over an hour. Late in the afternoon additional thunderstorms developed in eastern New Mexico in the drier air and moved eastward into the South Plains. A very dry sub cloud layer allowed these storms to produce several severe wind gusts as they marched eastward towards the Interstate 27/US Highway 87 corridor. By the time storms reached Lubbock County late in the evening, they were moving very slowly which produced heavy rainfall over the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County). Numerous city roads on the south side of the city of Lubbock were inundated with water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Reese Center measured a wind gust to 68 mph at 2001 CST. At 2032 CST, an off duty NWS employee reported that several power poles were blown over south of Wolfforth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and unstable air mass was in place across South Texas, with surface dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s and strong daytime heating producing moderate to strong instability. Sea-breeze boundaries along the Middle Texas Coast served as a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon. While upper-level winds were relatively weak, sufficient instability and moderate deep-layer shear supported organized convection capable of producing damaging wind gusts. A compact MCS developed near Corpus Christi and moved along the coast, where a favorable thermodynamic environment allowed it to intensify. The storm complex produced severe wind gusts, including measured gusts of 53-59 kt in Corpus Christi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KRKP in Rockport measured gusts up to 41 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 40 mph with LGA ASOS reporting a 52 mph gust at 6:04 am, a 61 mph gust at 6:30 am at the Fordham NYSM station, and a 64 mph gust at Kew Garden Hills NYS mesonet at 3:20 am; along with frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at the LGA ASOS. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged from mainly 20 to 23 inches across the zone via public reports, and a trained spotter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported golf ball sized hail in Groesbeck.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began near Mount Olive Road and tracked northeastward across Shell Oil Lane and MS Highway 583 before lifting near Highway 583 and Bethel Road. Along the tornado path, the roof of an outbuilding was damage on Shell Oil Lane and a house on Highway 583 sustained roof damage. Several trees were snapped and uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated strong summer thunderstorms formed during the afternoon in southern Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high based shower collapsed near the Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport to the east of Rock Springs and produced a 58 mph wind gust.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts along the east central Florida coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: USSF wind sensor on tower 211 measured a peak wind gust of 48 knots from the southwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed over the upper Ohio Valley along a passing cold front on the afternoon of January 14th. As temperatures cooled across the Western and north Central New York areas, rain mixed with and then changed to snow. Snow continued across much of the Buffalo forecast area through the day on Thursday January 15th as the surface low tracked from Northwestern Pennsylvania to Central New York. Cold air filtering into the region, along with mid-level troughs over the region helped increase lake enhancement off of both Lake Erie and Ontario. The snow finally tapered off later in the day on January 15th as drier air and a ridge built into the region. While snowfall amounts weren't overly impressive by Buffalo standards, the widespread nature of the snowfall did cause more disruptions to daily activities than snow from a lake effect event with similar amounts. ||While most snowfall ranged from six to ten inches across most of the Buffalo forecast area, there were some larger amounts closer to the foot and a half to two foot mark where lake enhancement really increased snow rates. Notable snowfall amounts from around the Buffalo forecast area include: 21.6 inches in Eden, 17.0 inches in North Boston, 16.0 inches in West Falls, 16.0 inches in Newfane, 13.3 inches in North Tonawanda, 12.1 inches in Lockport, 9.5 inches in Perrysburg, 9.4 inches in Mexico, 9.0 inches in Hamlin and 9.0 inches in Cassadaga.

A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail that was three quarter inch in diameter was reported near Forest, VA in Bedford County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level jet was positioned over the Pacific Northwest from March 8 through 13. As it mixed down to the lower levels, it brought periods of high winds sustained in the 30 to 40 mph range and gusts up to 70 mph for portions of the region. It was followed by a cold front that brought snow amounts ranging from 2 to 9 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of gusty southwest winds up to 56 kts (64 mph) impacted the Coeur d'Alene area. A gas station sign was damaged. There were a couple of reports of downed trees and power lines with one sparking a fire in a backyard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening hours on June 5th, storms move into portions of Buffalo and Trempealeau counties producing large hail and strong winds. Eventually, these storms formed into a line and pushed southeast into portions of La Crosse, Monroe and Juneau Counties bring additional large hail, damaging wind gusts and an EF-0 tornado in eastern Monroe County prior to storms exiting to the southeast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported trees onto powerlines 2 miles north-northwest of Elroy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A roof was blown off of a business in Crewe. Additionally, broadcast media shared pictures  from and individual claiming that five roofs were flown off with debris extending for around two blocks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed across the southern North Carolina Piedmont during the early morning of the 25th. The precipitation began as mostly sleet before mixing with, and eventually changing to freezing rain later in the morning. The precipitation finally tapered off during the evening. Total sleet accumulations of around an inch occurred, with 0.10 to 0.25 inch of ice accreting on top of the sleet. This made for very hazardous driving conditions. Due to unusually cold weather following the event, a couple of days of refreezing resulted in travel difficulties continuing during the overnight and morning hours.
A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was blown down at the Taylor Fire Department on Littlefield Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of convection earlier in the day, a meso-low moved through far northwest Indiana and southwest Michigan, producing a widespread swath of 45-55+ mph wind gusts. The highest wind gust report was a 70 mph gust that occurred at the South Bend Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimated 50 to 55 mph wind gusts. KPPO recorded a 52 mph wind gust. As a result, numerous reports were received of trees and powerlines down, as well as large branches down in and around La Porte.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oklahoma Mesonet station near Vinita measured thunderstorm wind gusts up to 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees fell down. Additionally, a steel heater was blown off of a back deck.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A broadcast media storm chaser shared images of large trees uprooted near the intersection of U.S. Highway 62 and Jackson Avenue, with several blocking roadways. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. An isolated severe thunderstorm developed during the early evening hours over the east side of Shreveport in Central Caddo Parish, producing quarter size hail in the Cedar Grove community before diminishing. While a lull in the storms were observed through the remainder of the evening into the overnight hours, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana. These storms eventually progressed east and exited Central Louisiana by midday on the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power lines were blown down between Many and Florien.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts downed an approximately 60 foot tall and 3 ft diameter tree on to a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 3 to 6 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system brought a widespread moderate accumulation of snow to northwestern Connecticut on January 17, 2026. Snowfall amounts of 3 to 7 inches were common, resulting in slippery travel conditions on area roadways.||Key impacts: travel delays.

A dynamic storm system brought a sharp transition from record-breaking warmth to severe weather across eastern Kentucky on March 11th. Ahead of an approaching cold front, unseasonably warm air surged into the region on a potent low-level jet, with temperatures reaching record levels at London and Jackson. Widespread non-convective wind gusts between 30 and 50 mph occurred during the afternoon.||As the cold front moved in during the evening, a pre-frontal squall line (QLCS) developed in a high shear environment and tracked across the Commonwealth. The most intense measured wind gust was 70 mph at the London-Corbin Airport ASOS. Elsewhere, the storms resulted in structural damage, scattered downed trees, and a few power outages before a sharp cold front crossed the area, ushering in a much drier and colder airmass.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An amateur radio operator reported that a metal carport had been flipped and mangled in the Keavy area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down in Pinson, including on Pinson Valley Parkway.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm moving offshore produced strong winds near Melbourne.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of pea to penny size hail and estimated wind gusts near 50 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system brought two rounds of storms to the region on June 17th. The second round during the afternoon produced isolated hail up to golf ball size.

While somewhat mild by January standards, a moisture rich system brought a period of valley rain and mountain snow, with some higher accumulations noted particularly in portions of Utah's northern mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utah Highway Patrol and Utah Department of Transportation reported a multi vehicle crash near mile post 5 on US-40 westbound between Mayflower and Quinns. This accident resulted in a period of road closure for cleanup, and is assumed to be the result of ongoing winter weather.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally dry spring led to expansion of ongoing drought conditions across Central Alabama during the month of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) conditions persisted across Russell County through April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple of different rounds of thunderstorms brought heavy rain to portions of the headwaters of the Big Sioux River. This heavy rain resulted in the upper portions of the Big Sioux rising above flood stage for a short period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Big Sioux River near Bruce rose above flood stage the morning of June 5th, cresting around 1.51 feet above flood stage (9.51 feet) on June 6th. The river then fell below flood stage on the morning of June 7th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of moderate to heavy snow moved across southern Wisconsin on the back side of a strong low pressure system moving into Lower Michigan, bringing a wide range of 4 to 16 inches of snow accumulation to southern Wisconsin. Snow was accompanied by frequent wind gusts of 35 to 60 mph and white-out conditions with visibilities down to 1/4 to 3/4 mile for an eight to twelve hour period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals of 7 to 13 inches and winds of 40 to 50 mph caused frequent white-out conditions across the county. There were several reports of disabled vehicle and slide-off calls reported through the county dispatch center. All schools were closed. There were 335 customers without power for a few hours in Cross Plains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong wind gusts with a cold frontal passage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sixty mph wind gusts were measured at Craters of the Moon and Tom Cat Summit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure and a warm front brought a round of severe thunderstorms to southern WI during the evening. Large hail and damaging straight-line winds occurred.

A number of organized thunderstorm complexes affected eastern Oklahoma during the month of June, which resulted in widespread heavy rainfall across the region. Most of the area received between six and fifteen inches of rain, with as much as around twenty inches occurring locally. This rainfall corresponded to 150 to 450 percent of average monthly rainfall amounts across much of the region during the month. As a result of this abundant, widespread heavy rainfall, severe (D2) drought conditions across portions of Muskogee, Cherokee, and Mayes Counties, and extreme (D3) drought conditions across portions of Choctaw County, improved to abnormally dry (D0) drought conditions or better by the end of the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in Crescent City along south Highway 17 and Union Camp Rd. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.
Multiple severe storms occurred, producing winds up to 67 mph and hail up to 3 inches in diameter. Some minor flooding occurred as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report.  Measured pea to quarter  sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, D2 (Severe Drought) conditions returned to Bibb County on January 13. This degradation followed a brief mid-winter reprieve, which had interrupted an initial three-week period of Severe Drought that began on November 25. By the end of January, the County had recorded a cumulative total of six weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the drought���s inception in the fall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increased drought conditions expanded eastward during the last week of this month into portions of Petroleum, northern Phillips, and northern Valley Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions increased from the west into the northern half of northern Phillips County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An ice storm crippled areas from northern Mississippi through middle Tennessee, clipping far northwest Alabama from the 24th through the 27th. Freezing rain accumulated up to 1 inch in far northwest Alabama, with accumulations dropping off quickly going further east and southeast in north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. The initial onset of precipitation was a mixture of snow, sleet and freezing rain, changing to all freezing rain in far northwest Alabama. A surge of warm air on the 26th changed precipitation to moderate to heavy rain for much of north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee, as temperatures warmed well above freezing. The exception was the far northwest tip of Alabama which remained in the colder air. A reinforcing cold front eventually brought temperatures back below freezing quickly during the late afternoon and early evening hours of the 25th which ended the steady rainfall. However, areas of light freezing drizzle redeveloped and produced a light accumulation of glaze across much of the area, and existing water on roadways from earlier heavy rain also began to freeze. The freezing drizzle changed to light snow and flurries during the overnight, lasting into the morning hours of the 26th. Very light accumulations were reported, with a dusting up to one half inch. Sunshine melted  the snow quickly during the day.||Impacts from these events were most severe in far northwest Alabama, including devestating tree damage, including numerous trees and limbs being knocked down, split or toppled onto power lines. Power outages occurred in northwest Alabama, including the Quad Cities/Shoals metro area. A water treatment facility in parts of western Lauderdale County was damaged, and a boil order was declared for about 1500 residents affected. Schools and businesses were shut down for multiple days in northwest Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. In north central and northeast Alabama, impacts were much less severe, and schools and businesses were shut down on the 26th due to cold and icy spots on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Intermittent sleet changed to freezing rain and freezing drizzle during the morning hours lasting into the afternoon hours, especially atop the Cumberland Plateau. A light glaze of ice was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rare strong and damaging downslope wind event started in the early morning hours of March 12th and continued through March 13th. Intense mountain wave activity was also a contributing factor to widespread wind gusts between 80 to 110 MPH across southeast Wyoming. Numerous reports of tree damage, power outages, and property damage including flipped over sixteen-wheeler tractor trailer trucks were reported to WYDOT and the National Weather Service. Areas of blowing dust also resulted in lower visibility on area roadways, which added to the already difficult travel scenario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of persistent strong wind gusts over 58 MPH over eastern Laramie County. Peak gust of 81 MPH measured at the WYDOT site at Gun Barrel, along US Highway 85.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four power poles were snapped along U.S. Highway 177, south of Hubbard Road. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked wires down near Aspen Road and Renovo Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds overturned a semi north of Lamar Heights. This was an injury accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across eastern Arkansas. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill value of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to its neighbors across the Mississippi River, West Tennessee spent April 2026 battling a persistent, long-term moisture deficit dating back to July 2025. While central and northern parts of the Midwest received heavy spring rains that broke their droughts, West Tennessee experienced a highly regionalized spring recharge gap. Abnormally hot temperatures and meager rainfall caused drought conditions to actively worsen across the region during the first half of the month, though patchy late-month systems provided highly localized stabilizing relief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions worsened to D3 by mid month and persisted into May.

CZ_NAME: GULF OF AMERICA FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO HALFMOON SHOAL OUT TO 5 FATHOMS
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary from a collapsed thunderstorm moved west over Gulf of America waters north of Big Pine Key, producing isolated gale-force wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An east wind of 34 knots was measured at a WeatherFlow station at Harbor Bank Light.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed a long a cold front that was sagging southward from Iowa into far northeast Missouri during the afternoon and evening hours. These storms remained below severe limits produced hail up to the size of pennies.

Supercell storms early in the day dropped large hail and across Oglala Lakota and the Pine Ridge areas. These storms turned into a linear cluster and moved into Todd and Tripp counties where it produced damaging wind gusts with reports of structure damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Updated report. Hail fell in the Wakpamani area. Numerous vehicles significantly dented. Vehicle side  windows smashed out and windshields cracked. Hail damage  to trees and vegetation. Time estimated based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree on transformer on Montgomery Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through eastern Pennsylvania. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees down with roads impassable. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a southeastward moving cold front, broken lines of showers and thunderstorms developed in the evening hours. A surge of mid 70s temperatures with upper 50s dew points resulted in sufficient destabilization with MLCAPE up to 1000 J/kg, effective shear of 30-40 knots, and a gradient of 700-900 DCAPE. This allowed for some thunderstorms to become severe with large hail and damaging wind as the result, including two measured 58 mph gusts in southwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down in Hazelton.

CZ_NAME: SIERRA NEVADA OF TEHAMA-BUTTE-PLUMAS COUNTIES BETWEEN 1000-3000 FT
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure strengthened across the region in mid June, and brought Moderate to Major HeatRisk to northern California. Hot daytime and very warm overnight temperatures were observed in the northern/central Sacramento Valley and surrounding terrain. Highs neared 110 degrees and lows approached 80 degrees at night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cohasset RAWS reached 99 degrees for the high temperature, and 7a degrees for the low temperature at 1733 ft. Weather stations in the area measured highs between 90 and 105 degrees and lows between 65 and 75 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With deep cold air in place following the strong Atmospheric River system and strong cold front, a third low pressure trough dropped down from the Pacific Northwest and passed through the Four Corners region. This brought moderate snowfall accumulations favoring the central and southern mountains of eastern Utah and western Colorado with much lighter amounts over the north. Since cold air was already in place, many lower valleys also received light to moderate snowfall accumulations particularly the central and southern valleys from along and south of the Interstate 70 corridor. Gusty winds led to blowing snow with some snow squalls across the southwest Colorado valleys at times due to the combination of snow, wind and visibilities less than a quarter mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 5 to 12 inches of snow fell across the area with 7 inches reported at Crested Butte 6.2 N and 9 inches reported at McClure Pass. Winds gusted in the 45 to 55 mph range with a peak wind gust of 58 mph at Cinnamon Mountain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Upson County remained under D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on October 7, 2025, the county sustained 26 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought conditions persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms continuously grew upscale along US Highway 380 in Garza County west of Post. On the evening of the 31st, law enforcement in Garza County reported flooding along US Highway 380 near Farm to Market Road 399. An NWS storm survey revealed portions of area roadways previously had water running over them as evidenced by mud on the road.
