EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist southwest flow between low pressure passing well inland and high pressure offshore led to an environment supportive of strong thunderstorms across warm Atlantic waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The CHR60 Buoy measured a peak wind gust of 40 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening of June 11 into the early morning of June 12, a severe thunderstorm complex tracked west to east across Southeast Michigan, producing scattered pockets of damaging straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media photo showed a large branch split from a tree onto a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving boundary was the focus for afternoon thunderstorms as the day's capping inversion lifted. Pea and dime-size hail reports were common, with a handful of reports for 1 inch hail or larger.

A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking both lanes of travel along the 1700 block of Old Halifax Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice and sleet storm occurred across portions of southeastern Arkansas and the surrounding region. Ice accumulations in Ashley and Chicot counties were up to 0.25 inches, and sleet accumulations up to 7 inches were measured in Ashley County. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Ashley and Chicot counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations from Ashley County through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. ||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm. Wind chills were as low as 4 degrees at Crossett. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred in Ashley County. Freezing rain accumulations were estimated to be 0.25 inches, with significant sleet accumulations as high as 6 to 7.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hardwood tree branches broken (1-3 inch diameter).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds occurred in the early morning hours on the 2nd with a cold frontal passage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Idaho Falls ASOS recorded a 68 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service survey determined that an EF0 tornado with winds up to 80mph briefly touched down north of Pumpkin Center. Damage included several outbuildings including a concrete block milk barn. Roofing tin from another barn was blown north, east and south of the barn. Trees were also uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall resulted in significant rock slides across Kanan Dume Road near mile marker 12.24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms produced hail over the Houston Metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public submitted an mPING report, indicating quarter inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad forcing for ascent in the left exit region of a 60 knot mid-level jet allowed for scattered thunderstorms in an environment with upper 70s temperatures and low 60s dew points. A sufficiently unstable airmass with 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 40-60 knots of effective shear beneath the core of the jet supported some storm organization with an all hazards day in discrete cells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking half the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed southeast through the region during the day, starting near daybreak. Snow quickly tapered off from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and was banded in nature within the northwest-southeast axis.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The EMA measured 2.3 inches of snow in Sardinia. A public report from Georgetown indicated that 2 inches had fallen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A widespread high wind event occurred across the entire CWA from the 16th through the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WYDOT Mesonet station WY48 7 miles northeast of Buford gusted 59 mph at 7:46 AM on February 17th. This was the first gust recorded for this zone.|UPR Mesonet station UP204 9 miles southeast of Buford gusted 80 mph at 10:42 AM on February 17th. This was the highest gust recorded for this zone.|WYDOT Mesonet station KVDW at Vedauwoo gusted 60 mph at 4:26 PM on February 17th. This was the final gust recorded for this zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front swung through the area in the evening kicking off mostly sub severe storms, though a few did produce damaging winds in MA and CT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Worcester, power lines were down on Sunderland Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills. By Friday morning, much of the area was seeing temperatures of at least 20 degrees below zero, and as cold as 25 degrees below zero measured at the South Dakota State University mesonet stations in Gettysburg and 23 miles north of Highmore. With these cold temperatures and a northwest breeze, wind chills across much of the area had fallen to 40 degrees below zero and colder, with the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Summit coming in with a wind chill of 53 degrees below zero. Temperatures failed to warm much during the day, with highs in the single digits to teens below zero. Watertown set a record for the lowest daily high temperature, reaching only 11 degrees below zero.

A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 3 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system and arctic blast brought strong winds and pockets of light to moderate snow showers.  ||A peak wind gust of 71 mph was observed 1 mile north northwest of Lees Corner in Buffalo County by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Information Weather System (RWIS), and by a personal weather station 2 miles north of the Pierre Regional Airport. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded by the SDDOT RWIS station 1 mile northeast of Stephan in Hyde county, while 66 mph wind gusts were measured by the SDDOT RWIS stations 5 miles south southwest of Klein Ranch in Corson county and 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake in Dewey county.  A total of 39 weather stations recorded a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. These high winds flipped a semi and damaged a grain elevator near the town of Murdo on the morning of the 16th. ||While snow accumulations were limited, snow showers of moderate intensity combined with these strong winds to produce temporary white-out conditions. No Travel Advised was issued by both the Walworth and Day county Sheriffs. Various SDDOT RWIS webcams showed visibility in blowing snow fluctuating significantly over short distances in the matter of a few minutes. An emergency vehicle rendering assistance for an accident on Interstate 29 near Watertown was struck with minor injuries. A separate accident along Interstate 90 resulted in a 5 vehicle chain reaction crash which resulted in 2 fatalities and a number of injuries.  ||80 residents of Deuel county reported power out during the event.

A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down and sheared numerous trees, with one structure sustaining roof damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D3-D4 drought conditions prevailed to start the month of May across southwest and south central Georgia. However, beneficial rain during the month reduced the drought to D2 by the end of the month near a line from Albany to Bainbridge and westward. D3-D4 drought still prevailed farther east across south central Georgia.
A winter storm brought widespread 40 to 50 mph winds with higher gusts in combination with heavy snow. Near impossible travel and scattered power outages occurred with this storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread 6 to 12 inches of snow across the County. This fell in combined with wind gusts over 50 mph. Travel disruption was significant with scattered power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Garrison ASOS reported wind gusts up to 75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed south into west Texas and southeast New Mexico on the 19th. This front stalled in the Trans-Pecos area. A few thunderstorms developed south of this front and east of a dryline in the eastern Permian Basin and Lower Trans-Pecos. One thunderstorm produced large hail in Big Lake while another produced flash flooding in Terrell County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public sent a picture of approximately quarter-sized hail in Big Lake. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front set up across central Kansas later in the afternoon and eventually, storms began to develop along it. The strongest storms were mainly across southeast Kansas with damaging wind reported in Montgomery and Labette counties; Parsons Airport had a measured wind gust to 86 mph. As the front slowly tracked to the southeast through the evening, storms became more widespread and trained across the same areas. There was a stronger storm within the activity which produced quarter sized hail in Sedgwick County, but the associated heavy rain was the bigger show. The hardest hit area was the Wichita metro and southern Sedgwick into northern Sumner County where a widespread 4 to 7 inches fell, most of it in a 2 to 3 hour period. Flash flooding reports from Wichita and surrounding areas were plentiful with around 112 reports of stalled vehicles in Wichita alone. Homes along the creeks were also threatened and impacted by flood waters. Basement apartments were evacuated in west Wichita. Just after 10:30 PM KAKE News shared reports on social media from the following intersections of flooded roadways: 13th and Maize, 8th and West, 21st and 295th, Custer and Pawnee, 13th and Rock, Pawnee and Seneca, Central and Tyler. The number of flooded intersections only increased through the next several hours as rain continued. Some of the flooding was due to quickly rising creeks, including the Cowskin in west Wichita, which led to additional street and property flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of tree branches and limbs were snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A pine tree was snapped three miles east of Loves Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ongoing severe drought (D2) persisted across portions of southeast West Virginia, including: Boone, southern Braxton, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Lincoln, Logan, McDowell, Mingo, Nicholas, Raleigh, southern Roane, southern Wayne, and Wyoming counties.  Moderate drought (D1) also remained present just north and west of the D2 area. ||Significant improvements occurred during the second half of the month as multiple rounds of rain and storms produced four to eleven inches of rain that resulted in weekly category improvements. By the second week of the month, D2 was confined to Mingo, McDowell, and portions of Kanawha, Clay, Nicholas, Fayette, Raleigh, Wyoming, and Logan counties. Minimal improvements to D1 also occurred. In the third and fourth weeks of the month, both D2 and D1 eroded from all but McDowell, and parts of Wyoming and Raleigh counties.
A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines down in Florence Township.

CZ_NAME: PARADOX VALLEY / LOWER DOLORES RIVER BASIN
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering approximately 80% of Colorado Zone 020 - Paradox Valley/Lower Dolores River Basin, with the remaining 20% under Severe (D2) Drought. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, the area of Extreme (D3) Drought was reduced to 20% coverage, with 80% of the zone now under Severe (D2) Drought. Impacts from the drought are not being felt as yet, but concerns are increasing about future impacts. Particularly, there are concerns of the drought's impact on the upcoming summer wildfire season. Additionally, there are concerns about water availability for home irrigation, farming, and ranching through the rest of the year.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Some siding damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking roadway on County Road 14.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary.  With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.

Thunderstorms developed around midday over the central Nebraska Panhandle. This activity tracked to the east and southeast into the evening hours, producing numerous damaging wind and large hail reports. The greatest damage was at the eastern end of Lake McConaughy. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 81 MPH were reported. Hail up to golf ball size was reported near Imperial.
Thunderstorms moved through the area, producing strong winds, mainly along the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KPSX Palacios measured a 60 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure supported by vigorous mid-level shortwave moved across northern NY and northern New England during the afternoon and evening hours of June 18th.||Moderate instability combined with directional wind shear at multiple levels and a cold front helped develop a line of thunderstorms in NY that increased in intensity and coverage as it moved across VT with wind damage as well as weak, isolated tornadoes in VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS storm survey found EF-1 tornado damage in the woods near York Hill Road in  the town of Lincoln. Maximum estimated winds were 105 mph and the estimated track length was 0.31 miles. A stand of trees was uprooted and snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged a boat dock at mile marker 3 of the Niangua River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts flipped a semi-truck on US 31.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down near the intersection of Fox Run Boulevard and Chesapeake Boulevard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a tree onto a camper. Additional sporadic damage reported in the western and southern portions of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms developed in north central Kansas during the mid afternoon on 4/26 and tracked eastward through northeast Kansas, producing large hail to ping pong ball size and wind gusts estimated to around 70 mph. Clusters of late evening severe storms impacted much of northeast Kansas through the early morning of 04/27. Large hail to Golfball size and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported. Flash flooding also occurred in Shawnee, Jefferson, and Douglas counties as in upwards of 5 inches of rain fell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The area of 29th street and Kansas Ave. was reported to be impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The roof of Sunset Beach Traders restaurant was blown off early in the morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in wind damage and a large number of power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof mounted weather station measured gust. Heavy damage to trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak brought 4 tornadoes to portions of western Wisconsin during the mid to late afternoon hours on April 17th. One of these tornadoes was a strong EF-3 tornado near the unincorporated community of Cream, Wisconsin. This intense tornado was responsible for substantially damaging a home with much of its exterior walls collapsed. Additional tornadoes occurred as these storms traveled into Trempealeau and Jackson counties, with tree and minor structural damage along their paths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began west of Blair and tracked northeast resulting in damage to outbuildings, trees, and minor damage to one residence. The tornado continued into the hills north of Blair as its damage path became more intermittent, eventually dissipating west of the Trempealeau/Jackson County line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful, but rather moisture starved low pressure system moved across the Northern Plains March 12-13. Widespread high winds raced across the region late on the 12th and into the early overnight of the 13th with gusts ranging from 58 to 78 mph behind a strong cold front. With little to no snow on the ground, there were no significant reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 51 mph at times, with gusts as high as 66 mph at a South Dakota Mesonet site at White Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reports tree down near the intersection of pannell road and old monroe madison highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of March with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across coastal Miami-Dade County in March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.

A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in western Maryland across Garrett and western Allegany counties where 3 to upwards of 15 inches of snow fell. A secondary max associated with an inverted trough was observed from the Catoctins down to northern Montgomery county where 3 to 8 inches fell. Upwards of 12 inches were observed across the Catoctins. Another max of 3 to 6 inches was observed across Calvert and St. Mary's counties. The final max was Carroll to Cecil counties where 4 to 9 inches fell. Elsewhere across the DC and Baltimore metro, there was a relative minimum of 2 to 4 inches. Very little snow fell across eastern Allegany into far western Washington County.
During the afternoon hours of March 10th, supercells brought massive hail to portions of eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail reported near 175th and Renner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deepening low-pressure system located across the western Canadian Prairies moved into Manitoba on April 23rd, 2026. A surface cold front associated with this low was stretched across Minnesota. This aided the development of showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. A few stronger storms did produce large hail measuring quarter size (Freeborn Co.) and half-dollar size (Meeker Co.). Additionally, in southern Minnesota, the AWOS station located in Albert Lea measured a 62-mph wind gust.

An active weather pattern brought rounds of rain, mountain snow and gusty southerly winds from January 1st through January 5th. There were numerous flooding reports from moderate to heavy rain, along with some reports of mud and rock slides in the foothills. Ski resorts, Caltrans and the UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 1 to 4 feet of heavy snow in the mountains. There was one fatality of a hiker who had gone missing with these storms. Gusty southerly winds of 35 to 50 mph were also observed at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at US Highway 50 and Interstate 5 from heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated wind gust up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, and continued below normal precipitation during February, drought conditions worsened and became Severe (D2) during the month. The Severe Drought (D2) persisted through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northeast Illinois during the late evening of March 30th producing large hail.

On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing ping pong ball-sized hail (1.50 inches) and damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60 mph. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.

A low pressure over the Northern Plains, combined with a moist and unstable air mass, led to a conditional threat of severe thunderstorms as an upper level jet streak moved over North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed in the early afternoon along a quasi-stationary surface trough that was placed across central North Dakota. Numerous large hail and damaging thunderstorm wind gusts were reported across southwest and central North Dakota through the afternoon and evening as storms moved through. The largest hail reported was 2.25 inches in diameter in Max in McLean County. The strongest wind gust was also measured in McLean County, with a 77 mph wind gust reported at a US Air Force Weather station just south of Max.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One window on house was broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of damaging wind gusts. A few destructive wind gusts were noted in north-central Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and wires blew down along Wakefield Circle due to thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station College St Station - KFLJACKS5022 measured 2.07 inches of rainfall during the one hour span from 8:59pm to 9:59pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were down on N Kossuth Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought widespread 40 to 50 mph winds with higher gusts in combination with heavy snow. Near impossible travel and scattered power outages occurred with this storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread 10 to 16 inches of snow across Allegan County. This fell in combined with wind gusts over 50 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, daytime heating pushed temperatures into the upper 80s and lower 90s, combining with surging humidity to drive heat indices near 100��F and create a highly unstable environment with MLCAPE values reaching 2,500 J/kg. Weak low-level convergence initially triggered severe storms over Wayne County, which dropped 1 to 1.25-inch hail across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights. Later in the evening, a destructive Midwestern squall line tracked into southern Lower Michigan, though it steadily weakened as it moved through Southeast Michigan before completely clearing the state by midnight. While the broader system left over 85,000 customers without power statewide, wind damage, downed trees, and power outages within Southeast Michigan remained isolated to scattered, impacting communities primarily along and west of U.S. 23.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values of 100 to 103 degrees were observed in Monroe during the afternoon and early evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms moved across NE Louisiana during the afternoon/evening hours of March 15 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of golf ball-size hail across the Jonesville area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down along the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.

A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 70 mph knocked multiple trees down in Halifax township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Uneeda, tree and power line damage was observed along Jarrells Branch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. Despite the rain Hays, Medina, and Travis Counties stayed in D3 and Blanco and Williamson stayed in D2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. Despite the rain Hays, Medina, and Travis Counties stayed in D3 and Blanco and Williamson stayed in D2. |The Edwards Aquifer level rose 12.6 feet but was still 26.2 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 0.2 feet but was 16.8 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in March and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.2 feet and was 69.1 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped 0.2 feet and was 87.4 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina River; below normal on the Blanco River; and below normal to normal on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal. Most water providers encouraged conservation while San Antonio and Universal City imposed stage 3 restrictions and New Braunfels and Austin had stage 2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser provided video of a brief tornado occurring in an open field. No damage occurred, so an intensity rating could not be assigned.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms impacted the southeast Georgia coast in the early evening hours. One storm became strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts in the Savannah area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chatham County Emergency Management reported a tree down near the intersection of East Park Avenue and Drayton Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system for mid-June brought two rounds of thunderstorm on Wednesday June 17th. The strongest round of storms occurred during the morning hours that brough damaging winds (some significant), heavy rain, and two EF-1 tornadoes occurred in Iowa. One of these tornado was in Linby in Jefferson and the second touched down in far southeast Lee County and moved into Clark County Missouri and then into Warsaw Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree snapped due to strong wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree on house along Putnam Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Approximately 86% of Arkansas was locked in Severe Drought (D2) or worse. Crucially, Northeast Arkansas remained the epicenter of Exceptional Drought (D4) and Extreme Drought (D3) conditions. Because the topsoil lacked the basic moisture required for seed germination, row-crop farmers across the Northeast Arkansas Delta had to run irrigation pivots continuously through the first three weeks of May just to get cotton, corn, and soybeans to sprout. Relief finally arrived during the last week of May, with widespread storms dropping several inches of rain across the region. Despite the rain, it took a bit of extra time to make up for the extreme rainfall deficits and drought continued into June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D4 Exceptional Drought persisted through the month of May, but did shrink spatially.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercell thunderstorms developed near a slow-moving frontal boundary during the afternoon and evening hours on February 26. Cold temperatures were present aloft with strong deep layer shear but relatively weak low-level shear. Scattered severe hail reports were received, with the largest hailstones falling in portions of Blount, Jefferson, and St. Clair counties, as large as two inches in diameter. Damaging winds also occurred, with the most significant wind damage in Pinson where a microburst occurred. A hail storm associated with the microburst resulted in accumulating hail that covered the ground and resulted in the formation of hail fog. In addition, a brief EF-0 tornado also moved through Trussville, damaging some commercial and industrial buildings as well as homes, most of which was minor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping-pong to golf ball-sized hail in the Trussville area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak wind gust in Lipscomb County was 70 mph, which was observed at the mesonet site located eight miles west of Lipscomb at 1242CST. Gusts greater than 58 mph were observed in the county from about 1220CST through 1600CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a slow moving cold front as it pushed south through the state. Scattered strong to severe storms also developed just ahead of this front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A road was flooded in the Colony Park area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong southerly winds ahead of a line of thunderstorms caused a tree to fall across the road at Overnack Road and Roysden Drive in Ethridge. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down onto County Road 250 near US 250.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread, slow-moving showers and storms trained over the same areas and resulted in locally heavy rainfall and scattered flash flooding across central and eastern Virginia on May 25.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video was shared showing flooded roads along Route 1 in the Bellwood area just north of I-288 with water estimated to be six to ten inches deep. Additionally, at least three cars were stranded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leading to far southern portions of the Jackson Purchase in West Kentucky entering Severe (D2) Drought at the very end of March. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation slightly below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, the southern Jackson Purchase was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

A strong upper level low pressure system passed through the Pacific Northwest and over the Northern Rockies into the Northern Plains. This system brought heavy snow primarily to the southern half of North Dakota, with the heaviest snow generally south of Interstate 94. The greatest snow amount reported was 16 inches at Napoleon in Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Locations northeast of Hague received 12 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level disturbance interacting with a surface trough triggered clusters of showers and thunderstorms across central Illinois from the late morning through the afternoon of June 8th.  With surface dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s and copious moisture within the atmospheric profile, the storms were efficient rain-producers.  There were pockets of rainfall of 1.50 to 3.00, with a few spots exceeding 4.00.  The most widespread heavy rainfall and flash flooding was focused along the I-57 corridor from Douglas County southward to Effingham County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads were inundated with standing water in Canton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of upper disturbances and fast moving cold fronts cause multiple rounds of stormy weather across portions of Louisiana. Several severe storms occurred. Behind the fast paced systems, tides fell below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The American Red Cross reported a tree was downed onto a home in Lecompte. Multiple trees were downed between Elmer and Glenmora. Beauregard Electric also reported powerlines were downed at East River and Sunset Roads near the community of Calcasieu. A street sign was blown down on Highway 181 near Lecompte.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm chaser reported golf ball size hail 5 miles west southwest of Annetta South.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bulloch County 911 Call Center reported a tree down near the intersection of East Highway 80 and Mud Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimate of 0.5 inch of accumulated freezing rain in Greenwood with downed trees and powerlines with thick ice cover.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough couple with an area of low pressure north of the region allowed for ample lift and moisture to funnel into northern Pennsylvania during the early afternoon hours of January 17th. Afternoon clearing ahead of snow showers allowed for marginal instability to form, allowing for a couple of snow squalls to form across Warren and McKean Counties. As the squalls moved farther east, limited instability allowed for the snow squalls to weaken with scattered snow showers continuing across northern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. Webcams in Warren outlined near-zero visibility with heavy snowfall being observed on the webcam. Roads rapidly became snow covered over the course of 5 to 10 minutes within the snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
