The atmosphere north of the warm front across eastern Oklahoma became moderately unstable during the afternoon and early evening, and the deep-layer wind shear was strong with the approach of the upper level disturbance. Some of the thunderstorms were able to develop into supercells due to the favorable combination of instability and wind shear. Large hail up to tennis ball size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms, as well as isolated damaging wind.

An upper-level low-pressure center progressed eastward through the Plains on the afternoon and evening of March 10, leading to the development of thunderstorms. These storms were able to initiate along a dryline across the Big Country. As the storms moved east through the forecast area, some generated large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported downed trees on highway 101 north of Chico.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions across much of central Pennsylvania persisted throughout the late fall and early winter months, allowing for severe drought to form across portions of southern and eastern Pennsylvania in January 2026. Multiple counties across central Pennsylvania were put under a Drought Watch by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, with Fulton County being put under a Drought Warning. Multiple instances of voluntary water reductions were put throughout central Pennsylvania, with two boroughs and a township in Schuylkill County put under a mandatory water conservation notice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 (severe) drought conditions began across Adams County on January 13, 2026 with dry conditions continuing through the end of January 2026. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection issued a Drought Watch for Adams County on January 8th. Voluntary water consumption reduction by 10% to 15% was urged due to the Drought Watch declaration by Pennsylvania American Water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of January with much of South Florida entering a severe drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe (D2) drought developed over inland Broward County during the middle of January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.
A warm front lifted into the Ohio Valley region, producing showers and thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Atmospheric patterns between strong low pressure and strong high pressure continued to direct strong and severe gusty winds into portions of northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple observations in southwest Phillips County recorded wind gusts in excess of 60 mph, the strongest of which was 76 mph, measured at the Zortman BLM RAWS site (ALDM8).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Slow-moving showers and storms resulted in locally heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding across central Virginia on May 26.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video was shared via social media showing water, several inches deep, completely covering a yard in Hopewell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 29, a shortwave trough brought with it ample mid-level moisture to produce virga and isolated rain showers across eastern Utah. For valleys, where surface conditions remained extremely dry, inverted-V profiles supported strong downdrafts from virga showers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 7:31 PM MDT, the KVEL ASOS at the Vernal Regional Airport recorded a gust of 58 mph. Other sensors around the zone recorded gusts of 47-53 mph. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received associated with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached a brief afternoon peak as high as 102 degrees near Truesdale and 100 degrees 3 miles south-southwest of Storm Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported inside of multiple apartments near the Villages of Roll Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak gust of 62 mph was measured at the KSME AWOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts to Greenbrier County. Surface air temperatures in the mid-70s and dew points in the 60s provided enough instability for storms to intensify. While DCAPE was only a few hundred and low compared to the areas east of the Blue Ridge, surface CAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots allowed severe thunderstorms to evolve and knock over several trees in the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and power line down reported near the intersection of Hollywood/Childers Road and Montvue Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced a low end squall line of thunderstorms, which in turn produced several reports of damaging winds. After the cold front's passage, a much colder airmass moved in and snow showers developed, leading to light snowfall for much of northeastern Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down by severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system became stationary over northeast Montana and introduced much colder air from the northeast. This combined with consistently gusty winds to produce white-out blizzard conditions for some locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported white-out blizzard conditions at the location 20 miles W of Circle. Wind speeds were sustained at 30 mph with gusts to 40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low off the Southern California coast pulled in some deep atmospheric river moisture ahead of a shortwave trough dropping southward across northwest Colorado. This led to moderate snow accumulations in the northern and central Colorado mountains with much less elsewhere. Warm temperatures also resulted in high snow levels with most accumulations above 9000 feet and rain or rain/snow mix in the valleys limiting accumulations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 5 to 12 inches of snow fell across the area with 12 inches reported at Crested Butte 6.2 N. Winds gusted in the 45 to 50 mph range at the onset of the event with a peak wind gust of 49 mph at Irwin Guides Ridge Top.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Facebook photo showed large hail estimated to be up to 3 inches in diameter around Dallas Baptist University. Windows of cars were blown out.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Southeastern New York. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Southeastern New York with blizzard conditions across Southern Westchester, New York City, and Long Island.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Southeastern New York. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.||A college student died from carbon monoxide poisoning while charging his cell phone during the blizzard. Also, there were 5 snow shoveling-related deaths on Long Island after the blizzard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 40 mph with JFK ASOS reporting a 62 mph gust at 5:17 am, and Bayonne mesonet reporting a 53 mph gust at 2:47 am, and Brooklyn college reporting a 57 mph gust at 5:10 am; and frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at surrounding ASOS stations, including Central Park. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged from mainly 20 to 23 inches across the zone via the public, and an official NWS observation from Central Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages in the American Falls area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed ahead of a cold front across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 12. These storms produced damaging winds as they moved east.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree branches were down onto Ladysmith Road at US-1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources confirmed widespread roadway flooding occurred in and near the outlined event area. This included several high-water rescues, road closures and erosion/damage in at least one location. The event time is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across the area with a line of showers and thunderstorms. The storms produced several tornadoes and gusty winds across southwest Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The EF-1 tornado began just west of Wildflower Rd south of|highway 84 near Isney Alabama. The tornado resulted in a few|uprooted and snapped trees as it passed over Wildflower Rd. The|tornado reached its peak intensity likely between Wildflower Rd|and Poultry Rd where it snapped several softwoods, uprooted other|trees and did damage to several chicken farm buildings. Total|damage to the chicken farm was difficult to determine given the|buildings were already damaged from a prior storm but satellite|imagery was able to assist in determining there was at least some|new damage to the buildings. As a result peak intensity was given|to the tree damage and a lower bound estimate was given to the|chicken farm. The tornado then proceeded towards highway 84 as it|slowly weakened before crossing highway 84 near Lone Star Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms with embedded supercells briefly intensified along the Interstate 85 corridor, causing several instances of wind damage in Chambers, Elmore, and Montgomery counties. The northern part of the city of Montgomery was most impacted, with numerous trees and several power lines downed and some trees falling on homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed along County Road 23 north of Elmore.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of March 15th. Several tornadoes occurred within this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed two trees in Alton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and moderately unstable airmass along a cold front moving through the region  supported development of thunderstorms across southeast Louisiana late afternoon and evening of May 11th. Although weak low-level flow limited the overall severe-weather organization, locally heavy rainfall occurred in Baton Rouge metro as well as a brief tornado and associated wind damage in St. James Parish near Grand Point and Paulina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media shared a photo of flooding on Corporate Boulevard in Baton Rouge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nebraska mesonet station measured wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stagnant, moist air mass just north of a stationary front allowed areas of dense fog to develop late on May 9th and early on May 10th. The fog dissipated shortly after dawn.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Somerset Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across eastern Arkansas. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill value of 5F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening hours on the 22nd, a couple clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of east-central and northeast Colorado. Yuma County was hit especially hard, with 81 mph winds and four inch diameter hail reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Per a social media photo, there were multiple hailstones compared to a one-dollar bill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elongated low pressure along a cold front brought an low end advisory accumulating snowfall to portions of Northeastern New Jersey.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cocorahs reported 2.6 inches in Little Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages reported in Springfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the 5 above to 2 below zero range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped as low as 1 above zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front blasted across northern NY during the early morning hours of February 7th sending temperatures plummeting near and below zero on brisk northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts creating dangerous windchill temperatures of 20 to 35 below zero for the daylight hours of February 7th. ||Although winds diminished somewhat on the night of the 7th, sub-zero temperatures still accounted for 25 to 40 below wind chills through midday on February 8th with daytime wind chills still 15 to 25 below zero.||Arctic high pressure crested across the region on the night of February 8th into the morning hours of February 9th. This allowed temperatures to radiate down to 10 to 25 below zero across northern NY.||This was the 3rd such cold spell within the past month that attributed to the Ice Over of Lake Champlain on February 13th, the first time since 2018.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime temperatures falling to below zero on Saturday (2/7) combined with northwest winds of 10 to 20 mph with higher gusts created wind chills of 20 to 30 below zero during the daylight hours. ||Saturday night (2/7) - Sunday morning (2/8)...although winds diminished to 5 to 10 mph and gusty at times, actual air temperatures fell to 10 to 15 below zero creating dangerous wind chills of 25 to 40 below zero. During Sunday (2/8) temperatures were around 0 degrees above zero but a persistent wind around 10 mph created wind chills of 10 to 20 below zero. High pressure crested across the region during the overnight into the early morning hours of February 9th, allowing temperatures to fall to 10 to 20 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A car was stranded with a person inside due to flooding waters at exit to pr-22 toward avenue Jose de Diego.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A section of a hog house near the 1000 block of Hollerin Road was severely damaged and the roof was blown off. A home on Hickory Green Lane also had its garage door partially pulled out. Four or five homes in the neighborhood  had shingles and shutters pulled off, and there were multiple trees down in that area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of excessive heat impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa from June 28 into June 30, 2026. The heat was supported by a strong mid- to upper-level ridge building into the central Plains. A warm front lifted northward across the area early on June 28, with temperatures rapidly rising in its wake. Daily high temperatures peaked in the upper 90s to low 100s, while southerly low-level flow ushered in dewpoints in the 70s. As a result, daily maximum heat index values peaked in the 105 to 115-degree range. In addition, little overnight relief was observed, with heat index values remaining at or above 75 degrees for at least 48 consecutive hours throughout the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KRDK AWOS recorded minimum temperatures above 75 degrees for at least 48 hours, paired with daily maximum heat index values peaking around 105-107 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines blew down on Harney Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration snow event produced 4 to 12 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, moderate to heavy at times, developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 6 and 8 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. There was a report of 7.0 inches 1 mile southeast of Winona Lake. Roads were snow covered and slick with numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow accumulation of 1 to 2 inches over the western part of Lafayette County, followed by 1/2 to 1 inch of ice over the entire county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic storm system brough gusty northwest winds to many locations across northeast Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Malta W MDA Montana Climate Office agrimet site (MTM69) measured a 59 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak weather system combined with an arctic blast to bring high winds and light snow to the region on the morning of January 21. The Pierre Regional Airport ASOS measured the strongest wind gust at 76 mph. Matching 75 mph gusts were recorded by a personal weather station north of Pierre and the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station southeast of Reliance. While the Watertown COOP recorded 2.4 inches of snow, most other locations received an inch or less. The combination of wind and snow prompted No Travel Advised notices for Walworth, Hand, Faulk, Spink, Roberts, and Hamlin counties. Slick roads and intermittent low visibility resulted in a number of slide-ins across Roberts county.

A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow accumulation generally around 6 inches was reported by the Public across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens. There were numerous social media posts of frozen and burst water pipes across the area.

A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across southern Vermont for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were cold, but not quite to dangerous levels. Feels-like temperatures this first night ranged from about -18 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -13 to 0 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -8 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -30 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -11 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -36 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook report relayed 1.75 inch hail just north northeast of Wills Point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) interacted with a sheared and unstable environment to produce numerous supercells in southeast Illinois on June 21st.  13 tornadoes were documented, the strongest being two EF-2 tornadoes near Newton.  Storms training over the same areas led to widespread heavy rainfall and several occurrences of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six inches of water was flowing across Co Rd 650 E near Clear Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours, decaying eastward-moving thunderstorms south, southeast, and east of the region produced a 58 mph non-thunderstorm wind gust at McCook.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The high winds blew out of the south, and were measured at the McCook Ben Nelson Regional Airport. They were likely associated with outflow from decaying eastward-moving showers and thunderstorms well south, southeast, and east of the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS damage survey confirmed that an EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 100 mph began in far northeastern Whiteside County west of Palmyra before moving northeast into Lee County. It tracked for over 6.5 miles before lifting near the town of Woosung. The tornado damaged or destroyed multiple farm outbuildings, downed several trees and power poles, and caused minor damage to a few residences.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and powerlines down in the area from smokey rd to franklin rd west of doctor bruce jackson rd and east of the  county line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported on roads near Greensburg area from 2.5 to 4 inches of heavy rain that fell in a few hours. No building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across upstate South Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts occurred, including an area of significant damage in Gaffney.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey found an area of straight-line wind damage in Gaffney. Damage was first observed within the city limits, where corrugated metal roof panels, wooden joists, and fascia were ripped off the front of a small business along West Frederick Street. The wind also shifted the exterior metal wall of a nearby auto parts store, causing the corner panels to buckle and separate. East of there, a large tree was uprooted next to a house between Marion Avenue and Mill Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of light freezing rain moved west to east across the UP during the afternoon and evening of the 6th into the early morning hours of the 7th. Although amounts were light, a glaze of ice resulted in treacherous travel conditions on untreated roadways. A few traffic accidents were reported, including a school bus carrying a high school girls' basketball team that flipped on its side between Marquette and K.I. Sawyer.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light freezing rain resulted in a glaze of ice on untreated surfaces. Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, school closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A portion of Francis Lane was washed out by rushing water, with parts of the roadway washed away.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills dropped below 0 degrees across the county between Saturday evening and Tuesday morning, January 24th through 27th. The lowest wind chill of 0 was recorded at KPRX the morning of January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions covered much of East Texas and eastern Central Texas throughout the month of April 2026, though minor improvements occurred during the latter half of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions at the beginning of April improved to moderate by the middle of the month for all but the southern part of the county, which remained in Extreme Drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The southern stream of the jet remained over the area for multiple days driving a series of short waves across the region. This resulted in a few days of unsettled weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles and trees were downed in Lake Charles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of June saw overall above normal temperatures and a mixed bag of precipitation with some areas seeing above normal precipitation and others below normal precipitation. This is very reflective of the early summer thunderstorm activity that saw daily rounds of thunderstorms pass over some areas repeatedly, while missing other areas entirely. As a result, most of New Mexico saw no change in drought conditions while around a quarter to a third of the state saw either a 1 class degradation or improvement in drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought was introduced to nearly all of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were three calls for downed trees and wires as the storm moved through.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions alleviated thanks to an abundance of rainfall, ending their formal inclusion as of the 5/26/2026 Drought Monitor issuance for most counties in Northern AL. At this time, only the following counties remain in D2 through the end of May: portions of Jackson, Dekalb, Colbert, and Franklin County, AL. All other counties were downgraded to Moderate Drought (D1) conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions finally end with the 5/26/2026 Drought Monitor issuance thanks to abundant rainfall that occurred across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of southwest Georgia ahead of a frontal boundary.  A few storms were severe with hail and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were down on Mussel White Store Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on Route 80.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail estimated up to 1 inch in diameter in Falls City, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts moving through western and central North Dakota combined with a series of short-wave troughs resulted in an extended period of strong winds. The strongest reported wind gust was 74 mph at the Bowman Airport in Bowman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tatanka Prairie RAWS reported wind gusts to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) swept across portions of central, southern and eastern Oklahoma on the morning of the 8th. This convective system was tied to the passage of a compact upper wave across the region, resulting in very strong wind fields within a weakly unstable boundary layer. In addition to sporadic pockets of thunderstorm wind damage, and generally sub-severe hail, a few tornadoes occurred in a corridor from near Purcell, OK to Shawnee, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed near 180th Street and Ladd Road southwest of Purcell and moved northeast. One home about 3 miles southwest of Purcell had the roof removed. A semi on Interstate 35 just west of Purcell was pushed over injuring one person. The tornado then moved through Purcell causing roof damage to a few homes and damaging utility poles and trees. Moving out of the northeast side of Purcell, the tornado crossed the Canadian River into Cleveland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over the region, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D2 to include all of the Coastal Mississippi counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of Harrison County according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bacon county 911 call center reported several trees reported down  just west of Alma. Time of event based on  radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kessinger School Road was closed due to downed powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ema reports at least one tree down on the 600 block of w haynes st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

Plummeting snow levels in the wake of a cold front interacted with strong northwest upslope flow to result in snow shower development beginning during the afternoon of the 16th across the counties bordering Tennesse. The snow showers continued through the overnight hours before beginning to wind down during the morning of the 17th, before tapering off during the afternoon. Total accumulations of 3-6 inches, with locally higher amounts were reported in the higher elevations along the Tennessee border. Accumulations up to 3 inches occurred in the valleys northeast of I-40, while valley locations beneath the Smokies saw little more than a dusting.

A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Southwest and south-central Georgia started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

A surface boundary was in the vicinity of the combined Panhandles through the afternoon and evening hours of June 29th. This combined with daytime heating, ample instability and enough dry air in the higher levels of the atmosphere to bring scattered showers and thunderstorms to the region. Some of these storms intensified to be severe with damaging winds being the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 62 MPH wind gust was measured at the mesonet site located six miles northeast of Pantex, on the northwest side of Pantex Lake. Severe gusts persisted for two minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and embedded thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the late morning and early afternoon of April 27th.  On the back side of this precipitation, a wake low developed, producing wind gusts between 50 and 70 mph, which blew down trees, tree limbs and power lines.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across east central Illinois during the evening of April 27th producing isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large branches were broken and fell onto power lines in Sandwich. The upper portion of a large tree was broken and landed on a house north of Sandwich. Nearby personal weather stations recorded gusts to between 60 and 70 mph at the time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked trees and wires down on Black Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near normal temperatures and precipitation led to a brief period of severe (D2) drought around mid to late month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief period of severe (D2) drought conditions developed mid-month and improved to moderate (D1) again by late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the parish fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am  on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures were below freezing over western Sargent County. The Brampton, ND NDAWN reported a low temperature of 31 at 4:25 AM CST. The NDAWN 3W of Stirum, ND also reported a low temperature of 31 during this period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees blew down around Cove Point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. A swath of 1 to 1.75 inch hailstones were observed from Putnam and Logan Counties over to Kanawha and Clay Counties. The severe risk subsided as the sun began to set for the evening and the cold front began its passage through the forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Central Avenue near downtown Wayne.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree Snapped  and fell across the street Near St. George Elementary School In St. George, Ga. Time Estimated  Based Off Radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down in Hodgesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of precipitation. The first round produced mixed precipitation across the county. The second round fell as mostly wet heavy snow that melted on contact with the ground. Snow accumulations measured 2 to 4 inches across the western portion of the county. A CoCoRaHS observer 3 miles E of Rice measured 3.0 inches of total snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Street flooding reported on Calle A in Barrio Palomas near a local church at the intersection with Callejon Viqueira. Water is observed covering the roadway and reaching the chassis level of parked vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown on a powerline and both were laying on the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Immediately following the strong winds, snow enveloped much of the state. Many areas saw 6 to 15 inches of snow across the lower elevations, much higher in the mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received over 12 inches of snow and breezy winds caused blowing snow impacts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported several trees down and debris in the road along MS Hwy 37 near the Smith Covington line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions persisted across the tri-state area through April and into May with D3-D4 drought continuing.

A strong mesoscale convective system of thunderstorms dropped southward out of Ontario into Central NY, moving into an unusually unstable and sufficiently sheared environment. This supported severe thunderstorms with widespread damaging winds, an isolated EF1 tornado, and hail. Heavy rainfall also occurred as deep moisture surged northward from the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down trees and wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down on West Commerce Street and Elm Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very cold winter, a significant amount of ice, with substantial depth, developed on main-stem rivers across eastern New York. Periodic multi-day stretches of late-season, above-normal temperatures subsequently led to considerable ice melt over a short amount of time. This ultimately led to flooding in Warren County in early to mid March after an ice jam broke loose on the Hudson River from the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg. NWS Albany was made aware of the flooding and its requisite impacts from communication with both local news outlets and emergency managers in the area. According to these sources, water and large chunks of ice flowed rapidly downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In Thurman, portions of River Road became inundated, specifically near The Glen Bridge, by both rapidly flowing water and large pieces of ice. This lead to the closure of the road for several days. In Warrensburg, portions of the Warren County Fish Hatchery also became inundated with some water and ice from a nearby branch of the Hudson River. Additionally, Cronin's Golf Course, which lies right along the Hudson River, became inundated with significant amounts of water. Areal drone images from a local news outlet showed what appears to be the entire golf course covered in water and ice. Due to the substantial nature of this ice jam, flooding impacted these areas for several days after the initial onset.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Warren County Emergency Managers, with the help of local broadcast media partners, reported that at 10 A.M. on Thursday, March 12th, an ice jam that had accumulated near the Route 28 Bridge at The Glen in Johnsburg, NY broke free and rapidly flowed downstream. Large chunks of ice were swiftly carried downstream towards the towns of Thurman and Warrensburg. In the town of Thurman, portions of River Road became inundated, specifically near The Glen Bridge, by both rapidly flowing water and large pieces of ice which lead to the closure of the road for several days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on wires with small fire on Milwaukee Ave near Oxford Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed powerlines in the 3000 block of Highway 412 West. Trees were also downed which blocked Highway 13 South near Highway 128. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages reported in Georgetown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of wires down and power outages near Plattsburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours. Strong storms developed and produced damaging wind gusts and localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the zero to 5 above zero range at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped as low as 1 above zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on the bridge along Rod Alston Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, as well as one of the driest Februarys on record, drought conditions worsened and became Severe (D2) during the month. The Severe Drought (D2) then persisted through the end of the month. Streamflows and soil moisture values across the region ranged from well below normal to near record lows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass persisted across northwestern Connecticut during the early morning hours on February 2, 2026. The combination of cold temperatures and a lingering breeze resulted in some wind chill values (or feels-like temperatures) to reach 10 to 15 degrees below zero, though coverage was not as widespread as previous days.

A powerful blizzard tracked through the Upper Great Lakes, bringing widespread blizzard conditions, with high winds and heavy snow to the U.P. Portions of the central and eastern U.P. experienced up to 4 feet of snowfall. Extreme conditions resulted in road departments pulling crews and pausing snow removal. Extreme snowfall and drifting resulted in cars being stranded and emergency officials advising people to not venture outside by foot or vehicle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds and heavy snow brought blizzard conditions to Delta County.  ESC/MNM ASOS reported blizzard conditions. Snowfall of over two feet fell across much of the county. Up to 7% of the county was without power during the event. A few FM radio towers became inoperable. Plowing operations suspended due to severe weather conditions. MI Governor declared a state of emergency. Flights cancelled to/from ESC. Vehicles were reported stranded, especially in the Escanaba area.  A Local Area Emergency was issued by request from the EM for impassable roads and extreme travel conditions and to advise people to stay off the roads.  An elderly person had to be rescued from their home using snowmobiles and side-by-sides due to impassable roads after loosing power in the Garden Peninsula. Key impacts: school closures, power outages, impossible travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

A warm and moist airmass was in place across southeast Louisiana on April 2nd, with scattered to numerous thunderstorms developing during the afternoon and evening hours. Storms became oriented north to south and repeatedly redeveloped while slowly shifting east across Tangipahoa Parish. This allowed heavy rainfall to fall over some of the same areas for an extended period. A stronger storm also produced localized wind damage near Tickfaw.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported roads in Independence covered with water with vehicles taking on water along Hwy 40. Reported via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The low pressure over Southern California responsible for bringing up the abundant Atmospheric River moisture moved eastward across the Desert Southwest with the low center passing south of the Four Corners across northern New Mexico. This resulted in additional light to moderate snowfall accumulations across the southwest Colorado mountains with the Southwest San Juan Mountains receiving the higher amounts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: About 7 inches of snow fell at Columbine Pass at the higher elevations with 3 to 5 inches at the lower elevations with 5.5 inches of snow reported at Ridgway 5.3 NNW.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments. It's along those stronger segments where multiple marine locations were impacted by severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Petit Bois Island station measured a wind gust of 43 mph or 39 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent area of low pressure stationed across southern Ontario allowed for a surface cold front to begin tracking across the Great Lake region during that afternoon and evening hours of February 6, 2026. As this cold front approached portions of central Pennsylvania, rapid drops in visibility were beginning to be observed on webcams due to snow squalls. These snow squalls continued across portions of southwestern Pennsylvania during the late evening hours of February 6th, mainly across Somerset County. As the cold front continued progressing across the region, snow showers intensity waned; however, an isolated snow squall in Schuylkill County was also observed with a rapid drop to near-zero visibility on Interstate 81. Cold air and gusty winds in the wake of the cold frontal passage allowed for dangerously cold wind chills across much of western Pennsylvania. No injuries or fatalities were reported with these snow squalls and the extreme cold that followed the cold frontal passage as temperatures began to warm during the late morning and early afternoon hours of February 7th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bitterly cold temperatures and gusty winds led to dangerously cold wind chills during the morning hours of February 7th across Elk County. The coldest wind chill observed was -27 degrees in Saint Marys during the early morning hours of February 7, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
