EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down near the intersection of Jersey Mountain Road and Orchard Point Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across eastern North Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NDAWN station at Finely 1 NNW consistently reported wind chill values -40 or lower from the morning of January 22 through midday on January 23. The lowest wind chill value during that period was -50.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with occasional severe weather reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and powerlines were down across Wakulla County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms tracked over parts of southeast and east-central Wisconsin during the evening hours on June 11, 2026. Storms organized into a linear complex along the Wisconsin-Illinois state line, producing several reports of thunderstorm wind damage from Walworth County east toward the Lake Michigan shoreline. Damage surveys would also confirm a brief tornado in the city of Kenosha. Additional severe storms formed over Sheboygan County, producing wind gusts to 60 MPH.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief tornado began on the south side of 18th Street west of 72nd Ave.  Two barn outbuilding structures were heavily damaged with metal roofing lofted and deposited several hundred yards downwind.  Several trees were damaged, uprooted or received large limbs damage.  Tree limbs with damage toward the end of the track along 72nd Ave were blown and deposited across the street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 degrees) across western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 28th.

During the evening hours on June 5th, storms move into portions of Buffalo and Trempealeau counties producing large hail and strong winds. Eventually, these storms formed into a line and pushed southeast into portions of La Crosse, Monroe and Juneau Counties bring additional large hail, damaging wind gusts and an EF-0 tornado in eastern Monroe County prior to storms exiting to the southeast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported trees down onto powerlines 2 miles southwest of Hustler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving shortwave upper level trough followed by a shortwave ridge tracking near the International Border produced a strong surface pressure gradient on the 7th and accompanying strong winds across North-Central MT.  Heading into the 8th, the upper level ridge broke down. This day brought a longer duration of strong sustained winds and widespread strong wind gusts over North-Central MT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KHLN Helena Airport measured a 67 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report indicated that several trees were blown down at Lake Bridgeport. Part of a roof was reportedly blown off a house, and a bay door was blown in at the fire department.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down across northern James City County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down in Enterprise.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system moved east-southeastward through central Mississippi into southwestern Alabama late on April 24. Although it mostly missed Central Alabama, it clipped southern Sumter County, resulting in a few downed trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed along County Road 9 near Highway 17.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very isolated rain events brought some moisture to the eastern Panhandles during the month. However, this did not put a dent in the 120 departure from normal with values staying 2 to 4 below normal. Mites were appearing on stressed winter wheat crop and wildfires became an increasing concern across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate Drought (D1) conditions persisted in the NW TX Panhandle until the third week of March. At that point, the drought intensified, with Dallam, Hartley, Sherman, and Moore Counties all escalating to Severe Drought (D2). This transition was marked by an additional 1 to 2 being added to the existing 120-day precipitation deficit. Furthermore, the severity of the drought's impact on winter crops was worsened by record monthly maximum temperatures recorded during the month.

CZ_NAME: LONG ISLAND SOUND EAST OF NEW HAVEN CT/PORT JEFFERSON NY TO THE MOUTH OF THE CONNECTICUT RIVER
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet site FW2389 in Orient measured a 38 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level jet was positioned over the Pacific Northwest from March 8 through 13. As it mixed down to the lower levels, it brought periods of high winds sustained in the 30 to 40 mph range and gusts up to 70 mph for portions of the region. It was followed by a cold front that brought snow amounts ranging from 2 to 9 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer measured 6 inches of snow. Other reports in North Idaho ranged from 2 inches near Spirit Lake, 3 inches near Sandpoint, and 3.9 inches near Athol.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms moved down the Space and Treasure Coasts in the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The WeatherFlow station at Rocky Point measured a peak wind gust of 41 knot from the north.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the community of Enterprise, a tree was blown down on Fish Hatchery Road near WV-5.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong upper level troughing diving southeastward from central BC toward southern AB/SK resulted in a sharp transition to strong zonal flow aloft across the Northern Rockies April 7. Favorable timing of the system, arriving during the day, allowed for daytime mixing to translate stronger gusts to the surface in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Montana mesonet station Bynum W measured a 78 mph gust. Other sensors measuring strong winds or gusts include Salmond Ranch Salmt, Delmt Dellwo, MTPND Pendfory MT Dot, MTCTS Chouteau S MT Dot, HODMT Hodgkiss, and RICMT Rice Ridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted into the central US with a deformation zone setting up across central Iowa, resulting in a band of heavy snow bisecting the state. Light precipitation fell ahead of the main deformation zone, however dry air and warm temperatures meant this largely fell as rain to start. The main deformation zone set up across Iowa in the afternoon with rain transitioning over to snow and temperatures fell. Heaviest snow fell through the overnight with rates over one inch per hour at times. Snow tapered off quickly through the morning hours. Roads across central Iowa were snow covered with impacts to the morning commute on the 20th, including an accident with injury. Operations were also paused overnight at the Des Moines airport.

At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Simultaneously and ahead (i.e. south) of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward and produced sporadic peak straight-line convective wind gusts of gale-to-storm-force along the OH shore amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. Within the warm and relatively-moist sector south of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward over and near Lake Erie and generated sporadic gale-force peak straight-line convective wind gusts along the OH shore during the predawn hours of the 15th amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Fairport Harbor C-MAN Station (FAIO1) recorded a peak straight-line convective wind gust of 64-mph from a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold frontal boundary progressed across the southeastern states on the 23rd of June before slowing progress and nearly stalling over the northeast FL/southeast GA region. Plenty of summer moisture and instability in the vicinity of the boundary resulted in numerous to widespread showers and thunderstorms for several days in a row.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees on powerlines reported in Callahan. Time of event based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique snow setup for South Carolina continued into February 1st as a strong coastal low strengthening offshore, while a upper level disturbance shifted over our area. This provided sufficient synoptic and mesoscale lift to continue across portions of northern and eastern SC with unusually high snow to liquid ratios between 15-20 to 1 and highest amounts in the Pee Dee region of SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple measurements across the county of between 2 and 5.3 inches of storm total snowfall with accumulating snow continuing into February 1st. Highest measured amount in the county was 5.3 inches near Bishopville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured mostly around one quarter of an inch of rain across the county. Gray County ended the month about 1.5-2.2 inches below normal. The 120 day departure below normal was around 3.5 inches in the west to 4.5 inches in the central and east. The entire county remained in D2 drought through the month until the western half of the county degraded further into Extreme Drought (D3) near the middle to end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.||In addition, locally repeated heavy rainfall produced some urban flash flooding in Rock Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds gusts up to 68 mph were measured by ASOS station KSPW at the Spencer Municipal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree branch was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation continued to lack across much of northwest Iowa with 25 percent to 75 percent of normal during the month for areas west of U.S. Highway 59.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions worsened to severe (D2) very late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed near a warm front across central and east-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours on Wednesday (6/24).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to golf ball size along with flash flooding in Green Bay.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny size hail fell in Plover.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low in the Central Plains moved northeast into the Great Lakes late on Sunday the 15th. Ahead of its attendant cold front that passed later in the evening, a low level jet developed in the late morning and moved east. Daytime heating gave added energy to mix the lower levels of the atmosphere and bring strong winds from this feature to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Richmond Municipal Airport twice measured a gust to 49 mph. The first occurred at 12:15 pm EST, and the second at 11:35 pm EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system pressing through the Great Lakes region on March 13th resulted in a windy day across northeast Kentucky. This was due to the combination of a tightened pressure gradient and strengthening low level jet aloft. Daytime heating helped to create turbulent mixing of these stronger winds down to the surface, especially during the afternoon and early evening hours. Wind gusts in excess of 40 to 50 miles per hour noted in northeast Kentucky resulted in downed trees and power lines across the area. The wind gradually declined after sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area.

Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through New Jersey producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires reported down. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The fire department reported knee deep water over Highway 80 near Big Tex Trailers at the Wills Point city limit. Wills Point Fire and Edgewood Fire were working multiple calls for flooding of stranded occupants in vehicles on Highway 80.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported a tree down on County Road 114 in Scottsboro blocking both  lanes. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm temperatures and moist upslope winds fueled thunderstorm development in eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the 15th. This cluster of thunderstorms moved into West Texas during the evening hours producing isolated wind damage. It was reported that power poles were snapped in Parmer County while shingles were blown off of a roof in Abernathy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported at least three snapped power poles along Farm to Market Road 1731 north of Bovina.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An strong upper-level low with an associated surface cold front allowed to ample lift in an environment with sufficient shear and instability for a line of showers and isolated thunderstorms to form during the afternoon and evening hours of March 13, 2026. Strong-to-damaging wind gusts were observed across northwestern Pennsylvania with these features with the most widespread wind damage in portions of Clearfield County during the late afternoon to early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of showers producing wind gusts estimated at 70 mph knocked a telephone pole down onto a roadway approximately 2 miles southeast of Hyde.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (108F) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April saw below to well below normal precipitation across a majority of New Mexico, with the exception of a small area of the northwestern mountains. The average temperature anomaly was also generally 1 to 5 degrees above normal over nearly all of the state. This led to a notable expansion of extreme drought conditions over northeastern NM, and severe drought conditions over the eastern plains. While western areas saw below normal precipitation, the actual difference from normal was still low given April is climatologically a very dry month already. This allowed for little to no change in drought conditions over this portion of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought spread across nearly all of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of March 15th. Several tornadoes occurred within this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado briefly touched down approximately 5 miles southwest of Akers in Shannon County. Strong winds caused the roof of a single wide home to be torn off as well as the windows to be blown in. Other damage included large trees uprooted and healthy trees snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam County emergency management reported a power line blown down. Time estimated from radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms moved across South Florida on April 8, 2026. A mesoscale area of low pressure followed the earlier round of storms producing widespread strong winds across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video footage of street flooding was shared by Riviera Beach PD as well as reports of manhole covers floating off on President Barack Obama Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold air in the wake of a winter storm that brought widespread snowfall to central Pennsylvania allowed for many locations to experience a prolonged period of cold weather beginning on January 27th and continuing into January 31, 2026. Cold air in the wake of the winter system allowed for a period of much cooler than average temperatures with gusty winds also allowing for dangerously cold wind chills across western Pennsylvania January 26th and into January 27th. High pressure in the wake of an Arctic Front passage on January 30th allowed for bitterly cold temperatures to continue into January 31st, especially across western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures impacted Northern Centre County on the morning of January 30. Much of the area saw low temperatures in the -10 to -15 degree range. The coldest temperature of -20 degrees was observed near South Philipsburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface front produced strong winds across northern North Dakota. There were a few isolated thunderstorms early in the day before non-thunderstorm wind gusts reached around 60 mph. The highest observed non-thunderstorm wind gust was 62 mph in Rolette.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station 5 W Coulee reported wind gusts up to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep occluded low approaching the UP from the west on the 18th brought a warm front just south of the UP and eventually the occluded front moved over the UP as the low weakened by the 19th. This brought a mess of heavy wet snow and freezing rain as well as high winds. Impacts included a majority of school districts closed, municipal facilities closed, power outages, and near-impassible roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow and freezing rain reports varied throughout the county, but the highest verifiable report was from a NWS Employee at 1 N Trowbridge Park with a report of 9.5 inches with a glaze of ice on top. Key impacts: school closures, municipality closures, hazardous travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across northwest and west central Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station FW9117 Gonvick, MN reported periodic wind chills -40 during this period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 146 near Highway 167 in Vienna was closed due to flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 8 Ball Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately 12 miles west of Clarendon, or ten miles west of Howardwick, along the US 287 corridor in Armstrong County. The fire was fueled by freeze-cured tall grasses and brush, driven by critical fire weather conditions including wind gusts up to 45 mph and low humidity. It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is human related with a connection to passenger vehicle or motorized RV usage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist onshore flow above the existing snow pack ahead of an advancing warm front resulted in widespread dense fog late on February 17th and early on February 18th. The fog dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Millville Executive Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

A hot and humid air mass led to strong destabilization with surface based CAPE near 4000 J/kg in the Central Savannah River Area. While shear was weak, dry air aloft and strong low level lapse rates supported a few storms reaching severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported quarter sized hail in the Oak Ridge Plantation Neighborhood near  Hephzibah, GA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of snow set up across northeast South Dakota on the morning of February 28th. 8.3 inches of fluffy light snow was measured 4 miles north of Bristol, with 6.1 inches in Doland. Observers in Chelsea, Columbia, Garden City and 2 miles north of the Hamlin Education Center all submitted 6 inches of total snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter 1 mile south of Chelsea measured 6 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper shortwave trough moved across Texas and generated thunderstorms. Some storms formed along a dryline over the western edge of South-Central Texas. Other storms formed east of the dryline in a conditionally unstable, moist airmass. Storms produced all severe hazards and locally heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that knocked down some 2.5 inch diameter tree branches in the city of Uvalde.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report relayed via emergency management. The hail was reported to be covering the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The beginning of February featured very cold temperatures and wind chills that began during late January across southwest Virginia. Temperatures as low as minus 8 degrees were recorded by a local cooperative observer in Clintwood during the first few days of the month, with similar temperatures observed in Buchanan County. The cold across this portion of the Appalachians was short-lived for the month, as temperatures quickly rebounded above freezing on February 3rd and once again by the middle of the month, where afternoon highs ranged in the 50s and 60s.
Multiple severe storms occurred, producing winds up to 67 mph and hail up to 3 inches in diameter. Some minor flooding occurred as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station 11 miles sse of Billings reported winds gusting up to 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Anawalt, a tree fell onto power lines along County Road 84.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active weather pattern brought rounds of rain, mountain snow and gusty southerly winds from January 1st through January 5th. There were numerous flooding reports from moderate to heavy rain, along with some reports of mud and rock slides in the foothills. Ski resorts, Caltrans and the UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 1 to 4 feet of heavy snow in the mountains. There was one fatality of a hiker who had gone missing with these storms. Gusty southerly winds of 35 to 50 mph were also observed at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding in Woodland due to heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The center of a major Nor���easter passed nearby to the east of southeastern New York during the morning of February 23, 2026. The resulting strong pressure gradient brought high winds to the area during this time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A measured high wind gust was recorded at mesonet station XBLU - Blue Point at 800 AM Local Standard Time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two water rescues occurred at State Highway 86 and Douglas Fir Road.

CZ_NAME: CENTRAL GUNNISON AND UNCOMPAHGRE RIVER BASIN
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong moisture transport flowed through the Intermountain West around a deep upper-level trough in late January, bringing widespread precipitation to Colorado's west slope. While much of the region continued to be impacted by active weather through the night and morning, drying mid-levels cleared skies over the Grand and Paradox Valleys. Dense fog already began to develop at this point, but as the frontal boundary supporting the precipitation dipped south, cooling temperatures prolonged dense fog throughout the majority of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Areas of dense fog developed within lower valleys along US-50 during the morning of January 24. The KAJZ AWOS at the Blake Field Delta Airport reported about two hours of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog following a prolonged period of snowfall. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scott County received heavy snow and sleet totaling 5 to 6 inches. Scott County also saw light ice accumulation around 0.10 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dryline pushed to about the Rio Grande Valley while a subtle upper level disturbance moved through southwest flow helping to produce severe thunderstorms and flash flooding.  Many locations across El Paso reported over 1 inch of rainfall with the thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports received from KVIA of flooded roadways and stalled vehicles near Lomaland and Vista del Sol.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon on June 16, a few supercells developed. Photos of wall clouds were received and hail as large as 2 inches in diameter was recorded (in Michigan). Two EF-U tornadoes occurred as well.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Lincoln and Union Parishes in North Louisiana through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 2 to 4 inches across much of North Louisiana, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only further expanded during the month of April.

A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began just south of Highway 412, damaging a grain bin and snapping a few trees along County Road 300. The tornado then caused damage to a camper along County Road 208. This tornado continued east-northeast and damaged an outbuilding on County Road 205 and caused tree damage at the intersection of County Road 205 and 214. This tornado resulted in EF-0 damage with 85 mph winds. The tornado lifted east of County Road 214.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly sinking cold front provided lift for thunderstorm development during the evening hours across north Mississippi. Partial clearing of skies prior to the frontal arrival resulted in moderate destabilization. Climatologically, February is cooler, which increases confidence in very cold air aloft. The lift from the front, an unstable environment, and cold air aloft raised a primary concern for large hail. Elevated MUCAPE values (up to 1500 J/kg) and steep lapse rates resulted in hail up to golf ball size to occur.

A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to 3 inches in size was reported in a mainly rural area. Damage occurred to a home, several outbuilding and a few vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal system brought widespread light to moderate snowfall accumulations to the area. Total snowfall amounts ranged from a light coating to 1 near the coast to 1-4 farther inland. Temperatures near freezing during daytime snowfall fell well below freezing overnight, resulting in slippery road conditions in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 2-4. The highest reported amount was 4.9 in Belle Mead.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A cold front dropped south into the region and combined with a warm, moist and unstable airmass to bring isolated showers and thunderstorms to the region on the afternoon and evening of June 13. Storms primarily affected the east and northeast Texas Panhandle with damaging winds and small hail.

A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages due to downed trees or limbs damaging equipment.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 58 mph was measured at the Rockford Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures persisted in April across western and north central Nebraska. This coupled with a continuation of well below normal precipitation, led to drought expansion across all of western and north central Nebraska in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions, persisted through the end of April across most of Deuel County. Over the far northwestern portion of the county, extreme (D3) drought deteriorated to exceptional (D4) drought by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation was only 25 to 50 percent of normal across most of southeast South Dakota, and a low as 10 to 25 percent of normal in south central South Dakota during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions worsened to severe (D2) late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of observing platforms in southern Hidalgo County (City of Edinburg, McAllen, Mission, Weslaco, etc) recorded minimum temperatures in the upper 20s on January 26th.  Freezing (32F or lower) temperatures arrived around 4 AM, and continued through around 930 AM before sunshine rapidly warmed temperatures above freezing.||An unknown amount of minor damage was likely to winter crops, mainly due to the sharp temperature change from prior to the freeze until after it.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were reported down in the Columbia area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked multiple trees down around Colchester.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed a tree down blocking Hunkins Hill Rd. in  Sanbornton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages in Lyon County reached approximately 25% at peak outage level.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front stalled along the Ohio Valley region, sparking showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced heavy rainfall, which resulted in flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported over Murphysville Road near U.S. Route 62.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of strong thunderstorms shifted into northwest Alabama during the late afternoon and early evening hours.  The storms produced strong and gusty winds knocking down a few trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down blocking the eastbound lane of CR 14.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record dry winter in Southeast Missouri led to dry conditions heading into April from Bollinger to Mississippi Counties. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. Severe (D2) drought developed mid-month along that corridor, diminished some with heavy rain the following week, then expanded for the end of April with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

A few isolated to scattered thunderstorm moved east to southeast across far southwest Nebraska during the afternoon hours on the 20th, ahead of deepening High Plains low pressure. Hail up to three-inches in diameter occurred in Hitchcock county, and winds up to 60 mph occurred in Dundy county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report came through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western Oklahoma on the evening and night of the 25th. An initial supercell thunderstorm (previously tornadic across Beaver County, Oklahoma) moved into northwestern Oklahoma and produced hail and severe winds. Additional thunderstorm activity moved eastward off of a dryline across the eastern Texas Panhandle, producing occasional reports of large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.
