EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak southwesterly flow around a deepening trough brought mid-level moisture over Colorado, prompting snow showers to portions of the region overnight from January 7 to 8. Some weak moisture from previous days' precipitation lingered in some valleys still, and brief breaks in cloud cover enabled enough radiational cooling to saturate some locations. Localized dense fog was able to develop as a result, though lingering cloud cover over central Colorado in the hours around sunrise kept fog development primarily to the lower valleys of western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed within the lower valleys along US-50 on the morning of January 8. The KMTJ ASOS at the Montrose Regional Airport reported about a half an hour of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog occurring between two snow showers shortly after sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 62 mph wind gust measured at Mink Creek mesonet station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Shortly before sunrise on 3/2, fog developed and briefly became dense enough for a couple stations to reach a quarter mile. Visibilities quickly recovered after diabatic heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station KHYS Hays Regional Airport Awos Site reporting quarter-mile visibility in dense freezing fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of May saw below normal precipitation through the Four Corners region and portions of the central highlands of New Mexico, while areas along the Rio Grande Valley, southwestern, and eastern NM saw near to above normal precipitation. Mean temperatures trended near to slightly above normal through western NM and near to slightly below normal across eastern NM. This led to a modest expansion of extreme drought conditions across western NM and portions of the eastern plains of NM along the TX border. Gaps of severe drought through the northern mountains were filled in. Due to ongoing drought conditions and record low snowpack the previous winter, the Rio Grande dried up through the Albuquerque metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought expanded to a majority of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued through the month of May. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May which helped in the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: By the 20th of April, the Pineland Road fire that ignited over southern Clinch County crossed into Echols County. On May 1st, the fire was 32,575 acres with 40% containment. The mandatory evacuation order issued for Echols County by the Georgia Forestry Commission (GFC) and Echols County EMA was lifted on May 1st. Road closures continued for Pineland Rd, Gopher Lope Rd, Register, Worth Ln, Joes Ln, Will Rewis Rd, New Barnes Rd, Gaddis Rd, King Rd, Jesse Ln, May Ln, Chauncey Rd, and Hendley Rd. On May 2nd, a passing cold front brought a soaking, beneficial rain of 1-1.5 inches across the fire with minimal lightning activity. Will Rewis Rd reopened on May 4th. On May 5th, the fire was 65% contained, per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC). On May 9th, the fire was 87% contained per the NIFC. On May 11th, all Echols county roads were reopened. Only private roads (company and club roads) remained closed. The fire was 32,575 acres with 90% containment per the NIFC. On May 15th, the Georgia Forestry Commission revised the fire to be 32,031 acres. The fire was 95% contained on May 22nd. On May 27th, the Level 2 (Set) and Level 1 (Ready) Evacuations were lifted, per Echols County Emergency Management Agency with no evacuations remaining. The estimated cost of the wildfire was around $14-15 million.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. With abnormally high amounts of atmospheric moisture, these thunderstorms were able to produce very heavy rainfall with rain amounts of five to seven inches reported across portions of Sumner and Robertson counties. This caused flash flooding for these areas, particularly in low-lying areas and those along area creeks. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain caused flooding along Slaters Creek Road in Millersville. Extent of damages is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power line were blocking County Road 61.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northerly to northwesterly winds behind a potent cold front overspread much of the western two-thirds of Kansas during the day of March 15. Many locations experienced prolonged sustained winds of at least 40 mph, and some locations experienced brief period of wind gusts between 58 and 67 mph. Additionally, several powerlines were knocked down across Harvey County as a result of these strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS site at Kingman-Clyde Cessna Airport measured sustained winds in excess of 40 mph between 10 AM CDT and 7 PM CDT. The peak sustained wind of 44 mph was measured at 10:23 AM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.

Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in late February and early March. Large wildfires that began in late February continued into early March, with some additional wildfires beginning in the first few days of March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 10,000 acres in Latimer County, over 2500 acres in Pittsburg County, over 1600 acres in Pushmataha County, and more than 500 acres in Cherokee County and Le Flore Counties.

An inside slider pattern developed over May 15 to May 18 as a low pressure system over the Great Basin and high pressure in the eastern Pacific combined to create a strong pressure gradient, resulting in strong gusts and turbulent wind-driven seas. A Beach Hazards Statement was placed in effect for the entire weekend, while two separate Wind Advisories were put in place, one for coastal regions through Saturday and another for the interior mountains of the Bay Area Sunday night through Monday morning. The strong winds caused an estimated 13,000 customers across the Bay Area to lose power.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The North Peak Access Road station operated by PG&E reported a gust of 52 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of 3 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -16 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement in the drought. Bexar, Lavaca, Lee, and Williamson Counties improved from Severe (D2) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was above normal across the area in May. The Hill Country, Coastal Plains, and Winter Garden areas received up to three times normal rain. This resulted in improvement in the drought. Bexar, Lavaca, Lee, and Williamson Counties improved from Severe (D2) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued lack of rainfall combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 10th drought monitor update, continuing through the rest of the Month of February. Wildfires sparked in Duval county in the month of February resulting in road closures, I-295 closure and railroad closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power line were blown down along Gardenview Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was observed at the intersection of Bills Creek Road and Marysville Run Road in Belington, Pea Ridge Road and Nestorville Road in Philippi, and Union Road. Flooding also occurred on multiple sections of Buckhannon Road, including in Volga and on Marjorie and Wellington View Lanes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across eastern North Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NDAWN station at Hillsboro 7SE consistently reported wind chill values -40 or lower from the morning of January 22 through midday on January 23. The lowest wind chill value during that period was -47.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought contributed to dry conditions which allow wildfire activity to return across portions of Hendry County in March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The FPL Solar Field fire in Hendry County went from March 4th to 9th and burned 724 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 2.0 inches of snow, up to 2.8 inches of sleet, and up to 0.50 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was down on Robertson Mill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Approximately half a foot of water on Highway 24 north of US Highway 90 in Gray. A car is stalled in the water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds occurred over Southeastern New York during the daytime hours of February 7, 2026 after a cold front passed through earlier in the morning and low pressure strengthened over the western Atlantic Ocean, tightening the pressure gradient over the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A measured wind gust of 58 mph occurred at 246 PM Local Standard Time at mesonet station EW5678 - Stony Brook at an elevation of 159 feet above ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -3 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -12 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.
With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of wires down around Cinnaminson. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Taylor County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 14, 2025, the county sustained 20 consecutive weeks at or above the D2 threshold as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of April 27, a line of severe storms moved into west-central Indiana, becoming a more organized QLCS. A few sporadic wind damage reports and a few measured 60-70 mph wind gusts occurred in Cass, Grant, and Blackford counties.

Multiple thunderstorm cells were observed training across the Flat Rock Community, located just northeast of the town of Mt Airy in Surry County. Cells began crossing the area at around 5:45 pm EDT, and continued passing across the area repeatedly until around 8:15 pm EDT before rainfall became light in intensity. Rainfall rates rose to as high as 5 inches per hour multiple times through the event. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D2: Severe Drought highlighted for the northern half of Surry County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 142-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration in the Flat Rock area, with rainfall totals reaching 120 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow was unimpressive however, reaching into the 300 to 400 cfs per mi^2 by around 8:00 pm EDT. The heavy rain produced runoff around 6 inches deep across Highway 103 from a nearby hillside drainage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto a house on Eleanor Avenue northeast of the Flat Rock Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak continued into the first couple days of February. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, as it extends well back into January. For portions of western Maryland, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. For central Maryland, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed. For the I-95 corridor, minimum wind chills of 0 to -10F were observed. The coldest wind chills were overnight.

On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Column anchorage failed on metal building system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow began to fall across central Kansas Friday night January 23rd and continued to fall through the 24th before ending early Sunday morning on the 25th.  Despite the long duration of snow most areas received modest amounts ranging from 5 to 8 inches. Air temperatures were unusually cold in the 0 to 5 above range making the snow very dry and powdery.  Winds were not strong with this event mainly staying in the 5 to 15 mph range so widespread blowing and drifting was not a widespread problem.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS report of 5 inches at Wakefield and 12.4 NNE of Clay Center.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wishek NDDOT site reported wind gusts to 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Space and Treasure Coasts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mesonet station K4ZZR PORT ST. LUCIE measured a peak wind gust of 34 knots from the north.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media post shows flash flooding from heavy rainfall during the afternoon of the 18th in Malaeloa Village. Pictures show significant overflow from Fuafua stream. Monetary damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued in Appomattox county in May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a six-month respite (since early-September 2025) with no worse than Moderate Drought (D1) assigned to any portion of this 24-county South Central Nebraska area by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM), unfortunately March 2026 brought a steadily worsening drought situation back into the spotlight as much of the area not only spiraled into Severe Drought (D2), but also Extreme Drought (D3). This marked the first D3 within the area in 10 months (since May 2025) and marked the highest areal coverage of D3 in at least 2.5 years (since Sept. 2023). These rapid degradations not only stemmed from an incredibly dry March, but also from the inevitable consequence of cumulative dryness that had been building for six months...as October 2025-March 2026 ranked among the Top-4 driest October-March periods on record across most of the area (see below for more detailed precipitation info).  Breaking down the significant changes in county-level USDM drought categories during March, the month opened with the vast majority of the 24-county domain assigned either D1 (mainly counties along/north of Interstate 80) or Abnormally Dry/D0 (most places south of I-80). Only a small sliver of the area (around 2 percent of it) was void of all drought categories whatsoever...mainly southeast Thayer County. As March unfolded, degradation came swiftly, with portions of several counties designated D2 on the very first USDM issuance of the month, and a steadily expanding introduction of D3 arriving just a few weeks later. As a result, the end-of-March categorical breakdown stood as follows (in order of drought severity): 1) roughly 52% of South Central Nebraska featured D3 (most prevalent within counties along/north of I-80)...2) approximately 32% of real estate contained D1...3) around 15% of the area was in D1 (almost entirely within southern-most counties along the Kansas border)...4) the remaining sliver of the area (far southern Thayer/Nuckolls counties) was allotted D0. ||Turning to the dire precipitation details, and starting with the longer-term dryness (including a pronounced lack of snow) that defined Oct. 2025-March 2026, this six-month stretch registered among the Top-4 driest on record across South Central Nebraska. More specifically, based on a mix of observations from over 100 NWS and NeRAIN/CoCoRaHS observers along with some radar estimation, the majority of the 30-county area (roughly 80% of it) measured merely between 1.65-4.45...only 25-67% of normal. The highest concentration of amounts 2-or-less focused within primarily far northern and western counties, particularly: Dawson, Gosper, Furnas, Valley, Greeley, Buffalo. Citing six-month totals from just a few longtime NWS Cooperative Observer sites, the Canaday Power Plant (near Lexington) incredibly registered just 0.87 (17% of normal...driest on record), Arcadia 2W reported only 1.29 (21% of normal...driest on record) and Elwood 8S tallied just 1.36 (25% of normal...driest on record). At the Tri Cities airports, October-March ranked between the 2nd-4th driest on record, with totals ranging from 1.69 (Kearney) to 2.68 (Hastings). The only part of the area where precipitation amounts were even remotely close to normal (but still below it)...with at least 5...focused within portions of Thayer and Nuckolls counties. Drilling down to March itself, while October-February were dry enough, March truly brought things to a whole other level. In fact, the majority of South Central Nebraska measured somewhere between a paltry trace and 0.27 (essentially zero to 20% of normal). In fact, around 96% of the 24-county area observed LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH NORMAL March precipitation. Among the very driest of the dry, the following NWS stations were just a few of several that received a paltry trace for the month: Cambridge, Elwood 8S, Beaver City and Orleans 2W. In the Tri Cities, the airports registered just 0.12-0.14. Even the wettest parts of the domain were still significantly below normal, including totals of 0.63 at Hebron, 0.36 in St. Paul, and 0.35 at Belgrade. Needless to say, the significant dryness that spanned the end of 2025 into the start of 2026 set the stage for not only a rough start to the 2026 agricultural growing season in South Central Nebraska (meager soil moisture profiles) but also sparked an above-average early-spring wildfire threat. In addition to several smaller fires across the 24-county area, portions of southwestern Dawson County were ravaged by the massive Cottonwood Fire that ignited on March 12th in far southeastern Lincoln County.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on a vehicle on Brownsville Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced a low end squall line of thunderstorms, which in turn produced several reports of damaging winds. After the cold front's passage, a much colder airmass moved in and snow showers developed, leading to light snowfall for much of northeastern Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three inches of snow was measured by the co-op observer in Monteagle, 1.2 inches of snow was measured in Whitwell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Most locations saw a dry start and middle of the month before more numerous convective systems impacted parts of the area toward the end of the month. This was especially true across far north-central Oklahoma and near the Red River, with central Oklahoma seeing near- to below-normal monthly rainfall totals. As a result, severe (or worse) drought persisted during the month, with some general category improvement towards the last days of the month.

During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, a line of multicell rain showers and thunderstorms generated sporadic straight-line convective wind damage in Wyandot and Marion Counties to Ashland County as the line persisted generally eastward in northern OH. Behind the line, a cluster of multicell rain showers generated a severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust at the Lorain County Airport ASOS as the cluster of showers persisted generally northeastward. These showers and storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in northwestern Crawford County, between Sycamore and Chatfield. Damage was caused by a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mosher NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 86 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of April, persisting extreme drought (D3) and  exceptional drought (D4) conditions area-wide. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of beneficial rainfall in April continued the Exceptional (D4) drought for the rest of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 5 degrees or less across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 7F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at the 1300 Block of North Friendship Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread showers and storms pressed through southeast Ohio on the first day of April ahead of a cold frontal passage. Strong to severe thunderstorms were first noted shortly after midday along the border of Kentucky and West Virginia, with more quickly infiltrating Ohio by peak heating hours. Storms grew strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts, 1 to 1.5 inch hail stones, and heavy downpours. Aside from numerous reports of large hail across Washington County, downed trees and power lines were observed, along with an isolated instance of flash flooding in Marietta. Storms pressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia by the middle of the evening, bringing the severe weather threat to an end for southeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed power lines were observed on Pike Street in Marietta.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report from the public of several large tree branches down in Plattsmouth. Time estimated with radar. Wind gusts were estimated at 65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A viewer submitted video to KRQE showed flash flooding down Ca��ada Ancha road where the road merges with and is in the Arroyo de la Ca��ada Ancha for a stretch of several blocks, flowing into the Santa Cruz River in Chimayo, but just south of the county line in Santa Fe County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January 2026's final week and February 1st, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  The cold outbreak's final embedded short wave plunged the farthest south, from the Middle Mississippi Valley on January 31st to the Carolina coast on the 1st.  Associated arctic surface high pressure centered over the Louisiana Gulf coast early on the 1st, extended its amplified ridge axis back over Indiana and into southeastern Canada, amid a weak surface gradient.  Resultant clear skies and light winds prevailed over central Indiana's remnant 5-10 inch snow pack from the January 31st late evening through daybreak on the 1st.  Temperatures fell generally as low as -5 to -15F with widespread resultant wind chills of -5F to -27F over the majority of central Indiana, with criteria wind chills limited to only Putnam, Hancock and Shelby Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 1st pre-dawn to early morning, temperatures as low as -17F, and light winds sustained under 5 mph...resulted in extreme wind chills as low as -27F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front draped along the southern Appalachians promoted isolated to scattered showers and storms in the afternoon to early evening, some of which produced damaging winds across the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down near Swift Creek School Road and Straight Gate Road.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Edisto Buoy measured a peak wind gust of 42 knots.
