EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minot NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in along the Blue Ridge where 4 to locally 12 inches were observed. Higher terrain in the Shenandoah Valley also received localized totals of 2 to 6 inches. In western Highland County, the upslope snow continued longer resulting in 4 to 10 inches. Across northern Virginia, a general 2 to 5 inches were observed.

A prolonged winter storm affected the Southern Plains on January 23rd through the 25th. Central and eastern Kansas saw all snow for this event. It snowed for 40 straight hours in Wichita. Most locations across central, south central and southeast Kansas picked up between five to a little above nine inches; near Smolan in Saline County measured 9.1 inches for the event.||Extreme cold air spilled south across the Plains with this event.  Nine temperature records were either set or tied during the January 23rd through January 26th time frame. Both Russell and Salina saw low temperatures of -16 with widespread wind chills in the 10 to 20 below zero range. In Wichita, the homeless shelter provided housing for over 365 guests which is above average and near their capacity. There is one unconfirmed fatality of an unhoused individual who didn't seek shelter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding reports as well as reports from around the county, an estimated 5 to 7 inches of snow fell across Reno County. The highest reported total was 5.8 inches about three miles southwest of Sylvia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.

Another shot of arctic air punched into the region on the evening of the 28th into the morning of the 29th, with cold temperatures depending mainly on radiational cooling combined with light winds to drop wind chills to around -15 to -20F.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -24F at the Mackinac Island airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.
Persistent isentropic lift generated showers and thunderstorms that led to excessive rainfall and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flooding of River Ranch at Leon Creek in Leon Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across Maryland. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 12 to 16 across Garrett County, with a general 8 to 12 across the remainder of the area aside from southern Maryland where 4-8 was observed. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed across southern Maryland. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state.

A very strong cold front moved across the area during the evening hours of January 15th. Strong winds continued overnight and into the following day. Numerous power outages, damages, and road closures were reported with the abnormally strong northwest winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 63 MPH was observed at the Agate Fossil Beds sensor at 6:13 PM MST on 1/15.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over western Kentucky allowed for clear skies and calm winds the morning of the 27th. Residual low-level moisture from a cold front that sagged south the previous day supported areas of dense fog during the early morning hours.

Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local fire department reported 6 to 12 inches of water over roadways throughout Tecumseh.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread and consistent rainfall following a pattern change in mid-May led to reductions in drought severity across Central Alabama from late May into early June. As two-month rainfall totals heading into June were near or above average, along with recovery in stream flows around the state, Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Central Alabama during the first week of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lingering Severe (D2) drought conditions across the southeastern half of Autauga County were removed in early June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a slow moving cold front as it pushed south through the state. Scattered strong to severe storms also developed just ahead of this front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 64 mph was measured with a handheld anemometer west of Gallman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and embedded thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall along a boundary that was stalled out over the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A portion of Hussey Road was closed due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between a quarter and three tenths of an inch of ice accumulation occurred, along with a half inch of snow and sleet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In a warm southwest flow regime ahead of a weak cold front, a very moist air mass combined with moderate instability and improved shear resulted in a couple of organized lines of storms with damaging winds. One moved across the far northeastern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain, including Warren and Halifax counties, while the other affected Chatham, Moore, and Lee counties. There were numerous reports of downed trees and power lines in these areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages were reported to be caused by fallen trees or limbs damaging equipment.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D4) continued from February through the month of March across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area. Those conditions were driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Although several inches of rain did fall over the region, most did not fall where drought conditions existed. The only appreciable change in March was an expansion of D2 to include all of the Coastal Mississippi counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long term D2 to D4 drought persisted through the whole month of March for portions of Wilkinson County according to the US Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree was blown down on Indian Creek Road near WV-18 in Blue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms increased across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 27th, as an upper level low pressure system approached the region. The air mass became moderately unstable during the afternoon, and wind shear northeast of the surface low pressure center across southeastern Oklahoma became supportive of rotating storms. Two tornadoes developed from these thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado damaged the hospital, damaged a few homes, uprooted a tree, and snapped numerous large tree limbs. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 85 to 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching surface low with a trailing cold front, southern winds brought warmer temperatures and moisture into central Kentucky. Highs temperatures and dew points reached into the 60s. This helped to generate enough instability to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. A couple of these storms dropped severe hail in Nelson and Fayette Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail was a little larger than quarter size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station reported wind gusts up to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on NY 22 with two lanes blocked.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm complex developed during the morning hours in northeast SD and tracked through far southeast ND and across west central MN and parts of northwest MN producing severe thunderstorm winds and large hail. A wake low developed as a result of this MCS with non thunderstorm high winds lingering over parts of west central MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down with tree branch diameter between 12 inches to 15 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend, persistent dry conditions through late January led to worsening drought and critically low soil moisture, limiting agricultural progress and stressing rangeland. Periods of unseasonably warm weather were followed by hard freezes and a winter storm, though precipitation was generally limited, with only modest rainfall of up to around an inch in parts of the Coastal Bend providing minor short-term improvement to soil moisture. Producers largely completed field preparation but delayed spring planting due to insufficient moisture for germination. Winter pastures and forage growth struggled under the dry conditions, resulting in poor to fair range conditions and increased reliance on hay and supplemental feed for livestock. While citrus and cool-season vegetable harvests continued, drought stress remained a concern for crop development and pasture recovery, and additional rainfall will be needed to improve soil moisture and support the upcoming planting season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple segments of heavy showers and a few thunderstorms moved across north Alabama during the evening hours.  One segment moved northeast during the late evening from central into northeast Alabama which exhibited a bow echo. This resulted in a power pole being snapped and trees being knocked down in Jackson and Marshall Counties.  A couple of trees were also knocked down blocking roads in Lauderdale and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple softwood trees and limbs were knocked down at 279, 620, and 1180 Skyline Shores Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An Effingham County emergency manager reported several small to medium trees snapped off at varying heights and a small outbuilding destroyed at a farm on Boaen Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems moved over southern California during the mid part of the month of February, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms, strong and gusty winds, and high elevation snow from the 10th thru the 11th, and then again on the 16th thru 18th. This resulted in a few reports of damage due to strong winds from thunderstorms. There were also several reports of flooding/flash flooding due to heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dept. of Highways reported mud/dirt/rock on road at I-805 n and I-8  near normal heights. 0.65 inches of rain has fallen in the past 6 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system passed through the area brought windy conditions, with gusts as high as 40 mph in the Valley and above 60 mph in the Mountains. As the longwave trough continued east, a shortwave trough along its west side evolved into a cutoff low over Baja California, where it stalled. As a result, the prevailing flow over the area shifted to the northeast, leading to a Mono wind event over the southern Sierra Nevada Mountains and high winds over the Tehachapi Mountains, Mojave Slopes, and Mojave Desert, including downslope acceleration and drying in these areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station 444SE Cottonwood Canyon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms produced localized wind damage, localized flooding and one brief tornado during the afternoon and evening of June 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of quarter size hail were received from Algonquin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooded roads across the county. Total rainfall for the event was around 2 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 6.8 to 8 inches from both the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the eastern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 25 to 30 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-half mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree knocked down power lines on Bosley Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed on the nose of a low level jet during the very early morning of June 1st. As they approached central Missouri, these thunderstorms congealed into a mesoscale convective complex. This complex produced wind damage extending from Boone County through Washington County, and produced flash flooding in Columbia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree onto a home on Maddox and Fowler in Overland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local law enforcement reported two trees down. The first was on Jackson Summit Road and the other on County Road 106. This was likely due to an outflow boundary as the damage was removed from the main storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were flood waters inundating a residence in Wahiawa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain across portions of Pickett and Fentress counties on June 28, 2026. An estimated five to seven inches fell across the area from Byrdstown to Jamestown which caused flash flooding. The Wolf River near Byrdstown crested to 15.29 inches, the second highest crest of record. Roadways along the river and nearby creeks were inundated with water and rendered impassable. One home in Byrdstown also reported being inundated with water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 5 to 7 inches of rain in the Jamestown area caused flash flooding. Portions of Delk Creek Road along the Wolf River in Jamestown were inundated with water and impassable. Damages are unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low rapidly deepened off the coast of Virginia from 1004mb along the Outer Banks on the morning of February 22 to 968mb off the Mid-Atlantic and New England coastline on the morning of February 23. This brought heavy snow and occasional blizzard conditions to the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore from February 22 into February 23.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain changed over the snow during the afternoon of February 22 in Wicomico County. Heavy snow and gusty winds lasted from the afternoon of February 22 into the morning of February 23 with occasional blizzard conditions. Snowfall totals ranged from 8 to 14 inches across the county. A maximum report of 14 inches was received 2 miles (NE) from Pittsville. Additionally, winds gusted to 49 mph at the Salisbury Regional Airport (KSBY). Several trees were down across the county with at least one tree snapped onto a power line in Parsonsburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 16th, storms brought all severe hazards to Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees, limbs, and wires down in Laredo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved down the state from the northwest and brought strong south to southwest winds ahead of it. These winds were strongest downslope of the mountains and primarily impacted north and east portions of Kauai and Oahu.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to Hawaiian Telcom, 4 utility poles in Kaneohe were blown down around 1pm. As a result, Kaneohe Bay Drive was closed through the evening for repairs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably warm and humid airmass developed across central Illinois on March 26, 2026, with some locations recording record high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s. Dewpoints also surged into the lower 60s. As a cold front approached during the evening, scattered to widespread strong to severe storms developed along and ahead of the front, primarily in areas north of I-70. These storms produced hail as large as golf balls, as well as a few wind damage reports.

The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought was observed in early June, but around normal to slightly above normal precipitation was observed for 3 of the 4 weeks of June. A very dry week around mid-June managed to reduce or flip any normal to above normal rainfall that had been present to normal or below normal for the month. Still, some spotty normal to above normal anomalies were observed in Dallam and Hartley counties. Moore county was almost entirely below normal for the month. Drought conditions improved by 1 category due to the rainfall observed, but Moderate (D1) to D2 persists due to a 1-4 inch rainfall deficit over the previous 180 days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low level frontogenesis developed ahead of a cold front, and an upper level shortwave provided lift to create a period of snow as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A spotter in Tollesboro measured 3.8 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree occurred along I-79 south just before the Mink Shoals exit, blocking the right lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record breaking winds across southeast Wyoming gradually spread east into the high plains of western Nebraska late in the morning and afternoon on March 12th. Power outages and some minor damage were reported with isolated wind gusts up to 78 MPH.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most observation sites across Scotts Bluff County reported strong wind gusts over 58 MPH late in the morning through the afternoon. Peak wind gust of 76 MPH measured at a Union Pacific Railroad sensor four miles west of the city of Scottsbluff. Scottsbluff Airport measured a peak gust of 68 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The third and final weather system in a series moved across the Four Corners and southern Rockies February 20th. A snow squall along the cold front resulted in a very brief period of quarter mile visibility at several locations across western New Mexico during the mid to late morning hours, including Farmington, Gallup, and Grants. This snow squall also resulted in a vehicle crash on U.S. Highway 550 just west of Cuba, NM. The snow squall along the cold front dissipated as it moved east into the Rio Grande Valley, resulting in some high wind gusts in the zone. Upslope flow resulted in light to moderate snow across the north central mountains with a localized area of heavy snow across Taos Ski Valley. Snow across the north central mountains tapered off midday February 20th. Additional high wind gusts were observed across eastern NM along and just behind the cold front during the early afternoon hours before winds tapered off around sunset.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Clines Corners measured high wind gusts peaking at 64 mph. A NMDOT weather station at the same location measured peak high wind gusts of 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong low pressure area swung through southern Virginia, dragging a cold front across Eastern NC by the evening hours. Ahead of it, bands of thunderstorms formed in the afternoon due to unstable conditions and wind shear in place. Scattered severe wind gusts embedded in some of the storms produced wind damage across the area. There were also several reports of hail up to nickel size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tideland EMC reports power outages in the Belhaven area due to trees and powerlines  down damaging equipment.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure area and frontal boundary brought a west to east swath of 2 to 5 inches of snow. Slick roads resulted in numerous vehicle slide-offs and accidents on highways and secondary roads.  There were major travel disruptions on the interstates and highway 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulation of 1-2 inches in the northern portion of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts caused damage to a carport in Sullivan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Higher moisture along and east of the central mountain chain combined with a disturbance moving north into the state ahead of an upper low over California resulting in the development of scattered thunderstorms across the central mountain chain and nearby highlands during the afternoon and evening hours. A few storms became strong to severe resulting in nickel size hail in Santa Fe and half dollar to ping pong ball size hail in northern Union County east-northeast of Des Moines, NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail was observed 9 miles east-northeast of Des Moines from a severe thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough positioned itself to support the development of a strong mid-level frontogenesis band. It took advantage of tremendous mid-level moisture and lift. Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 7.5 inches of snow fallen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over far southwestern Nebraska and the Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon hours of May 30th. As this activity progressed slowly east into the evening hours, numerous large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported. A couple of tornadoes were also reported. Hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported.

A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.5 inches in diameter near Lincoln, NE. Damage also reported to vehicle hood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 90 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
