Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds associated with thunderstorms in the areas resulted in periods of blowing dust and reduced visibility. Utah Highway Patrol reported that this dust storm led to a multi-vehicle traffic accident on U.S. Highway 91 in northern Cache County, which resulted in multiple serious injuries. A patrol sergeant reported that injuries included one critical injury, and six serious but non life-threatening injuries. The largest crash(es) were reported near mile marker 44. The incident resulted in the closure of the highway for four hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, sparking thunderstorms in a moist airmass. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over a foot of standing water inundated at least eleven cars at a local car dealer and portions of the corner gas station. Several homes also had water over their porches, up to their front doors.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reports 1.75 inch diameter hail in Watertown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak clipper system moved from the Great Lakes across NY and New England during the night of January 6th through the morning of January 7th. Snowfall developed during the late evening of January 6th and ended across VT around daybreak on January 7th.||Snowfall totals ranged from 1-3 inches across the International border with Canada to 4 to 6 inches across the eastern slopes of Vermont's central and southern Green Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches fell across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A 500 acre wildfire in northwestern Calhoun county caused significant damage to property.  There were a total of 43 displaced occupants, 15 dwellings destroyed, 7 outbuildings destroyed, along with 7 vehicles, 2 boats and 1 utility trailer destroyed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 500 acre wildfire in northwestern Calhoun county caused significant damage to property. There were a total of 43 displaced occupants, 15 dwellings destroyed, 7 outbuildings destroyed, along with 7 vehicles, 2 boats and 1 utility trailer destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree resulted in a motor vehicle accident near Highway 195 and CR 25.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Hackberry measured a wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak brought 4 tornadoes to portions of western Wisconsin during the mid to late afternoon hours on April 17th. One of these tornadoes was a strong EF-3 tornado near the unincorporated community of Cream, Wisconsin. This intense tornado was responsible for substantially damaging a home with much of its exterior walls collapsed. Additional tornadoes occurred as these storms traveled into Trempealeau and Jackson counties, with tree and minor structural damage along their paths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dispatch in Eau Claire County relayed a report of nickel sized hail in Mondovi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were reported down on Route 519.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long duration extreme cold every took place across the region starting the 22nd and lasting into the morning of the 24th. An area of very cold high pressure worked into the Plains on the 22nd and became established on the 23rd into the 24th. Air temperatures remain below zero during the event with light winds dropping wind chills into the 40s and 50s below zero. A few locations even dropped into the 60s below zero one morning with light winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -63F were reported in the northern parts of Cook and Lake counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of northwestern Arkansas experienced above average precipitation during April, with the exception of Carroll County, and portions of Crawford and Franklin Counties. In general, four to ten inches of rain fell across the region, which corresponded to as much as 150 to 200 percent above monthly average precipitation amounts. Much of Carroll County, and portions of Crawford and Franklin Counties received between four and five inches of rain during the month, which corresponded to only 75 to 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Carroll and Madison Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

An Arctic cold front moved through western Kentucky on the morning of the 30th, bringing cold temperatures down to the teens. Blustery northwest winds caused wind chills to fall around -5 to -7 the night of the 30th into the morning of the 31st. Intervals of dangerous wind chills was variable across the region with northern portions of the Kentucky Purchase and Pennyrile remaining above threshold.

An impressive, long-duration atmospheric river brought copious snowfall and high winds to western Montana.  Some high-elevation areas received a few feet of snow.  Impacts from this storm included power outages and impacts to travel.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Montana Department of Transportation reported severe driving conditions on MT Highway 83 from milepost 14.0 to 47.8, Seeley Lake to Condon due to blowing and drifting snow, heavy snow.  There was a slide-off accident on Highway 83 south of Seeley Lake.  Obstructions blocked travel on Highway 200 and Interstate 90 on the morning of March 14.  Missoula Electric COOP reported 2500 customers without power at 0930 MST March 14 plus a major infrastructure failure: two main feeders from the Clinton substation were damaged, cutting power to 505 members.  Some storm total snow amounts were 26.7 inches in Seeley Lake, 16 inches at Clearwater Junction, 14 inches at Lubrecht Forest, and 32.6 inches at the Ovando CoCoRaHS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from quarter (1.00) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, a storm near Kewanee Illinois in Henry County produced a funnel cloud.
A strong cold front moved into an warm and unstable airmass primarily west of I-95. This resulted in bands of showers and thunderstorms that produced localized damaging wind and spotty large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was reported near Cross Junction.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful and expansive storm system brought widespread heavy wintry precipitation across nearly two thirds of the width of North America, stretching from the southern Rockies and southern Plains, across portions of the Midwest, Deep South, and Southeast, into the Mid-Atlantic and New England. For the Mid-Atlantic region, this was an overrunning precipitation event, with a very cold and dry, arctic airmass in place ahead of the storm. The main low pressure center passed offshore just to the south of the forecast area.||Precipitation began as all snow across the local region during the very early morning hours of January 25th. A transition to sleet occurred from south to north after dawn through midday. Some freezing rain occurred across the coastal plain of New Jersey and Delmarva during the afternoon and evening hours. Temperatures warmed above freezing across far southern New Jersey and southern Delaware where the marine front moved inland, resulting in a period of rain before precipitation ended. The marine front remained south and east of the I-95 to I-195 corridors. North of the front (along and north of the I-95 to I-195 corridors, including much of the Philadelphia metropolitan area, central and northern Delmarva) into the I-78 corridor, temperatures remained in the 10s when snow changed to sleet. Total sleet accumulations between 1-3 were reported in this region, on top of approximately 2-6 of snow.||The snow and sleet proved very challenging to remove following the storm due to the weight and density of the ice-capped snowpack and below freezing temperatures. At least 3 fatalities related to snow removal occurred in the Lehigh Valley. Snow removal took a few days in some places. Untreated or unplowed pavement remained covered in snow and/or ice for one to two weeks following the storm.||A 17 day period of largely well below freezing temperatures began the day before this storm on January 24th and continued through February 9th. This was one of the coldest 17 day periods in several decades for much of the region at the time. Mean temperatures in the period ranged from the mid 10s to low 20s. The extreme cold preserved the ice-capped, glacier-like snowpack for approximately 3 to 4 weeks following the storm. The snowpack remained across the entire region until about the third week of February, before melting away completely in most areas due to light rainfall and low temperatures remaining above freezing for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow and sleet accumulation totals mainly ranged from 4-7 based on reports from within and surrounding the county. The highest report received was 5.2 in Royal Oak.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough developed across the Coastal Plain during the afternoon hours of Sunday April fifth out ahead of an eastward moving cold front. An ongoing line of scattered showers and thunderstorms quickly tracked east from central North Carolina to the coast and strengthened as they interacted with the surface trough in the coastal plain with a few of these storms becoming strong in nature bringing strong and damaging winds to portions of the northern sounds and Pamlico river.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was recorded on a personal weather station as thunderstorms moved through the area. Report came in via WeatherFlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house and injured a child in the 1000 block of Red Oak Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was knocked down onto a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of East Texas along with an isolated report of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail reported in Jacksonville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the second time in a week, a winter storm impacted the North Carolina Piedmont  as an area of low pressure intensified across the Deep South. In this case, all precipitation fell as snow. Snow began falling during the early morning of the 31st and continued off and on for almost 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the afternoon. By the time the snow tapered off, 6 to 10 inch totals were reported across much of the area. An axis of around a foot occurred from east Charlotte to High Rock Lake and vicinity.

The right entrance region of a jet within stronger flow across the northern tier of the U.S. helped to increase convergence by late afternoon and early evening along a cold front working eastward through northwest Iowa.  Mixed-layer instability reached up to 1500-2000 J/kg courtesy of 8C/km mid-level lapse rates with deep-layer shear of 40 to 50 knots. Initially discrete cells produced large hail, with a tendency to evolve toward more linear structures.

A similar environment to 5/24 took shape during the afternoon of 5/25, continuing into the late evening. Seasonal instability brought summertime pulse convection that was slow moving with efficient rain rates as PWAT's neared 2. This led to a couple instances of flash flooding in southern Lancaster County, SC early in the afternoon before bringing a couple more instances later in the evening near Augusta GA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Richmond County Dispatch reported flooding on the 2400 block of Windsor Spring Road  leading to a road closure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across western Wisconsin, with RCX in Ladysmith reporting the coldest wind chill of -49F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -49F.||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F.||The lowest wind chills were:|-49F at KRCX (Rusk).|-47F at KRNH (St Croix).|-45F at KEAU (Chippewa).|-43F at KUBE (Barron).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearby KRGK reported wind gusts as high as 25 mph during the evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -20F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -41F at 1AM on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of southern Illinois. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Roads were particularly bad near Glendale in Pope County, IL. Ice on rural roadways in Saline County, IL caused one vehicle to overturn with a person trapped. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The first round of storms arrived during the early morning hours of the 27th, associated with a warm front lifting northeastward across the region. Being elevated storms, large hail was the primary impact. Additional isolated to scattered storms developed during the midday hours, also tracking northeastward with large hail.||In Southwest Indiana, midday MLCAPE values were around 500J/kg, DCAPE was 600-800J/kg, effective bulk shear was a robust 40-50kts, and mid-level lapse rates were around 6.5C/km.||Cells tracking northeastward in Southwest Indiana midday resulted in several hail reports in Gibson and Warrick Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was measured northeast of Melody Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts and hail in Volusia County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The WeatherSTEM station at Ponce Inlet Town Hall measured a peak wind gust of 55 knots from the southeast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm brought significant rainfall and gusty winds to Southwestern California. Rainfall totals ranged from 0.50 to 1.50 inches across coastal and valley areas up to around 2.50 inches across the foothills and mountains. With this rainfall, numerous reports of nuisance roadway flooding was reported along with one report of flash flooding on Interstate 5. Along with the rain, gusty southerly winds developed across the higher terrain with gusts reaching up to 72 MPH.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong and gusty southerly winds impacted the eastern range of the San Gabriel Mountains. Some peak wind gusts include: Yucca Circle (gust 72 MPH), Ford Observatory (gust 63 MPH) and Barley Flats Road (gust 62 MPH).

CZ_NAME: EASTERN ALASKA RANGE SOUTH OF TRIMS CAMP
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: More to come.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Storm Watch to a Winter Storm Warning for the Eastern Alaska Range South of Trims Camp at 1113AKST on April 18. The Look Eyrie SNOTEL site measured 11 inches of snowfall between 1100AKST on April 19 and 1100AKST on April 20. Additionally, the Alaska Department of Transportation recorded 11 inches of snowfall along the Richardson Highway at the Trims DOT Camp (TRDA2). No fatalities, injures, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported 1 inch hail just southwest of Arlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Leftover boundaries from June 3 thunderstorms and diurnally driven MLCAPE up to 1500-2000 J/kg triggered rapid storm development in the mid-James River Valley by mid-to-late afternoon. These storms intensified due to 40-45 kts of effective shear, producing hail as large as baseballs.

Weak ascent atop a very hot/unstable boundary layer fostered clusters of thunderstorms - generally disorganized/multi-cell in nature - from southwestern into north-central Oklahoma on the 29th. Damaging wind gusts and hail were observed with activity throughout the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clearing skies and light winds under high pressure, along with lingering low-level moisture, allowed for widespread dense fog formation to develop late evening across most of Southern Illinois. Dense fog continued until the early to mid-morning hours. Many locations reported low temperatures slightly below freezing but no reports were made of freezing fog development.

The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency managers reported river flooding impacting PR-114 near the intersection of PR-103, where the Rio Guanajibo & Rio Rosario converge. Several vehicles, approximately 15 cars, were stranded in floodwaters. At 9:45 PM AST, the USGS HORP4 gauge on the Rio Guanajibo, located downstream of this area, measured 20.06 feet, which is above flood stage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reports indicated flooding at the intersection of PR-446 and PR-111 in San Sebasti��n. Floodwaters covered the roadway, creating hazardous travel conditions and rendering it nearly impassable. No injuries or structural damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure moved through the eastern U.S. bringing a plume of deep moisture over top of an arctic airmass which brough 1-2 feet of snow to southern New England Sunday through Tuesday morning. The biggest total was 27 inches in Gloucester, MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 12 to 14 inches of snow fell with some of the higher amounts being 15 inches in Tiverton and 12.5 inches in Middleton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager sent images of measured 1.5 inch hail at HWY 171 and CR 304.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on house in the Blackwoods area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A complex mix of snow, sleet, freezing rain, and rain fell across Jackson County beginning as all snow on the afternoon of the 24th and continuing for most of the 25th. A picture from just past 0900EST on the 25th showed an estimated 0.3 inches of flat ice accretion in Annville with trees starting to snap.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly unstable environment developed across western Montana, fueled by pooling moisture and steep lapse rates. Shortwave energy rotating around a broader upper-level trough provided the necessary lift for convective initiation which resulted in large hail. As storms moved into the Idaho Panhandle and interacted with the local terrain, they organized into two distinct quasi-linear convective systems, producing widespread severe wind gusts across Lincoln and Flathead Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A quasi-linear convective system produced widespread wind damage across the county. Fallen trees blocked Highway 2 northwest of Troy, while snapped large cottonwoods caused minor damage to a carport on Missoula Avenue. Severe blowdown forced the closure of Callahan Creek Park disc golf course, and utility damage left 1,440 customers without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing theta-e, steep mid level lapse rates, strong shear and limited MUCAPE allowed for the development of several thunderstorms which moved from White county to northern portions of Allen county during the morning hours. Additional storms developed in the afternoon. Low freezing levels and the elements noted above resulted in efficient hail producing storms, with one in particular leaving a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path. A few severe level hail stones were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS observer measured at least one hailstone just over 1.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front led to a line of showers and storms that tracked across central North Carolina during the morning to early afternoon hours. Damaging wind reports, including trees and power lines down, were reported across Moore, Harnett, and Johnston Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down, blocking Youngs Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northerly to northwesterly winds behind a potent cold front overspread much of the western two-thirds of Kansas during the day of March 15. Many locations experienced prolonged sustained winds of at least 40 mph, and some locations experienced brief period of wind gusts between 58 and 67 mph. Additionally, several powerlines were knocked down across Harvey County as a result of these strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS site at Lyons-Rice County Municipal Airport recorded sustained winds of at least 40 mph between 10 AM CDT and 7 PM CDT. The peak sustained winds were 44 mph recorded at 4:55 PM CDT. The peak wind gust across the county was 56 mph recorded by a Kansas Mesonet 2 miles west Little River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening upper level trough across CA and vicinity sent an embedded wave northeastward toward the Northern Rockies Feb 17, which resulted in surface low pressure developing and moving across Southwest Montana. This resulted in a strong cold front progressing through the area, bringing brief snow squalls, synoptic high winds, localized impactful snow, and very cold wind chills to various portions of the region into Feb 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple strong wind observation reports were received, including a peak report of 64 mph from mesonet station MTM51 Gildford which measured a 64 mph gust. Other sensors to measure criteria winds include Montana mesonet stations Fox Crossing and Lake Thibadeau and ASOS station KHVR Havre Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-0 tornado with maximum sustained winds estimated near 85 mph tracked across parts of southwest and central Washington Parish, south of Franklinton, LA. This tornado began near Sam Smith Rd where it snapped a rotted large hardwood tree. Additional tree debris and minor damage to skirting of a manufactured home was noted nearby. The tornado continued east-northeast where more abundant tree damage was identified including snaps of smaller tree trunks and branches along Daniels Rd, west of LA Hwy 25. This was where the tornado appeared to be at its strongest and widest, spanning about 75 yards wide. The tornado continued across the Bogue Chitto River, and additional minor tree damage was found by the survey team along LA Hwy 16, Tullos Rd, and Gene Williams Rd. Near Lee Rd and Thigpen Rd was where the last area of more concentrated minor tree damage was noted and this was the estimated end point of this tornado damage path. No additional damage was identified on Moore Rd nor LA Hwy 439, however, minor sporadic tree damage did continue farther east, north of Bogalusa, LA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the night of the 3rd and 4th of March, an upper level system moved in to the combined Panhandles sparking a line of thunderstorms running southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle. The southern most storm developed into a severe storm that dropped hail up to 2 in diameter across Potter and Randall County.  On the evening of the 5th of March increase moisture advection in the southeastern Panhandles provided instability for severe thunderstorms. This time in the southeastern Panhandles. One of these storms dropped hail up to 1.7 in Collingsworth County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of mostly nickel to quarter size fell across the western and northwestern side of Amarillo. However, hail of two inches in diameter fell near I-40 and Coulter Street. In addition, hail of golfball size fell to the west-northwest of Amarillo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary arctic frontal zone crashed southeast across the region with yet another increase in winds, spotty light snowfall, and areas of blowing snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite snowfall of only a few tenths of an inch, northwest winds gusted as high as 45 to 55 mph and produced periodic near-blizzard conditions, with visibility briefly as low as one-quarter to one-half mile near Trosky at times of light snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally dry spring led to expansion of ongoing drought conditions across Central Alabama during the month of April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Elmore County was upgraded to Severe (D2) drought in late April, with the southern third in Extreme (D3) drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable but relatively weak shear atmosphere brought storms to the region on the evening of June 11. One notable storm formed just east of the City of Roanoke and passed across Bedford County. It produced 1 size hail and blew down a few trees as a result. While much of the Mid-Atlantic had CAPE of 2000-4000 J/kg, better synoptic ascent from mid-level shortwaves were located to the north.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of Bunker Hill Loop and McDaniel Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The start of the new year was rung in with heavy snow showers that set up primarily along the northeast West Virginia mountains. Snow was ongoing from the night of New Years Eve, which was the result of a passing clipper system. This disturbance jetted off the eastern seaboard by the middle of the day on January 1st, leaving behind 5 to 8 inches of snow along the foothills and around a foot of snow for the higher mountainous areas of Randolph and Pocahontas Counties. For the lowlands, a few passing snow squalls contributed to light snow amounts between 1 to 3 inches.
Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 80 mph touched down approximately 3 miles southeast of Saybrook in McLean County and crossed into Ford County just west of Route 54. The tornado damaged trees, power lines and an outbuilding in Harpster. The tornado then impacted a campground along E 200N Road, two miles south of Gibson City where it rolled over and damaged several campers. Trees and farm outbuildings were also damaged at a farmstead one mile east of the campground. The tornado then tracked east northeast for a few miles, primarily producing tree damage before ending in a field north of E 300N Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic cold front shifted winds out of the northwest, increasing gusts to around 30 to 45 mph across the region. At the same time, 1/2 to 2 inches of light fluffy snow fell across the entire region. The strongest wind gusts and greatest snow amounts were measured across southwest and southern MN during the afternoon and evening, resulting in occasional periods of near-blizzard conditions with visibilities as low as 1/2 to 1/4 mile.||The strongest measured wind gusts on January 21 were:|42 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.|41 mph at KCNB in Canby, MN.|40 mph at KSTP in St Paul, MN.|39 mph at KMIC in Crystal, MN.|39 mph at KRWF in Redwood Falls, MN.|38 mph at KFRM in Fairmont, MN.|38 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of very strong winds and light snow showers resulted in reduced visibility from blowing snow. Occasional near blizzard conditions were reported at the height of the storm. The AWOS at nearby KFRM and MNDOT sensors in Wells and Blue Earth noted visibility as low as 1/2 mile and wind gusts between 35 to 45 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early evening hours on the 17th, an isolated severe thunderstorm moved east out of east-central Colorado and into northwest Kansas, ahead of a strong cold front approaching from the northwest. Large hail up to ping-pong ball size was reported in Sherman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo showed the large hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving system produced 3 to 6 inches of snow from portions of northwest Indiana into far northeast Indiana. Most of the heavier snow accumulation occurred roughly along a line from South Bend, IN to Fort Wayne, IN. The timing of the event produced moderate to high impacts for the morning commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bands of snow produced 2 to 5 inches of snow accumulation during the early morning hours of February 6th. Snowfall rates briefly reached as high as 1 to 2 inches per hour in association with the heavier bands of snow. A snowfall report of 2.1 inches was received from a CoCoRaHS observer 2.9 miles south of Albion, IN. The morning commute was impacted with numerous slide-offs and accidents reported across the region.

CZ_NAME: LONG ISLAND SOUND EAST OF NEW HAVEN CT/PORT JEFFERSON NY TO THE MOUTH OF THE CONNECTICUT RIVER
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet site FW5754 in Southold measured a 35 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Bland county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Walker Creek, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Florida ahead of a frontal boundary. Several severe weather reports were received with the main impacts to trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were down west of Paxton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southeast South Dakota during the evening of February 17 and into the morning of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 50 mph with gusts as high as 66 mph were reported across the area. The strongest winds were along and west of the James River Valley. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of wind gusts from 45 to 55 mph and light snow resulted in brief reductions in visibility to one mile or less, resulting in difficult travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a few trees southwest of Shelbyville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts and hail in Volusia County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed picture of quarter size hail in New Smyrna Beach in the Oliver Estates subdivision near S Glencoe Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous small limb debris and scattered larger limbs with diameter greater than 3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple elevated thunderstorms moved across the Ozarks during the afternoon. Some of the storms were moving as slow as 10 miles an hour. This produced localized flooding in Barton County, but one storm in Miller County was able to take advantage of the environment and produced hail up to 3 inches in size as is moved slowly over the town if Iberia, MO. Another storm then moved along a similar track approximately 3 hours later producing hail up to tennis balls in size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front from the northwest maintained their strength to deliver damaging wind gusts resulting in downed trees and power lines across southeast West Virginia. In spite of the early morning hours, there was Effective Bulk Shear of 30-40 kts and a few hundred MLCAPE to keep the system alive. These storms dissipated after crossing the Appalachian mountains and encountering relatively stable air.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down over Anvil Rock Lane near the Anvil Rock Training Center.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portion of east-central and northeast Nebraska during March. Monthly precipitation totals were generally 0.5 to 1.5 inches below average.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A D2 (Severe) drought was introduced across the southern portion of the county on March 24, persisting through the remainder of the month. The cooperative observer near Fremont, Nebraska recorded 0.13 inches of precipitation for the month, which was 1.44 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from severe drought to moderate drought as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 100th to 200th percentile across much of SE West Virginia. Rainfall totals over the past 30 days ranged from 5.0 to 8.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to near normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Both Mercer and Monroe counties continued to remain in Severe drought as portions of those counties received rainfall totals closer to 3-4 inches over the 30 day period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from Severe drought to Abnormally dry conditions as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 110th to 125th percentile range across Western Greenbrier County. Rainfall totals ranged from 8.0 to 10.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to just below normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Soil moisture improved to the 30th to 70th percentile based off the NASA Sport LIS 0-100 cm soil moisture percentile, while stream flows improved to the 75-90th percentile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another in a week of extremely strong winds occurred with the strongest wind day with a peak of 89 mph at East Butte and several gusts over 70 mph throughout the state.  Interstate 15 was pre-emptively closed from Shelley to north of Idaho Falls in anticipation of the extreme event.  It was a widespread event with some damage and power outages occurring as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: US Highway 20 closed from Ashton to the Montana border due to extremely strong winds causing blowing snow and whiteout conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in along the Blue Ridge where 4 to locally 12 inches were observed. Higher terrain in the Shenandoah Valley also received localized totals of 2 to 6 inches. In western Highland County, the upslope snow continued longer resulting in 4 to 10 inches. Across northern Virginia, a general 2 to 5 inches were observed.

A broken line of snow showers and localized snow squalls pushed across eastern New York ahead of a secondary cold front during the afternoon hours on January 11, 2026 leading to some brief visibility reductions to one quarter of a mile or less and wind gusts up to 30 mph. Behind the front, strong winds developed across the region with peak gusts between 40 and 50 mph in some locations.||Key impacts: travel delays.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This weak tornado tracked from along Arm Road northeastward across Saint Stephens Road before lifting. Relatively minor tree damage occurred along the path with trees uprooted and several tree limbs broken. Max wind 85 mph, max path width 200 yards, path length 2 miles.

CZ_NAME: TELLER COUNTY / RAMPART RANGE ABOVE 7500 FT / PIKES PEAK BETWEEN 7500 & 11000 FT
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quick-moving shortwave brought a brief period of accumulating snow to the mountains, while strong winds were seen just east of the terrain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a 66 mph wind gust measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large cluster of showers and thunderstorms developed along the southeast Georgia coast in the afternoon hours and produced a few instances of flash flooding in Chatham County. Several rain gauges in the area observed rainfall totals of 3-4 inches, with hourly rainfall rates of 2-3 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chatham County Emergency Management reported that the intersection of Canal Street and Park Avenue was closed due to flooding. The roadway intersection was covered with 12-18 inches of water and one vehicle was stalled out in the flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak surface high pressure ridging was centered just to the south of the JAX CWA on both the 26th and 27th, resulting in a west to southwest flow across the region. Sufficient moisture and summertime instability resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms, with some strong to severe storms causing isolated reports of damage across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report of a roof blown off a shed and a few trees down in Daytona North. Time  estimated via radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Decaying convection from across the eastern Texas Panhandle produced several heat burst episodes across western Oklahoma during the mid to late evening of the 30th into the 31st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weatherford (WEAT) Mesonet observation. Severe (>50-knot) wind gusts occurred during the event time, with the peak wind gust of 51 knots occurring at 2150 LST. This event was caused by a probable heat burst.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe weather impacted lower Michigan on March 6th. 1 tornado occurred in the Grand Rapids County Warning Area while 3 occurred in the Northern Indiana County Warning Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Exit sign on the highway was blown over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large mid-level trough pushed through the Pacific NW into the northern Great Basin throughout June 6-8, bringing a few scattered severe wind gusts to Tooele county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Dugway DPG18 Causeway mesonet station measured a thunderstorm wind gust to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power line downed at Sledd Creek Rd and Beshears Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked down trees and power lines near the intersection of Snake Lane and Old Philadelphia Pike approximately 3 miles north of Gap.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold morning temperatures near normal across Southeastern Arizona. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that cold and hypothermia was the primary factor in the cause of death for two individuals, one in Tucson and one in Sahuarita.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cold morning temperatures were 2 to 4 degrees below normal across Southeastern Arizona. Tucson International Airport ASOS reached a low temperature of 39 degrees Fahrenheit. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that environmental cold exposure was the primary factor in the cause of death for two individuals, one in Tucson and one in Sahuarita.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This was a delayed report received via emergency management.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Exceptional Drought (D4) to Extreme (D3) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report on Facebook relayed 2 inch hail just south of Grand Saline, along VZCR 1110 south of Hwy 280.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged a metal frame barn and tossed it into the power lines along with debris tossed across J Highway into a field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow southward-moving cold front tracked into South-Central Texas, producing a line of strong to severe thunderstorms which advanced ahead of the front as it encountered a moist and unstable airmass on the evening of May 19 into the early hours of May 20. The storms produced swaths of severe winds and some large hail. Locally heavy rain that led to some flash flooding mainly north of the Austin area and in the Hill Country.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping Pong ball sized hail relayed by EM near Enchanted Rock State Natural Area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Florida ahead of a frontal boundary. Several severe weather reports were received with the main impacts to trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were down around the De Funiak Springs area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals were generally 1 to 2 feet across Kewaunee County. In addition, winds gusting to 40 to 60 mph caused blizzard conditions on Monday March 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down along North Carolina Highway 56.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May started with severe drought (D2) present across much of eastern WV, including: Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and most of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Moderate drought (D1) also persisted across most of western and north-central WV, with the exception of Pleasants, Wood, northwest Jackson, northern Mason, western Ritchie, western Tyler, and western Wirt counties where conditions were merely abnormally dry (D0). Only minimal changes to D0 and D1 occurred in the second week of the month. D2, however, spread out across all of Boone and Kanawha counties; most of Lincoln, Logan, and Putnam counties; and portions of eastern Cabell, southern Jackson, southern Roane, and eastern Wayne counties. Conditions worsened even more the following week, as D2 engulfed most of southern, central, and eastern West Virginia, and a sliver of extreme drought (D3) crept into eastern McDowell, southeast Raleigh, and eastern Wyoming counties. Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth. Fortunately, enough precipitation fell at the end of the month to eradicate D3 and confine D2 to mainly Boone, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Nicholas, Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Raleigh, Webster, Wyoming, southern Braxton, eastern Lincoln, southern Roane, and southern Wayne. D1 improved to D0 in southern Tyler, Doddridge, northern Harrison, northern Taylor, part of northern Barbour, Ritchie, Wirt, northwest Gilmer, northern Calhoun, northern Roane, northern Jackson, northwest Mason, northwest Cabell, and part of northern Wayne. Meanwhile, drought was completely eliminated from counties, or at least portions of counties, bordering the Ohio River.||Generally less than an inch of rain fell during the first week of May. Around an inch or less accumulated during the second week. During the third week of the month, much of the area received around an inch and a half or less of rain, though a strip of up to two inches fell along the Ohio River. More substantial precipitation occurred at the end of the month, when one to three inches of rain fell to the south of I-64 and one and a half to over four inches fell to the north of I-64. Highest amounts were observed across portions of Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Taylor, Randolph, and Upshur counties. Multiple rounds of rain during this time finally allowed for significant improvement to drought conditions, particularly across the northern and western part of the state.||The six climate sites in West Virginia were evenly split between above and below normal total precipitation for the month, with Beckley, Charleston, and Elkins on the below normal side and Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg on the above normal side. On the 22nd, Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg each received enough rain to break their existing daily precipitation records. Beckley was also able to tie a standing daily precipitation record on the 24th of the month.

Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southern Illinois on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Williamson County, IL on the 26th. Northwest portions of southern Illinois and areas south of route 13 only experienced advisory criteria with values of -9 to -14. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the early morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Alexander, Pulaski, and Massac County, IL where wind chills warmed above -5 the morning of the 26th due to calmer winds.

On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado developed just east of the Missouri River at approximately 4:31 AM CST. The tornado produced minor tree damage as it tracked east towards Interstate 29. As the tornado reached Interstate 29, the tornado intensified. EF1 damage was produced at a residence located along Western Ave with most of the roof lifted off this residence. The tornado then crossed Interstate 29 and produced tree damage along the interstate before dissipating at approximately 4:32 AM CST. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second day of high winds occurred for Southwest Nebraska.  High wind gusts started after 9 AM MT and continued through mid afternoon before declining.  The peak wind gust was 66 MPH from a personal weather station near Culbertson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts around 60 MPH were reported in Yuma, Cheyenne, and Hitchcock counties.  As such these winds should have also occurred in Dundy County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lines and clusters of severe thunderstorms ahead of a cold front approaching from the Ohio River Valley resulted in widely scattered damaging wind gusts, a few of which were considerable mainly during the mid to late afternoon and early evening hours. In many cases east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Monutains, severe wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph preceded any precipitation by at least several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were mutliple reports of trees and power lines down throughout the City of Alexandria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe storms developed along a slow moving cold front as it creeped across the area through the afternoon and into the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 2-inch hail along with estimated winds up to 90 mph. Multiple structures were damaged across south-central Kansas due to these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed near Blue Spring Road just west of State Highway 48 north of Coleman where a barn lost part of its metal roof and trees were snapped. The tornado moved east-southeast damaging trees and another outbuilding at the county line as it crossed into Atoka County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 10 degrees or less across eastern Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 9F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large storm system moved across the Midwest March 15 to the 16th, initially bringing rain and thunderstorms to the area on the morning of the 15th. This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. Local news reported that most areas schools were closed and several Department of Transportation districts reported snow covered road ways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP Observer in Hennepin reported 1.6 inches of snow. There were widespread automated weather observation reports of visibilities between 1/2sm to 1sm along with frequent wind gusts between 45 to 55 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down onto a power line along Wells Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties.
