In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.

Severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning, afternoon and evening hours of April 26 through April 29 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail and a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very large hail fell near Vaughn. Multiple large hailstones in the area were between 2 and 3 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas. Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches!!  Unfortunately 3 fatalities were confirmed due to flooding in Madison County, KY, and 1 fatality indirectly related to the flooding occurred on Floyds Fork in Jefferson County, KY.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A truck was submerged up to its headlights at Payneville Road and Grandview Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.
Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.

As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service survey determined that an EF0 tornado with maximum winds of 70mph produced an intermittent damage path to the east northeast of Buffalo, MO. Reports of a funnel cloud near the ground were received from the Springfield Street area southeast of Buffalo, with the first damage viewed north of Quarry Road in a wooded area. The tornado did the majority of its damage as it crossed Ozark Trail. One mobile home suffered broken glass on the south and north sides of the structure and another on the east side of the structure. Additional damage was noted to several outbuildings. Additional large limbs were noted on Steelman Road and west of Engle Road via Sentinel-2 satellite data analysis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued lack of rainfall combined with hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 10th drought monitor update, continuing through the rest of the Month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough was moving southeast through southern New Mexico with some mid level moisture available for thunderstorms to develop.  A very dry surface with dew point depressions over 65 degrees allowed for gusty thunderstorm winds to occur.  Blowing dust also developed over the Lordsburg Playa causing the interstate to be closed for a short period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air moved into eastern Colorado the 23rd and linger into the 24th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three large trees downed at the intersection of Canterbury and Detroit Roads in Westlake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through New Jersey producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree reported down. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across southeastern Oklahoma and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the area was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. A tornado, isolated damaging wind, and large hail up to two inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

Winds gusting in the 35 to 50 mph range combined with air temperatures in the single digits to result in minimum wind chills of -5 to -15 across the valleys. Beneath weak, broad high pressure, minimum wind chill values generally dropped into the negative single digits with isolated colder patches including KUCP and KDUJ which recorded wind chills into the -20s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. For some areas in the central and western UP, this was the coldest 3 and 4 day stretch since January 2019. Numerous schools, businesses, and services were closed on Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th.||In addition to the cold temperatures, blizzard conditions accompanied the initial push of cold air during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd in the Keweenaw, with whiteout conditions leading to several traffic accidents and road closures. Another round of heavy accumulating lake effect snow occurred in the northeastern UP on the 23rd, with very low visibilities resulting in at least one road closure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -40F were observed on the 23rd and 24th, and as low as -25F on the 25th and 26th. Key impacts: school and business closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was uprooted and a metal sign blown over west of Pistakee Highlands.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from October 2025 through the first half of January 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of East Texas from the second week of January through the end of the month. During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 5-8 inches, which was only 25-30% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. Conditions deteriorated to extreme drought across Franklin and Titus Counties by January 22nd through the end of the month as only 1.0-1.5 inches of precipitation fell during the month. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

Multiple mesoscale convective vortices triggered a line of storms that brought damaging wind gusts the New River Valley and the Piedmont. Mesoscale conditions were not the most ideal for severe weather development. Bulk shear struggled to get above 20 knots, mid-level lapse rates were about 5.5 C/km, and DAPE only up went up 500 J/kg. However, sufficient surface heating and moisture resulted in CAPE of at least 1000 J/kg which allowed for some decent thunderstorm development after the MCV trigger. There was one notable storm that brought down a swath of trees in Roanoke County and went straight eastward and brought more trees down in Charlotte County. Broad rotation was noted in the SRV data by the time it reached Charlotte County with a 59.3 mph velocity gate recorded at around 7250 feet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds across Hillcroft Road in between railroad tracks and Austin Creek.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 35 knots (40 MPH) was measured by a mesonet (MSI05) adjacent to the tidal Patapsco River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An ice jam on the Koyukuk River near Hughes impounded a significant volume of water. This caused water levels to submerge properties in the lower sections of the community, directly impacting local residences, school property, and the airport. Local residents and members of the Alaska State EOC indicated that the ice set up late Friday night and then released Saturday afternoon. However, a secondary jam set up soon after which was responsible for sending most of the water into the community.  Numerous families were sheltered at the local community hall which is located on higher ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second wave of wintry precipitation occurred 24 hours after a light mix of snow and freezing rain fell the day prior. This round was heavier and temperatures were right around freezing, leading to a mixture of snow, freezing rain, and rain. For most locations, the main period of freezing rain occurred very early in the morning on January 6th as rainfall rates were lighter. Rates then increased throughout the morning of the 6th which made it difficult for ice accretion to continue as temperatures hovered right around the freezing point. During the morning commute, most areas saw more of a crunchy slush on the ground as the heavier rain attempted to melt the coating of ice that developed overnight. The heaviest impacted area was St Croix, Polk, and Barron counties where temperatures were slightly cooler and the rain rates were not as heavy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at KEAU reported several hours of freezing precipitation during the morning of January 6th. A CoCoRaHS observer also reported freezing rain in Chippewa Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Almost record below normal rainfall continued during the month of March, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions area-wide and upgraded the Suwannee Valley and inland southeast Georgia into an exceptional drought (D4) by the end of March. Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down across the street from church.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Remnant convection from the southern Plains entered central Missouri during the evening of March 6th. These thunderstorms congealed into a QLCS and produced wind damage in Boone County. Antecedent saturated conditions paired with an inch to two inches of additional rain also caused isolated flash flooding in southeast Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Bradford Farm Missouri Mesonet weather station measured wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 13, 2026, a potent late-winter occluded storm system tracked across the Great Lakes while slowly filling, from early morning at 985 mb in northeastern Wisconsin, to late day at 989 mb over the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan.  The system's cold front crossed northern and northeastern portions of central Indiana from 1000 to 1230EST.||Both an earlier corresponding low-level jet stream axis and a later tighter surface pressure gradient crossed the region, promoting widespread gusty winds veering from southwest to west-northwest while gusting to 45 to 57 mph.  When these two features briefly overlapped following the frontal passage, through midday to early afternoon hours, and also coupled with increased boundary layer mixing under plentiful sun, isolated highest wind gusts reached 58-67 mph.  Winds subsided quickly through evening hours.||This unusually intense gradient wind episode for the central Indiana region included measured gusts of 58+ mph at seven reporting stations;  four reports from Tipton County to Delaware County of semi trucks traveling on north-south roads being blown over to the east;  and widely scattered tree, power line, and minor property (mainly roof) damage that was most prevalent in Delaware County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Rockdale County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 14, 2025, the county experienced a period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in February. In total, the county sustained approximately 15 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two back to back winter storm systems impacted northern and central NM with the first from late January 7th through the morning of January 8th with the second colder system crossing the state late January 8th through the afternoon of January 9th. The first storm brought snow to mainly the mountains and nearby highlands, with valley and plains locations receiving mainly rain. Gusty west winds were observed across the central highlands midday on January 8th between the two storm systems with a peak wind gust of 65 mph at a Ziamet station southeast of Vaughn. The second storm system approached the state during the afternoon hours of January 8th with western New Mexico impacted by a band of snow on the leading edge of the storm. This band of snow moved into the middle Rio Grande Valley during the evening. This band contained a convective storm with large hail and graupel across the Albuquerque metro area. Accumulating graupel and hail forced the closure of I-40 west of Albuquerque with one inch diameter hail and graupel observed at the National Weather Service office. As the core of the system moved into western NM the night of January 8th and early morning of January 9th, a wraparound snow band brought moderate to heavy snow across northwest and north-central NM, including Farmington, Taos, and Santa Fe. Moderate to heavy snow then shifted to northeast NM on the north side of the storm during the morning and midday hours of January 9th. North wind gusts of up to 45 mph resulted in blowing snow and near whiteout conditions and the temporary closures of I-25 at Raton Pass and U.S. Highway 64/87 between Raton and Clayton. Snow across northeast NM tapered off during the early evening hours as the system exited into the central Great Plains. A lingering band of snow across Espanola, Los Alamos, Santa Fe, and Glorieta brought some light snow during the evening hours of January 9th before skies finally cleared up and temperatures plummeted overnight.||In the end, snowfall amounts of 2 to 6 inches were observed across lower elevations of northwest and north central New Mexico, 4 to 7 inches across the Jemez and Tusas Mountains with an estimated 10 inches at the Bateman SNOTEL site in the southern Tusas Mountains. The Sangre de Cristo Mountains observed 1 to 2 feet of snow with the higher end of this range observed at Ski Santa Fe and the Santa Fe SNOTEL site. The eastern foothills of the Albuquerque Metro observed 1 to 2 inches of a snow and graupel mix and the Sandia and Manzano Mountains observing around 5 to 9 inches of snow with locally a foot on the Sandia Crest. The west-central and southwest mountains observed around 3 to 5 inches of snow with locally up to an estimated 16 inches at Whitewater Baldy Peak. Finally, the Ruidoso area observed around 1 to 4 inches of snow with 10 inches at Sierra Blanca Peak and Ski Apache.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS observers on the northern and eastern areas of Taos observed 8 to 9.5 inches of snowfall. CoCoRaHS observers in Ranchos de Taos observed 5.5 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No observations within the county. Estimated maximum wind gusts of 58-60 mph based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong area of low pressure brings strong front through the region and brought high winds that impacted much of the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 11th slowed down a cold front moving through the area but also provided a focus for thunderstorm development. Strong instability, resulting from the warm temperatures and high moisture, ahead of the front fueled the rapid development of severe thunderstorms from the late afternoon into the evening hours. Thunderstorms initially developed over the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains where temperatures in excess of 100 degrees allowed updrafts to break through a capping inversion. Atmospheric flow was weak which allowed storms to move slowly and create torrential rainfall in some locations. Some roads within the city of Levelland (Hockley County) became impassable because of water over the road. The most significant thunderstorm developed over southern Lubbock County and moved southward producing severe wind gusts and wind damage throughout Lynn County. These winds caused minor but widespread damage throughout the towns of Tahoka and Wilson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS cooperative weather observer reported quarter size hail approximately nine miles southeast of Floydada.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked multiple trees down onto Gold Mine Road near Tower City. Multiple cars were stuck on the road as a result of the downed trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There were a few rounds of thunderstorms through this period. A few storms were severe with large hail and damaging winds and an isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported golf ball size hail along county line southeast of Woodson by Woodson VFD.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph, knocked down numerous trees and power lines down in Middlecreek Township. This included a large tree down that blocked portions of Barron Church Road for multiple hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over the course of the weekend, a meandering front and an unseasonably strong upper trough triggered widespread showers and thunderstorms across the region. Heavy rain from training storms ultimately resulted in flash flooding, particularly affecting several Central Texas counties. A significant flood event occurred in and around Waco costing millions of dollars.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire and rescue reported that the CR 232 Loop north of Rockdale was impassable due  to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms moved eastward into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening as they organized into a squall line. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oklahoma Mesonet station near Webbers Falls measured thunderstorm wind gusts up to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported penny size hail near Trevino and Championship Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approximately 50 kt jet passed across the region the afternoon of June 16. Combine this with deep vertical mixing and several areas ended up observing strong wind gusts through the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few mesonsets measured gusts of 58+mph, including GW3546 Whitlash 7 S, GW1986 Lothair 9N, GW1952 Riverview Colony, GW4015 Chester 4 NE, and GW3478 TCTiber. The peak observed gust was 62 mph at TCTiber.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of thunderstorms formed downstream of a mid-level wave in an environment with around 500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 40 knots of effective shear. Despite the meager instability, thunderstorms were able to reach severe levels with areas of tree and power line damage reported in Northwestern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received from Mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed north of a semi-stationary front during the late afternoon hours on Wednesday (5/27).  The strongest storms produced damaging winds and large hail up to 2 inches in diameter as they tracked through central Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell in Wausau.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown onto a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power lines were blown down across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper shortwave moved through the area during the afternoon of 6/27. With a moderate to strong destabilization with MLCAPE approaching 2000 J/kg, scattered thunderstorms developed across the area. A favorable downburst environment was in place with strong low level lapse rates and DCAPE between 700-800 J/kg. While most downbursts were sub-severe, one storm reached severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aiken County Dispatch reported trees fell on a power line leading to a fire near the  intersection of Kathwood Rd and Old Jackson Hwy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper level storm moved into the western U.S. early on February 17th with a lead disturbance moving over the Four Corners and Intermountain West. Strong mid and upper level winds at the base of this shortwave moved over New Mexico during this time. The Pacific cold front associated with this disturbance moved across the state during the morning hours of the day resulting in brief high wind gusts at several sites along and west of the central mountain chain coinciding with a period of rain and snow west of the Rio Grande Valley and the north central mountains. A peak gust of 84 mph was measured at Kachina Peak within the Taos Ski Valley, while two reports of downed trees with one knocking out a power line came in from Ruidoso. Subsidence behind the cold front allowed stronger winds aloft to translate down the surface resulting in an extended period of high winds along and east of the central mountain chain. High winds tapered off during the late afternoon and evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A ZiaMet station east of Fort Sumner measured high wind gusts peaking at 64 mph. Additionally, a ZiaMet station at Canyon Blanco measured a high wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding across eastern Nebraska. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||Sinitially presenting a significant large hail threat before transitioning into a destructive wind event. Through the early to mid-evening hours, widespread hail ranging from quarter (1.00 inch) to baseball (2.75 inches) size bombarded Platte, Saline, Seward, Gage, Lancaster, and Jefferson counties. The most intense hail occurred in Jefferson and Saline counties, highlighted by 2.75-inch hailstones measured near Plymouth and 2.50-inch hailstones reported near De Witt.||As the storms progressed into the late evening and early morning hours of May 17, the primary hazard shifted to severe and damaging straight-line winds. Jefferson County absorbed the brunt of this impact, with multiple mesonet stations and emergency management officials measuring extreme wind gusts between 75 and 88 mph in and around Fairbury. These intense winds caused significant impacts, including downed trees, widespread power outages, and near-zero visibility. The line of storms maintained severe intensity as it pushed eastward, producing gusts in excess of 60 mph across Gage and Richardson counties before eventually clearing the region.||In addition to the severe weather, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall brought flash flooding to southeast Nebraska, primarily impacting Gage, Johnson, Jefferson, and Saline counties. Widespread precipitation totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the region, with localized maximums of 5.80 to 7.00 inches concentrated in Gage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several public reports of hail measured up to 1.75 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The fire department reported multiple houses were flooding on Pecan Ave in Wills Point. Local FD requested a boat and were going door to door evacuating residents. Four to five feet of water was prohibiting egress on foot.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: We had a few wildfires that occurred in early April.  A couple in Hutchinson County (North and South Twin), and another Fire in Potter County (Meadow View).  The fires ranged from 365-1262 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The North Twin Fire was reported around 12:30 pm CDT about 2 miles northeast of Bugbee, TX. The fire is believed to be human caused by a vehicle.  The fire would go on to burn 518 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down, and a roof was damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported at PR-115 near Kayuris Restaurant, and the intersection with Calle Las Flores (street), due to rio Culebrinas (river) and its tributaries being out of their banks. No one was reported as trapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into an warm and unstable airmass primarily west of I-95. This resulted in bands of showers and thunderstorms that produced localized damaging wind and spotty large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down onto a power line at the intersection of Ewing Street and Dawson Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.

A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -12 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -29 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed across East Liberty Road near State Route 347.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles downed in Collins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down on King Avenue in Shamokin Dam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of significant thunderstorm wind damage occurred in the area between Old Cabin Road and Bold Springs Road, north of Fillmore. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped and at least two outbuildings were destroyed. The path is estimated and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked a tree onto a leaking propane tank, with possible damage to a building on Reading Road, according to the county dispatch feed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 16th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were a couple of blown transformers reported in Tift county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported an overturned trailer northwest of Jacksboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stationed across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours allowed for thunderstorm development to form across the Shenandoah Valley during the late morning hours of March 16, 2026 that began to surge towards southern Pennsylvania. Severe thunderstorms in a favorable unstable and highly sheared environment across Virginia and Maryland began to shift into the a more stable and less sheared environment; however, momentum from these thunderstorms allowed for isolated instances of tree damage during the afternoon hours. As the cold front continued to track eastward, slightly more instability was available across eastern Lancaster County during the evening hours, with more readily available lift and moisture, allowing for more robust winds that caused more significant wind damage in eastern Lancaster County. The most notable wind damage came in the form of significant roof damage in New Holland along with significant damage to a barn and a nearby residence near Terre Hill. Multiple trees were also knocked down near Terre Hill and near Gap.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 70 mph knocked trees down onto wires along Lincoln Highway approximately 2 miles west-northwest of Gap.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. In southern Michigan, damaging wind gusts occurred downing trees, some onto houses. Powerlines were reported to be down in multiple areas as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Shavehead Lake on the southside Chanel has very large trees uprooted and landed on a  house, a gazebo was destroyed. A shed was also destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. Storm development occurred both along a quasi-stationary boundary across northern Oklahoma and along an accelerating Pacific Front from far western Oklahoma into western-north Texas. A mix of supercells and a well-developed quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) yielded reports of large to very large hail and wind damage across portions of the area. A brief tornado was also documented in far eastern Wilbarger County in Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines and power poles were blown down along U.S. Highway 287 on the east side of Quanah. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 5 degrees or less across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An embedded shortwave moved northeast through a broad upper-level trough while increasing midlevel winds aided thunderstorm organization across the central Gulf Coast. Ample atmospheric moisture in the local soundings and strong instability supported expanding afternoon convection with very efficient rainfall. Stronger cells produced damaging winds and large hail from the northshore and southshore of Lake Pontchartrain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees reported down on several streets in the Folsom and Goodbee area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on Main Hewett Creek Road in Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pace CT wildfire continued through most of April at 318 acres with 75% containment. On April 21, the fire grew to 343.35 acres with 85% containment. The fire continued to burn through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported quarter sized hail 1 mile east of Dexter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts moving through western and central North Dakota combined with a series of short-wave troughs resulted in an extended period of strong winds. The strongest reported wind gust was 74 mph at the Bowman Airport in Bowman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fryburg NDDOT site reported wind gusts to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were three separate downed tree reports in the Mount Airy area. One was at the intersection of Rockford Street and Old Highway 601 near Iglesia Misionera Cristo Vive Mount Airy. Another was at the intersection of Lambert Farm Trail and Rockford Street. The last was at the intersection of Rockford Street and Smith Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds at the 136.1 mile marker of I-81.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a southeastward moving cold front, broken lines of showers and thunderstorms developed in the evening hours. A surge of mid 70s temperatures with upper 50s dew points resulted in sufficient destabilization with MLCAPE up to 1000 J/kg, effective shear of 30-40 knots, and a gradient of 700-900 DCAPE. This allowed for some thunderstorms to become severe with large hail and damaging wind as the result, including two measured 58 mph gusts in southwest Pennsylvania.

A cold front moved into South-Central Texas and stalled. The airmass the front moved into was warm and very moist. Thunderstorms formed in the vicinity of the front and some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. Leander Rd. was closed due to flooding near Mason Creek in Leander.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall total in northern Marinette County was 22.4 inches in Athelstane.  In addition, winds gusting to 40 to 50 mph caused blizzard conditions on Monday March 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree down.

CZ_NAME: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of March continued the trend of much above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation that characterized the winter of 2025-2026. Very little precipitation fell across the region, with all ten climate sites finishing the month with below normal totals. Likewise, temperatures were well above normal, with mean temperatures running 8-10 degrees above normal. As a result, drought remained, and worsened significantly in many locations. And in areas that had, to this point, remained drought free, drought developed and worsened rapidly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of March, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought as covering approximately 35% of Colorado Zone 010 - Gore and Elk Mountains/Central Mountain Valleys. Approximately 50% of the zone was under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, with the remaining 15% under Severe (D2) Drought. With the 3/24 US Drought Monitor update, Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded to cover approximately 75% of the zone, with the remaining 25% under Extreme (D3) Drought. With the 3/31 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought covered 100% of the zone. No reports of impacts or losses related to drought conditions in the zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most of this region was in Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought to begin June. Normal to well above normal precipitation was observed through most of the June except for a dry middle of the month. Well above normal precipitation was observed for the month across eastern portions of this region, while normal to below normal precipitation was observed elsewhere. The drought category improved this month but areas of D2 to D3 persist due to a 2-6 inch 120 day rainfall deficit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Gusty to strong west downslope winds developed along the east slope of the Front Range Mountains and Foothills during the morning of the 25th. Windy conditions spread east across the plains with gusts of 45 to 55 mph with a few local gusts reaching 65 mph. The strong winds combined very warm and dry conditions fuel two wildfires. One on the north Denver metro area and a second in northern Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph wind gust was recorded at the Fort Morgan airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large cyclonic trough occupying the eastern third of the US was the instigating force behind snow showers and northwest orographic snow. This snow resulted in light snow at lower elevations, with several inches of accumulating snow at higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell at the top of Mount LeConte, with 8 inches of snow falling over the course of portions of 3 calendar days. At Newfound Gap, the automated sensor measured 2.4 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reports a tree down in the 1000 block of howser mill road.

CZ_NAME: WEST JACKSON & WEST GRAND COUNTIES ABOVE 9000 FEET
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest flow transport Pacific moisture into the region producing heavy snowfall across the northern Colorado Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on snow/water equivalent, an estimated 9 to 15 inches of snow fell across the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm produced hail from golf ball to tennis balls in size over a swath nearly 32 miles in length from south of Nevada, MO to locations north and east of Nevada. Along this mostly rural path, damage occurred to some roofs of homes and structures, vehicles, multiple RV's, equipment and crops.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving south along the west coast brought a strong cold front with valley and mountain snow across southern Oregon on 02/16 into 02/17. Snow showers followed on 02/18 before they increased in coverage and intensity late on 02/18 into the morning of 02/19.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Gridded Snowfall Analysis indicated storm totals of 1 to 6 inches at elevations below 3000 feet. Precipitation amounts in the zone included 0.35 inches at Toketee Lake, 0.40 inches at Grandad, 0.60 inches at Toketee Airstrip, and 0.61 inches at Buckeye.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave brought about windy thunderstorms across much of southern MT. In it's wake, a cold front crossed the area, and strong winds behind the front persisted well into the 14th. Non-convective gusts up to 80 mph were observed, with convective gusts up to 80 mph observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lavina N mesonet gusted to 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a strong April cold front spread south through North and Central Texas during the early morning hours of April 18. Isolated instances of hail occurred, along with a wind gust of 61 MPH at Fort Worth Alliance Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook report relayed penny to quarter size hail in Athens along with torrential rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry spring continued across Middle Tennessee during April 2026. Precipitation amounts were generally 3 to 5 inches across with most of this rain recorded during the last week of the month. While these rain amounts were higher compared to the past couple months, it was still below normal for the month. Drought conditions worsened through the month of April. By the end of the month, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least severe drought with about 38 percent of this classified as extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Abnormally dry conditions from March 2026 worsened in April with severe drought conditions developing across Overton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought continued across portions of Deep East Texas through the first week of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. However, widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 2.00+ inches fell across much of Cherokee, Nacogdoches, and Angelina Counties during the last few days of April into the first week of May, resulting in a one category improvement to Moderate (D1) drought across these areas by the May 7th release of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Timely near to above normal rainfall continued across these areas through the remainder of May, with monthly rainfall totals ranging from 3-6+ inches, near to slightly above the monthly normals. Thus, some improvement to pasture greenup, stock pond levels, and streamflows across area rivers, bayous, and creeks were observed, especially as the additional timely rains fell through the remainder of the month.

A warm front lifted north through the region Monday morning (6/29) allowing daytime temperatures to soar into the upper 80s to lower 90s with dew points in the middle to upper 70s Monday (6/29) afternoon across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. The warm front lifted north Monday night, which brought the hot and humid weather further north and east to include northeast Wisconsin and the lakeshore with similar temperatures and dew points. The combination of hot temperatures and high dew points allowed heat index values to soar to 105 to 110 degrees both days. ||In addition to the hot temperatures, overnight lows only fell into the upper 70s to lower 80s Monday night (6/29) into early Tuesday morning (6/30), providing minimal relief from the hot temperatures. The heat wave broke when an area of showers and thunderstorms tracked through the area Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday evening (6/30).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures and high humidity caused heat index values to rise as high as 108 degrees during the afternoon on Tuesday.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant street flooding occurred in the city of West Plains. Numerous streets were closed due to flooding. A home was flooded, a vehicle was submerged and extensive flooding occurred at a Dollar General store.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second weather system in a series of storms across the western U.S. moved into the Four Corners area February 18th. This system brought light to moderate snow to the Tusas and northern Sangre de Cristo Mountains. However, the more significant hazard to the region was the strong to damaging wind gusts. Daytime mixing allowed stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface resulting in high wind gusts across the highlands of far west central NM and eventually the central mountain chain and adjacent central highlands. A band of snow accompanying the Pacific cold front moved across western and north central NM during the evening hours of February 18th. Heading into the overnight hours February 18th into February 19th, strong to damaging wind gusts shifted to the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and adjacent northeast highlands as the shortwave moved across the southern Rockies. High winds across the eastern highlands tapered off slowly during the late morning hours as the shortwave exited northeast outside of a brief high wind gust east of Puerto de Luna in Guadalupe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Edgewood SWCD mesonet station measured a peak wind gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mainly zonal flow aloft with embedded low amplitude perturbations resulted in scattered thunderstorm development across central Virginia with heavy rainfall and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A caller reported that the on-ramp to the Downtown Expressway from I-95 was flooded with a depth of about 3 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface boundary kicked off a marginal line of thunderstorms that produced sporadic wind damage across central and eastern MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Belchertown, a large tree and wires were down on Michael Sears Rd and North Liberty  St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A boundary set up across eastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania allowed for ample lift ahead of the cold frontal passage given sufficient instability and ample shear in place across the region during the afternoon and evening hours of March 31, 2026. These thunderstorms began to develop across western Ohio and gradually developed stronger as they continued tracking across central and eastern Ohio and into portions of western Pennsylvania. This line of thunderstorms along the boundary caused multiple instances of tree damage across Warren and McKean counties with no injuries reported despite all of the tree damage. A secondary surge of thunderstorms later in the evening allowed for a tree to get knocked down in Clearfield County, with no injuries reported from this incident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down across Six Mile Road approximately 3 miles south-southeast of Clarendon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media photo showed a 2.75 to 3 inch hailstone in Emory.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure in the gulf states moved northeast and intensified along and off the Mid Atlantic coast with the consolidated of mid level energy resulting in a major Nor'easter which brought blizzard and near blizzard conditions to Northeastern New Jersey. The storm became vertically stacked and it slowly pulled away to the east and brought a heavy to major snowfall across Northeastern New Jersey with blizzard conditions across the eastern zones.  Winter storm and near blizzard conditions were reported across the remainder of Northeastern New Jersey. A major snowfall occurred region wide, with portions of the region receiving historic snowfall totals.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Frequent wind gusts of over 40 mph with Newark ASOS reporting a 54 mph gust at 3:07 am, and Bayonne mesonet reporting a 53 mph gust at 2:47 am, and frequent visibilities of a quarter mile or less were reported at the Newark ASOS. Snowfall amounts reported across the zone ranged from mainly 19 to 24 inches across the zone via trained spotters, Cocorahs, and an official NWS observation from Newark.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving and narrow snow band brought remarkably heavy snowfall rates to much of northeast Iowa during the late evening hours on February 19th through the morning on February 20th. Some locations likely received snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the overnight hours with the highest totals being in a narrow band through portions of Floyd, Chickasaw, Winneshiek, Fayette and Allamakee counties where 12 to 16 inches of snow fell. Widespread totals in excess of 6 inches were noted across much of northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This snow band brought heavy snow to Howard County with snowfall totals ranging from 5 to 8 inches. The highest reported snowfall total was in Cresco where 8 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Destructive hail up to baseball sized and strong winds in Westby right before 5pm on April 14th resulted in widespread damage across the entire town and surrounding areas. Roughly 1100 residences in this area sustained roof, window and siding damage with many vehicles having significant damages as well.
