EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across inland Miami-Dade County in March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Infrequent brief wind gusts over 58 MPH were observed over two southeast Wyoming wind prone areas along Interstate 80. Impacts were minimal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Vedauwoo WYDOT site reported a few gusts around 58 MPH the morning of March 24th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light to moderate snow occurred as relatively warm and moist air spread over cold valleys.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light to moderate snow fell across the region, with the heaviest accumulations of 2 to 3 inches occurring across the Flathead Valley. These totals resulted in slick road conditions for much of the area. Further south, the Mission Valley saw only minor accumulations, with totals generally remaining under 1 inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms rolled across the Denver Metro area mid afternoon on June 8th producing up to golf ball sized hail. Isolate severe wind gusts were recorded as well. As the storms progressed east of the Denver their intensity increase. A supercell thunderstorm continued to track eastward, stay south of I-70. Farther north, thunderstorms organized into a broken line, producing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph across far northeast Colorado.

At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across the state.  Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 1%, D2 - 54%, D1 - 55%.  January  brought little relief to Maine's drought conditions, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge.  January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas in the 50 to 75% of normal range.  Snowfall remained below normal, especially for interior areas with snow water equivalent below normal for all areas except the immediate coast.  Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins.  Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the immediate coastline in the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought conditions remained in a steady state by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 46 mph wind gust was recorded at the Saratoga National Historical Park. A tree and wires were downed on New York Route 32 between Reynolds Road and Reservoir Road in the Town of Moreau. A tree and wires were downed on New York Route 32 between Grange Hall Road and U.S. Route 4 in the Town of Northumberland.  A tree was downed on New York Route 29 between Hudson Lane and Pine Grove Lane in the Town of Milton. A pole, tree and wires were downed on U.S. Route 9 between Old West Road and Old Saratoga Road in the Town of Moreau. A tree and wires were downed on New York Route 9N between Bockes Road and Greene Road in the Town of Greenfield. A pole and wires were downed on New York Route 9N between Antone Road and Elaine Edelson Lane in the Town of Corinth. An estimated 8700 people were without power throughout Saratoga County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous large tree limbs were snapped along Goddard Youth Camp Road, on the south edge of Lake of the Arbuckles. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough positioned itself to support the development of a strong mid-level frontogenesis band. It took advantage of tremendous mid-level moisture and lift. Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 6.5 inches of snow fallen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While occasional precipitation events occurred in January 2026, including an impactful winter storm in the late month, most areas saw continued precipitation deficits relative to January normals. Rather widespread severe (or worse) drought conditions continued in areas near and south of the Interstate 40 corridor.

A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began on the 24th with 3.0 inches of snow and sleet reported in Frenchburg by 0730EST on the 25th. A CoCoRaHS observer near Means estimated at least 1 inch of sleet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th late morning into the early evening, temperatures were as low as -1F, with sustained winds around 15-20 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -22F.  During the 26th late evening into the overnight, temperatures were as low as -1F, with sustained winds around 20 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -24F.  During the 28th pre-dawn and early morning hours, temperatures were as low as -8, with sustained winds around 5-10 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -23F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS evolved within a strongly sheared environment to produce multiple tornadoes across south central Mississippi. The most prominent feature was the northern bookend vortex of the line. The line also produced wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This very brief tornado resulted in minor tree damage south of Taylorsville as it tracked across Charlie Red Drive and Ben Stroud Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed at approximately 4:07 PM CST near the intersection of 646 Avenue and 708 Road, about 1 mile northeast of Salem. Intermittent damage to trees and farm outbuildings was noted between 646 and 647 Avenues. The tornado continued northeast, damaging more trees and breaking power poles along 650 Avenue. Additional damage to trees and farm outbuildings was noted near the intersection of 651 Avenue and 710 Road. The tornado then crossed US Highway 73 and lifted the roof off another farm outbuilding east of 652 Avenue before dissipating shortly thereafter. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 107 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills. By Friday morning, much of the area was seeing temperatures of at least 20 degrees below zero, and as cold as 25 degrees below zero measured at the South Dakota State University mesonet stations in Gettysburg and 23 miles north of Highmore. With these cold temperatures and a northwest breeze, wind chills across much of the area had fallen to 40 degrees below zero and colder, with the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Summit coming in with a wind chill of 53 degrees below zero. Temperatures failed to warm much during the day, with highs in the single digits to teens below zero. Watertown set a record for the lowest daily high temperature, reaching only 11 degrees below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roadway flooding reported at California Highway 1 and Highland Drive near Point Pinos.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina during the afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in the Piedmont, while an isolated flash flood event occurred in Caldwell County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple sources reported flash flooding developed along Buffalo Creek after 2.5 to 4 inches of rain fell in the area where Caldwell, Watauga, and Wilkes Counties come together. Water from the creek inundated a portion of Stone Mountain Rd. The bridge at Camp Carrolwood Rd was reportedly overtopped, while several culverts were washed out along lower portions of Buffalo Cove Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 13th, a strong cold front moved across the Intermountain West. A tight surface pressure gradient along and behind of this front resulted in strong northwesterly winds across southwest and south central Idaho.

A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was uprooted onto a fence on Hersperger Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms moved east through northern West Virginia on the periphery of an MCS diving through Kentucky in the early morning hours. Despite the unfavorable timing, weak MLCAPE values of 250-500 J/kg was enough when coupled with strong effective shear values of 50-70 knots beneath a seasonably very strong 90-100 knot mid-level jet to support sporadic wind damage in northern West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees reported down along Route 219.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported 4.5 inch hail on 171 between Cresson and Godley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed multiple trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snowfall across the county ranged from 16-20 inches, and locally as high as 2 feet. Some sleet and freezing rain occurred during this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Continued dryness in May, led to deterioration of drought conditions for much of western and north central Nebraska. There was one pocket of drought improvement across far southwestern Nebraska. By the end of May, 87 percent of western and north central Nebraska was in extreme (D3) or exceptional (D4) drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across the southern 2/3rds of Sheridan County through the end of May. Over the remainder of the county, severe (D2) drought conditions  deteriorated to extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of May. The cooperative observer at Gordon 6N reported 2.32 inches of precipitation for May. This was 0.92 inches below the normal of 3.24 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions alleviated thanks to an abundance of rainfall, ending their formal inclusion as of the 5/26/2026 Drought Monitor issuance for most counties in Northern AL. At this time, only the following counties remain in D2 through the end of May: portions of Jackson, Dekalb, Colbert, and Franklin County, AL. All other counties were downgraded to Moderate Drought (D1) conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) Conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Richland County Emergency Management reported trees fell on a residence along Adger Rd in Columbia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An ice storm crippled areas from northern Mississippi through middle Tennessee, clipping far northwest Alabama from the 24th through the 27th. Freezing rain accumulated up to 1 inch in far northwest Alabama, with accumulations dropping off quickly going further east and southeast in north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. The initial onset of precipitation was a mixture of snow, sleet and freezing rain, changing to all freezing rain in far northwest Alabama. A surge of warm air on the 26th changed precipitation to moderate to heavy rain for much of north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee, as temperatures warmed well above freezing. The exception was the far northwest tip of Alabama which remained in the colder air. A reinforcing cold front eventually brought temperatures back below freezing quickly during the late afternoon and early evening hours of the 25th which ended the steady rainfall. However, areas of light freezing drizzle redeveloped and produced a light accumulation of glaze across much of the area, and existing water on roadways from earlier heavy rain also began to freeze. The freezing drizzle changed to light snow and flurries during the overnight, lasting into the morning hours of the 26th. Very light accumulations were reported, with a dusting up to one half inch. Sunshine melted  the snow quickly during the day.||Impacts from these events were most severe in far northwest Alabama, including devestating tree damage, including numerous trees and limbs being knocked down, split or toppled onto power lines. Power outages occurred in northwest Alabama, including the Quad Cities/Shoals metro area. A water treatment facility in parts of western Lauderdale County was damaged, and a boil order was declared for about 1500 residents affected. Schools and businesses were shut down for multiple days in northwest Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. In north central and northeast Alabama, impacts were much less severe, and schools and businesses were shut down on the 26th due to cold and icy spots on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Areas of freezing drizzle moved in during the late afternoon and evening of the 25th. This precipitation changed to light snow and flurries during the overnight hours and ended during the late morning of the 26th. An additional light glaze of ice and fluffy snow accumulation under 0.5 inch was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to form along a stationary boundary stationed near the Interstate 80 corridor in an environment with ample instability and shear. Steep low-to-mid level lapse rates allowed for severe thunderstorms to begin forming hail with multiple reports of quarter-sized hail in portions of Clearfield and Centre counties during the evening hours of March 22, 2026. Within severe thunderstorms, some instances of wind damage across Clearfield, Centre, and Clinton counties as thunderstorms continues to form along the aforementioned stationary boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked multiple trees down across Drane Highway approximately 4 miles northwest of Osceola Mills.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above average precipitation the 2nd half of the month, especially over Cheyenne, Rawlins, Sherman, and Thomas counties supported improved drought conditions from west to east by mid to late month, especially over the aforementioned counties. D3 Extreme Drought over central and northern portions of Cheyenne, Rawlins, Decatur, and Norton counties was gradually replaced with mostly D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought.  However an area of D0 Abnormally Dry Drought was introduced over southwest Cheyenne and central to western Sherman counties by late month. Elsewhere, a mix of D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought persisted. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from one and one-half inches over eastern and southern counties, to nearly seven inches over west-northwest counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over far west-northwest counties near the Colorado border, to over three and one-half inches over far eastern counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one and one-half inches over eastern portions of the county (one and one-half inches below average), to nearly four inches over far western portions of the county (about one inch above average). Normal monthly precipitation amounts are around three and one-quarter inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and storms developed ahead of a slow moving cold front on the evening of April 1, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large trees and power lines were blown down around Clayton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms occurred across the Texas Panhandle from during the late afternoon through late evening hours on May 22nd through May 24th. On the 22nd the environment was such that a few isolated storms were able to produce hail between one inch and 2.75 inches across parts of the southern Texas Panhandle. On the 23rd, thunderstorms produced straight line winds in excess of 58 mph across the central to northern Texas Panhandle. Additional severe wind gusts also occurred on the 24th. Several landspouts also occurred during this time period. An additional landspout also occurred on May 26th in the southwest Texas Panhandle.

A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

A line of strong thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 7, 2026. This line was non-severe as it moved through the area, but did produce wind gusts up to 50 mph which caused minor sporadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds caused tree branches to fall and resulted in a small shed losing its roof near Alridge Circle south of Lobelville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Slow moving thunderstorms resulted in 2-3 inches of rain over portions of eastern Allegheny County, PA in the afternoon on the 28th. Flash flooding lead to road closures along Thompson Run Road, Rodi Road and Route 48.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State official reported a car stuck in floodwaters along Thompson Run Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D3-D4 drought conditions prevailed to start the month of May across southeast Alabama. However, beneficial rain during the month reduced the drought to D2 by the end of the month.

The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-35 Corridor, Coastal Plains, and southern Rio Grande Plains received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to improvement in drought conditions. Fayette County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) drought. Medina County went from Severe (D2) Drought to no drought. Maverick and Zavala Counties went from D2 to Abnormally Dry (D0). Atascosa, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties went from D2 to D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds uprooted multiple trees in Creve Coeur.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 90 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and outbuilding damage occurred to a couple of farmsteads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over the course of the weekend, a meandering front and an unseasonably strong upper trough triggered widespread showers and thunderstorms across the region. Heavy rain from training storms ultimately resulted in flash flooding, particularly affecting several Central Texas counties. A significant flood event occurred in and around Waco costing millions of dollars.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported that multiple people were stranded near the intersection of 60th and Sanger in Waco. During this event, Waco reported 73 vehicles involved in water incidents and at least 6 structures flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a ruler-measured hailstone was shared on social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions continued during the month of March as below-normal rainfall was observed through the first three months of the year. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across southeastern Central Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lowndes County began March with the southern half in Severe (D2) drought. D2 conditions were removed for a week but added back during the second week. D2 was expanded to include more of the county toward the end of the month, with Extreme (D3) conditions introduced across the southern quarter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas received less than 50% of normal precipitation during the month, and most counties stayed in the same drought category. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the heavy snow did move into southern New Hampshire. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed in areas along and near the Blue Ridge escarpment during the late evening of the 24th, beginning mainly as sleet. The sleet, occasionally mixed with snow continued into the early morning of the 25th, when it began to mix with and eventually change to freezing rain. The freezing rain was mostly light until a band of heavy freezing rain moved over the area late in the afternoon. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with around 0.5 inch (locally as high as 0.75 inch) ice accretion on top of the sleet, resulting in very hazardous driving conditions. Unusually cold temperatures following the event resulted in travel difficulties that lingered for several days.

Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 14th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Furthermore, dry lightning initiated a wildfire just west of Matador. This wildfire was named the Crooked Cook Fire and burned approximately 1388 acres before being contained on the 15th. No known damage occurred from this wildfire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gust measured by anemometer.

Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active weather day transpired on May 19th in southeast Ohio as a quick succession of storms passed through the area. The first round was observed during the late afternoon, when scattered thunderstorm development that moved in a southwest to northeast fashion. This clipped portions of Jackson County and resulted in several downed trees and power lines around the area. A few hours later, a line of thunderstorms slowly progressing through the Ohio Valley arrived into Perry and Morgan Counties around sunset. Decaying storms due to the loss of daytime heating caused downburst winds that promoted hundreds of homes to be without power due to downed trees and power lines. The weakening trend prospered into the late evening hours, bringing the severe threat over southeast Ohio to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the community of Ringgold, over 500 homes were without power in response to tree and power line damage.

During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of thunderstorm wind damage including multiple large trees down. Wind gusts were estimated at 60-70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down wires on Academy St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered several homes and buildings in Detroit. Report from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a period of above normal temperatures through the first half of January, a series of cold fronts brought a significant pattern change and much colder conditions for the latter part of the month.  An Arctic cold front that pushed through central Illinois during the evening of January 22nd dropped temperatures below zero by the morning of January 23rd.  Due to the falling temperatures and brisk northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph, wind chill values plummeted into the -25 to -35 degree range along and north of a Macomb to Bloomington line.  Despite the dangerously cold temperatures, no cold-related injuries or deaths were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bitterly cold wind-chill values of -25 to -35 occurred across Knox County during the morning of January 23rd. The coldest hourly wind-chill reading observed at the Galesburg Airport (KGBG) was -35.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of North Carolina Highway 54 West and  Hatch Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto US-6 near Ludlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first microburst occurred over the open water of  Lake Winnipesaukee shortly after 4:00 PM on June 18th. Based on damage reports this likely occurred in the vicinity of Round and Welch Islands in Gilford, New Hampshire. There were pictures of trees snapped on Round Island and reported damage on parts of Welch Island. The microburst continued unimpeded by friction towards Sandy and Cow Islands in Tuftonboro, New Hampshire. There were at least three camps damaged by tree falls on Sandy Island. On the southwest side of Cow Island there was significant tree damage. At least three additional camps were damaged by falling trees, as well as at least two docks that sustained damage. An estimated 1,500 trees, mostly softwood, were either snapped or uprooted by the winds. The open water and lack of friction likely allowed this microburst to expand beyond on the accepted definition of areal extent.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe thunderstorms tracked across portions of central and northeast South Dakota during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 3, generating high winds, large hail, and heavy rainfall.  ||One cluster tracked along the North Dakota border, where a personal weather station in Frederick recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph. These high winds destroyed the football field scoreboard and a storage shed in Frederick, knocked down trees and a radio tower, downed power lines in Hecla, and snapped power poles and flipped an irrigation pivot six miles north of Britton. The city of Britton lost electrical power. Three additional weather stations in Marshall County clocked wind gusts in excess of 60 mph. ||A second storm cluster moved out of eastern South Dakota into the southern Glacial Lakes region. Quarter-sized hail occurred at several locations. Heavy rainfall topping out at 4.40 inches in Clear Lake resulted in water six inches deep running over roads and caused a creek near the golf course to overflow its banks. Across central South Dakota, storms produced hail ranging from penny to golf ball size south of Interstate 90.
Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hart County received significant ice accumulation of 0.25 to 0.50 inches, in addition to 3 to 4 inches of snow and sleet. The wintry precipitation caused very slick and hazardous travel conditions on Interstate 65. A large truck pulling a trailer slid into and through a guardrail and went over an embankment. This crash resulted in one injury. A large SUV also slid 40 feet off Interstate 65 North, resulting in the closure of the far right lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust observation from personal weather  station, relayed through broadcast media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western Oklahoma on the evening and night of the 25th. An initial supercell thunderstorm (previously tornadic across Beaver County, Oklahoma) moved into northwestern Oklahoma and produced hail and severe winds. Additional thunderstorm activity moved eastward off of a dryline across the eastern Texas Panhandle, producing occasional reports of large hail and damaging winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rare June high wind events occurred in the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming during the second week of June. This was the first event which produced gusts as high as 67 MPH along Interstate 80.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four WYDOT sites reported wind gusts over 58 MPH for multiple hours. Peak gust of 67 MPH observed at Halleck Ridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed trees on wires in Strafford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions continued through the end of February as the region saw a lack of moisture and precipitation. Dry fuels, sustained winds of 20-30mph and gusts up to 40mph, along with relative humidity in the single digits contributed to an environment supportive of wildfire development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Willard Fire ignited on February 24, 2026, in Dallam County.  The fire occurred near Willard Lane and Farm to Market Road 807. This is located about ten miles southwest of Stratford. This fire burned 540 acres. The cause of the fire is unknown as the origin of it was destroyed according to fire department reports. It did threaten one home and one structure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A creek overflowing and some yard and basement flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall reports from the public, trained spotters, and CoCoRaHs data showed between ten and sixteen inches of snowfall fell across Lenoir County between the morning of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.

A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hardwood tree trunks snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The MARSH mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Hempstead and Nevada Counties in Southwest Arkansas by late March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) drought expanded across more of Southwest Arkansas by the end of the month.

Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.

Strong zonal flow aloft combined with cold frontal passage, a strong pressure gradient, and ridgetop stability combined to result in an extended stretch of strong winds across the region February 26th into the 27th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A short lived tornado touched down near the intersection of Madison Road and Ebenezer Road where tree damage was observed. The tornado continued northeast where it snapped trees and destroyed an outbuilding at Ruby Lane. The tornado lifted just east of Ebenezer road. Max winds were 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado uprooted trees as it moved along Rough River Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred from southwestern Mississippi northeast through the Delta region into North Mississippi. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Sharkey and Issaquena counties and southern Washington County, through Humphreys, Holmes, and northwestern Yazoo counties, through Leflore, Carroll, and Grenada counties. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 189,000 customers in Mississippi lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in Attala, Bolivar, Carroll Grenada, Holmes, Humphreys, Issaquena, Leflore, Madison, Montgomery, Sharkey, Sunflower, Warren, Washington, Webster and Yazoo counties. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 to 3 inches occurred in parts of northwest Mississippi. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. Additional injuries were reported in Grenada, Hinds, Sharkey, Smith, Warren, and Washington counties. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the county fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas from the evening of the 14th into early morning hours of the 15th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of East Texas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.

An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and moist trough pushed inland during the middle portion of February, leading to several days of impactful weather. On 2/18/26 in particular, the combination of precipitating snow and winds with blowing snow resulted in periods of very limited visibility and roadway hazards.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wyoming Highway Patrol in addition to other law enforcement and first responders reported that a multi-vehicle accident occurred on I-80 near Evanston at mile marker 18 at approximately 3:00 PM 2/18/26. The crashes are said to have happened more or less simultaneously, involving 32 vehicles (20 semi trucks, 12 passenger vehicles), which blocked and closed both the westbound and eastbound lanes. The interstate was closed from mile marker 6 to mile marker 34, lasting from roughly 3:28 PM  until 4:00 AM the following morning. As a result of the collisions, 2 fatalities were confirmed, as were 22 injuries, 3 of which required helicopter transportation to Utah emergency facilities. Additionally, a tractor trailer carrying livestock suffered severe enough impact to kill 6 of the cattle inside. Around the time of the pileup a nearby mesonet sensor was observing conditions including gusts in excess of 30 mph and visibility around one quarter of a mile, likely due to blowing snow. Wyoming Highway Patrol suspects excessive speed for the ongoing poor winter weather conditions to be a likely cause.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.

Antecedent arctic air mass on the 29th, combined with radiational cooling and a light wind going into the morning of the 30th, led another chilly night, with some sites dropping into the -20 to -30F range for apparent temperatures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong atmospheric river and associated jet streak moved over the Northern Rockies, with mid-level winds peaking between 50 and 60 knots.  Strong, gusty winds caused widespread power outages.
