On top of Mount Sentinel at 5,000 feet MSL, wind gusts reached 62 mph at 1345MST. A flipped trailer was reported south of Florence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of May, D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Issaquena County to Forrest County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Clay County decreased in intensity from D2 (Severe Drought) to D1 (Moderate Drought).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms moved northeast across portions of east-central and northeast Colorado during the mid to late afternoon hours on the 29th, in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline and ahead of a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest. The highest wind gust was 66 mph in Kit Carson County, and the largest hailstone was slightly larger than quarter size in Cheyenne County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Kit Carson County Airport. Gusts ranged from 63 to 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity resulted in an unsettled weather pattern across the Ohio Valley for the start of June. Each day yielded developing showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest and travelling eastward along the front before dissipating after sunset. On June 6th, storms remained strong to severe as it dashed across Ohio, and caused scattered tree and power line damage across Perry County from the damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the community of Bristol, a tree blew down onto Township Road 128.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed and blocked Gilcrease Road near Stinson Road east of Montgomery.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm impacted the region from the 3rd to the 5th of January. This produced between 1 to 2 feet of snow in the Tahoe Basin with 2 to 4 feet for the higher elevations. This system also produced winds upwards of 90 mph on the ridges, with gusts commonly upwards of 55 mph elsewhere.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 40.4 inches of snowfall and CO-OP observer at Tahoe City measured 11.5 inches of snow. This was from the 3rd to the 5th. In addition,|Northstar Ski Base reported 29 inches, Palisades Tahoe Ski Base reported 17 inches, and CoCoRaHs station CA-NV-51 Truckee 1.6 N reported 18.3 inches. These were storm totals for the event from the 3rd to 5th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum windchill of -2F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Artic air behind a cold front ushered in dangerously cold wind chills of -15 to -25F for Extreme Cold areas and -10 to -18F for the Cold Weather areas. Winds gusted up to 35 mph at times.

A band of steady light to moderate snow overspread western Maryland during the early afternoon of January 21. This continued steadily through the evening before tapering to light snow showers and freezing drizzle. Total snowfall accumulations of two to five inches were observed along with a few hundredths of an inch of ice. The highest snowfall reports were across western and northern Garrett County.

A Clipper system moved across NY and New England during the evening and overnight hours of February 10-11th to into the Gulf of Maine by the morning of February 11th.||Light to moderate snow spread across VT during the late afternoon and evening hours causing some hazardous travel for evening commute. The steadiest snow exited the region around midnight but more scattered orographic enhancement snow redeveloped around daybreak of the 11th and continued during the day and evening with travel issues the morning and evening commutes in some locations as well. ||Snowfall totals across the region were generally 3 to 5 inches with slightly lower amounts in the Champlain Valley of Addison and Rutland counties with some locally higher amounts in orographic favored higher terrain in central and northern VT with the first round of snow. Additional snowfall during the day and evening hours of February 11th led to an additional 3 to 6 inches along some communities along the western slopes of the Green Mountains. Two-day snowfall totals were generally 3 to 6 inches with locally 8 to 12 inches along western foothills of the central and northern Green Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across the region were 4 to 9 inches with localized amounts in excess of 10 inches along the western slopes of the Green Mountains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across the South Carolina  Piedmont and foothills continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.

A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two power poles were broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blew down blocking MD-355 Frederick Road near Prescott Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed through eastern Utah and western Colorado in the days prior to these high winds, turning the upper level frow from zonal to northwesterly. The cooler air moving in behind the front limited mixing for lower elevation locations, but high peaks continued to tap into the 50-70 knot 500 hPa jet. These winds mixed down in the days following the cold front passage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 2:35 PM MDT, the KMYP AWOS located on Monarch Pass, CO recorded a wind gust to 79 mph. The only other gust recorded in the region was at the Carbonate Hill mesonet site, where a gust to 56 mph was recorded at 1:00 PM MDT. The KMYP AWOS is the highest elevation wind sensor in the zone. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Morgan County remained in D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout the month of February. Following the initial onset of D2 on January 27, the county sustained five consecutive weeks of D2 conditions as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power line were blown down near Dean Road and Highway 109.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limbs were broken and utility poles were leaning. The wall and roof of an old barn were damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The breakdown of an upper-level ridge brought increased wind speeds aloft. These winds mixed to the surface along the Rocky Mountain Front on the morning of the 16th, spreading out to mainly the North-Central plains by the afternoon. The peak winds occurred on the morning of the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTM76 Cascade E Mda measured a 66 mph wind gust.  ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport also measured a high wind gust and an averaged sustain wind of 42 mph between 9:00pm to 10:00pm MST on the 17th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure moved through the eastern U.S. bringing a plume of deep moisture over top of an arctic airmass which brough 1-2 feet of snow to southern New England Sunday through Tuesday morning. The biggest total was 27 inches in Gloucester, MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 14 to 19 inches of snow fell with the heaviest being 19.1 inches in Columbia and 10 inches in Tolland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A cluster of rapidly weakening showers produced high winds in central South Dakota. A peak wind gust of 65 mph was recorded on the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet (SDDOT) station 3 miles southeast of Reliance in Lyman county, with a 62 mph gust measured at the SDDOT station 2 miles west of Oacoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles north of Reliance recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph that originated out of elevated showers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe weather impacted lower Michigan on March 6th. 1 tornado occurred in the Grand Rapids County Warning Area while 3 occurred in the Northern Indiana County Warning Area.

Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS survey team confirmed a short, narrow path of tree damage consistent with an EF0 tornado between Spokane and Highlandville in Christian County. Additionally, Sentinel 2 satellite data analysis revealed tree damage at the start of the track near Camp Creek, southwest of Stoneshire Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 1.72 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.68 inches below normal, marking the 5th driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 92% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). It was the driest June through February stretch on record, approximately 11 inches below normal for that 9 month period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms moved across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois and produced 50+ mph winds, causing some areas of damage to trees, roofs, and a few outbuildings.  The line of very gradually fading storms produced surges of straight-line wind damage. These were most pronounced to the immediate south of mesovortices (small scale circulations within the thunderstorm line that can in themselves result in tornadoes). Based on the nature of damage, observations, and radar, these reflect 65-80 mph wind gusts.||Two main areas of damage that experienced enhanced wind surges were:  1.) Kalona, IA (Washington Co)  and 2.) the east-southeast side of Iowa City (Johnson County).||A third area of isolated wind damage from Miles to Sabula, IA (Jackson County) was a little different in that it was much more of an outflow surging from decaying storms, but again straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Door blown off a small outbuilding, and a window blown out of a barn. A tree blown down nearby. The time was estimated using radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 10th, a discrete supercell moved from Illinois into northwest Indiana. It produced an EF-2 tornado in Starke County with maximum winds of 115 mph, prompting a rare Tornado Emergency for the area near Knox, IN. Following the initial supercell, a line of storms moved through on the morning of March 11th. Training storms produced significant rainfall between 1 and 3, with localized amounts reaching 4-5, resulting in Flash Flood Warnings and Flood Advisories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video obtained from storm chasers claiming to be on the south-|southeast side of the parent mesocyclone clearly show two|distinct tornadoes occurring at the same time. One larger circulation|with numerous power flashes, with a smaller 2nd circulation off to |the southwest. Based on the unusual damage path that the NWS damage |assessment uncovered, this aligns with the idea that a small, |short-lived circulation formed on the southern periphery of the |large wedge tornado, producing brief EF-0 damage before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am  on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures ranged from 28 to 32 across much of Pembina County. The lowest value of 28 was reported at the Cavalier, ND Airport AWOS at 5:15 AM CST and the Walhalla, ND Airport AWOS at 3:35 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact short-wave within northwest flow aloft moved across the Northern Plains late February 27 into February 28. Mid-level frontogenesis and sufficient moisture resulted in a narrow band of light to moderate snow mainly along and north of a De Smet, SD to Windom, MN line. These areas received 1-4 inches of snow, with a few locations exceeding 5 inches. Winds were light during the snowfall, limiting blowing and drifting.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 3.0 inches in Windom.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at the intersection of Perch Road and Grassy Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms produced strong and gusty winds in far northwest Alabama during the early to mid afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down and blocking both lanes fo the roadway at 11884 CR 14.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: South Perimeter Road and entrance to Veterans Cemetery covered by unknown amount  of water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Unknown tree damage and power outages reported on the back side of the line of storms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems affect portions of northern Nevada the first half of the week, bringing in high winds and much needed snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station (CMP26) Warm Springs Summit, Elevation 7550 ft.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between large air masses funneled strong and severe winds through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few observations in Garfield County recorded wind gusts in excess of 62 mph, the strongest of which was 69 mph, measured at the South Sawmill Creek RAWS site (SSMM8).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree in a backyard near Lakeland and Donelson Pike in Hermitage. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down and knocked over along and in the vicinity of Brookside Court  between Strong Avenue and Great Neck Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across southwest Indiana, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. A lull in the dangerous wind chills occurred on the 25th when a major winter storm was ongoing.

A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The US-89 at USU mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blocking lanes across Brannon Stand Road and State Highway 52.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northeast Illinois during the late evening of March 30th producing large hail.

A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of River Siloam Road and Romie Snow Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sporadic trees were reported down across the county, with the highest concentration in and around Adrian.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The CWOP observer in Sanders measured a 48 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 3, 2026, central Indiana experienced a wave of isolated severe weather fueled by record-breaking warmth and high humidity. The most significant severe report occurred in Hendricks County, where intense storms dropped 1 inch hail that was thick enough to completely cover road surfaces in areas like Avon. While the storms were scattered, they packed enough punch to create hazardous driving conditions and frequent cloud-to-ground lightning across the Interstate 74 corridor.||In addition to the hail, heavy rainfall led to localized flash flooding that caused significant disruptions in the southern suburbs. Near New Whiteland, rapid water accumulation forced the closure of several roads and led to a dangerous situation where a vehicle became stranded in floodwaters. This evening of activity was a precursor to a larger regional flooding event, as the 2 to 4 inches of rain saturated the ground and caused several local rivers to rise rapidly toward flood stage over the following 24 hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large volume of hail which covered the roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through eastern Pennsylvania. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and wires down in East Malvern. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail estimated at 1.75 inches in diameter with all windows broken on the west side of a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow overspread the Midcoast by the afternoon on the 25th. Within an hour or two snow was moderate to heavy at times as an intense band of lift moved into the region. Snowfall rates were one to two inches per hour during the heavy snow. Snow continued overnight into the 26th, with occasional breaks or lighter snowfall before the storm center moved into the Atlantic. Snowfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of East Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree downed at the corner of Baylor Drive and Karen Drive in Tyler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the second time in a week, a winter storm impacted the mountains and foothills of North Carolina as an area of low pressure intensified across the Deep South. In this case, all precipitation fell as snow. Snow began falling during the late evening of the 30th and continued off and on for around 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the morning of the 31st. By the time the snow tapered off, 5 to 8 inch totals along with locally higher amounts were reported across the area.

Unseasonably mild air moved into the region ahead of a strong low pressure system. These conditions, on top of a fairly dry February across western South Dakota allowed a fire to develop northeast of the community of Green Grass and spread rapidly southeast. 991 acres of mostly prairie and pasture were burned in the fire, with a portion of Highway 63 closed due to smoke and the threat of the fire crossing the Highway. ||Winds picked up dramatically with the passage of the low pressure system, with a peak wind gust of 81 mph recorded at the Pierre Regional Airport ASOS. The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) station 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind gust of 77 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 6 miles southwest of Joe Creek Rec Area and 9 miles north northwest of Vivian both recorded peak winds of 71 mph. 6 additional weather stations would go on to observe a peak wind gust in excess of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid-level jet moved into the Rocky Mountain Front. This combined with a strong surface pressure gradient and mountain wave activity brought isolated strong winds to the Rocky Mountain Front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mt Lebanon SE Montana Mesonet site averaged a sustained wind of 41 mph from 4:10 PM until 5:35 PM MST. This site also measured a 65 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a two foot diameter pine tree fell near the intersection of Highway 119 and Reedsville Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough, slow moving cold front, and continued presence of a dryline resulted in additional severe thunderstorm development on April 28 and 29. Large hail was the primary severe weather occurrence. Destructive hail damaged several locations in North and Central Texas with hail sizes ranging up to 3.5-4 inch hail in Johnson County. On April 28th 4 tornadoes occurred including an EF-3 tornado in Mineral Wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported golf ball size hail at 460 Hwy 75 North.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in far eastern Whiteside County just north of Fulfs Road and just west of the Whiteside-Lee county line, where satellite imagery showed the beginning of a narrow southwest-northeast path of disturbed soil through farm fields. Drone footage taken along Mound Hill Road in Lee County revealed swirl marks in the field to the west that aligned with the path that was evident in the satellite imagery, confirming that the tornado remained on the ground continuously as it tracked into Lee County. The tornado crossed Mound Hill Road, downing a number of power poles and impacting a property on the east side of the road. The tornado reached its peak intensity here, destroying multiple outbuildings and snapping several trees at this property. The tornado left additional swirl marks in a field to the northeast of the property before causing damage to trees, a residence, and a metal outbuilding along and just south of Lenox Road. As the tornado reached Timber Creek Road, it caused damage to a barn, at least one power pole, and several trees. On the north side of the road, the tornado pushed an old barn off of its foundation into a grain leg, causing the grain leg to collapse. A concrete silo was also toppled at the same location. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing tree and roof damage at a property along Peek Home Road, then damaging an outbuilding, a house, and more trees at a property at Penrose Road and Swarts Road. The tornado produced its last instance of damage at the Hey Tree Service facility along U.S. Route 52/State Route 26 southeast of Woosung before dissipating prior to reaching the Ogle County line. Straight-line wind damage was also observed to the south and east of the tornado's track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving shortwave upper level trough followed by a shortwave ridge tracking near the International Border produced a strong surface pressure gradient on the 7th and accompanying strong winds across North-Central MT.  Heading into the 8th, the upper level ridge broke down. This day brought a longer duration of strong sustained winds and widespread strong wind gusts over North-Central MT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous weather stations in this zone hit high wind gusts with a few stations hitting high sustained winds over a span of 4 to 6 hours. The highest wind gust was reported at Mesonet station MTCHK Chinook (DOT) of 70 mph, they also averaged a sustained wind of 45 mph between 1pm to 2pm MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust to 58 mph was measured at the Rockford Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm winds onto a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with a gusts to around 60 mph occurred across west central, southwest, and central Nebraska during the early morning hours until the early afternoon hours on March 15th. Peak wind gusts reached 60 mph or higher at the Imperial, Broken Bow and North Platte ASOS stations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts to around 50 mph or higher were common across Frontier County during the morning hours into the mid afternoon hours. The nearby McCook ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph 907 am CST. The nearby North Platte ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 1107 am CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through northwest Connecticut, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Warming temperatures led to a mix of both rain and snow during this event with some short-duration sleet and freezing rain. ||The highest accumulations of snow fell across northern portions of Litchfield County where 0.5 to about 2 inches were reported. For the southern portion of the county, generally a trace to 0.5 were common. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into South-Central Texas and stalled. The airmass the front moved into was warm and very moist. Thunderstorms formed in the vicinity of the front and some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. FM 1021 was closed due to flooding north of El Indio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front draped across the southern tier of Pennsylvania began to shift further south and east during the afternoon and evening hours of May 20, 2026. This served as a lifting mechanism in an unstable airmass with 1500 to 2000 J/kg of CAPE across the Lower Susquehanna Valley and favorable bulk shear. Showers and storms began to form and upscale growth allowed for strong-to-severe storms to continue into south-central and southeastern Pennsylvania with tree damage being the main hazard observed within these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down at the intersection of Charlestown Road and PA 741 north of Millersville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Northwest Florida started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 59 mph in the Township of Brigham. Frequent wind gusts in the 50 mph range across the county. Many branches down and some power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF1 tornado touched down on the east bank of the MS River snapping and uprooting trees and breaking power poles near Jefferson Highway and Airline Highway.  Empty rail cars were also derailed just to the south of Airline Highway. This tornado exited Jefferson Parish Parish, entering Orleans Parish near the intersection of Bamboo Road and Palmetto Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video showed a two foot diameter tree uprooted with the entire root ball destroying nearby pavement. The tree fell on a garage which was destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley region, bringing rounds of heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water reached the front doors of homes along Runkle Road and at the intersection of Church Road and State Route 560. Additionally, water was reported in basements in St. Paris.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large trees were uprooted two miles northwest of Kerrick on the west side of Highway 287.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In central Kansas, a lack of precipitation led to severe drought conditions (D2) in all or portions of six counties in central and south central Kansas. This started in the last 10 days of the month. The first 20 days of the month had around 0.1 to 0.25 of an inch for much of the included areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate drought (D1) for earlier in the month worsened to severe drought (D2) for all but a tiny portion of the northeast corner of the county on the 21st. Only around 0.25 of an inch had fallen in that time period. There were showers and storms that moved in and brought 1.25 to 1.75 inches based on cooperative observer and CoCoRaHS reports. This led to improvement over northern portions of the county with a southern swatch from middle of the county in the west to the bottom quarter in the east.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (105) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of strong storms moved across the western coastal waters with measured gusts of 34 knots or greater.

An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system and arctic blast brought strong winds and pockets of light to moderate snow showers.  ||A peak wind gust of 71 mph was observed 1 mile north northwest of Lees Corner in Buffalo County by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Information Weather System (RWIS), and by a personal weather station 2 miles north of the Pierre Regional Airport. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded by the SDDOT RWIS station 1 mile northeast of Stephan in Hyde county, while 66 mph wind gusts were measured by the SDDOT RWIS stations 5 miles south southwest of Klein Ranch in Corson county and 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake in Dewey county.  A total of 39 weather stations recorded a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. These high winds flipped a semi and damaged a grain elevator near the town of Murdo on the morning of the 16th. ||While snow accumulations were limited, snow showers of moderate intensity combined with these strong winds to produce temporary white-out conditions. No Travel Advised was issued by both the Walworth and Day county Sheriffs. Various SDDOT RWIS webcams showed visibility in blowing snow fluctuating significantly over short distances in the matter of a few minutes. An emergency vehicle rendering assistance for an accident on Interstate 29 near Watertown was struck with minor injuries. A separate accident along Interstate 90 resulted in a 5 vehicle chain reaction crash which resulted in 2 fatalities and a number of injuries.  ||80 residents of Deuel county reported power out during the event.

A strong section of the jetstream between two upper level systems brought a brief period of high wind gusts to a portion of central NM January 8th. Peak gusts of 58 mph to 65 mph were measured by the New Mexico Ziamet station southeast of Vaughn, NM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum winds chill of 7F recorded.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado tracked across parts of St. Charles and Jefferson Parishes, affecting the community of Avondale, LA. This tornado began over the Salvador Wildlife Management Area as evidenced by a well-defined 15-20 yard wide path of damage to marsh vegetation oriented southwest to northeast that was collocated with an intensifying area of rotation on both TMSY and KHDC. This damage path gradually broadened and fluctuated in intensity causing minor damage to trees as it traveled over uninhabited and inaccessible marsh areas. The tornado damage path evidently became larger and more noticeable again near Bayou Verret. A clear path of tree damage was evident on high resolution satellite imagery spanning to approximately 300 yards wide with numerous trees damaged or displaced as the tornado exited St Charles Parish and crossed into Jefferson Parish 1.35 miles south of Highway 90 along Bayou Verret.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on wires down on Oxford Road, Oneill Road and Coppermine Road in Oxford  CT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong atmospheric river and associated jet streak moved over the Northern Rockies, with mid-level winds peaking between 50 and 60 knots.  Strong, gusty winds caused widespread power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 160 people in the Lakeside to Angel Point area of Flathead Lake were without power. A tree was reported in the power line at Angel Point.

On Oahu, the heavy rain developed and remained persistent for several hours, which led to flooding and flash flooding over the eastern and northern portions of the island. Particularly the Koolau Mountain Range was impacted. Portions of Maui and Kauai also experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A River/Creek reportedly overflowed and flooded cropland, a yard, and a basement.

As the storms progressed east of the Denver their intensity increase. A supercell thunderstorm continued to track eastward, stay south of I-70. Farther north, thunderstorms organized into a broken line, producing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph across far northeast Colorado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level system drove strong cold front eastward across the region, including adjacent coastal waters. Ahead of the boundary, a robust low-level jet brough in warm, buoyant, and very moist air northward from the Gulf. Night timing of the line of storms that developed along the front did limit low level instability, however, elevated instability and frontal lift were more than enough to overcome the lack of surface heating. Several locations across coastal waters observed severe convective wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weatherflow mesonet at Mid point of the Causeway measured a wind gust of 40 mph or 34 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic trough pushed through Southcentral Alaska on February 24. A 980 mb surface low formed over the northeastern Gulf of Alaska coast. A strong pressure gradient formed between the coastal low and high pressure over the Bering, which, combined with a strong temperature gradient over and through the mountains, triggered northerly gap winds across the region, including Thompson Pass and Kodiak Island. Thompson Pass saw strong winds, which combined with transportable snow, led to blizzard conditions that lasted through February 26. Kodiak Island saw a period of gusty winds on February 25.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Alaska Department of Transportation (AKDOT) reported on February 24 that winds were gusting up to 60 mph with zero visibility from Paxson Camp to Trims Camp. There was significant drifting of snow that completely obscured the road with the plow operator having to stop at times and make sure that he was still on the road. AKDOT closed Isabel Pass due to ground blizzard conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved along the US Highway 54 corridor during the late evening of March 10th. Damaging winds occurred along this line of storms with damage to trees and structures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small shed was blown over in the city of Versailles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second of two cold front passages resulted in convective snow shower development in the afternoon hours. Convergence along the boundary was strongest north of Pittsburgh coincident with where impactful snow squalls developed. Numerous reports from ASOS and Department of Highways sensors measured visibility of a quarter mile or less with quick accumulation on surfaces.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With the Drought Monitor issuance on May 12th, Extreme Drought (D3) Conditions were formally removed thanks to an abundance of rainfall across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought (D3) Conditions are finally removed thanks to an abundance of rainfall across the area on the May 12th Drought Monitor issuance.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-afternoon thunderstorms both in broken line segments and single cells developed along and ahead of a cold front. Marginal effective shear values up to 30 knots and MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg supported severe thunderstorms producing both wind and hail. Wind was primarily confined to northern West Virginia along a DCAPE gradient of 600-700 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates up to 6.5 C/km and up to 300 J/kg of hail growth zone CAPE supported numerous reports of quarter size within storms across western Pennsylvania.

A weak short wave trough moved overhead on the evening of the 21st within the larger cyclonic flow aloft. Most of region remained cool and stable with cloud cover persisting for much of the day. Areas across New Mexico saw clearing in the afternoon which allowed isolated thunderstorms to develop and drift into West Texas. One of these storms moved into western Cochran County producing penny size hail near Bledsoe.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree and power lines blocked Stone Lick Road outside of Belgrove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 7th record-setting early March warmth in the upper 70s and low 80s primed eastern Kentucky for isolated severe weather ahead of an advancing cold front. Strong wind shear and sufficient instability supported a convective line that tracked northwest to southeast across the region during the late afternoon and evening. The primary hazard was damaging straight-line winds, which caused localized utility damage and a power outage in the Jackson area. A sharp temperature drop followed the front, ending the anomalous warmth.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A retired NWS employee reported a tree blown down onto power lines about a mile up Lick Branch Road resulting in a power outage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle was stuck in water near the Blair Post Office.

As the system approached the local area, mid-level temperatures cooled, increasing atmospheric instability. These cooler temperatures aloft, combined with near-record surface temperatures in the mid 80s, supported robust thunderstorm development during the afternoon hours. One thunderstorm became severe and produced large hail across portions of East Feliciana Parish.

Continued culling of cattle herds, as well as delays in spring planting and impacts on early spring growth, was noted by farmers and ranchers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Jessamine County received 4 to 5 inches of snow and sleet, in addition to around 0.40 inches of ice accumulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tekamah ASOS measured wind gust of 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread showers and storms developed across south-central and southeast Kansas during the morning hours of June 18th. Strong thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of March 7th during a period of record warmth. These storms formed a broken line of loosely organized convection west of the area that afternoon ahead of a cold frontal passage. While some of the storms proved to be severe in Ohio, the threat waned quickly as they progressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia that evening. Strong wind gusts were still associated with storms as they swept through the state, which caused isolated tree damage in Wood, Ritchie, and Upshur Counties. Further deterioration of storms took place on the evening of the 7th due to the loss of daytime heating, bringing the severe threat to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong 1033 mb high pressure nosing ridging in from the west allowed for efficient radiational cooling and minimum wind chill values ranging from -5 to -15F and as cold as -22F at KDUJ.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill values generally ranged from -5 to -15 degrees across the county with the exception of the Dubois ASOS which recorded -22 degrees in the morning of the 20th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and several power lines were downed around Calera.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roadway flooding across both lanes at San Andreas Road and Seawind Road near Manresa State Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked trees and wires down near Fall Creek and College Ave, numerous other wires down throughout Ithaca area as per county dispatch feed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and development of extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of North Louisiana through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought developed/expanded across portions of Northwest and North Central Louisiana throughout the month.

Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on Highway Z near Trophy Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Picture of water flowing over the street and at least one truck inundated with water in Westchester subdivision.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Continued dry conditions in February, coupled with very warm temperatures, led to expansion of drought conditions across western and north central Nebraska in February. Locations in the western Sandhills, portions of southwestern Nebraska, the eastern Nebraska Panhandle and portions of north central Nebraska, saw drought conditions reaching severe (D2) and even extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions, deteriorated to severe (D2) drought conditions over the eastern third of Holt County by the end of February. Over the remainder of the county, moderate (D1) drought persisted through the end of the month. The cooperative observer at Atkinson 3SW reported 0.07 inches of precipitation for February. This was 0.63 inches below the normal of 0.70 inches. The cooperative observer at O'Neill reported a trace of precipitation for February. This was 0.67 inches below the normal of 0.67 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most of the hail was penny to quarter size, but some stones were as large as hen eggs.

Snow began falling during the late evening of the 30th and continued off and on for around 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the morning of the 31st. By the time the snow tapered off, 5 to 8 inch totals along with locally higher amounts were reported across the area.

Thunderstorms developed during the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
