EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Worsening drought conditions continued into early May across Central Alabama. Following a severe weather event on May 6-7 in which 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across southern counties of Central Alabama, conditions began to slowly improve. A pattern change came by mid-May as ridging retreated off the East Coast and a persistent troughing setup over the Central U.S. served to return moist southerly flow to Alabama. With it, rainfall increased drastically across the region, and drought conditions improved by late month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pike County remained in Extreme (D3) drought for most of May before improving to Severe (D2) by late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal precipitation amounts continued through much of January 2026. The largest deficits of 2 to 3 inches were found across northwest Middle Tennessee which saw severe drought conditions develop across portions of Stewart, Houston, and Montgomery counties. A major winter storm with substantial liquid precipitation brought slight improvement to Middle Tennessee during the end of the month. By the end of January, 30 percent of the area was in at least moderate drought conditions with 6 percent of this classified as severe drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions across eastern Cumberland County from December 2025 continued through January 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A one-foot diameter tree limb was snapped.

An upper level shortwave lifting north from the Ozarks into the Upper Midwest during the day, lead to widespread shower and thunderstorm activity across the forecast area, resulting in some flash flooding primarily in the Knoxville metro area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The two separate lines of severe thunderstorms began to congeal across eastern Lebanon County, with a line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocking down a tree onto Strack Drive northwest of Myerstown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were reported down on Wilgus Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front passed through Central Alabama on January 17-18. By the early morning of the 18th, rain associated with the front began to transition to snow southeast of Interstate 85. Some areas of Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties received 1-2 inches of snow by 9 AM. By mid-morning, cloud cover cleared, and the snow quickly melted. Impacts to roadways were minimal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure tracked across the central Great Lakes, into southern Ontario and then into southwest Quebec on December 29th. Moderate to heavy lake effect snow at times, combined with breezy conditions, prompted the issuance of Winter Storm Warnings for many counties in the Buffalo County Warning Area. Lake effect bands shifted north to south and south to north with passing troughs and cold fronts during the week, leaving a large footprint of significant snowfall. The third and final weather system in a series moved across the Four Corners and southern Rockies February 20th. A snow squall along the cold front resulted in a very brief period of quarter mile visibility at several locations across western New Mexico during the mid to late morning hours, including Farmington, Gallup, and Grants. This snow squall also resulted in a vehicle crash on U.S. Highway 550 just west of Cuba, NM. The snow squall along the cold front dissipated as it moved east into the Rio Grande Valley, resulting in some high wind gusts in the zone. Upslope flow resulted in light to moderate snow across the north central mountains with a localized area of heavy snow across Taos Ski Valley. Snow across the north central mountains tapered off midday February 20th. Additional high wind gusts were observed across eastern NM along and just behind the cold front during the early afternoon hours before winds tapered off around sunset.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow Squall resulted in visibility below a quarter of a mile and a vehicle crash on U.S 550 at mile marker 97 just west of Cuba. The crash led to the brief closure of the highway. The extent of any injuries is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of excessive heat impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa from June 28 into June 30, 2026. The heat was supported by a strong mid- to upper-level ridge building into the central Plains. A warm front lifted northward across the area early on June 28, with temperatures rapidly rising in its wake. Daily high temperatures peaked in the upper 90s to low 100s, while southerly low-level flow ushered in dewpoints in the 70s. As a result, daily maximum heat index values peaked in the 105 to 115-degree range. In addition, little overnight relief was observed, with heat index values remaining at or above 75 degrees for at least 48 consecutive hours throughout the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Citizen Weather Observer Program (CWOP) measured peak heat index of 113 degrees within the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations and very cold wind chill temperatures. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Analysis shows that widespread snow resulted in accumulations ranging from 2 to 3 inches across the Allendale County. The highest reported amounts were 2 inches around the Allendale area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In February 2026, New Hampshire���s drought conditions remained steady in their classification while experiencing ongoing hydrologic strain. By the end of the month, the state���s drought extent held firm with 41% categorized as Severe Drought (D2), 37% as Moderate Drought (D1), and 22% as Abnormally Dry (D0). Although seasonal snowpack remained near normal across much of the state, particularly on the slopes of the White Mountains, the water content was relatively low, and the snowpack peaked in late February, nearly three weeks earlier than usual. Deep soil frost depths between 6 and 20 inches created a cap that blocked melting snow and rain from recharging deep aquifers. Consequently, the majority of groundwater monitoring levels remained at or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grafton County averaged 0.81 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.96 inches below normal, marking the 4th driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 90% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 10% in Moderate Drought (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.

A tornado warning was issued on January 5 for the Pacific coast near the border between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties due to a radar indicated rotation signature. Around 3,400 customers in San Francisco lost power on the 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding was reported on both lanes of Empire Grade at the Santa Cruz Waldorf School.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across northwest Connecticut for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Feels-like temperatures this first night ranged from about -8 to 2 degrees Fahrenheit. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -9 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -20 to -8 degrees Fahrenheit. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of a funnel cloud 4 miles east of Swanton.

Northerly winds increasing to 4-7mph before dawn brought an end to fog conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Warren County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on December 2, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 9 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system brought a widespread light to moderate accumulation of snow to eastern New York on January 17, 2026. The highest snowfall totals occurred across portions of the eastern Catskills, mid-Hudson Valley, Taconics, Saratoga region and into the southern foothills of the Adirondacks with amounts of 3 to 6 inches common. This resulted in slippery travel conditions on area roadways.||Key impacts: travel delays.

With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: From spotter network, tree damage reported west of Felton between Sandtown Road and Burnite Mill Road. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reports 3.5 inch diameter hail east of Maple Bluff.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had resulted in Extreme Drought (D3) over north-central Indiana by late 2025 generally expanded and intensified throughout January 2026. While D2 and D3 levels were maintained from the previous month, a significant degradation occurred on the January 6th update, where D3 intensity expanded across the heart of the region. These drought conditions remained entrenched without improvement through the end of the month and continued into at least February 2026.||This status quo included a primary sub-region where D3 conditions expanded to cover the entirety of Howard County and much of Carroll and Delaware counties. Significant expansion of Severe Drought (D2) was also noted, moving to encompass the remainder of Clinton, Hamilton, and Vermillion counties. Meanwhile, D2 intensity was maintained across northern Henry County and northwestern Vigo County, with a small additional expansion into north-central Vigo. In the northeast, Tipton County saw an intensification as D3 pushed into its northern portions, while D3 remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County.||Precipitation throughout January for these areas was critically low, with many totals falling between 0.75 and 1.25 inches. Specifically, Carroll, Randolph, and Howard counties saw meager totals of 0.75 to 1.10 inches, which directly triggered the expansion of D3 intensity. Even in areas like Henry County, which received a slightly higher 1.50 to 2.25 inches, the moisture was not enough to warrant improvement. These sustained deficits, often totaling less than 50% of normal monthly rainfall, ensured that the drought not only persisted but worsened across the central Indiana landscape.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 0.90 to 1.10 inches across the month of January. This maintained D2 conditions across northwestern Vigo county. On the January 6th update, there was a very small expansion across north central Vigo county. These drought conditions continued into at least February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front moved across the area during the evening hours of January 15th. Strong winds continued overnight and into the following day. Numerous power outages, damages, and road closures were reported with the abnormally strong northwest winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 72 MPH was observed at the Kings Canyon sensor (7 S Chadron) at 11:22 AM MST on 1/16. Multiple sensors across the county recorded strong wind gusts over 60 MPH. Downed tree branches and power flashes were also reported in the city of Chadron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down, blocking both lanes of Knox Daniel Road near Union City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small Ferris wheel was blown over and damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Video showed a well-developed landspout tornado northeast of Donovan just west of the Illinois Indiana state line that persisted for several minutes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several videos were shared of a slow-moving landspout tornado that occurred a few miles east of Beaverville and north northeast of Donovan in rural northeast Iroquois County. No known damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near average rainfall for many areas kept drought conditions the same in May. The one change was in northern Sierra county where there was slightly below normal precipitation and the area was put in Extreme(D3) drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe(D2) drought continued across the zone in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drier and warmer than average conditions contributed to worsening drought across southwest Nebraska during March 2026. D2 Severe Drought was introduced by early to mid March, and deteriorated to D3 Extreme Drought by late March over northern portions of the county. Monthly precipitation amounts were very light, with only around one-hundredth of an inch or less reported. Normal monthly precipitation amounts are a little over one inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts were very light, with only around one-hundredth of an inch or less reported. This was a little over one inch below average. Normal monthly precipitation amounts are a little over one inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.25 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the waters and bays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station EPTT2 near Eagle Point measured a 37 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elongated low pressure along a cold front brought an low end advisory accumulating snowfall to portions of Northeastern New Jersey.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters observed 2.9 inches at 1 N River Vale and 2.9 inches at 1 WSW Wallington. Cocorahs reported 2.4 inches at 1 SSW River Edge. The public reported 2.8 inches in Waldwick.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of storms impacted the Bay Area and Central Coast from January 1st to the 5th, causing numerous flooding impacts and scattered thunderstorms. A low pressure system on the 1st was followed by a strong cold front and associated atmospheric river late on the 2nd into the morning of the 3rd.  A second cold front followed on the 4th. A tornado warning was issued on January 5 for the Pacific coast near the border between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties due to a radar indicated rotation signature. Around 3,400 customers in San Francisco lost power on the 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The gage along Mark West Creek at Mirabel Heights reached Moderate flooding with a peak stage of 59.79 ft.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought began to expand across portions of southern Pennsylvania throughout the month with near-to-slightly below average precipitation values observed across much of the region throughout May 2026. Severe drought was expanded into Adams, Cumberland, and York counties due to well-below average long-term precipitation and slightly below near-term precipitation values, with a Drought Watch issued across York County and Drought Warnings in effect for Adams and Cumberland County throughout the month according to the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought was expanded across portions of southern Pennsylvania for the middle of the month due to initially dry conditions during the month of May 2026. This expansion entailed the southern half of York County being added into severe drought due to longer-term precipitation deficits, where a Drought Watch was issued for the county for much of May 2026 by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front attendant to a southern Canada low pressure center moved slowly through northwest North Carolina, causing showers and storms to form. Bulk shear of around 30kts in the North Carolina High Country encouraged some isolated severe thunderstorms to form during the afternoon of May 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lightning struck a church steeple, setting it on fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A widespread freeze event the morning of 5/12. Most inland areas across WNY saw temperatures dip into the mid to upper 20s due to a combination of cold air, surface high |pressure overhead, light winds, and clear skies. Notable observations: Belmont 27 F, Franklinville 26 F, Clymer 26 F, East Aurora 28 F, Philadelphia 28 F, Osceola 26 F, Dansville               29 F, Honeoye Falls 28 F, Hastings 26 F, Walworth 29 F .

On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered heavy thunderstorms developed across north-central Oklahoma during the early to mid-morning hours of the 24th. Provided slow movement and heavy rainfall rates, scattered flooding occurred, especially across far eastern Payne County, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple images showing large sections of 19th Avenue, between Underwood Road and Greenwood Road, eroded or collapsed due to flooding were shared on social media. The event time is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.
Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were downed throughout Springfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Beaufort County 911 Call Center reported a tree down at Azalea Drive and Ridenour Pl.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in the Piedmont of Virginia. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree as well as multiple power lines were reported down along Tavern Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough with a cold front swept across Kansas. This brought strong upper-level winds up to 50-60 KTs. As winds mixed down to the surface, very strong winds were recorded up to multiple 67 mph gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station UR350 Kismws recorded a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across northwest Indiana during the morning of January 14th with a band of heavy snow and snow squalls.  Wind gusts were between 40 mph and 50 mph with a few higher gusts, including a gust to 58 mph near Lake Station. Visibility was reported to be near zero in many locations. A band of lake effect snow then move across far northwest Indiana through early afternoon. Snowfall amounts were 2 to 4 inches near Lake Michigan and 1 to 2 inches elsewhere.

An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 5.3 inches of snow and up to 3.0 inches of sleet. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grandfield (GRA2) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms dropped southeast into southern middle Tennessee and north Alabama during the afternoon and early evening hours.  Damaging winds were reported in northwest Alabama including the Shoals metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and a powerline were reported down at the intersection of Rose Street and CR 26. Time was estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a weak surface front/pressure trough across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 26th. This activity produced damaging winds, hail and flooding as it progressed south/southeastward into the early morning of the 27th. Significant damaging winds and hail were noted with a trio of more organized thunderstorms (supercells) during this time impacting areas around Enid, Stillwater, Oklahoma City and Chandler, OK.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A cabin was destroyed, large trees were uprooted and power poles were blown down. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported quarter sized hail 2 miles south of Millston.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong backdoor front moved south and west across eastern New Mexico late March 26th into early March 27th resulting in strong north winds at several locations. The strong northerly winds aided the rapid spread of the Old 66 Wildfire that began just north of I-40 near San Jon, jumping south of the highway. This fire destroyed two structures, but did not cause any injuries or loss of life. The cold front surged through the gaps of the central mountain chain just before sunrise resulting in strong to high east canyon winds across the Tularosa Valley and middle and lower Rio Grande Valley. Mesonet sites across White Sands Missile Range measured wind gusts up to 93 mph. Winds across eastern New Mexico tapered off during the late morning hours while winds across the Tularosa and Rio Grande Valley tapered off during the mid to late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Old 66 Wildfire was discovered mid-day March 27th, and quickly grew out of control north of I-40 near San Jon, NM. It burned quickly southward through grasslands crossing I-40 aided by strong northerly to northeasterly winds behind a strong cold front, growing to a final size of 4,111 acres. The fire came under control as winds subsided heading into March 28th. The fire caused a closure of NM 469 and Main Ave. in San Jon, NM. Emergency management reported the fire destroyed two structures, and that a wind farm that was threatened did not suffer any damage. No injuries or loss of life was reported. Damage is an estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic airmass brought very cold temperatures to the entire region Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).  Winds of 15 to 25 mph combined with low temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero brought wind chill values down to 30 to 55 below zero Thursday evening (1/22) through Friday morning (1/23). Temperatures did not warm much Friday afternoon, with daytime highs ranging from 5 to 15 below zero, offering little relief from the cold, with wind chill values at or near extreme cold criteria, even in the afternoon. Plummeting overnight temperatures Friday night (1/23) into Saturday morning (1/24) of 15 to near 40 below zero once again pushed wind chill values down to 30 to near 50 below zero. Temperatures had finally warmed to above extreme cold criteria late Saturday morning (1/24) but remained cold through the weekend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds caused wind chill values to fall to -30 to -45 degrees from late Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into central NY, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds brought down a tree, power lines, and three utility poles on Mormon Hollow Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Bitterly cold air moved across northern Illinois on January 23rd and January 24th with wind chills between 25 below and 35 below zero.  Wind chills 35 below to 40 below zero occurred across far northern and northwest Illinois.

Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.
A long duration snow event produced 6 to 10 inches of fluffy snow accumulation late January 24th into January 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow, moderate to heavy at times, developed during the evening hours of January 24th and continued through the early evening hours of January 25th. The snow accumulated to between 8 and 10 inches and was fluffy in nature as temperatures were in the single digits and teens. There was a report of 9.6 inches of total snow accumulation in Van Wert. Roads were snow covered and slick with numerous reports of accidents and slide-offs across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree downs. Another tree down on County Highway L just to the south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms moved across the area on the evening of the 30th into the early morning hours of the 31st, producing a couple rounds of heavy rain and several reports of accumulating hail, with hailstones as large as ping pong balls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail fell again in the Lake City area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was observed in an open field by a storm chaser around 2 miles northwest of Terril. The tornado was estimated to touch down northeast of the intersection of 290th Avenue and 220th Street. The tornado tracked northeast for around one minute before it lifted west of 300th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 25 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As an upper level low moved through the region, severe thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front that moved through North Dakota. Scattered showers and non-severe thunderstorms were ongoing during the morning before increasing in strength throughout the afternoon. A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to the size of quarters reported. Nearby, there was a report of smaller hail but larger quantity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas from the evening of the 14th into early morning hours of the 15th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of Elk City, Oklahoma (and vicinity), producing large hail and significant wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A measured wind gust from a broadcast media storm chaser.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported on Mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms developed along a trough axis during the evening hours on June 6, resulting in multiple reports of thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms including several supercells developed over parts of  west central and northwest MN during the afternoon and evening period, with very large hail and severe winds reported. One supercell produced 3 inch hail in Moorhead, MN. One EF-0 tornado developed with a supercell in Clay County 6 miles northwest of Hawley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report relayed by mPING of ping pong ball size hail 1 SW of Dilworth, MN.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reports 3 inch diameter hail near Maple Bluff.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds impacted much of Montana. However, it was spotty if the high winds made it down to the surface, with a few counties not seeing gusts at or above 58 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ingomar gusted to 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the St Clara area, a tree blew down onto County Road 29.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved through the region in early February, spawning deepening surface low pressure offshore. A very steep pressure gradient resulted in strong winds across southeast Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow sensor at Rudee Inlet experienced strong winds as low pressure deepened offshore. Sustained winds were above 40 mph from midnight through 5 AM with a peak gust of 54 mph measured at 3:21 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media post showed what appears to be a small creek overflowing and impacting the entrance and exit of Playa Buye, preventing people from leaving the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front attendant to a southern Canada low pressure system moved slowly through western and central Virginia, triggering showers and thunderstorms. Bulk shear of around 30kts just east of the Blue Ridge supported damaging wind gusts from a few storms, which resulted in localized tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds along Angel Place Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several tree limbs snapped by thunderstorm winds.

High winds were the main impact around the Tahoe basin for April 1-2, with peak gusts of 60-95 mph, and Sierra ridge gusts up to 135 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amidon NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over far southwestern Nebraska and the Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon hours of May 30th. As this activity progressed slowly east into the evening hours, numerous large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported. A couple of tornadoes were also reported. Hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured at the Ogallala Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was draped from the Ohio Valley into the northern Mid-Atlantic region. A mid-level system tracked in from the west and led to numerous showers and storms across the Coastal Plain and Piedmont of Central North Carolina. Numerous wind damage reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on Buffaloe Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A third consecutive day of isolated dryline thunderstorms developed across the Rolling Plains on the afternoon of the 14th. Strong moisture returned to areas off the caprock and sufficient heating resulted in convective thunderstorm development. One of these storms became severe as it moved over eastern King County producing a severe wind gust of 64 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Guthrie measured a severe wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds along South Constitution Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills across the parish fell as low as -5 degrees during the early morning of January 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions due to strong westerly winds and very low humidity were present over the northeastern highlands of NM allowing for the Helen Wildfire to quickly grow to over 1,000 acres. The fire was reported in Mora County on private land just west of Wagon Mound, NM and west of I-25. NM 120 was temporarily closed to allow firefighters safe access to the incident. There have been no reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Helen Wildfire ignited during the afternoon of March 3rd, quickly growing to over 1,000 acres on private land in Mora County west of Wagon Mound, NM. While NM 120 was temporarily closed to allow firefighters access to the wildfire, there were no other reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries. The fire reached a final size of 1,180 acres by March 5th before activity subsided.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the area Friday the 29th, bringing scattered showers during the afternoon and evening as it tracked south across the region. Even with limited instability, strong shear supported a few thunderstorms, mainly across the Mohawk Valley and Tug Hill Plateau. The tightening pressure gradient along and behind the front also produced widespread gusty winds of 30-40 mph, especially across the higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on a house causing the front of the  house to partially collapse. There were no known injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercell thunderstorms developed near a slow-moving frontal boundary during the afternoon and evening hours on February 26. Cold temperatures were present aloft with strong deep layer shear but relatively weak low-level shear. Scattered severe hail reports were received, with the largest hailstones falling in portions of Blount, Jefferson, and St. Clair counties, as large as two inches in diameter. Damaging winds also occurred, with the most significant wind damage in Pinson where a microburst occurred. A hail storm associated with the microburst resulted in accumulating hail that covered the ground and resulted in the formation of hail fog. In addition, a brief EF-0 tornado also moved through Trussville, damaging some commercial and industrial buildings as well as homes, most of which was minor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to golf ball-size hail fell on the Blount County side of Altoona.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered afternoon storms developed across southeast Texas with a couple storms becoming severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A gauge site on Lawhon Road indicates the creek out of its bank and rising slowly over nearby streets. Street flooding was also reported in Beaumont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media photo showed a 2.75 inch hailstone west of White Settlement.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms moved across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the late evening hours of June 20th into the morning hours of June 21st. Several reports of damaging winds were gathered along with a brief tornado near the Harvey-Sedgwick County line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Russell Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down into the road near the intersection of US Route 68 and A H Boston Road. Another tree was reported down near the intersection of Columbia Road and Mosby Ridge Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first of two tornadoes in Pottawatomie County began west of Dale and north of I-40, near S3340 Road. This tornado produced sporadic damage between I-40 and Westech Road, just south of Dale. Damage to trees and a few power lines was noted |as the tornado curved to the northeast. A tree was uprooted just south |of Garretts Lake Road and US Highway 177 north of Shawnee. The tornado |dissipated a short time later.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.
During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought very large hail and damaging wind gusts to portions of far eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tennis ball sized hail reported west of Paola.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of the 29th, a dryline moving eastward stalled out around the Interstate 27/US Highway 87 corridor. Strong heating along the boundary created an unstable atmosphere and storms were able to form. A lack of deep layer shear kept storms from becoming organized and led to pulse type thunderstorms. However, one storm did produce a severe wind gust near Floydada (Floyd County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Floydada measured severe wind gusts from 2146 CST through 2147 CST with a peak gust of 66 mph at 2147 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead of a potent cold front pushed through Central Alabama from late March 15 into the early morning of March 16. Scattered instances of wind damage were observed across many counties in Central Alabama as the line moved through. After a significant temperature reduction, a band of snow developed during the late morning hours, with counties such as Winston, Jefferson, Shelby, Blount, Etowah, and St. Clair picking up 0.5 to 1.5 inches of accumulation. With warm ground and road temperatures, the snow quickly method and travel impacts were little to none.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Fulton Springs Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surge of Arctic air invaded Southwest Arkansas during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across Southwest Arkansas from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

Scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 90 mph gust was measured at the Guymon ASOS in relation to a heat burst. A tin roof was ripped off of a building and scattered across another nearby yard. Additionally, tree limbs and branches were broken around town and some fencing damage occurred. No noted damage occurred at the airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably cold temperatures developed during the growing season across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, with hard freeze conditions observed at some locations during the morning hours before sunrise. The 2026 Spring growing season officially began at 12am on May 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station at Hadler, MN observed a low temperature of 31 at 5:10 AM CST. The NDAWN at Ada, MN observed a low of 32 at 5:25 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An emergency manager estimated wind gusts of 75mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The incredible stretch of severe weather continued on Wednesday June 10th with more severe storms and a few small tornadoes across Dickinson county.  The storms also dumped  more flooding rains across parts of Kansas that were already saturated from days of torrential rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Old highway 40 is impassable due to flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water over a foot deep on Dedeaux Road.  The road is impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS Station KLBL measured high wind gusts multiple times throughout the day, peaking 51 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported golf ball sized hail roughly 2 miles south-southeast of Price.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received from Mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and powerlines down in the area along miller farmer rd near corn crib dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique snow setup for South Carolina developed as a strong coastal low strengthening offshore, while a upper level disturbance shifted over our area. This provided sufficient synoptic and mesoscale lift for widespread heavy snow across SC along with unusually high snow to liquid ratios between 15-20 to 1. A brief period of sleet-graupel occurred at the onset of the event following by 12 hours of light-moderate snow across the area, with highest amounts in the Pee Dee region of SC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple measurements across southern Lancaster county of between 3 and 6 inches of storm total snowfall. Highest measured amount in southern Lancaster was 6 inches northeast of the city of Lancaster.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens. There were numerous social media posts of frozen and burst water pipes across the area.

Extreme (D3) drought continued across the southern half of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the first half of June, before tapering back to Severe (D2) drought as appreciable rainfall helped to ease drought conditions and impacts. June monthly rainfall totals ranged significantly from 5-10 inches across McCurtain County with isolated higher amounts in southern parts of the county, generally near and along the Red River where as much as a foot of rain fell.  As a result, drought conditions continued to improve through the last half of the month as additional rain fell, although amounts were less than those that occurred earlier in June. Despite the improvement, all this rainfall was not enough to completely erode the severe drought in the southern half of the county, which persisted through the end of the month.

Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Storm Survey confirms an EF-1 tornado with maximum wind of 100 mph.

Temperatures did not warm much Friday afternoon, with daytime highs ranging from 5 to 15 below zero, offering little relief from the cold, with wind chill values at or near extreme cold criteria, even in the afternoon. Plummeting overnight temperatures Friday night (1/23) into Saturday morning (1/24) of 15 to near 40 below zero once again pushed wind chill values down to 30 to near 50 below zero. Temperatures had finally warmed to above extreme cold criteria late Saturday morning (1/24) but remained cold through the weekend.
