EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals ranged from 5 to as much as 20 inches or more across the county, much of which was mixed with or solely sleet. Some freezing rain occurred as well. County offices were proactively closed for the 16th due to conditions. Road clearing in the county was slowed by the thick, dense sleet/snowpack overwhelming county trucks, requiring equipment repairs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hailfall near the intersection of U.S. Highway 277 and Kleeman Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level system drove strong cold front eastward across the region, including adjacent coastal waters. Ahead of the boundary, a robust low-level jet brough in warm, buoyant, and very moist air northward from the Gulf. Night timing of the line of storms that developed along the front did limit low level instability, however, elevated instability and frontal lift were more than enough to overcome the lack of surface heating. Several locations across coastal waters observed severe convective wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KNEW recorded a wind gust of 60 mph or 52 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of short wave moved across Southeast Texas and produced a few severe storms during late May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed in Fannett.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northeastern Colorado during the late afternoon hours of June 9th. As this activity pushed east, it encountered favorable moisture and shear, and became severe. Activity was isolated initially, but became more numerous into the evening hours. Hail up to the size of baseballs was reported in McPherson County while 79 MPH wind gusts were reported in Holt County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter sized from social media picture.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall totals across Outagamie County included 27.5 inches in Appleton, 24.8 inches in Shiocton, 24 inches in Greenville, and 22.8 inches in New London. In addition, winds gusting to 35 to 45 mph caused blizzard conditions on Monday March 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front, combined with scattered thunderstorms embedded in southwest flow, interacted with an anomalously warm and dry air mass across southwest Montana. High temperatures were in the 80s, creating large dewpoint depressions. High winds aloft, reaching 65 knots between 16,000 and 18,000 feet MSL, were brought to the surface by both convective downdrafts and evaporative cooling, as well as the passing cold front. This synoptic setup led to severe and high wind gusts across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-convective winds occurring behind a cold front resulted in high winds across the zone. In the city of Deer Lodge (Powell County), a 53 MPH wind gust was measured at 1754MST, which blew a few shingles off a roof. The DRLM Agrimet station south of Deer Lodge measured gusts up to 49 mph between 1800MST and 1815MST. MacDonald Pass also recorded a 55 MPH wind gust. At 1815MST, a 59 mph wind gust was measured at Warm Springs (Deer Lodge County).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Breezy southerly winds shifted to southwesterly later into the evening of the 8th ahead of a cold frontal passage. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours in Southeast Missouri. Gusty gradient winds of near and above 40mph developed in portions of Southeast Missouri during the evening hours ahead of the storms.

A major winter storm system impacted the State of Tennessee starting late Friday, January 23 and continuing into Sunday, January 25, 2026. Cold air moved into Tennessee Friday evening, setting the stage for winter weather through the weekend. This cold air along with a potent storm system resulted in primarily snow Friday night into Saturday morning. However, as warm air aloft moved north into Tennessee, this changed the precipitation from snow to sleet and then finally to freezing rain Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon. By the time precipitation came to an end, snow accumulations were highest across northwest Middle Tennessee where generally 3 to 5 inches were measured. A swath of ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inches was reported from Wayne County northeast through Nashville and to the Tennessee/Kentucky border. Locally higher amounts over one half inch were reported around the Nashville metro area.||These accumulations caused widespread, crippling damage in the form of broken and downed trees and power lines, dangerous to impossible travel conditions, and hundreds of thousands of power outages. Nashville Electric Service (NES) alone reported 230,000 customers without power which is the largest number of outages at one time NES has ever experienced. ||The other major impact from this winter storm was frigid temperatures. Cold air already in place over the weekend was reinforced Sunday night as arctic air moved into Tennessee behind this winter storm. The coldest temperature readings were recorded Monday and Tuesday mornings with widespread readings in the single digits and wind chills below zero. With these very cold temperatures, impacts were felt long after the precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mixture of snow, sleet, and ice impacted Jackson County during the early morning hours of January 24th into the afternoon of January 25th. A variety of reporting sources measured snow accumulations of 1 to 2 inches with ice accumulations of 0.20 to 0.30 inches. This led to several reports of treacherous travel and downed powerlines, trees, and tree branches. Total power outages were around 300 customers across Jackson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Pacific low-pressure system moving into the area brought high winds to portions of southern Nevada.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station at the Nevada National Security Site recorded high winds for a brief period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front moved across Minnesota and proceeded into western Wisconsin on April 17th which ultimately produced two rounds of thunderstorms. The first line of storms was associated with a warm front which produced quarter size hail across south-central Minnesota mid-morning. The secondary and stronger line of storms tied to the cold front itself moved through in the early afternoon across eastern MN and western WI. This line produced a swath of large hail measuring from quarter size up to half dollar size hail 4 miles NNW of Bay City (Pierce County) which ended up being the largest measured hailstone from this event.

A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding observed in 7600 Block of Laurel Creek Road near Clothier. People were stuck in homes with no power in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on wires near the intersection of State Street and South Ferry Street in Schenectady.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, well above normal precipitation occurred across the region during March. By mid-March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Crawford County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Hummingbird Wildfire, which began April 20th, continued into the first week of May. This wildfire burned within the old Whitewater Baldy burn scar in the Gila National Forest, eventually growing to 5,720 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Hummingbird Wildfire was a lightning caused fire starting in a remote region of the Gila Wilderness in Catron County. The wildfire began April 20th and continued into the first week of May burning within dead and downed trees within the old 2012 Whitewater-Baldy burn scar. The fire reached a final size of 5,720 acres by May 2nd before activity subsided. Evacuations for the Willow Creek Subdivision were finally lifted by May 6th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of downed traffic lights at the intersection of Dominion Blvd and Scenic Parkway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees downed and tree limbs snapped in Garrettsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed behind a home on White Street in Schenectady. An estimated 5500 people were without power throughout Schenectady County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Metal roof cover partially removed from a mobile home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad low pressure system over the Northern Plains combined with an upper level trough pushing through the region to produce heavy snow over northwest and north central North Dakota. The greatest snow amounts reported were around nine inches, which occurred in Divide, Bottineau, and Pierce Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Locations northeast of Bottineau received nine inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Electrical Transmission Lines (ETL)/wood poles broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across the state.  Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 1%, D2 - 54%, D1 - 55%.  January  brought little relief to Maine's drought conditions, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge.  January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas in the 50 to 75% of normal range.  Snowfall remained below normal, especially for interior areas with snow water equivalent below normal for all areas except the immediate coast.  Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins.  Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the immediate coastline in the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought conditions remained in a steady state by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot conditions prevailed across the Panhandles during the week of June 8 through 12. However, the combination of lingering moisture, a dryline and these hot conditions allowed for a few thunderstorms to develop each day during the afternoon and evening. Some of these storms were severe with hail and damaging winds being the main hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 63 mph wind gust was measured at the mesonet site located 11 miles southwest of Romero. Gusts above 58 MPH lasted from 1756 to 1800.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting the eastern West Virginia panhandle during the late afternoon hours with damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down near the intersection of Daniel Road and Shenandoah Junction Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few thunderstorms across far southeast Wyoming produced isolated strong wind gusts up to 66 MPH.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Warren Air Force Base recorded a 60 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees and wires near Beechwood Road near Truman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A barn sustained minor siding damage along York Road. Additionally, several power poles were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours.||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KMAE Madera Airport reporting near 0 mile visibility at times.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down at Route 29 and Carpenters Mill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Jayton measured a severe wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed across Highway 43.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northeast Illinois during the late evening of March 30th producing large hail.

A slow moving cold front sagged southeast across the area sparking a broken line of thunderstorms that moved across eastern OH and northwestern PA in the evening hours. A narrow axis of 100-250 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30 knots of effective shear supported a localized damaging wind threat resulting in power poles and trees down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking the entirety of the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A 985mb low pressure system caused winds to increase dramatically out of the northwest overnight March 12 into the morning of Friday the 13th. The strongest winds were measured across the southwest portion of the state with 30 to 40 mph sustained winds and frequent gusts over 50 mph. Slightly weaker, yet still high winds, extended as far east as the Twin Cities metro (primarily the southwest and central portions) as well as Mankato and Owatonna. Xcel Energy reported over 300 power outages across the state of Minnesota due to downed trees and power lines.||The highest measured wind gusts were:|71 mph at KBBB in Benson, MN.|67 mph at KRWF in Redwood Falls, MN.|66 mph at KAQP in Appleton, MN.|66 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.|64 mph at KJYG in St James, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds were sustained around 35 to 45 mph overnight, with frequent gusts over 50 mph. A max wind gust of 62 mph was recorded at near KFRM around 3:00am.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May 2026 in West Tennessee was a textbook example of weather whiplash. The month began with the region enduring the peak of a grueling, multi-season drought that originally took hold in late 2025. Because a persistent weather pattern had largely cut off moisture from the Gulf of Mexico for months, West Tennessee completely missed its traditional winter and early spring recharge window.||However, the narrative flipped abruptly during the second half of May. A significant atmospheric shift finally broke the dry dome, bringing heavy, consistent rainfall and improving conditions to West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 Extreme Drought conditions improved to D2 Severe Drought by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front moved across Minnesota during the early morning of April 17th which ultimately produced two rounds of thunderstorms.  The first line of storms was associated with a warm front which produced quarter size hail across south-central Minnesota mid-morning. The secondary and stronger line of storms tied to the cold front itself moved through in the early afternoon across eastern MN. This line produced a swath of large hail measuring from quarter size up to ping pong ball size hail in Cannon Falls (Goodhue County) which ended up being the largest measured hailstone from this event.

Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, blew the metal roof off of a single story unoccupied building on the 6500 block of Hokes Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clearing skies and light winds under high pressure, along with lingering low-level moisture, allowed for widespread dense fog formation to develop late evening across most of Southern Illinois. Dense fog continued until the early to mid-morning hours. Many locations reported low temperatures slightly below freezing but no reports were made of freezing fog development.
Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds across northwest Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down on Township Road 135. Time was estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought continued across parts of the area through June, especially in the eastern zones.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: To begin the month, all but the western edge of Western Roosevelt County was in D2 drought conditions. On the last day of the month, D2 drought conditions exited from this zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lightning damaged two homes in North Carolina during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lightning started a fire in the attic of a home on Cascade Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of April with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across mainland Monroe County in the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant short-term drought relief was observed across Maine in May 2026, highlighted by a mid-May soaking rain that markedly improved drought categories in the mountains and foothills. In the single week ending May 19, the state's Severe Drought (D2) coverage fell from 11% to 2.2%. While this spring precipitation effectively mitigated immediate agricultural and hydrological impacts���replenishing topsoil moisture, restoring streamflows, and bringing surface water storage like lakes and reservoirs back to near-normal seasonal baselines���long-term deficits endure. Deep groundwater aquifers are slower to react, leaving deep water table levels substantially below historical averages due to these ongoing groundwater deficits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had 58% of Oxford County in Severe Drought (D2), but by the end of May severe drought was completely resolved (0%), with 58% remaining in Moderate Drought (D1) and 42% in Abnormally Dry (D0). May rainfall averaged 5.36 inches, well above normal by 1.80���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 12-month period ending May 2026 held a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong winds were observed across multiple locations in southeast Ohio on February 20th as they accompanied a cold front. The initial burst of winds arrived in the late morning timeframe with the frontal passage, and continued to be breezy to strong through the day as stronger winds from aloft mixed down to the surface. The strongest winds in the area measured that day was reported from an AWOS observation site in the town of Jackson with a 47 mile per hour gust noted around the time of the front's passage. Several trees were blown down in the midst of these stronger winds as a result. High pressure building in from the west helped to ease the stronger winds just before midnight that evening.

An intense low-pressure system tracking through the northern Great Lakes brought damaging winds of 50 to 71 mph to much of southeast Michigan. The strongest gusts were concentrated along and south of the M-59 corridor, where numerous trees and power lines were downed across the Detroit Metro area. Both Detroit City Airport and Ann Arbor Airport recorded peak gusts of 71 mph during the height of the storm. The most intense winds occurred in the afternoon following the passage of a strong cold front, leaving around 200,000 DTE Energy customers without power at the peak of the event. Tragically, the storm claimed the life of a Huntington Woods public works employee, who was struck by a falling tree limb while working to clear a roadway during the evening hours.

During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail reported in Grant City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low level frontogenesis developed ahead of a cold front, and an upper level shortwave provided lift to create snow showers as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report of 3.5 inches of snow was received from the Vevay area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic airmass brought very cold temperatures to the entire region Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).  Winds of 15 to 25 mph combined with low temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero brought wind chill values down to 30 to 55 below zero Thursday evening (1/22) through Friday morning (1/23). Temperatures did not warm much Friday afternoon, with daytime highs ranging from 5 to 15 below zero, offering little relief from the cold, with wind chill values at or near extreme cold criteria, even in the afternoon. Plummeting overnight temperatures Friday night (1/23) into Saturday morning (1/24) of 15 to near 40 below zero once again pushed wind chill values down to 30 to near 50 below zero. Temperatures had finally warmed to above extreme cold criteria late Saturday morning (1/24) but remained cold through the weekend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds caused wind chill values to fall to -30 to -44 degrees from late Thursday evening (1/22) through Saturday morning (1/24).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down around Bowling Green.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad upper level low centered offshore from northern California produced numerous thunderstorms in southern Oregon. One thunderstorm produced a lightning strike that burned a hole through the roof of a home.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm in the city of Ashland produced  a lightning strike that burned a hole in the roof of a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across western and central Wyoming and brought a scattering of showers and thunderstorms. With large dew point depressions and supportive upper level dynamics, strong wind gusts occurred across much of central Wyoming. The most widespread high wind gusts were in Johnson County. After the cold front passage, a brief period of high wind driven by a tight pressure gradient and northwest flow brought strong synoptic winds to Johnson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around a 1 hour period of high wind occurred behind a cold front passage. The highest wind gust was 69 mph at the Johnson County airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front moved into a warm, moist airmass over South-Central Texas and generated thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. There were multiple water rescues at FM 471 N at San Geronimo Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a southeastward moving cold front, broken lines of showers and thunderstorms developed in the evening hours. A surge of mid 70s temperatures with upper 50s dew points resulted in sufficient destabilization with MLCAPE up to 1000 J/kg, effective shear of 30-40 knots, and a gradient of 700-900 DCAPE. This allowed for some thunderstorms to become severe with large hail and damaging wind as the result, including two measured 58 mph gusts in southwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees snapped in half in a backyard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level low-pressure center progressed eastward through the Plains on the afternoon and evening of March 10, leading to the development of thunderstorms. These storms were able to initiate along a dryline across the Big Country. As the storms moved east through the forecast area, some generated large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm spotter reported tennis ball sized hail 9 miles south of Breckenridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough crossed Wyoming and brought scattered showers and thunderstorms. Very dry air at the low levels led to the showers and thunderstorms to be high based, and numerous locations saw dry microbursts as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary moved north off of the Wind River Mountains andbrought strong wind to much of central Fremont County. The highest wind reported was 86 mph at Red Canyon. In the lower elevations, some gusts included 64 mph at the Lander airport and 58 mph at the Riverton airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Thornton, a tree blew down and blocked parts of the road around the 900 block of  Irontown Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees fell down onto Ridge Road at Deer Gap.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were reported down in Henderson Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto Stumpknocker Trail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Limited rainfall during this period led to further worsening of drought conditions. In addition, recent hard freeze events have dried available fuels, resulting in an increasing wildfire risk throughout our area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall during January combined with multiple freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) drought by the end of January.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the 12000 block of North Carolina Highway 125, near US Highway 301.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions continued across LaSalle, Livingston, Ford and Iroquois counties in east central Illinois during most of March with extreme drought conditions easing at the end of March.

Similar to May 19th, thunderstorms were able to develop across west Texas thanks to pulses in the southwesterly flow aloft, a stationary front, and plentiful moisture east of the dryline. A few storms became severe, producing large hail. Flash flooding was also recorded in a few locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from the IBHS Hail Field Research team measuring hailstones up to 1.89 inches. The time of occurrence is estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed on Lee Road 213, 309, and 240.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Part of a large tree was blown down onto the hood of a car near the Abraham Lincoln Historical Home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across northeast Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued lack of rainfall combined with hard freeze events resulted in worsening drought conditions into Extreme (D3) with the February 10th drought monitor update, continuing through the rest of the Month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant snowstorm struck portions of East Tennessee at the end of the month, thanks to strong lift from a deep upper trough diving from north to south. A couple of long term cooperative weather stations saw top 10 snowfalls during this storm. This storm led to 3 confirmed fatalities in East Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow fell in Hancock County, with 4 inches of snow reported north of Bean Station and 5 inches of snow measured in Kyles Ford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds gusted as high as 59 mph at the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site at Fort Randall Dam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down in northern Isle of Wight County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

Strong thunderstorms developed into northeastern Oklahoma during the late evening of the 23rd, as a cold front moved into the area. These thunderstorms organized into a line of thunderstorms and moved into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 24th, the strongest of which produced damaging wind. ||Another round of thunderstorms developed along the cold front over east central Oklahoma and west central Arkansas during the afternoon of the 24th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind snapped large tree limbs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between large air masses funneled strong and severe winds through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple observations in central and southeast Phillips County recorded wind gusts in excess of 64 mph, the strongest of which was 67 mph, measured at the Saco US-2 DOT site (MTSCO).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Spur Highway EE was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed social media report of hail estimated up to 1.25 inches in diameter. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Locally induced afternoon thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall over Aguada, causing minor flooding on May 27th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency managers reported standing water from recent heavy rainfall along PR-115 at km 21.9 near Cielo Mar Bakery.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather system resulted in a light wintry mix of precipitation during the early afternoon on January 4th. Surface temperatures were about 5 to 10 degrees below freezing, under a slightly warmer air mass just above the surface. This resulted in a few hours of light freezing rain or drizzle, and ultimately light ice accretion, creating slick surfaces for a number of counties in east-central Minnesota. Farther north, the airmass just above the surface was slightly cooler, resulting in more snow mixing in with any freezing precipitation. This limited impacts for areas north and west of St Cloud, Princeton, and Rush City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several CoCoRaHS observers reported a mixture of sleet and light freezing precipitation that resulted in a glaze of ice throughout the county, including in Anoka, St Francis, Coon Rapids, and Lino Lakes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of strong winds and light snow just the day prior, many locations saw a second cold front move through the region, producing gusty winds and light snow from the morning of the 18th through the morning of the 19th. Since there was little to no snowpack on the ground, any reductions in visibility depended on how heavy the falling snow was and how strong winds were. Conditions were generally worst in open, rural areas where the snowfall was able to blow around easier.||Winds gusted up to 45 mph in parts of western and southern Minnesota, and generally under an inch of snow fell across the region. Visibilities dropped to 1/4 mile in several locations, though it was often brief due to the showery nature of the snowfall. The snowfall was heaviest before the strongest winds developed, limiting overall impacts from this event.||The strongest measured wind gusts from January 18-19 were:|46 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN.|45 mph at KBDH in Willmar, MN.|44 mph at KAXN in Alexandria, MN.|44 mph at KDXX in Madison, MN.|44 mph at KJYG in St James, MN.|43 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearby KSTC measured strong winds gusting to 40 mph and scattered snow showers resulting in periodic reductions in visibility as low as a 1/2 mile at times, though generally remaining around 1 to 3 miles. The strongest winds were during the afternoon as snowfall became lighter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 30 to 45 mph with gusts as high as 55 to 65 mph across southwest Minnesota.  When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted to as high as 57 mph at Florence, 47 mph at Tracy, and 45 mph at Marshall. These winds combined with periods of snow totaling 1 to 2 inches to produce periods with visibility of one-quarter mile or less.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought continued across portions of East Texas through the first three plus weeks of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. However, widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 2.00+ inches fell across much of Rusk, Gregg, San Augustine, and Sabine Counties between the 19th  and 26th, resulting in a one category improvement to Moderate (D1) drought across these areas by the May 28th release of the U.S. Drought Monitor. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2.50-4+ inches across Rusk and Gregg Counties, and between 5-8+ inches across San Augustine and Sabine Counties, which was near to as much as twice the monthly normals. Thus, some improvement to pasture greenup, stock pond levels, and streamflows across area rivers, bayous, and creeks were observed by month's end. ||Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana. Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

During the morning of June 7th, training thunderstorms caused flooding across nearly the entire southern half of Boone County. Most of the flooding consisted of inches of water over roadways and flooded creeks. That afternoon through evening, additional thunderstorms exacerbated the problem, creating even more dangerous conditions through the morning of the 8th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding caused two swift water rescues in Columbia with three individuals rescued in total. No injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple of thunderstorms pushed across southern Vermont during the early evening hours on June 6, 2026 within the warm sector of a low pressure system. One such storm became severe near Bennington downing a tree and utility poles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very large tree fell onto power lines and took down four utility poles on Depot Street in Bennington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning on January 21st, a weak winter system brought light snow to portions of southeast Minnesota. While accumulations were generally on the lighter side of around 2 inches or less across the region, a few vehicle accidents occurred which resulted in 7 combined non-life threatening injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Accumulating snow during the morning hours on January 21st resulted in snow covered roadways across Fillmore County. During this period of accumulating snow, a two vehicle collision occurred on Highway 52 near Chatfield resulting in 4 individuals receiving non-life threatening injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the midday of the 17th, west-southwesterly winds began gusting up to close to 70 MPH ahead of a cold front.  Behind the front high winds continued.  The west-southwesterly winds did loft dirt into the air, causing widespread visibilities to drop to around 1-2 miles with isolated pockets of intense plumes leading to brownout conditions. One such location was at mile marker 66 on I-70 where a two vehicle accident occurred, causing one fatality.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were 58 MPH or greater in surrounding counties.  As such, high winds also occurred in Sheridan County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The bridge on CR30E between 130S and 140S had enough flood water over it that the bridge was blocked by debris and not passable.

The low tracked from southern Piscataquis county to northern Washington county exiting across New Brunswick during the morning of the 16th. Snow developed to the north of the low track during the early morning hours of the 16th...persisting into the afternoon. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fallen pine trees blocked Wallace Blue Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large trees downed in Vandalia area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With 2 to 4 inches of precip and snow melt, minor flooding issues were reported along the some of the Cascade creeks and streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mission Creek flooded a residence due to debris from 2025 Labor Mountain fire burn scar causing a backup on the river. Other than this spot, creek was within its banks. Time estimated from river crest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.
A cold front produced showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Delaware Valley. A few of these storms produced heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A water rescue was needed on a flooded roadway in Lansdowne.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds caused a window to shatter at the Gallatin Civic Center. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active severe weather and flooding event impacted the WFO Norman Forecast Area form the morning into early evening of the 23rd. An initial complex of severe thunderstorms moved from northwestern into southwestern Oklahoma and eventually western-north Texas during this time, producing reports of large hail and observations of severe winds. A separate complex of slow-moving thunderstorms entered southeastern Oklahoma during the mid-morning, fostered by ascent atop a strong outflow boundary. Slow storm movement and rich boundary layer moisture combined to yield significant flash flooding across portions of Atoka County, Oklahoma. Eventually, these two separate areas of thunderstorms merged across central Oklahoma, yielding additional severe weather (mainly damaging winds) and flooding during the afternoon and early evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a strong mid-month winter storm which produced substantial mountain snow accumulations, many avalanches were reported across Utah's mountains due to snowpack conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two skiers left the Butler Fork trailhead in Big Cottonwood Canyon Saturday morning 2/21 with the plan to do a run known as The Triangle. This is in Butler Basin, a Big Cottonwood Canyon drainage east of Gobblers Knob. The skiers ascended a steep north-facing slope next to the desired run, when near the top an avalanche broke. Both skiers were caught and carried around 100 feet down the slope, becoming fully buried at the bottom. Other groups of skiers in the basin witnessed the avalanche occur, and notified 911, Alta Central, and began rescue efforts. Around 10 minutes after the avalanche, one of the bystanders made their way to the debris, conducted a beacon search, and eventually found a splitboard binding still attached. Additional bystanders arrived and helped uncover the first victim, cleared their airway, allowing them to breathe and gain consciousness. The victim had suffered a leg injury, but was moved to a safer location. Around this time others began transceiver searching for the other victim, eventually exposing the boot. The skier was buried around 150 cm and face down. The second victim was unburied and CPR efforts were initiated. An EMT was longlined to assist the first victim who had regained consciousness, and the second victim was airlifted from the scene but later succumbed to their injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Part of a tree down on a house resulting in a collapsed front porch awning along North 7th Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions developed in a few of our eastern counties during the last week of February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions developed across the western half of the county the last week of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed along Lakeshore Parkway and Green Springs Highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent clipper low brought rain and/or snow to the Western and North Central New York areas, along with windy conditions. Most of the lower elevations remain primarily as rain, but mixing with and changing to snow at times did allow for some light accumulations. Across the higher terrain snowfall and accumulations increased, especially for areas east of Lake Ontario where warning level snowfall amounts were observed. ||Another component of this storm was the winds associated with the system. Several reports of winds reaching 58 to 63 MPH were observed across the Western New York area. ||Notable snowfall reports include: 10.7 inches in Copenhagen, 9.8 inches in Highmarket and 8.0 inches in Constableville. Notable winds gusts include: 63 MPH in Lime Lak/Machias, 62 MPH at the Rochester Airport, 61 MPH in Warsaw and 60 MPH at the Niagara Falls Airport, Kenmore, and in Dunkirk.

On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding throughout southern Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The roadway was flooded at the viaduct at the corner of Eastern Boulevard and Sodrel Drive.
