EVENT_NARRATIVE: The entire zone remained in Severe(D2) drought through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought sleet/snow to much of west central Texas. Some freezing rain resulted in a light glaze of ice across the Northwest Hill Country. The snow/sleet amounts ranged from 1 to 4 inches across the northern 2/3 of the area. The winter storm caused disruptions to travel and one fatality due to an accident on Interstate 10 east of Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 2 to 4 inches of snow/sleet across Sterling County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation continued to lack across much of northwest Iowa with 25 percent to 75 percent of normal during the month for areas west of U.S. Highway 59.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions worsened to severe (D2) very late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media user reported a tree blown down onto a road about 1 mile west northwest of the Bethany community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front stalled across the Ohio Valley region during the morning, eventually lifting north in the evening hours. Showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary with locally heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported near Cedar Mill Road and State Route 348.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1.50 inches in diameter. Report received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of a metal roof ripped off of a warehouse along State Route 666.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: System snow overspread far northern Indiana during the evening hours of January 18th which was followed by periods of lake effect snow on January 19th behind an arctic front. Storm total snowfall accumulations ranged from 2 to 4 inches across portions of far northern Indiana generally along and north of Interstate 80. Strong winds coupled with the snow and blowing snow produced significant visibility reductions at times and hazardous travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light system snow during the late afternoon and evening of January 18th was followed by bands of lake effect snow.  The combination of west wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph and the snowfall resulted in significant visibility reductions at times due to snow and blowing snow. While storm total snow accumulations only ranged from 1 to 2 inches, the combination of snow and blowing snow produced hazardous travel conditions. A band of snow affected the area during the early morning hours of January 19th producing brief snowfall rates of 1 inch per hour.  Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported across the region.  In addition, wind chills dropped to as cold as 20 below during the early morning hours of January 19th extending into early afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously deep upper low barreled into the region on Saturday, January 31, bringing very cold temperatures. As the low dropped southeastward into the Carolinas, moisture wrapped around the backside of the low, bringing bands of snowfall across much of northeast and east-central Georgia. Snowfall totals were maximized where these bands occurred, reaching as high as 4-7 in many areas. ||Given the narrow nature of these snow bands, areas just a few miles to the west (including much of metro Atlanta) saw very little snowfall, though windy and very cold conditions occurred areawide. Wind chills reached dangerously cold subzero levels across much of the area by the night of January 31 into the morning of February 1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow showers began in the morning of the 31st and continued through the afternoon. Total snowfall amounts ranged from 2 to 4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather outbreak unfolded across central and north-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening of Friday (4/17). The event was triggered by a surface low-pressure system and cold front across the upper Midwest. ||NWS storm surveys confirmed 2 tornadoes that resulted in structural damage. A tornado formed 3 miles northwest of Glandon around 4:44 PM CDT and tracked into southeast Lincoln County producing EF-1 damage before dissipating around 4:55 PM CDT. Another tornado formed 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle in Marathon County around 4:46 PM CDT and dissipated around 5:03 PM CDT 5 miles southwest of Hogarty. This tornado produced EF-3 damage and destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. ||Beyond the tornadic threat, the storms produced isolated large hail up to half dollar size and damaging winds. Heavy rainfall was another impact, with localized totals ranging from 1 to 4 inches. These torrential downpours caused flash flooding, particularly in Marshfield where 2.65 inches of rain fell and multiple vehicles were reported stranded in deep water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed trees and power lines southwest of Phelps. The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media report showing multiple trees and power lines down as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.
A moist air mass ahead of advancing low pressure resulted in widespread dense fog late on February 20th and early on February 21st. The fog dissipated before dawn.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Delaware Coastal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms along with heavy rain moved across parts of northeast Illinois during the evening of January 8th, producing flash flooding and localized wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video shared on social media showed street flooding in multiple locations in Joliet.  Rainfall reports included 2.92 inches in Rockdale and 2.77 inches near Lockport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rather anomalous Arctic Outbreak settled in ahead of the January 25th Winter Storm with reinforcing shots through the last week of January. The remarkable aspect of this outbreak was the duration, especially for the Mid-Atlantic. The coldest nights (January 27th, 30th, and 31st) featured Extreme Cold Warnings. Other nights, Cold Weather Advisories were in effect. For the Allegheny Mountains, minimum wind chills of -20 to -30F were observed. Further east, minimum wind chills of -10 to -20F were observed.

A solid mid-month snow storm brought a few feet of fresh snow to the Colorado Divide mountains. This fresh snow fell atop a shallow layer of faceted, old, and unstable snow, creating an overall unstable snowpack. However, as this winter has been very snow poor, the fresh snow enticed a number of backcountry tourers, despite dangerous avalanche conditions as analyzed by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center. As a result, two avalanches resulted in injuries to two different backcountry tourers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the accident day, the avalanche danger in the area was rated 3/5 - Considerable at all levels, below, near, and above treeline. Avalanche danger was rated on all aspects, with large to very large avalanches likely west through north to east aspects, and small avalanches possible on southwest through southeast aspects. Avalanche discussion indicated that recent avalanches in the area had been large enough to bury, injure, or kill a person, and could be triggered remotely, from a distance or below, and could travel long distances. The accident group consisted of three backcountry tourers, 1 split board rider and 2 skiers, and the intention was to ski a southwest slope from a sub-peak south of Bonita Peak into Minnehaha Basin (37.893, -107.625). Before ascending toward their destination, they stomped on several areas of drifted snow with no reaction. South slopes noted to have shallow snowpack. Rider 1 descended first and made two ski cuts with no reactivity, then started down the slope. A number of turns into Rider 1's descent the avalanche broke and the Rider was caught, tumbling end over end down the rocky path. Rider 1 came to a stop in a standing position at the bottom of the path, buried from the waist down. A second avalanche, triggered by Skier 1 in the hangfire, struck Rider 1 and pushed them further downhill, leaving them in a seated position. Skier 1, who triggered this avalanche, was also caught and carried, bouncing over rocks and left with their legs buried and an injured arm. Rider 1 was able to self-extricate and moved to Skier 1 to extricate them. Skier 2 chose to descend the way they had ascended, and all met and returned to the trailhead. The larger of the two avalanches was rated R2/D2, meaning it was small relative to its path but was large enough to catch, bury, injure, or kill a person. The smaller avalanche was rated R1/D1, meaning it was very small relative to its path and was small enough to be mostly harmless.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front produced wide spread wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph across east central Florida.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Melbourne International Airport measured a peak wind gust of 50 knots from the west.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 10th, a discrete supercell moved from Illinois into northwest Indiana. It produced an EF-2 tornado in Starke County with maximum winds of 115 mph, prompting a rare Tornado Emergency for the area near Knox, IN. Following the initial supercell, a line of storms moved through on the morning of March 11th. Training storms produced significant rainfall between 1 and 3, with localized amounts reaching 4-5, resulting in Flash Flood Warnings and Flood Advisories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Road closed with a vehicle accident due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from pea to quarter size covered the ground just south of Tyler in the Gresham area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mobile home rolled over on Braznell Concrete Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gusts at the Coffeyville Municipal Airport ASOS site ranged from 62 to 79 mph in a 10-minute time frame.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 4:33 AM CST, a brief tornado developed north of Tabor, Iowa, and moved east. The tornado produced sporadic tree damage near 235th Street and Pathfield Road, with estimated maximum estimated winds around 65 mph. Shortly after this damage occurred, KOAX radar displayed a tornadic debris signature associated with the tornado. The tornado was estimated to have a maximum width of 20 yards. The tornado dissipated at approximately 4:35 AM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado that began in Hancock County entered Harrison County at Deschamp Road. The tornado then evidently weakened and the damage path become more intermittent until it reached the Wolf River where another swath of trees was rated low-end EF-1. The tornado damage path became intermittent once more after crossing the intersection of Cemetery and Steel Bridge Rd. The tornado then evidently reached its third peak as an EF-1 tornado as it crossed Cemetery Rd and MS Hwy 53 where swaths of trees were damaged and uprooted. The tornado then rapidly dissipated as it continued northeast and it's estimated to have lifted prior to reaching Herman Ladner Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds from weak showers in East Central CO pushed an outflow boundary into Northwest Kansas.  Wind gusts up to 60 MPH were measured at the Goodland airport as the boundary moved through.  As the outflow boundary continued eastward it collected enough dust to cause dust storm conditions in Wallace, Thomas, Logan, and Gove counties along and behind it.  The high winds blew over a semi and sparked a grassfire between MM 46 and 47 on I-70.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A semi pulling an empty enclosed trailer was blown over between MM 46-47 on I-70 from the outflow boundary that moved through.  The blow over also caused a grassfire.  No information about the size or if the fire burned anything else besides grass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on power lines in the Hunters Ridge subdivision in Prince George.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low moved across northern Mexico bringing a strong cold front through South-Central Texas. This resulted in very cold air in the boundary layer with a layer of above freezing air aloft which produced sleet and freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind chill temperature dropped to 5 degrees at the San Marcos Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms moved northward through Southeastern Arizona the afternoon and evening of June 17th, 2026. These storms caused thunderstorm wind damage causing 8 power poles to be downed and 7,000 customers to be without power in the Tucson Metro and damage to a power transformer that caused a power outage for Tohono O'odham Nation. Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms caused flash flooding in normally dry rivers and washes that resulted in multiple swift water rescues that resulted in 1 fatality and 2 injuries. Additionally, multiple roadways in Cochise County was impassible due to flooding. An estimated penny sized hail was reported on the SW side of Tucson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large palo verde tree downed due to thunderstorm wind gust.  Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 5 to 7 inches of snow across Piatt County.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a tree.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist onshore flow above the existing snow pack ahead of an advancing warm front resulted in widespread dense fog late on February 17th and early on February 18th. The fog dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Atlantic City International Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system developed along a baroclinic zone off the coast of Georgia during the overnight hours between Friday January thirtieth and Saturday January thirty-first. This low then began to rapidly deepen during the evening hours of January thirty-first while tracking northeastwards along the Carolina Coast making its closest point of approach to the coastal waters near North Carolina during the early morning hours of Sunday February first with a minimum pressure around 994 mb before the system departed off to the north and east. With strong high pressure ridging building in from the north and west a tight pressure gradient spread over most of our waters bringing Storm Force wind gusts to much of the coastal and interior waters of eastern North Carolina during the evening of January thirty-first to the morning of February first.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oregon Inlet CG XORE WeatherFlow site measured several hours of frequent storm force wind gusts between the evening of January thirty-first and the morning of February first. Reports came in via WeatherFlow.
