EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in a brief but widespread period of gale-force winds during the early to mid-morning hours across the Chesapeake Bay (north of Smith Point VA) and the tidal Potomac River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A squall produced an estimated wind gust to 34 knots (39 MPH) near a personal weather station (KMDSOLOM16) adjacent to the tidal Patuxent River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on State Route 35, near Rebecca Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-afternoon thunderstorms both in broken line segments and single cells developed along and ahead of a cold front. Marginal effective shear values up to 30 knots and MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg supported severe thunderstorms producing both wind and hail. Wind was primarily confined to northern West Virginia along a DCAPE gradient of 600-700 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates up to 6.5 C/km and up to 300 J/kg of hail growth zone CAPE supported numerous reports of quarter size within storms across western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree uprooted along Kingwood Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed and blocked both lanes of Highway 71 near Highway 477 in the Saint Maurice community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low top supercell developed in Hubbard county and produced an EF-0 tornado near Laporte, MN during the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Per video and pictures along with real time reports a weak tornado tracked ESE to the south of HWY 200 for about 7 minutes with intermittent kicking up of dust, leaves, and other small debris. No damage could be seen either in pictures or via high resolution satellite so the track is an estimate based on video evidence of time and location. Max estimated winds 65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front interacting with an unseasonably warm early January airmass with temperatures in the lower to middle 60s triggered a couple lines of strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of January 8th.  A few of the storms produced minor wind damage in Tazewell County and toppled two semis further east in Champaign County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown across the road near the intersection of Springfield Road and Par 3 Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak weather system combined with an arctic blast to bring high winds and light snow to the region on the morning of January 21. The Pierre Regional Airport ASOS measured the strongest wind gust at 76 mph. Matching 75 mph gusts were recorded by a personal weather station north of Pierre and the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station southeast of Reliance. While the Watertown COOP recorded 2.4 inches of snow, most other locations received an inch or less. The combination of wind and snow prompted No Travel Advised notices for Walworth, Hand, Faulk, Spink, Roberts, and Hamlin counties. Slick roads and intermittent low visibility resulted in a number of slide-ins across Roberts county.

Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms ahead of a slow moving cold front led to runoff flooding across portions of Montgomery County, Maryland. Rain rates of a half an inch to one inch per hour were observed yielding storm total rain amounts between one to two and half inches in a 3 hour period. Emergency management within the county notified us of multiple instances of small streams and poor drainage flooding. This included flooding from Rocky Run near McLean, VA and Accotink Creek near Annadale, VA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Woodburn Road closed at Spicewood Drive due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful winter storm developed on 24 January and did not fully let up until early on 26 January. After a strong Arctic cold front arrived the prior day, an area of low pressure tracked across the southeastern United States, bringing a plume of moisture into the Carolinas. A wintry mix of freezing rain, sleet, and snow developed, with the greatest snow and sleet accumulations over the Piedmont and the highest ice accumulations over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between a half inch to an inch of snow and sleet fell across the county, with a tenth of an inch or less of ice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Southeast 100th Lane near Highway U was washed out with 6 to 8 feet of fast flowing water over the road. Some road material was removed for the water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High based thunderstorms developed ahead of an upper level trough around the Lordsburg Playa.  Due to the very dry air at the surface, wind gusts in excess of 75 mph developed and brought near zero visibilities to the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NMDOT cameras captured near zero visibilities around mile marker 11 on Interstate 10.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex of thunderstorms developed across portions of north-central Kansas during the late afternoon hours of June 8th. These thunderstorms rapidly intensified and moved south and southeast across the I-70 corridor. Widespread wind damage occurred across portions of Lincoln, Ellsworth, Saline, McPherson, Marion, and Chase counties. In fact, a wind gust of 113 mph was measured at the Salina Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured via a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of March 15th. Several tornadoes occurred within this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed small to medium size tree limbs southwest of Winona.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. This resulted in blizzard conditions with widespread travel impacts from the early morning through the afternoon of February 18. ||Peak winds associated with the system included a gust measuring 72 mph by a mesonet station owned by a trained spotter in Faulkton, a 71 mph gust recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 4 miles north of Altamont (Deuel county) and a 67 mph gusts measured by the SDDOT RWIS 7 miles east of Clark. 47 additional weather stations would record a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. ||The Andover and Westport COOP observers reported blizzard or ground blizzard conditions at the time of their observations.||Not much overall snowfall occurred with the system, but within the band snowfall averaged about 4 inches with the COOP observers in Westport and Clark reporting a total of 4.1 and 4.0 inches of snowfall respectively. Additionally, the National Weather Service office just outside the Aberdeen Regional Airport measured 3.7 inches.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hailfall near the intersection of U.S. Highway 81 and Oklahoma Highway 45.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Southeast 1000 Rd east of Hwy J near the Birdsong Conservation area west of Collins was impassable due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary began the day nearly stationary near the Florida/Georgia border on the morning of the 2nd, progressing towards south of the region by that same evening. Widespread stratiform rainfall accompanied the front, with some embedded thunderstorms across northeast FL. Modest instability ahead of the front, as well as moderate to strong wind shear associated with the base of an upper level trough, supported isolated severe thunderstorms despite convection occurring during the first half of the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree limb fell on an RV and damaged the slide-out portion. A large tree limb fell on a car near US 441 and SE 80th St causing damage to the rear left side of the car. The nearby AWOS station KOCF Ocala Airport - Jim Taylor Fld measured 45 mph at 113 PM EDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and development of extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of Southwest Arkansas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-2.00+ inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought developed across Northern Howard County Arkansas by the second week of the month.

Severe thunderstorms occurred across the Texas Panhandle from during the late afternoon through late evening hours on May 22nd through May 24th. On the 22nd the environment was such that a few isolated storms were able to produce hail between one inch and 2.75 inches across parts of the southern Texas Panhandle. On the 23rd, thunderstorms produced straight line winds in excess of 58 mph across the central to northern Texas Panhandle. Additional severe wind gusts also occurred on the 24th. Several landspouts also occurred during this time period. An additional landspout also occurred on May 26th in the southwest Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail started around 2000CDT and would continue for about 15 minutes. Accumulating hail occurred as well. Hail started small but would eventually peak at the size of quarters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree branches up to eight-inches in diameter were blown down in Oakley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Near to below normal precipitation amounts over southwest New Mexico kept Severe(D2) drought conditions going through the month of March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The entire zone remained in Severe(D2) drought through the month of March.  The Cooperative Observer in Cliff received 0.64 inches of precipitation which was 0.01 inches above normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At 10:45PM on June 19, 2026, the Iron fire ignited on private land northwest of Eureka in Juab county, Utah. Given exceptionally hot, dry, and windy conditions through much of its early life, it would go on to grow rapidly through the next few days while exhibiting extreme fire behavior as it grew across portions of Juab, Utah, and Tooele counties (encompassing portions of public zones 102, 106, and 115). Thankfully, no structures were harmed with no reported injuries or fatalities. This fire has been contained as of July 3, 2026 and reached a total of 41,842 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

A strong surface low deepened as it moved through North Dakota, leading to high non-thunderstorm wind gusts. By the early afternoon, the strong winds were producing blowing dust and significantly reduced visibility across western North Dakota, with a Blowing Dust Warning and Blowing Dust Advisory issued for much of western and central North Dakota. Visibility was under one quarter of a mile at times. The strongest wind gust reported was 76 mph near Crosby in Divide County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fortuna NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed the area, with most robust activity occurring in the afternoon and evening of the 23rd and 24th. The majority of the area received one to three inches of rain during this time, with a few pockets between three and four inches.  Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Raleigh, Taylor, and Upshur Counties and led to a mud slide in Kanawha County. A couple of severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds which downed trees and power lines in Logan and Mingo counties the evening of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three large trees were uprooted along Yeager Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were downed in the Dublin area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While somewhat mild by January standards, a moisture rich system brought a period of valley rain and mountain snow, with some higher accumulations noted particularly in portions of Utah's northern mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utah Highway Patrol reported numerous traffic accidents on I-15 between approximately the Nephi exit and roughly two miles northward. The volume of accidents resulted in the southbound lanes of I-15 being closed and traffic being detoured through the city itself. The winter weather is assumed to be the likely cause of the incident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper shortwave trough moved across Texas and generated thunderstorms. Some storms formed along a dryline over the western edge of South-Central Texas. Other storms formed east of the dryline in a conditionally unstable, moist airmass. Storms produced all severe hazards and locally heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. Numerous roads were closed in the Cibolo area due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak replenishing arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 29th bringing colder air on northwest winds. Minimum air temperatures dropped to Zero to 15 below zero across much of VT with wind chill temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero across much of VT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures 5 to 15 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 20 to 30 below zero during the overnight of January 29th into the midday hours of January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
A few severe thunderstorms producing wind damage developed over Macomb, St. Clair, and Wayne counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local media reported roof damage to a home after a large tree limb fell on the structure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms trained over portions of Barton, Russell, Ellsworth, and Lincoln counties during the afternoon and evening hours of May 17th. Several reports of large hail and flash flooding were received. The largest hail report was near Milberger in Russell County with a size of 2.25 inches in diameter.

Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in mid to late March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 5500 acres in Adair County, more than 3800 acres in Cherokee County, more than 2300 acres in Latimer County, more than 2100 acres in Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Okfuskee Counties, more than 1100 acres in Mayes County, more than 500 acres in Le Flore County, and more than 450 acres in Sequoyah County.

On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.

Multiple rounds of severe weather moved northeast across south-central and southeast Kansas during the evening hours March 10th. These severe thunderstorms produced numerous reports of large hail and damaging winds.

The first of April saw the third consecutive day of severe thunderstorms across the region. An upper level storm system moving out of the Rockies into the Central Plains brought moisture and lift over West Texas creating widespread rain showers and thunderstorms. Surface conditions across the caprock were relatively dry which led to numerous virga showers that brought severe wind gusts. Once this activity reached better moisture off the caprock, the showers developed into severe thunderstorms producing severe wind gusts. ||High wind gusts (non-thunderstorms) from Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites are listed below:||67 mph at New Deal (Lubbock County),|64 mph at Shallowater (Lubbock County),|62 mph at Reese Center (Lubbock County), |58 mph at Floydada (Floyd County), and|58 mph at Olton (Lamb County).||High wind reports (non-thunderstorms) from Automated Surface Observing Systems (ASOS) are listed below:||64 mph at Lubbock International Airport (Lubbock County).

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Toombs County remained under D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on November 4, 2025, the county experienced a very brief period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in late January. By the end of February, conditions intensified to D3.  In total, the county sustained 18 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread and consistent rainfall following a pattern change in mid-May led to reductions in drought severity across Central Alabama from late May into early June. As two-month rainfall totals heading into June were near or above average, along with recovery in stream flows around the state, Severe (D2) drought conditions were removed from Central Alabama during the first week of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lingering Severe (D2) drought conditions across the southern half of Elmore County were removed in early June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds developed across all of northern Illinois during the morning of March 13th with widespread wind gusts to 60 mph with some higher peak gusts.  Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of Southwest Arkansas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged around 3 to 4 inches across much of Southwest Arkansas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A backyard was flooded due to excessive rainfall filling a usually dry stream, in PR-4441. Flood depth appears to be near 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported 1.25 inch hail in Point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding across eastern Nebraska. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||Sinitially presenting a significant large hail threat before transitioning into a destructive wind event. Through the early to mid-evening hours, widespread hail ranging from quarter (1.00 inch) to baseball (2.75 inches) size bombarded Platte, Saline, Seward, Gage, Lancaster, and Jefferson counties. The most intense hail occurred in Jefferson and Saline counties, highlighted by 2.75-inch hailstones measured near Plymouth and 2.50-inch hailstones reported near De Witt.||As the storms progressed into the late evening and early morning hours of May 17, the primary hazard shifted to severe and damaging straight-line winds. Jefferson County absorbed the brunt of this impact, with multiple mesonet stations and emergency management officials measuring extreme wind gusts between 75 and 88 mph in and around Fairbury. These intense winds caused significant impacts, including downed trees, widespread power outages, and near-zero visibility. The line of storms maintained severe intensity as it pushed eastward, producing gusts in excess of 60 mph across Gage and Richardson counties before eventually clearing the region.||In addition to the severe weather, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall brought flash flooding to southeast Nebraska, primarily impacting Gage, Johnson, Jefferson, and Saline counties. Widespread precipitation totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the region, with localized maximums of 5.80 to 7.00 inches concentrated in Gage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the evening of May 16, 2026, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across central Jefferson county. Emergency management reported several streets flooded in Fairbury, NE. The surge was driven by an intense downpour with rainfall rates of 1.00 to 2.00 inches per hour, resulting in total accumulations of 2 to 4 inches into the early morning hours of May 17, 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across Maryland. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 12 to 16 across Garrett County, with a general 8 to 12 across the remainder of the area aside from southern Maryland where 4-8 was observed. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed across southern Maryland. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state.

An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Realitos, TX recorded minimum wind chill values at or below 30F degrees (Cold Weather Advisory Criteria) for 9.5 hours from 2:24-11:54am CST on Sunday January 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm system impacted the State of Tennessee starting late Friday, January 23 and continuing into Sunday, January 25, 2026. Cold air moved into Tennessee Friday evening, setting the stage for winter weather through the weekend. This cold air along with a potent storm system resulted in primarily snow Friday night into Saturday morning. However, as warm air aloft moved north into Tennessee, this changed the precipitation from snow to sleet and then finally to freezing rain Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon. By the time precipitation came to an end, snow accumulations were highest across northwest Middle Tennessee where generally 3 to 5 inches were measured. A swath of ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inches was reported from Wayne County northeast through Nashville and to the Tennessee/Kentucky border. Locally higher amounts over one half inch were reported around the Nashville metro area.||These accumulations caused widespread, crippling damage in the form of broken and downed trees and power lines, dangerous to impossible travel conditions, and hundreds of thousands of power outages. Nashville Electric Service (NES) alone reported 230,000 customers without power which is the largest number of outages at one time NES has ever experienced. ||The other major impact from this winter storm was frigid temperatures. Cold air already in place over the weekend was reinforced Sunday night as arctic air moved into Tennessee behind this winter storm. The coldest temperature readings were recorded Monday and Tuesday mornings with widespread readings in the single digits and wind chills below zero. With these very cold temperatures, impacts were felt long after the precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mixture of snow, sleet, and ice impacted Pickett County during the early morning hours of January 24th into the afternoon of January 25th. A variety of reporting sources measured snow accumulations of 1 to 2 inches with ice accumulations of 0.10 to 0.15 inches. This led to several reports of treacherous travel and downed powerlines, trees, and tree branches. Total power outages were around 1,000 customers across Pickett County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in Missouri during the morning of May 31st. As they passed through central Missouri, one cell was able to produce minor flooding in Boone and Moniteau counties. The thunderstorms then congealed before producing a swath of wind damage in southeast Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds estimated to be about 60 mph in magnitude downed large, healthy trees around St. Francois county. One large branch fell onto a metal outdoor pool, bending its frame in Doe Run.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 5 to 9 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.

A complex setup characterized by moisture overrunning an entrenched wedge of cold air at the surface led to freezing rain and sleet beginning across north Georgia late on the night of January 24 and persisting through much of the day on January 25. Widespread ice accretion of one-tenth to one-quarter inch ice occurred with some areas receiving over a half inch of freezing rain accumulation. ||Significant tree damage and power outages occurred in the worst-affected areas of northeast Georgia, while spotty tree damage and isolated power outages occurred in other areas. Additionally, a layer of sleet occurred in much of northeast Georgia, leading to hazardous roadways. ||The hardest hit areas locally were White County as well as portions of Dawson and Lumpkin counties. The vast majority of the White County lost power with many locations remaining without power for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light rain showers began on the evening of the 24th. Rain briefly transitioned to ice on the morning of the 25th, however temperatures warmed through the day and quickly melted any accumulations which managed to stick on elevated surfaces. Northern portions of the county which were in the wedge were able to remain colder for a little longer and resulted in ice accumulations on elevated surface up to 0.2 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree branch was blown down onto a fence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The first round of storms arrived during the early morning hours of the 27th, associated with a warm front lifting northeastward across the region. Being elevated storms, large hail was the primary impact. Additional isolated to scattered storms developed during the midday hours, also tracking northeastward with large hail. ||In Southern Illinois, early morning MLCAPE values were around 750-1000J/kg, DCAPE was 700-900J/kg, effective bulk shear was a very robust 50-60kts, and mid-level lapse rates were around 6.5C/km.||Southern Illinois received primarily hail with early to mid morning thunderstorms, with the largest reports to golf ball size in Vergennes and Dowell. The one wind damage report involved portions of trees falling at a home in Anna, damaging a porch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to quarter size fell north of Macedonia. Report submitted via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 65 MPH EF0 tornado touched down north of Albany, LA and tracked southeast. The damage was large branches and tree debris along the line that also lines up with the radar signature. The tornado exited Livingston Parish and entered Tangipahoa Parish just west of Kinchen Road about one half mile south of Highway 442.

Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Dimmit County improved from Exceptional (D4) Drought to Extreme (D3) Drought. Atascosa, Bastrop, Bexar, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Lavaca, Lee, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties all improved from D3 to Severe (D2) Drought. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second round of high winds and snow showers created hazardous travel conditions across northeast South Dakota. Although snow accumulations were minor, totaling only 2 inches or less, the light snow led to slick roads and intermittent near-blizzard conditions. These conditions resulted in several accidents, including a vehicle rollover on Interstate 90 near Vivian and a jackknifed semi-trailer on Highway 12 west of Aberdeen. The highest wind gust of 63 mph was recorded by South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet stations near Roscoe and Bowdle.

The incident was caused by high winds and light snow which led to poor visibility in the area, along with icy road conditions. A peak wind gust of 54 mph was recorded on the South Dakota State University mesonet station 12 miles south of Vivian at 12:50 pm.

In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens and lower 20s by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across East and Northeast Texas from late evening on January 25th through late morning on January 27th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds on Wray Street and another tree was reported down over Overton Street near the Martinsville Futbol Soccer Field.

Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over far southwestern Nebraska and the Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon hours of May 30th. As this activity progressed slowly east into the evening hours, numerous large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported. A couple of tornadoes were also reported. Hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported.

The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.

The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lexington County EM reported trees down near the intersection of Tindal Rd and Cedar Creek Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Siding was ripped off of buildings and small tree limbs were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of strong thunderstorms slowly spilled into northeast Kentucky ahead of a cold front, arriving into Lawrence County by the afternoon of May 20th. Damaging winds accompanying the storms resulted in a few instances of downed trees and power lines before progressing northeastward. The cold front passed through shortly after, bringing the risk for severe weather to an end across northeast Kentucky.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Verona NDDOT site reported wind gusts to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in Madison Township.
