EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surge of Arctic air invaded Northern Louisiana during late January with bitterly cold temperatures and light northerly winds. In wake of the this Arctic air arriving on the evening of January 24th, overnight low temperatures plummeted into the teens and lower 20s by the morning on January 26th and again on the 27th. Although northerly winds were relatively light throughout much of the event, they only further contributed to the dangerously cold temperatures across Northern Louisiana from late evening on January 24th through late morning on January 27th.||The following is a list of the 7 direct and indirect fatalities per parish from this period of very cold temperatures: ||Caddo Parish: 2 fatalities...A 63 year old male and an unknown aged male died in Downtown Shreveport due to hypothermia. |Desoto Parish: 3 fatalities...An 86 year old male died due to carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in his garage. A 79 year old female died of hypoxia when her oxygen generator failed during a power outage. A 74 year old male died of hypothermia due to an extended power outage at his home. |Sabine Parish: 1 fatality...A 59 year old female died of hypothermia due to an extended power outage at her home. |Jackson Parish: 1 fatality...A 65 year old male died at his home due to hypothermia due to an extended power outage at his home.

The vast majority of the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw significant rainfall deficits, ranging from 4 to 8 inches below normal, from January through the end of June. Only some small areas scattered across the region had near normal rainfall by the end of June. After seeing winter wheat failures this year, summer crop planting and emergence were delayed. Soil moisture had been too short to support seed germination, stunting cotton, corn and sorghum crops. Dryland cotton that did sprout did not establish uniform stands. Much of the rangelands were unable to grow, leaving ranchers relying heavily on supplemental feeding and watering, leading some producers to start considering herd reductions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought was observed in early June, but around normal to slightly above normal precipitation was observed for 3 of the 4 weeks of June. A very dry week around mid-June managed to reduce or flip any normal to above normal rainfall that had been present to normal or below normal for the month. Still, some spotty normal to above normal anomalies were observed in Dallam and Hartley counties. Moore county was almost entirely below normal for the month. Drought conditions improved by 1 category due to the rainfall observed, but Moderate (D1) to D2 persists due to a 1-4 inch rainfall deficit over the previous 180 days.

Thunderstorms developed along and ahead of the front during the afternoon hours, then became increasingly influenced by storm outflow as they moved south faster than the front itself. The strongest storms produced a mix of large hail and damaging wind across portions of southwest Mississippi.

The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough axis extending from the eastern Great Lakes into the Mid-Atlantic states and a ridge centered over the central and southern Plains placed the forecast area directly between both features. These storms produce isolated flash flooding and severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines downed by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Evidence of a high-end EF-1 (110mph) tornado was found in south- central Victoria County. Drone footage showed a scour track that began over farmland between Crouch Rd and HWY-185, and ended near Crouch Rd east of York Rd along with a track of debris. In between, several manufactured homes on Jared Rd, Lexie Ln, and York Rd suffered significant roof damage, broken windows, and scattered debris correlated to circulation of a tornado. One manufactured home was completely destroyed along Jared Rd. The tornado track was found to be around 1.1 miles long and a width of around 400 yards, spanning from 2:02-2:06pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 21, 2026, a shortwave disturbance moving across the northern Plains drove a cold front through eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Ahead of the frontal passage, northwesterly winds strengthened throughout the afternoon, driven by a tightening surface pressure gradient and deep mixing that tapped into stronger winds aloft. Consequently, strong, non-thunderstorm wind gusts overspread the region, with measured peak gusts ranging from 58 to 71 mph. Notable observations included 71 mph in Tekamah, NE, 64 mph near Verdel, NE, and 61 mph in Harlan, IA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 57 mph near Woodbine, IA. Personal weather station measured gust of 61 mph just north of the county line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct clusters of severe thunderstorms impacted central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon and evening of June 4. In the northeast, severe storms generated large hail up to golf ball size five miles south-southeast of Cottonwood Lake and nine miles southeast of Tulare. The Huron Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) 12 miles east-southeast of Sunshine Bible Academy recorded a peak wind gust of 86 mph.||A separate cluster of storms tracked through mainly central and south central South Dakota producing peak wind gusts of 71 mph and 68 mph at the South Dakota Department of Transportation Road Weather Information System (RWIS) stations six miles southwest of the Joe Creek Recreation Area and nine miles north-northwest of Vivian, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public estimated thunderstorm winds gusted as high as 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into February in northern and central Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of February was 21 inches at the Caribou office, gradually increasing to 26 inches by February 24th. All climate sites recorded below average precipitation, with generally 1.5 - 2.0 inch deficits. At the end of January, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In February,  drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Interior Hancock led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late January and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

In the wake of convection earlier in the day, a meso-low moved through far northwest Indiana and southwest Michigan, producing a widespread swath of 45-55+ mph wind gusts. The highest wind gust report was a 70 mph gust that occurred at the South Bend Airport.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued, and worsened across Wilkes county through April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure passing through Ontario dragged a strong cold front west to east across the region in the afternoon hours. Boundary orthogonal bands of snow squalls developed ahead of the front with steep low level lapse rates and non-zero surface-based CAPE. The result was a widespread area of snow bands reducing visibility to a quarter mile or less with gusty wind greater than 35 mph and rapid accumulation on roadways resulting in at least one highway accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS KPJC measured quarter mile visibility in a snow squall.

Isolated thunderstorms began forming east of the dryline around 1500CDT, including a long-tracked supercell which produced a brief tornado, strong winds, and a swath of large to very large hail from the Del Rio area to the Hill Country. A line of thunderstorms formed along the dryline over Val Verde County after 1900CDT which tracked across the southern Edwards Plateau and Hill Country through the evening, producing some strong winds before weakening near the I-35 corridor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front stationed across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours allowed for thunderstorm development to form across the Shenandoah Valley during the late morning hours of March 16, 2026 that began to surge towards southern Pennsylvania. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video of homes flooding in the Bayou Cane area.

A weakening mesoscale convective system (MCS) advanced east southeast into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours on June 24th, just north of an outflow reinforced frontal boundary which extended from Northeast Texas into North Central Louisiana and eastward into Mississippi. Behind the MCS, showers and thunderstorms increased in coverage from North Louisiana into Southwest Arkansas. Wind profiles in the 925-850 millibar layer showed some modest strengthening into the 25-30 knot range from the south southwest, helping to remove lingering lower level convective inhibition centered near 850 mb. Low level flow overrunning the surface boundary set up a convergence axis in the 925-850 millibar layer, aligned from Southeast Oklahoma into Northwest Louisiana. This zone of convergence focused increasing coverage of elevated thunderstorms throughout the morning, beneath increasingly diffluent flow aloft in the 300-400 millibar layer. The convergence axis was aligned with a gradient in MLCAPE of 500 to 1500 J/kg noted to the southwest of the axis. Precipitable water (PWAT) values ranged from 1.7 to near 2 inches across the region. As a result, hourly rainfall rates of 1 to 2+ inches occurred within areas of training storms with localized rainfall totals of 2 to 6+ inches common across Southwest Arkansas. Thus, numerous reports of flash flooding were recorded throughout the morning into the mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Barton Bethel Road closed due to flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This system dropped 2 to 4 of snow in the northern two thirds of the county from Canyon to Amarillo. While it is possible there was up to 5 inches in the south, closest to the heavier swath of snow, there were no measurements confirmed. 2.4 to 3 inches of snow fell around Canyon and Palo Duro Canyon. The south and southwest side of Amarillo measured 2 to 3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Garrison NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Dade County entered January under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Following a period of improvement, the county saw a reduction in drought intensity, officially falling below the D2 drought thresholds on January 12. This event, which originally reached the D2 threshold on December 30, 2025, peaked in both spatial extent and intensity on January 6. In total, the county sustained two weeks of D2 conditions during this brief event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in a brief but widespread period of gale-force winds during the early to mid-morning hours across the Chesapeake Bay (north of Smith Point VA) and the tidal Potomac River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A squall produced an estimated wind gust to 34 knots (39 MPH) near a personal weather station (KMDSTEVE164) adjacent to the Chesapeake Bay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across western Wisconsin, with RCX in Ladysmith reporting the coldest wind chill of -49F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -49F.||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F.||The lowest wind chills were:|-49F at KRCX (Rusk).|-47F at KRNH (St Croix).|-45F at KEAU (Chippewa).|-43F at KUBE (Barron).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KEAU reported wind gusts as high as 35 mph during the evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -24F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -45F at 8AM on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a quasi-stationary front extending across southern Missouri and northwest Tennessee during the afternoon hours of June 13, 2026.  These storms were supported by SBCAPE values of 3000 to 4000 J/kg and 0-6km bulk shear values of around 30 knots. The storms formed into a line by late afternoon, with several reports of damaging winds. Slow-moving storms combined with precipitable water values around 2 inches to produce heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down, blocking the northbound lane of Munford Giltedge Road near Sturdivant Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave brought about windy thunderstorms across much of southern MT. In it's wake, a cold front crossed the area, and strong winds behind the front persisted well into the 14th. Non-convective gusts up to 80 mph were observed, with convective gusts up to 80 mph observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Harlowton S DOT gusted to 72 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front attendant to a southern Canada low pressure system moved slowly through western and central Virginia, triggering showers and thunderstorms. Bulk shear of around 30kts just east of the Blue Ridge supported damaging wind gusts from a few storms, which resulted in localized tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Cottontown Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of southwest Indiana on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -15 to locally -18 in Vanderburgh County, IN on the 26th. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th with wind chill values warming above -5.

On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines downed in Fillmore.
