EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms fired along a stalled frontal boundary throughout the day, resulting in localized heavy rainfall and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Old Columbus Road between West Choctaw Drive and East Choctaw Drive was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A shed was destroyed from a nearby trailer park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercells developed and moved into north central Kansas in the late afternoon period. Hazards reported were initially large hail to 2 inches in diameter before the convection formed into a line, tracking southeast during the evening hours. The storms produced winds around 70 mph and heavy rainfall amounts to 3.5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Union Pacific railroad observation site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moving across the area combined with a strong jet stream to produce high wind gusts across portions of western and central Wyoming. The highest recorded wind gust was 89 mph at Red Canyon along South Pass. In the lower elevations, wind gusts of 70 mph or greater occurred in Johnson and Natrona Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at the Hidden Creek weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms near 9 AM in the Missouri Bootheel with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of the Bootheel, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A metal roof was blown off a home and a few outbuildings were damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Disturbances in the upper-level flow, coupled with upslope flow in the higher terrain, caused shower and thunderstorm development across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. Dry low-levels allowed several storms to produce strong downbursts, the strongest of which occurred in Seagraves, where damage to multiple buildings was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported 2 broken power poles southwest of Seagraves. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar. The total cost of damages and the maximum wind gust is also estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a southeastward moving cold front, broken lines of showers and thunderstorms developed in the evening hours. A surge of mid 70s temperatures with upper 50s dew points resulted in sufficient destabilization with MLCAPE up to 1000 J/kg, effective shear of 30-40 knots, and a gradient of 700-900 DCAPE. This allowed for some thunderstorms to become severe with large hail and damaging wind as the result, including two measured 58 mph gusts in southwest Pennsylvania.

Under strong 1027 mb high pressure, light wind allowed for efficient radiational cooling and minimum wind chill values to dip to -10 to -20F areawide with some spots below -20F, mostly in sheltered areas and higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill values generally ranged from -10 to -15 degrees with the exception of a -20 degree reading at the Zelienople Airport AWOS in the early morning hours of the 31st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal moisture moved into the Four Corners from the southwest due to remnant Atmospheric River moisture ahead of a strong closed low pressure system and cold front that brought mountain snow above 9000 feet and valley rain. Temperatures were very warm ahead of this system and fell to below normal levels afterwards with abundant moisture resulting in heavy, wet snow favoring the central and southern mountains with the heaviest accumulations above a foot at the higher elevations where the winds were also the strongest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 9 to 18 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 22 inches at Wolf Creek Summit. Winds gusted in the 45 to 60 mph range with a peak gust of 60 mph at Wolf Creek and a peak wind of 49 mph at Lewis Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting northern to central Maryland during the late afternoon hours with swaths of 60 to 70 mph wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees blew down north of Reisterstown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 1.25 inch hail from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Calm winds and clearing skies behind a cold frontal passage resulted in a few hours of dense fog formation near dawn in portions of Southeast Missouri near Cape Girardeau.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on County Roads 15 and 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Richland County Emergency Management reported trees fell on a residence along Howard St in Columbia.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power line down on the 2000 block of bethlehem church rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into an warm and unstable airmass primarily west of I-95. This resulted in bands of showers and thunderstorms that produced localized damaging wind and spotty large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were a couple reports of trees and large tree limbs down in Romney.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Gulf low moved inland over the Alaska Panhandle along with a ridge over the Southcentral and the Al-Can border. These features allowed for easterly waves to move over the Susitna Valley and into the East Kuskokwim Valley. These easterly waves, further enhanced by an upper low dropping into Southwest Alaska, combined with warmer temperatures and ample moisture allowed for many thunderstorms to form over the Susitna Valley and the East Kuskokwim Valley. There were 2420 lightning strikes over the Susitna Valley and Talkeetna Mountains from thunderstorms on June 19. By 9:30 PM that day, six fires were confirmed over the Susitna Valley. In the Susitna Valley, the greatest concentration of lightning strikes was northeast of Skwentna around the Petersville area. In the East Kuskokwim Valley, there were many lightning strikes around Lime Village.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous lightning strikes from thunderstorms were observed around Lime Village during the afternoon hours of June 19. There were numerous fire starts but the Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Protection (DFFP) immediately deployed aviation and ground assets to suppress the starts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cooperative observer at Michigan State University Extension Lake City Experimental Farm measured a storm total snowfall of 10.4 inches, and reported ice buildup of 0.4 to 0.5 inch; additional reports of radial ice around 0.25 inch across the county, with tree and infrastructure damage resulting in at least 60 percent of utility customers losing power by the morning of the 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across western North Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Several isolated, weak tornadoes occurred, along with sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Utility company reported trees blown down on power lines and causing an outage along Dutch Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported a downed tree from thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tennis ball size hail was reported in Flat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum windchill of -7F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 18-22 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported along with flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down near Hawkinstown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills. By Friday morning, much of the area was seeing temperatures of at least 20 degrees below zero, and as cold as 25 degrees below zero measured at the South Dakota State University mesonet stations in Gettysburg and 23 miles north of Highmore. With these cold temperatures and a northwest breeze, wind chills across much of the area had fallen to 40 degrees below zero and colder, with the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Summit coming in with a wind chill of 53 degrees below zero. Temperatures failed to warm much during the day, with highs in the single digits to teens below zero. Watertown set a record for the lowest daily high temperature, reaching only 11 degrees below zero.

A significant severe weather outbreak across northeast Louisiana and central and southern MS amid a favorably sheared environment. A capping inversion limited early convection, which allowed for higher instability. Supercell initiation began in the afternoon and eroded the capping inversion to allow a long track supercell to take root. This supercell produced a long track EF-3 tornados. Several other brief, weak tornadoes occurred. Supercells also produced hail as large as baseballs and straight line wind damage also occurred. The duration of rainfall also lead to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado downed multiple trees along a path in a wooded area west of LA Highway 15 just north of the Deer Park community. The tornado was observed from LA 15 by a storm chaser. The maximum estimated wind speed was 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked east of the Ohio Valley before redeveloping off the Northeast coast on Sunday the 25th. Snow spread from south to north Sunday morning, becoming heaviest from mid-morning through the early evening. The snowfall gradually tapered off early Monday morning, though pockets of freezing rain and drizzle lingered across central New York. Light snow showers and flurries continued into Monday afternoon, accompanied by strong, gusty winds that caused localized blowing snow and reduced visibility. By Monday night, lake-effect snow showers developed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulated between 6 and 11 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread crop damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms again developed late in the afternoon of the 23rd in two separate locations. Isolated thunderstorms initially developed across the western South Plains into the Permian Basin which produced large hail. Numerous outflow boundaries interacted with each other creating new convection and several landspout tornadoes. A second area of thunderstorms moved into the southern Texas Panhandle from eastern New Mexico. Both areas of thunderstorm activity merged into a single complex of thunderstorms producing severe wind gusts as it moved across the Rolling Plains through the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Hackberry measured severe wind gusts from 2318 CST through 2320 CST. A peak wind gust of 64 mph was measured at 2319 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple confirmations, including mPING reports and shared social media images, of ping pong ball-size hail in Chandler. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across northeast Georgia by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 10 driest on record across the area. Unusually warm weather developing during March and April of 2026 exacerbated drought impacts. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large branches up to 12 inches in diameter reported down in Avondale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm chances increased across South Texas on February 14th as a large-scale upper-level trough moved east from the western United States and pushed an associated surface low and cold front toward the region. Ahead of the front, a strengthening low-level jet transported Gulf moisture northward, gradually increasing atmospheric moisture and supporting scattered showers overnight into the morning hours. Early activity remained relatively light and limited in coverage, primarily affecting the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads, and northern Brush Country as modest lift interacted with increasing low-level moisture.||By the afternoon and evening, the approaching cold front provided stronger lift across the region while upper-level jet support enhanced large-scale ascent. Atmospheric moisture values rose to well above seasonal normals, and modest instability developed with CAPE values near 1000 J/kg. These ingredients allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop along and ahead of the advancing boundary, with the greatest coverage focused across northern portions of the area where mid-level capping was weakest. Storms were expected to organize into a broken line as they moved from northwest to southeast through the afternoon and evening.||Although the overall severe weather risk remained limited, portions of the northern Brush Country, northern Coastal Plains, and Victoria Crossroads were placed under a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms. South Texas largely remained on the southwestern edge of the more favorable severe environment centered farther north and east across Southeast Texas. However, a few storms briefly intensified as the front moved through, producing isolated damaging wind gusts, and severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station FW9607 Kingsville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex, multi-day weather system moved across the region bringing rounds of wind, snow, and when combined, blizzard conditions. Strong winds aloft brought a round of high winds to the region beginning late on the 11th through the 12th. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Copper Camp SNOTEL measured 13 inches of new snow on the 13th. On the afternoon of the 14th, Rogers Pass was reported to have had severe driving conditions and required tire chains by the Montana Department of Transportation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported 1.75 inch hail just south of Rockwall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak area of low pressure and warm front produced widespread light precipitation across the region. For locations near and northwest of the I-95 corridor, temperatures where near or just below freezing at precipitation onset the morning of March 3rd. Precipitation began as a very light wintry before changing to a period of light freezing rain, then eventually turned to all rain as temperatures warmed above freezing as the day progressed. A light glaze of ice was reported across these areas, with reports ranging from a trace to a few hundredths of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A light glaze of ice from freezing rain occurred across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed north of a semi-stationary front during the late afternoon hours on Wednesday (5/27).  The strongest storms produced damaging winds and large hail up to 2 inches in diameter as they tracked through central Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel size hail fell near Wausau.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported power lines down across the road near 1980 Low Ground Road and power outages in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Erie during the afternoon and evening of Monday, May 19, 2026. Several severe thunderstorms within this line generated thunderstorm wind damage and wind gusts across Northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public weather station reported a wind gust of 65 mph. In addition, several tree limbs were snapped and minor roof shingle damage occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An inverted trough of low pressure moved into Texas from the Gulf of Mexico and generated thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail over South-Central Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced wind gusts measured at 51 kts by the AWOS at San Marcos Regional Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June had areas that received above and below normal precipitation in what is typically a dry month. There was little change to the drought conditions around Southern New Mexico with Moderate(D1) to Severe(D2) drought the most common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The entire zone remained in Severe(D2) drought through the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported on several roads near Locust Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines fell down at Holland Road and Farlow Road in New Church. Multiple power outages were reported in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down on Black Hawk Drive in the Love Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front draped across Arkansas in tandem with an approaching upper level trough axis would spur multiple days of severe winds, flash flooding, and heavy rain totals for the multi-day event across the state of Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple county roads were blocked off in and around Amagon due to high water covering them completely making them impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Northeast Pennsylvania. and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region. With one storm, lightning struck a church and led to a fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees, resulting in road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed and a shed destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power outages reported southwest of Malad City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold/Wind Chill: KRBO and KCRP reported wind chills at or below 15 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Extreme Cold Warning criteria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving boundary was the focus for afternoon thunderstorms as the day's capping inversion lifted. Pea and dime-size hail reports were common, with a handful of reports for 1 inch hail or larger.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo on Facebook shows quarter-size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple elevated thunderstorms moved across the Ozarks during the afternoon. Some of the storms were moving as slow as 10 miles an hour. This produced localized flooding in Barton County, but one storm in Miller County was able to take advantage of the environment and produced hail up to 3 inches in size as is moved slowly over the town if Iberia, MO. Another storm then moved along a similar track approximately 3 hours later producing hail up to tennis balls in size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tennis ball sized hail was reported. multiple homes, out buildings, vehicles and businesses received damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex, multi-day weather system moved across the region bringing rounds of wind, snow, and when combined, blizzard conditions. Strong winds aloft brought a round of high winds to the region beginning late on the 11th through the 12th. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTNOR Norris Hill measured a 59 mph wind gust and averaged a sustained wind of 40 mph between 1:30am to 2:30am MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper low brought heavy snow to much of eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota on February 17th and 18th. Snowfall totals ranged from a few inches to nearly 17 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received a public report of 10 inches of snow in Minnewaukan, ND.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure tracked across the Northern Plains, leading to moisture advection and isolated severe thunderstorms across central North Dakota. Supercells developed during the evening hours, continuing until the late evening. The strongest wind gust report was near Minot Air Force Base in Ward County, where a trained spotter reported wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. The largest hail occurred in McHenry County, with hail of 2 inches in diameter observed near Velva and Drake. A tornado was observed approximately 4 miles east-southeast of Riverdale in McLean County around 9 PM CDT. There was no known damage from this tornado, therefore there is no estimated wind speed and it is assigned a rating of EF-Unknown per NWS policy.

A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limb downed within 8100 block of Pine Road. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 10 degrees or less across eastern Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 4F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam County Emergency  Management reported that a 40 acre wildfire  was triggered by a lightning strike late on  Saturday night. Time of event based on  lightning strike data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 13, heavy rain began to fall and quickly led to extensive damage across  Maui. This damage included widespread infrastructure damage, property and home losses, and emergency rescues. At 1030 AM HST, heavy rain washed away Lower Kula Road near Ohala Place, and all of South Kihei Road closed due to severe flooding. On March 14, 40 people were reportedly stranded in Hana due to flooding. Honoapiilani Hwy (Hwy 30) was closed from  Kuihelani Hwy to the Olowalu dump due to flooding, swift water, and the integrity of  the Ukuhehame bridge. At approximately 3:45 pm on March 14, a section of South Kihei Road collapsed. Many other roads across Maui were also closed. A home in Iao Valley collapsed into the Iao River. A Target store in Kahului reported severe flooding with several inches of water inisde the store.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms moved across SE Arkansas during the evening hours of March 15 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a transformer that was damaged due to winds. This caused power outages for a few hours for parts of W Crossett.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions persisted across parts of northeastern Minnesota during the month of March. A slight reduction in the area of D2 Severe Drought was realized with the updates on the 17th and 31st, but no significant changes were observed. Precipitation for the month was around 0.25 to 0.50 inches below normal in the western portion of the D2 Severe Drought area with 0.5 to 1 inches above normal in the eastern portion where the reduction in area occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought covered the northern 2/3rds of the county at the start of March. Precipitation over the month was around 0.25 to 0.75 inches above normal which led to improvements in the drought status with the updates on the 17th and 31st. This left just the northwestern corner of the county in D2 Severe Drought at the end the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were knocked down in Covington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Broad southwesterly flow aloft on the eastern side of a western CONUS trough carried several weak disturbances across the central Gulf Coast, while southeasterly low-level flow maintained deep moisture. Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi. A thunderstorm over the local marine areas produced a waterspout near the Interstate 10 Twin Span as well as severe wind gusts at other coastal locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet XGPT in Gulfport on Highway 90 measured a thunderstorm wind gusts of 41 mph or 36 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Moderate (D1) drought to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the region Wednesday and Thursday that brought heavy rain, damaging wind, and several brief tornadoes to eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO.  The more widespread wind damage occurred Wednesday afternoon June 10th from a derecho that developed in eastern Iowa and moved east. This downed trees, power lines primarily along and north of I-80. The more significant winds between 70-80 mph winds were seen north of the Hwy 20 corridor. A second round of storms later on produced isolated wind damage, including some damage north of Geneseo, IL that was due to straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak wind gust was measured by COOP observer.  Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A sharpening High Plains dryline, in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest, spawned scattered thunderstorms across western to northwest Kansas during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 30th. Storms moved north to northeast. A measured wind gust to 68 mph and half-dollar sized hail both occurred in Norton County. Additionally, portions of Graham County received dime to nickel sized hail.

Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to tennis ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This weak tornado crossed into Olmsted County from Dodge County, damaging trees and farm outbuildings before dissipating as it moved northeast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed north of a semi-stationary front during the late afternoon hours on Wednesday (5/27).  The strongest storms produced damaging winds and large hail up to 2 inches in diameter as they tracked through central Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell in Wausau.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning hours of June 13, 2026, severe thunderstorms tracked through eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa, producing hail and damaging wind gusts. The storms were driven by moisture return from a low-level jet impinging on a slowly sagging cold front. Elevated showers and thunderstorms developed over eastern Nebraska prior to sunrise before moving eastward into an environment characterized by sufficient instability and shear to support severe weather. Notable reports included quarter-sized hail (up to 1.00 inch in diameter) in and around the Omaha metro area���including Fremont (Dodge County), Douglas, and Sarpy counties in Nebraska, as well as Mills and Pottawattamie counties in Iowa. Measured wind gusts ranged from 58 to 60 mph, with an estimated wind gust of 70 mph recorded near Valley, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Employee estimated wind gusts of 55-60 mph with dime-size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Rock River at Newville rose to Moderate flood stage. Flood waters surrounded some homes near East Mallwood Drive and were into yards and roads across eastern Newville. Floodwaters affected a riverside restaurant and its parking lot on the south side of the river.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong long track tornado with estimated peak winds of 165 mph touched down near the intersection of Grand Boulevard and Clay Street just east of Interstate 65 in rural Lake County. The tornado caused tree and crop damage until it crossed into Porter County, just east of where Dike Road turns into Union Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across Augusta Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tin roofing material removed from a fishing camp. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail to baseballs in size was reported with multiple homes and vehicles in town damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An overall active pattern continued into June 2026 with daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received generally 3 to 8 inches of rain with the highest amounts favoring areas along and near the Tennessee River as well as areas near the Tennessee/Alabama border. It was also these areas that received more than their monthly normal precipitation while other areas continued to run a deficit. Fortunately, these repeated rounds of rain continued to improve drought conditions. For the first time since April 2026, none of Middle Tennessee was in extreme drought. About 11 percent of the area continued to be in severe drought, an improvement from 34 percent in May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from May 2026 improved in June to moderate drought conditions across Putnam County.

CZ_NAME: KUSKOKWIM DELTA COAST AND NUNIVAK ISLAND
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front atop a ridge in the East Bering moved into the Southwest Alaska Mainland, bringing a swath of precipitation and gusty southerly winds. The southerly winds brought about warm air advection, causing temperatures to increase. However, before temperatures rose above freezing in the Kuskokwim Delta, the gusty winds with the front allowed for a period of blizzard conditions in the Kuskokwim Delta Coast on February 13.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Toksook Bay ASOS (PAOO) observed a several hour period of blizzard conditions (Visibility less than or equal to 1/4 statute miles, winds gusting to around 35 mph, and blowing snow) from 9:30 AM to 3:21 PM AKST on Feb 13. Temperatures warmed afterwards and precipitation transitioned to freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in Lauderdale County, Alabama and tracked into southern Middle TN. After the tornado crossed the Tennessee and Alabama state line, it traveled for ten more miles through Lawrence and Giles counties. In Bonnertown, many residences were impacted with several homes damaged. A few manufactured homes were moved off their piers, and a couple mobile homes were lofted or slid, but remained in tact. Other structural damage included missing awnings, removed shingles, carports thrown, and trees falling onto the structures. Several farm outbuildings were damaged. Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted. Beyond Bonnertown, the tornado continued east along Appleton Road, downing trees and destroying a chicken farm. The tornado then crossed into Giles County. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong clipper low tracked through the Upper Great Lakes, bringing widespread heavy snowfall which transitioned to lake enhanced/effect as the storm progressed. Over a foot of snow fell at several locations. Many school districts, colleges and a few businesses were closed across the U.P.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall created difficult travel conditions in Gogebic County.  Snowfall analysis and observations showed 6-12 of snowfall over much of the county, lesser amounts were observed close to the lakeshore.  Key impacts: travel delays, school closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of March 15th, a QLCS moved through southern and south-central Illinois. Stronger segments of the QLCS produced wind damage across the region. The QLCS ended up producing 8 tornadoes while it passed through the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado moved into Montgomery County from Macoupin County, where it caused minor damage to a home on W County Line Road. The tornado then took on a near due northerly track as it occluded and caused minor tree damage before it dissipated completely just north of Saint Johns Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the sixth consecutive month, much of the region experienced below normal precipitation, with deficits of 1 to 2 inches common during the month of January. Mean temperatures were above normal for much of autumn, but below normal during December and January. While precipitation was below normal for the month, a disturbance brought almost an inch of rainfall west of I-55, which led to modest improvement in the drought conditions. Elsewhere, the ongoing drought expanded across central and eastern Illinois. Streamflows, lake levels, and regional water tables remained well below normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe (D2) Drought was ongoing at the start of the month. The official observation for Lincoln measured 1.13 inches of precipitation during the month of January, which was 1.04 inches below normal. The continued below normal precipitation resulted in Severe Drought persisting through the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was received from mPing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms pushed through southeast Texas, producing damaging winds and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee shared a photo of 1 inch hail, around the size of a quarter. They noted that the hail lasted around 3 to 5 minutes in duration.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold frontal boundary progressed across the southeastern states on the 23rd of June before slowing progress and nearly stalling over the northeast FL/southeast GA region. Plenty of summer moisture and instability in the vicinity of the boundary resulted in numerous to widespread showers and thunderstorms for several days in a row.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Duval County Emergency Management has  reported over a dozen reports of power lines  down through portions of western Duval  county in the vicinity of Herlong Recreational Airport. Over 18,000 people are currently without power in Duval County. Damage costs estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above normal temperatures and minimal precipitation continuing from late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of northeast LA. Through the month of June, D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions expanded to affect all of our northeast LA parishes as depicted on the U.S Drought Monitor. Average temperatures for the month ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 50 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 10 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Catahoula Parish decreased from D2 (Severe Drought) to D1 (Moderate Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually extreme, early-season heat wave impacted central California during the middle of March, setting several monthly heat records across the region. Radiosonde observations from Oakland reported a monthly record for highest 850 mb temperature at 23.4 degrees Celsius, or around 74.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Notably, this temperature would also break the monthly record for April, had it occurred during that month. Given the extreme and unusual levels of heat for this time of year, a Heat Advisory was issued from Monday, March 16 through Friday, March 20, throughout the Bay Area and northern Central Coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ben Lomond station reported a monthly record high of 99 on March 19 and March 21.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms after 8 AM in northeast Arkansas with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of northeast Arkansas, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles (3-4) were knocked down on AR 135 Hwy S near the Twin Oaks Motel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two utility poles were blown down by thunderstorm winds near East 256th Street and Carson road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam county EM reported trees down along South Moody Rd near pine Oak Way and South State Rd 19. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-strong low pressure system produced heavy snow across central Indiana January 24th through January 25th. Over a foot of snow fell in most counties across south-central Indiana. Indianapolis broke the daily record snowfall total on January 25th with 9.1 inches. The heavy snow led to 29 Travel Warnings, 9 Travel Watches, and 1 Travel Advisory.||Indiana State Police in the Indianapolis district alone responded to 264 crashes (33 with injuries), 158 slide-offs, and 529 motorist assists for vehicles stuck in snow or broken down from Saturday afternoon on January 24th through Tuesday morning on January 27th. Any accidents responded to by local entities would have been in addition to this number.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts ranged from 10.0 to 12.5 inches. A Travel Warning was issued for the county due to the impacts of snow on road conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power poles were blown down at KY-94 as an embedded supercell moved into Fulton County. To the southeast, tree limbs took down power lines off of KY-309 and a tree fell onto Mikel Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow-reinforced front moved into the area during the morning of June 22nd, and a dryline set up over west Texas. These features, combined with lift from a disturbance in the upper-level flow, yield thunderstorm development during the afternoon. One storm in rural Pecos County interacted with remnant surface vorticity from the decaying boundary and managed to produce a weak tornado. Another storm moved through Midland and produced up to ping-pong ball sized hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report was received via mPING of dime-sized hail on the south side of Midland. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts across State Road 32.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak disturbance moving across the Intermountain West combined with intense daytime heating resulting in scattered high based evaporating showers and dry thunderstorms across western and central New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 13th. These showers resulted in dry microbursts at the Farmington Four Corners Regional Airport and the NMDOT weather station along I-40 at SR6 in Laguna Pueblo. High based shower and thunderstorm activity across western and central New Mexico dissipated around sunset with the loss of daytime heating. Two rounds of high based shower and thunderstorm activity developed across the eastern plains of New Mexico during the afternoon hours on May 14th and 15th with dry microbursts in Clayton. High based shower and thunderstorm activity exited east into west Texas and tapered off during the evening hours, with one area of collapsing showers resulting in a heat burst at the Fort Sumner Municipal Airport late on May 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station near Clayton Municipal Airport measured a brief 60 mph wind gust due to a microburst from a high based thunderstorm.
