EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were reported down on Kittanning Pike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pre-frontal trough triggered a few clusters of thunderstorms across central Illinois from the late morning through the early evening of June 9th.  Thanks to copious atmospheric moisture, one cell dropped heavy rainfall and caused localized flash flooding in parts of Fulton County.  Another storm later in the day produced damaging wind gusts and flash flooding in rural Edgar County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down and corn was damaged by thunderstorm winds about 3 miles north-northeast of Oliver.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across eastern North Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS KBAC at Valley City, ND consistently reported wind chills -40 or lower from the morning of January 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. The lowest wind chill value during that period was -47.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.
A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down along Main Street in Berryville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters and broken lines of thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of 4/15 in Ohio and progressed east into the local area. Beneath a belt of enhanced mid-level flow, effective shear values reached 40-50 knots with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE in place. This supported swaths of straight-line wind damage with damage to trees, power lines, and structures as well as hail up to golf ball sized.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of downed trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Erie during the afternoon and evening of Monday, May 19, 2026. Several severe thunderstorms within this line generated thunderstorm wind damage and wind gusts across Northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Erie County 911 Dispatch reported several tree limbs down in Perkins Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of March saw abysmally dry conditions alongside record heat stretch across much of the Desert Southwest, including New Mexico. Albuquerque in particular saw a record high average monthly temperature, roughly 6 degrees warmer than any other month on record. The record warmth and record low snow pack limiting snow melt and lack of precipitation otherwise allowed for a degradation of drought conditions across the state. Severe drought (D2) was introduced back to a significant segment of northeastern NM, and spreading further across northwestern and west-central NM. Extreme drought (D3) also spread across a portion of the Northwest Plateau and highlands area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought was introduced to the western third of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong southwesterly flow ahead of a cold front brought hot humid air northward into the region. The front's passage heralded the end of the heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The heat index at Philadelphia International Airport reached 105 degrees on June 11th and 106 degrees on June 12th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed south through the combined Panhandles during the afternoon and late evening of April 17, 2026. As the pressure fell across the region, this resulted in increased wind speeds. A few locations measured winds above 58mph through the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Dalhart Municipal Airport measured a 69mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell near the Turnertown community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photo was received of a tree down on a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wildfire near Flagler burned part of the railroad, including the railroad bridge.  Smoke from the fire also impacted I-70 westbound traffic.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wildfire started near MM 392, one and a half miles west of Flagler, north of I-70 near the railroad. The railroad bridge nearby was a total loss. The fire risk continued for days afterward from the creasode in the railroad ties smoldering. Westbound traffic was closed on the order of minutes at Siebert due to smoke blowing across the highway.  The fire ended up being 364 acres in size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was stalled over the coastal Mississippi.  At the same time, a weak upper level trough was moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley.  Both of these features tapped into a warm and unstable airmass to produce thunderstorm activity in coastal Mississippi.  These thunderstorms produced some severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on a power line in Millard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado began just west of Martha Comer Drive, snapping several hardwood tree trunks before moving across the southern portion of a community college campus. The Kentucky Mesonet site on campus measured a wind gust of 114 mph. The tornado then tracked east and northeast across open field, eventually hitting several businesses along Kentucky Highway 9 (AA Highway), causing roof and structural damage. As the tornado approached East Maple Leaf Road, it quickly intensified. A couple of residences were severely damaged, including an outbuilding demolished with pieces and contents of the structure thrown between 100 to 200 feet. This included a 690 pound four wheeler and a large cinder block. A dual axle trailer jacked up on a block was pushed nearly 100 feet before being stopped by a cement barrier. A house suffered extensive roof damage. A property on the east side of East Maple Leaf Road was also heavily damaged with the debris in a convergent path. This included the roof and siding of a house, several snapped and uprooted hardwood trees, and a couple of hardwood fences that were posted well into the ground, that were pulled toward the circulation. Splatter was observed on the east and south sides of the home, further suggesting a cyclonic rotation. |The tornado then took a left turn toward the northeast as it snapped more trees and destroyed another portion of a fence. Additionally, on the southern side of the tornado, a couple of large barns were heavily damaged with both roofs a total loss, as outflow winds occurred on the south side of the tornado. As the tornado continued on a northeast track across a field, a metal outbuilding was pulled down a hill as the circulation neared. Additional tree damage was observed east of Hill City Road before the tornado dissipated. Sporadic tree damage was reported farther northeast toward the Ohio River as a result of outflow winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms moved across southwest Missouri and southeast Kansas on the evening of June 11. Large hail occurred with some of the storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree on Highway 59 past Two  Sons Campground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated supercell thunderstorm developed across Kingman and Reno Counties during the afternoon hours of April 11. This storm produced winds up to 80 mph and up to golf ball size hail as it tracked across far northern Kingman, southern and eastern Reno, northern Sedgwick, and Harvey Counties.

Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms that moved through Arkansas. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced a number of damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles around Big Cabin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2-D4 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon hours of May 17th, storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of NW Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Private weather sensor measured a 56 knot wind gust SW of Cameron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large diameter tree damage was reported around 123rd Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front draped over the Ohio Valley tracked into the central and southern Appalachians by the late evening and overnight period. Ahead of the front, scattered showers and storms tracked from the North Carolina mountains into the Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the evening hours. Numerous wind damage reports were observed over the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were snapped and broken near the intersection of Martin Street and North Carolina Highway 66.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills. By Friday morning, much of the area was seeing temperatures of at least 20 degrees below zero, and as cold as 25 degrees below zero measured at the South Dakota State University mesonet stations in Gettysburg and 23 miles north of Highmore. With these cold temperatures and a northwest breeze, wind chills across much of the area had fallen to 40 degrees below zero and colder, with the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station in Summit coming in with a wind chill of 53 degrees below zero. Temperatures failed to warm much during the day, with highs in the single digits to teens below zero. Watertown set a record for the lowest daily high temperature, reaching only 11 degrees below zero.

Amid unseasonably hot temperatures for the middle of May, isolated thunderstorms formed around southwest Virginia on the afternoon of the 18th. These storms produced damaging wind gusts as they quickly collapsed after their initiation, which resulted in a tree to knock down onto a trailer in the town of Vansant. The loss of daytime heating at sunset brought the threat for additional thunderstorm damage to an end on this particular day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell onto a trailer along Dry Fork Road in Vansant.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours as a low pressure system lifted northeast across the Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed in Fountain City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A blown transformer occurred near Publix along Highway 19.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon and early evening hours of June 24th. As activity moved to the east and southeast, storms became severe with strong winds and large hail. Hail up to the size of baseballs was reported near Wauneta and wind gusts up to 77 MPH were reported near Grant. Thunderstorm wind damage, with winds estimated at 80 MPH overturned multiple pivots and damaged buildings south of Madrid.

Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines down in Crucible.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions at the start of the month worsened to D3 on March 3rd before heavy rains trimmed the drought levels weekly until ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 9 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snapped pine tree falling onto a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over northeastern Colorado and the southern Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon and early evening hours of June 24th. As activity moved to the east and southeast, storms became severe with strong winds and large hail. Hail up to the size of baseballs was reported near Wauneta and wind gusts up to 77 MPH were reported near Grant. Thunderstorm wind damage, with winds estimated at 80 MPH overturned multiple pivots and damaged buildings south of Madrid.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Caller reported 8 inch diameter branch downed. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across eastern Arkansas.||Thermal profiles across eastern Arkansas favored predominantly snow north of Interstate 40, however, with the development of the surface low, a shallow warm nose aloft overspread the area, causing a changeover to sleet. Poor road conditions continued for nearly two weeks after the storm, causing difficult travel and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow and sleet accumulations of 5 to 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado with maximum sustained winds estimated near 80 mph touched down near US Hwy 98 in far northeast Amite County, MS causing minor tree damage and removing a few metal panels from an outbuilding. The tornado continued northeast into Pike County where additional minor tree damage was found on Kenna Rd. This tornado continued northeast into Lincoln County, MS where it strengthened into a large, strong EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds near 110 mph southwest of Norfield, MS in NWS Jackson's area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles snapped due to thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down with some down on homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation continued to lack across much of southwest Minnesota with only 25 to 50 percent of normal during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions worsened to severe (D2) very late month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power lines were downed along IL-17 west of I-55 near Dwight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of winter weather affected South Texas during the final week of January 2026, beginning with the arrival of a strong Arctic front early on January 24. The front surged southward faster than initially anticipated, producing a rapid temperature drop across the region and widespread rain behind the boundary. As colder air deepened overnight, precipitation continued while temperatures approached or fell below freezing across parts of the region, creating a narrow window for freezing rain and drizzle late January 24 into the morning of January 25. The greatest risk for ice accumulation occurred across the Victoria Crossroads, where light ice totals of up to around a tenth of an inch were possible. Elsewhere, the combination of lingering precipitation and wet roadways raised concerns for patchy black ice, particularly on bridges and overpasses as temperatures briefly dipped to freezing.||Once the precipitation ended on January 25, the primary hazard transitioned to extreme cold as a deep Arctic air mass settled over South Texas. Temperatures struggled to rise above the 40s during the day, while overnight lows dropped into the teens across northern inland areas and the lower to mid-20s closer to the coast. Persistent northerly winds produced dangerously low wind chills, with values falling into the single digits in some inland locations and the teens elsewhere. Extreme Cold Warnings and Freeze Warnings were issued across the region as the prolonged cold posed risks to infrastructure, agriculture, and vulnerable populations. Clearer skies and lighter winds early in the week allowed efficient radiational cooling, reinforcing the cold conditions through January 27 before gradual moderation began.||Although temperatures slowly recovered into the 50s and 60s by midweek, the pattern remained active with additional frontal passages. A brief warmup ahead of another cold front late in the week pushed temperatures into the 70s before colder air returned by January 30. This secondary surge brought another round of below-freezing temperatures and widespread cold weather headlines, particularly across inland counties where lows fell into the 20s and wind chills dropped into the teens. While precipitation with this second front remained limited, the extended period of repeated freezes and persistent cold made this late-January event a notable winter episode for South Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Cold/Wind Chill: KBEA reported wind chills at or below 15 degF for at least 2 hours, which is our local Extreme Cold Warning criteria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across north Mississippi. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. Ice-laden trees and infrastructure remained stressed in subfreezing conditions, slowing restoration efforts and prolonging outages in affected areas. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northwest Pennsylvania. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northwest Pennsylvania, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters, particularly near the OH/PA border across Northwest Pennsylvania where a few tornadoes also occurred. At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed around midday over the central Nebraska Panhandle. This activity tracked to the east and southeast into the evening hours, producing numerous damaging wind and large hail reports. The greatest damage was at the eastern end of Lake McConaughy. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 81 MPH were reported. Hail up to golf ball size was reported near Imperial.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms brought intense storms to the region during the late evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The storms delivered a severe combination of damaging wind gusts, large hail, and an isolated tornado. Moving through the state in the overnight hours, a line of storms impacted Jasper and Newton counties with heavy rain, wind, and lightning. Early morning video documented significant tree damage and downed power lines near 1st and Schifferdecker in Joplin. Widespread wind damage tore the roof off the Joplin Parks and Recreation building and leveled several metal outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Storm Survey determined that a grain silo was toppled over by estimated 70mph straight line winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm system impacted the State of Tennessee starting late Friday, January 23 and continuing into Sunday, January 25, 2026. Cold air moved into Tennessee Friday evening, setting the stage for winter weather through the weekend. This cold air along with a potent storm system resulted in primarily snow Friday night into Saturday morning. However, as warm air aloft moved north into Tennessee, this changed the precipitation from snow to sleet and then finally to freezing rain Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon. By the time precipitation came to an end, snow accumulations were highest across northwest Middle Tennessee where generally 3 to 5 inches were measured. A swath of ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inches was reported from Wayne County northeast through Nashville and to the Tennessee/Kentucky border. Locally higher amounts over one half inch were reported around the Nashville metro area.||These accumulations caused widespread, crippling damage in the form of broken and downed trees and power lines, dangerous to impossible travel conditions, and hundreds of thousands of power outages. Nashville Electric Service (NES) alone reported 230,000 customers without power which is the largest number of outages at one time NES has ever experienced. ||The other major impact from this winter storm was frigid temperatures. Cold air already in place over the weekend was reinforced Sunday night as arctic air moved into Tennessee behind this winter storm. The coldest temperature readings were recorded Monday and Tuesday mornings with widespread readings in the single digits and wind chills below zero. With these very cold temperatures, impacts were felt long after the precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mixture of snow, sleet, and ice impacted Overton County during the early morning hours of January 24th into the afternoon of January 25th. A variety of reporting sources measured snow accumulations up to 2 inches with ice accumulations of 0.10 to 0.15 inches. This led to several reports of treacherous travel and downed powerlines, trees, and tree branches. Total power outages were around 500 customers across Overton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One last burst of winter weather for the season took place across southwest Virginia beginning on the afternoon of March 16th in the wake of a cold front. A surge of sub-freezing temperatures sweeping into the area on the backside of the front resulted in a transition from rain to snow. Snow showers progressed into the afternoon of March 17th before building high pressure promoted the return of quiet weather. In the midst of the snow, an average of one to three inches of snow fell across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties, with locally higher amounts taking place along the higher elevations.

Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. An EF-1 tornado was confirmed in northern Davidson and southern Robertson counties. The strongest straight-line wind damage was reported in northern Lawrence County where numerous downed trees and other structural damage was found in the Summertown area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree on Moss Glen Road in Lebanon. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 82 and other nearby roads flooded in De Kalb.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported on Mping.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May started with severe drought (D2) present across much of eastern WV, including: Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and most of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Moderate drought (D1) also persisted across most of western and north-central WV, with the exception of Pleasants, Wood, northwest Jackson, northern Mason, western Ritchie, western Tyler, and western Wirt counties where conditions were merely abnormally dry (D0). Only minimal changes to D0 and D1 occurred in the second week of the month. D2, however, spread out across all of Boone and Kanawha counties; most of Lincoln, Logan, and Putnam counties; and portions of eastern Cabell, southern Jackson, southern Roane, and eastern Wayne counties. Conditions worsened even more the following week, as D2 engulfed most of southern, central, and eastern West Virginia, and a sliver of extreme drought (D3) crept into eastern McDowell, southeast Raleigh, and eastern Wyoming counties. Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth. Fortunately, enough precipitation fell at the end of the month to eradicate D3 and confine D2 to mainly Boone, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Nicholas, Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Raleigh, Webster, Wyoming, southern Braxton, eastern Lincoln, southern Roane, and southern Wayne. D1 improved to D0 in southern Tyler, Doddridge, northern Harrison, northern Taylor, part of northern Barbour, Ritchie, Wirt, northwest Gilmer, northern Calhoun, northern Roane, northern Jackson, northwest Mason, northwest Cabell, and part of northern Wayne. Meanwhile, drought was completely eliminated from counties, or at least portions of counties, bordering the Ohio River.||Generally less than an inch of rain fell during the first week of May. Around an inch or less accumulated during the second week. During the third week of the month, much of the area received around an inch and a half or less of rain, though a strip of up to two inches fell along the Ohio River. More substantial precipitation occurred at the end of the month, when one to three inches of rain fell to the south of I-64 and one and a half to over four inches fell to the north of I-64. Highest amounts were observed across portions of Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Taylor, Randolph, and Upshur counties. Multiple rounds of rain during this time finally allowed for significant improvement to drought conditions, particularly across the northern and western part of the state.||The six climate sites in West Virginia were evenly split between above and below normal total precipitation for the month, with Beckley, Charleston, and Elkins on the below normal side and Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg on the above normal side. On the 22nd, Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg each received enough rain to break their existing daily precipitation records. Beckley was also able to tie a standing daily precipitation record on the 24th of the month.

An upper-level trough positioned itself to support the development of a strong mid-level frontogenesis band. It took advantage of tremendous mid-level moisture and lift. Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 7 of snow fallen via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon, slow-moving thunderstorms produced heavy to locally extreme rainfall, including a public observation of 3.14 inches in the Wichita Hill neighborhood of  far southwestern Marion County.  Flash flooding was limited to adjacent far northeastern Morgan County, focused along Mann Road.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Road 700 East flooded south of US Highway 52 from 2.20 inches of rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in Big Beaver.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong low pressure area swung through southern Virginia, dragging a cold front across Eastern NC by the evening hours. Ahead of it, bands of thunderstorms formed in the afternoon due to unstable conditions and wind shear in place. Scattered severe wind gusts embedded in some of the storms produced wind damage across the area. There were also several reports of hail up to nickel size.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were blown down with winds estimated at 55 to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dust storm conditions were reported along the leading edge of outflow winds which initially emanated from the thunderstorm complex that was north then east of Greeley County.  The narrow corridor of dust storm conditions moved south across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 80 mph, knocked down multiple wires near Rockwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent strong winds was in place across the region. A cold front passage combined with rain showers helped mixed these stronger winds to the surface mainly across the Rocky Mountain Front and Little Belts foothills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ambient Weather Station Howards Lodge measured a 67 mph wind gust. Mesonet station SNPMT Sunpoint and Ambient Weather Station Glacier Park Trading Company, East Glacier Park Village also measured a high wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first damage produced by the tornado occurred on Texas Gas Road, where a large tree was uprooted and other smaller trees were downed. Farther east along Cole Lane, an attached garage was destroyed and a large tree was downed onto a house. In addition, a roof was lifted from another garage and several trees were snapped at their trunks. ||The tornado strengthened and proceeded east near East Laughery Creek Road, where it completely destroyed a house and two outbuildings. Debris from these buildings was strewn east along the path of the tornado across a large field. Based on this damage, estimated wind speeds were around 130 mph in this area, and the damage also resulted in a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar at this time. ||The tornado continued toward Alta Vista Ave, where a large number of hardwood trees were snapped. The tornado then moved across Laughery Creek and into Switzerland County at 2317EST, about 2.8 miles southeast of Dillsboro. The tornado continued east across Ohio County, eventually moving into Boone County, Kentucky, before dissipating at 2326EST, just across the Ohio River near Belleview Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Numerous damaging wind reports occurred across eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind damaged the Eufaula Cove Marina.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to exceptional (D4) drought conditions continued across portions of eastern Nebraska through the month of June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) drought conditions degraded further across Knox County during the month of June, leading to the introduction of exceptional (D4) drought. Exceptional drought coverage expanded to around 18 percent by the end of the month, while coverage of extreme drought or greater encompassed 100 percent of the county. The cooperative observer at Orchard 9NNE recorded 4.55 inches of precipitation, 0.31 inches below average. The CoCoRaHS observers at Crofton 4.4 WNW and Crofton 0.7 NNW recorded 2.20 and 2.39 inches of precipitation, respectively. These values were 1.87 and 1.81 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: EM reports multiple trees down near Spring Rd and Bethlemhem Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High surf conditions on February 6 resulted in two separate water rescue incidents off the coast of Santa Cruz. At 11:45 AM, surfers rescued a family of 6 from a boat that capsized off Steamer Lane. Later that day, the Coast Guard started a search at around 6:30 PM for two surfers who were seen going away from the water off the Santa Cruz Lighthouse. A High Surf Advisory was in effect for the day due to breaking waves of 17 to 22 feet. There was also a higher than normal tourist load for the region due to Super Bowl weekend activities in the San Jose and San Francisco areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A boat carrying six people, two adults and their four children, capsized off Steamer Lane near Santa Cruz around 11:45 AM on February 6. The children were wearing life vests, but the parents were not. Around ten surfers, one of whom was 14, helped to rescue the family and bring them to safety; patrol boats and ambulances arrived within minutes. The people were taken to a hospital and recovered. At the time of the incident, buoy 46236 reported swell waves of 8 ft at 16.7 seconds from the west, with wind waves of 4 ft at 9.9 seconds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. While there were isolated severe storms during the afternoon, widespread storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Aiken County EM reported a tree down along Old Friar Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-phased system brought a combination of system and lake enhanced snow to northwest and portions of north central Indiana Saturday night into early Sunday morning followed by more organized lake effect snow showers late Sunday into Monday. This prolonged snow event coupled with gusty north to northwest winds lead to hazardous travel conditions and numerous slide-offs and accidents across favored lake effect snow region across northwest and north central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of system and lake enhanced snow Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by a more organized lake effect snow phase Sunday afternoon through midday Monday. Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 5 to 10 inches. A CoCoRaHS observer 1.9 miles north northeast of Mill Creek, IN reported 8.3 inches of snow. In addition to the snow, north to northwest winds gusting to 30 to 35 mph resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow along with periods of significantly reduced visibilities. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout June 2026, New Hampshire experienced short-term drought relief driven by soaking rains, though long-term groundwater deficits persisted in the southern half of the state. Spurred by a remarkably wet May and continued rainfall in June, total drought coverage in New Hampshire fell from a high of over 68% Severe Drought (D2) in late 2025 to 35.9% total drought (D1���D2) by June 23. Northern and western New Hampshire saw drought designations completely erased due to localized rainfall exceeding 150���200% of normal. D2 Severe Drought covered 3.2%���10.9% area in the state, confined mostly to southern Rockingham and Hillsborough counties along the Massachusetts border and the Seacoast. Despite geographical shrinkage, lingering Moderate (D1) and Severe (D2) drought areas overlapped with higher-density southern counties. As a result, approximately 75% of New Hampshire's residents (997,000 people) remained within a classified drought zone in late June. Deep subsurface water tables, reduced in the drought of 2025, lagged considerably due to slow infiltration rates in thicker surficial aquifers and long-term rainfall deficits. Well monitoring confirmed several southern New Hampshire wells remained in the Below to Much Below Normal categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on June 2nd had 12.57% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), and 87.17% in Moderate Drought (D1). By June 30th, this was reduced to 5.73% Severe Drought, and 78% Moderate Drought. Precipitation for June averaged 3.70 inches across Rockingham County, roughly at monthly norms. Surface conditions remained steady with few notable impacts to drought. However, the groundwater deficit inherited from 2025 remained. For instance, while the monitoring well in Greenfield demonstrated active surface recharge during the month, overall groundwater levels remained stalled below the 5th percentile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite a rather volatile airmass for severe weather across Oklahoma and north Texas on the 26th, misaligned synoptic features (i.e., neutral-to-rising mid-level heights) and remnant convective inhibition limited the overall number/coverage of thunderstorms during the evening. The most significant storm was a slow-moving supercell storm near and north of Wichita Falls, Texas. This thunderstorm produced large to very large hail and yielded a pair of left-moving supercells that went on to produce hail into portions of adjacent southern Oklahoma. This included confirmations of baseball-size hail in areas east of Lawton, Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface boundary kicked off a marginal line of thunderstorms that produced sporadic wind damage across central and eastern MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near Maynard a tree was reported down on Sudbury  road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front was approaching the region during the evening of May 3rd. Concurrently, a low-level jet was ramping up in the area. This resulted in the development of thunderstorms, some of which became severe and produced large hail in Macoupin and Madison counties.

With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through eastern Pennsylvania. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees and wires down with entire blocks having wires down. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down onto the Petersburg Battlefield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through eastern Pennsylvania. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees down along Upper Mountain Road between Route 413 and Forest Grove Road. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moves through the area especially across Hennepin and Ramsey Countines. Due to the rate and quantity of hailstones, a few areas had observed hail accumulation on the ground. The largest hailstone diameter was 2.25 inches observed 2 miles NNE of St. Paul.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf Ball sized hail fell near hwy 36 and I35.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2) expanded across southeast Kansas especially towards the end of the month impacting all or portions of five counties. The combination of below normal precipitation by an inch to two along with early season temperatures in the low to mid 90s were two factors.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2) encompassed the county at the start of the month after being in moderate drought (D1) in February. D2 conditions persisted through the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto Aughwick Creek Road near Runk Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Bedford county in late June  after a few rainfall events brought some rain to the county. Drought conditions lingered; however, after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th to 10th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of thunderstorms formed ahead of an outflow boundary along the Mississippi River around midday on June 10th.  Some of the stronger cells within the line produced 60mph wind gusts and scattered damage along and north of a Jacksonville to Clinton line through mid-afternoon.

An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began near Pleasant Hill Drive and Elm Lane in southeastern Lincoln County and tracked eastward, crossing MS Highway 583 in the Ruth community. It then continued along Greenwood Road and Raiford Trail, crossing Primitive Drive in the Bristerville community, then across Monument Trail and Junction Lane before crossing into southwestern Lawrence County near the Verna community. It crossed Holmesville Road and paralleled Verna Road before lifting near Excell Boyd Road. Along the path, countless trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths, multiple outbuildings sustained damage, utility poles were damaged, a mobile home sustained roof and skirting damage, and a site built home sustained minor wind damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of April 15th, severe storms brought very large hail and damaging wind gusts to portions of far eastern Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail larger than baseballs on the east side of Paola.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 3-5. The highest reliable measurement received was 4.7 from Weatherly.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking Snake Hill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. The strongest winds were generally west of the James River Valley where gusts to 60 to 70 mph were common. While areas of light snowfall generally on the order from a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, there were only very spotty and brief instances of visibility below one mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 30 to 39 mph at times with a peak gust of 57 mph at a South Dakota Mesonet site 7 miles north of De Smet and an Automated Weather Observing System site 2 miles north-northwest of De Smet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms moved through SE Texas and produced strong winds and heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple mPing reports were received, spanning from the north Freeway around Independence Heights to the Sugarland area. Four indicated street flooding with vehicles stranded. One indicated a building had been inundated with water. Additionally, a storm chaser shared a video on social media showing water over the North Freeway frontage Road at West Rocky Creek Road. In the video, one vehicle appears to be stalled out, though others can be seen passing through.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As the third week of May 2026 unfolded, the dynamic breakup front stalled repeatedly along the Lower Yukon, creating a cascading sequence of severe jams and flooding. This period involved massive downstream surges as well as backwater effects in tributaries like the Andreafsky and Chuilnuk.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS River Watch team reported a 3 mile-long ice jam composed of large, intact ice sheets blocked the channel downriver from the town of Russian Mission, backing up roughly 60 miles of chunk and pan ice upstream. The jam released on Wednesday evening (May 20), allowing water levels to drop by about a foot by Saturday, though low-lying areas remained impacted with flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Jeff Davis 911 call center reported a tree was down over power lines along Charles  Rogers Blvd. Time was estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved from Illinois through southwest Michigan and northern Indiana. The line of storms eventually weakened, but prior to this, damaging wind gusts were recorded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reports powerlines downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front brought several days of showers and thunderstorms to the region as it moved through the area, stalled, and then retreated back to the north. Isolated instances of hail, severe winds, and flooding occurred with this activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny and nickel sized hail lasted for 4 minutes off of FM 920, approximately 1.7 miles south of Poolville, Texas, in Parker County. At 12:19 pm, penny sized hail resumed for another two minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow southward-moving cold front tracked into South-Central Texas, producing a line of strong to severe thunderstorms which advanced ahead of the front as it encountered a moist and unstable airmass on the evening of May 19 into the early hours of May 20. The storms produced swaths of severe winds and some large hail. Locally heavy rain that led to some flash flooding mainly north of the Austin area and in the Hill Country.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain from slow-moving thunderstorms caused rises along Berry Creek. The combination of elevated streamflow and accumulation of water in a nearby detention basin led to a washout across both lanes of Berry Creek Drive between Airport Road/Briarcrest Drive and Mourning Dove Boulevard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A post on social media reported 2 inch hail in between Reno and Paris.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Calm winds and clearing skies behind a cold frontal passage resulted in dense fog formation in the Kentucky Pennyrile and Western Coal Fields areas of Western Kentucky overnight into the early morning of the 25th. Fog duration was longest in areas to the east, with fog observed for several hours at Hopkinsville, Madisonville, Greenville, and Owensboro.
An isolated thunderstorm over central Montana produced gusts up to 59 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Awos station K1KM 2 ENE Harlowton gusted to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew a semi-truck onto the median of I-55.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported quarter size hail southeast of Lubbock International Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western SD with large hail, damaging wind gusts and reports of minor damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust report at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant snowstorm struck portions of East Tennessee at the end of the month, thanks to strong lift from a deep upper trough diving from north to south. A couple of long term cooperative weather stations saw top 10 snowfalls during this storm. This storm led to 3 confirmed fatalities in East Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inches of snow fell in Oneida.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across southeastern Oklahoma and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the area was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. A tornado, isolated damaging wind, and large hail up to two inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The right entrance region of a jet within stronger flow across the northern tier of the U.S. helped to increase convergence by late afternoon and early evening along a cold front working eastward through northwest Iowa.  Mixed-layer instability reached up to 1500-2000 J/kg courtesy of 8C/km mid-level lapse rates with deep-layer shear of 40 to 50 knots. Initially discrete cells produced large hail, with a tendency to evolve toward more linear structures.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

Above normal moisture ahead of a strong cold front that pushed southward across the western Colorado Divide resulted in light to moderate snowfall accumulations across the western Colorado mountains along the Divide with locally heavier accumulations and rates. Better snowfall accumulations and impacts occurred above 9000 feet with some gusty winds to 50 mph at higher elevations along the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 4 to 10 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 20 inches at Tower.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms along the leading edge of a cold front pushing across the Florida Peninsula down a few trees near Brandon and Willow Oak in Hillsborough County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County fire rescue reported a tree down across power lines near Willow Oak.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down blocking two lanes of HWY 264 east of Washington, NC. The time was based on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of sleet and snow during this event, producing 4 to 6 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (6 inches) was reported southwest of Elmore City. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms moved northward through Southeastern Arizona the afternoon and evening of June 17th, 2026. These storms caused thunderstorm wind damage causing 8 power poles to be downed and 7,000 customers to be without power in the Tucson Metro and damage to a power transformer that caused a power outage for Tohono O'odham Nation. Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms caused flash flooding in normally dry rivers and washes that resulted in multiple swift water rescues that resulted in 1 fatality and 2 injuries. Additionally, multiple roadways in Cochise County was impassible due to flooding. An estimated penny sized hail was reported on the SW side of Tucson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reports Highway 92 flooded due to heavy rains across both sides of  highway. MRMS estimated that between 0.5 and 1.0 inches of rainfall fell in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough positioned itself to support the development of a strong mid-level frontogenesis band. It took advantage of tremendous mid-level moisture and lift. Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 5 inches of snow fallen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were blown down in the Lake Seminole area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winds behind yet another arctic front reached speeds from 35 to 55 mph with gusts as high as 75 mph across southeast South Dakota. When periods of light snowfall occurred that would total between one and two inches north of Highway 18, gusty winds produced considerable near-blizzard and very brief blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds were sustained from 30 to 32 mph with gusts as high as 50 mph at a South Dakota Mesonet site 3 miles north-northeast of Flandreau.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another in a week of extremely strong winds occurred with the strongest wind day with a peak of 89 mph at East Butte and several gusts over 70 mph throughout the state.  Interstate 15 was pre-emptively closed from Shelley to north of Idaho Falls in anticipation of the extreme event.  It was a widespread event with some damage and power outages occurring as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter recorded a 60 mph wind gust in Challis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved into northeastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 11th. The atmosphere became very unstable during the late afternoon and evening ahead of these thunderstorms, and wind shear increased as an upper level disturbance approached the region. As a result, the strongest thunderstorms produced severe weather in the form of damaging wind. Locally heavy rainfall also resulted in isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a couple trees and some power lines in Miami.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed just ahead of a strong cold front and moved into southeast Georgia in the early morning hours. The environment ahead of these storms was supportive of damaging wind gusts, and a few of the clusters of thunderstorms became strong enough to produce severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Screven County dispatch reported a powerline down along Mercer Road.
