EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across northern Illinois during the morning of January 14th with a band of heavy snow and snow squalls. Wind gusts were between 40 mph and 50 mph with a few higher gusts, including a gust to 61 mph near Crescent City. Visibility was reported to be near zero in many locations. Snowfall amounts were generally between 1 and 2 inches and with temperatures falling below freezing as the snow began, roads became icy.  Hundreds of vehicle accidents were reported across northern Illinois.

Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. The strongest winds were generally west of the James River Valley where gusts to 60 to 70 mph were common. While areas of light snowfall generally on the order from a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, there were only very spotty and brief instances of visibility below one mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 40 to 44 mph at times with a peak gust of 59 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 3 miles east-southeast of Parker.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong northwest winds moved into central and south central Kansas starting in the evening hours of the 15th and continuing through the early evening of the 16th with a tightened gradient from a low pressure system. Generally winds had speeds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 55 mph. The peak gust was at Russell Airport overnight with a measured gust of 63 mph. No damage was reported.

A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked a tree down on East Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure arrived by January 27 in the wake of a departing winter storm. However, the pressure gradient between the high arriving and the low departing provided gusty winds that combined with the cold air to provide dangerously low wind chills. Wind chills dropped below -15��F during the early morning hours of January 27 in Bath, Grayson, and Tazewell counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at Hot Springs reported a wind chill value down to -26��F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As storm clusters crossed into Missouri from Kansas a line of storms spawned several embedded circulations. Tornado watches and warnings were triggered across multiple counties in Ozarks. High winds impacted local areas, causing thousands of power outages, particularly in Benton and Morgan counties, where multiple buildings sustained roof damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to golf balls in size was reported. Some minor home and vehicle damage occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree on Bear Mountain Bridge Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 30, 2026, an oppressive tropical airmass fueled by extreme heat warnings collided with a sharp mid-level shortwave across the NWS Buffalo CWA, prompting the Storm Prediction Center to issue a Severe Thunderstorm Watch as strong boundary-layer destabilization produced widespread severe convection across Central New York and the North Country. NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions highlighted surging moisture and extreme instability that unleashed powerful multi-cell clusters and isolated supercells, leading to severe straight-line microbursts with winds up to 100 mph and an EF-1 tornado touchdown in Lewis County. Concurrently, deep warm-cloud processes and precipitable water levels approaching 2.0 inches fueled torrential precipitation efficiency, driving Weather Prediction Center Excessive Rainfall concerns for localized flash flooding in poor-drainage areas. As the pre-frontal convective line swept east toward nightfall, loss of daytime heating and post-frontal drying rapidly stabilized the region, bringing an end to the severe weather threat into the overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees, large branches, and wires down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in the Piedmont of Virginia. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of Renan Road and Starkey Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms produced strong winds across portions of central, north central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon of June 15th. A peak wind gust of 69 mph was recorded on the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 5 miles west of Seneca (Potter county), with a 68 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT mesonet station in Waubay (Day county). Rapidly decaying showers also generated strong winds in Lyman and Buffalo counties, with a 66 mph gust recorded on the SDDOT station 5 miles north of Reliance and a 64 mph gust on the SDDOT station 3 miles north of Gann Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota State University mesonet station near the Lower Brule community recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph associated with decaying showers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Androscoggin County averaged 3.13 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.76 inches below normal, marking the 4th driest start to the new year. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).  It was the driest June through March stretch on record, approximately 10.24 inches below normal for that 10 month period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across east-central Wisconsin during the afternoon on Tuesday (6/16).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to quarter size in the Fox Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell near Oshkosh.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough and Arctic high pressure over the Mid-Atlantic combined to produce a period of high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet in Indian Head measured a peak wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observations from several locations in the northern half of inland Cameron County reached the freezing level (32F or lower) early on the 27th.  This included Harlingen, San Benito, Santa Rosa, and La Feria.  Harlingen/Valley International Airport fell to 30F, while mesonet platforms in Santa Rosa and northwest Harlingen fell to 28F. Durations were much shorter than on the 26th, as low level winds veered to the northeast.  Duration of freezing temperatures (32F or lower) was around 2 hours.  Locations in inland southern Cameron, including Brownsville, remained above freezing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms along the leading edge of a cold front pushing across the Florida Peninsula produce a waterspout offshore Fort Myers Beach, and gusty winds from the Tampa Bay area waters southward through Charlotte Harbor area waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 19th, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the Ohio River, with storms moving from southwest to northeast across northern Kentucky and southern Indiana. While effective bulk shear was relatively unsupportive of organized convection around 20 knots, a few stronger cores were able to develop thanks to 2000-2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. These stronger cells were able to produce a few instances of wind damage vai downed trees as well as near-severe level hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto power lines along Fairview Court in Eminence.

Severe thunderstorms produced wind damage, mostly to trees and vegetation, in portions of central and southwestern Mississippi during the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down on Mississippi Road 550 in Union Church.

The clusters of storms tracked southeastward through south central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening. Sporadic wind damage to trees and power lines occurred including hail around one inch in diameter.
A strong low pressure system moving into the area from the Pacific Northwest brought high winds to portions of southern Nevada.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet site on the Nevada National Security Site recorded high winds for much of the day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Completely flattened crops.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved across the Upper Midwest the afternoon of the 4th into the early morning of the 5th. This brought a wintry mix to the Northland with snow, sleet, and freezing drizzle. An area of heavy banded snow along the lake and terrain enhancement set up along the North Shore around Grand Marais and areas further inland in northern Cook County. This led to snowfall amounts of 5 to 8 inches in this area with upwards of 9 inches reported near Grand Marais in about 6 hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow was heavier than expected and quickly piled up along the North Shore of Lake Superior. Snowfall totals of 6 to 8 inches were received with a high report of 9.5 inches from 3.8 miles north-northeast of Grand Marais.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media Report of estimated 70-80 mph winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 13th.

Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported that Davilla Ave at Scarborough St, the 1900 block of CR 446, and FM 908 at Beverley Dr were flooded and closed in the city of Rockdale. High water was also reported near the intersection of Highway 79 and Childress Dr in Rockdale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms coming off the mountains of southern MT and northern WY produced hail up to 2 in diameter and gusts up to 70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to 2 in diameter reported by a spotter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front swung through the area in the evening kicking off mostly sub severe storms, though a few did produce damaging winds in MA and CT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Auburn, a tree was down blocking both lanes of travel in  the vicinity of 2 Millbury Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Camas mesonet site on Interstate 15 recorded a 61 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex setup characterized by moisture overrunning an entrenched wedge of cold air at the surface led to freezing rain and sleet beginning across north Georgia late on the night of January 24 and persisting through much of the day on January 25. Widespread ice accretion of one-tenth to one-quarter inch ice occurred with some areas receiving over a half inch of freezing rain accumulation. ||Significant tree damage and power outages occurred in the worst-affected areas of northeast Georgia, while spotty tree damage and isolated power outages occurred in other areas. Additionally, a layer of sleet occurred in much of northeast Georgia, leading to hazardous roadways. ||The hardest hit areas locally were White County as well as portions of Dawson and Lumpkin counties. The vast majority of the White County lost power with many locations remaining without power for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light rain showers began on the evening of the 24th. Rain briefly transitioned to ice on the morning of the 25th, however temperatures warmed through the day and quickly melted any accumulations, less than 0.1 inches, which managed to stick on elevated surfaces.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report indicated significant underpass flooding at Harry Hines and Spur 482, with cars submerged up to the windshield. Additionally, all intersections along Northwest Highway near Bachman Lake were flooded and closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. In southern Michigan, damaging wind gusts occurred downing trees, some onto houses. Powerlines were reported to be down in multiple areas as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines are down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper wave dropping south across the Great Lakes and it's associated cold front brought widespread accumulating snow to the region New Year's Eve and into the new year across the ridges of western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Enhanced orographic lift resulted in higher totals across the Laurel Highlands and eastern West Virginia ridges, with relatively high snow ratios between 18:1 and 21:1. Widespread Advisory level snow was also observed across the region, ranging from 2.5 inches to 5.5 inches outside of the ridges of Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall, generally exceeding advisory criteria but falling short of warning criteria, fell across the county with amounts ranging from 3-5 inches and the highest total of 5.8 inches reported by the Public 5 miles west-southwest of Ohiopyle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought sleet/snow to much of west central Texas. Some freezing rain resulted in a light glaze of ice across the Northwest Hill Country. The snow/sleet amounts ranged from 1 to 4 inches across the northern 2/3 of the area. The winter storm caused disruptions to travel and one fatality due to an accident on Interstate 10 east of Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 2 to 4 inches of snow/sleet across Haskell County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were down near I-75 with debris across the highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported numerous trees down and damage to power lines in Paris.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple downed trees and three snapped power poles were observed along Route 36 in Clover.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough crossed Wyoming and brought scattered showers and thunderstorms. Very dry air at the low levels led to the showers and thunderstorms to be high based, and numerous locations saw dry microbursts as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph wind occurred at the Riverton airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong sized hail was reported in Newport News.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moving through the central Appalachian mountains during the peak heating of the afternoon triggered scattered showers and thunderstorms to form. The presence of modest instability allowed a couple of these storms to grow intense enough to produce damaging wind gusts, which resulted in localized damage to trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down several large tree limbs near the intersection of Ingalls Street and Chestnut Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system (987 mb) moved across Illinois during the afternoon of Sunday, March 15, 2026. The environment was characterized by high shear and weak instability. A line of storms swept across the state, producing scattered wind damage and eight tornadoes within the NWS Central Illinois coverage area.  The tornadoes occurred southeast of the I-72 corridor and all were rated EF-0 or EF-1. No injuries occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began about two miles southwest of Tuscola where it snapped several large trees along N County Road 800 E. The tornado tracked northeast through Tuscola, producing more tree and fence damage, then continued towards Villa Grove, producing additional tree damage in rural parts of Douglas County. The tornado snapped multiple power poles on the north side of Villa Grove, along with additional tree damage, before dissipating north of Villa Grove prior to reaching the Champaign-Douglas county line. The tornado was rated EF-1, had a path length of over 11 miles, and was in progress for 10 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elongated low pressure which eventually intensified offshore along a cold front brought an low end advisory accumulating snowfall to Southern Connecticut.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cocorahs observers reported 3.2 inches in Killingworth and 3.0 inches at 1.4 NW Middlefield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong short wave moved across the region creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across southeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power poles were downed near Lumberton while a business had a sheet metal roof damaged in near Village Mills.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first storm of the month brought snowfall to the Sierra on the 10th and 11th, with 3-7 inches below 7000 feet and up to 1 foot near the crest west of Tahoe. The heaviest snow fell in far southern Mono County, with storm totals of 2 feet at Mammoth Mountain near 9000 ft elevation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm totals for the event were the following: Mammoth Mountain Ski Base measured 28 inches, June Mountain Ski Base measured 18 inches, and CoCoRaHs observer CA-MN-6 Mono City 1.9 SW measured 10.2 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals between 1.5 and 5 inches were reported across Parker County. The highest sleet and snow totals were reported just southwest of Reno. The Emergency Manager reported a roof collapse at GNJ Pickleball in Willow Park. The estimated damage to the metal warehouse facility was $2 million.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1.25 inch diameter hail in Shorewood Hills. Time confirmed via radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Cold temperatures and very cold wind chills infiltrated northeast Kentucky starting on January 20th, and extended into the end of the month amid reinforcing shots of cold air. Most nights during this time featured Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

The weather pattern began to turn more rainy/stormy during April 2026 across Oklahoma and western-north Texas, especially late in the month along and east of the Interstate 44 corridor. This helped to generally improve drought conditions here. Continued below-normal early spring rain totals across western and portions of northern Oklahoma intensified prolonged drought conditions for this region.
A warm moist air mass moving over cold ground helped cause widespread fog to form late on March 3rd and early on March 4th. The fog dissipated by noon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Delaware Coastal Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The gust was recorded by MnDOT station MN124 0.5N Motley.

CZ_NAME: BEARS PAW MOUNTAINS AND SOUTHERN BLAINE
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong mid level winds aloft moved in over the Hi-line and Central MT during the evening. This caused a few strong winds to mix down to the surface and produce isolated high winds across the North-Central MT plains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station FBLM8 Fort Belknap RAWS measured a 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of minor weather disturbances moved through the region from April 9th through the 11th. These combined with increased moisture to bring showers and storms to the region. With enough wind shear available in the atmosphere, some of these storms brought severe wind gusts to the region.  Dry and windy conditions were in place on April 9th and that helped drive the spread of a wildfire known as Mary 15 to almost 900 acres.  Additionally, the Lightning Roll Wildfire would be sparked due to dry lightning in Beaver County on the evening of April 9th.  That fire would go on to burn 2,412 acres.

Drought conditions continued during the month of February as below-normal rainfall was observed through the first two months of the year. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across southeastern Central Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) conditions persisted across Barbour County throughout the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low amplitude shortwave and accompanying 40 kt speed max approached the Mid-South and allowed lapse rates to steepen above 7 C/km. Ahead of this activity, the Mid-South housed around 750 J/kg of SBCAPE and bulk shear in excess of 45 kts. Small, organized clusters impacted the Mid-South in the late afternoon and brought damaging winds and large hail. Heavy rain showers ahead of the thunderstorm activity also brought on an urban flash flood threat.

A prolonged winter storm affected the Southern Plains on January 23rd through the 25th. Central and eastern Kansas saw all snow for this event. It snowed for 40 straight hours in Wichita. Most locations across central, south central and southeast Kansas picked up between five to a little above nine inches; near Smolan in Saline County measured 9.1 inches for the event.||Extreme cold air spilled south across the Plains with this event.  Nine temperature records were either set or tied during the January 23rd through January 26th time frame. Both Russell and Salina saw low temperatures of -16 with widespread wind chills in the 10 to 20 below zero range. In Wichita, the homeless shelter provided housing for over 365 guests which is above average and near their capacity. There is one unconfirmed fatality of an unhoused individual who didn't seek shelter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on surrounding reports as well as reports from within the county, an estimated 5 to 8 inches of snow fell across Russell County. The highest reported snow total was 8.0 inches about eight miles northwest of Russell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms moved eastward into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening as they organized into a squall line. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This is the first segment of a two-segment tornado. The tornado developed south of W 81st Street S and just west of S 39th West Avenue. The tornado moved east-northeast damaging the roofs of several homes, some severely, destroying outbuildings, snapping or uprooting numerous trees, and snapping power poles before it crossed into Tulsa County near W 81st Street S. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in this segment of the tornado was 100 to 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station Treatment - KGANICHO18 reported a one hour rainfall accumulation of 2.45 inches.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts along the east central Florida coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mesonet station Valkaria Airport measured a wind gust of 36 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A secondary cold front from an associated upper-level low pressure system tracking from the Ohio Valley allowed for snow shower development during the morning hours of January 11th. Clear skies with cold advection aloft allowed for meager, but sufficient, instability across the western half of Pennsylvania in an environment of ample lift and moisture to produce snow squalls. These snow squalls produced multiple instances of visibility below one-quarter of a mile, with multiple accidents with one reported on US Route 6 in McKean County and another accident on US Route 322 near Port Matilda. No injuries were reported from these accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall moved across Southern Centre county during the late morning of January 11, 2026. Webcams along Interstate 99 showed visibility less than one quarter of a mile with snow accumulating on the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front attendant to a southern Canada low pressure system moved slowly through western and central Virginia, triggering showers and thunderstorms. Bulk shear of around 30kts just east of the Blue Ridge supported damaging wind gusts from a few storms, which resulted in localized tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds near the 2800 block of Camp Hydaway Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on car on Route 12 in Gales Ferry CT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad upper level low centered offshore from northern California produced numerous thunderstorms in southern Oregon. One long-lived thunderstorm produced damaging winds across a portion of Jackson and Josephine counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long-lived thunderstorm produced strong winds across the city of Gold Hill. Damage included multiple trees falling across roads and power lines, and a fallen tree that damaged a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported golf ball sized hail 4 miles east-northeast of Strum.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Shed damaged at farmstead along County Road 53 near McComb.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Under strong 1027 mb high pressure, light wind allowed for efficient radiational cooling and minimum wind chill values to dip to -10 to -20F areawide with some spots below -20F, mostly in sheltered areas and higher elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill values generally ranged from -10 to -20 across the county with the exception of a -21 degree reading at a CWOP site 2 miles west of Washingtonville in the early morning hours of the 31st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moist upslope low level flow and hot temperatures allowed thunderstorms to develop on the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the 24th. This thunderstorm activity consolidated into several loosely organized segments as they moved into West Texas. The strongest storms remained anchored to a remnant surface boundary draped across the southern Texas Panhandle. These storms were able to produce widespread severe wind gusts across the extreme southern Texas Panhandle due to a very dry sub-cloud layer.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Hart measured severe wind gusts from 2253 CST through 2254 CST with a peak gust of 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 26th an approaching cold front associated with an upper level shortwave trough brought strong shear and modest mid level instability to New Hampshire.  Daytime heating was near seasonable norms, but still enough to create amble low level instability as highs reached the lower 80s.  A few long track storms created a swath of hail and wind damage from Sullivan to Rockingham Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed trees on wires on NH 11 near Grandliden Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted southeast Missouri on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th. Along and south of Route 34 towards Highway 60, a period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 5 to 11 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in areas that experienced mixing. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassable closer to the Mississippi River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces. Snow and ice covered roads, including portions of Interstate 57, were too dangerous for travel, and led to multiple accidents and traffic pileups across the region, making it difficult for first responders to provide assistance for several hours. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow, especially in Perry County, MO where drifts up to 21 inches were observed near Perryville. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures.
Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell along Raccoon Crossing Road in the vicinity of Cary Shop Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado developed south of Villisca at approximately 5:11 AM CST. The tornado would track along 110th St between V Ave and Willow Ave before dissipating near the county line at 5:13 AM CST. Along the tornado's path, trees were damaged, a farm outbuilding lost part of the roof and wall, and a carport was destroyed. The tornado had estimated wind speeds of 90 mph earning a rating of EF1. The maximum estimated width of the tornado was approximately 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave trough moved through the Northern Plains and brought high winds, heavy snow, and blowing snow across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. The highest winds occurs to the south of the main areas of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report relayed by broadcast media of 6.3 inches of measured snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.
With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through New Jersey. These storms produced widespread damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down, fences damaged in the Timberbirch development near Lynwood and Prospect Lane; time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were in place across most if not all of Martin, Pitt, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, northern Craven, southern Craven, Inland Onslow, Coastal Onslow, East Carteret, West Carteret, Jones, Pamlico, Washington, Northern Outer Banks, Outer Banks Hyde, and Beaufort Counties through the entire month of May according to the US Drought Monitor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions were noted across all of Lenoir County through all of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. This storm was unique as it had several local maxima across the state. The greatest amounts were in western Maryland across Garrett and western Allegany counties where 3 to upwards of 15 inches of snow fell. A secondary max associated with an inverted trough was observed from the Catoctins down to northern Montgomery county where 3 to 8 inches fell. Upwards of 12 inches were observed across the Catoctins. Another max of 3 to 6 inches was observed across Calvert and St. Mary's counties. The final max was Carroll to Cecil counties where 4 to 9 inches fell. Elsewhere across the DC and Baltimore metro, there was a relative minimum of 2 to 4 inches. Very little snow fell across eastern Allegany into far western Washington County.

Hot and humid conditions under high pressure along with an afternoon sea breeze circulation shifting inland led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported downed trees along 5 Chop Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning of March 11th, a QLCS pushed through portions of southern Illinois. The QLCS caused thunderstorm wind damage as it passed and produced 4 tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado moved through the communities of Moro and Midway, IL early in the morning of March 11, 2026. This tornado produced wind damage indicative of maximum wind speeds of approximately 110 miles per hour. Damage to trees, homes, and grain bins was observed. One injury was also reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Concho Valley and Northern Edwards Plateau. Also, a lightning strike destroyed a hotel in Brady.

A prolonged hot and dry period was set up for the Panhandles in mid May.  And with the lack of significant rainfall to help transition the grasses from cured to green, the fuels were well above the 90th percentile in dryness.  While it's not uncommon for a high based storm or two to occur west of the dryline and create dry thunderstorms, on May 14th it was certainly more scattered to nearly widespread storms that occurred.  Several lightning ignitions occurred, and given that the storms had severe dry microbursts associated, the fires that ignited would spread quickly.  Thereafter the Panhandles would go through several consecutive days of critical to extremely critical conditions.  And the issues of any new starts, as well as active fires that ignited on May 14th would take another run were of high concern.  Overall 20 wildfires ranging from over 34,000 acres to some as small as a few acres would ignite in the TX/OK Panhandle between the 14th and the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lightning sparked a wildfire in Hartley County Texas on May 14th and it was known as the Roman Fire.  This fire would quickly spread to over 2,000 acres due to the winds and dry fuels.  At one point the fire caused a shutdown of US highway 54 from RM3296 all the way to NM, due to smoke and low visibility.  Mandatory evacuations for areas near highway 54 and FM 767 were briefly needed.  On outbuilding structure was lost to this fire.  The fire would go on to burn 6,294 acres.  before being contained on the afternoon of the 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The lack of rainfall during winter 2025/2026 resulted in a continuation of drought conditions across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to begin March. D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) was common to start March, with a small area of Exceptional Drought (D4) across the Brush Country.  Additionally, the area saw deepening/expansion of these categories and the month we on. From the last week in February to the first week of March, D4 (Exceptional Drought) increased across 8% of the area from 18% to 26%, and the combination of D2 to D4 increased from 91 to 97% of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beginning on March 3, D2 (Severe Drought) developed in northern coastal Willacy County, and continued through Through March 16, before spreading to cover all of coastal Willacy County. These conditions would continue through March 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limbs were blown down and fences were damaged. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports from Emergency Managers of rotation and a funnel cloud near Fruitland,|IA. Location and time estimated from radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure passed to the south of Wyoming and brought snow to central and southern portions of the state. The heaviest amounts of snow fell in the favored northeast upslope areas. Some notable amounts in the mountains included 23 inches on Casper Mountain and 19 inches above Sinks Canyon Park near Lander. In the lower elevations, 8 inches of new snow fell in Casper and Jeffrey City and 5 to 12 inches fell near Lander. In Eastern Sweetwater County, the Green Mountains and Wind River Range, winds gusting as over 55 mph brought local blizzard conditions, leading to closure of Interstate 80, US 287 and South Pass during the storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to 14 inches of snow fell along the eastern Slopes of the Wind River Range. The snow and strong wind led to the closure of Highway 28 over South Pass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Outflow from thunderstorms caused multiple reports of wind damage throughout Franklin County, including at least 18 trees blown down in the northern portion of the county. A tree was also blown down at the 200 Block of Sample Road. One power line was reported down across the road near the intersection of Middle Valley Road and Green Ridge Drive, and another tree was blown down on Indian Run Trail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires down reported around Charlestown Township. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over Mother's Day weekend, a slow-moving cold front triggered scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across North and Central Texas. The majority of these storms occurred on Mother's Day (May 10), with many reaching severe levels and large hail becoming the most frequent report. Hail up to 4.5 was reported in Hamilton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio operator reported tennis ball size hail near South Mountain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving north of the area brought periods of rain Wednesday morning (13th), followed by scattered showers as a cold front approached. Partial clearing during the afternoon allowed for modest destabilization across western portions of the area. Combined with wind shear and unstable temperature lapse rates, thunderstorms organized along the front as they moved east through the evening. A few storms produced isolated damaging wind gusts and small hail. The strong gusts and small hail resulted in some crop damage according to a state emergency declaration, though estimated costs were unknown.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds brought down a tree and wires near Flume Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved along the US Highway 54 corridor during the late evening of March 10th. Damaging winds occurred along this line of storms with damage to trees and structures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An outbuilding was flipped upside down northeast of Harper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hinton (HINT) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from Wunderground station KMDSTEVE109. Time given in report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms moved east to southeast across Yuma and Kit Carson Counties during the evening hours on the 26th. Ping-pong ball size hail and a 68 mph measured wind gust were both reported in Cheyenne County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a Davis Weatherlink station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Henry County received 5 to 8 inches of heavy snow and sleet, in addition to 0.10 to 0.25 inches of ice accumulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across northeastern Minnesota on the afternoon of the 17th. These storms mainly produced large hail to the size of half dollars and gusty winds snapped a few trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The majority of the hail was three quarters to one inch in size but some pieces were as large as 1.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late season snow storm below across southeast Wyoming and dumped several inches of snow across the area. This was the heaviest snowfall event of the Winter 2025/2026 season with 8 inches of heavy, wet, snow falling in Cheyenne.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported 16 inches of snow 1 mile north of Buford during the duration of the event. The report came into the office via a social media post with a ruler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the night of June 21st, 2026 and into the early morning of June 22nd, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System moved through southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. This system brought multiple lines of storms and some supercells. Several tornadoes occurred along with flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado started along County Road 160 doing damage to some trees and a home along the east side of County Road 160. The tornado intensified as it approached Salem Drive, where the worst of the tree damage was noted with roughly 10 trees uprooted in a |small area. The tornado weakened and quickly lifted just to the east of Route 3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 10 degrees or less across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 8F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong coastal storm developed offshore of the Mid-Atlantic during the daytime hours on February 22nd, bringing high winds and heavy snow to portions of the Mid-Atlantic by that evening and through the morning hours of February 23rd. Blizzard conditions were confirmed for coastal New Jersey and Delaware, with heavy snow and windy conditions extending farther inland. The heavy snow was wet enough to stick to trees, which caused scattered tree damage and power outages across Delmarva, New Jersey, and the Philadelphia metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall amounts generally ranged from around 16-24. The highest reliable measurement received was 25.2 from Jackson Township. Blizzard conditions were confirmed based on nearby photos, videos, and weather station observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Breezy southerly winds shifted to southwesterly later into the evening of the 8th ahead of a cold frontal passage. Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the late evening hours in Southwest Indiana. Gusty gradient winds of near and above 40mph developed in portions of Southwest Indiana during the evening ahead of those storms.
On the afternoon on June 16, a few supercells developed. Photos of wall clouds were received and hail as large as 2 inches in diameter was recorded (in Michigan). Two EF-U tornadoes occurred as well.

A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around 2.5 to 5.5 inches of snow fell from Saturday night into Sunday morning. The highest report was 5.5 inches in Upsala. The snow was heavy at times, impacting visibility and driving conditions Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the mid-60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2500J/kg in Southeast Missouri with DCAPE of 900J/kg, 0-6km shear of 35-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from Southeast Missouri were primarily hail based. The largest hail occurred in the town of Advance which had numerous reports of golf ball to tennis size hail and a couple reports of baseball size hail, producing damage. Straight line wind damage was observed with a supercell in Bollinger County, downing a tree and damaging a barn roof.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports and pictures of hail in Advance were sent in from a variety of sources, many of which were golf ball to tennis ball size. The largest reports were measured at baseball size. Damage to roofs, windows, and vehicles occurred with this storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought sleet/snow to much of west central Texas. Some freezing rain resulted in a light glaze of ice across the Northwest Hill Country. The snow/sleet amounts ranged from 1 to 4 inches across the northern 2/3 of the area. The winter storm caused disruptions to travel and one fatality due to an accident on Interstate 10 east of Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 1 to 2 inches of snow/sleet across Irion County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low amplitude shortwave and accompanying 40 kt speed max approached the Mid-South and allowed lapse rates to steepen above 7 C/km. Ahead of this activity, the Mid-South housed around 750 J/kg of SBCAPE and bulk shear in excess of 45 kts. Small, organized clusters impacted the Mid-South in the late afternoon and brought damaging winds and large hail. Heavy rain showers ahead of the thunderstorm activity also brought on an urban flash flood threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A driver was stranded in flood waters on Sandhill Ave. They were able to escape without injury.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Alleghany county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Jackson River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper wave dropping south across the Great Lakes and it's associated cold front brought widespread accumulating snow to the region New Year's Eve and into the new year across the ridges of western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Enhanced orographic lift resulted in higher totals across the Laurel Highlands and eastern West Virginia ridges, with relatively high snow ratios between 18:1 and 21:1. Widespread Advisory level snow was also observed across the region, ranging from 2.5 inches to 5.5 inches outside of the ridges of Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall, exceeding advisory criteria and topping out just above warning criteria, fell across the county with amounts ranging from 3-5 inches and the highest total of 6.5 inches reported by the Public 2 miles northeast of Eastvale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were down and tree debris was downed due to thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Behind the northward retreat of a warm front, a cluster of showers moved along and just ahead of a cold front from Virginia into northwest North Carolina during the evening hours. These showers deepened and led to growing clusters of storms, along with one sustained supercell that brought a swath of large hail (0.75 to 1.25) and sporadic power outages and downed trees to the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One thousand power outages were reported from trees on powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Missouri during the afternoon and evening of March 15th. Several tornadoes occurred within this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged a barn roof 6 miles south of West Plains.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Repeated rounds of rainfall throughout May significantly improved drought conditions across South Texas and the Coastal Bend. Early-month rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches along the Coastal Bend and 1 to 10 inches across South Texas, with additional rainfall continuing through mid-May. Several storms produced strong winds, hail, and tornado warnings, resulting in localized damage. A more significant rainfall event occurred during the last week of May, when multiple storm systems produced widespread totals of 1 to 12 inches, with localized amounts exceeding 5 inches along portions of the Coastal Bend. The heavy rainfall led to localized creek flooding and more widespread flooding in portions of Refugio County. By month's end, topsoil and subsoil moisture had improved from short to surplus in many locations, substantially alleviating drought impacts and improving rangeland, pasture, and water availability across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 5/26, ending inclusion in Storm Data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure tracked across the central Great Lakes, into southern Ontario and then into southwest Quebec on December 29th. Its strong occluded front crossed the area during the morning into the early afternoon hours, ushering in much colder air to the region. ||The colder air and repeated passages of troughs and cold fronts for the remainder of the New Years week developed into a prolonged lake effect snow event, bringing at least light snow to the entire area. Moderate to heavy lake effect snow at times, combined with breezy conditions, prompted the issuance of Winter Storm Warnings for many counties in the Buffalo County Warning Area. Lake effect bands shifted north to south and south to north with passing troughs and cold fronts during the week, leaving a large footprint of significant snowfall. Snow and breezy conditions impacted New Years Eve celebrations across the areas as well. The hardest hit areas for snowfall were mainly east to southeast of both Lake Erie & Ontario. Some snow amounts from the entire event were as high as 4 to 5 feet off of Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.||Some of the notable snowfall amounts from this event include: 59.0 inches in Lacona, 56.5 inches in Richland, 51.5 inches in Colden, 44.0 inches in Glenwood, 34.5 inches in Cattaraugus, 33.6 inches in Silver Creek, 31.0 inches in Highmarket, 29.2 inches in Arcade, 25.5 inches in Batavia and 20.5 inches in Copenhagen.

A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms around 11 AM in northwest Mississippi with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of northwest Mississippi, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few fences were knocked down as well as a storage shed north of Lewisburg Schools, off of Craft Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down along Pilot Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Menokin Road in Richmond County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ponce emergency managers reported a landslide at Calle J (Street J), Parcela La Yuca, near PR-505 km 5.2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager relayed a report of a down tree across highway 114 near hoskin drive, blocking both lanes. As well as near smallen rd and oak hill rd.
