EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees blew down in the 13300 block of Round Hill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on Cameron Ridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Discrete severe thunderstorms developed off of Lake Michigan, tracked southeast, and congealed into multicell clusters. Along the way, storms produced quarter-sized hail. Most reports of quarter-size hail came from Putnam County, Ohio.

A major winter storm impacted the Ozarks region from January 23���25, 2026, bringing significant snow, ice, record-breaking cold to southwestern Missouri and far southeastern Kansas. The event, which peaked between Saturday, Jan 24, and Sunday, Jan 25, resulted in double-digit snowfall totals in some areas and widespread, dangerous travel conditions. Heaviest snowfall occurred near the Missouri-Arkansas border, with many locations receiving over 6 inches of snow. Some areas recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall with the highest amounts occurring along the Arkansas State line as bands of heavy snow developed. Roads and highways were severely impacted, with partial to full coverage reported across the region, including I-44 and I-49, making travel difficult or dangerous. Numerous crashes were reported with significant portions of I-44 experiencing closures, accidents, and hazardous conditions, particularly in Southwestern Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began to push into the County during the late evening hours of January 23 as the first round of snow that would continue into January 25th. Moderate to heavy snowfall then occurred during through the day January 24 and into midday January 25th. Between 4-7 inches of snow were reported across the County, causing multiple schools to close. Additionally, Interstate 49 was reported covered and partially closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees down throughout Berwick Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening coastal storm that passed by New Jersey resulted in strong onshore winds, resulting in elevated tides and moderate coastal flooding along the Jersey Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread roadway flooding occurred in the tidal communities of southeastern Burlington County. Water entered vulnerable buildings causing some damage. The tide gauge at Tuckerton reached 5.63 feet MLLW.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

The start of the new year was rung in with heavy snow showers that set up primarily along the northeast West Virginia mountains. Snow was ongoing from the night of New Years Eve, which was the result of a passing clipper system. This disturbance jetted off the eastern seaboard by the middle of the day on January 1st, leaving behind 5 to 8 inches of snow along the foothills and around a foot of snow for the higher mountainous areas of Randolph and Pocahontas Counties. For the lowlands, a few passing snow squalls contributed to light snow amounts between 1 to 3 inches.

Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few hail reports from north and northwest of Buckingham ranged in size from 2.5 to 3.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An ice storm crippled areas from northern Mississippi through middle Tennessee, clipping far northwest Alabama from the 24th through the 27th. Freezing rain accumulated up to 1 inch in far northwest Alabama, with accumulations dropping off quickly going further east and southeast in north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. The initial onset of precipitation was a mixture of snow, sleet and freezing rain, changing to all freezing rain in far northwest Alabama. A surge of warm air on the 26th changed precipitation to moderate to heavy rain for much of north Alabama and southern middle Tennessee, as temperatures warmed well above freezing. The exception was the far northwest tip of Alabama which remained in the colder air. A reinforcing cold front eventually brought temperatures back below freezing quickly during the late afternoon and early evening hours of the 25th which ended the steady rainfall. However, areas of light freezing drizzle redeveloped and produced a light accumulation of glaze across much of the area, and existing water on roadways from earlier heavy rain also began to freeze. The freezing drizzle changed to light snow and flurries during the overnight, lasting into the morning hours of the 26th. Very light accumulations were reported, with a dusting up to one half inch. Sunshine melted  the snow quickly during the day.||Impacts from these events were most severe in far northwest Alabama, including devestating tree damage, including numerous trees and limbs being knocked down, split or toppled onto power lines. Power outages occurred in northwest Alabama, including the Quad Cities/Shoals metro area. A water treatment facility in parts of western Lauderdale County was damaged, and a boil order was declared for about 1500 residents affected. Schools and businesses were shut down for multiple days in northwest Alabama and southern middle Tennessee. In north central and northeast Alabama, impacts were much less severe, and schools and businesses were shut down on the 26th due to cold and icy spots on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain produced and estimated ice accretion of 0.25 to 0.5 inches, and possibly higher in far northwest Lincoln County. Some sleet accumulation was also reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated thunderstorm moved east to slightly southeast across northeast Colorado during the afternoon hours on the 14th, ahead of an approaching upper level disturbance. Wind gusts up to 58 mph were reported between Yuma and Wray.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported by a trained spotter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Occluding low pressure system to the north moves east, further into Canada. Associated warm front moved through the state Tuesday evening, March 31st, and associated cold front moved through Maine quickly behind it on Wednesday, April 1st. Downeast region saw some snowfall early Tuesday morning, and alongside the warm front, mid-level warm air advection created a prime environment for some sleet development. Precipitation began as snow in the north, freezing rain/sleet in the Central Highlands, and rain Downeast. As the cold front quickly swept through the region, temperatures tanked, and resulted in more mixed precipitation. By the time the system fully moved through the region by Wednesday, roughly, 1/2 to just under 1 inch of sleet fell in Aroostook county. Roughly 0.1 to 0.25 inches of freezing rain fell in southern Aroostook, Piscataquis and northern Penobscot counties. Event began in March. System resulted in messy travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-2 inches of snowfall and sleet fell during the evening of the 31st. Trained spotter measured 0.20 inches of freezing rain by the morning of April 1st in Greenville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Diurnal convection interacted with a very moist atmosphere across portions of Louisiana. These slow moving storms produced flooding and a report of damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The stream gauge at Surrey  Street reported the Vermilion River rapidly rose 3 feet into minor flood. This flooded low areas along the river including areas around Vermilionville.

The more widespread wind damage occurred Wednesday afternoon June 10th from a derecho that developed in eastern Iowa and moved east. This downed trees, power lines primarily along and north of I-80. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Artic air behind a cold front ushered in dangerously cold wind chills of -15 to -25F for Extreme Cold areas and -10 to -18F for the Cold Weather areas. Winds gusted up to 35 mph at times.

These thunderstorms rapidly intensified and moved south and southeast across the I-70 corridor. Widespread wind damage occurred across portions of Lincoln, Ellsworth, Saline, McPherson, Marion, and Chase counties. In fact, a wind gust of 113 mph was measured at the Salina Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the early evening of the 14th, ahead of a dry line and an approaching upper level disturbance. The thunderstorms moved eastward into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening as they organized into a squall line. The line of thunderstorms produced several tornadoes and damaging wind.||Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 28th, an upper low was over the Great Basin. A shortwave propagating around this low helped prime the atmosphere for thunderstorm development. A dry, well-mixed boundary layer was present over far southwest Idaho leading to a severe wind threat. Further north into the west central Idaho mountains, effective shear was to 30-40 knots. This increased the hail threat north, in addition to the wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Idaho Transportation Department Mesonet CN2T6 measured a 59 mph wind gust associated with thunderstorm outflow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 drought conditions redeveloped during the middle of January and continued into February.

During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 66 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May started with severe drought (D2) present across much of eastern WV, including: Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and most of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Moderate drought (D1) also persisted across most of western and north-central WV, with the exception of Pleasants, Wood, northwest Jackson, northern Mason, western Ritchie, western Tyler, and western Wirt counties where conditions were merely abnormally dry (D0). Only minimal changes to D0 and D1 occurred in the second week of the month. D2, however, spread out across all of Boone and Kanawha counties; most of Lincoln, Logan, and Putnam counties; and portions of eastern Cabell, southern Jackson, southern Roane, and eastern Wayne counties. Conditions worsened even more the following week, as D2 engulfed most of southern, central, and eastern West Virginia, and a sliver of extreme drought (D3) crept into eastern McDowell, southeast Raleigh, and eastern Wyoming counties. Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth. Fortunately, enough precipitation fell at the end of the month to eradicate D3 and confine D2 to mainly Boone, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Nicholas, Logan, Mingo, McDowell, Raleigh, Webster, Wyoming, southern Braxton, eastern Lincoln, southern Roane, and southern Wayne. D1 improved to D0 in southern Tyler, Doddridge, northern Harrison, northern Taylor, part of northern Barbour, Ritchie, Wirt, northwest Gilmer, northern Calhoun, northern Roane, northern Jackson, northwest Mason, northwest Cabell, and part of northern Wayne. Meanwhile, drought was completely eliminated from counties, or at least portions of counties, bordering the Ohio River.||Generally less than an inch of rain fell during the first week of May. Around an inch or less accumulated during the second week. During the third week of the month, much of the area received around an inch and a half or less of rain, though a strip of up to two inches fell along the Ohio River. More substantial precipitation occurred at the end of the month, when one to three inches of rain fell to the south of I-64 and one and a half to over four inches fell to the north of I-64. Highest amounts were observed across portions of Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Lewis, Taylor, Randolph, and Upshur counties. Multiple rounds of rain during this time finally allowed for significant improvement to drought conditions, particularly across the northern and western part of the state.||The six climate sites in West Virginia were evenly split between above and below normal total precipitation for the month, with Beckley, Charleston, and Elkins on the below normal side and Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg on the above normal side. On the 22nd, Clarksburg, Huntington, and Parkersburg each received enough rain to break their existing daily precipitation records. Beckley was also able to tie a standing daily precipitation record on the 24th of the month.

An upper shortwave trough moved across Texas and generated thunderstorms. Some storms formed along a dryline over the western edge of South-Central Texas. Other storms formed east of the dryline in a conditionally unstable, moist airmass. Storms produced all severe hazards and locally heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 65 mph that knocked down a tree in the city of Uvalde.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm system impacted the State of Tennessee starting late Friday, January 23 and continuing into Sunday, January 25, 2026. Cold air moved into Tennessee Friday evening, setting the stage for winter weather through the weekend. This cold air along with a potent storm system resulted in primarily snow Friday night into Saturday morning. However, as warm air aloft moved north into Tennessee, this changed the precipitation from snow to sleet and then finally to freezing rain Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon. By the time precipitation came to an end, snow accumulations were highest across northwest Middle Tennessee where generally 3 to 5 inches were measured. A swath of ice accumulations of 0.25 to 0.50 inches was reported from Wayne County northeast through Nashville and to the Tennessee/Kentucky border. Locally higher amounts over one half inch were reported around the Nashville metro area.||These accumulations caused widespread, crippling damage in the form of broken and downed trees and power lines, dangerous to impossible travel conditions, and hundreds of thousands of power outages. Nashville Electric Service (NES) alone reported 230,000 customers without power which is the largest number of outages at one time NES has ever experienced. ||The other major impact from this winter storm was frigid temperatures. Cold air already in place over the weekend was reinforced Sunday night as arctic air moved into Tennessee behind this winter storm. The coldest temperature readings were recorded Monday and Tuesday mornings with widespread readings in the single digits and wind chills below zero. With these very cold temperatures, impacts were felt long after the precipitation ended.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mixture of snow, sleet, and ice impacted Wilson County during the early morning hours of January 24th into the afternoon of January 25th. A variety of reporting sources measured snow accumulations of 1 to 2 inches with ice accumulations of 0.30 to 0.60 inches. This led to several reports of treacherous travel and downed powerlines, trees, and tree branches. Total power outages were 2,458 customers across Wilson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Mountainair RAWS measured a 60 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms moved over Lake Erie in the evening hours.

An unusually extreme, early-season heat wave impacted central California during the middle of March, setting several monthly heat records across the region. Radiosonde observations from Oakland reported a monthly record for highest 850 mb temperature at 23.4 degrees Celsius, or around 74.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Notably, this temperature would also break the monthly record for April, had it occurred during that month. Given the extreme and unusual levels of heat for this time of year, a Heat Advisory was issued from Monday, March 16 through Friday, March 20, throughout the Bay Area and northern Central Coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Mount Hamilton station reported a monthly record high of 81.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a tree onto a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple shortwaves were able to spark clusters of severe thunderstorms in a moderately unstable, weakly sheared environment. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and wires down in Middle Island.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper low was moving along the International Border which helped to trigger thunderstorms along the Rio Grande Valley.  Modest instability and dry low levels helped to produce a 64 mph wind gust at Spaceport America.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Spaceport America AWOS recorded a peak gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS office measured a gust to 53 mph. The Clinton County Airport AWOS measured a gust to 48 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.

A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A dairy farm sustained significant damage to numerous outbuildings.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple images showing thunderstorm wind damage in/around Tuttle were shared on social media. Damage included: A large horse trailer blown onto its side, A garage door blown inward, trees snapped, large tree branches and limbs blown down and various damages to outbuildings. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning, afternoon and evening hours of April 26 through April 29 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail and a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered trees were blown down in the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure trough moved eastward out of the Great Basin and tracked across eastern Utah into western Colorado, with above normal moisture pulled in ahead of it. This resulted in moderate snowfall for most mountain ranges in eastern Utah and western Colorado with the central and southern Colorado mountains receiving the heavier snowfall as colder air wrapped into the center of the low as it tracked further south over the Four Corners.  This favorable northerly flow on the backside of the low along with colder air resulted in higher snowfall amounts in the Uncompahgre Gorge of the Northwest San Juan Mountains and the valleys upstream from Ouray to Montrose.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 6 to 12 inches of snow fell across the area with locally higher amounts up to 18 inches at Cumbres Trestle. A peak wind gust of 46 mph occurred at Wolf Creek Pass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees blew down near Worthington Manor and Western Run.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercell thunderstorms developed near a slow-moving frontal boundary during the afternoon and evening hours on February 26. Cold temperatures were present aloft with strong deep layer shear but relatively weak low-level shear. Scattered severe hail reports were received, with the largest hailstones falling in portions of Blount, Jefferson, and St. Clair counties, as large as two inches in diameter. Damaging winds also occurred, with the most significant wind damage in Pinson where a microburst occurred. A hail storm associated with the microburst resulted in accumulating hail that covered the ground and resulted in the formation of hail fog. In addition, a brief EF-0 tornado also moved through Trussville, damaging some commercial and industrial buildings as well as homes, most of which was minor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter-size hail was reported in Fayette.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low in the area brought two rounds of isolated strong to severe thunderstorms to the region. The main hazard with storms was severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Straight-line winds knocked down multiple tree limbs and caused the power to go out.  Nearby automated sensors were gusting 35-40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multicell thunderstorms over eastern Indiana moved into northwest Ohio resulting in sporadic reports of damaging wind gusts and sub-severe hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damage to aluminum roofing at a  manufacturing building.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of freezing rain moved across portions of central and southern MN. Despite ice accumulations accreting to less than a tenth of an inch, travel conditions were very slippery which results to numerous vehicle accidents and spin outs across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The neighboring AWOS stations located at the Olivia Regional Airport and Glencoe Municipal Airport observed approximately an hour of freezing rain. There was less than one tenth of ice accretion but did make morning travel conditions incredibly slippery.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59mph wind gust was measured at Central Illinois Regional Airport (KBMI).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

Strong northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with a gusts to around 60 mph occurred across west central, southwest, and central Nebraska during the early morning hours until the early afternoon hours on March 15th. Peak wind gusts reached 60 mph or higher at the Imperial, Broken Bow and North Platte ASOS stations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph with gusts to around 50 mph or higher were common across Keith County during the morning hours into the mid afternoon hours. A mesonet site 4 miles southwest of Brule recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 227 am MST. The nearby North Platte ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph at 1107 am CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a mid-level wave moved out of Nebraska toward southeast South Dakota during the overnight, convective clusters blossomed near and ahead of a frontal boundary with MUCAPE from 2000-3000 J/kg and effective shear of up to 50 knots. Initial, more isolated storms produced hail across northeast Nebraska up to golf ball size, but quickly evolved into bowing segments with damaging wind gusts mainly from 60 to 85 mph across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.  At one point, there were around 600 customers without power due to downed lines and poles in parts of Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by a NDAWN mesonet station 4 miles north-northwest of Bergen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper-level low over the Eastern Arctic tracked southwest toward the Bering Strait during the last week of January. This system pushed a cold front across the region, producing very strong winds along and immediately behind the boundary. These winds triggered initial blizzard conditions along the Northwest Arctic coast, which then spread westward toward the western Seward Peninsula.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: For the second consecutive day the Eastern Beaufort Sea coastline experienced blizzard conditions. The AWOS at Point Thomson (PAAD) began reporting wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph along with visibility reading of 1/4 mile or less. This trend continued for more than two full days resulting in a long duration blizzard that persisted for 55 hours before letting up.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of scattered tree, power line, and structural damage across central and southern Jefferson County. This included many uprooted and snapped trees, power lines down, and fallen trees on homes and vehicles especially in Fort Atkinson and Jefferson. The entire roof of a home was removed by the strong winds in Jefferson near the high school. Lakeview Cemetery in Fort Atkinson suffered significant tree damage with trees down on grave sites. An agricultural business near Hellenville sustained damage to fences and shelters built for animals. A 60 mph wind was estimated at the National Weather Service office several miles southeast of Sullivan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

A line of severe storms developed in north central Kansas during the mid afternoon on 4/26 and tracked eastward through northeast Kansas, producing large hail to ping pong ball size and wind gusts estimated to around 70 mph. Clusters of late evening severe storms impacted much of northeast Kansas through the early morning of 04/27. Large hail to Golfball size and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported. Flash flooding also occurred in Shawnee, Jefferson, and Douglas counties as in upwards of 5 inches of rain fell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured with handheld anemometer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather station Home - KGAFOLKS16  measured a storm total of 3.64 inches. Rain began around 12 PM EDT. Heaviest rain fell  between noon and 130 PM EDT where 2.85  inches fell. Surrounding sites measured 3  inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low pressure system passed over North Dakota and deepened over the Red River Valley.  This, combined with strong winds aloft mixing down, resulted in very strong wind gusts over much of western and central North Dakota. The strongest wind gust reported was 89 mph which occurred at Hettinger in Adams County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Denhoff NDDOT reported sustained winds to 44 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front draped across Arkansas in tandem with an approaching upper level trough axis would spur multiple days of severe winds, flash flooding, and heavy rain totals for the multi-day event across the state of Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down at the intersection of Arkansas Highway 315 and Arkansas Highway 359 east of the town of Lamar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure moved through the eastern U.S. bringing a plume of deep moisture over top of an arctic airmass which brough 1-2 feet of snow to southern New England Sunday through Tuesday morning. The biggest total was 27 inches in Gloucester, MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 12-18 inches of snow fell with some of the higher amounts being 19.5 inches in Warren and 15.1 inches in Barrington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of creeks leading to flooded roads at the intersection of County Highway F and FF, and State Highway 104 north of Brodhead.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A two foot diameter tree was down and blocking the southbound lane of Somonauk Rd just north of Pratt Rd in Sandwich.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

During the last two days of June, a favorable synoptic weather pattern brought extreme heat to portions of northeast Iowa as ample moisture resulted in remarkably high dewpoints. Consequently, heat indices soared well above 100 degrees with numerous locations seeing heat indices of 110 to 115 degrees or even higher in some locations. June 29th was the hottest day but extreme heat persisted into the 30th where heat indices in excess of 100 degrees were still common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme heat moved into the region during the end of June with widespread heat indices over 100 degrees. On June 29th, heat indices ranged from 110 to 116 degrees across the county during the afternoon and early evening. The highest heat index observed in the county was 116 degrees in Lawler. On June 30th, continued heat indices over 100 degrees persisted throughout much of the daytime hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated light rain showers and virga associated with a weak shortwave led to strong wind gusts across parts of North Texas the evening of May 15. Wind gusts around 60 MPH were measured, and trees were blown down in a few locations within the DFW Metroplex.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A local official reported that a tree was down at Schooling Road and Palm Lake in Roanoke. Strong winds of 50-60 mph were measured beneath virga moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Road PR-2 km 164.7 was impassable due to flash flooding. At 1:36 PM, Emergency managers reported that they reopened the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Antecedent arctic air mass, combined with some radiational cooling on the night of the 7th into the 8th, resulted in a very cold night. Light winds of 5mph or less resulted in apparent temperatures of -15F or colder in many locations, some for several hours, but briefly in a few sites.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: RAWS site near Atlanta, MI reported an apparent temperature of -32F. Low temperature reported by Atlanta, MI cooperative observer was -14F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Early summer environment of moderate shear and instability contributed to the development of strong storms that produced wind damage near Sebring in Highlands County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local EM reports tree and roof damage at an auto dealership near Sebring.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass entered the UP late on the 22nd, with very cold wind chills of -25F or lower persisting at times through the morning of the 26th. The coldest wind chills occurred during the mornings of the 23rd and 24th, when minimum values ranged from -30 to -55F in the central and western UP, and -25 to -25F in the eastern UP. For some areas in the central and western UP, this was the coldest 3 and 4 day stretch since January 2019. Numerous schools, businesses, and services were closed on Friday the 23rd and Saturday the 24th.||In addition to the cold temperatures, blizzard conditions accompanied the initial push of cold air during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd in the Keweenaw, with whiteout conditions leading to several traffic accidents and road closures. Another round of heavy accumulating lake effect snow occurred in the northeastern UP on the 23rd, with very low visibilities resulting in at least one road closure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds, accumulating snow, and cold temperatures resulted in blizzard conditions during the afternoon and evening of the 22nd. Key impacts: traffic accidents, transportation delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm tracked across northern Denver and nearby suburbs producing hail up to 1.75 inch in diameter. Additional severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 2 inch in diameter to the eastern Colorado plains.

A second wave of wintry precipitation occurred 24 hours after a light mix of snow and freezing rain fell the day prior. This round was heavier and temperatures were right around freezing, leading to a mixture of freezing rain and rain. For most locations, the main period of freezing occurred overnight from the 5th into the 6th as rainfall rates were lighter. Rates then increased during the morning of the 6th which made it difficult for ice accretion to continue as temperatures hovered right around the freezing point. By the morning commute, most areas saw more of a crunchy slush on the ground as the heavier rain started to melt the coating of ice that developed overnight. The heaviest impacted area was western Hennepin, Wright, Anoka, and Chisago counties where temperatures were slightly cooler and the rain rates were not as heavy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The AWOS at KROS reported several hours of freezing precipitation mainly falling during the early morning hours of the 6th. Several CoCoRaHS observers reported light ice accumulation overnight, especially on trees, driveways, and walkways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A continued lack of rainfall allowed pre-existing drought conditions to worsen in the month of March with much of South Florida remaining a severe to extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought continued across coastal Broward County in March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 2 to 3-foot diameter tree was snapped about halfway up the base.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were down and blocking Eldridge St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down across a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.
Orographic lift and mid-level moisture lead to accumulating snow in the Sierra Madre Range on January 5th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak snowfall reported in the Sierra Madres came from the Old Battle SNOTEL (OLDW4) with 15.6 inches. Several other SNOTELs reported snow accumulations above 6 inches.
