EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front pushed through the U.P. during the morning hours on Jan 14th, associated with a clipper low that passed north of Lake Superior.  Strong winds and heavy lake effect snow behind the front brought blizzard conditions to Marquette and Alger Counties.  Periods of near blizzard conditions were observed in the Keweenaw Peninsula.  Law enforcement reported near zero visibility and the runway at Sawyer Regional Airport was closed.  Snowfall amounts of 5 to 10 inches were reported across the northern half of Marquette County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pick City NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of passing frontal boundaries, surface lows and troughs during the week of January 18th resulted in yet another snowy period for Western and North Central New York. These passing cold and warm fronts also provided a variability to temperatures during this period as well. Toward the end of the week, behind a passing Arctic front, temperatures dropped to some of the coldest values of the season with daytime highs only in the single digits to low teens for most areas. Overnight windchill values dropped to -30 degrees Fahrenheit or lower at times for Jefferson and Lewis counties on the night of January 23rd. ||Notable windchill values for the end of the week include: -49 degrees Fahrenheit at Copenhagen, -47 degrees Fahrenheit at the Watertown Airport, -46 degrees Fahrenheit at Belleville, and -39 degrees Fahrenheit at Harrisburg.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous observations and reports from around Lewis County of wind chill values between -30 and -49 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Discrete thunderstorms in southeast Oklahoma congealed into a mesoscale convective complex as they moved southeast into northern Louisiana early morning of May 9th. The system consisted of clusters and linear segments moving rapidly eastward, while localized cell mergers and brief training occurred within the broader complex. The storms produced widespread severe wind gusts over local coastal waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Weatherflow mesonet on Ship Island XSHI measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 52 mph or 45 kts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Em reports tree down at lone oak rd near bass cross rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power poles were snapped along Dickson Mounds Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pictures showed hail stones around 4 inches in diameter in Trenton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were estimated to be around 60 to 70 mph by the public.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were blown down.  A photo showed an uprooted evergreen tree.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS KOMA reporting peak gust of 63 mph at Omaha Eppley Airfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, well above normal precipitation occurred across the region during March. By late March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Schuyler County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph, tore a roof off of a house in the 5900 block of Warrensville Road in Warrensville. There were no injuries reported from this storm damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had resulted in Extreme Drought (D3) over north-central Indiana by late 2025 generally expanded and intensified throughout January 2026. While D2 and D3 levels were maintained from the previous month, a significant degradation occurred on the January 6th update, where D3 intensity expanded across the heart of the region. These drought conditions remained entrenched without improvement through the end of the month and continued into at least February 2026.||This status quo included a primary sub-region where D3 conditions expanded to cover the entirety of Howard County and much of Carroll and Delaware counties. Significant expansion of Severe Drought (D2) was also noted, moving to encompass the remainder of Clinton, Hamilton, and Vermillion counties. Meanwhile, D2 intensity was maintained across northern Henry County and northwestern Vigo County, with a small additional expansion into north-central Vigo. In the northeast, Tipton County saw an intensification as D3 pushed into its northern portions, while D3 remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County.||Precipitation throughout January for these areas was critically low, with many totals falling between 0.75 and 1.25 inches. Specifically, Carroll, Randolph, and Howard counties saw meager totals of 0.75 to 1.10 inches, which directly triggered the expansion of D3 intensity. Even in areas like Henry County, which received a slightly higher 1.50 to 2.25 inches, the moisture was not enough to warrant improvement. These sustained deficits, often totaling less than 50% of normal monthly rainfall, ensured that the drought not only persisted but worsened across the central Indiana landscape.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.00 inches across the month of January. This maintained D2 conditions across far southwestern Vermillion county. On the January 6th update, D2 expanded to cover the remainder of the county. These drought conditions continued into at least February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A QLCS moved into western Georgia during the mid morning hours of the 10th. The strongest storms were located south of I20 with several bowing and comma-head sections which lead to pockets of strong wind damage and a brief tornado in Carrol county. Storms quickly weakened as they moved eastward, as a wedge was in place over northern Georgia.||Storms in north Georgia became nearly stationary ahead of the main line with high proficient rainfall rates along and south of the southern Appalachians. This resulted in areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree down at n butts mill rd and hamilton rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance rounding the top of an upper-level ridge along with a nearby stationary boundary resulted in shower and thunderstorm development mainly across portions of southeast New Mexico. One storm managed to produce a severe wind gust at the Tatum Mesonet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 58 mph at WTM 2SW Tatum NM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Alleghany county by the end of April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One tree blew down into the road on Parsons Road near Thornhill Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. Cold temperatures (wind chill) below 30F arrived during the late evening of the 24th across the ranchlands and spread to the lower Rio Grande Valley before daybreak on the 25th.  A cold afternoon set the stage for the overnight of the 25th into the morning of the 26th, as skies cleared but fresh breezes/stronger winds near the coast prevailed.  The 26th was the coldest ambient and feels-like temperature of the calendar year so far, with a freeze in all areas, and wind chill below 20F in most areas.  ||Clear skies and calm winds allowed rapid temperature drops during the evening of the 26th, with many inland locations recording their second hard freeze in as many nights early on the 27th. Locations closer to the coast saw winds veer to the northeast above the surface, precluding a second freeze/hard freeze. ||The hard freeze caused minor damage to tender vegetation and crops in Hidalgo, Willacy, and Cameron County.  Dollar values were unknown as of this writing (end of March 2026) but some estimates are included, and will likely be updated.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The locus of observations on the Yturria ranch (northern Willacy, near the Kenedy line), northern Cameron (near the Willacy line), and the Texas AgriScience Center (northeast Hidalgo,  near the southwest Willacy border) gave a proxy duration of freezing temperatures (32F degrees or lower) for 13.5 hours from 9 PM Jan. 25 through 1030 AM CST on Monday January 26th. A Hard Freeze (temperatures at or below 27F degrees) occurred for 7.5 hours from 2 until 930 AM CST January 26th.  Minimum temperatures were in the lower to mid 20s.||An unknown amount of minor damage was likely to winter crops, mainly due to the sharp temperature change from prior to the freeze until after it.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably mild air moved into the region ahead of a strong low pressure system. These conditions, on top of a fairly dry February across western South Dakota allowed a fire to develop northeast of the community of Green Grass and spread rapidly southeast. 991 acres of mostly prairie and pasture were burned in the fire, with a portion of Highway 63 closed due to smoke and the threat of the fire crossing the Highway. ||Winds picked up dramatically with the passage of the low pressure system, with a peak wind gust of 81 mph recorded at the Pierre Regional Airport ASOS. The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Huron RAWS, located 5 miles east of Danforth recorded a peak wind gust of 75 mph, while the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles east of Orient recorded a peak gust of 72 mph. 3 additional weather stations in Hand county recorded a peak wind gust in excess of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought persisted in January and continued into February.

Two rounds of severe storms developed across north-central Kansas on the evening of May 16. The first was a cluster of supercells that produced large to very large hail and isolated strong winds, while the second was a line of storms that mostly produced damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CWOP station measured 63 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few severe storms produced damaging winds which downed trees across portions of central and southern Mississippi. A brief, weak tornado also occurred near Midway Road in Hinds County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down near Onward.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet accumulation in southern Indiana January 24-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy snowfall rates and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky and into far southern Indiana, changing precipitation over to sleet for a short period of time in some counties. The winter storm dropped a swath of heavy snow and sleet totaling 6 to 13 inches across southern Indiana. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of snow-covered roads and dangerously cold wind chills. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow and sleet totaling 6 to 12 inches fell across Perry County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions across Pickett County from April 2026 continued in May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic, record-setting winter storm impacted northeast Wisconsin from Saturday evening (3/14), through Monday evening (3/16). A potent Colorado low deepened as it tracked from the central Plains toward Chicago and eventually Lake Huron, placing a long duration of heavy precipitation directly over the region. The storm began as snow Saturday evening (3/14) before transitioning to a wintry mix of snow, freezing rain, and sleet across central and east-central Wisconsin after 3 AM Sunday (3/15). This mix produced a few hundredths of an inch of ice in east-central Wisconsin before changing back to all snow early Sunday afternoon (3/15).||Snow became very heavy over central Wisconsin early Sunday morning (3/15) with snowfall rates up to 4 inches per hour. Cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were observed at times in thundersnow and thunder sleet. These heavy snowfall rates shifted east through the morning, reaching northeast Wisconsin around midday Sunday. Blizzard to near-blizzard conditions developed Sunday afternoon, fueled by northeast winds gusting between 35 and 50 mph. Peak gusts reached 59 mph at the Green Bay Airport (Brown Co.) and 60 mph in De Pere (Brown Co.). This combination of heavy falling snow and high winds created whiteout conditions and massive drifting.||After a brief lull in snowfall Sunday evening, heavy snow redeveloped from south to north early Monday morning (3/16). This second round of precipitation was intense, with snowfall rates reaching 1 to 3 inches per hour at times across the Fox Valley and lakeshore. The combination of this heavy snow and powerful north winds, gusting between 40 and 55 mph, resulted in a return to blizzard conditions. Visibility frequently dropped to a quarter mile or less, creating whiteout conditions that made travel impossible. By Monday morning (3/16), this overnight surge had dumped an additional 6 to 12 inches of snow on top of what had already fallen.||Final snowfall totals were historic, with a widespread 1 to 2 feet across the area and localized amounts exceeding 30 inches from Wausau (Marathon Co.) to Marinette and Door counties. Green Bay (Brown Co.) recorded 26.6 inches, marking its second-largest snowstorm on record. Impacts were severe and wide-reaching. Travel became nearly impossible, leading to numerous flight cancellations and significant road drifting, including a 10-foot drift reported in Ephraim (Door Co.). Roads were severely impacted throughout the event with tow bans in place and some municipalities suspending plowing. No Travel Advised was posted for an extended period on the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (DOT) webpage. The heavy snow load and high winds caused widespread power outages, most notably in Door and Marinette counties, and building collapses were reported in Sturgeon Bay (Door Co.) and Kewaunee County. Many schools and businesses remained closed through Monday (3/16) and even on Tuesday (3/17).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall totals across Marathon County included 30.9 inches in Wausau, 28 inches in Brokaw, 25.8 inches near Mosinee, and 24 inches in Knowlton. In addition, winds gusting to 35 to 45 mph caused near-blizzard conditions at times on Sunday March 15 and Monday March 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region during the afternoon and evening. An initial pre-frontal boundary led to the developed isolated strong to severe storms. A secondary line of storms were also tied with the main cold front, leading to widespread damaging winds as the front moves from the Piedmont into the Coastal Plain of central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house near the 3400 block of Silver Pine Circle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An inside slider pattern developed over May 15 to May 18 as a low pressure system over the Great Basin and high pressure in the eastern Pacific combined to create a strong pressure gradient, resulting in strong gusts and turbulent wind-driven seas. A Beach Hazards Statement was placed in effect for the entire weekend, while two separate Wind Advisories were put in place, one for coastal regions through Saturday and another for the interior mountains of the Bay Area Sunday night through Monday morning. The strong winds caused an estimated 13,000 customers across the Bay Area to lose power.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Poverty RAWS reported a gust of 47 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In response to a powerful upper-level trough barreling into the Central Plains, digging further south and deepening in the process, an area of low pressure at the surface also strengthened as it shifted east across Kansas and eventually into Illinois by the end of the day on the 15th. The accompanying surface cold front and resulting strong pressure gradient allowed legitimate High Wind criteria conditions to overtake the entire forecast area, with sustained winds commonly 35-45 MPH with gusts 55-65 MPH, and even a few localized 70+ MPH gusts. The brunt of the highest wind gusts occurred mainly during the 10AM-4PM CDT timeframe, with reports more scattered in nature outside of that period. Across north central Kansas, some of the highest gusts included the following: 63 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located near Agra; 61 MPH, measured by the Smith Center Airport AWOS as well as mesonet stations located near Jewell and four miles east-southeast of Long Island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained speeds near 40 MPH and wind gusts exceeding 50 MPH were common throughout the day based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex system brought severe winds to much of northern UT with a brief tornado along the border of Cache and Rich counties. Later on, this system would result in a flash flood event across southern UT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported 1.25 hail via MPING near Logan, UT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system and arctic blast brought strong winds and pockets of light to moderate snow showers.  ||A peak wind gust of 71 mph was observed 1 mile north northwest of Lees Corner in Buffalo County by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Information Weather System (RWIS), and by a personal weather station 2 miles north of the Pierre Regional Airport. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded by the SDDOT RWIS station 1 mile northeast of Stephan in Hyde county, while 66 mph wind gusts were measured by the SDDOT RWIS stations 5 miles south southwest of Klein Ranch in Corson county and 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake in Dewey county.  A total of 39 weather stations recorded a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. These high winds flipped a semi and damaged a grain elevator near the town of Murdo on the morning of the 16th. ||While snow accumulations were limited, snow showers of moderate intensity combined with these strong winds to produce temporary white-out conditions. No Travel Advised was issued by both the Walworth and Day county Sheriffs. Various SDDOT RWIS webcams showed visibility in blowing snow fluctuating significantly over short distances in the matter of a few minutes. An emergency vehicle rendering assistance for an accident on Interstate 29 near Watertown was struck with minor injuries. A separate accident along Interstate 90 resulted in a 5 vehicle chain reaction crash which resulted in 2 fatalities and a number of injuries.  ||80 residents of Deuel county reported power out during the event.

April saw below to well below normal precipitation across a majority of New Mexico, with the exception of a small area of the northwestern mountains. The average temperature anomaly was also generally 1 to 5 degrees above normal over nearly all of the state. This led to a notable expansion of extreme drought conditions over northeastern NM, and severe drought conditions over the eastern plains. While western areas saw below normal precipitation, the actual difference from normal was still low given April is climatologically a very dry month already. This allowed for little to no change in drought conditions over this portion of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought remained persistent over the far northwestern portion of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As an upper level low moved through the region, severe thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front that moved through North Dakota. Scattered showers and non-severe thunderstorms were ongoing during the morning before increasing in strength throughout the afternoon. A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to be golf ball sized. Public report relayed by broadcast media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms produced high wind gusts in southwest Alabama.
Scattered thunderstorms developed and tracked east across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail was the main storm threat with three inch diameter hail being reported near Wiggins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was from mPing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The S-Turns - Big Cottonwood Canyon mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 60 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Wyoming as a strong cold front moved across the state. Several areas had multiple lines move through the same region during the event. Severe Thunderstorm Watch was in effect for most of the afternoon through the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station near Douglas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into northwestern Connecticut on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of southern Litchfield County both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms led to some downed trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of trees and wires were downed in West Cornwall including on Lower River Road and on River Road just north of the center of town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires down with power outages per Eversource. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix changed over to snow as temperatures plunged well below freezing behind an arctic front. This created an icy flash freeze environment under a half inch to two inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front moved through with a mixture of sleet and rain changing to a period of snow. Snow accumulations were generally an inch or two at best. However, the cold air rushing in with the front and snow allowed the wet pavement to freeze late morning into the afternoon and early evening. This resulted in reports of slide-offs and accidents across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of rapidly weakening showers produced high winds in central South Dakota. A peak wind gust of 65 mph was recorded on the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet (SDDOT) station 3 miles southeast of Reliance in Lyman county, with a 62 mph gust measured at the SDDOT station 2 miles west of Oacoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 9 miles east southeast of Rosseau recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph that resulted from decaying elevated shower activity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal rainfall in portions of north central, central, southwestern and western Nebraska led to improvements in drought conditions across western and north central Nebraska in June. There were a few local areas where drought conditions remained unchanged in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Exceptional (D4) drought conditions improved to extreme (D3) drought across most of Grant County by the end of June. Across far northern and far eastern portions of the county, extreme (D3) drought improved to severe (D2) drought the end of June. The cooperative station at Whitman 5 ENE reported 4.45 inches of precipitation for June. This was 1.68 inches above the normal of 2.77 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of a large downed tree branch in Edgerton. Wind gust estimated from radar data and damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak ascent atop a very hot/unstable boundary layer fostered clusters of thunderstorms - generally disorganized/multi-cell in nature - from southwestern into north-central Oklahoma on the 29th. Damaging wind gusts and hail were observed with activity throughout the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 6 to 8 inches of snow across Moultrie County...including 7.4 inches in Lovington.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree over the roadway at the corner of E  Benton Ave and Malone St. in Ava.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. Training along the boundary mostly resulted in a flash flooding threat, though moisture pooling ahead of the front supported MLCAPE values reaching 1000 J/kg, and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported some storm organization for a damaging wind and embedded tornado threat with locally backed surface wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Picture on social media of water covering Kruger Street and the sidewalk across the  street. Estimating at least 6 inches of water on the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One category improvements were noted in drought severity in areas that had previously been in Extreme(D3) or even some Severe(D2) drought.  By the end of the month, there were no areas in southern New Mexico in Extreme(D3) drought or worse.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was no change in drought conditions through the month of January.  The western half of the zone remained in Severe(D2) drought and the east in Moderate(D1) drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing across IL-121 near its intersection with County Road 1200 North.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous hail-producing thunderstorms (supercells) developed along a slow-moving frontal boundary across south-central into southeast Oklahoma from the early afternoon into evening of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado with path length of 2.02 miles and a path width of 50 yards moved through portions of Martin County. Much of the damage limited to trees with one metal roof partially ripped off.  Nearby, there was sporadic straight line wind damage.  Peak tornado winds were 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms rolled across the Denver Metro area mid afternoon on June 8th producing up to golf ball sized hail. Isolate severe wind gusts were recorded as well. As the storms progressed east of the Denver their intensity increase. A supercell thunderstorm continued to track eastward, stay south of I-70. Farther north, thunderstorms organized into a broken line, producing wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph across far northeast Colorado.

An unseasonably warm and humid airmass developed across central Illinois on March 26, 2026, with some locations recording record high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s. Dewpoints also surged into the lower 60s. As a cold front approached during the evening, scattered to widespread strong to severe storms developed along and ahead of the front, primarily in areas north of I-70. These storms produced hail as large as golf balls, as well as a few wind damage reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large pine tree branch was blown down onto playground equipment on the west side of Pana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A snow squall crossed through Wythe County during the morning hours to produce gusty winds, blowing snow, a sudden drop in temperature, and near whiteout conditions. The snow squall caused the visibility to drop under one quarter of a mile at several locations in Wythe County with a state department of transportation camera capturing its passage along Interstate 77 at mile marker 26.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow Squall - A snow squall crossed Speedwell where a picture was taken that showed the visibility dropped to under a quarter of a mile.  Key Impacts:  traffic delays, reduced visibility, blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and large tree limbs were blown down across Homer Glen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across Lorain County.

Heading into the 8th, the upper level ridge broke down. This day brought a longer duration of strong sustained winds and widespread strong wind gusts over North-Central MT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous weather stations in the zone measured high wind wind gusts and a few measured sustained winds of up to 4 to 6 hours. The highest wind gust was measured at Montana mesonet station Frenchman Ridge of 71 mph and measured an average sustained wind of 46 mph between 9:25am to 4:50pm MST. Law enforcement also reported reduced visibility from blowing dust due to the strong winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 4F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A messy mix of snow, sleet and freezing rain fell across the county, beginning initially as snow on the afternoon of the 24th. A picture on social media shows at least an estimated 0.25 inches of flat ice accretion in the Sizerock area at 857EST on the 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Highway Z was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 6 to 8 inches fell. The highest report was 6.8 inches in Amhurst.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several very large cottonwood trees were uprooted at Snyder Bend Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deepening surface low pressure system was centered over Illinois and an attendant cold front extended south-southwestward sweeping from west to east across Arkansas during the afternoon and evening hours of March 15, 2026. Multiple severe thunderstorms developed in a well-defined warm sector positioned across the state where storms matured and quickly became severe producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny sized hail fell near the town of Heber Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were pictures of shed damage between Midland City and Pinckard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -50F. ||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F. ||The lowest wind chills were:|-50F at AXN in Alexandria, MN.|-49F at STC in St Cloud, MN.|-49F at OWA in Owatonna, MN.|-49F at GHW in Glenwood, MN.|-47F at MSP in the Twin Cities, MN.|-47F at BDH in Willmar, MN.|-47F at CFE in Buffalo, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearby KMSP reported wind gusts as high as 35 mph during the early evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -21F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -47F at 2AM on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana.  Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed around Cropwell.

CZ_NAME: SANTA LUCIA MOUNTAINS AND LOS PADRES NATIONAL FOREST
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cyclone approached the Central Coast on February 10, resulting in the first substantial rainfall in over a month for much of the Bay Area and Central Coast. A Wind Advisory was issued for all of Monterey and San Benito Counties as wind gusts up to 50 mph were expected across the region late on the 10th and into the early morning of the 11th. The orientation of the low favored rainfall for the Santa Cruz and Santa Lucia ranges, where rain totals reached 1-3 inches in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and 2-5 inches in the Santa Lucias.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Old Coast Tower station operated by PG&E measured two gusts of 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours.||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station KDLO Delano Airport reporting quarter-mile visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused a washout on Cleveland Hill Road in Tamworth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a low pressure system moving to the north of Wyoming with the passage of a shortwave brought widespread high wind to much of western and central Wyoming. There were numerous reports of hurricane force wind gusts, with some around 100 mph. Transportation was severely impacted as there were numerous truck blow overs, with many highways closed to truck traffic for much of the day. Tree damage was commonplace, with reports of damage to roofs, sheds, fences and outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured gusts of 68 mph at the Cottonwood Merna PC sensor, and 59 mph at the Farson WYDOT sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall and persistent heat allowed Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to expand farther east into Hidalgo County for the final week of February, 2026.  Farmers in the area had mixed results, with early spring planting being delayed due to the top five-ten warmest conditions combined with no rainfall.

In this farm-rich area, spring planting was delayed due to the lack of rainfall, and citrus blooms were slowed as soil moisture values remained very low.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a large tree.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Behind the northward retreat of a warm front, a cluster of showers moved along and just ahead of a cold front from Virginia into northwest North Carolina during the evening hours. These showers deepened and led to growing clusters of storms, along with one sustained supercell that brought a swath of large hail (0.75 to 1.25) and sporadic power outages and downed trees to the northern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of New Hope Church Road and Indian Creek Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms crossed over the Eastern Great Lakes and moved across the Niagara Frontier and North Country producing sporadic reports of damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and wires down near Akron St. and Davison Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

On the afternoon of the 30th, a dryline moved back into the Rolling Plains of West Texas allowing for low level moisture to surge into the region. Areas on the caprock saw scattered high based showers and thunderstorms generating severe wind gusts over Lubbock and Floyd Counties. Stronger moisture in the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle allowed for more robust thunderstorms. These storms produced severe wind gusts as well as hail as large as golf ball size in the city of Memphis (Hall County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Memphis measured severe wind gusts from 1805 CST through 1808 CST. A peak wind gust of 60 mph was measured at 1805 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing clipper system helped southeast Ohio ring in the new year in the form of snow squalls. Shortly after the clock struck midnight on January 1st, snow squalls ventured into the Ohio River Valley and dropped around an inch of snow. Local CoCoRaHS volunteers measured close to two inches of snow on the morning of the 1st in the wake of the squall. One snow squall in particular in Athens County resulted in a brief, sharp drop in visibility with heavy snow and strong wind gusts. This event was short-lived, as the clipper system quickly jetted off the east coast by the middle of the day on the first and high pressure built into the Ohio Valley.

Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, one storm produced three different EF-1 tornadoes in Lee County near Donnellson.

During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along Bridgeport Road.
