EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep low pressure system tracked east through the Great Lakes, combining with a low level jet over the Ohio Valley that shifted east in the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured at the Delaware Municipal Airport (KDLZ). The emergency manager reported that a tractor trailer was blown over on US Route 23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 13th.

On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Electrical Transmission Lines (ETL)/wood poles leaning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 degrees) across western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 28th.

On June 30, 2026, an oppressive tropical airmass fueled by extreme heat warnings collided with a sharp mid-level shortwave across the NWS Buffalo CWA, prompting the Storm Prediction Center to issue a Severe Thunderstorm Watch as strong boundary-layer destabilization produced widespread severe convection across Central New York and the North Country. NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions highlighted surging moisture and extreme instability that unleashed powerful multi-cell clusters and isolated supercells, leading to severe straight-line microbursts with winds up to 100 mph and an EF-1 tornado touchdown in Lewis County. Concurrently, deep warm-cloud processes and precipitable water levels approaching 2.0 inches fueled torrential precipitation efficiency, driving Weather Prediction Center Excessive Rainfall concerns for localized flash flooding in poor-drainage areas. As the pre-frontal convective line swept east toward nightfall, loss of daytime heating and post-frontal drying rapidly stabilized the region, bringing an end to the severe weather threat into the overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of a few trees and wires downed in the Town of Champion.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-thunderstorm wind gusts downed trees and powerlines throughout the county. EMA response units were also assisting with a field fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough positioned itself to support the development of a strong mid-level frontogenesis band. It took advantage of tremendous mid-level moisture and lift. Despite the initial more progressive nature of the system, it stalled out over SW Kansas creating some locally high amounts in excess of a foot of snow. The heavy snow brought widespread travel impacts. The snow started early on 1/9 and ended in the evening of the same day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 6.5 inches of snow fallen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of May 27th into the morning of the 28th, plenty of atmospheric moisture and lift led to training thunderstorms across the northeastern combined Panhandles. Some flooding eventually occurred in northern Lipscomb County due to the heavy and repeated rainfall. Going into the 29th, moisture and lift continued to lead to thunderstorms, some of which became severe with hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 75 to 80 mph. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.

Low pressure tracked east of the Ohio Valley before redeveloping off the Northeast coast on Sunday the 25th. Snow spread from south to north Sunday morning, becoming heaviest from mid-morning through the early evening. The snowfall gradually tapered off early Monday morning, though pockets of freezing rain and drizzle lingered across central New York. Light snow showers and flurries continued into Monday afternoon, accompanied by strong, gusty winds that caused localized blowing snow and reduced visibility. By Monday night, lake-effect snow showers developed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulated between 6 and 13 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anomalous low pressure system tracked north and east of the region, producing a tight pressure gradient and strong winds. A cold front moved through around midday, bringing showers and thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts. The highly sheared and modestly yet adequately unstable environment also produced EF0 and EF1 tornadoes across Central NY, although damaging winds remained the primary hazard.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down power lines, causing arcing on Terrace Lane, according to the county dispatch feed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station CasaVerdie - KFLBRYCE33 measured 2.1 inches of rainfall. Rain began at 7:59 pm EDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures and high humidity combined to create dangerous heat indices (in excess of 105 to 110 degrees) across the western two-thirds of Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 8th through 11th.

Drought conditions continued during the month of February as below-normal rainfall was observed through the first two months of the year. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across southeastern Central Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) conditions persisted across the southern third of Chambers County throughout the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur moved into the southeastern US which led to a significant surge of moisture into the area. The air mass became highly unstable in the afternoon and evening with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg. Storms developed along a surface trough in Georgia with strong low level convergence which led to a line of storms that moved through the area producing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a vehicle on Tailboard Way in Martinez.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm straight line winds in central Martin County near the EF0 tornado, uprooted or snapped several large tree branches and a few whole trees, from Dover Hill to the Shoals area.  Carport damage also occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 24th's late day, a broad and deep stacked area of low pressure over northwestern North America, carried a trailing weak cold front and secondary disturbance across the western Midwest with a much weaker area of surface low pressure over the Lower Peninsula of Michigan.  This placed central Indiana in the warm sector of the secondary disturbance, where a brief overlap of up to 1200 J/kg of CAPE to the west, and moderately strong vertical wind shear to the east produced a single severe cell that crossed the Indianapolis Metro before rotating, east of the city to Henry County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed numerous trees with multiple trees on trailer homes in Garden City area along US Highway 36 and one person injured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching cold front and trough of low pressure combined with a very unstable airmass producing conditions conducive to robust thunderstorm development. Showers and thunderstorms developed across the Coastal Plain and along the immediate coast of South Carolina and quickly pushed northeastwards tracking mainly east of Hwy 17 and along the coastal waters of Eastern North Carolina while strengthening during the late morning to early afternoon hours of June nineteenth. A few of these storms became severe in nature and brought strong winds to the Crystal Coast and Pamlico Sound.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was recorded at the Hatteras Airport KHSE ASOS station as thunderstorms moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm impacted northern and central NM from January 23rd through January 27th, with a combination of heavy snow, ice, and extreme cold impacts. A subtropical upper low beginning off the coast of the northern Baja Peninsula transported abundant moisture into the Desert Southwest and New Mexico in particular, much of it overriding an anomalously bitter cold and shallow Arctic airmass over eastern NM. This warmer moisture laden air overriding subfreezing surface temperatures set the stage for freezing rain and sleet for areas along the south-central highlands to the south-central mountains and southeastern plains of NM January 23rd through January 24th. Slick icy travel conditions were reported in these areas alongside ice and snow downing limbs and trees across the Ruidoso area burn scars. Power outages and road closures in the Ruidoso area lasted multiple days from January 24th to at least January 28th. While the entire event was snow for the northeastern plains and northern mountains, the transition from rain to snow through the middle Rio Grande Valley and an icy wintry mix to all snow through the aforementioned areas of ice did not occur until late January 25th when a trailing upper level system over the Four Corners area brought snow levels down to valley floors. The highest snow accumulations of 30 plus inches fell atop Sierra Blanca Peak just west of Ruidoso. A Village Disaster Declaration was made January 27th. General amounts of 2 to 8 inches of snow fell elsewhere across the northern mountains, highlands, and southeastern plains. Extreme cold settled into eastern NM behind the Arctic airmass where 72 to 96 hours of subfreezing temperatures lasted in many areas. Freezing fog limiting visibility in these areas were present during the first 48 hours of the event, with extreme cold wind chills falling below zero to negative 10 to 15 degrees below zero during the nights thereafter through the morning of January 27th. Conditions from ice and snow began improving January 26th while the extreme cold and wind chills persisted for the southeast plains particularly near Roswell through January 27th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A CoCoRaHS observer 14.4 miles south of Causey measured 6 inches of snowfall. Elsewhere in the zone, another CoCoRaHS observer 5.7 miles west of Elida measured 4.6 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a few trees in the Goodlettsville area. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet accumulation in southern Indiana January 24-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy snowfall rates and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky and into far southern Indiana, changing precipitation over to sleet for a short period of time in some counties. The winter storm dropped a swath of heavy snow and sleet totaling 6 to 13 inches across southern Indiana. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of snow-covered roads and dangerously cold wind chills. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow and sleet totaling 9 to 12 inches fell in Jefferson County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down near Old Route 73 and Greenville School Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported a gust to 52 knots (60 miles per hour). Tree branches also fell down in the Willow Oaks subdivision.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A post on social media reported that lightning struck a power line which caused it to fall onto the road below. The downed power line caused a power outage and a portion of Osborne Road near Spence St to be closed. Time estimated off of radar and  Lightning data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported multiple main roads in Balch Springs were flooded with stranded motorists. Several houses had water of an unknown depth inside. Numerous side streets were also flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions allowed a grass fire to rapidly spread across portions of Woodbury County from near Bronson to Lawton, IA during the afternoon and evening of March 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wildfire ignited southeast of Bronson around 3:00 pm and rapidly spread northeastward. The wildfire ended just north of U.S. Highway 20 east of Lawton around 9:00 pm. The wildfire perimeter was approximately 7.1 miles long by 1.4 miles wide, burning 3400 acres. No fatalities were reported, but one injury occurred. Multiple pets and livestock were killed. Two single-family homes, 15 to 20 outbuildings, and one county bridge were destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A broken pole was reported on M and M Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th, 2026, severe weather fueled by record humidity and high temperatures impacted the Duluth County Warning Area, leading to 27 total warnings across northeast Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin. Two waves of severe storms swept through the area, producing golf ball-sized hail (1.75 inches), damaging straight-line wind gusts to 60���65 mph, several reported funnel clouds, and one tornado in central St. Louis County during the overnight round of storms. The severe winds uprooted trees, damaged structures, and knocked down power lines across multiple counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were reported down in Bovey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the evening of June 10th.  Scattered wind damage was observed along and north of the I-72 corridor, with the most concentrated damage focusing across portions of Menard, Logan, Sangamon, and Macon counties where the cells interacted with an existing outflow boundary from earlier storms.  Six tornadoes touched down within this corridor, including an EF-1 tornado that tracked across Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport and the north side of Springfield.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were damaged between Riverton and Sherman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant, non-thunderstorm wind event, occurred on March 13th resultant of a strong pressure gradient with cold front passage, mixing into strong wind aloft, and a sting jet. Areawide measured gusts of 50 mph or greater were common with numerous measured from 60-70 mph and as high as 75 mph. Widespread tree and structural damage was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CWOP site 4 miles north of Waynesburg measured 62 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 Tornado with a path length of 3.71 miles and path width of 100 yards moved through this area. The estimated peak winds were 105 mph with damage including snapped trees and two barns destroyed. The tornado touched down just east of Co Road 300E where multiple trees were snapped about 15 to 20 ft above ground. The tornado then moved northeast and caused substantial damage to barns and to at least one home across a three to four mile path before lifting near Co Road 600E to the north of County Road 1000N. The tornado may not have been on the ground continuously for the whole track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked along the Iowa and Illinois border northeast across southeast WI. The low spread a swath of moderate snowfall across southwest WI affecting the panhandle of Sauk County and Marquette and Green Lake Counties. Several inches of snow fell in the early morning hours and some schools were cancelled. Some vehicle slide-offs occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Approximately 2 to 5 inches of snow accumulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

Scattered to widespread storms developed across central Virginia in the afternoon of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. Upscale growth into a few storm clusters produced swaths of damaging winds across central Virginia, eventually progressing eastward toward eastern Virginia in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: VDOT reported a tree down on Route 815 in Lancaster County, in the vicinity of Benson Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -16 degrees Fahrenheit recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a dryline and some of these storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that blew down a large, free-standing flagpole south of Carta Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures during the 26-27th overnight were as low as 0F, while breezy winds were sustained as high as 15-20 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing theta-e, steep mid level lapse rates, strong shear and limited MUCAPE allowed for the development of several thunderstorms which moved from White county to northern portions of Allen county during the morning hours. Additional storms developed in the afternoon. Low freezing levels and the elements noted above resulted in efficient hail producing storms, with one in particular leaving a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path. A few severe level hail stones were reported.

Snow began to fall across central Kansas Friday night January 23rd and continued to fall through the 24th before ending early Sunday morning on the 25th.  Despite the long duration of snow most areas received modest amounts ranging from 5 to 8 inches. Air temperatures were unusually cold in the 0 to 5 above range making the snow very dry and powdery.  Winds were not strong with this event mainly staying in the 5 to 15 mph range so widespread blowing and drifting was not a widespread problem.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS report of 8.5 inches measured in Concordia from KS-CD-9 station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced damaging winds in northeastern Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few power lines were blown down with many power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail of 1 inch in diameter was observed near the community of Deep Gap, NC.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system moves northeast towards Maine on Wednesday, as an occluded front passes over the state on Thursday.  High pressure builds over Canada Wednesday, surging cold air into northern and eastern Maine. Cold air at the surface, plus plenty of warm air aloft, led to significant mixed precipitation accumulations mid-afternoon on Wednesday, through Thursday morning. Precipitation began as snow Wednesday morning in the north, a freezing rain/sleet mix in central regions, and rain Downeast. Snow in the north transitions generally over to sleet by Wednesday afternoon. Wednesday night, freezing rain fell south to north. Roughly 2 to 3 inches of sleet in the St. John Valley, North Woods, and Aroostook regions. Around 0.5 to 0.25 of an inch in Aroostook county, and 0.25 to 0.50 in Penobscot region. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow in the north.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-3 inches of sleet fell Wednesday into Wednesday evening in Northern Penobscot.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and large branches snapped or uprooted by thunderstorm straight line wind gusts, focused on County Road 375 East, about a half mile south of concurrent EF1 tornado.  Multiple vehicles and several houses were also damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system became stationary over northeast Montana and introduced much colder air from the northeast. This combined with consistently gusty winds to produce white-out blizzard conditions for some locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observations from the Glasgow Airport ASOS, DOT reports of severe driving conditions and an NWS Employee confirmed near-zero visibility in blowing snow. Additionally at 9:15 AM, DOT reported a semi-truck slide-off resulting in blocked lanes of traffic.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down along Carson Bunkerhill Road, moved east across Bass Burkett Road and Lofton Drive, and dissipated as it crossed MS Highway 35. A few trees were snapped, but most trees were uprooted along the path. A couple power lines were down as well. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 90 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air behind a cold front ushered in dangerously cold wind chills of -15 to -25F for Extreme Cold areas and -10 to -18F for the Cold Weather areas. Winds gusted up to 35 mph at times.
Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Southwest and south-central Georgia started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.

An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. Storm development occurred both along a quasi-stationary boundary across northern Oklahoma and along an accelerating Pacific Front from far western Oklahoma into western-north Texas. A mix of supercells and a well-developed quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) yielded reports of large to very large hail and wind damage across portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moisture rich Alberta Clipper moved into the Appalachians during the late afternoon of December 31. Ahead of the snow, light freezing drizzle developed resulting in a glaze of ice. Light to moderate snow developed through the late afternoon and continued steadily through the evening. Just after midnight, a snow squall along an Arctic Front moved through. Thundersnow was observed with this band as it dropped a quick 1-2 in about a half an hour. Total snow accumulations for the event were four to nine inches in western Maryland. Winds gusted to 45 mph resulting in significant blowing and drifting snow. Further east, a snow squall along an Arctic front brought a quick coating in inch or snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A snow squall produced a quick coating to inch of snow. Visibilities were below one quarter of a mile and winds gusted to 30 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface trough draped from eastern Virginia into northeastern sections of central North Carolina led to isolated thunderstorm developing in the afternoon and evening. Several reports of wind damage occurred across Nash, Edgecombe, Wake, Wayne, and Hoke Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down in the towns of Middlesex and Bailey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed southeast through the region during the day, starting near daybreak. Snow quickly tapered off from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and was banded in nature within the northwest-southeast axis.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Walton, 1.7 inches of snow was measured. At the Cincinnati airport, 1.6 inches of snow had accumulated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper low brought heavy snow to much of eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota on February 17th and 18th. Snowfall totals ranged from a few inches to nearly 17 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received a public report of 7 inches of snow 4 miles miles southwest of Oberon, ND.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down along Robert Rd most of the damage was between Chanticleer Dr and Haas Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid conditions ahead of a sea breeze circulation along with a broad surface trough inland led to an environment favorable for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Screven County 911 Call Center reported a tree down on Huckleberry Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave trough moved through the Northern Plains and brought high winds, heavy snow, and blowing snow across eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. The highest winds occurs to the south of the main areas of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 6 inches measured snowfall 4 miles south of Bagley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a home off CR 300. There were five occupants in the home, with one sustaining a minor head injury.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped into the 5 above to 2 below zero range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures dropped as low as 4 above zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of mainly snow and some sleet during this event, producing 6 to 10 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (10 inches) was reported near Ponca City. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave brought about windy thunderstorms across much of southern MT. In it's wake, a cold front crossed the area, and strong winds behind the front persisted well into the 14th. Non-convective gusts up to 80 mph were observed, with convective gusts up to 80 mph observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTLRH Livingston River Hill gusted to 94 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of beneficial rain throughout the month of May brought slight improvements to the long term extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below normal rainfall as well as multiple hard freezes inland continued during the month of February, persisting extreme drought (D3) conditions for the same areas as January, and also upgrading some severe drought zones (D2) to extreme drought (D3). Severe to extreme drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in numerous wildfires developing across southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall during February combined with multiple hard freeze events resulted in continuing Extreme Drought (D3) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down blocking the road at intersection of Melcroft Road and Buchanan Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down near Concord, Ohio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-15 @ Tremonton mesonet station recorded an initial wind gust of 60 mph, followed by a peak gust of 63 mph, as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted into the Ohio Valley region, producing showers and thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed. Additionally, a power pole was downed along with power lines in the same vicinity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail north of Watertown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down near the intersection of Bean Rock Road and McDermont Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house on Avenue K in the Lipscomb/Brighton area.

Extreme high winds occurred north of Fort Collins/Wellington area to the Wyoming/Colorado border. Gusts peaked at 85 to 95 mph. U.S. Highways 287 and 85 as well as I-25 were closed before of the strong winds. There were reports of trees blown down and roof damage in Fort Collins.

These events contributed to short-term surface moisture gains. Despite these events, precipitation was not sufficient or consistent enough to fully eliminate long-term deficits, especially in areas that experienced prolonged dryness during fall 2025.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Abnormally Dry and D1 Moderate Drought conditions worsened to D1 and D2 Severe Drought conditions, respectively by the end of the month. The Drought Monitor first revealed D2 conditions in southern portions of the county on January 13 and persisting for the rest of the month.

At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.

There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active weather pattern brought rounds of rain, mountain snow and gusty southerly winds from January 1st through January 5th. There were numerous flooding reports from moderate to heavy rain, along with some reports of mud and rock slides in the foothills. Ski resorts, Caltrans and the UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 1 to 4 feet of heavy snow in the mountains. There was one fatality of a hiker who had gone missing with these storms. Gusty southerly winds of 35 to 50 mph were also observed at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at Lo Hi Way with the entire southbound lane flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines downed in the town of Otto.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two back to back winter storm systems impacted northern and central NM with the first from late January 7th through the morning of January 8th with the second colder system crossing the state late January 8th through the afternoon of January 9th. The first storm brought snow to mainly the mountains and nearby highlands, with valley and plains locations receiving mainly rain. Gusty west winds were observed across the central highlands midday on January 8th between the two storm systems with a peak wind gust of 65 mph at a Ziamet station southeast of Vaughn. The second storm system approached the state during the afternoon hours of January 8th with western New Mexico impacted by a band of snow on the leading edge of the storm. This band of snow moved into the middle Rio Grande Valley during the evening. This band contained a convective storm with large hail and graupel across the Albuquerque metro area. Accumulating graupel and hail forced the closure of I-40 west of Albuquerque with one inch diameter hail and graupel observed at the National Weather Service office. As the core of the system moved into western NM the night of January 8th and early morning of January 9th, a wraparound snow band brought moderate to heavy snow across northwest and north-central NM, including Farmington, Taos, and Santa Fe. Moderate to heavy snow then shifted to northeast NM on the north side of the storm during the morning and midday hours of January 9th. North wind gusts of up to 45 mph resulted in blowing snow and near whiteout conditions and the temporary closures of I-25 at Raton Pass and U.S. Highway 64/87 between Raton and Clayton. Snow across northeast NM tapered off during the early evening hours as the system exited into the central Great Plains. A lingering band of snow across Espanola, Los Alamos, Santa Fe, and Glorieta brought some light snow during the evening hours of January 9th before skies finally cleared up and temperatures plummeted overnight.||In the end, snowfall amounts of 2 to 6 inches were observed across lower elevations of northwest and north central New Mexico, 4 to 7 inches across the Jemez and Tusas Mountains with an estimated 10 inches at the Bateman SNOTEL site in the southern Tusas Mountains. The Sangre de Cristo Mountains observed 1 to 2 feet of snow with the higher end of this range observed at Ski Santa Fe and the Santa Fe SNOTEL site. The eastern foothills of the Albuquerque Metro observed 1 to 2 inches of a snow and graupel mix and the Sandia and Manzano Mountains observing around 5 to 9 inches of snow with locally a foot on the Sandia Crest. The west-central and southwest mountains observed around 3 to 5 inches of snow with locally up to an estimated 16 inches at Whitewater Baldy Peak. Finally, the Ruidoso area observed around 1 to 4 inches of snow with 10 inches at Sierra Blanca Peak and Ski Apache.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bateman SNOTEL in the southern Tusas Mountains observed an estimated 10 inches of snowfall. An estimated 4 to 7 inches of snowfall was observed across the rest of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near Blue Street and Murchison Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level low-pressure center progressed eastward through the Plains on the afternoon and evening of March 10, leading to the development of thunderstorms. These storms were able to initiate along a dryline across the Big Country. As the storms moved east through the forecast area, some generated large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported downed trees on CR 420 and FM 932 just southeast of Hamilton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure stationed across southern Ontario gradually shifted eastward throughout the afternoon hours of May 13, 2026. Some showers and thunderstorms forming ahead of a surface cold frontal passage and along the cold front was stationed in an environment of sufficient deep-layer shear along with steepening low- and mid-level lapse rates that brought a marginal wind threat during that afternoon and evening hours. This severe wind threat allowed for scattered instances of tree damage across central Pennsylvania with the most damage across the Lower Susquehanna Valley where slightly better shear and moisture was available during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph knocked multiple trees down north of Harrisburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level low which had been nearly stationary over Hudson Bay in Canada was producing several disturbances moving across the upper Midwest in early to mid-June.  On June 15th, enough mid-level instability and surface moisture was in place to generate scattered showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. In Mille Lacs County, one storm briefly pulsed up strong enough to produce a 67-mph wind gust approximately 9 miles north of Milaca. The storm continued southeast into Isanti County where a couple trees were downed in Dalbo and Stanchfield.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds downed a tree in Dalbo. An RWIS station near MP 200 on Hwy 169 in Mille Lacs had earlier recorded a 67-mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a southeastward moving cold front, broken lines of showers and thunderstorms developed in the evening hours. A surge of mid 70s temperatures with upper 50s dew points resulted in sufficient destabilization with MLCAPE up to 1000 J/kg, effective shear of 30-40 knots, and a gradient of 700-900 DCAPE. This allowed for some thunderstorms to become severe with large hail and damaging wind as the result, including two measured 58 mph gusts in southwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down near the intersection of George Street and Trolist Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southeast South Dakota during the evening of February 17 and into the morning of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 50 mph with gusts as high as 66 mph were reported across the area. The strongest winds were along and west of the James River Valley. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain shower induced sustained winds were briefly between 40 and 44 mph, with gusts as high as 60 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Freeman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of March saw abysmally dry conditions alongside record heat stretch across much of the Desert Southwest, including New Mexico. Albuquerque in particular saw a record high average monthly temperature, roughly 6 degrees warmer than any other month on record. The record warmth and record low snow pack limiting snow melt and lack of precipitation otherwise allowed for a degradation of drought conditions across the state. Severe drought (D2) was introduced back to a significant segment of northeastern NM, and spreading further across northwestern and west-central NM. Extreme drought (D3) also spread across a portion of the Northwest Plateau and highlands area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought was introduced to the northern half of the zone.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures in Southeastern Arizona were 2 to 8 degrees above normal with Minor to Moderate HeatRisk. The Pima County Medical Examiner found that heat was a factor in the cause of death for 16 individuals, with 10 having heat as the primary factor and 6 as a secondary factor in their deaths.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.

EF- 2 damage occurred downtown on Commerce St. where roofing material was peeled off three adjacent low-rise buildings. After crossing a swampy area, a significant number of snapped trees were observed on either side of the SR 52 bridge over the Choctawhatchee River. The tornado continued east causing sporadic damage on McDougald St. in Eunola, Spring Creek Road, and East CR 4 before lifting near Spring Creek itself. Both EF-2 areas had maximum winds of 115 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong winds were observed across multiple locations in southeast Ohio on February 20th as they accompanied a cold front. The initial burst of winds arrived in the late morning timeframe with the frontal passage, and continued to be breezy to strong through the day as stronger winds from aloft mixed down to the surface. The strongest winds in the area measured that day was reported from an AWOS observation site in the town of Jackson with a 47 mile per hour gust noted around the time of the front's passage. Several trees were blown down in the midst of these stronger winds as a result. High pressure building in from the west helped to ease the stronger winds just before midnight that evening.

Extreme Drought conditions expanded into SE West Virginia after the previous three months of  February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with pockets of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 19th of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New, and Greenbrier River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Western Greenbrier county in early May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Greenbrier River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A roof was blown off of a barn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air settled into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest resulting in a prologued period of extreme cold and wind chills across northwest and west central Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KTVF AWOS at Thief River Falls, MN periodically reported wind chills -40 or lower from the morning of January 25 through the early morning hours of January 26.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in mid to late March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 5500 acres in Adair County, more than 3800 acres in Cherokee County, more than 2300 acres in Latimer County, more than 2100 acres in Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Okfuskee Counties, more than 1100 acres in Mayes County, more than 500 acres in Le Flore County, and more than 450 acres in Sequoyah County.

A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees downed across weeks road near hwy 90.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The atmosphere had a few impressive characteristics including mid-lapse rates of 7-7.5 C/km, DCAPE of at least 1000 J/kg, and surface based CAPE of 2000-4000 J/kg in the afternoon. A mid-level ridge, however, was too strong to support any serious and widespread storm development and the absence of shear prevented any storm organization. Even so, orographic lift caused a storm to form and briefly form a landspout in Wythe County. A survey was conducted, but no tornadic or wind related damage was found. PWAT values of 1.5-1.75 did contribute to torrential rainfall in the storms that did form, resulting in a Flood Advisory for Watauga.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photographs were shared on social media depicting a landspout along Interstate 81 near the community of Wytheville. A storm survey was sent to investigate further but no wind damage was found.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large hail, wind damage, and three tornadoes in Illinois.
Light to moderate snow in a post-frontal, cold advection regime brought generally 3-5 inches of accumulation with as high as 8.5 inches in Eastern Tucker County, WV.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Accumulation ranging from 1-3 inches with the highest amount of 3.5 inches reported by the public 1 mile south-southwest of East Liverpool.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Route ZZ was closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was reported down along Newsome Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm moved across the state between January 23rd and January 25th. Mixed precipitation was observed with significant accumulations of sleet and snow over the northern two-thirds of the state and freezing rain mixed with sleet over the southern third of the state. A very cold air mass followed this event prolonging accumulations to well beyond a weeks time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mainly sleet, mixed with snow at times, was measured at 2 inches in Mena.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.

Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peachtree city police relayed a report of a downed tree and power lines near highway 54 and stevens entry.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front on the afternoon of April 5, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The buoy at Ship John Shoal measured a 39 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Explosive cyclogenesis of a low pressure center off the Mid Atlantic coast brought a strong winter storm with blizzard conditions to central and eastern Massachusetts as well as Rhode Island on Monday. The storm tracked from east of the Carolinas to the 70w/40n benchmark bringing extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour and winds gusting to hurricane force along the coast and 50 to 60 mph inland. The heaviest snow was centered over central Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts where over 30 inches of snow fell. The highest amount for the storm was 37.9 inches at T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island.  Snow tapered off Monday evening. There was some minor to moderate coastal flooding along the eastern Massachusetts coast but impact from coastal flooding was minimal. This was a record breaking storm in some aspects including state snowfall records for Rhode Island. The storm crippled movement across much of southern New England especially southeast Massachusetts and Rhode Island where plows could not keep up and some municipalities actually halted plowing for a time at the peak. The combination of heavy, wet snow and strong winds led to many power outages especially over southeast Massachusetts where some did not get power for 4+ days. Cape Cod was especially hard hit with power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 12 to 18 inches of snow fell. Some of the highest reports were 20 inches in Malden and 18.5 inches in Winchester. Winds generally gusted 50 to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving and narrow snow band brought remarkably heavy snowfall rates to much of northeast Iowa during the late evening hours on February 19th through the morning on February 20th. Some locations likely received snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the overnight hours with the highest totals being in a narrow band through portions of Floyd, Chickasaw, Winneshiek, Fayette and Allamakee counties where 12 to 16 inches of snow fell. Widespread totals in excess of 6 inches were noted across much of northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest snowfall total report in Mitchell County was in Osage where 2 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and development of extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across portions of North Louisiana through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought developed/expanded across portions of Northwest and North Central Louisiana throughout the month.

A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from Facebook of tree falling on a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few thunderstorms moved through Eastern NC during the later evening hours of April 5th. One particular storm became severe and produced damaging straight line winds of up to 80-90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In coordination with Pamlico County Emergency Management, a survey of damage along HWY 55 in Stonewall found damage consistent with straight line winds of 80 to 90 mph. In this area, a mobile home strapped down with hurricane ties was moved 3 to 4 feet off its foundation. The ties were ripped out of the ground. The home sustained damage to siding and windows. An occupant inside the home during the storm sustained injuries. The home was blown off the foundation towards the east. A nearby home on Spain Farm Road sustained minor damage to a patio and outdoor light fixtures. The time was estimated based on observer report and radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms swept over Lake Superior in late June as minor disturbances pivoted around a mid-level ridge over the southeastern CONUS. These disturbances caused multiple incidences of thunderstorm-driven outflow and gusty winds on Lake Superior from the afternoon of the 29th to the early morning hours of the 30th.  A strengthening low level jet and wake lows trailing the thunderstorms resulted in additional periods of gusty winds, above gale force.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 45 mph wind gust was observed by the public at station KMIONTON26 in Ontonagon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system developed over the Northern Plains and tracked across the Upper Midwest.
