This brought a series of heavy snow bands to eastern ND and Northwest MN from the afternoon of April 3 through the evening of April 4. A large swath of heavy snow was reported across northwest Minnesota, with highest values 10 to 17 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured storm total snowfall of 8.0 inches by CO-OP observer station ITAM5 Lake Itasca MN 2 SSE. There was a public report 7.0 inches of snow measured 4 S of Bagley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 5.0 inches of snow, up to 3.0 inches of sleet, and up to 0.50 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: power outages, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong area of low pressure brings strong front through the region and brought high winds that impacted much of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated wind gust 15 miles south southeast of Mission.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary frontal boundary as well as both a Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coast sea breeze combined with plentiful diurnal instability to produce robust thunderstorms across northeast FL during the afternoon and evening hours. Along with isolated severe thunderstorm activity, PWATs around 1.8 inches and slow moving/training convection resulted in very heavy rainfall and localized minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several Large Trees were reported down on a property along Musselwhite Road near Callahan. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very powerful winter storm brought heavy rain, strong thunderstorms and gusty winds to Southwestern California Rainfall totals generally ranged from 1.50 to 4.00 inches across coastal and valley areas with 3.00 to 7.00 inches across the foothills and mountains with significant snowfall at the higher elevations. With this rainfall, numerous reports of flash flooding were received. Strong thunderstorms were also observed, resulting in strong outflow winds and wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds, gusting to 59 MPH, were reported at the Refugio RAWS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few shingles were blown off a roof. Tree limbs that were 6 to 8 inch in diameter are downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof damage occurred in Hammock Bay with soccer goals destroyed at the middle school athletics fields.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a strong arctic high pressure system and very dry air resulted in very cold temperatures ranging from zero to 10 degrees above zero on the morning of January 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Low temperatures ranged form 5 to 10 degrees across Shackleford County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system over the Pacific Coast pushed into the western CONUS which produced spring and winter weather. Nevada experienced strong gusty winds across the state with tightening pressure gradients ahead of the storm front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Station (CRSN2) Crane Springs, Elevation 6414 ft.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines downed onto road by thunderstorm straight line winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snow accumulation generally ranging from 9 to 14 inches was reported across the county with the highest total of 18 inches reported by the public 2 miles southwest of West Newton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The passage of an intense cold front, associated with a deepening midlatitude cyclone across the central CONUS, fostered a non-convective wind and wildfire episode across Oklahoma and western-north Texas during the morning into early evening of the 15th. Strong winds over very dry topsoil also led to sporadic reductions in visibility (and vehicle incidents) due to blowing dust. High Wind events included in this episode capture the first, last and highest magnitude wind gust in a particular zone/county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Medicine Park (MEDI) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27th, as a low pressure system moved east towards the Lower Ohio Valley, the system's warm front brought a line of convection east along the Ohio River and Interstate 64. This produced widespread wind damage with limited flash flooding across north central Kentucky. On April 28th, the system's cold front dropped southeast, bringing a line of thunderstorms through central Kentucky. This produced additional wind damage and multiple small tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking both lanes on the 1600 block of Omar Chaney Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported baseball sized hail on the east side of Charles City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree and power line damage was observed along Ranch Lake Boulevard in Bancroft.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front set up across central Kansas later in the afternoon and eventually, storms began to develop along it. The strongest storms were mainly across southeast Kansas with damaging wind reported in Montgomery and Labette counties; Parsons Airport had a measured wind gust to 86 mph. As the front slowly tracked to the southeast through the evening, storms became more widespread and trained across the same areas. There was a stronger storm within the activity which produced quarter sized hail in Sedgwick County, but the associated heavy rain was the bigger show. The hardest hit area was the Wichita metro and southern Sedgwick into northern Sumner County where a widespread 4 to 7 inches fell, most of it in a 2 to 3 hour period. Flash flooding reports from Wichita and surrounding areas were plentiful with around 112 reports of stalled vehicles in Wichita alone. Homes along the creeks were also threatened and impacted by flood waters. Basement apartments were evacuated in west Wichita. Just after 10:30 PM KAKE News shared reports on social media from the following intersections of flooded roadways: 13th and Maize, 8th and West, 21st and 295th, Custer and Pawnee, 13th and Rock, Pawnee and Seneca, Central and Tyler. The number of flooded intersections only increased through the next several hours as rain continued. Some of the flooding was due to quickly rising creeks, including the Cowskin in west Wichita, which led to additional street and property flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported ditches overflowing near YMCA along highway 54. Water was flowing into his garage about ankle deep. Water was also flowing over the roadway at the intersection of Southwest 70th and Ohio Street. Numerous roadways were impassible in Augusta due to flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Central New York and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree on Baltimore Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure building east into the west coast brought clear skies and widespread freezing temperatures to inland valleys located west of the Cascades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing temperatures were recorded with a low of 28 at Rogue Valley International Airport, 30 at Central Point, 27 at Eagle Point, 30 at Hammel, 29 at Rogue River, 29 at Medford Agrimet, and 27 at Ashland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 26, 2026, a potent cold front tracked across central Indiana, interacting with a warm and unstable airmass to trigger severe storms.  Severe thunderstorms developed rapidly, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across northern central Indiana that downed trees and power lines, leading to over 1,700 power outages as residents dealt with the abrupt onset of hazardous weather.||Significant structural damage was observed, including a destroyed pole barn and a garage roof failure in Clinton County. While the environment supported supercellular rotation and prompted numerous tornado warnings, the only severe modes were straight-line damaging winds and large hail, with reports of 1.5-inch hail in Veedersburg. The convective activity gradually weakened as it progressed south of the I-70 corridor and encountered a more stable airmass, effectively concluding the active weather event for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees, limbs, and utility poles were blown down by thunderstorm winds across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary dropping southward on the 19th of June, combined with both weak upper level support with a mid level trough of low pressure and remnant moisture from Post Tropical Cyclone Arthur moving across the area from the Gulf Coast, resulted in widespread showers and thunderstorms across the JAX CWA. Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred, however the primary impacts to the region was areas of flooding due to very heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Jeff Davis 911 call center reported that portions of Broxton Hwy flooded due to excessive rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local fire and rescue in Alta Vista reported golf ball sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds and isolated flash flooding to northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power lines and large tree branches were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary frontal boundary was draped across northern NY east across central VT and New England during the afternoon of April 16th. A weak area of low pressure was traversing this frontal boundary as well. Temperatures and dewpoints were summerlike along and south of the boundary allowing for thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon and evening hours. A few thunderstorms contained gusty winds in excess of 40 mph and some hail. One severe thunderstorm impacted the Cranberry Lake area with damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down along Mill Street near Silver Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass that was in place across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and large limbs were downed near U.S. Route 36 and Jaysville-St Johns Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down near intersection of Mae West Road and Tub Run Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of extensive damage to a kennel, well, and barn at county road 120 and sumac ln  southeast Jasper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Minor wind damage occurred in a few areas along the Red River associated with thunderstorms which accompanied a cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported that a few trees, power lines, and power poles were blown down in Nocona.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into February in northern and central Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of February was 21 inches at the Caribou office, gradually increasing to 26 inches by February 24th. All climate sites recorded below average precipitation, with generally 1.5 - 2.0 inch deficits. At the end of January, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In February,  drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Southern Penobscot led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late January and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold upper level trough along with deep moisture and southeasterly winds allowed heavy rainfall to develop over the Koolau mountain range of Oahu, over Kauai, and over windward portions of Maui. On Oahu, the heavy rain developed and remained persistent for several hours, which led to flooding and flash flooding over the eastern and northern portions of the island. Particularly the Koolau Mountain Range was impacted. Portions of Maui and Kauai also experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Hana Police Department reported a landslide on the Hana Highway. The roadway was |temporarily closed to remove rock and debris. A nearby resort in the Hana area also reported trees downed from landslides.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and isolated severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station 3 miles (E) from Knotts Island measured a gust to 50 knots (58 miles per hour).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure along the Georgia coast on 31 January intensified as it tracks off the North Carolina coast into the early morning hours of 1 February. With abundant cold air in place with cold high pressure over the northern Middle Atlantic, widespread snow fell across central North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 5 to 11 inches of snow fell across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitation associated with an intensifying low pressure system over the Deep South developed along the I-40 corridor in the North Carolina foothills and Piedmont during the afternoon of the 24th, beginning as a mix of snow and sleet. The precip quickly transitioned to mostly sleet, which continued into the overnight and early morning of the 25th. The sleet began to mix with freezing rain after sunrise on the 25th, briefly becoming all sleet before ending early in the evening. Total sleet accumulations of 1 to 2 inches occurred, with up to 3 inches reported across Davie County. Ice accretion was Generally around 0.1 inch, with amounts up to 0.25 inch reported closer to the Blue Ridge escarpment.

A supercell thunderstorm dropped between 2 and more than 4 inches, perhaps 5 inches, along and just north of the Rio Grande late March 7 into early March 8, allowing for one category of drought improvement along the US 83 corridor.  Meanwhile, the supercell missed the remainder of the county, which continued with no rain, warm to hot conditions, and periods of low humidity to increase the coverage of Exceptional (D4) Drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 7 into early March 8, torrential rain, accompanied by wind and hail, dropped between 2 and up to 4-5 inches along the Rio Grande from Roma to the Hidalgo County line.  This allowed drought conditions to improve one category, from Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) along and near the river.  Meanwhile, the same storm completely missed central and northern Starr, and Extreme to Exceptional (D4) Drought continued.  D4 conditions expanded southward to eventually include all of northern Starr by the 24th.||Cattle ranchers in northern and central Starr continued to cull herds due to the lack of sufficient grazing land, which became dusty in many spots.  Water hauling was required to maintain the herds that remained. Unknown was the impact of the drought on any calving.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 1 inch fell across Rains County, along with freezing rain accumulations up to 0.25 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave moved across Louisiana creating a line of thunderstorms that produced severe weather across the area. A total of 13 tornadoes occurred along this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado damaged and uprooted pine trees. Large branches of 1-3 inches in diameter were snapped. Max estimated winds were 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

The start of the new year was rung in with heavy snow showers that set up primarily along the northeast West Virginia mountains. Snow was ongoing from the night of New Years Eve, which was the result of a passing clipper system. This disturbance jetted off the eastern seaboard by the middle of the day on January 1st, leaving behind 5 to 8 inches of snow along the foothills and around a foot of snow for the higher mountainous areas of Randolph and Pocahontas Counties. For the lowlands, a few passing snow squalls contributed to light snow amounts between 1 to 3 inches.

An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of sleet and snow during this event, producing 4 to 6 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (6 inches) was reported near Roosevelt. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed a band of heavy snow over Eastern Washington from the east slopes of the Cascades to far Eastern Washington and stalled over the Spokane area. It brought heavy snow amounts to Eastern Washington ranging from 4 to 11 inches. It caused a 3 hour traffic delay along I-90 at the Four Lakes area with two semis jackknifed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported 8.2 inches of snow 9 miles West of Lucerne. Another report of 5.5 inches reported 12 miles Northwest of Lucerne. Stevens Pass recorded 36 inches of snow for January 6 through January 9.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation around an inch below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile following a record to near record dry winter, resulted in development of Severe (D2) Drought at the very end of April in the southernmost portions of Illinois. The late month start of D2 drought kept April agricultural impacts minor initially, though farm pond levels were very low and planting was ahead of schedule. Drought continued into May in far southern Illinois.

Drought conditions continued into early January across southern portions of Central Alabama. Several inches of rainfall on January 9-10 greatly reduced drought conditions in southwestern counties. Drought expanded across the southeast in areas that received less rainfall during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of Marengo County remained in Severe (D2) drought through January. Extreme (D3) conditions were removed and D2 area was reduced following several inches of rain on January 9-10.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1 inch in diameter in Logan, IA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tennis ball size hail reported near Lake Sam Rayburn between the Broaddus and Pineland communities.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across northeast Georgia  continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.

A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 47 mph wind gust was recorded at the New York State Mesonet site near Cold Brook.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A measured 67mph gust was recorded on the south side of Republic. Several trees were reported down with two on homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weakly sheared and unstable environment south of a quasi-stationary frontal boundary stalled over the central Florida peninsula supported convection over southwest Florida that produced a funnel cloud near Fort Myers Shores in Lee County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media relayed video of a funnel cloud near Fort Myers Shores taken from the River Hall Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms, including supercells, developed along a trailing frontal boundary from western-north Texas into north-central Oklahoma on the afternoon into evening of the 15th. The strongest storms produced large to very large hail and sporadic damaging wind reports. Repeated thunderstorm activity across southeastern Oklahoma also led to localized flooding here.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant roadway flooding, with an estimated water depth of one foot, near the intersection of Broadway Street and Wheeler Street. The event time is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed public report of several hailstones up to ping pong ball sized. Time estimated with radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down on John Small Ave/US Highway 264.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees blew down at spotter's home location on Grinstead Court. Trees down onto houses on this street according to County EM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While the wintry precipitation created the initial impacts, it was the multi-day period of subfreezing temperatures that prolonged and, in many cases, worsened those impacts. The lack of meaningful thawing effectively extended the storm���s footprint from a 2���3 day event into a nearly week-long hazard across West Tennessee. Limited melting during the day and refreezing each night kept roads hazardous well beyond the end of precipitation, especially on secondary roads and bridges. Prolonged freezing temperatures increased the risk of burst pipes, particularly in homes and buildings without adequate insulation or during extended power outages. The duration of cold posed risks for hypothermia and exposure, especially for vulnerable populations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 2F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unsettled weather pattern unfolded across the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians for the start of June amid a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity. This combination allowed for daily storm initiation across the Midwest that eventually tracked into Ohio and northern West Virginia. On June 6th and 7th, storms tracking into the area reached Harrison and Taylor Counties late in the evening and caused tree and power line damage before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down across Ford Lane outside of Irontown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted north through the region Monday morning (6/29) allowing daytime temperatures to soar into the upper 80s to lower 90s with dew points in the middle to upper 70s Monday (6/29) afternoon across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. The warm front lifted north Monday night, which brought the hot and humid weather further north and east to include northeast Wisconsin and the lakeshore with similar temperatures and dew points. The combination of hot temperatures and high dew points allowed heat index values to soar to 105 to 110 degrees both days. ||In addition to the hot temperatures, overnight lows only fell into the upper 70s to lower 80s Monday night (6/29) into early Tuesday morning (6/30), providing minimal relief from the hot temperatures. The heat wave broke when an area of showers and thunderstorms tracked through the area Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday evening (6/30).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures and high humidity caused heat index values to rise as high as 107 degrees during the afternoon on Monday and 109 degrees Tuesday afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms preceding a cold front briefly intensified over Coosa and Tallapoosa counties, producing sporadic wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A bowing segment embedded within a line of strong thunderstorms produced isolated damage around the Kellyton community in eastern Coosa County on the morning of February 21, 2026. This damage was surveyed by NWS meteorologists and was determined to be the result of straight-line winds. A manufactured home sustained major roof damage on Trailer Park Rd, but this was an isolated incident with no further damage noted to the surrounding homes or trees. The bowing segment continued east with a localized area of several uprooted and a few snapped pines noted along Moon Rd. A metal outbuilding in this area also sustained minor roof damage with a corner of tin peeled back. Minor tree and power line damage was noted at times as far east as Dobbs Rd and Greenleaf St near Highway 63 in Tallapoosa County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system passed through the Pacific Northwest and over the Northern Rockies into the Northern Plains. This system brought heavy snow primarily to the southern half of North Dakota, with the heaviest snow generally south of Interstate 94. The greatest snow amount reported was 16 inches at Napoleon in Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ellendale received 11 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped into the area after a prolonged period of humid conditions. A few bands/clusters of thunderstorms developed resulting in several damaging wind gusts and sporadic large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a call for trees blown down onto wires near the intersection of VA-649 Mill Pond Road and Todds Tavern Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large trees blew down on Howard Lodge Drive, River Road, and Taylor Park Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level low pressure system associated with Post-Tropical Storm Arthur pushed slowly through the area resulting in several rounds of thunderstorms over the coastal waters.  Some of these storms produced strong downburst winds over the waters resulting in several marine thunderstorm wind events.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station PTBM6 Petit Bois Island (Port of Pascagoula MS).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the morning of March 31st producing isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of dime to quarter size hail were received from the Joliet Junior College.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak disturbance within a buoyant environment forced thunderstorms that caused damaging severe winds in Michigan's Upper Peninsula on the 29th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were multiple reports of downed trees from outflow winds. Some tree limbs were reported on power lines, resulting in sparking.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and embedded thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall along a boundary that was stalled out over the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small tree was uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level low which had been nearly stationary over Hudson Bay in Canada was producing several disturbances moving across the upper Midwest in early to mid-June.  On June 15th, enough mid-level instability and surface moisture was in place to generate scattered showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. In Mille Lacs County, one storm briefly pulsed up strong enough to produce a 67-mph wind gust approximately 9 miles north of Milaca. The storm continued southeast into Isanti County where a couple trees were downed in Dalbo and Stanchfield.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: RWIS Sensor located on U.S. 169 MNDOT near MP 200 measured a 67-mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: North winds pushed the tides below normal for multiple days along the coast of southeast Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tide fell below -1 foot MLLW for multiple hours falling to a low of -1.64 foot at Sabine Pass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough brought strong winds aloft. The timing of these stronger winds aloft coincided with deep daytime mixing in the atmosphere, which brought those stronger winds to the surface across mostly North-Central MT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: MT Mesonet Eden NW measured a 65 mph wind gust. A few other site including MT mesonet Belt NW, Mesonet station MTM76 Cascade E Mda, Mesonet station FW1843 Great Falls, and ASOS station KGTF Great Falls Airport also reported a high wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.

Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down onto a mobile home resulting in one injury.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A grazing shortwave trough north of Utah sent a cold front into the region. Ahead of and along this boundary there was enough moisture to result in isolated to scattered convective development, with much of this activity higher based in nature. As a result, numerous strong to severe wind gusts were recorded or reported. Additionally, a period of strong winds downsloping off of terrain was noted in portions of northwest Utah following the passage of the frontal boundary.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The I-15/2400 S Spaghetti mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of March continued the trend of much above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation that characterized the winter of 2025-2026. Very little precipitation fell across the region, with all ten climate sites finishing the month with below normal totals. Likewise, temperatures were well above normal, with mean temperatures running 8-10 degrees above normal. As a result, drought remained, and worsened significantly in many locations. And in areas that had, to this point, remained drought free, drought developed and worsened rapidly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of March, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering approximately 12% of Colorado Zone 002 - Central Yampa River Basin. The remaining 88% of the zone was under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 3/11 US Drought Monitor update, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover 20% of the zone, with the remaining 80% still under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 3/24 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought had developed, covering approximately 5% of the zone, with the remaining 95% now under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. With the 3/31 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought had expanded to cover 100% of the zone. No reports of impacts or losses related to the drought conditions in this zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front moving across the southern half of the Northland during the late afternoon and early evening hours of the 26th. A few of the storms were strong to marginally severe producing mainly hail to 1.25 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Size was estimated to be around quarter-sized, but the appearance of the hail in photos suggested slightly larger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms moved across southern Virginia during the afternoon of June 10. One storm became severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 911 call center reported downed trees and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front and associated QLCS system moved through central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 12th. Storms within the line were able to produce a few spots of wind damage, however the main hazard ended up being the numerous short lived and brief spin-up tornados which occurred in central Georgia. The strongest tornado was an EF2 near Marshallville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on a house on old louvale road .

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated wind gusts of 75mph.

CZ_NAME: WINTHROP HARBOR TO WILMETTE HARBOR IL
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon of June 10th producing severe wind gusts.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated ping pong sized hail with photo and US quarter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper low brought heavy snow to much of eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota on February 17th and 18th. Snowfall totals ranged from a few inches to nearly 17 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received a CoCoRaHS report of 6.5 inches of snow 6.3 miles south of Fargo, ND. Station ND-CS-77.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought, dry fuels, and breezy days triggered numerous wildfires in southeast Georgia and northeast Florida in April that continued to burn into June. Multiple rounds of beneficial rain fell across the wildfires in May helped the final containment of local ongoing wildfires in June.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history across three counties, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. Per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC), the fire was 98% contained on June 3rd. The fire became 100% contained on June 10th. The total cost of the fire across three counties was $19,371,895.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Breezy conditions on the afternoon on May 4 resulted in instances of zero to near-zero visibility as soil and dust was stirred up in northwest Indiana. Later on, isolated severe thunderstorms produced small hail and gusty wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of a few trees downed just west of North Liberty.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Artic air behind a cold front ushered in dangerously cold wind chills of -15 to -25F for Extreme Cold areas and -10 to -18F for the Cold Weather areas. Winds gusted up to 35 mph at times.

CZ_NAME: COLORADO SPRINGS VICINITY / SOUTHERN EL PASO COUNTY / RAMPART RANGE BELOW 7500 FT
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Closer to the middle of the month, an upper level jet maximum passed by a bit north of our forecast area. This produced some stronger, damaging wind gusts and brief moderate snowfall across portions of SE Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was 5.0 inches of snow measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 1/2 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 20 mph with frequent gusts over 25 mph. The 2-day snowfall estimates ranged from about 5 to 9 inches throughout the county, with the highest report being 8.5 inches in Benson. Road conditions became dangerous Saturday night and much of Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system emerged out of the Southern Plains and Texas and rode northeast through the Tennessee Valley and the Appalachians, before emerging just off the New Jersey coast. This produced a heavy snowfall across all of Southeastern New York, with sleet, some of it heavy across a large portion of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS Employee reported  9.4 inches in 3 WNW Riverhead. The following subsequent snowfall reports are as follows; 12.0 inches in Orient, 12.0 inches in Mattituck, 11.0 inches in 3 ENE Orient, 10.1 inches in Upton, and 10.0 inches in Baiting Hollow. Estimated average snowfall across the zone was more than 10 inches, but less than 1 foot.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The time was estimated from radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed along Harper Road in Elkins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple supercells developed during the mid to late afternoon hours, lasting into the mid evening hours.  All of these thunderstorms produced hail, some of it large.  Hail up to 2 inches in diameter was reported, and many locations reported large accumulations of hail with drifts up to a couple feet.  Strong and gusty winds in a couple of the thunderstorms produced wind driven hail damage as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball sized hail was reported in in the north side of Russellville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed southeast through the region during the day, starting near daybreak. Snow quickly tapered off from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and was banded in nature within the northwest-southeast axis.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An observation from Lancaster came in with 2 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals between 0.5 and 1.8 inches were reported across Hood County, along with reports of freezing rain accumulations up to 0.02 inches. The highest sleet and snow total was reported in Oak Trail Shores.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic front moved across NY and northern New England on January 23rd with sub-zero temperatures (5 to 20 below zero) and brisk winds to create dangerous wind chills of 20 to 40 below zero across the region for the overnight of January 23rd into the morning hours of January 24th. Very strong arctic high pressure across the region during the night of January 24th allowed for more sub-zero temperatures (10 to 20 below zero) across the region but winds were calm or light.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Actual air temperatures of 10 to 15 below zero combined with winds to create wind chill values of 20 to 30 below zero during the night of January 23rd into the morning hours of January 24th. Morning low temperatures on January 25th were 15 to 25 below zero with light winds creating colder wind chill values.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across Maryland. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 12 to 16 across Garrett County, with a general 8 to 12 across the remainder of the area aside from southern Maryland where 4-8 was observed. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a quarter of an inch were observed across southern Maryland. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state.
Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Space and Treasure Coasts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Vero Beach, Vero Beach Municipal Airport measured a peak wind gust of 40 knots from the northwest.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across portions of central and eastern Virginia on June 14. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree branches fell down onto power lines on Midlothian Turnpike near Huguenot Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds peeled up a local business's metal roof in Pulaski. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon of March 7th, a line of showers and thunderstorms tracked into the Chautauqua County from Pennsylvania. As the storms tracked northeast, they became severe causing a few reports of damage in Chautauqua and then Cattaraugus counties. The storms were within the warm sector of a surface low located near Lake Huron, developing and strengthening along a pre-frontal trough that was crossing the region. Timing with afternoon heating and a strong low level jet that increased shear over the area coincided with the trough passage to cause a cluster of thunderstorms to become severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large pine tree down across Cherry Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving east from off the Mexican Baja coast phased with a strong northern stream low pressure system over the Southern Plains. Precipitation began across eastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 23rd, as these systems approached the area. A couple rounds of heavy wintry precipitation fell across the region through the morning of the 25th. During the first round of precipitation, widespread snow, some heavy, fell north of I-40, with a mixture of sleet and freezing rain south of I-40. The second round began during the evening of the 24th and continued through the morning of the 25th. Heavy snow fell generally north of I-44, with a mixture of heavy sleet and snow south of I-40. Storm totals of up to 12 inches of snow and up to 6 inches of sleet fell across the area. Far southeastern Oklahoma also received up to one quarter of an inch of glaze from freezing rain, before the precipitation changed to sleet and snow.

During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.||The second supercell developed northwest of Seward, Nebraska, and tracked northeastward to Wahoo, Nebraska, before gradually weakening as it approached the northern side of the Omaha metropolitan area. Notable severe reports from this storm included two-inch in diameter hail south-southwest of Dwight, Nebraska, and golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) within Dwight itself, which resulted in visual damage to residential vinyl siding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Pre-frontal convection ahead of a cold front moving across the region produce a severe wind gust near Brooksville in Pasco County and downed trees and power lines near Chiefland in Levy County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed at NW 140th St and NW 30th Ave near Fanning Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, however precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon.||In the first twenty-four hours of the event, precipitation amounts ranged from around half an inch to two inches across northern West Virginia. Meanwhile, amounts generally remained under an inch within the southern half of the state. Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. Rises on local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers primarily led to flooded roads in Wood, Gilmer, and Ritchie Counties on the 4th, then runoff prompted minor flooding to develop on the Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek the morning of the 6th. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off during the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A water rescue occurred on River Road along Buckhannon River just off Hall Road. Water rose up to the car windows with a rear window open. The vehicle began filling with water and the lone occupant was rescued via raft.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding across eastern Nebraska. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||Sinitially presenting a significant large hail threat before transitioning into a destructive wind event. Through the early to mid-evening hours, widespread hail ranging from quarter (1.00 inch) to baseball (2.75 inches) size bombarded Platte, Saline, Seward, Gage, Lancaster, and Jefferson counties. The most intense hail occurred in Jefferson and Saline counties, highlighted by 2.75-inch hailstones measured near Plymouth and 2.50-inch hailstones reported near De Witt.||As the storms progressed into the late evening and early morning hours of May 17, the primary hazard shifted to severe and damaging straight-line winds. Jefferson County absorbed the brunt of this impact, with multiple mesonet stations and emergency management officials measuring extreme wind gusts between 75 and 88 mph in and around Fairbury. These intense winds caused significant impacts, including downed trees, widespread power outages, and near-zero visibility. The line of storms maintained severe intensity as it pushed eastward, producing gusts in excess of 60 mph across Gage and Richardson counties before eventually clearing the region.||In addition to the severe weather, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall brought flash flooding to southeast Nebraska, primarily impacting Gage, Johnson, Jefferson, and Saline counties. Widespread precipitation totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the region, with localized maximums of 5.80 to 7.00 inches concentrated in Gage County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the evening of May 16, 2026, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across northeastern Gage County. Authorities received multiple public reports of flooded roads and overflowing creeks. The surge was driven by an intense downpour with rainfall rates of 1.50 to 2.50 inches per hour, resulting in total accumulations of 4.80 to 7.00 inches by the end of the evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down along the the intersection of Zion Road and Pristine Place outside of Salisbury, Maryland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multivortex tornado documented southwest of Richmond.  Multiple sheds with sheet metal damage along County Highway M before entering Walworth County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from a 911 call center of a downed tree on a house in Ripon. Wind gust estimated from radar data and damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed on Coal Heritage Road near Pennys.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms on June 10th brought severe wind gusts and isolated large hail to portions of western Wisconsin throughout the day. The most prolific of these rounds was during the afternoon, where wind gusts as high as 85 mph were reported with a bow echo that clipped southern Grant County and continued eastward across southern Wisconsin. This intense complex that was later classified as a derecho by SPC.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported trees down and sign damage 1 mile south-southeast of Lancaster.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree blocked most of Berwind Mountain Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite below the monthly average rainfall, enough rain fell which allowed drought conditions to improve with only Moderate (D1) drought to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions  remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina Piedmont during the morning in advance of a cold front. The relative slow movement of the cluster resulted in heavy-to-torrential rainfall that continued for a couple of hours along the Mecklenburg/Union County line, with flash flooding developing across northern Union County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Although heavy rainfall tapered off across northern Union County during late morning, high water conditions continued across mainly the Crooked Creek basin as runoff from the earlier rainfall continued to result in elevated stream levels and flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of a strong low pressure system, hot temperatures, just enough humid air, and an unstable atmosphere, created widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms, some of which included severe wind gusts for many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bredette NE Montana Climate Office mesonet site (BDEM8) recorded a 64 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Driven by a weak frontal zone over southern Oklahoma, two separate thunderstorm complexes tracked from west to east over the same areas, causing flash flooding across Lamar County. The bulk of the flooding occurred on June 23 in connection with the second complex. The systems also produced isolated large hail and a single severe wind gust.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads, buildings and vehicles were flooded in and around Blossom, including an  RV park, apartment complex, and several homes. Highway 82 through town was flooded and approximately 35 water rescues were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Comal County saw the greatest improvement going from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought. Kendall, Kinney, and Val Verde improved from Severe (D2) Drought to D1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South-Central Texas had above normal rainfall during the month. More than half of the area had two to three times normal. This led to improvement in the ongoing drought. Comal County saw the greatest improvement going from Extreme (D3) Drought to Moderate (D1) Drought. Kendall, Kinney, and Val Verde improved from Severe (D2) Drought to D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across northeast Georgia  continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.
