By the time the snow tapered off, 5 to 8 inch totals along with locally higher amounts were reported across the area.

From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds gusted as high as 59 mph at the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Dell Rapids.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following two rounds of showers and thunderstorms in the morning, a third round later in the day produced damaging wind gusts over northwest Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from mPING of 0.75 inch hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dynamic breakup front finally arrived at the lower reaches of the Yukon River across the Yukon Delta by late May 2026. This resulted in severe, cascading flood impacts for multiple communities as the high water made it's way to the mouth of the Yukon River, inundating the coastal delta.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS River Watch team reported that the Alakanuk Slough jammed at its mouth, causing minor flooding that primarily impacted the south riverbank. Roads leading to the airport were covered in water by Tuesday afternoon (May 26th). However, because the upstream Yukon River was largely clear of ice, the flood threat diminished quickly, and water levels dropped 2 feet below bankfull by Tuesday night.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong jet stream was located over the region, with strong winds mixing down to the surface during the late morning to afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured gusts of 59 mph at the Casper Airport ASOS and I25 Twenty Mile Hill WYDOT sensor.

CZ_NAME: CHESAPEAKE BAY DRUM PT TO SMITH PT VA
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front resulted in a brief but widespread period of gale-force winds during the early to mid-morning hours across the Chesapeake Bay (north of Smith Point VA) and the tidal Potomac River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts of up to 38 knots (44 MPH) were measured by the ASOS at Patuxent River Naval Air Station (KNHK) adjacent to the tidal Patuxent River and the Chesapeake Bay beginning at 8:26 AM EDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm began Saturday night and continued through Sunday as it passed over an entrenched arctic airmass. A strengthening surface low over the Tennessee Valley combined with upper level dynamics to produce snowfall of up to a foot in some areas. The Dayton airport DAY set its highest 24 hour snowfall on record with 12.4 inches on the 25th, breaking the previous record of 12.2 inches set on January 26, 1978.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The observer southeast of Hamersville measured 7.4 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A classic ice storm setup developed across the Midlands of South Carolina January 25th. Cold air damming at the surface and strong overrunning aloft produced light and moderate freezing across the Central Midlands with sleet predominant in the Northern Midlands. The southern Midlands saw a shorter period of freezing rain and rain. Damage was primarily due to tree and limb damage along with associated hazardous and impassable roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of small limbs down and measured 0.15 ice accumulation near Gloverville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds occurred along and behind an advancing cold front.  The peak gust was 72 MPH near Aroya.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak gust in the county was reported at the airport.

CZ_NAME: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The historically poor snowpack across Colorado through the 2025-2026 Winter season allowed for a shallow, weak snowpack to develop in the accident location. Recent fresh snowfalls in the weeks prior to the event allowed for a layer of soft, fresh snow to develop atop a stronger layer of storm snow, which was itself on top of the weakened initial snowpack. Strong winds in the days leading up to the fatal avalanche also provided wind-loading issues, continuing to weaken the overall snowpack conditions. Avalanche conditions in the Vail Pass area, where the fatal avalanche occurred, were rated at Considerable (3/5) at and above treeline, and at Moderate (2/5) below treeline.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: All information paraphrased from the Colorado Avalanche Information Center report on the incidence. The fatal avalanche was triggered by a solo backcountry skier in an area known locally as Boss Basin, in the area of Vail Pass, CO. Boss Basin is comprised of a series of northeast-facing slopes that are low-angled at the top, descending into steeper slopes below, ending at a flat bench. Conditions in the Vail Pass area on the accident day were rated by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center at Moderate (3/5) near and above treeline, with a Considerable (2/5) rating below treeline. The main concern was listed as Persistent Slab Avalanches, favoring slopes northwest through north to northeast facing at all elevation bands. The likelihood was listed as Likely, and size expected listed as Large to Very Large (up to D3), meaning these avalanches would be capable of burying, injuring, or killing a person as well as potential bury cars and break trees.  The avalanche forecast also included wording stating that humans could easily trigger avalanches where [they] find more than about 10 inches of snow, that avalanches that break on buried weak layers would be difficult to survive, and that remote triggering of avalanches would be possible. The backcountry skier that triggered the fatal avalanche, referred from here on as Skier 1, started the day at approximately 7AM local time in the Vail Pass Winter Recreation Area. Skier 1 used a snowmobile to access various terrain through the morning before heading toward Boss Basin around 1:15 PM local time, parking his snowmobile at the top of a nearby ridge. Skier 1 successfully made one descent and climbed back up the slope for a second. On the second descent, Skier 1 triggered the avalanche and was caught and buried near the toe of the avalanche with only the tip of one ski visible. As Skier 1 was alone, no rescue action was taken until family members noticed they were overdue at approximately 11:30 PM local time that evening. Members of Summit County Rescue Group searched through the night, finding the accident location by 6:00 AM local time the next morning. Two rescuers and a search dog were at the avalanche location by 8:00 AM, and the dog quickly alerted on an area of interest. In this location, the rescuers located Skier 1, now deceased, with their head buried approximately 1 foot below the snow surface. Skier 1 was dug out and eventually removed from the location by helicopter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station reported wind gusts up to 65 mph.

Thunderstorms developed along and ahead of the front during the afternoon hours, then became increasingly influenced by storm outflow as they moved south faster than the front itself. The strongest storms produced a mix of large hail and damaging wind across portions of southwest Mississippi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Warren County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions through March. Following the initial onset of D2 on December 2, 2025, the county experienced a period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in January. In total, the county sustained 14 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed north of Gilmer along FM Road 2088 just west of U.S. Highway 271.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hen egg sized hail was reported in a mainly rural area. Minor damage occurred to a few vehicles, a home and some outbuildings.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on home in Bedico Trace Subdivision.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms again developed late in the afternoon of the 23rd in two separate locations. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Private weather station reported wind gusts up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above normal temperatures and minimal precipitation continuing from late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of northeast LA. Through the month of May, D2 (Severe Drought) and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions expanded to affect all of our northeast LA parishes as depicted on the U.S Drought Monitor. Average temperatures for the month ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 50 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 10 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Richland Parish mitigated from D3 (Extreme Drought) to D2 (Severe Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours. Strong storms developed and produced damaging wind gusts and localized flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed at Ziegler and Versailles Roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms with sufficient shear and instability produced severe weather across central Mississippi. The main feature, a mesovortex within a broken line of storms, produced several weak, brief tornadoes and some damaging winds in central Mississippi. This event featured multiple rounds of storms as well as heavy rainfall, which led to flash flooding across southeastern portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A hardwood tree was uprooted along County Road 155. Several small tree limbs were also found scattered along this road as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and early evening on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, extending along the Middle Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across the area, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, extending well into the afternoon and early evening. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. As a result, several damaging wind reports were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed onto a power line on Old Mill Road in the Wesson community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small streams flooded Old Mill Road heading north towards Jackson Mill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of trees and power lines down.

In Barbour County, an EF1 tornado caused damage to trees and structures along a 1.2 mile path.||Showers and storms generally produced one to two inches of rain, though training storms did lead to a swath of three to six inches of rain across parts of Mingo, Logan, Boone, Wyoming, and Raleigh counties. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep Pacific trough brought moist southwesterly flow to much of the western CONUS on January 1. A weak upper-level jet streak arrived in coincidence with the surge of moisture, prompting widespread precipitation in western Colorado throughout the morning of the 1st. Strong cold air advection behind the storms rapidly saturated valleys, and areas of dense fog developed during throughout the night and into the morning of January 2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Patchy dense fog developed within the San Juan River Basin overnight on January 1 and 2. The KPSO AWOS at the Stevens-Pagosa Springs Airfield reported brief 1/4-mile visibility from dense fog near midnight. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto power lines on Fishing Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of power outages and traffic accidents. One traffic accident resulted in the death of a boy in Pittsylvania County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 6.8 inches of snow and up to 0.10 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moist and unstable weather pattern affected Puerto Rico from March 24 through March 28, 2026, as a mid- to upper-level trough interacted with abundant tropical moisture and favorable upper-level dynamics. Periods of heavy showers and thunderstorms developed across the island, resulting in flooding concerns, urban and small-stream flooding, and rapid rises on rivers and streams. The threat was enhanced by strong upper-level support associated with a strengthening jet stream and persistent moisture across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused the R��o Cibuco to overflow, resulting in flash flooding across multiple roadways in Vega Alta. Floodwaters inundated portions of PR-620, PR-647, PR-675, PR-690, and PR-676, creating hazardous travel conditions and temporary transportation disruptions. Debris and sediment deposited by the floodwaters required cleanup operations before affected roadways could safely reopen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong upper level troughing diving southeastward from central BC toward southern AB/SK resulted in a sharp transition to strong zonal flow aloft across the Northern Rockies April 7. Favorable timing of the system, arriving during the day, allowed for daytime mixing to translate stronger gusts to the surface in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: MT DOT sensor Bozeman Pass MTBZH measured a 64 mph gust late in the afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Temperatures averaged near normal, but precipitation was mostly 50 to 75 percent of average during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted through the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the afternoon of 4/25, two strong storms both producing severe hail with one producing 2.5 hail. Some severe wind gusts were also reported. A cold front bisected the area and interacted with a shortwave that produced organized convection with low level moisture and deep-layer shear. The shear CAPE available generated numerous reports of severe winds while the steep lapse rates aided in generating severe wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Hummingbird Wildfire was a lightning caused fire starting in a remote region of the Gila Wilderness, in Catron County. The wildfire was discovered during the afternoon of April 20th, growing rapidly to several thousand acres thanks to several days over critical fire weather conditions. The fire grew within dead and downed trees within the old 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire burn scar. It's remote location slowed firefighting and containment. An evacuation order was put in place for the Willow Creek Subdivision April 26th, lasting at least to the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Hummingbird Wildfire was a lightning caused fire starting in a remote region of the Gila Wilderness, in Catron County. The wildfire was discovered during the afternoon of April 20th, growing within dead and downed trees within the old 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire burn scar, reaching 4,364 acres at month's end and continuing into May. An evacuation order was put in place for the Willow Creek Subdivision April 26th, lasting at least to the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 12th through March 14th of 2026, a large and powerful kona storm setup over the northern central Pacific, and brought numerous impacts across the state. This low was supported by a broad and potent upper level trough that lingered for many days. Impacts included flash flooding, wind damage, large surf, and strong thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Persistent heavy rain fell across the island of Oahu. Water flooded a residence in Waialua and over a foot of water was reported on Farrington Highway. Flooding was also reported at Waialua High and Intermediate School, and Komo St and Waialua Beach Rd, Waialua.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy band of snow set up along a strong area of convergence along a slow-moving boundary draped from Lakes of the North toward Onekama. Snowfall rates of around an inch per hour beneath this band, resulting in 6-9 inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS observer in the Mancelona area observed 8.0 inches of snowfall by the morning of the 18th.

Meanwhile, as the front swept through the area high winds were recorded at a couple of Mesonet sites in west Texas and southeast New Mexico.

The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Clipper system moved across NY and New England during the evening and overnight hours of February 10-11th to into the Gulf of Maine by the morning of February 11th.||Light to moderate snow spread across northern NY during the afternoon and evening hours causing some hazardous travel for the evening commute. The steadiest snow exited the region by the 8-9 pm but more scattered orographic enhancement snow redeveloped during the early morning hours of February 11th and continued during the day. Snowfall totals across the region ranged from a few inches in St. Lawrence county to 2 to 5 inches elsewhere with some locally higher amounts near 8 inches in orographic favored higher terrain in southeast Franklin and western Essex counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across the area were 3 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.
Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line swept through the tri-state area ahead of a cold front on March 12th. Numerous reports of severe weather were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were down on County Road 79.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above normal temperatures and high humidity created heat index values up to 110 degrees across much of North and Central Texas on June 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees occurred across the county on June 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front dropped into the area after a prolonged period of humid conditions. A few bands/clusters of thunderstorms developed resulting in several damaging wind gusts and sporadic large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down in the 1900 block of Old Mill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front brought gale- to storm-force winds in snow showers to the tidal waters of the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay early on New Year's morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 37 knots (43 MPH) was measured by the Baltimore CBIBS sensor (44080).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mature mesoscale convective system (MCS) impacted portions of far northern Oklahoma during the very late evening of the 1st into the early morning hours of the 2nd. Several severe wind gusts were observed across this area during that time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Medford (MEDF) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front produced showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Delaware Valley. A few of these storms produced heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roadways flooded around Darby Township due to heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong winds aloft moved into the North-Central MT plains on the 15th. A cold frontal passage helped bring these stronger winds down to the surface, resulting in isolated high winds across Central MT and the Hi-line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Montana mesonet site Coffee Creek N measured a 65 mph wind gust. Montana mesonet site Forestgrove, MTBCH Beacon Hill, and AWOS station KMVH N Bar Ranch also measured a high wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For the second time in a week, a winter storm impacted the mountains and foothills of North Carolina as an area of low pressure intensified across the Deep South. In this case, all precipitation fell as snow. Snow began falling during the late evening of the 30th and continued off and on for around 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the morning of the 31st. By the time the snow tapered off, 5 to 8 inch totals along with locally higher amounts were reported across the area.
On the afternoon on June 16, a few supercells developed. Photos of wall clouds were received and hail as large as 2 inches in diameter was recorded (in Michigan). Two EF-U tornadoes occurred as well.
A line of severe storms that produced widespread wind damage in Alabama moved into the Florida panhandle and gradually weakened but not before producing a few more reports of wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At least two trees were down in the Bascom area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell down onto Crestwood Road in Richmond.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elongated low pressure along a cold front brought an low end advisory accumulating snowfall to portions of Northeastern New Jersey.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported 3.8 inches in Elizabeth. An official NWS observation of 2.3 inches was reported at Newark Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The eastern part of Deaf Smith County started April in Moderate Drought (D1) and the remainder of the county continued into April in Severe Drought (D2) as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. However, this area of Moderate Drought quickly eroded within the first week and became Severe Drought. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured around three quarters of an inch in the west to around one tenth of an inch in the east. Deaf Smith County ended the month about one quarter to one third of an inch below normal in the west to one inch below normal in the east. The 120 day departure from normal was around 1.5 inches in the west to 2.75 inches in the east below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.
A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting the eastern West Virginia panhandle during the late afternoon hours with damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several calls for trees down along River Road in different locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic front brought prolonged frigid temperatures to southeast Wyoming Sunday, January 25 through the morning of Monday, January 26. The coldest temperatures occurred Sunday night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overnight low temperatures ranged from -15 F to -20 F across Converse County from 1/25 into 1/26. The combination of cold temperatures and gusty winds resulted in a prolonged period of extreme wind chills under -25 F. Minimum observed wind chill values reached -33 F at the Douglas Airport ASOS at 12:25 AM MST on 1/26.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large tree branches and a tree snapped. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.
Drought conditions worsened during March with below average rainfall. Southwest and south-central Georgia started the month in D2 to D3 status and ended the month in D3 to D4 status.
A line of quick-moving low topped convection developed ahead of a cold front and produce damaging wind gusts over the waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet site ROBN4 at Robbins Reef measured a 52 knot wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. Large to very large hail was the main storm hazard with several supercell thunderstorms during this time. Sporadic wind damage was also observed, including on the southwest side of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough brought an increase in southerly winds aloft on the 13th. This combined with a strongly unstable atmosphere brought severe thunderstorms producing scattered severe wind gusts across the region. High synoptic wind gusts also accompanied thunderstorms on the 13th and 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter measured a 70 mph wind gust. ASOS station KBZN Bozeman Yellowstone Airport also measured a 68 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed over the Midwest and tracked quickly eastward, affecting the eastern West Virginia panhandle during the late afternoon hours with damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were three calls for trees down near Glengary.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale upper trough was in place across the northeastern US. A disturbance in the southwest flow aloft led to early thunderstorm development across the region with most of the convection translating offshore by mid to late afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines fell on Nike Park Road in Isle of Wight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions persisted across parts of northwestern Wisconsin to begin the month of March. Precipitation for the month was around 0.25 to 1 inches above normal in the area with most of that occurring over the first half of the month. This led to the complete removal of D2 Severe Drought conditions across northwestern Wisconsin with the update on the 17th, leaving a mix of D1 Moderate Drought and D0 Abnormally Dry conditions in place.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought conditions covered the northern 1/3rd of the county at the start of March. Precipitation for the month was around 0.25 to 0.75 inches above normal across the county, with much of that falling over the first half of the month. This led to the complete removal of D2 Severe Drought conditions in the county with the update on the 17th leaving a mix of D1 Moderate Drought and D0 Abnormally Dry conditions across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Eight healthy trees downed by thunderstorm wind gusts, all were 12 to 14 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low tracking eastward across the Midwest dragged a cold front south into Texas and east toward the Mid-South by the morning of March 11. Delayed arrival of the frontal boundary allowed diurnal instability to increase, interacting with 40 knots of bulk shear. As the front swept swiftly across the region, it triggered severe thunderstorms capable of producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A single tree was downed along Hwy 59 S.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An elderly female suffered from heat exposure and dehydration in Florence in Lauderdale County and was ambulanced for treatment at a local hospital in Florence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An elderly female was treated for heat exposure and dehydration.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Crawford County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 on November 18, 2025, the county sustained 15 consecutive weeks at or above the D2 threshold as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light snow moved across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours of January 18, bringing accumulations generally between 0.5 and 1 inch, with some locally higher totals. While accumulation was light, the newly-fallen snow combined with increasing & gusty winds to result in reduced visibilities into the morning of January 19. The blowing snow and lowered visibilities brought some impacts to the morning commute on January 19.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulations near 0.5 inches observed countywide, with locally higher totals. Greatest accumulation of 0.8 inches observed near Port Washington. Blowing snow and reduced visibilities continue following the end of snowfall, leading to lingering travel impacts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.

An Arctic cold front moved through southern Illinois on the morning of the 30th, bringing cold temperatures down to the teens. Blustery northwest winds caused wind chills to fall around -5 to -7. Intervals of dangerous wind chills were variable across the region during the morning hours on the 30th and 31st with the far southern counties remaining above threshold.

An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local law enforcement reported a tree and wires down on West State Street in the town of Johnstown. This damage was likely caused by an outflow boundary as it occurred away from the main storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front brought several days of showers and thunderstorms to the region as it moved through the area, stalled, and then retreated back to the north. Isolated instances of hail, severe winds, and flooding occurred with this activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: HAM radio operator reported nickel size hail north of Aubrey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of flooding from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The start of the new year was rung in with heavy snow showers that set up primarily along the northeast West Virginia mountains. Snow was ongoing from the night of New Years Eve, which was the result of a passing clipper system. This disturbance jetted off the eastern seaboard by the middle of the day on January 1st, leaving behind 5 to 8 inches of snow along the foothills and around a foot of snow for the higher mountainous areas of Randolph and Pocahontas Counties. For the lowlands, a few passing snow squalls contributed to light snow amounts between 1 to 3 inches.

A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -34 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -19 degrees Fahrenheit recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-phased system brought a combination of system and lake enhanced snow to northwest and portions of north central Indiana Saturday night into early Sunday morning followed by more organized lake effect snow showers late Sunday into Monday. This prolonged snow event coupled with gusty north to northwest winds lead to hazardous travel conditions and numerous slide-offs and accidents across favored lake effect snow region across northwest and north central Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of system and lake enhanced snow Saturday night into Sunday morning, followed by a more organized lake effect snow phase Sunday afternoon through midday Monday. Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 5 to 10 inches. A CoCoRaHS observer 1.8 miles east northeast of Granger, IN reported 8.5 inches of snow. In addition to the snow, north to northwest winds gusting to 30 to 35 mph resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow along with periods of significantly reduced visibilities. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm produced 1 inch hail in South Rockwood.

A compact short-wave within northwest flow aloft moved across the Northern Plains late February 27 into February 28. Mid-level frontogenesis and sufficient moisture resulted in a narrow band of light to moderate snow mainly along and north of a De Smet, SD to Windom, MN line. These areas received 1-4 inches of snow, with a few locations exceeding 5 inches. Winds were light during the snowfall, limiting blowing and drifting.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 6.4 inches in Minneota, 6.3 inches 4.7 miles south of Cottonwood, 6.0 inches 2.1 miles southeast of Balaton, and 3.0 inches in Marshall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were reported down in a two-mile-wide band spanning along the Lawrence and Barry county lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A round of severe thunderstorms, a tornado and flash flooding occurred during the evening of June 21, lasting into the morning of June 22.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed a tree on Spring Valley Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry spring continued across Middle Tennessee during April 2026. Precipitation amounts were generally 3 to 5 inches across with most of this rain recorded during the last week of the month. While these rain amounts were higher compared to the past couple months, it was still below normal for the month. Drought conditions worsened through the month of April. By the end of the month, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least severe drought with about 38 percent of this classified as extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from March 2026 worsened in April with all of Perry County in extreme drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and isolated severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees fell down in Hertford County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weather pattern in the upper atmosphere favored the development of showers and thunderstorms across the local area. At the surface, a stalled frontal boundary stretched from west to east near the I-10 corridor and provided a focus for repeated thunderstorm development. Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of coastal Mississippi over the two-day period and resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: MDOT camera showed Beach Boulevard was flooded near the intersection with Porter  Avenue. Water depth on the eastbound side was 1-2 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of southern Illinois. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Roads were particularly bad near Glendale in Pope County, IL. Ice on rural roadways in Saline County, IL caused one vehicle to overturn with a person trapped. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday January 31st. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly strengthened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred. Snow began during the morning hours on Saturday January 31st mainly along the Crystal Coast and Inner Banks, though a period of light snow occurred across portions of the Coastal Plain as well Saturday morning. By Saturday afternoon the low pressure system off the coast began to deepen quickly resulting in heavier and more widespread snowfall across much of Eastern North Carolina. Snowfall rates became heavy at times resulting in periods of whiteout conditions as 30-50 mph wind gusts (60-65 mph on the Outer Banks) also impacted the area making travel treacherous across the region. Snow finally pushed completely offshore by the late morning hours on Sunday February 1st. Over 10 inches of snowfall were measured across most counties of Eastern North Carolina outside of Hatteras Island and Ocracoke with several counties reporting over a foot of snowfall. The strong winds associated with the low also produced coastal flooding on the Outer Banks of Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands. Highway 12 was closed for a time, and 4 more homes in the Buxton area collapsed into the ocean due to the coastal flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall reports from trained spotters, the public, and CoCoRaHs data showed between ten and twelve inches of snowfall fell across mainland Hyde County between the morning of January thirty-first and the morning of February first.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 31st, severe thunderstorms moved across Lake Erie and into portions of southwestern New York as a potent shortwave trough crossed the area with a stationary front draped across the south shore of Lake Ontario and lake breeze boundaries found across the area. Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received report with photo via Facebook of hail in Collins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually extreme, early-season heat wave impacted central California during the middle of March, setting several monthly heat records across the region. Radiosonde observations from Oakland reported a monthly record for highest 850 mb temperature at 23.4 degrees Celsius, or around 74.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Notably, this temperature would also break the monthly record for April, had it occurred during that month. Given the extreme and unusual levels of heat for this time of year, a Heat Advisory was issued from Monday, March 16 through Friday, March 20, throughout the Bay Area and northern Central Coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 41-year old man died on the western side of San Jose early on the morning of March 18. The Santa Clara County Medical Examiner-Coroner's office reported that while the immediate cause was hypertensive cardiovascular disease, environmental heat exposure was a significant factor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Similar to its neighbors across the Mississippi River, West Tennessee spent April 2026 battling a persistent, long-term moisture deficit dating back to July 2025. While central and northern parts of the Midwest received heavy spring rains that broke their droughts, West Tennessee experienced a highly regionalized spring recharge gap. Abnormally hot temperatures and meager rainfall caused drought conditions to actively worsen across the region during the first half of the month, though patchy late-month systems provided highly localized stabilizing relief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D1 conditions worsened to D3 conditions mid month and persisted through the end of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th into the early morning hours on April 26th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and extreme North Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across parts of extreme North Louisiana in addition to isolated damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported just north of Interstate 20 between Grambling and Ruston.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D3-D4 drought conditions prevailed to start the month of May across southwest and south central Georgia. However, beneficial rain during the month reduced the drought to D2 by the end of the month near a line from Albany to Bainbridge and westward. D3-D4 drought still prevailed farther east across south central Georgia.

A long duration extreme cold every took place across the region starting the 22nd and lasting into the morning of the 24th. An area of very cold high pressure worked into the Plains on the 22nd and became established on the 23rd into the 24th. Air temperatures remain below zero during the event with light winds dropping wind chills into the 40s and 50s below zero. A few locations even dropped into the 60s below zero one morning with light winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills as low as -47F were reported in the southern part of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 68 mph at Mitchell Field. Many branches down throughout the county, and over 20,000 customers without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 5.2 to 8 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the northwestern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 20 to 25 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-quarter mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The short-term drought entered its sixth month in March, as a lack of winter precipitation and unseasonably warm temperatures exacerbated dry conditions statewide. The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). The most severe deficits persisted in east-central Georgia, where totals of 1.25 to 2 inches (25% to 50% of normal) were common, with localized areas receiving less than 1 inch. While the western Atlanta metro area saw higher totals of 3.5 to 5.5 inches (60% to 95% of normal), streamflows and soil moisture failed to recover due to the widely spaced nature of the rain events.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected this aggressive expansion. D2 (Severe Drought) or worse conditions grew from 70.94% to 80.19% of north and central Georgia over the month. Most alarming was the rapid intensification of D3 (Extreme Drought), which surged from 15.34% to 40.00%. Condition Monitoring Observer Reports and Drought Impacts Reporter reports highlighted the cost: farmers reported failing pastures, an inability to plant forage crops, and dry holding ponds. Meanwhile, fire officials were forced to re-strategize prescribed burns while other officials discouraged outdoor burning following an uptick in emergency calls. ||The drought persisted and intensified through April as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued, evolving into the largest footprint of D2 Severe Drought or higher in US Drought Monitor history.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Gilmer County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in March. Following the initial onset of D2 (Severe Drought) on December 30, 2025, the county experienced a period of marginal improvement before drought officially returned in late January. In total, the county sustained 13 weeks at or above the D2 threshold through the end of March, with drought persisting into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms that would eventually become a derecho, produced widespread wind damage across much of northeast Illinois during the afternoon of June 10th. Two brief tornadoes also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down in multiple locations in Elk Grove Village.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent hurricane force North Pacific Low moved into the Bering on January 4. This, combined with potent shortwave troughs and cold air advection behind the low allowed for gusty, westerly to southwesterly winds across the Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula. The Eastern Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula saw strong, gusty winds for a time. As the low moved eastward, heavy snowfall and blizzard conditions were observed over the Southwest mainland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Adak ASOS (PADK) had a max wind gust of 70 mph at 10:25 AM AKST January 4 before the wind sensor went out. Another observation site on Adak Island had multiple instances of greater than 70 mph wind gusts between 9:48 AM and 8:12 PM AKST on January 4. The highest wind gust for this site was 80 mph at 5:06 PM AKST January 4.
