EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist airmass with mid 80s temperatures and low to mid 70s dew points supported initial thunderstorm development in central Ohio with geographically moderate to strong MLCAPE values up to 3000 J/kg and 15-25 knots of effective shear. As the storms progressed east, they became more congealed along cold pools and the wind threat increased into western Pennsylvania with notable tree damage and some damage to structures as well within a line of storms producing 60-75 mph wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: US 30 closed in both directions between PA 151 and Pittsburgh Grade Road due to downed trees and wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large wildfire ignited across western portions of Woods County, Oklahoma due to the combination of thunderstorm activity (i.e., lightning) and very dry fuels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The School Lands Fire burned 2,411 acres in western Woods County. This wildfire is believed to have been started by a lightning strike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough moved across Wyoming during the afternoon bringing high-based showers and thunderstorms. Dry air below storms lead to strong outflow wind gusts for much of central and western Wyoming. Wind gusts over 58 mph were reported in Fremont, Natrona, Johnson, Park, Lincoln and Sublette Counties. The highest wind gust reported was 83 mph at Red Canyon along Highway 28 through South Pass in Fremont County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph wind gust was reported to the north of Etna.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front tracked across Eastern North Carolina during the morning and afternoon hours of May thirtieth. As the front tracked across the coastal waters of Eastern North Carolina, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the coast with an isolated storm or two becoming strong in nature. The strongest storm that developed produced a waterspout in the Core Sound given the favorable environment.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several public reports of an ongoing waterspout in the Core Sound between Stacy and Davis North Carolina as thunderstorms moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across SE Arkansas during the late evening hours of April 28, 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines. Some of these storms produced hail. One of these storms produced a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple power lines were blown down across Lakeside Street. A large tree was uprooted and fell across powerlines along Mulberry Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video shows quarter-size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple widely scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds above in the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds onto a vehicle along Mike Stuart Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As the month of February continued hot and dry, there was no relief from the worsening drought conditions. Extreme (D3) Drought either redeveloped or expanded across northwest Colorado and into the southern portion of the central Colorado Divide mountains. No areas of Exceptional (D4) Drought developed or expanded during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: With the 2/11 US Drought Monitor update, Colorado Zone 012 - West Elk and Sawatch Mountains were analyzed as having developed Extreme (D3) Drought over roughly 2% of the zone. Severe (D2) Drought covered 48% of the zone, with the remaining 50% under Moderate (D1) Drought conditions. From this point through the end of the month there was no change to drought conditions in the zone. No reports of impacts or damages related to this drought were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A push of dangerously cold air spread across the Upper Midwest behind a series of strong arctic fronts from January 21 through January 23. Wind chills dropped into the -40s across much of the region, with AXN in Alexandria reporting the coldest wind chill of -50F during this stretch of extreme cold. The strongest winds did not line up with the coolest temperatures, limiting wind chills from getting any colder than -50F. ||The peak of the coldest conditions occurred from the evening on the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd. Very cold air temperatures around -10 to -20 below continued until the morning of the 26th, though winds were generally at or below 10 mph, limiting wind chills from dropping below -35F. ||The lowest wind chills were:|-50F at AXN in Alexandria, MN.|-49F at STC in St Cloud, MN.|-49F at OWA in Owatonna, MN.|-49F at GHW in Glenwood, MN.|-47F at MSP in the Twin Cities, MN.|-47F at BDH in Willmar, MN.|-47F at CFE in Buffalo, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KRWF reported wind gusts as high as 25 mph during the evening as air temperatures dropped from -15F to -22F overnight. The lowest measured wind chill was -41F at 8AM on the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stagnant, moist air mass just north of a stationary front allowed areas of dense fog to develop late on May 9th and early on May 10th. The fog dissipated shortly after dawn.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at South Jersey Regional Airport.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were a few reports of trees and and power lines down in Hagerstown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed eastern New York on March 13-14, 2026 bringing periods of snow and strong winds. The heaviest snow fell across portions of the southern Adirondacks with amounts ranging from 4 to 10 inches. In the wake of the clipper's cold front, wind gusts on the order of 40 to 50 mph were observed on March 14.||Key impacts: travel delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 46 mph wind gust was recorded at the New York State Mesonet site near Ballston Spa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

Anomalously dry conditions persisted across much of central Pennsylvania through April 2026, with severe drought persisting across portions of southern Pennsylvania with slight expansion into southeastern Pennsylvania towards the latter portions of the month due to lack of widespread rainfall, with month-to-date precipitation values generally one inch below average for the month of April across the southeastern half of Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drier than average conditions over the course of multiple months lead to the addition of severe (D2) drought across conditions persisted across much of eastern Lancaster County during the second half of April 2026. Drier than average conditions were observed throughout the first half of the month with generally light rainfall across the region with slightly more beneficial rainfall coming in the final week of the month. The Drought Warning was downgraded to a Drought Watch by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection on April 27, 2026 after the aforementioned beneficial rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed around Tallassee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Anomalous cold air settled into the eastern US for late January, with the coldest period for the Upper Great Lakes from the night of Jan 22nd through the morning of the 24th. Actual air temperatures struggling to break 0 degrees Fahrenheit, combined with winds gusting as high as 15-25mph at times, resulted in extreme cold apparent temperatures of -15 to -25F, and -25 to -35F during the overnight hours on the 22nd into the 23rd, and the 23rd into the 24th. The 23rd into the 24th was the coldest of the two nights. Strong gusty winds and some snowfall resulted in significant blowing and drifting snow, reducing visibilities to whiteout conditions at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dickerson Rd in Gaylord closed between Van Tyle Rd and O'Rourke Blvd near the airport due to whiteout conditions.

This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded into Buckingham county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a week of temperatures running close to 30 degrees above normal, and a continued lack of precipitation, drought expanded significantly across eastern Utah and western Colorado. Areas that had been in Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) Drought now worsened into Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) Drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: With the 3/24 US Drought Monitor update, an area of Extreme (D3) Drought was analyzed as covering approximately 50% of Colorado Zone 009 - Grand and Battlement Mesas, with the remaining 50% under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 3/31 US Drought Monitor update, Exceptional (D4) Drought had developed, covering approximately 35% of the zone. Extreme (D3) Drought now covered approximately 55% of the zone, with 10% of the zone still under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. No reports of impacts or losses related to drought conditions in the zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening surface low crossed northern Maine during the 1st. At the same time...a secondary low developed across the Gulf of Maine and tracked toward Nova Scotia with a trof extending between the lows. Snow developed during the early morning hours of the 1st...persisting into the evening. A meso-scale snow band developed along the trof axis...running across central and coastal portions of Washington county. Localized snow fall rates of up to 4 inches per hour occurred with this band. The greatest storm total snow accumulation occurred with the band...with totals of 8 to 14 inches. Storm totals across Washington county...outside of this band...ranged from 5 to 8 inches. Warning criteria snow accumulations occurred during the late afternoon of the 1st. Storm total snow accumulations of 4 to 6 inches occurred to the north of Washington county across the remainder of eastern Maine along the trof axis. Snow totals tapered to 1 to 2 inches across western portions of the forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 7 to 12 inches...locally up to 14 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large branch was blown onto powerlines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry, mid-level shortwave aid in the push of another cold front in late January. Another arctic airmass residing behind this boundary resulting in another bitterly cold period. Cold temperatures combined with elevated northerly winds resulted in sub zero wind chill values across north Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 1F recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of low pressure systems moved over southern California during the mid part of the month of February, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms, strong and gusty winds, and high elevation snow from the 10th thru the 11th, and then again on the 16th thru 18th. This resulted in a few reports of damage due to strong winds from thunderstorms. There were also several reports of flooding/flash flooding due to heavy rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Fire reports a tree went through a roof into a bedroom near the intersection of  Grass Valley Rd and Club House Dr. Wind gusts estimated to be 40-50 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A northwest flow aloft was in place across the Four State Region during the morning of May 10th, developing on the east side of an upper level ridge of high pressure over the Rockies and Desert Southwest. A shortwave trough embedded in this flow regime traversed the Oklahoma/Texas Panhandle during the early morning hours, before moving into East Texas by late morning and North Louisiana during the afternoon. Diurnal heating contributed to an unstable air mass by late morning/early afternoon, with the approaching trough helping to enhance large scale forcing for the development of scattered severe thunderstorms across portions of East Texas and North Louisiana, where multiple reports of large hail and damaging winds were received. These storms eventually exited the region by late afternoon with the departure of this disturbance aloft.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell at the intersection of Desiard Street and Kansas Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado damage was first observed on Hendricks Church Road where a few small pine trees were snapped. Damage continued across Hurricane Creek where approximately 20-30 trees were knocked down or uprooted in private farmland. The path continues with damage to a small outbuilding before reaching Ellerbeetown Rd where some additional tree damage was noted. The track continues eastward towards the intersection of McCard Rd and 74 where additional tree damage was observed as well as some minor structural damage to a home. After crossing Womble Creek, the|tornado uprooted trees along Thurston School Rd before continuing east where it caused some minor tree and outhouse damage near the intersection of Butts Rd and Pickard Rd. From there, the path ends and the tornado appears to have lifted. This damage was in line with the estimated maximum wind speed of 78 mph and an|EF0 rating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mature mesoscale convective system (MCS) impacted portions of far northern Oklahoma during the very late evening of the 1st into the early morning hours of the 2nd. Several severe wind gusts were observed across this area during that time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freedom (FREE) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-afternoon thunderstorms both in broken line segments and single cells developed along and ahead of a cold front. Marginal effective shear values up to 30 knots and MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg supported severe thunderstorms producing both wind and hail. Wind was primarily confined to northern West Virginia along a DCAPE gradient of 600-700 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates up to 6.5 C/km and up to 300 J/kg of hail growth zone CAPE supported numerous reports of quarter size within storms across western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees reported down on Pricketts Fort Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions persisted across the tri-state area through April and into May with D3-D4 drought continuing.

A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and adjacent power lines were blown down in Sweeneysburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house, causing the roof to cave in along Morganton Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms developed on June 1st mostly across central and southern Mississippi as afternoon heating of a very moist airmass contributed to substantial atmospheric destabilization. The primary observed impacts were from damaging winds though at least one report of large hail was recorded. Additional thunderstorms developed in the afternoon of June 2nd in a similarly unstable summer airmass.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along Highway 12 at Caldwell Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave moving across the Rockies brought snow to the mountains. Precipitation was confined largely to the high terrain with little impacts noticed at lower elevations. The highest snowfall amounts were above 9000 feet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak snowfall reported in the Sierra Madres came from the Little Snake River SNOTEL (LITW4) with 21.8 inches. Several other SNOTELs reported heavy snow accumulations above 12 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm from Sunday, February 15th into Friday, February 19th brought heavy snow, rain, and gusty winds. This brought from 1 to 7 inches of rain, with totals of around 5 to 9 feet of heavy snow above 5000 feet, 1 to 4 feet from 3500 feet to 5000 feet, and 1 to 12 inches from 500 feet to 3000 feet. ||Gusty southerly wind gusts of 25 to 50 mph in the Valley, 40 to 60 mph in the mountains and foothills were recorded. Roads were reported to be flooded, as well as covered with mud and rocks in some mountain and foothill areas. Numerous downed trees were reported during this time, along with mountain highway closures and chain restrictions, with roadway flooding in the Central Valley. Numerous roads were closed from flooding and storm damage in the Valley. Up to 80,000 power outages were reported across the mountain and foothill areas from Butte County down to Tuolumne County for an extended period. There were numerous school closures in the mountains and foothills from the storm. Water storage and pump stations were also impacted, leaving homes without water for an extended period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding with 2 feet of water over the surface.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Wednesday April 15th, a southwest flow pattern sent a mid-level shortwave disturbance into northeast PA, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. The combination of instability, strong wind shear, and ample moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and evening. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50-60 knots knocking down trees and wires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down wires on Coryland Road near Church.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity resulted in an unsettled weather pattern across the Ohio Valley for the start of June. Each day yielded developing showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest and travelling eastward along the front before dissipating after sunset. On June 6th, storms remained strong to severe as it dashed across Ohio, and caused scattered tree and power line damage across Perry County from the damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on Winegardner Road near Somerset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The damage path of a brief EF-0 tornado was identified via high resolution satellite imagery in northwest Harrison County. This tornado caused predominantly damaged to trees over inaccessible areas between West Wortham and McHenry roads. This focused damage path closely aligned with a strong tornado vortex signature that crossed through the area. The tornado apparently lifted as it crossed McHenry Rd as no other damage could be identified as the circulation lifted northward.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wall partially separated from house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of calm winds and a moist boundary layer allowed for a few hours of dense fog development early morning in Southwest Indiana on the 19th.

Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in an open warm sector behind a morning warm front passage. A modestly unstable environment with 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, strong effective shear values of 40-50 knots, and a gradient of 600-800 J/kg of DCAPE contributed to damaging wind reports ranging from trees and power lines down to removal of a metal roof of an outbuilding. A few sporadic reports of quarter size hail occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Part of a roof was reported to be ripped off of a barn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front and retreating dryline combined to create thunderstorms late on the evening of the third. A quasi-line of storms developed initially across the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle and moved east-southeast. Strong instability allowed some of these scattered thunderstorms to become severe producing hail up to the size of half dollars and wind gusts up to 65 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local broadcast media relayed a report of quarter size hail in the town of Littlefield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong cold raced south across eastern Colorado during the early morning hours of March 15th bringing wind gusts up to 65 mph across northern Colorado. Snow also developed behind the front. Most of the snowfall was light (less than 4 inches), however the northerly upslope flow across the northern slopes of the Palmer Divide dropped 4 to 10 inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the AWOS sensor at the Akron airport during the early morning hours, and then a 61 mph wind gust was recorded mid morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system that moved through the region brought a brief period of gusty winds to Central MT. This caused isolated strong sustained winds to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTBCH Beacon Hill averaged 41 mph sustained winds over an hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas on the evening of the 14th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of eastern Foard County, producing reports of large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reported by a broadcast media storm chaser. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant home damage from very strong thunderstorm wind gusts reported north of Beulah. Attached double garage was ripped away from home and destroyed, with debris scattered across the yard. Garage doors were facing west into the wind. Some damage to the siding and roof of the main part of the house, especially on the southern side where the garage was attached. Some larger tree branches were snapped off of the few trees directly east of the house. The barn at the northeast side of the property had some minor roof and siding damage, as well as broken windows. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level disturbance interacting with a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across the Deep South produced a prolonged overrunning snowfall event across central and southern Illinois from the morning of January 24th to the morning of January 25th.  ||By the time the snow tapered off and came to an end, significant amounts had been observed...especially along and south of the I-70 corridor where amounts of 8 to 12 inches were common.  Some of the highest totals were recorded across southern Richland County around Olney where a few reports indicated 13-14 inches.   Amounts decreased further north, with 4-8 inches along the I-72 corridor from Jacksonville to Danville...and just 1 to 3 inches along and north of a Macomb to Peoria line. Northeasterly winds gusting 20-25mph on January 24th and north-northwesterly winds gusting 25-30mph on January 25th created considerable drifting of the snow in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weather observers measured 5 to 7 inches of snow across Logan County...including 5.5 inches in Lincoln.  Due to both falling and drifting snow, travel became extremely hazardous...leading to numerous traffic accidents on area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Waldo County averaged 3.08 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.89 inches below normal, marking the third driest start to the new year, and the driest June through March stretch on record. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: D2-D3 drought conditions continued through February and into March.

Low pressure system from the west moved over Maine, late on 02/10 into 02/11. Occluded front moves over the state, bringing precipitation in the form of snow from west to southeast. Low began to slow down over eastern Maine, and alongside a surface low developing, heaviest snowfall occurred over eastern Maine. Warning criteria snowfall occurred in central and costal Washington county, with accumulations around 7-9 inches during the afternoon of the 11th. Storm total accumulations around 6-8 inches in southern Aroostook. Northern and eastern Aroostook, alongside Hancock county, had accumulations around 3-5 inches. The rest of the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Bangor region received about 2-4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved across southeast Missouri, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -5 to -12 degrees during the afternoon and evening hours and continued into the afternoon of the 24th. After a brief lull at night, another interval of dangerous wind chills occurred during the morning and early afternoon hours on the 25th. The one exception was New Madrid County, MO where wind chills remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

A cold front continued to move through the Mid-Atlantic on Friday, June 12th. This sparked additional clusters of thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced estimated gusts to 70 mph and sporadic hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were multiple reports of trees down across southern Madison County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although most of the activity was in western Nebraska, far eastern Wyoming experienced isolated severe thunderstorms with large hail and a few strong wind gusts reported. Severe thunderstorm Watch was in effect along and east of the Interstate 25 corridor for the afternoon and evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Niobrara County Emergency Management reported quarter size hail west of Lusk.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough and associated surface cold front approached from the west. Out ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough moved through the area. The pre-frontal trough sparked convection in an area characterized by about 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 35 kt of 0-6km bulk shear. Several severe thunderstorms formed and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limb down on roadway on Washington Street in Middletown CT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief tornado started south of Beaver Dam and went through a garage near Shaw Hill Rd, west of the Shaw Marsh Wildlife Area.  Other wind damage was noted on the southern side of the tornado path, attributed to downburst winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system crossed eastern New York on March 13-14, 2026 bringing periods of snow and strong winds. The heaviest snow fell across portions of the southern Adirondacks with amounts ranging from 4 to 10 inches. In the wake of the clipper's cold front, wind gusts on the order of 40 to 50 mph were observed on March 14.||Key impacts: travel delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 41 mph wind gust was recorded at the New York State Mesonet site near Duanesburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree limbs and power lines were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed along Clyburn Street in Sprague.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in Nashville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sunshine and nice weather changed quickly to scattered storms with hail and wind during the afternoon on June 19th, 2026. Many places in east-central Minnesota and then western Wisconsin saw large amounts of hail fall as the initial storms moved through the area, covering the ground completely at times.||The second round of storms followed about 30 to 60 minutes behind and produced scattered wind damage to trees and a few power lines. The very southern portion of Eau Claire County saw a highly visible funnel cloud near Osseo, which briefly touched down on the west side of town near the Merchants Baseball Field off US Highway 10. This tornado falls within NWS La Crosse's forecast jurisdiction, and more detail on the tornado can be found there.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated near 50kts downed trees in Boyceville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Route 56 East was closed beyond Dogwood Ridge Road to State Route 356 due to flooding from Hewett Fork.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper low brought heavy snow to much of eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota on February 17th and 18th. Snowfall totals ranged from a few inches to nearly 17 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Received a report of 5.9 inches of snow from a CoCoRahs station 1 mile NNE of Park Rapids. Station MN-HB-40.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A clipper system and arctic blast brought strong winds and pockets of light to moderate snow showers.  ||A peak wind gust of 71 mph was observed 1 mile north northwest of Lees Corner in Buffalo County by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Information Weather System (RWIS), and by a personal weather station 2 miles north of the Pierre Regional Airport. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded by the SDDOT RWIS station 1 mile northeast of Stephan in Hyde county, while 66 mph wind gusts were measured by the SDDOT RWIS stations 5 miles south southwest of Klein Ranch in Corson county and 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake in Dewey county.  A total of 39 weather stations recorded a peak wind gust at or in excess of 58 mph. These high winds flipped a semi and damaged a grain elevator near the town of Murdo on the morning of the 16th. ||While snow accumulations were limited, snow showers of moderate intensity combined with these strong winds to produce temporary white-out conditions. No Travel Advised was issued by both the Walworth and Day county Sheriffs. Various SDDOT RWIS webcams showed visibility in blowing snow fluctuating significantly over short distances in the matter of a few minutes. An emergency vehicle rendering assistance for an accident on Interstate 29 near Watertown was struck with minor injuries. A separate accident along Interstate 90 resulted in a 5 vehicle chain reaction crash which resulted in 2 fatalities and a number of injuries.  ||80 residents of Deuel county reported power out during the event.

Severe thunderstorms swept through the Missouri Ozarks during the evening and overnight hours of June 7th and 8th. Several tornadoes occurred along with significant flash flooding. Between 2 and 6 inches of rainfall fell over a short period of time across portions of southwest Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Highway U had water over the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front and a subtle upper-level disturbance interacted with a moist and unstable airmass to produce a line of thunderstorms that moved north to south across the Mid-South on June 12, 2026. Precipitable water values approaching 2 inches combined with SBCAPEs over 2000 J/kg supported locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding, along with isolated wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kirby Whitten Road was flooded north of I-40.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local media reported that heavy rainfall during the afternoon of the 18th caused multiple flooded homes in Nu'uuli village. An American Samoa Power Authority/University of Hawaii stream gauge in the village rapidly rose to over three times its initial height in a single hour. Fiscal damage is estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. With abnormally high amounts of atmospheric moisture, these thunderstorms were able to produce very heavy rainfall with rain amounts of five to seven inches reported across portions of Sumner and Robertson counties. This caused flash flooding for these areas, particularly in low-lying areas and those along area creeks. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree onto a powerline on Rocky Fork Road in Nolensville. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across southern Vermont for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were cold, but not quite to dangerous levels. Feels-like temperatures this first night ranged from about -18 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -13 to 0 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -8 degrees Fahrenheit. A brief respite came on January 30th when extensive cloud cover maintained sufficient insulation to limit temperature falls, but by the next night, February 1, minimum feels-like temperatures once again fell to -30 to -5 degrees Fahrenheit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -9 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -32 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the evening of June 10th.  Scattered wind damage was observed along and north of the I-72 corridor, with the most concentrated damage focusing across portions of Menard, Logan, Sangamon, and Macon counties where the cells interacted with an existing outflow boundary from earlier storms.  Six tornadoes touched down within this corridor, including an EF-1 tornado that tracked across Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport and the north side of Springfield.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were downed throughout the Town of Dummerston.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across northwestern Arkansas on the 28th, as a warm front stretched across the area and an upper level disturbance approached from the west. The atmosphere across the region was moderately unstable with strong deep-layer wind shear, the combination of which supported the development of some supercell thunderstorms. Very large hail up to three inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball size hail damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across North and Central Texas on May 27 and 28, triggered by a slow-moving upper-level disturbance. Although the majority of these storms remained sub-severe, a few produced large hail. Additionally, the slow progression of the system led to heavy rainfall and flash flooding in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Facebook post reported quarter to half dollar size hail off Hwy 281 north of Stephenville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized flooding observed in and around Griffithsville. Some pictures showed Straight Fork close to going over its banks and covering roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm moved across the state between January 23rd and January 25th. Mixed precipitation was observed with significant accumulations of sleet and snow over the northern two-thirds of the state and freezing rain mixed with sleet over the southern third of the state. A very cold air mass followed this event prolonging accumulations to well beyond a weeks time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Total collapse of a building in downtown Benton due to the weight of the winter precipitation on the roof. As the building collapsed, additional damage was done to adjacent businesses.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two waves of precipitation impacted the area March 2nd into March 3rd. The first wave moved through during the daylight hours of March 2nd bringing a coating to localized 2 inches of snow to parts of the state. The second wave of precipitation moved in during the overnight to morning of March 3rd bringing light freezing rain. Freezing rain accumulations of a light glaze to locally two tenths of an inch were observed.

The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms fired along a stalled frontal boundary throughout the day, resulting in localized heavy rainfall and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported on Selma Pike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Across South Texas and the Coastal Bend during February, persistent drought and very limited rainfall continued to strain agricultural conditions. Periods of freezing temperatures early in the month caused damage to several leafy vegetable crops and burned back pasture grasses, while most areas received little meaningful precipitation despite occasional scattered showers. Soil moisture remained very short across much of the region, with some irrigation canals and stock tanks running low or dry. These dry conditions delayed widespread planting of corn, sorghum, and other row crops, as many producers waited for sufficient soil moisture to support germination, though limited planting began where moisture allowed. Irrigated small grains such as oats and wheat generally held up better than dryland fields, and onion harvest began with strong yields despite earlier cold stress. Rangeland and pasture conditions remained poor to very poor, forcing livestock producers to rely heavily on hay and supplemental feed as supplies tightened and forage availability declined. As drought impacts persisted, some producers reduced herd sizes, though strong cattle markets continued to provide some financial support.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought. Introduction of D3 on 2/24.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.

A cold front moved across South-Central Texas on the evening of May 10, encountering an unstable airmass and producing a line of strong to severe storms with damaging wind gusts and some severe hail. Most of the  observed wind damage occurred in the Austin area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large snapped tree limb was observed in Pflugerville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Patrick county in early April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Mayo River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Treutlen County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 in fall 2025, the county experienced a period of mid-winter improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels on January 13. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 13 weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the original fall onset, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe storms ahead of a cold front brought damaging wind gusts and a few tornadoes to the tri-state area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant tree damage was reported near Bonifay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees onto wires near Forest Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system passed through the area brought windy conditions, with gusts as high as 40 mph in the Valley and above 60 mph in the Mountains. As the longwave trough continued east, a shortwave trough along its west side evolved into a cutoff low over Baja California, where it stalled. As a result, the prevailing flow over the area shifted to the northeast, leading to a Mono wind event over the southern Sierra Nevada Mountains and high winds over the Tehachapi Mountains, Mojave Slopes, and Mojave Desert, including downslope acceleration and drying in these areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station 649SE Sce Cottonwood Creek West.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper-level system brought scattered showers and storms across central North Carolina in the afternoon and early evening. A few storms produced damaging winds across Moore, Randolph, and Chatham Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down with power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of wires down along Clayton Road. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 16th, a Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved from west-southwest to east-northeast across the lower Ohio Valley, providing forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. Thunderstorms were able to feed off of a seasonably high amount of instability, with around 2000 J/kg Mixed-Layer CAPE present in the pre-storm environment. While synoptic scale ridging over the southeast US meant that large scale flow was fairly weak, the MCV provided a mesoscale enhancement to the wind shear profile, with around 30-35 knots of effective shear supporting organized multicell clusters. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across southern Indiana, producing several reports of quarter sized hail and downed trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was observed in and around Corydon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed near State Route 40 and Cottrell Road in the Town of Greenwich.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds to eastern Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust report from this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic airmass descended upon the tri-state area during the early morning hours of February 1st.  Actual low temperatures reached the upper teens to lower 20s in many location, but the combination of strong winds drove wind chills down into the single digits to lower teens. There were numerous social media posts of frozen and burst water pipes across the area.

Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This episode is part 2 of 2 from two rounds of severe weather that occurred on June 10th. ||Two clusters of storms redeveloped across Minnesota during the early afternoon of June 10th. The first cluster developed over Douglas and Stevens Counties and rapidly intensified as it entered Pope County. This cluster produced golf ball to tennis ball size hail in Glenwood and Villard (Pope). This storm would weaken some as it continued to the NNE into Stearns, Todd, and Morrison Counties where a brief funnel cloud was observed just south of Sobieski (Morrison). ||The second cluster of storms developed farther east across eastern MN along the I-35 corridor. A supercell entered Chisago County and produced quarter size to golf ball size from Wyoming to Center City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo report provided via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Above average precipitation the 2nd half of the month, especially over Cheyenne, Rawlins, Sherman, and Thomas counties supported improved drought conditions from west to east by mid to late month, especially over the aforementioned counties. D3 Extreme Drought over central and northern portions of Cheyenne, Rawlins, Decatur, and Norton counties was gradually replaced with mostly D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought.  However an area of D0 Abnormally Dry Drought was introduced over southwest Cheyenne and central to western Sherman counties by late month. Elsewhere, a mix of D2 Severe Drought and D1 Moderate Drought persisted. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from one and one-half inches over eastern and southern counties, to nearly seven inches over west-northwest counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over far west-northwest counties near the Colorado border, to over three and one-half inches over far eastern counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one and one-half inches over northwest portions of the county (two inches below average), to nearly four inches over south-central portions of the county (near and either side of average). Normal monthly precipitation amounts are around three and three-quarter inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With low pressure strengthening and tracking northeastward towards Chicago, the Quad State region experienced breezy southerly to southeasterly winds throughout the daytime hours. Spotty wind gusts to 40+mph were observed in Southeast Missouri, with the strongest gust measured 49mph at the Cape Girardeau Regional Airport's ASOS site. Showers and a few thunderstorms moved eastward across Southeast Missouri during the late afternoon hours.

An upper-level jet provided ascent for multiple inches of snow to fall. A stronger and heavier band of snow set up across the northern zones produced 5-6 inches across Finney to Ellis county. The isentropic lift prevented the rest of the area seeing similarly high amounts. The higher amounts were assisted by higher SLR rates of 20:1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public report of 5.5 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Pacific low-pressure system moving into the area brought high winds to portions of southern Nevada.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mountain Springs RAWS briefly recorded high wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: House suffered siding and shingle damage near North Main Street and Nicholas Street in Arlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of mini-supercells developed during the late morning into the early afternoon hours. One of the thunderstorms produced a tornado in northeast Cullman County.  Repetitive rainfall caused excessive rainfall and flash flooding across parts of Cullman County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down blocking the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was the second part of the prolonged wind event which started on March 11th and the 12th. There was a twelve-hour lull in the strong winds outside of the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming, but winds quickly increased by late morning on March 14th. Although winds weren't quite as strong, nor as widespread, compared March 12th, peak wind gusts between 70 to 85 MPH were observed along with travel impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WYDOT sensor at Shirley Rim measured a wind gust around 58 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak midlevel low over eastern Texas and multiple mesoscale convective vortices maintained widespread convection along the central Gulf Coast on May 25th. Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. Flash flooding affected New Orleans from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Intersection of Curran Blvd and Benson St flooded according to Streetwise NOLA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold air moved across northern Illinois during the morning of January 19th and continued into the early afternoon.  Wind chills 25 below zero were common across northern Illinois with a few locations across northwest Illinois in the 25 below to 30 below zero range.

On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed an 18 to 20 inch healthy tree limb.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper-level low tracked south and then southeast from the Upper Midwest to the Southeast during the weekend of Friday January 30th to Sunday February 1st. At the same time, a baroclinic zone set up along the offshore waters of Georgia, westwards to the Deep South. A surface low then developed along this baroclinic zone just off the coast of Georgia during the early morning hours on Saturday. As the upper level low neared the developing surface low, this resulted in a Miller-A low pressure system. The associated offshore low pressure system then rapidly deepened as it tracked northeastwards just off the North Carolina coast during the overnight hours between Saturday and Sunday. This very strong low then pulled away from the Carolinas and moved out into the open waters of the North Atlantic during the late morning hours on Sunday. With an unusually cold airmass in place across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, a rather widespread and historic snowstorm for almost all of Eastern North Carolina occurred.
