EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front associated with a strong Bering low pushed across the Kuskokwim Delta late April 21 into the morning of the April 22, bringing notable winter weather impacts to the region. As the front entered the region, strong southwesterly winds (gusting 40-50mph) blew onshore. This, combined with moderate to heavy snowfall, promoted blowing snow conditions for the Kuskokwim Delta Coast, reducing visibility to a quarter mile or less through the late afternoon/evening hours on April 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Toksook Bay ASOS (PAOO) recorded blizzard conditions with 40 to 50 mph wind gusts, visibility less than a quarter of a mile, and blowing snow from 6:40 PM AKDT April 21 to 12:15 AM AKDT April 22.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.
A stagnant, moist air mass just north of a stationary front allowed areas of dense fog to develop late on May 9th and early on May 10th. The fog dissipated shortly after dawn.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Heritage Field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active weather day transpired on May 19th in southeast Ohio as a quick succession of storms passed through the area. The first round was observed during the late afternoon, when scattered thunderstorm development that moved in a southwest to northeast fashion. This clipped portions of Jackson County and resulted in several downed trees and power lines around the area. A few hours later, a line of thunderstorms slowly progressing through the Ohio Valley arrived into Perry and Morgan Counties around sunset. Decaying storms due to the loss of daytime heating caused downburst winds that promoted hundreds of homes to be without power due to downed trees and power lines. The weakening trend prospered into the late evening hours, bringing the severe threat over southeast Ohio to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few utility poles were snapped in Jackson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D0 conditions worsened to D2 and persisted through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In response to a powerful upper-level trough barreling into the Central Plains, digging further south and deepening in the process, an area of low pressure at the surface also strengthened as it shifted east across Kansas and eventually into Illinois by the end of the day on the 15th. The accompanying surface cold front and resulting strong pressure gradient allowed legitimate High Wind criteria conditions to overtake the entire forecast area, with sustained winds commonly 35-45 MPH with gusts 55-65 MPH, and even a few localized 70+ MPH gusts. The brunt of the highest wind gusts occurred mainly during the 10AM-4PM CDT timeframe, with reports more scattered in nature outside of that period. Across south central Nebraska, some of the highest gusts included the following: 74 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located two miles west of Doniphan; 71 MPH, measured by the Hastings Airport ASOS; 67, measured by mesonet stations located three miles north-northeast of Kearney  as well as seven miles west-southwest of Ragan; 66 MPH, measured by the Grand Island Central Nebraska Regional Airport ASOS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained speeds near 40 MPH and wind gusts exceeding 50 MPH were common throughout the day based on surrounding observations.

In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Bolivar, Sunflower, and Washington counties for an entire week, with some of the deeper sleet accumulations through Bolivar County persisting through at least Sunday, February 8th.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 11 at Bluff Lake, 12 at Natchez and Starkville, 13 at Ackerman, Collins, Crystal Springs, Forest, and Golden Triangle Airport; 14 at Brookhaven, Canton, Columbia, Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, Louisville, Madison, Newton, and Philadelphia; 15 at Jackson International; 16 at Greenville, Indianola, Meridian, and Vicksburg; and 17 at Cleveland, Laurel, and Rolling Fork. Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||Severn deaths occurred in the Mississippi counties in the NWS Jackson area - four due to exposure to the cold in Hinds, Sharkey, Warren, and Yazoo counties, and three in fire-related incidents in Adams, Leflore, and Jefferson counties. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of eastern New York from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across eastern New York from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The expansive impacts that this storm had on New York State as a whole led Governor Kathy Hochul to declare a widespread State of Emergency which encompassed all of our portion of eastern New York. NWS Albany received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across eastern New York. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, travel restrictions, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.

The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two feet of coastal flooding was reported on Redwood Highway at the Frontage Road just south of Hamilton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense lake effect snow band produced dangerous travel and near whiteout conditions. Snowfall totals exceeded a foot in portions of western Cass and Berrien counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A single band of heavy lake effect developed behind an arctic front during the morning hours of January 14th, becoming nearly stationary and intensifying during the late afternoon through early morning hours of January 15th. Snowfall rates of more than 2 inches per hour were reported with near zero visibility. Snowfall totals across the country were generally greater than a foot, with a report of 16.4 inches in Niles. There were innumerous slide-offs and crashes across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deepening surface low pressure system was centered over Illinois and an attendant cold front extended south-southwestward sweeping from west to east across Arkansas during the afternoon and evening hours of March 15, 2026. Multiple severe thunderstorms developed in a well-defined warm sector positioned across the state where storms matured and quickly became severe producing large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three power poles were snapped in the community of Rose Bud.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reports a tree down near the intersection of bouldercrest road and  key road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two strong back to back frontal passages followed by a period of post-frontal showers led to heavy snowfall across the Oregon Cascades. Convection along the Oregon coast was robust enough to produce a funnel cloud on January 7th as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Red Hill SNOTEL at 4410ft recorded 24 inches of snowfall from 0700 01/06 to 0900 1/08 with 12 inches reached 0500 01/07. The Blazed Alder SNOTEL at 3660ft also recorded 19 inches of snow from 0700 1/06 to 0700 1/08 with 12 inches reached 2200 1/07.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One large tree was blown down by thunderstorm winds along Walton Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Calm winds and clearing skies behind a cold frontal passage resulted in dense fog formation in the Kentucky Pennyrile and Western Coal Fields areas of Western Kentucky overnight into the early morning of the 25th. Fog duration was longest in areas to the east, with fog observed for several hours at Hopkinsville, Madisonville, Greenville, and Owensboro.

Strong low pressure tracked east across northern WI to Lake Huron. Westerly wind gusts of 50-68 mph were recorded. Numerous branches down and some power lines. Power outages in the tens of thousands mainly over southeast WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust of 58 mph in Brookfield. Many branches down throughout the county, and over 20,000 customers without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours on January 22nd and morning on January 23rd, an arctic airmass moved into the Upper Midwest resulting in dangerously cold temperatures across the region. Many locations saw low temperatures colder than 20 degrees below zero with widespread wind chills ranging between 30 to 55 degrees below zero across western Wisconsin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme cold moved into the region beginning on January 22nd and continued into January 23rd. During this period extremely cold wind chills of around 35 to 45 degrees below occurred in Juneau County with the coldest observed wind chill being 46 degrees below zero at Volk Field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Moderate (D1) drought to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large, long-period northwest to northerly swell impacted the Atlantic waters and local passages of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands from February 9 through February 11, 2026. This swell developed over the western Atlantic, maintaining hazardous marine conditions across the region.||Seas built to hazardous levels, with buoy observations indicating wave heights near 9 feet and long periods of 14 to 15 seconds. These conditions generated large breaking waves along north- to northeast-facing coastlines, with surf heights estimated between 10 and 16 feet.||The swell produced dangerous marine and coastal conditions, including life-threatening rip currents, high surf, and minor coastal flooding across exposed coastal areas of Puerto Rico, Culebra, Vieques, and the northern U.S. Virgin Islands. The most significant impacts occurred from February 9 through February 10, with hazardous conditions gradually subsiding by February 11.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coastal flooding and erosion occurred in Parcelas Su��rez in R��o Grande during the morning of February 10, 2026. Swell-driven wave action caused significant erosion, leading to the collapse of the intersection at Calle 3 and Calle 10 in Lo��za. The damage impacted roadway infrastructure and surrounding areas. The event was caused by large breaking waves associated with a long-period northerly swell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms moving across north central and northeast South Dakota generated high winds from the evening of June 7th into the early morning hours of June 8th. The South Dakota State University mesonet station 1 mile southwest of Timber Lake recorded a peak wind gust of 65 mph, while the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet stations 1 mile northeast of Timber Lake and 2 miles north of Herreid peaked at 64 mph.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. One person was injured as a tree fell onto a house on E 12th St in Hopkinsville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail measured to two inches fell south of Freemont and dented back porch wood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down at the intersections of SW 119th Ave and SW 36th St and SW 102nd Ave and SW 36th Trail. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms tracked across eastern Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours of the 24th. Hail, strong winds, and two tornadoes were observed. In addition heavy rainfall in the Evergreen area produced flash flooding late on the 24th and early on the 25th.

Breezy northwesterly winds and a very dry airmass develop in the wake of departing cold front. This resulted in critically low humidity values and dangerous fire conditions and the issuance of a Red Flag Warning for portions of southeast Georgia south of Waycross.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerline broke from non-thunderstorm winds near the 8000 block of Highway 301. Peak wind gusts during the day were around 45 mph. This led to the development of the wildfire that spread southeastward just north of Folkston.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 18th, as a cold front moved into the area. The strongest storms produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a tree near the intersection of Waldron Road and Grand Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: New Hampshire faced a pronounced north-south divide in precipitation amounts during April 2026. Northern New Hampshire benefited from wetter short-term precipitation patterns and a gradual snowmelt, which yielded localized improvements in overall drought intensity and shallow groundwater conditions. Conversely, coastal and southern areas faced substantial precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This poor spring recharge actively drove drought degradation, prompting the reintroduction of Moderate Drought (D1) across southern New Hampshire. Groundwater levels across regional monitoring networks remained critically low, heavily constrained by long-term moisture deficits. Despite minor surface-level recoveries in soil layers and small reservoirs, water levels in waterways underperformed expectations, with streamgages finishing the month exhibiting below-normal to much-below-normal streamflows. No flooding or significant runoff events were reported anywhere in the state, mirroring the quiet hydrologic conditions seen throughout the region. Overall drought conditions improved in the north, and worsened in the south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Carroll County averaged 3.91 inches of precipitation in April,  which is near normal. The heavier precipitation fell in the mountains, while the lakes in the southern part of the county received over an inch below normal precipitation. The USDM on March 31st had 98% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), which was reduced to 58% by the end of the month. It was the driest July through April stretch on record. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 11 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

The right entrance region of a jet within stronger flow across the northern tier of the U.S. helped to increase convergence by late afternoon and early evening along a cold front working eastward through northwest Iowa.  Mixed-layer instability reached up to 1500-2000 J/kg courtesy of 8C/km mid-level lapse rates with deep-layer shear of 40 to 50 knots. Initially discrete cells produced large hail, with a tendency to evolve toward more linear structures.

Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to ping pong ball size damaged homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a dryline and cold front along with strong instability resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms across much of the area. The strongest storms produced very large hail and damaging winds.

The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered trees and utility lines were downed from thunderstorm straight line winds north of Bicknell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on a daily basis across the region over Memorial Day weekend as a result of several passing upper level disturbances. Some storms produced severe hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Significant flash flooding occurred in North Richland Hills in Tarrant County on May 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager relayed photos of a fence blown down and several large trees with large branches snapped in a small area of Colleyville. The tree damage was consistent with severe microburst winds over 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough brought an increase in southerly winds aloft on the 13th. This combined with a strongly unstable atmosphere brought severe thunderstorms producing scattered severe wind gusts across the region. High synoptic wind gusts also accompanied thunderstorms on the 13th and 14th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Landspout. High quality video of dust-wrapped circulation in contact with the ground ahead of destructive thunderstorm outflow containing significant dust. Time estimated from radar rotation signature along leading edge of storm. No damage reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Canadian airmass encompassed the region on the morning of February 1. This airmass intensified to 1040mb allowing temperatures to fall below freezing to kick off the month. Clear skies and a light northerly wind resulted in wind chill values at 5 degrees or less across West Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of 0F reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A disturbance moved through Northeast Pennsylvania. and kicked off scattered showers and thunderstorms. Warm, humid conditions led to an unstable environment with many storms becoming strong to severe. Damaging wind gusts were observed with these storms as there were multiple reports of downed trees and wires throughout the region. With one storm, lightning struck a church and led to a fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees throughout Montrose.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds surged behind a strong arctic cold front which moved across the region early on January 16. Winds persisted into the midday on January 17, with occasional gusts as high as 35 to 50 mph. Areas of light snowfall generally on the order of a dusting to an inch fell before and concurrent with the strong winds, and locations mainly near Highway 71 experienced considerable time with visibility near or below one quarter mile with travel not recommended in areas surrounding Windom.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Occasional light snowfall totaled generally less than one inch during a period of enhanced northwest wind gusts as high as 35 to 45 mph. This led to a brief degradation in visibility to around one-quarter mile. With little or no pre-existing snow cover, impacts due to the lowest visibility periods were quite spotty and very brief.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were blown down along Dosh Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.

A strong cold front moved through northeast Pennsylvania on Sunday, April 19th, ushering in a much colder air mass. Temperatures dropped into the mid-20s to lower 30s overnight and remained well below normal through Tuesday, April 21st. This event occurred before the Frost Freeze program was even underway for the season, but due to how far below freezing some areas reached, this unfortunately led to costly crop damage in northeast Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell below freezing for multiple nights in April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and northern Oklahoma from the late evening of the 5th into early morning hours of the 6th. This activity developed in the vicinity of a dryline as a deep upper trough began to establish across the Four Coners. As a nocturnal low-level jet strengthened after sunset, a pair of cyclic tornadic thunderstorms emerged from the eastern Texas Panhandle into northern Oklahoma. In addition to several tornadoes, including a deadly tornado west of Fairview in Major County, large hail and eventually damaging wind gusts were observed with severe convection across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tractor-trailer was blown over along U.S. Highway 281. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist airmass fueled slow moving storms in southeast Texas. Flooding was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very heavy rain produced flooding across large portions of Groves, Nederland, and Port Arthur. Many roads were flooded and impassable while numerous homes flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked wires down on Moonlite Pike Road near Benson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado appeared to develop in the Lisbon Oaks subdivision, causing mainly tree damage before intensifying closer to Highway 164.  The tornado was at it's most intense near Indian Grass Lane where it caused damage to multiple businesses.  The strongest damage was to an insurance car shop port that had a well anchored roof that was completely blown off and found approximated 3 to 4 blocks to the east near Highway 164.  Damage then occurred to a church near Wildwood Way and multiple homes along Conservancy Court.  Tornado appeared to end near Waukesha Ave along Linda Dr.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southeast portion of Ochiltree County was in Moderate Drought (D1) to start April while the remainder of the county was in Severe Drought (D2). By the middle of the month, the entire county was in Severe Drought, with some Extreme Drought (D3) creeping into the far northern and far southern portions of the county by mid to late April. This worsening drought was due to the lack of continuous, significant rainfall. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county but amounts were sparse. In total, the county measured 0.1 to 0.4 inches of rain. Ochiltree County ended the month about 1.4-1.7 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 3.5-4.2 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Relatively abundant moisture and cold temperatures aloft allowed for a few thunderstorms over southern Nevada, one of which produced severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm wind gust was recorded at an automated observation station on the Nevada National Security Site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix associated caused by a disturbance aloft resulted in snow accumulations less than one inch with a glaze to few hundredths of an inch of ice accretion.

Breezy northwesterly winds behind a cold front resulted in gusts reaching up to around 40mph in portions of Southeast Missouri during the midday to afternoon hours as high pressure moved towards the Midwest.

CZ_NAME: EASTERN SIERRA SLOPES OF INYO COUNTY
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought mountain snow and valley rain to much of Inyo County, causing flood impacts in Death Valley and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Event snow totals ranged between 15 and 20 inches at several SNOTELs in the Eastern Sierra.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An widespread area of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall of 2-4 inches in a short period of time during the morning that resulted in flash flooding and some downed trees in Cullman county. Isolated strong storms occurred in the afternoon hours as well. One storm downed a tree in Morgan county, Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down nea rthe intersection of CR 87 and CR 166.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and humid air mass advected into eastern New York on June 11-12, 2026 ahead of an approaching low pressure system and cold front. Heat index values (feels like temperatures) reached the mid-90s to lower 100s across portions of the Hudson Valley into Washington County and the southern Taconics on one or both days.||In addition, isolated to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developed both days, mainly during the afternoon hours. Some of these storms produced some large hail along with downed trees and wires. The Town of Pawling was hardest hit on June 11 as an intense thunderstorm produced hail in excess of 2 inches in some areas and widespread tree damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail in Wingdale was estimated to be between 1.25 and 1.50 inches based on pictures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported a small downed tree with thunderstorms in Elk Grove. Nearby wind gusts measured 42 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Severe to Extreme Drought that characterized Fall 2025 persisted into January 2026 as north and central Georgia failed to benefit from the typical 'recharge' period. A more active weather pattern in the second half of the month allowed for several rounds of beneficial, albeit non-drought-breaking, rainfall, particularly over the north and northwest portions of the state. While these systems helped stabilize soil moisture in some areas, deep-layer moisture deficits remained significant, and led to the redevelopment of D3 Extreme Drought over portions of the state.||Precipitation for January varied across north and central Georgia. Much of north Georgia and the Metro Atlanta area received between 3.0 and 5.0 inches of rain, which neared 60 to 100 percent of the monthly normal. In contrast, central Georgia continued to lag behind, with many areas receiving only 1.5 to 3.0 inches (approximately 40 to 60 percent of normal). Despite the uptick in surface moisture, the cumulative rainfall deficit since August 2025 remained between 8 and 14 inches for a large swath of the Piedmont. Consequently, while topsoil showed signs of recovery, subsoil moisture and groundwater levels remained low for mid-winter.||Agricultural impacts continued to be reported through the Condition Monitoring Observer Reports (CMOR). The winter wheat crop, already stunted by the dry fall months, showed uneven growth and poor tillering in the most affected central Georgia counties. Livestock producers remained in a critical state; although January rains provided some minor recharge to stock ponds, many remained at dangerously low levels. The reliance on supplemental hay feeding remained total across central Georgia, and the high cost of feed continued to drive reports of decreasing herd size as producers looked toward a potentially dry spring.||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of slow expansion of drying conditions. At the start of January, roughly 15.4 percent of north and central Georgia was in D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, this figure had shifted slightly to 50.96 percent. Although there were some improvements over portions of the western and northern greater Metro Atlanta area, there were also pockets of D3 Extreme Drought that expanded, including Harris, Chattahoochee, Muscogee, Madison, Oglethorpe, and Wilkes counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, D2 (Severe Drought) conditions returned to Wilkinson County on January 13. This degradation followed a brief mid-winter reprieve, which had interrupted an initial three-week period of Severe Drought that began on November 25. By the end of January, the county had recorded a cumulative total of six weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the drought���s inception in the fall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. The rate of falling and blowing snow reduced visibility to whiteout conditions, making many roadways impassible. Snow lingered for several hours before finally dissipating the afternoon of the following day. Storm total snowfall ranged between a few inches up to 9.5 inches.||The highest measured snowfall totals from this event are:|9.5 inches ENE of Prior Lake (Scott)|8.5 inches in Shorewood (Hennepin)|7.7 inches in Waconia (Carver)|7.0 inches 1 E of Granite Falls (Chippewa)|7.0 inches 3 SSW of Elko New Market (Rice).||The strongest wind gusts measured from this event were: |50 mph at Canby Municipal Airport (Yellow Medicine)|48 mph at Redwood Falls Municipal Airport (Redwood)|48 mph at New Ulm Municipal Airport (Brown)|44 mph at Mankato Regional Airport (Blue Earth).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall with rates near one inch per hour produced 6 to 9 inches across the northern half of the county. The Minneapolis St. Paul International Airport reached 6 inches of snow during the official midnight observation but continued to fall through the morning commute. CoCoRaHS observers in 3 miles ENE of Prior Lake measured 9.5 inches, 7 inches in Savage, and 6 inches in Shakopee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Had extreme high wind verification from a thunderstorm outbreak as a system raced through Idaho.  Several power outages occurred with many recorded over 60 mph thunderstorm outflow wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Medicine Lodge mesonet station recorded a 78 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Complete uplift of roof; most walls remain standing on a manufactured home/single wide.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered supercell thunderstorms developed near a slow-moving frontal boundary during the afternoon and evening hours on February 26. Cold temperatures were present aloft with strong deep layer shear but relatively weak low-level shear. Scattered severe hail reports were received, with the largest hailstones falling in portions of Blount, Jefferson, and St. Clair counties, as large as two inches in diameter. Damaging winds also occurred, with the most significant wind damage in Pinson where a microburst occurred. A hail storm associated with the microburst resulted in accumulating hail that covered the ground and resulted in the formation of hail fog. In addition, a brief EF-0 tornado also moved through Trussville, damaging some commercial and industrial buildings as well as homes, most of which was minor.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong to golf ball-sized hail in the Chalkville and Clay areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm and humid air to the south of a warm frontal boundary spawned heavy rain producing thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Storms repeatedly moving over the same regions produced pockets of 3 to 4 inches of rain which triggered areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Officials reported Mecklenburg Road flooded in several spots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After an active period of multiple systems moving through the area bringing periods of high winds to the southern panhandle, a stronger system arrived bringing high winds to majority of the Panhandle on the 13th into the 14th. This low center tracked northward through the eastern gulf, while deepening, along with a storm force front. The low center moved onshore along the NE Gulf Coast in vicinity of Yakutat overnight Tuesday the 13th. As the low jumped inland, winds spiked up through the inner channels, lasting longest for the Skagway area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Sitka area saw high winds during the afternoon and evening of the 13th. The Sitka Airport ASOS measured high winds consistently between 345pm and 1040pm, including a period of sustained winds in excess of 40mph and a peak gust of 76mph at 852pm.The Marine Exchange station at the AML Dock measured a peak gust of 69mph at 911pm and the boat harbor saw a peak of 72mph at 854pm. A report on social media stated that boat lines were being snapped at the harbor during the high wind and the USCG reported a sunken vessel the following day. The local newspaper noted that emergency responders dealt with downed trees, a power outage, and other damages. Total monetary damage from this event is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lee trough ignited widely scattered thunderstorms that produced locally damaging wind gusts over western Maryland, eastern West Virginia, and northwestern Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County 911 center reported a tree down onto the roadway at the 400 block of Fishel Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto Route 35 N northeast of Mifflintown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms dropped southeast into southern middle Tennessee and north Alabama during the afternoon and early evening hours.  Damaging winds were reported in northwest Alabama including the Shoals metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down along CR 457 in Pisgah. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. Storm development occurred both along a quasi-stationary boundary across northern Oklahoma and along an accelerating Pacific Front from far western Oklahoma into western-north Texas. A mix of supercells and a well-developed quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) yielded reports of large to very large hail and wind damage across portions of the area. A brief tornado was also documented in far eastern Wilbarger County in Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust captured by a vehicle anemometer along Texas Highway 25, south of Mankins. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms push through Southeast Texas on Valentines day, producing damaging winds and some hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XLEV Levee measured a 69 mph wind gust.

CZ_NAME: VOLUSIA-BREVARD COUNTY LINE TO SEBASTIAN INLET 0-20NM
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms produced strong to severe wind gusts along the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: USSF wind sensor on tower 513 (SLF North) measured a wind gust of 41 knots from the north.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing the trunk of a large tree snapped was shared on social media. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down on the far east side of Havana near the Laurel Hill Cemetery at 11:52 PM CDT.  The tornado tracked northeastward, snapping trees and downing numerous power poles along County Road 2130.  A horse barn was partially destroyed and a horse was killed near the intersection of County Road 2200 and County Road 1900 about 1 mile west-northwest of Topeka before the tornado dissipated at 11:58 PM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low level frontogenesis developed ahead of a cold front, and an upper level shortwave provided lift to create a period of snow as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An observation in Carrollton indicated that 2.5 inches of snow fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted through the Ohio Valley, sparking thunderstorms in a moist airmass. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in flooding and flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: West Main Street flooded under the railroad overpass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rounds of showers and thunderstorms improved drought conditions across central Kansas early in the month. A couple areas went from severe drought (D2) to none. By the end of the of the month, remaining counties or portions of counties improved to moderate drought and abnormally dry categories. Monthly rainfall totals ranged from 4.5 inches to around 15 inches in the drought stricken areas with the highest amounts across south central Kansas. These values were 7 to nearly 9 inches above seasonal normal.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southern third of the county entered the month in extreme drought (D3) with much improvement by June 16th to the moderate drought (D1) except the far southern corners which eventually improved for a removal of severe drought (D2) by the 23rd. In this time period, southern portions of the county measured around 5 inches according to CoCoRaHS observers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms, including one tornado occurred during the evening of March 6th as both supercells and a squall line moved through the area. Widespread 1-3 inches of rainfall fell across portions of southern Missouri, causing localized flooding of low water crossings and some river flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several low water crossings were flooded in Carl Junction due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm chaser video showed a well-defined funnel cloud extending at least half way to the ground approximately four miles west of Chauncey. However, no evidence of a tornado was found in this area. This thunderstorm went on to produce a tornado in Crawford County four minutes after this funnel cloud was sighted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.64 miles and a path width of 300 yards began in eastern Vigo County. Within Vigo county the peak width was 75 yards, path length of 2.14 miles and peak winds of 95 mph. The peak winds were 110 mph after it moved into Clay county. Damage within Vigo county was limited to tree damage along East Dallas Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through southern New England during the late afternoon and evening. While the bulk of the severe weather remained in northern New England some wind damage was reported in northern MA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Greenfield, multiple trees were down on Beacon St.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated storms developed along a prefrontal trough by mid day on May 20. Later in the afternoon, a broader multicellular cluster of storms associated with the slow moving cold front moved into the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several large tree limbs and some trees were blown down in Edison and Metuchen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and humid conditions persisting across the region and a closed low across the Deep South led to an environment favorable for strong to severe thunderstorms across Southeast South Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported a tree down near the intersection of Cane Branch Road and Lucky Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of strong to severe storms became organized as it progressed mostly across the I-20 corridor and surrounding areas in Louisiana. This thunderstorm activity produced numerous reports of wind damage as it was aided in its progression and intensity by an ongoing Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and utility pole were downed in Jonesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 43 mph wind gust was recorded at the New York State Mesonet site near Duanesburg. An estimated 5500 people were without power throughout Schenectady County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry month of March, with monthly rainfall deficits on the order of one to two inches, led to a continuation of expanding/worsening drought across Oklahoma and western-north Texas.

Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana.  Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

Yet another QLCS moved through portions of north and central Georgia in the early morning hours of the 16th. Pockets of concentrated winds damage were found mostly in north Georgia where the storms held together best. A few more brief tornados were found via surveys, including one just southeast of the metro and two further south to Macon and Pine Mountain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The emergency manager relayed a report of a tree and powerlines down 1.0 n of nelson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. Cost of debris cleanup in Hyde county alone topped out at 1.4 million dollars. ||Electrical infrastructure was severely disrupted, causing $2.4 million in utility distribution damage across Hyde and Hand counties. Power was knocked out to 1,072 residents in Hyde County (94% of the county). Power generation was heavily impacted; at least 20 wind turbines were damaged or destroyed at the Triple H and North Bend wind farms, with replacement costs estimated at $50 million.||Day County suffered extensive damage, particularly around Andover, where straight-line wind speeds reached 100 mph. Extensive tree stands were leveled, grain bins dented, and buildings damaged at the Andover Threshing Grounds. Day County power damage reached $18,000, leaving 487 residents without electricity. A brief EFU tornado was confirmed near Andover.||Even as the storm system departed, wrap around high winds caused additional tree damage in areas that had just missed out on thunderstorm wind damage, with several trees and limbs down in parts of Aberdeen, and a peak wind gust measured on a personal weather station of 88 mph in the town of Westport (Brown county).||Governor Rhoden requested a Presidential Disaster Declaration to assist with damage cleanup and repairs for Hyde, Hand, Hughes, Buffalo and Stanley counties including Lower Brule and Crow Creek reservations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damage to several metal buildings was observed at the Andover Threshing Grounds. Two shops had their doors blown in with roofs partly blown out. One building had a window also blown out. A set of bleachers had also been knocked over. Thunderstorm winds were estimated at 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure passing through Ontario dragged a strong cold front west to east across the region in the afternoon hours. Boundary orthogonal bands of snow squalls developed ahead of the front with steep low level lapse rates and non-zero surface-based CAPE. The result was a widespread area of snow bands reducing visibility to a quarter mile or less with gusty wind greater than 35 mph and rapid accumulation on roadways resulting in at least one highway accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video provided of less than a quarter mile visibility in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portion of east-central and northeast Nebraska during March. Monthly precipitation totals were generally 0.5 to 1.5 inches below average.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A D2 (Severe) drought was introduced across the western portion of the county on March 3, persisting through the remainder of the month. No rainfall reports were available within the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe line of storms swept across most of Alabama from north to south, causing numerous trees and power lines to fall across the state.  Southeast Alabama was not spared and saw numerous reports of downed trees and lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on Highway 134 near Newton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface trough draped from eastern Virginia into northeastern sections of central North Carolina led to isolated thunderstorm developing in the afternoon and evening. Several reports of wind damage occurred across Nash, Edgecombe, Wake, Wayne, and Hoke Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sawyer road was closed due to trees that fell on along the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a significant ridge was over the southeastern US, hot and unstable air was over Michigan's Upper Peninsula by the 30th. This warm and moist air caused unseasonable heat impacts, and forcing from an approaching upper level disturbance over the Canadian Prairie initiated thunderstorms that caused multiple forms of severe weather, including the first confirmed tornado for the Upper Peninsula since 2020.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pelkie RAWS site PIEM4 reported heat index values in excess of 100 degrees from 10 AM EST through 2 PM, with a peak heat index of 105 at 2 PM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was the second part of the prolonged wind event which started on March 11th and the 12th. There was a twelve-hour lull in the strong winds outside of the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming, but winds quickly increased by late morning on March 14th. Although winds weren't quite as strong, nor as widespread, compared March 12th, peak wind gusts between 70 to 85 MPH were observed along with travel impacts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Alpha AWOS site between Gun Barrel and Pine Bluffs Wyoming measured a brief strong wind gust early in the morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed in Reform.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light snow developed over eastern Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of January 15, 2026. While snow accumulations were less than one half inch, a quick burst of snow resulted in slick road conditions near Cookeville in Putnam County. Slick roads and poor visibility resulted in a multi-car crash on Interstate 40.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A quick burst of snow resulted in slick roads and poor visibility on Interstate 40 near Cookeville. Near mile marker 285, these poor conditions caused an eleven chain-reaction crash that forced the closure of the Interstate for several hours. Three injuries were reported in the accident. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal moisture moved into the Four Corners from the southwest due to remnant Atmospheric River moisture ahead of a strong closed low pressure system and cold front that brought mountain snow above 9000 feet and valley rain. Temperatures were very warm ahead of this system and fell to below normal levels afterwards with abundant moisture resulting in heavy, wet snow favoring the central and southern mountains with the heaviest accumulations above a foot at the higher elevations where the winds were also the strongest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 7 to 10 inches of snow fell across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There were a few rounds of thunderstorms through this period. A few storms were severe with large hail and damaging winds and an isolated tornado.

Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Florida ahead of a frontal boundary. Several severe weather reports were received with the main impacts to trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two power lines were on the road near West Bonita Street in Chattahoochee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level low-pressure center progressed eastward through the Plains on the afternoon and evening of March 10, leading to the development of thunderstorms. These storms were able to initiate along a dryline across the Big Country. As the storms moved east through the forecast area, some generated large hail and damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from mPING: Baseball (2.75 in.).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed near Benton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-afternoon thunderstorms both in broken line segments and single cells developed along and ahead of a cold front. Marginal effective shear values up to 30 knots and MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg supported severe thunderstorms producing both wind and hail. Wind was primarily confined to northern West Virginia along a DCAPE gradient of 600-700 J/kg. Mid-level lapse rates up to 6.5 C/km and up to 300 J/kg of hail growth zone CAPE supported numerous reports of quarter size within storms across western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down on Smithtown Road near Route 119.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with widespread moderate drought (D1) conditions already present across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties. Although around an inch of rain fell during the first week of the month, it was not enough to improve conditions. This was followed by relatively dry weather, which allowed for a further degradation to a severe drought (D2) by the third week of the month. Showers and storms brought some additional precipitation during the third and fourth weeks of the month, but once again did nothing to improve or resolve the D2 state in Buchanan and Dickenson.||Impacts included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals up to 1.3 inches were reported in Hill County. The highest sleet and snow total was reported between Whitney and the Lake Whitney Dam.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed throughout the day along a boundary that was draped across the Ohio Valley region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree and power pole were downed near Denune and Joyce Avenues.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
